Field manual · Single-file edition

Modern Interface Practice

Opinionated infrastructure for outcomes — and the product practice that keeps goal progress legible, recoverable, inclusive, and measurable.

Start reading Choose a path

One congruent manual

This single HTML edition merges four source works into one field curriculum: the Modern UI infrastructure textbook, its Part I–VI examples companions, the Modern UX practice textbook, and the Volume B worked examples. The chrome, type, space, and color follow the material’s own contracts — locked role scale, semantic tokens, quiet tool chrome, docs measure.

Volume A spine

Modern UI is opinionated infrastructure for outcomes.

  • ClearHierarchy encodes priority; chrome yields to work.
  • TalkativeEvery intentional action is acknowledged.
  • ReversiblePrefer undo; confirm only for external irreversibility.
  • SystematicSemantic contracts scale humans and generators.
  • InclusiveExclusion is a defect; lived experience can block ship.
  • MeasurableCraft follows trust × frequency (L14).

Volume B spine

UX makes goal progress legible, recoverable, inclusive, and measurable.

  1. 1 · SafetyIrreversible harm, exclusion from essential action.
  2. 2 · ModelMental model & recovery before polish.
  3. 3 · InclusionDiverse abilities, languages, devices, bandwidth.
  4. 4 · OutcomesMeaningful job progress with confidence.
  5. 5 · SystemsPlatform, performance, operational reality.
  6. 6 · DelightOnly after the layers above are solid.

Two tests that never go out of date

Brand test. Remove the navigation. If the first viewport of a marketing surface could belong to another company, branding failed.

Tool test. Inside the product, if chrome competes with the user’s work, the product failed.

This manual’s cover answers the brand test; its reading chrome answers the tool test. Everything below lives in this one file.

How to use this manual

This manual is a practice surface, not a mood board. Use it when you ship product UI and UX — checkout, auth, create, delete, search, tables, account rights, AI review loops — under real constraints.

Who this is for

  • Product designers and UX generalists leveling up to senior practice
  • Design-systems engineers and accessibility specialists
  • PMs and engineers in product trios who share discovery ownership
  • AI-assisted UI authors who need enforceable contracts, not vibe prompts
  • Students and career-switchers who need a coherent modern canon

How the volumes work together

  1. Volume A (Modern UI) gives falsifiable laws, visual/interaction contracts, systems ops, and inclusion gates — the infrastructure spine.
  2. Volume B (Modern UX) gives human-centered foundations, strategy, research, content/trust, and weekly operating rituals — the practice spine.
  3. Volume A examples sit beside Parts I–VI with concrete scenarios, microcopy, named tokens, and Measure lines for every major law and tension.
  4. Volume B examples sit beside Volume B chapters with realistic product scenarios, UI copy, named states, and bad-vs-good contrasts.
  5. Appendices hold ship kits, evaluation methods, course maps, and instructor exemplars.

Design of this HTML edition

The manual’s own UI follows Volume A / Ch. 5–7 and Volume B / Ch. 5B:

  • Locked role scale — Display / Title / Body / Meta / Code only
  • Semantic color roles — canvas, surface, fg, accent, danger… (no raw hex in components)
  • Docs shell — sticky 240px nav, ~72ch measure, quiet chrome
  • Motion as meaning — cover entrance, nav open, hover acknowledgment; respects prefers-reduced-motion
  • Focus visible — ≥2px accent ring; skip link; forced-colors borders preserved

Modern UX: A Field Textbook of Product UX Practice

Version 2.2
Subtitle: Philosophies, Methods, Systems, and Operating Practice for Digital Products (2024–2026)

Front Matter

About This Book

This textbook is a practice-oriented synthesis of modern user-experience design. It was authored by independent specialist experts—Human-Centered Design, Interaction Design, Inclusive Design, Product UX Strategy, Design Systems, Content/Trust/Service Design, Research Methods, and Operating Practice—then assembled into one curriculum. Each specialist wrote in isolation so no single school of thought dominated; a later synthesis pass aligned vocabulary and cross-references.

The book treats UX as the discipline of making user goal progress legible, recoverable, inclusive, and measurable—under interruption, across modalities, through probabilistic AI, and under real business constraints. It is a field textbook: oriented to working product practice, not a claim to exhaust every UX tradition or method.

Who This Book Is For

  • Product designers and UX generalists leveling up to senior practice
  • PMs and engineers in product trios who share discovery ownership
  • Design-system and content designers connecting craft to outcomes
  • Students and career-switchers who need a coherent, modern canon—not a trend roundup

Part I — Foundations

What this part is for. Before tokens, components, and critique checklists, a team needs a shared answer to four questions: what is modern UI for, which philosophies and tensions govern trade-offs, which laws are falsifiable enough to ship against, and how company strategy and a design-quality operating system allocate craft. Part I establishes that spine. Later parts turn it into visual grammar, interaction playbooks, systems ops, and worked decisions.

How to read. Each chapter ends with takeaways you can paste into a kickoff or PR template. Part I closes with review questions that force prefer-when judgments, not vocabulary recall. Where the research gap audit flagged thin coverage—settings and admin IA, privacy and consent, trust and safety, help, AI disclosure, and notification preferences—those surfaces appear here as product obligations, not as afterthoughts in a completeness appendix.

Companion examples: See the Part I examples companion.

Chapter 1 — What Modern UI Is For

1.1 The spine, in one sentence

Modern UI is opinionated infrastructure for outcomes.

It is infrastructure because it must scale across surfaces, teams, platforms, and—increasingly—generators that consume your design contract. It is opinionated because neutrality is abdication: every default teaches a path, every silence is a state, every confirm dialog is a policy. It is for outcomes because craft without a job to be done becomes theater, and theater on a trust path is a defect.

That sentence is the spine of this textbook. Everything else is elaboration, tension management, or tactics that make the spine enforceable.

1.2 Six obligations

A modern product UI that fails any of the following is incomplete, even if it looks polished in a marketing screenshot.

Obligation Meaning in practice
Clear Hierarchy encodes priority. Chrome yields to work. The user can answer “what matters here?” in under a second without a tour.
Talkative Every intentional action is acknowledged. Intermediate and terminal states are visible. Silence after a click is a bug, not calm design.
Reversible Prefer undo and soft recovery over confirm dialogs for local, recoverable work. Confirm only when irreversibility is external—money moved, legal commitment made, mass notification sent, production destroyed.
Systematic Semantic contracts—roles, type, elevation, space, named states—scale humans and AI generators. Ambiguous APIs become industrial defects when multiplied.
Inclusive Exclusion is a defect. WCAG and market regulations (EAA, ADA, Section 508) set floors. Lived experience of disabled people can block ship on critical paths. Checklist-green is not the ceiling.
Measurable Craft follows trust × frequency. Arguments from pure taste lose to critical-path maps, override rates, recovery rates, and trust metrics that experiments must not worsen.

These obligations are not mood boards. They are release criteria in prose form. If your team cannot point to where each obligation is enforced—in primitives, in review, in CI, or in research gates—the spine is decorative.

1.3 Two tests that never go out of date

Brand test. Remove the navigation. If the first viewport of a marketing or acquisition surface could belong to another company, branding failed. Brand must be a hero-level signal on branded pages—not an eyebrow, not a logo in a corner fighting a louder headline.

Tool test. Inside the product, if chrome competes with the user’s work, the product failed. Quiet chrome and loud content are not aesthetic preferences; they are the tool test applied to layout.

Marketing and product surfaces often share a design system and still fail different tests. Stripe-like dual systems—marketing expression versus product quietness—exist because the brand test and the tool test pull in opposite directions. Treating them as one “look” produces either a pretty tool that forgets its job or a forgettable brand that cannot acquire.

1.4 What modern UI is not

Modern UI is not:

  • A gallery of cards, glass, and glow that substitutes atmosphere for hierarchy.
  • A default purple-on-white or cream-and-terracotta cliché that signals “AI SaaS” without encoding priority.
  • A dashboard of stats, schedules, and promo chips dumped into the first viewport of a landing page.
  • Infinite settings as a substitute for opinionated defaults.
  • Accessibility as a late audit rather than a property of primitives.
  • AI that silently mutates user work and optimizes only accept rate.

It is also not “whatever ships fastest” without naming the context. Pre-PMF speed of learning is a legitimate optimization. Shoddy checkout errors in a trust market are not the same choice wearing a different hat; they are a spine failure.

1.5 Outcomes as the unit of design

Design the job, then the surface. A critical-path map of three to five jobs—authenticate, create the first artifact, pay, invite, recover from error—starves theater elsewhere. Craft money where trust × frequency is highest: payment, identity, daily create/edit loops, shared destructive actions.

Expertise modes should fork mode, not fork product: templates and air for first-run; density, keyboard, and command palette for daily drivers. Onboarding is a curriculum—identity → artifact → share → return cue—not a twelve-step carousel that delays the first successful job.

Metrics sit in a hierarchy:

  1. North star — e.g., weekly successful jobs completed.
  2. Leading — time-to-first-value, payment success, task success without documentation.
  3. Craft — error recovery rate, keyboard completion on critical paths, design-system override rate.

Experiments may lift leading metrics only if trust metrics do not worsen: cancel clarity, “how do I cancel?” support tickets, chargebacks, lived-experience task failures. Activation that permanently damages trust is not growth; it is extracting from the brand test and the tool test at once.

1.6 Infrastructure for humans and machines

A semantic contract is a promise about meaning: color.text.danger means danger in every theme; elevation level 2 means temporary modality; a tone prop does not have three synonyms. Humans need that contract to stay consistent across squads. Generators and agents need it because ambiguous APIs scale into industrial defects—thousands of near-duplicate variants, color-only status, and focus-hostile patterns reproduced at machine speed.

AI in the product UI itself follows a different but related loop: intent → proposal → review → undo. Streaming and cancelability are talkativeness. Diff-primary apply flows are reversibility. Citations and disclosure are honesty about provenance. Tool side-effects that email customers or charge cards without approval are spine violations, not “agent autonomy.”

1.7 Product surfaces that are still UI

The research gap audit called out surfaces teams often treat as policy documents rather than designed products. They belong in Foundations because they are obligations, not features:

  • Settings — taxonomy for account, workspace, notifications, privacy, security, and appearance; opinionated defaults with progressive disclosure for long-tail controls.
  • Admin / operator consoles — mass actions, audit logs, impersonation, and blast-radius confirms that end-user UI must never silently inherit.
  • Privacy and data rights — consent minimization, preference centers, export and account deletion (harder than soft-delete trash).
  • Trust and safety — report, block, appeal, and enforcement messaging with clear next steps.
  • Help — findable mechanisms, plain-language recovery, and links from denial and error states (not a buried FAQ).
  • AI disclosure — when content or actions are model-assisted; provenance without theater.
  • Notification preferences — critical interrupt versus batched digest versus muteable; quiet hours; lifecycle email honesty.

Chapter 4 returns to these as strategy and ownership. Chapter 1’s claim is simpler: if these surfaces are ugly, silent, irreversible, or exclusive, the product failed the six obligations on paths users cannot avoid.

1.8 Chapter 1 takeaways

  1. Modern UI is opinionated infrastructure for outcomes—not decoration, not infinite preference.
  2. Clear, talkative, reversible, systematic, inclusive, and measurable are release obligations.
  3. Brand test for acquisition; tool test for work surfaces; do not collapse them into one look.
  4. Allocate craft by trust × frequency; measure so experiments cannot buy activation with trust debt.
  5. Semantic contracts serve humans and generators; AI product flows need propose → review → undo.
  6. Settings, admin, privacy, safety, help, AI disclosure, and notification prefs are first-class UI.

Chapter 2 — Philosophies & Managed Tensions

2.1 Why philosophies before laws

Laws (Chapter 3) are falsifiable. Philosophies are the reasons you prefer one failure mode over another when two laws collide. Teams that skip philosophies debate pixels. Teams that skip tensions pretend every principle can be maximized at once. Both fail under schedule pressure.

This chapter compresses seven philosophies, then tables the managed tensions with prefer-when columns and failure-if-wrong outcomes. Prefer-when is the operational unit: without it, a tension table is a mood.

2.2 Seven philosophies

1. Clarity is the product. Ornament that does not encode priority, state, or affordance is debt. Linear-like density and Apple HIG-like restraint share this root: the interface earns attention by removing competition with the work, not by decorating emptiness.

2. Interface as conversation. Silence is a bug. Presence, send states, save indicators, and selection chrome are conversational turns. Figma’s selection and presence, Slack’s send states—the mechanic to steal is acknowledgment, not the brand skin.

3. Systems over pages. UI is grammar: roles, type, elevation, space, and named patterns. Material 3, Spectrum, and Polaris succeed when product teams import semantics rather than inventing page-local paint. Pages are utterances; the system is the language.

4. Outcomes over aesthetics. Craft is a moat on critical paths—Stripe Checkout field honesty, Superhuman latency and keyboard—not a coat of polish on every dashboard tile. Aesthetics without a job is theater.

5. Opinionated defaults. Neutrality is abdication. Defaults teach the happy path. Changing a default is a migration, not a tweak. Infinite settings dump expert anxiety onto every user.

6. Accessibility is quality. Situational disability is normal (Microsoft’s framing). “Nothing about us without us” means paid lived-experience sessions can block ship. GOV.UK’s posture—AA floor, humane ceiling, plain language—beats compliance theater that is axe-green and task-red.

7. AI consumes your contract. Ambiguous component APIs and unnamed states become defects at generator scale. Agent UX is not autocomplete theater: intent, proposal, review, undo. Side-effects need approval; disclosure needs honesty.

2.3 Managed tensions

Use this table in critiques. For every heated debate, name the tension, pick a cell, and write the failure mode you are accepting.

Tension Prefer A when Prefer B when Failure if wrong
Density vs air Daily driver, tables, power users First-run, marketing, empty states Middling padding that serves neither
Consistency vs flexibility Auth, forms, focus, destructive patterns Brand moments, campaigns Flat brand or unmanageable debt
Optimistic vs pessimistic UI Cheap rollback, local edits Money, legal, mass notify, shared destroy Silent wrong state / confirm tax everywhere
Polish vs speed High trust×frequency; competitive post-PMF Discovery, internal tools, rare admin Theater before learning / shoddy fintech
Disclosure vs discoverability Long-tail expert actions Core path must be found without a tour Buried core action / chrome bloat
Growth vs trust Clear value, reversible trial, honest cancel — (do not prefer urgency theater) Activation↑ trust↓ permanent
Platform parity vs native Semantics, IA, tokens Gestures, nav chrome, materials Shrunk-web or three unrelated apps
Checklist floor vs lived-experience gate Low-risk Open surfaces; automated floor always Paths disabled people must complete axe-green, unusable
Brand expression vs forced-colors Marketing illustration System High Contrast / forced-colors modes Broken HC or lifeless product UI
Systemize vs leave local ≥3 real uses on a Locked surface One-off experiment Shadow libraries or premature API
Brand-hero vs quiet tool Marketing / acquisition Product work surfaces Pretty tool / forgettable brand

Reading the table

Density vs air is not “more whitespace is more premium.” A daily issue tracker with marketing padding fails the tool test. An empty state with table density fails first-run clarity. Middling padding is the characteristic failure of teams that average the debate.

Optimistic vs pessimistic is classified by blast radius and rollback cost. Optimistic list insert with undo is talkative and reversible. Optimistic “Paid!” before the bank responds is a trust defect. Confirm-on-archive with no soft delete is the opposite failure: confirm tax without safety.

Growth vs trust has an asymmetric prefer-when. Fake urgency, trap cancel, and decoy “Most popular” plans do not get a legitimate Prefer B column on Locked trust paths. Honest comparison and labeled defaults can live on Guided surfaces; they still obey contrast and focus laws.

Checklist vs lived experience prevents two opposite failures: shipping without automated floors, and shipping with floors only. Automated axe and contrast gates always run. Lived-experience sessions on auth, checkout, and create can block Locked releases even when the checklist is green.

Systemize vs leave local implements Law L12 early: three real uses and a Locked surface justify promotion; one clever wrapper “for consistency” is premature abstraction.

2.4 Philosophies applied to gap-audit surfaces

Philosophies are easiest to preach on buttons and hardest to keep on settings and safety.

  • Clarity in settings means a taxonomy and search, not a flat list of fifty toggles.
  • Conversation in privacy means confirming what was exported or deleted, with receipts—not a silent 204.
  • Systems in admin means Locked destructive and impersonation patterns, not per-squad scary modals.
  • Outcomes in help means recovery to the job, not article pageviews as a vanity metric.
  • Defaults in notifications means quiet hours and digests on by sensible default; critical interrupts reserved and explainable.
  • Accessibility in consent banners means operable, readable, and not contrast-hostile overlays that trap focus.
  • AI contract in disclosure means labeling assistance and provenance without burying the control to turn assistance off where policy requires it.

2.5 Chapter 2 takeaways

  1. Philosophies explain prefer-when; laws enforce falsifiable breaks.
  2. Every tension needs Prefer A, Prefer B, and Failure if wrong—or it is not managed.
  3. Growth theater does not earn a Prefer column on trust paths.
  4. Lived experience can block ship; checklist floors still always run.
  5. Settings, privacy, safety, and AI disclosure inherit the same philosophies as checkout.

Chapter 3 — Fourteen Laws

3.1 How to use the laws

Each law is falsifiable: the right column names observable breaks. If you cannot fail a PR against the break condition, the law is a slogan. Supporting constraints at the end of the chapter are near-laws—ship gates that rarely deserve exceptions.

Laws are numbered L1–L14 for citation in critiques (“breaks L7: confirm-on-archive”).

3.2 The fourteen laws

# Law Breaks when
L1 Roles, not hexes — product UI consumes semantic tokens only Raw palette values appear in components or app CSS
L2 Hierarchy before paint — weight, space, and position beat color; one focus per region Equal card shadows everywhere; status communicated by color alone
L3 Type & rhythm are contracts — named roles, locked role scale, 4/8 space Ad-hoc px type; seven unused sizes; spacing from taste
L4 Elevation means modality — raise = temporary; flat = durable Random shadows on static panels; durable pages that look like overlays
L5 Acknowledge ≤100ms — tiered latency budgets for press, work, and resolve Silent controls; blank full-page waits with no local pending state
L6 State is designed — empty, loading, partial, error, offline, denied, syncing “No data” for every gap; toast-only failure; spinner with no meaning
L7 Undo > confirm — confirm only for external irreversibility Confirm-on-archive; no soft delete; toast undo for team-visible destroy
L8 Progressive disclosure — primary → overflow → palette → settings Expert control dump on first run or core action buried
L9 Focus is a cursor — keyboard and AT peer paths; restore focus to trigger outline: none without replacement; focus dumped on body after modal
L10 Native first, APG second Fake roles without keyboard maps; div theater with ARIA lipstick
L11 Multi-channel + reflow — never color alone; usable at 320px CSS / 400% zoom Red-only errors; essential horizontal scroll at zoom; charts without labels/patterns
L12 Abstract after three — recipe → pattern → component One-off “shared” wrappers; prop soup; shadow libraries
L13 Version the contract — semver tokens/APIs; deprecate with CI bans Silent breaking renames; eternal dual APIs; Figma drift without code SoT
L14 Craft ∝ trust × frequency — polish money, identity, and daily paths Dashboard theater; shoddy checkout errors; rare admin polished before pay

3.3 Law notes — enough to apply without the tactics part

L1–L4 (grammar). Semantic color roles survive theme, high contrast, and generator use. Hierarchy before paint stops teams from fixing structure with accent color. Type roles (Display, Title, Body, Meta, Code) and space tokens (4/8/12/16/24/32/48) are contracts: product UI does not invent sizes outside the locked scale. Elevation is modality: menus and modals raise; tables and pages stay flat. Decorative shadow on a static settings card breaks L4.

L5–L8 (conversation and control). Acknowledgment can be a pressed state, inline pending, or optimistic row—within ~100ms for the ack, with separate budgets for work and resolve. The seven states in L6 are distinct: filtered-to-zero is not true empty; denied is not error; syncing is not loading. Undo classes: soft toast (5–10s), quarantine trash (e.g. 30 days), hard confirm (charge, production destroy, mass mail). Progressive disclosure keeps primary actions scented and parks expert power in overflow, command palette, and settings.

L9–L11 (inclusion). Focus visible (≥2px contrast-aware ring), DOM order, dialog focus trap with restore, and skip links are peer to pointer paths. Native elements beat ARIA reimplementation; APG patterns are for when native is insufficient. Multi-channel status (text, icon, pattern) and reflow at 320 / 400% are non-negotiable for L11.

L12–L14 (scale and allocation). Three real uses on a Locked surface justify promotion through recipe → pattern (docs, a11y, do/don’t) → component (semver, tests, Storybook). Token and API changes follow semver with a deprecation window (e.g. 90 days), codemods, and CI bans after sunset. L14 tells you where to spend: trust × frequency, not equal polish everywhere.

3.4 Supporting constraints

Treat these as default ship requirements unless a documented exception exists:

  • Primary touch: craft bar ≥44×44 (Apple HIG / Material). WCAG 2.2 2.5.8 AA floor is 24×24—meet 44 on primary actions; never ship below 24.
  • Honor prefers-reduced-motion (opacity/instant alternatives; motion in shared components limited to transform/opacity).
  • Logical CSS and RTL-aware layout; do not mirror meaning with physical left/right alone.
  • Tabular figures for numbers in tables and money.
  • Captions and transcripts for meaningful media; no seizure-risk flashing (>3/sec).
  • Password-manager-friendly auth (visible labels, correct autocomplete); passkeys/OTP preferred over puzzle CAPTCHA; always an accessible alternative if a challenge is required.
  • Help Mechanisms (WCAG 3.2.6) is AAA—still ship consistent help placement on Locked trust paths as craft; label conformance claims accurately (AA vs AAA).

3.4b Undo class taxonomy (L7) — Soft / Quarantine / Hard

Class Window / mechanism Prefer when Examples Rejected
Soft 5–10s toast with Undo Local, reversible, frequent Archive, Undo Send, dismiss Confirm modal every time
Quarantine Trash / recycle ~30d Recoverable destroy; regret common File/page delete Soft toast for team-visible destroy
Hard confirm Modal names blast radius; typed confirm for extreme Money, legal, mass notify, prod destroy, account erase Charge card, delete org, Case J One-click “for speed”

Rule: Confirm only for external irreversibility or shared blast that cannot be reconstructed cheaply.

3.5 Empty, zero, error, denied — sharpening L6

The gap audit stressed distinctions teams collapse into one illustration:

Situation Meaning Typical CTA
Never-used empty User has no artifacts yet Template / create
Filtered to zero Query or filters exclude all Clear filters / adjust query
True empty collection Intentionally empty after use Create / import
Error Load or action failed Retry / support
Denied Permission or policy blocks Explain + request access / settings link
Offline / syncing Connectivity or queue Indicator + queued changes / resolve conflict

Using one “No data” string for all of these breaks L6 and usually L8 (wrong disclosure of recovery).

3.6 Chapter 3 takeaways

  1. Cite laws by number; fail PRs on the break column.
  2. Grammar (L1–L4), conversation (L5–L8), inclusion (L9–L11), scale (L12–L14) are one system.
  3. Undo classes and state distinctions prevent confirm tax and false empties.
  4. Supporting constraints are default gates, not footnotes.
  5. L14 allocates craft; it does not excuse exclusion on rare paths users still must complete.

Chapter 4 — Company Strategy & Design-Quality OS

4.1 Strategy is context, not taste

The same fourteen laws apply in a pre-PMF startup and a multi-brand bank. What you optimize—and what you explicitly refuse—changes. Strategy tables prevent teams from cargo-culting Linear density into a first-run consumer app or marketing bento into a pro tool.

4.2 Company when / when-not

Context Optimize Do not
Pre-PMF / unknown problem Clarity + learning speed Visual theater, mega design system
Trust market (fintech, health, identity) Polish + pessimistic patterns + a11y on money/identity paths early Growth dark patterns on checkout
Daily pro tool Density, keyboard, latency, Cmd-K Marketing bento inside the app
Consumer viral Fast experiment; honest cancel Fake urgency as default growth
Multi-brand enterprise Shared grammar + forked tokens Forked component trees per brand
Multi-platform Shared semantics; native chrome/gestures Pixel-identical cross-platform fantasy

RACI sketch (adjust names, keep the seams):

Concern Accountable Responsible Consulted
Locked primitives + tokens Design Systems Design Systems + Eng Product Design
Guided surfaces Product Design Product Design Systems
A11y CI + lint Eng Eng Systems, A11y specialist
Critical-path metrics PM Eng + Design Research
Lived-experience sessions Research Research Product, Systems
Override-rate remediation Design Systems Product + Systems Eng

Override rate is a strategy metric: high overrides mean the system failed the product, or the product is forking without promotion. Remediation is Systems-accountable so shadow libraries do not win by neglect.

4.3 Design systems as operations

Strategy without ops is a slide deck. Minimum viable systems ops:

  • Token layers: Primitive → Semantic → rare Component. Product imports semantic only (L1).
  • Partition: Locked / Guided / Open. Label Open explicitly so “exception” does not become the unmarked default.
  • Promotion path: local recipe → documented pattern (a11y + do/don’t) → versioned component.
  • Source of truth: code is SoT for product; Figma Variables mirror token names; weekly drift check on renames.
  • Semver SLA: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH for tokens and components; ~90-day deprecation; codemod for renames; CI fails on deprecated imports after sunset. Token bumps: MAJOR = rename/remove or change meaning of a semantic role; MINOR = add role/alias; PATCH = primitive ramp tweak behind the same semantic (visual diff required).
  • Budgets (example): core kit JS ≤150KB gzip incremental; no raw hex/px in app CSS; motion in shared components only via transform/opacity.
  • Lint catalog: no-raw-color, no-synonym-variant, no-unlabeled-icon-button, no-banned-import, require-focus-visible.
  • Catalog schema (minimum): { id, name, props[], tokens[], a11yKeyboard, do, dont, status } for humans and codegen.
  • Adopt vs build: Prefer battle-tested behavior primitives (e.g. Radix, React Aria); skin with tokens. Build when the contract is missing—do not wrap once “for consistency.”

4.4 Interaction strategy (company level)

  • Feedback loop: trigger → acknowledge → work → resolve → undo.
  • Dual device models: not shrunk desktop; native nav and gestures where platform demands (parity table: semantics yes, chrome no).
  • Offline: sync indicator required. Conflicts—prefer-when: keep both (equal peer edits); choose (one clearly stale); merge (structured fields).
  • Interruptions: one modal at a time; toasts queue; never steal focus from typing unless assertive error.
  • Permissions: just-in-time at intent; denial explains, links to settings, and offers a degraded path—not a dead end.
  • AI: stream + cancel; citations; tool side-effects need approval; diff → apply → undo; track reject/override as trust metrics, not only accept rate.

4.5 Accessibility strategy

  • Bake inclusion into primitives: contrast-gated tokens, focus rings, labeled APIs, APG maps.
  • Release-blocking gates on critical paths: keyboard task pass; axe clean of serious issues; both-theme contrast; focus visible; screen-reader smoke on auth/checkout/create.
  • AT matrix: VoiceOver + Safari; NVDA + Chrome/Firefox; TalkBack + Chrome; JAWS for enterprise sales; Voice Control once on mobile core.
  • Legal floor: WCAG 2.2 AA baseline; EAA/ADA/508 by market; VPAT/ACR when enterprise sells.
  • Lived experience: paid sessions on critical paths each quarter; findings can block ship on Locked surfaces (checklist floor vs lived-experience gate from Chapter 2).

4.6 Design-quality OS

A design-quality operating system is the recurring ritual set that keeps L14 and inclusion from depending on heroics:

  1. PR critique against a short checklist (hierarchy, state matrix, undo class, focus/AT, contrast/reflow, system token use, growth/trust on Locked paths).
  2. Weekly failure-path review — empty/error/denied/offline plus about five session replays.
  3. Release gates — automated floors + critical-path manual/AT smoke.
  4. Quarterly usability + override review — promote, fix, or delete; kill UI bets that fail the competitive craft scorecard.
  5. Competitive craft scorecard (1–5 vs top rivals): trust-path quality · density honesty · opinionated defaults · undo honesty · checkout a11y · scent of core action.

Metric hierarchy (restated for PM ownership): north star → leading → craft; experiments must not worsen trust metrics (cancel clarity, support tickets, chargebacks, AT task success).

4.7 Product surface strategy — settings, admin, privacy, safety, help, AI disclosure, notifications

These surfaces were flagged in the completeness gap audit as absent or throwaway in many “modern UI” documents. They are strategy because they concentrate blast radius, legal risk, and trust.

Settings IA

Taxonomy beats a scroll of toggles. A durable starter map:

Area Holds Notes
Account Identity, email, password/passkeys, sessions/devices Security indicators belong here and in-session
Workspace / org Members, roles, billing entry points Separate end-user from admin depth
Notifications Channels, volume, quiet hours, digests See notification prefs below
Privacy & data Consent, export, delete, connected apps Hard delete ≠ trash soft-delete
Appearance Theme, density, language Density as token maps, not one-off CSS
AI assistance Disclosure, defaults on/off, data use for training where applicable Provenance ≠ mutation control
Advanced Long-tail expert controls Progressive disclosure (L8)

Provide in-settings search when the catalog exceeds what a new user can scan. Deep links from denial states (“Open notification settings”) are part of talkativeness.

Admin and operator consoles

Admin UI is not “the app with more checkboxes.” It needs:

  • Scoped mass actions with blast-radius copy and hard confirm (L7).
  • Audit logs that are readable and exportable.
  • Impersonation that is obvious in chrome while active, time-boxed, and logged.
  • Separation from end-user Guided surfaces so operator density does not leak into consumer IA.

Rare admin can tolerate less visual polish than checkout (L14), but not less inclusion on tasks operators with disabilities must complete, and never silent irreversibility.

Privacy, consent, and data rights

  • Minimize consent theater: ask when needed, explain in plain language, avoid dark-pattern “accept all” mazes.
  • Preference centers must be as findable as upgrade paths (growth vs trust).
  • Export and account deletion are hard workflows with receipts, delays where legally required, and confirmation matched to irreversibility—not soft-delete toast patterns.
  • Connected apps and scopes should be revocable without support archaeology.

Trust and safety

Report, block, mute, and appeal are product flows:

  • Clear categories and consequences.
  • Confirmation of receipt; timelines where you commit to them.
  • Appeal paths that do not dead-end in a void mailbox.
  • Enforcement messaging that distinguishes temporary limits from permanent bans.

Safety UI fails when it is only a legal footer. It is a critical path for people being harmed.

Help mechanisms

Help is successful when the user returns to the job:

  • Contextual links from errors and denials.
  • Plain-language articles with the GOV.UK instinct: short sentences, Error Summary-style diagnosis when forms fail.
  • Search that admits zero results and offers contact or status.
  • In-product curricula over carousels (Chapter 1).

WCAG’s help mechanisms mindset (findable, consistent) applies even when you are not citing the criterion number in every PR.

AI disclosure and provenance

Distinguish three layers:

  1. Mutation control — propose → review → undo (interaction law territory).
  2. Disclosure — user knows when content or actions were model-assisted.
  3. Provenance / watermarking — where policy or market requires machine-readable or visible signals.

Do not optimize only accept rate. Reject and override rates are trust metrics. Never allow agents to email customers, charge cards, or change permissions without approval.

Notification and messaging preferences

Class Behavior Prefs
Critical interrupt May break through; rare; explain why Hard to disable if safety/security; still explainable
Batched digest Default for non-critical product mail/push Cadence selectable
Muteable Social and marketing-adjacent Easy off; honest unsubscribe
Quiet hours Non-critical suppressed Default on where timezone known

Lifecycle messaging (trial ending, receipt, security alert) must not hijack marketing patterns. Security alerts remain distinct in scent and urgency. Email preference centers are UI: operable, labeled, and reversible.

4.8 Visual strategy (company posture)

  • Quiet chrome / loud content; content-shaped layouts on tool surfaces.
  • Type specimens and modular scale live in the system, not in slide decks.
  • Icon grid + metaphor glossary; label primary nav until learnability is proven.
  • Visualization: position and length first; color with labels; patterns for accessibility.
  • Marketing may use brand-hero full-bleed imagery; product UI does not import marketing gradients behind dense data (brand-hero vs quiet tool).

4.9 Chapter 4 takeaways

  1. Context decides optimize/do-not; laws stay constant.
  2. Systems ops (Locked/Guided/Open, semver, lint, budgets) make strategy real.
  3. Design-quality OS rituals beat heroic taste debates.
  4. Settings, admin, privacy, safety, help, AI disclosure, and notification prefs are strategic surfaces with blast radius.
  5. Accessibility is both floor (CI, legal) and gate (lived experience on Locked paths).

Part I Review Questions

Part I Review Questions

Work these without looking up the tables first. Prefer short written judgments (“Prefer A because…; failure if wrong is…”).

A. Spine and obligations

  1. Restate the spine sentence, then map each of the six obligations to a concrete artifact in a product you know (primitive, gate, metric, or ritual).
  2. Apply the brand test and the tool test to the same company’s marketing site and logged-in app. Where do they incorrectly share a look?
  3. A team wants “calm UI” that never shows pending states. Which obligations break, and which laws?

B. Philosophies and tensions

  1. For density vs air, pick prefer-when for: (a) first empty project, (b) a 50-row issue triage view. What does middling padding look like in each?
  2. A growth PM proposes fake scarcity on the Pay button in a fintech checkout. Name the tension, the correct prefer-when, and the trust metrics you would refuse to worsen.
  3. Your axe report is clean, but a screen-reader user cannot complete password reset. Which tension applies, and who should be able to block ship?

C. Laws

  1. A static settings page uses heavy drop shadows on every card “for hierarchy.” Which laws break, and what do you change first?
  2. Classify undo vs confirm for: (a) archive a personal draft, (b) delete a shared production database, (c) send a campaign to 40k recipients, (d) toggle a notification digest.
  3. List the seven L6 states and give a distinct CTA for filtered-to-zero versus never-used empty.
  4. A squad adds variant="primary" | "main" | "brand" to a Button. Which laws and systems ops rules fire?

D. Strategy and design-quality OS

  1. Choose optimize/do-not rows for a pre-PMF B2C app versus a post-PMF multi-brand bank. What systems investment differs?
  2. Draft a one-page RACI for tokens, Guided surfaces, a11y CI, and lived-experience sessions.
  3. An override rate spikes on CheckoutField. What does Design Systems do in the first two weeks?
  4. Fill a competitive craft scorecard (1–5) for your product versus two rivals on the six dimensions in §4.6. Name one ship and one kill.

E. Gap-audit surfaces

  1. Propose a settings taxonomy for a B2B workspace product. Where do AI disclosure and data export live, and why not under “Advanced” by default?
  2. Write blast-radius copy and confirm requirements for an admin “impersonate user” action. What chrome must remain visible while impersonating?
  3. Distinguish soft-delete trash, account deletion, and revoking an OAuth app. Which undo class or confirm class fits each?
  4. Design notification classes (critical / digest / muteable / quiet hours) for: security login alert, weekly product tips, “your export is ready,” and marketing newsletter.
  5. An agent proposes bulk-editing 200 issues and emailing assignees. Outline intent → proposal → review → undo, including what requires explicit approval.
  6. A consent banner fails contrast and traps focus. Which laws break, and how does the checklist vs lived-experience tension apply?

F. Integration

  1. Using Case instincts from the research spine: quiet chrome, pessimistic payment, field errors, Locked pay controls—list rejected alternatives for a checkout redesign pitch that wants marketing gradients and optimistic “Paid!” states.
  2. Walk a feature from Open experiment to Locked component using L12 and the promotion path. When do you refuse promotion?
  3. A quarterly review shows time-to-first-value up and “how do I cancel?” tickets up. What does the metric hierarchy say you must do?

Self-check

You are ready for Part II when you can: (1) cite L1–L14 in a PR without notes, (2) fill prefer-when for the eleven tensions, (3) place a UI bet on the when/when-not table, and (4) treat settings/admin/privacy/safety/help/AI disclosure/notifications as designed products with owners and gates.

End of Part I — Foundations.
Source synthesis: Modern UI research Round 3 (pass) + §10 completeness gap audit (settings/admin/privacy/safety/help/AI disclosure/notification prefs).

Part II — Visual Systems

Visual systems turn taste into contract. Roles, scales, elevation, motion, and media are the grammar that lets humans and generators produce coherent UI without reinventing hierarchy on every screen. Product surfaces stay quiet so work can be loud; marketing surfaces make the brand inevitable. Confuse the two and you get either a pretty tool nobody finishes work in, or a dense marketing page nobody remembers.

This part covers the locked visual contracts: type and space (Chapter 5), color/theme/materials/elevation (Chapter 6), motion and loading (Chapter 7), expressive media and dense lists (Chapter 8), and cross-surface visuals for email, print, and device safe areas (Chapter 9).

Laws in force here: L1 Roles not hexes · L2 Hierarchy before paint · L3 Type & rhythm are contracts · L4 Elevation means modality · L11 Multi-channel + reflow.

Companion examples: See the Part II examples companion.

Chapter 5 — Type, Space, Hierarchy

5.1 Hierarchy before paint

Hierarchy is encoded first by weight, size, position, and space—then by color. If every panel has the same card shadow and title weight, the eye has nowhere to land. One focal point per region is the rule; secondary content must step down deliberately through named type roles, not through inventing a seventh font size.

Prefer-when

Prefer When Failure if wrong
Weight / space / position Product UI, dense tools, status in tables Color-only status; equal card shadows
Color accent Single primary CTA; brand moment on marketing Accent on every chip and badge
Air + Display type First-run, empty, marketing hero Middling padding everywhere
Density + Body/Meta Daily driver lists, dashboards, power users Marketing bento inside the app

5.2 Locked type scale

Product UI does not invent sizes outside the locked role scale. The table below is a practical product contract (not a claim that every step equals ratio 1.125). Marketing may use Display; product pages use Title → Body → Meta. Code and money always use tabular figures.

Role Size (px) Weight Line-height Letter-spacing Use
Display 32 700 1.15 −0.02em Marketing / brand hero only
Title 22 600 1.25 −0.01em Page / section headings
Body 16 400 1.5 0 Reading, forms, primary UI
Meta 14 500 1.35 0.01em Secondary labels, timestamps
Code 14 400 (mono) 1.4 0 Code; tabular nums for money

Contract rules

  1. Named roles only in components (text.style = title), never raw font-size: 18px in app CSS.
  2. Do not ship seven unused intermediate sizes “for flexibility.” Flexibility without roles is drift.
  3. Pair one display/serif (or distinctive sans) for brand moments with one highly readable UI sans for product. Avoid default Inter/Roboto/Arial stacks as the brand voice.
  4. Specimens live in the design system: every role shown in light, dark, and on accent surfaces.

5.3 Optical craft

Optical alignment beats mathematical centering.

Situation Optical rule
Icon beside label Vertically center icon to cap height, not full line-box
Text field padding Often more padding-top than bottom so the glyph sits optically centered
Buttons with icon + text Icon optical middle; 8px gap; don’t center to emoji ascent
Mixed weight rows Align baselines across Title/Body/Meta in a toolbar
Caps / all-small-caps labels Slight positive tracking (+0.02–0.05em); never all-caps for long reading
Numerals in tables font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; right-align money

Tracking (letter-spacing) is a role property, not a one-off. Tighter tracking on Display/Title; neutral on Body; slightly open on Meta and uppercase chrome. Do not optically kern individual marketing words in CSS unless brand guidelines ship a tracked specimen—ad-hoc tracking is the typographic equivalent of raw hex.

5.4 Variable fonts and optical size

Variable fonts earn their keep when they replace multiple static files and expose axes the system actually uses.

Axis / feature Prefer when Avoid when
wght One family covers 400–700 without separate files You only need two weights forever
opsz (optical size) Display vs caption of same family; UI chrome at small sizes Fake opsz by shrinking Display masters
wdth Compact table headers; density modes Stretching body text for “personality”
Italic as axis True italic masters available Slanted roman sold as italic for UI

opsz guidance: At ≤14px Meta/Code, prefer a caption-optimized optical size (higher x-height, slightly looser forms). At Display 32+, prefer display optical size (tighter joins, finer contrast). If the chosen family lacks opsz, do not fake it with tracking alone—pick a pairing or accept the static cut.

Ship font-display: swap with size-adjusted fallback metrics (or ascent-override / size-adjust) so hierarchy does not jump on load. Subset aggressively for product UI; marketing can load a fuller set.

5.5 Space tokens and rhythm

Space is a contract, not a vibe. Use a 4-based token ladder; components consume tokens, not magic pixels.

Token Value Typical use
space-1 4 Icon-text micro gaps; tight inline
space-2 8 Control internal padding; label→control
space-3 12 Compact list row padding
space-4 16 Default control padding; field stack
space-5 24 Related field groups; card internal
space-6 32 Section breaks inside a view
space-7 48 Major page section separation

Form rhythm (locked recipe)

Relationship Spacing
Label → control 4–8
Control → next field 16–24
Field group → next group 32+
Helper / error under control 4–8; error replaces helper in place

Density modes (comfortable / compact / dense) remaps the same semantic roles to different token steps—they do not invent new type sizes. Example: comfortable list row uses space-4 vertical padding; compact uses space-3; dense uses space-2 with Meta still readable.

5.6 Measure and max-width by surface

Line length (measure) and content max-width are surface-specific. Marketing prose wants a comfortable reading measure; product tools want throughput and often full-bleed data.

Surface Max-width / measure Intent
Marketing body prose ~60–70ch; content ~640–720px Readability
Marketing hero headline Full bleed OK; text block ≤12–14 words Brand + one claim
Settings / forms (1-col) 480–560px control column Focused tasks
Settings (2-col label|control) 720–960px; labels ≤⅓ Desktop admin
Docs / long-form in-app 65–75ch Reading
Data tables / boards Full width of shell; horizontal scroll only for non-essential columns Throughput
Dialogs sm 400 · md 560 · lg 720 Task scoped
Toasts / banners Content width; wrap; never full-bleed paragraphs Glanceable

Rule: If removing a max-width makes a paragraph unreadably wide, restore it. If adding a max-width clips a table’s primary columns, remove it and redesign columns instead.

5.7 Breakpoints: intent, not device names

Name breakpoints by layout intent, not “iPhone.” Prefer container queries for local chrome; use viewport breakpoints for shell navigation.

Token Width Intent
bp-sm 320–639 Single column; stack; bottom or top primary nav
bp-md 640–959 Two columns possible; side panels become sheets
bp-lg 960–1279 Persistent nav + content; tables usable
bp-xl 1280+ Optional third rail; denser tooling

Container query recipes (visual)

Component Switch At
Toolbar Icon-only → icon+label min-width: ~280–320cqi
Entity card Drop side meta first; keep title + primary action When card < ~360cqi
Filter bar Horizontal chips → “Filters” sheet trigger Narrow container
Page header Inline actions → overflow menu Title + actions collide

Reflow law (WCAG 1.4.10): Usable at 320 CSS px and 400% zoom. Stack; DOM order = reading order; no essential two-dimensional scrolling.

5.8 Column and modular grids

Grid type Columns Gutter Use
Marketing modular 12 16–24 Hero + feature bands; align edges across sections
Product app shell Fluid content + fixed nav (240) / rail (320) 16–24 Tools; content not card-gridded by default
Form grid 1-col mobile; optional 2-col desktop for short fields 16 Never 2-col for long text or errors
Dense list Single column, full content width Row padding tokens Scan path vertical
Dashboard widgets CSS grid auto-fit minmax(280px, 1fr) 16–24 Only when widgets are peer objects

Anti-pattern: Card-grid everything. Cards are for interactive containers; flat sections with type hierarchy are the default for durable content (L2, L4).

5.9 Chapter 5 summary

Lock the scale. Align optically. Space on tokens. Size the measure to the job. Break on intent. Grid for alignment—not for card theater.

Measure (Ch 5)

Signal Pass when
Contrast / type Specimens reviewed; no ad-hoc px in product
Max-width Prose surfaces have measure; tables are full-bleed by intent
Density Compact/dense remaps tokens—does not invent sizes

Chapter 6 — Color, Theme, Materials, Elevation

6.1 Roles, not hexes (L1)

Product components consume semantic roles. Primitives (ramps) exist only in the theme layer. Raw palette in components is a defect lint can ban (no-raw-color).

Semantic role Purpose Notes
canvas Page background Lowest surface
surface Durable panels, tables Flat elevation 0
surface-raised Menus, popovers Elevation 1
fg-default Primary text ≥4.5:1 on canvas/surface
fg-muted Secondary text Still ≥4.5:1 if used as text
fg-on-accent Text on accent fills Contrast-gated
border-subtle Hairline separators ≥3:1 when conveying structure (1.4.11)
accent Primary actions / brand Scarce; one primary per view
danger / warning / success / info Status Never color alone—pair with text/icon
focus-ring Keyboard focus ≥3:1 against adjacent; ≥2px

Token layers: Primitive ramp → Semantic role → rare Component alias. Product imports semantic only. Semver: MAJOR = rename/remove or change meaning of a role; MINOR = add role; PATCH = ramp tweak behind same role (visual diff required).

6.2 Contrast floors

Pairing Ratio Standard
Normal text 4.5:1 WCAG 1.4.3 AA
Large text (≥18.66px bold / 24px) 3:1 1.4.3
Non-text UI (icons, boundaries, focus) 3:1 1.4.11
Disabled controls Exempt from AA as inactive; still must not look like primary —

Dual-theme audit: Every semantic pair ships light and dark. CI or visual regression fails contrast on both. Placeholder text and muted chrome are the usual failures—gate them.

Status must be multi-channel (L11): color + text and/or icon and/or pattern. Red-only errors fail.

6.3 Dark mode is not inverted light

Dark themes use separate tonal ramps, not CSS invert or naive hex flips.

Concern Light Dark
Surfaces Paper-like ascending elevation Desaturated darks; elevate by lightening slightly, not by heavy shadow alone
Hairlines Soft dark at low alpha 10–20% white hairlines
Accents Full brand chroma OK if contrast holds Dim chroma; check fg-on-accent
Shadows Soft dark umbra Prefer border/surface steps; shadows wash out
Danger/success Saturated Desaturate; rely on label

Prefer-when for dark: User preference (prefers-color-scheme) + explicit product toggle that persists. Do not force brand-dark marketing look into dense data tables without a product dark ramp.

6.4 Forced-colors and High Contrast

Forced-colors / Windows High Contrast / forced-colors: active remaps the UI to system colors. Do not force hex backgrounds that wipe system Canvas, ButtonText, Highlight, LinkText, etc.

Do Don’t
Preserve semantic meaning with system color keywords Paint over with brand purple fills
Keep borders that define controls Remove borders that only existed as shadow
Ensure focus remains visible via system Highlight outline: none without replacement
Test marketing illustration separately from product chrome Assume product glass survives HC

Tension (from research): Brand expression vs forced-colors — prefer illustration on marketing; preserve system semantics on product UI. Broken HC or lifeless product chrome are both failures; product must choose HC correctness.

6.5 Theme layers

Themes stack. Later layers override earlier ones without forking component trees.

Brand (primitive ramps + fonts)
  → Mode (light | dark)
    → Contrast (standard | high / forced-colors adaptation)
      → Campaign / seasonal (rare, time-boxed aliases)
Layer Owns Prefer when Avoid when
Brand Primitive ramps, type pairing, radius Multi-brand enterprise forks tokens not trees Forking component repos per brand
Mode Semantic remaps for light/dark Always for product Inverted-light hacks
Contrast HC borders, disable decorative blur System HC / user HC setting Shipping HC as a pastel gray theme only
Campaign Temporary accent alias, landing skins Marketing launches with sunset date Touching Locked checkout tokens

Override-rate on Locked surfaces after a campaign layer is a systems smell—remediate.

6.6 Elevation means modality (L4)

Raise means temporary. Flat means durable. Random shadows on static panels destroy hierarchy.

Level Surface treatment z-index Use
0 Flat No shadow; canvas / surface 0 Pages, tables, settings
1 Raise Light shadow or surface-raised 100 Menus, popovers, sticky bars
2 Overlay Stronger elevation + scrim 200 Modals, sheets, dialogs
3 Telemetry Toast surface 300 Toasts (above scrim, below critical blockers)
Critical blocker Full stop UI 400 Session expiry, legal hard-stops (rare)

Radius tokens: sm 4 · md 8 · lg 12 · full sparingly (avatars, icon buttons)—not on every card.

Sticky headers sit at elevation 1 visually but must not imply modality; use hairline borders more than shadow when the content is durable.

6.7 Materials: glass, blur, scrim, vibrancy

Materials encode temporariness and focus, not decoration.

Material token Spec (example) Prefer when Avoid when
scrim Neutral black 40–60% opacity Modal/sheet focus; dim durable UI beneath Soft decorative tint behind forms
blur-overlay backdrop-filter: blur(8–16px) + translucent fill Floating panels over rich canvases (design tools) Data tables, checkout, long reading
glass Blur + low-alpha surface + hairline Marketing overlays; rare tool palettes “Glass everywhere”; solid data
vibrancy Platform native (iOS) materials Native shells where HIG expects it Fake CSS vibrancy on dense web grids
solid-overlay Opaque surface-raised Accessibility, HC, reduced transparency —

Rules

  1. Glass/blur = overlays only; solid for data (research anti-pattern: glass/glow everywhere).
  2. Respect prefers-reduced-transparency (where available): swap blur → solid.
  3. Text on glass must still meet contrast against the worst-case backdrop—or place text on a solid scrim plate.
  4. Never use glow + multi-layer shadow stacks as hierarchy substitutes (L2).

6.8 Chapter 6 summary

Semantic roles only. Contrast both themes. Dark is tonal, not inverted. Forced-colors preserve system meaning. Elevation = modality. Materials are temporary; data stays solid.

Measure (Ch 6)

Signal Pass when
Theme audit Dual-theme contrast CI green on trust paths
Elevation No decorative shadow on durable flat panels
Materials Glass only on overlays; data stays solid

Chapter 7 — Motion & Loading

7.1 Motion as meaning

Motion acknowledges state change (L5 adjacency): press, open, resolve. Motion that does not change understood state is theater—cut it (decision cheat-sheet: “Decorates or changes known state?”).

Shared components animate transform and opacity only (compositor-friendly; systems budget).

7.2 Motion tokens

Token Duration Easing (typical) Use
motion-fast 100–150ms ease-out Press, hover, toggle knobs
motion-default 150–250ms ease-in-out State changes, expand/collapse
motion-slow 300–400ms ease-in-out Sheets, large overlays entering
motion-enter = default/slow decelerate Elements arriving
motion-exit ≤ enter accelerate Elements leaving (snappier exit)
motion-reduced 0–1ms or opacity only linear prefers-reduced-motion path

Latency tiers (interaction contract): Acknowledge control press ≤100ms (often CSS :active / optimistic). Longer work needs progress UI—not a longer animation.

7.3 Reduced motion

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  /* Swap distance animations for instant/opacity */
}
Full motion Reduced path
Sheet slides up 300ms Instant appear + optional 100ms fade
List item fly-in on create Opacity or instant insert
Parallax / scroll scrubbing Static layout; no scroll-linked movement
Skeleton shimmer Static pulse opacity ≤2Hz or solid placeholder
Confetti / success flourishes Checkmark + text; no particles

Reduced motion is not “less pretty”—it is a peer path. Ship both; test both.

7.4 Marketing scroll storytelling (anti-theater)

Marketing may use scroll to sequence claims. Product UI must not.

Rule Guidance
Hero budget First viewport: brand, one headline, one sentence, one CTA group, one dominant image—no stats strips, schedules, or secondary promos
Scroll scenes ≤3 deliberate scene changes; each with one job
Parallax Subtle or none; never required to understand content
Sticky storytelling Must remain keyboard operable; content in DOM order
Autoplay video Captions; pause control; no seizure-risk flash (>3/sec)
Product app No scroll-jacking, no bento theater inside tools

Anti-patterns: Dashboard confetti on every save; scroll-jacked product settings; pinning the user’s scroll until a Lottie finishes.

7.5 Loading and skeleton recipe

Loading is a designed state (L6), not a blank page.

Latency Visual treatment
<100ms No loader; in-place ack
100–300ms Control pending (spinner in button / disabled)
300ms–2s Local skeleton or inline progress
>2s Determinate progress if known; else skeleton + optional status text
Full-page rare Only for true route-level first paint without shell

Skeleton recipe (layout-matched)

  1. Shape match: Skeleton blocks mirror final content geometry (title bar, row heights, avatar circles)—not a generic gray card grid.
  2. Token surfaces: Use surface vs canvas contrast lightly; avoid harsh pure gray that flashes in dark mode.
  3. Shimmer: Optional horizontal gradient moving slowly; disable or static-pulse under reduced motion.
  4. No fake text: Do not put Latin gibberish in skeletons; shapes only.
  5. Preserve chrome: App shell (nav, user menu) stays mounted; skeleton the content pane.
  6. Exit: Crossfade ≤150ms to real content; avoid layout jump—reserve min-heights from skeleton.
  7. Failure handoff: Skeleton never spins forever—timeout → error state with retry (field-local or region-local).

Partial loading: Prefer streaming rows / section-ready over blocking the whole view. Optimistic list insert (Linear-style) beats full-page reload theater when rollback is cheap.

7.6 Chapter 7 summary

Tokenize time. Honor reduced motion. Marketing may sequence; product must not scroll-jack. Skeletons match layout and end in real states.

Measure (Ch 7)

Signal Pass when
CLS Skeleton→content layout shift within budget
Reduced motion No essential meaning lost under prefers-reduced-motion
Ack latency Controls acknowledge ≤100ms in profiling

Chapter 8 — Icons, Illustration, Photography, Data Viz + Dense-List Craft

8.1 Icon production system

Icons are a language. Uncontrolled metaphors create cognitive tax equal to synonym component APIs.

Production grid

Property Spec
Grid 24×24 master; also 16 / 20 / 32 derived
Live area 20×20 inside 24 (2px padding); keep strokes inside live area
Stroke 1.5–2px optical at 24; do not scale stroke thickness naively down to 16—use a 16 master or variable stroke
Corners Match radius tokens optically (slightly tighter than UI md)
Caps / joins Round caps for friendly sets; square for technical sets—pick one
Optical adjustments Circles and diagonals often need +0.5–1px visual weight
Color Icons use currentColor / semantic fg-*; never baked brand hex in SVG fills for product UI
Touch Primary actions: craft ≥44×44 hit target (HIG/Material); WCAG 2.5.8 AA floor 24×24. Dense rows may be 32–36 tall if the hit slop (padding/expand) still yields ≥44×44 or an expand-on-focus mode is offered. Visible glyph may be 20–24.

Metaphor glossary (required artifact)

Concept Approved metaphor Banned synonyms
Settings Gear or sliders (pick one product-wide) Wrench + gear mix
Delete Trash X in primary toolbars (X = dismiss)
Search Magnifier Spyglass variants
Share Node/branch or platform share “Send” airplane if Send exists
More Kebab or meatball (pick one) Hamburger for overflow

Labeling: Primary navigation stays icon + text until learnability is proven. Lint: no-unlabeled-icon-button for destructive and primary actions.

Decorative icons adjacent to visible text: aria-hidden="true". Alone: accessible name required.

8.2 Illustration system

Context Style job Rules
Marketing Brand atmosphere; memorable Real visual anchor (product/place/context); not generic purple blobs
Empty state Encourage one next action Air + one CTA + optional template; decorative alt=""; named CTA
Error / denied Calm clarity No blame humor that obscures recovery; always path forward
Onboarding Curriculum, not carousel Identity → artifact → share → return cue
In-product celebration Rare; trust×frequency paths Prefer quiet success text over confetti

Empty vs marketing art: Empty illustrations are quieter, smaller, and subordinate to the CTA. Marketing art can be full-bleed. Do not reuse a hero illustration as a permanent empty state—it becomes wallpaper and kills scent of the action.

Spot illustrations share a limited palette mapped to semantic tokens so dark mode does not break them. Prefer SVG or carefully compressed assets; provide dark variants when flat fills assume light canvas.

8.3 Photography

Concern Guidance
Crop Subject-aware; faces/products clear of UI chrome; define focal point for object-position
Grade Shared grade per brand; don’t mix cinematic teal-orange with flat product shots on one page
Text-safe zones Reserve clear space for overlaid type; never place Display text on busy midtones without scrim plate
Hero treatment Full-bleed edge-to-edge on marketing; not inset rounded media cards unless the design system requires it
Product UI photos Rare; avatars and entity previews—consistent aspect ratios (1:1, 4:3)
Alt text Informative photos get real alt; decorative get empty alt; never “image123”
Performance Responsive srcset; priority only on LCP hero

Brand test reminder: If you remove the nav and the first viewport could belong to another company, photography + type failed—not the logo size.

8.4 Data visualization encoding kit

Encode with position and length first; color second; never color alone.

Priority Channel Use
1 Position / length Bar, column, position on axis
2 Labels / values Direct labels on small-n series
3 Shape / pattern Patterns/hatching for a11y + print
4 Color Semantic ramps; dual-theme checked
5 Motion Transition on filter—not continuous distraction

Ramp rules

Ramp type Prefer when Notes
Sequential Magnitude One hue family; check dark mode
Diverging Deviation from midpoint Clear neutral midpoint
Categorical ≤6–8 categories After that, aggregate or facet
Status Success/warn/danger Pair with icon/text

Dual-theme: Export chart tokens (chart-1…chart-n, chart-axis, chart-grid) as semantics. Gridlines stay subtle but ≥3:1 if they define structure users rely on.

Fallbacks: Provide a data table or summary for complex charts (a11y). Tooltips are not the only access path—keyboard focusable points or a table toggle.

AI diffs / code hunks: Do not rely on red/green alone; include +/− markers and readable wording (Case D).

8.5 Dense-list visual craft

Daily tools earn density. Middling padding is the common failure (density vs air tension).

Element Comfortable Compact Dense
Row height 44–48 36–40 32–36 (still ≥44 touch via padding/hit slop on mobile)
Separator Full hairline border-subtle Hairline or zebra Zebra or hairline—not both heavy
Primary text Body Body Body (don’t shrink below 14)
Secondary meta Meta, muted Meta Meta; drop optional columns first
Leading icon/avatar 24 20–24 16–20
Trailing actions Visible primary + overflow Overflow-first Overflow; reveal on select/focus

Scan path

  1. Users scan down the primary column (usually title/id)—align it consistently.
  2. Status pills sit in a fixed column; multi-channel encoding.
  3. Sticky header: hairline + surface, elevation-1 treatment without modal implication.
  4. Selected row: surface-raised or accent wash at low alpha plus checkbox/aria-selected—not color alone.
  5. Keyboard focus: visible ring per row/action; do not steal horizontal scroll from columns.

Sticky headers & columns: Pin identity columns first; freeze header on vertical scroll. Shadow under sticky header only while stuck (scroll-driven class)—avoids permanent fake elevation.

Linear-style steal: Issue row density, instant insert, keyboard scent—without assuming every user is keyboard-native (offer progressive path).

8.6 Chapter 8 summary

Icons need a grid and a glossary. Illustration serves action or brand—never both at once. Photos are graded and text-safe. Viz encodes position first. Dense lists respect scan paths and tokenized density.

Measure (Ch 8)

Signal Pass when
Icon glossary No metaphor collisions in primary nav
Viz grayscale Chart meaning survives grayscale + labels
Dense list Scan path (identity · primary · meta) holds in usability
Dense touch Dense rows still provide ≥44×44 hit (padding/slop) or expand-on-focus

Chapter 9 — Cross-Surface Visual: Email, Print, Safe Areas

9.1 Email HTML visual kit

Email is a constrained visual runtime: limited CSS, unreliable webfonts, dark-mode quirks, image blocking.

Element Spec
Canvas width 600px content table common; fluid ≤100% on small screens
Type System stack fallbacks; 14–16px body; titles ≤22–24px
Hierarchy Weight + space; one primary CTA button
CTA Solid fill button (≥44px tall); single accent; link fallback text beneath
Colors Inline + hex with semantic intent; test dark-mode clients (some invert)
Images Width attributes; alt text always; important CTA not image-only
Spacing Padding on cells; avoid margin collapse assumptions
Footer Plain-language unsubscribe / manage preferences; equal clarity to upgrade paths

Do / Don’t

Do Don’t
One job per email Newsletter as dense dashboard
Live text for claims Critical copy baked only into images
Prefers-plain-text twin for transactional Rely on CSS grid/flex as primary layout
Test Apple Mail, Gmail, Outlook Assume browser CSS

Transactional email follows trust-path craft: quiet chrome, clear amounts with tabular lining if possible, no growth dark patterns.

9.2 Print and PDF UI

Print stylesheets and PDF exports are product surfaces for receipts, tickets, reports, and compliance.

Concern Guidance
@media print Hide nav, chrome, toasts; expand accordions; show link URLs where needed
Page breaks Avoid breaking mid-row in tables; break-inside: avoid on rows/cards that must stay whole
Color Assume B&W; patterns/labels for status; sufficient contrast without background fills
Type 10–12pt body for dense reports; margins ≥0.5in
Headers/footers Document title, date, page number; confidentiality if required
Forms Print user-entered values, not empty widgets
Accessibility of PDF Tagged PDF when enterprise sells; selectable text; real headings—not flattened screenshots

Export buttons preview a print-faithful layout when legal/money is involved (receipts). Do not ship “Download PDF” that screenshots a glass dashboard.

9.3 Safe areas, notches, foldables

Devices clip content into unsafe regions (notch, home indicator, rounded corners, fold creases).

Token / CSS Use
env(safe-area-inset-top/right/bottom/left) Padding on shell edges, fixed CTAs, sticky footers
Bottom primary CTA padding-bottom: max(space-4, env(safe-area-inset-bottom))
Side-edge gestures Keep destructive swipe actions away from system back-gesture zones
Notch landscape Don’t put primary controls in the camera cutout band
Foldables / dual pane Prefer two logical panes over stretching one form across the crease; avoid interactive targets on the hinge
Desktop PWA / electron Still honor OS traffic-light / drag regions; don’t place controls under window chrome

Touch: Primary targets ≥44×44. Hover-only affordances fail on mobile—sheets + buttons (anti-pattern table).

Orientation: Reflow; don’t lock landscape unless the task is inherently media-canvas and an alternative exists.

9.4 Cross-surface checklist

  1. Same semantic roles named across web, email (as far as hex mapping allows), and native.
  2. Brand-hero on marketing web/email headers; quiet tool in product and transactional mail.
  3. Safe-area padding on every fixed edge control.
  4. Print path verified for trust documents.
  5. Forced-colors / dark clients sampled for email and web.

9.5 Chapter 9 summary

Email is constrained hierarchy with one CTA. Print strips chrome and survives grayscale. Safe areas are part of layout—not an afterthought padding hack.

Measure (Ch 9)

Signal Pass when
Email clients Receipt readable in Gmail + Apple Mail light/dark
Print Critical content within margins; B&W still legible
Safe areas Primary CTA clear of home indicator / notch

Part II Review Questions

Part II Review Questions

  1. Type contract: A product squad adds font-size: 18px to emphasize a dashboard widget title because “Title (22) feels too loud and Body (16) feels weak.” Using Chapter 5’s locked scale and L3, what should they do instead—and how would optical craft and density tokens participate in the fix?

  2. Theme layers & elevation: You are shipping a seasonal campaign accent and a new settings page with three static cards that each use heavy drop shadows “to match the campaign site.” Map the correct theme layer for the accent, explain whether those card shadows obey L4, and propose the elevation/z treatment if one card opens a confirmation modal with toasts still able to appear.

  3. Motion & loading: A marketing page uses scroll-scrubbed parallax to reveal three product claims; the product app reuses the same Lottie as a full-page loader between every internal navigation, with no reduced-motion path. Critique both against Chapter 7 and specify a skeleton recipe for a dense issue list route.

  4. Media & viz: Design the visual system artifacts you need before drawing icons for a new “Share / Export / External link” cluster, and list the encoding priority you would use for a categorical bar chart that must work in dark mode and grayscale print.

  5. Cross-surface: Walk through visual decisions for a paid invoice: in-app receipt view, email receipt, and PDF download—covering type/measure, color/contrast under grayscale, CTA/hierarchy, and safe-area implications if the in-app view has a sticky “Pay now” bar on iOS.

End of Part II — Visual Systems

Part III — Interaction

Spine reminder: Modern UI is opinionated infrastructure for outcomes. Interaction is how that spine talks: every action acknowledged, every state designed, every irreversible path gated by honesty.

Interaction design is not decoration on screens. It is the conversation between person and system: trigger → acknowledge → work → resolve → undo. Laws L5–L8 (acknowledge ≤100ms; state is designed; undo > confirm; progressive disclosure) are the grammar of that conversation. This part turns those laws into shippable playbooks—including the findability and manipulation kit the research gap audit flagged as thin: search, filter, selection, tables, drag-and-drop, history, collab, and AI review loops.

Part objectives. After this part you should be able to:

  1. Assign latency tiers, undo classes, and a full state taxonomy (including empty vs zero vs error) to any control or list.
  2. Design search, filter, sort, and pagination as one findability system with URL persistence and recovery paths.
  3. Specify selection models, data tables, and accessible drag-and-drop with keyboard peers.
  4. Wire navigation, history, disclosure, teaching, share, autosave, clipboard, notifications, and live collab without stealing focus or burying core paths.
  5. Ship dual device models, JIT permissions, offline sync honesty, and AI propose → review → undo.

Laws in force: L5 Feedback · L6 State · L7 Undo · L8 Disclosure · L9 Focus · L10 Native first · L11 Multi-channel · L14 Craft ∝ trust × frequency.

Companion examples: See the Part III examples companion.

Chapter 10 — Feedback, Latency, Undo & State

10.1 The feedback loop

Every interactive control participates in one loop:

Phase Question the UI must answer Failure mode
Trigger What did I invoke? Ambiguous hit target; no scent
Acknowledge Did the system hear me? Silence; dead button
Work Is something happening? Blank page; spinner without meaning
Resolve Did it succeed or fail? Toast-only failure; lost context
Undo Can I reverse it? Confirm tax; hard delete by default

Interface as conversation: silence is a bug. Figma presence, Slack send states, and Linear optimistic inserts all treat acknowledgment as infrastructure—not polish.

10.2 Latency budgets (L5)

Acknowledge within ≤100ms. Beyond acknowledgment, use tiered budgets—never a blank full-page wait for a button press.

Tier Budget What the user feels UI pattern
Instant 0–100ms Press registered Press state, ripple/opacity, disable double-submit
Fast 100–300ms Continuous Inline pending on control; keep layout stable
Perceptible 300ms–1s Waiting but oriented Deterministic progress or layout-matched skeleton
Interrupt 1–5s Task paused Explicit progress; cancel if safe
Long >5s Background job Persist work; notify on complete; never hold the modal hostage

Prefer-when:

  • Optimistic UI when rollback is cheap (create draft, archive locally, star). Show the result immediately; reconcile on server ack.
  • Pessimistic UI when money, legal, mass notify, or shared blast radius is involved (checkout, prod destroy, invite-all). Wait for confirmation; use idempotent keys.

Failure if wrong: silent wrong state (optimistic without undo) or confirm tax on every archive (pessimistic everywhere).

Double-submit: disable the control and show in-place pending; use idempotent request keys on pay and other once-only actions.

10.3 Motion as feedback, not noise

Token Duration Use
fast 100–150ms Press / hover acknowledgment
default 150–250ms State transitions
slow 300–400ms Sheets / large reveals
reduced opacity or instant Honor prefers-reduced-motion

Motion must change known state (opened, selected, succeeded)—not decorate. Shared components should animate transform/opacity only. Never use motion as the sole success signal; pair with text or icon (L11).

10.4 Undo classes (L7)

Undo > confirm locally. Confirm only for external irreversibility (money left the building, email sent to a thousand people, production resource destroyed).

Class Window / mechanism Prefer when Reject
Soft undo 5–10s toast with Undo Archive, mute, send (Gmail/Superhuman), local delete Soft toast for team-visible permanent destroy
Quarantine Trash / recycle 30d (or product equivalent) Recoverable objects; user-owned content Pretending Trash is soft undo for shared ACL deletes without notice
Hard confirm Modal with blast radius named Charge, prod destroy, mass mail, revoke access for others Confirm-on-every-archive; custom scary modals per page

Steal mechanics: Gmail Undo Send; Drive Trash; GitHub dangerous zone (type to confirm when blast is extreme).

Bulk operations: show N selected; scoped select-all (see Ch. 12); on partial failure keep successes and report failures with retry—do not roll back the whole batch silently.

10.5 Interruptions & live regions

  • One modal at a time. Toasts queue (elevation tier 3 telemetry: above scrim, below critical blockers).
  • Never steal focus from typing unless an assertive blocking error requires it.
  • Live regions: polite for toasts and status; assertive for blocking errors—sparingly (WCAG 4.1.3 status vs alert vs log).
  • Toast actions must be keyboardable; do not move focus into the toast unless assertive.

10.6 The designed state matrix (L6)

“No data” is not a state. Design at least these seven, then expand with the empty/zero/error taxonomy below.

State User meaning Chrome / content
Empty Nothing here yet (never used or cleared) Teaching CTA; templates; one primary action
Loading Fetch in flight Layout-matched skeleton; preserve structure
Partial Some loaded, some pending Show known rows; inline pending for remainder
Error Request failed Field-local or region error + retry; preserve input
Offline No network; queue or read-only Banner + sync indicator (Ch. 14)
Denied AuthZ / permission missing Explain + settings/request path; degrade feature
Syncing Local ≠ server; reconcile in progress Explicit syncing affordance—not a mystery spinner

Forms: validate on blur vs change intentionally; preserve input on error; field-local errors + Error Summary pattern (GOV.UK: list errors linked to fields); layout-matched skeletons so content does not jump.

10.7 Empty vs zero vs error taxonomy (critical)

The gap audit called this out: never-used, filtered-to-zero, true empty, error, and denied need distinct CTAs. Collapsing them into one illustration destroys trust and recovery.

Situation Definition What to show Primary CTA Anti-pattern
Never-used (first empty) User has never created objects in this space Air + one CTA + optional templates Create / Start from template 12-step carousel; permanent empty art
True empty Space exists; all items removed or archived Honest empty + recreate path Create / Restore from Trash Same copy as never-used (“Welcome!”)
Filtered-to-zero Query/filters active; no matches “0 results” + active filter chips Clear filters / Adjust query “No projects yet” when filters are on
Search zero Query string yields no hits Ranking honesty: “No matches for X” Clear search; suggest spelling/scope Fake results or silent fallback to popular
Error Load/mutation failed Error message + retry; preserve context Retry / Contact support Toast-only failure with empty illustration
Denied Permission or entitlement missing Plain-language reason Request access / Upgrade / Open settings Dead end with no next step
Offline empty Cannot load; may have local cache Offline banner; show cache if any Retry when online Spinner forever
Partial / stale Showing cached or subset Staleness cue + refresh Refresh Presenting stale as live

Decision rule: If clearing filters or search would reveal items, you are in filtered-to-zero or search zero—never first-empty. If the API returned 403/401, you are in denied. If the API failed, you are in error. Only when the collection is legitimately vacant with no active refine do you use empty teaching UI.
