Case K — Table selection + bulk partial failure (new — R2)

Context. Ops table with filters on; user range-selects and bulk-archives. Selection and tables were completeness gaps; Capstone 3 is not enough—teach the decision.

Lens Choice Rejected
Visual Dense rows; sticky header; tabular status text+icon Card-per-row; color-only status
Interaction Shift-range; scoped select-all (page/filter); show N selected; selection toolbar; bulk soft-undo; partial failure keeps successes Silent whole-corpus select-all; all-or-nothing bulk with no per-row errors
Systems Shared DataTable + BulkBar Guided→Locked if ≥3 uses Per-squad table snowflakes
A11y <th scope>; keyboard row/cell model documented; select-all named (“Select all on this page”); DnD reorder has Move up/down peer Div grid without headers; drag-only reorder
Strategy Instrument bulk success/partial/fail; blast-radius copy for destructive bulk Optimize only “actions completed” vanity

Steal: Linear/Gmail scoped selection + bulk bar; partial-failure reporting.
Measure: bulk completion · partial-fail recovery · accidental whole-corpus selects · keyboard task success.
Lesson: Selection grammar and scoped select-all are safety rails. Tables without structure a11y and bulk without partial-failure UX are incomplete daily-driver surfaces.

Anti-pattern Why it fails Repair
AI-SaaS purple / cream-terracotta cliché Brand test fails; interchangeable marketing; forces weak product chrome Distinctive scarce accent; separate marketing vs product systems; dual-theme audit

Override-rate signal: If product forks Locked primitives often, the anti-pattern is often premature rigidity or wrong default—fix the system (Systems A), don’t blame squads alone.

Chapter 23 — North Stars: Steal the Mechanic (Expanded)

Steal behavior and structure, not skin. Each entry: mechanic → where to apply → avoid cargo-cult.

Linear
Steal Issue row density for daily drivers; Cmd-K for long-tail; optimistic create with instant list insert when rollback is cheap
Apply when Pro tool, high frequency, keyboard-willing users; reversible creates
Avoid Assuming all users are keyboard-native—pair with templates/empty guidance; optimistic create on money/legal paths

Stripe
Steal Dual systems (marketing vs product); Checkout label + error pairing; docs-as-product clarity
Apply when Trust markets; Locked checkout; public docs that reduce support
Avoid Marketing gradients inside dashboard tables; treating docs as afterthought

Figma
Steal Selection/presence as conversation; contextual toolbar on selection; state talkativeness
Apply when Multiplayer canvases; selection-scoped actions
Avoid Forcing desktop canvas IA onto mobile; presence noise on solitary form flows

Apple HIG
Steal Material = temporary vs durable (elevation-as-modality); VoiceOver craft; prefers-reduced-motion
Apply when Modals/sheets vs pages; native iOS chrome/gestures
Avoid Copying iOS materials onto dense web tables; decorative blur on data

Material 3
Steal Role-based color; tonal surfaces; systematic state layers
Apply when Building semantic token ramps; Android parity of roles
Avoid Default M3 purple as “your brand”; role soup without promotion rules

Polaris / Spectrum / Carbon
Steal Contribution model + docs + token discipline; do/don’t; escape hatches
Apply when Multi-squad enterprise; Locked kit governance
Avoid Monolith with no Guided/Open partition; contribution theater without semver SLA

Radix / React Aria / shadcn-style kits
Steal Behavior primitives (focus, APG maps); own the skin with tokens
Apply when Adopt-vs-build: prefer proven behavior, skin with semantics
Avoid Copying skin without understanding focus/ARIA; wrapping once “for consistency” (L12)

GOV.UK
Steal Error Summary (list linked to fields); plain language; one-column critical tasks
Apply when Forms, auth, legal, data-rights, high-anxiety tasks
Avoid Lifeless marketing; using plain language as excuse for weak product brand on acquisition surfaces

Gmail / Superhuman
Steal Undo Send window (soft undo class); density toggle; keyboard power with progressive path
Apply when High-frequency communication/productivity; reversible sends
Avoid Elitism without templates/empty guidance; undo window on hard legal erase

Chapter 24 — Decision Cheat-Sheet & Full PR Critique Checklist

24.1 Decision cheat-sheet

Ask in order. Bias toward the right column’s default unless prefer-when flips it.

Question Bias / action
Marketing or product? Brand-hero vs quiet tool
Pre-PMF or trust market? Speed-of-learning vs early polish
New or daily? Air + templates vs density + keyboard
Reversible? Assign undo class (Soft / Quarantine / Hard)
Money / identity / shared blast / legal erase? Pessimistic + Locked
≥3 real uses + Locked concern? Promote recipe→pattern→component; else keep local
Decorates or changes known state? Cut decoration
Color sole signal? Add text / pattern / icon (L11)
Synonym API? Rename before AI scales it
Growth on trust path? Move or kill
AI side effect? Diff + approve + undo
High override rate? Fix system (Systems A)
axe-green but task fail? Inclusion > compliance theater
Empty vs filtered-zero vs error? Distinct copy + CTA (Case I)
Search or command? Retrieval UX vs Cmd-K palette—don’t conflate
Table/grid needed? Headers, sticky plan, keyboard model, selection scope
Account/data rights? Hard flow ≠ document soft-delete (Case J)
Offline possible? Sync indicator + conflict prefer-when (Case H)

24.2 Full PR critique checklist

Use on UI PRs and design specs. Check N/A only with a one-line why. Fail any ship-gate row on critical paths.

A. Hierarchy & visual grammar

  1. Hierarchy — One focal point per region? Weight/space/position before paint (L2)?
  2. Type — Named roles only; modular scale; no ad-hoc px (L3)?
  3. Elevation — Raise = temporary modality; flat = durable (L4)?
  4. Space — 4/8 rhythm; forms label→control spacing; reflow at 320 / 400%?
  5. Color — Semantic tokens only (L1)? Text 4.5:1 / large 3:1 / UI 3:1 both themes?
  6. Forced-colors — No forced hex that breaks system ButtonText/Canvas?
  7. Motion — Meaning-bearing; transform/opacity in shared kit; reduced-motion path?

B. Interaction & state

  1. Feedback — Acknowledge ≤100ms; correct latency tier (L5)?
  2. State matrix — empty / loading / partial / error / offline / denied / syncing designed (L6)?
  3. Empty ≠ zero ≠ error — Distinct CTAs (esp. filtered-to-zero)?
  4. Undo class — Soft / Quarantine / Hard matches blast radius (L7)?
  5. Disclosure — Primary → overflow → palette → settings (L8)? Core action scent without tour?
  6. Double-submit — Disabled + pending; idempotent on pay?
  7. Bulk — Scoped select-all; N selected; partial failure keeps successes?

C. Search, filter & findability

  1. Query UX — Scope clear; ranking honesty; no fake fullness?
  2. Zero-with-filters — Explains filters; Clear filters primary; URL persists facets?
  3. Announcements — Result count in polite live region?
  4. Cmd-K vs search — Palette not pretending to be full retrieval (or vice versa)?

D. Tables, grids & selection

  1. Semantics — <table> headers/scope or APG grid—not unlabeled div grid?
  2. Keyboard — Cell/row navigation model documented; no keyboard traps?
  3. Sticky headers / columns — Don’t break reading order or focus?
  4. Selection — Shift-range if claimed; selection-anchored toolbar; destructive bulk confirm?
  5. Inline edit — Esc/cancel; save ack; error local to cell/row?

E. Accessibility structure (landmarks, headings, focus, live regions)

  1. Landmarks — Banner / main / nav / complementary as needed; skip to #main?
  2. Headings — One logical h1; no level-skipping for style; outline matches IA?
  3. Focus — DOM order = reading order; :focus-visible ring; restore to trigger (L9)?
  4. Names — Icon buttons labeled; no-unlabeled-icon-button clean?
  5. Live regions — Polite toasts; assertive only for blocking errors; status vs alert vs log (4.1.3) disciplined?
  6. SR smoke — Land → skip → primary CTA → hear errors → dismiss modal → focus restored?
  7. Touch — Primary targets ≥44×44?
  8. Auth/CAPTCHA — Visible labels; PM autocomplete; accessible alternative if challenged?

F. Systems & AI

  1. Partition — Locked / Guided / Open labeled; overrides justified?
  2. Tokens — No raw hex/px; semantic imports only?
  3. API — tone/size/density; no synonym variants; exhaustive unions?
  4. Promotion — <3 uses justified as local?
  5. AI — Diff → apply → undo; side-effects approved; override rate instrumented?

G. Strategy, growth & privacy

  1. Outcome — Which metric? Theater or critical path (L14)?
  2. Growth/trust — Dark patterns on Locked/trust paths? Cancel clarity?
  3. Data-rights — Export/delete/consent not softer than policy reality?
  4. i18n — Expansion budgets; Intl formats; RTL/logical CSS considered if in scope?

Ship gates (critical paths — release-blocking)

  • [ ] Keyboard task pass
  • [ ] axe clean of serious
  • [ ] Both-theme contrast
  • [ ] Focus visible
  • [ ] SR smoke on auth / checkout / create (as applicable)
  • [ ] Lived-experience findings addressed if Locked path

Chapter 25 — Capstone Exercises (5)

Complete each with: decision write-up (use Case format), wire or PR checklist pass, and metrics. Target self-score > 90 on the textbook rubric.

Capstone 1 — Trust-path checkout slice

Brief: Design and specify a single-page checkout for a subscription upgrade (card + tax + Pay). Trust market. No growth theater.

Must include: Locked field/button contracts; pessimistic submit; Error Summary; tabular money; both-theme contrast; idempotent pay note; receipt state; keyboard + SR smoke script.

Deliverables: Prefer-when table · rejected alternatives (≥3) · checklist Ch 24 with ship gates checked · measure plan (payment success, error recovery, chargebacks).

Fail if: Optimistic “Paid!”; placeholder labels; marketing gradient on fields.

Capstone 2 — Findability: search + filters + zero recovery

Brief: Specify product search for a resource list (projects/files/issues) with facets, URL persistence, and zero-with-filters recovery. Include Cmd-K only for commands—not as the sole finder.

Must include: State copy for no-query / zero-query / zero-filtered / error; chip dismiss; Clear filters; result-count live region; APG or native combobox notes; mobile filter sheet.

Deliverables: Decision tree (Case I) · IA for URL params · a11y structure notes (landmarks/headings on results page) · metrics (find success, clear-filter recovery).

Fail if: One generic empty; filters auto-clear silently; color-only active facets.

Capstone 3 — Data table with selection & bulk destroy

Brief: Design an admin-capable table: sortable columns, sticky header, row selection with scoped select-all, bulk delete with correct undo class for shared records.

Must include: Header/scope or grid keyboard model; N selected toolbar; partial failure behavior; DestructiveConfirm or Trash quarantine with blast radius; focus restore.

Deliverables: Selection model spec · undo-class justification · Ch 24 sections D+E filled · rejected “div soup grid.”

Fail if: Select-all across entire corpus without scope; soft toast for team-visible destroy; no keyboard path.

Capstone 4 — AI proposal review on a Guided surface

Brief: Specify an AI “apply suggestions across N items” flow: stream, cancel, diff, apply, undo. One tool side-effect (e.g., notify watchers) requires approval.

Must include: Diff readable without color; override/reject instrumentation; side-effects[] in contract; keyboard apply/reject; not silent mutation.

Deliverables: Case D-style matrix · trust metrics (override rate, undo-after-apply) · promotion plan (when to Lock).

Fail if: Accept-rate-only success metric; email/customers notified without approval; red/green-only diffs.

Capstone 5 — Privacy preference center + account delete

Brief: Design Settings → Privacy: consent minimize, export data, delete account. Legal erase ≠ document delete. Include grace-window copy only if policy supports it—and say so.

Must include: Hard confirm; what is erased vs retained; request status timeline; email receipt; session timeout warn+extend on export; accessible alt if fraud gate present; plain-language Error Summary.

Deliverables: Case J matrix · IA information architecture · contrast with Case C (one paragraph) · support-ticket metric plan · Ch 24 G rows.

Fail if: Soft toast account delete; buried cancel/delete; puzzle-only gate; reuse of file-delete strings unchanged.

Capstone scoring sheet (copy per exercise)

Criterion Weight Score (1–100)
Accuracy 20
Completeness 25
Pedagogical clarity 15
Tactical specificity 20
Cross-domain integration 10
Evidence 10
Weighted total > 90 to pass

Revision loop: If ≤90, list failing criteria → repair with numbers/rejects/measures → re-score.

Part VI close

Practice is where the spine becomes muscle memory: acknowledge, show state, pick an undo class, search with recovery, table with structure, delete with honesty, measure trust. Return to Parts I–V when a case exposes a missing law—then re-enter Chapter 21 with a sharper reject column.

End of Part VI — Practice

Volume A Examples — Companion Guide

Concrete, auditable examples for every major concept, law, tension, taxonomy, and pattern in
research/modern-ui-textbook.md (Edition 1.1).

How these were produced

Six independent domain-expert agents (one per textbook part, to avoid single-author bias) each drafted
an examples document for their assigned chapters. Each draft was then scored 1–100 by an independent,
skeptical judge agent against the weighted rubric below, revised by a revision agent acting on the judge’s
concrete deficiency list, and re-judged — a mandatory minimum of one full revision cycle per document,
continuing until the score exceeded 90.

Scoring rubric (weighted, 1–100)

Criterion Weight Excellence
Accuracy 20 Matches the textbook’s laws, WCAG floors (AA vs AAA labeled), undo classes, token/semver ops, exact numbers
Completeness 25 Every concept in the assigned chapters has a concrete example, with context and rejected alternatives
Pedagogical clarity 15 One concept per example; labeled with chapter/section; usable standalone
Tactical specificity 20 Real numbers, token names, code snippets, microcopy, schemas — no vagueness
Cross-domain integration 10 Examples spanning visual × interaction × systems × a11y × strategy
Evidence & realism 10 Realistic product situations with a Measure line where the textbook demands one

Pass bar: weighted total > 90, with at least one revision cycle regardless of first score.

Conventions

Each examples document mirrors the textbook’s chapter/section numbering, opens with a coverage index
table (concept → example section), and formats each example as Concept → Scenario → Example →
Why it passes → Rejected (where the textbook names a rejected alternative) with a Measure line
where the textbook demands one. Laws are cited as L1–L14, undo classes as Soft / Quarantine / Hard,
and WCAG 2.2 success criteria carry explicit AA/AAA labels.

Modern UI — Part I Foundations: Official Examples Companion

Covers: Chapters 1–4 of Modern UI: Philosophies, Principles, Strategies & Tactics (Edition 1.1).

Purpose. This document gives every major concept, law, tension, taxonomy, and pattern in Part I at least one concrete, auditable example: a realistic product scenario, real microcopy in quotes, real code where the concept is technical, real numbers (px, ms, ratios, percentages), and named tokens. Examples cite laws as L1–L14, use the textbook’s undo classes (Soft / Quarantine / Hard), its WCAG 2.2 numbers with AA/AAA labels, and its touch-target convention (≥44×44 craft bar; WCAG 2.2 2.5.8 AA floor 24×24). Recurring fictional products are used so no real company is imitated: Ledgerline (B2B invoicing SaaS in a trust market), Trellix (daily-driver issue tracker), Nestly (consumer meal-planning app), and Meridian Bank (multi-brand enterprise). Following the textbook’s chapter structure (“Measure — which metric decides the argument”), every tension, law, and strategy example carries an explicit Measure line naming the deciding metric.

Chapter 1 — What Modern UI Is For

Ch 1 — 1.1: The spine sentence — Example

Concept. “Modern UI is opinionated infrastructure for outcomes” (§1.1) — infrastructure (scales across surfaces/teams/generators), opinionated (defaults are policy), outcomes (craft serves a job).

Scenario. Ledgerline is deciding how invoices are archived. Three PRs are open: one adds a per-user setting “Ask before archiving? (on/off)”, one adds a confirm modal, one implements archive-with-undo.

Example. The team writes the decision in spine terms:

  • Infrastructure: archive behavior ships as one Locked pattern ArchiveAction consumed by web, mobile, and the AI bulk-edit agent — not three per-surface implementations.
  • Opinionated: no “Ask before archiving?” setting. The default is the policy: archive is Soft-undo, period. Microcopy: "Invoice archived. Undo" (toast, 7s).
  • Outcomes: the job is “clean up my invoice list in under a minute,” so the design is measured by archive throughput and mis-archive recovery rate, not by how calm the modal looks.

Why it passes. Every clause of the spine is enforced in an artifact (component, default, metric) — the spine is not decorative (§1.2 closing warning).

Rejected. The setting PR (“let users choose”) — neutrality is abdication; infinite settings dump expert anxiety onto every user (§1.4, Philosophy 5).

Ch 1 — 1.2a: Obligation — Clear

Concept. Clear: hierarchy encodes priority; chrome yields to work; “what matters here?” answerable in under a second (§1.2).

Scenario. Trellix issue-detail page redesign.

Example. Issue title set in type.title (20px/600), one primary action "Close issue" styled with color.bg.accent, everything else (labels, watchers, activity settings) demoted to type.meta (12px, color.text.secondary) or parked behind a ⋯ overflow. Sidebar chrome uses color.bg.surface-sunken so the issue body — the work — is the loudest region. Five-second test result: 9/10 participants name “the issue and its Close button” as what matters.

Why it passes. Priority is encoded by weight/space/position (also L2), and chrome yields to the user’s work (tool test, §1.3).

Rejected. Every panel in an equal white card with box-shadow: 0 2px 8px — equal emphasis is no hierarchy.

Ch 1 — 1.2b: Obligation — Talkative

Concept. Talkative: every intentional action acknowledged; silence after a click is a bug (§1.2).

Scenario. Ledgerline “Send invoice” button.

Example. Click → button enters pressed state within 100ms (L5), label swaps to "Sending…" with inline spinner; on resolve, row shows badge "Sent · just now" and a toast: "Invoice #10422 sent to accounts@acme.example." On failure: inline row error "Couldn't send — SMTP timeout. Retry" with a Retry button, not a silent revert.

Why it passes. Trigger, work, and resolve are each acknowledged; intermediate and terminal states are visible.

Rejected. Click → nothing visible for 2.5s → invoice list silently updates. Silence is a bug, not calm design.

Ch 1 — 1.2c: Obligation — Reversible

Concept. Reversible: undo and soft recovery over confirm for local recoverable work; confirm only for external irreversibility (§1.2, L7).

Scenario. Ledgerline delete actions.

Example. Delete a draft invoice → Soft: toast "Draft deleted. Undo" (7s). Delete a client record → Quarantine: moved to Trash, restorable for 30 days, list banner "In Trash — restores automatically expire Aug 14." Issue a refund → Hard confirm: modal "Refund $1,240.00 to Acme Corp? This moves money and can't be undone." with button "Refund $1,240.00".

Why it passes. Confirm is reserved for money moved (external irreversibility); local work gets recovery instead of a confirm tax.

Rejected. Confirm modal on draft delete (“Are you sure?”) — confirm-on-archive class failure, breaks L7.

Ch 1 — 1.2d: Obligation — Systematic

Concept. Systematic: semantic contracts (roles, type, elevation, space, named states) scale humans and AI generators (§1.2, §1.6).

Scenario. Trellix ships a status pill used by 14 squads and by a codegen agent.

Example.

// One contract, no synonyms:
<StatusPill tone="danger" />   // tone: "neutral" | "info" | "success" | "warning" | "danger"
// Consumes only semantic tokens:
// color.bg.danger-subtle, color.text.danger, border color.border.danger

The generator prompt library references the same enum; a lint rule no-synonym-variant blocks a PR adding tone="error".

Why it passes. One meaning per name; the ambiguity that becomes an industrial defect at generator scale is prevented at the API.

Rejected. tone="danger" | "error" | "critical" as accepted aliases — three synonyms for one meaning.

Ch 1 — 1.2e: Obligation — Inclusive

Concept. Inclusive: exclusion is a defect; WCAG/EAA/ADA/508 are floors; lived experience can block ship; checklist-green is not the ceiling (§1.2).

Scenario. Ledgerline checkout release candidate.

Example. Automated floor: axe clean of serious issues, text contrast ≥4.5:1 (WCAG 2.2 1.4.3 AA), focus ring 2px visible in both themes. Then a paid session: a screen-reader user (NVDA + Chrome) cannot find the card-error message because it renders in a visually adjacent div with no aria-describedby. Ship is blocked despite the green checklist; fix is aria-describedby="card-error" plus role="alert" on the error container.

Why it passes. Floor always runs; lived experience gates the Locked trust path (Tension T8).

Measure. AT task success on checkout ≥ target before release; zero serious axe issues in CI.

Ch 1 — 1.2f: Obligation — Measurable

Concept. Measurable: craft follows trust × frequency; arguments from taste lose to metrics (§1.2, §1.5, L14).

Scenario. A Trellix designer wants two weeks to re-polish the admin billing-history page.

Example. The critical-path map shows billing-history at trust 3/5 × frequency 1/5 = 3, versus issue-triage at 4/5 × 5/5 = 20. The two weeks go to triage keyboard flow instead. The decision record cites: override rate on IssueRow 11% (target <5%), keyboard completion of triage 62% (target 90%).

Why it passes. The argument is settled by the metric hierarchy and L14, not by whoever has more taste-confidence in the room.

Ch 1 — 1.3a: Brand test — Example

Concept. Remove the nav — if the first viewport could be another company, branding failed (§1.3).

Scenario. Nestly marketing homepage audit.

Example. Current hero: white background, generic headline "Plan smarter. Live better.", purple gradient CTA. With the nav cropped out, three of five test users guess “some AI productivity app.” Redesign: hero-level brand signal — Nestly’s signature illustrated dinner-table motif at full bleed, headline "Tonight's dinner, decided by 9 a.m.", brand token color.brand.saffron (#E8890C) carrying the CTA. Nav-cropped recognition rises to 5/5 among users who’ve seen the app.

Why it passes. Brand is a hero-level signal on a branded acquisition page, not a logo in a corner fighting a louder generic headline.

Rejected. Purple-on-white “AI SaaS” cliché hero (§1.4).

Ch 1 — 1.3b: Tool test — Example

Concept. Inside the product, if chrome competes with the user’s work, the product failed (§1.3).

Scenario. Trellix logged-in board view.

Example. Chrome inventory pass: top bar reduced to 48px, backgrounds color.bg.surface (near-neutral), all chrome text color.text.secondary; the only saturated elements on screen are user content — issue-priority badges and avatars. The marketing gradient that a previous PR added behind the board header is removed. Screenshot heuristic used in review: “squint — the brightest thing must be user data.”

Why it passes. Quiet chrome, loud content is the tool test applied to layout (§1.3, §4.8).

Rejected. Importing the marketing gradient behind dense data (brand-hero vs quiet tool, T11).

Ch 1 — 1.3c: Dual systems — Example

Concept. Marketing and product share a system yet pass different tests; Stripe-like dual systems exist because the tests pull opposite directions (§1.3).

Scenario. Ledgerline runs one token pipeline for both surfaces.

Example. Shared: primitives (palette.blue.600), type roles, spacing scale, a11y gates. Forked at the semantic layer: marketing maps color.bg.hero → palette.indigo.700 with full-bleed imagery allowed; product maps color.bg.surface → palette.neutral.0 and bans full-bleed brand imagery behind data via lint. One system, two postures.

Why it passes. Same grammar (Systematic), different tests satisfied — no “one look” collapse that yields a pretty tool or a forgettable brand.

Ch 1 — 1.4: What modern UI is not — Anti-pattern gallery

Concept. §1.4’s six negations, each with the concrete failure.

Scenario. A Nestly redesign pitch deck is reviewed against §1.4.

Example (each slide rejected with a reason).

  1. Cards/glass/glow gallery: frosted-glass recipe cards with 24px blur and no reading order — atmosphere substituting for hierarchy. Rejected (breaks L2).
  2. AI-SaaS cliché: cream-and-terracotta palette swap with no change to priority encoding. Rejected — signals a genre, encodes nothing.
  3. Dashboard-as-landing: first viewport shows streak stats, a schedule widget, and two promo chips before the “Plan this week” job. Rejected — the job is buried.
  4. Infinite settings: “Let users pick card density, corner radius, and animation speed.” Rejected — settings as a substitute for opinionated defaults.
  5. A11y as late audit: “We’ll run axe the week before launch.” Rejected — inclusion must live in primitives (§4.5).
  6. Silent AI mutation: “Autofix pantry quantities in the background; we track accept rate.” Rejected — AI that silently mutates work and optimizes only accept rate is a spine violation (§1.6).

Why it passes. Each negation is falsifiable in review, not a vibe.

Ch 1 — 1.5a: Critical-path map & craft allocation — Example

Concept. Design the job, then the surface; 3–5 jobs starve theater elsewhere; craft where trust × frequency is highest (§1.5).

Scenario. Ledgerline quarterly planning.

Example. Critical-path map (trust 1–5 × frequency 1–5):

Job Trust Freq Score Craft budget
Pay / get paid (checkout, payouts) 5 4 20 Highest — pessimistic patterns, field-level errors, AT smoke
Authenticate + recover account 5 3 15 High — passkeys, password-manager-friendly
Create/send first invoice 4 3 12 High — time-to-first-value path
Invite accountant 3 2 6 Medium
Export year-end report 3 1 3 Meets floors, minimal polish

The dashboard “insights” tiles score 2×2=4 and get no polish sprint.

Why it passes. L14 applied as an allocation table; theater is starved by construction.

Measure. Payment success rate, time-to-first-invoice, error recovery rate on checkout.

Ch 1 — 1.5b: Metric hierarchy + trust guardrail — Example

Concept. North star → leading → craft; experiments lift leading metrics only if trust metrics don’t worsen (§1.5).

Scenario. Nestly growth experiment: auto-enroll trial users into a paid plan reminder flow.

Example.

  • North star: weekly successful meal plans completed.
  • Leading: time-to-first-plan (target <4 min), trial-to-paid conversion.
  • Craft: plan-edit error recovery rate, keyboard completion of plan creation, DS override rate.
  • Trust guardrails (must not worsen): cancel-flow completion without support contact; "how do I cancel?" tickets (baseline 14/wk); chargebacks (baseline 0.3%); AT task failures.

Experiment result: conversion +9%, but cancel tickets 14→31/wk. Verdict per §1.5: roll back — “activation that permanently damages trust is not growth.”

Why it passes. The hierarchy makes the rollback non-negotiable rather than a debate.

Ch 1 — 1.5c: Expertise modes & onboarding curriculum — Example

Concept. Fork mode, not product; onboarding is a curriculum: identity → artifact → share → return cue (§1.5).

Scenario. Trellix serves both first-run PMs and daily-driver engineers.

Example. One product, two modes: first-run gets templates ("Start from: Bug triage · Sprint board · Blank"), airier rows (row height 44px), and inline hints; daily mode (auto-detected after 10 sessions or toggled in Appearance settings via a density token map, §4.7a) gets 32px rows, full keyboard map, and ⌘K palette. Onboarding curriculum: (1) identity — sign in with SSO; (2) artifact — create first issue from a template in <90s; (3) share — "Invite a teammate to see this board"; (4) return cue — digest email "3 issues changed since yesterday." No twelve-step carousel.

Why it passes. Same product spine; the mode fork serves both densities without middling padding (T1).

Ch 1 — 1.6a: Semantic contracts for humans and machines — Example

Concept. A semantic contract is a promise about meaning across themes and consumers (§1.6).

Scenario. Ledgerline token file consumed by web app, iOS, and an internal codegen agent.

Example.

{
  "color.text.danger":    { "light": "{palette.red.700}", "dark": "{palette.red.300}",
                            "meaning": "destructive or failing state text — never decorative" },
  "color.bg.surface":     { "light": "{palette.neutral.0}", "dark": "{palette.neutral.900}" },
  "elevation.2":          { "shadow": "0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.16)",
                            "meaning": "temporary modality: menus, popovers — never static panels" },
  "space.4": "4px", "space.8": "8px", "space.16": "16px", "space.24": "24px"
}

color.text.danger means danger in every theme, including forced-colors (mapped to CanvasText + iconography, T9); elevation.2 means temporary (L4). The codegen agent’s system prompt embeds the meaning fields.

Why it passes. Humans stay consistent across squads; generators cannot invent color-only status because the contract carries semantics, not hexes (L1).

Rejected. #B91C1C hardcoded in a component — a hex has no meaning to a theme or a generator.

Ch 1 — 1.6b: AI loop — intent → proposal → review → undo — Example

Concept. Product-AI loop; streaming/cancel = talkative, diff-primary apply = reversible, citations/disclosure = honesty; side-effects need approval (§1.6).

Scenario. Ledgerline’s “AI cleanup” for invoice line items.

Example.

  1. Intent: user types "standardize all line-item descriptions to Title Case and fix VAT rounding."
  2. Proposal: streams within 400ms, cancel button visible ("Stop generating"); output is a diff view — 34 rows, changed cells highlighted, per-row checkbox.
  3. Review: footer "Apply 34 changes" disabled until stream completes; rows cite source: "VAT rule: workspace setting › Tax › Rounding = banker's."
  4. Undo: after apply, Soft toast "34 line items updated. Undo" (10s) plus a version-history entry.
  5. Side-effect guard: the model also proposes "email the corrected invoice to the client" — rendered as a separate approval card "Requires your approval: send email to accounts@acme.example", never auto-executed.

Why it passes. Talkative (stream + cancel), Reversible (diff → apply → undo), honest provenance, approval-gated side-effect — the full §1.6 loop.

Measure. Track reject and override rates alongside accept rate (§4.4f) — accept-rate-only optimization is the named anti-metric.

Ch 1 — 1.7: Gap-audit surfaces as first-class obligations — Example

Concept. Settings, admin, privacy/data rights, trust & safety, help, AI disclosure, notification prefs are obligations, not policy documents (§1.7).

Scenario. Ledgerline pre-launch obligations audit.

Example. A one-page gate lists each surface with the obligation it must not fail: Settings must be Clear (taxonomy + search, not fifty toggles); Privacy export must be Talkative (receipt email "Your export of 2,118 records is ready — link valid 7 days", not a silent 204); Account deletion must be honestly irreversible (Hard confirm — harder than trash); Safety must be Reversible (block takes effect immediately and appeal exists) and Talkative (report receipt confirmed); Help must be Inclusive (linked from every denied state); AI disclosure must be Systematic (one AIProvenanceBadge component); Notifications must be Measurable (opt-out and complaint rates tracked). Each row has an owner from the RACI (§4.2g).

Why it passes. If these surfaces are ugly, silent, irreversible, or exclusive, the product failed the six obligations on unavoidable paths (§1.7). Full designs: Ch 4 — 4.7a–4.7g below.

Chapter 2 — Philosophies & Managed Tensions

Ch 2 — P1: Clarity is the product — Example

Concept. Ornament that does not encode priority, state, or affordance is debt (§2.2.1).

Scenario. Trellix issue list visual QA.

Example. Rule applied in critique: every visual element must answer “what does this encode?” Priority badge encodes priority (position + label "P1" + pattern, not color alone — L11). The 1px row separator encodes row boundary. The proposed decorative left-edge gradient stripe encodes nothing → deleted. Result: 0 non-encoding elements in the row template; row scan time in testing drops 210ms.

Why it passes. The interface earns attention by removing competition with the work — the Linear-density/HIG-restraint root.

Ch 2 — P2: Interface as conversation — Example

Concept. Silence is a bug; presence, send states, save indicators, selection chrome are conversational turns; steal the acknowledgment mechanic, not the brand skin (§2.2.2).

Scenario. Ledgerline collaborative invoice editor.

Example. Conversational turns implemented: presence avatars ("Maya is viewing"), field-level save indicator cycling "Saving…" → "Saved just now" (never omitted), selection chrome showing "2 line items selected", send-state ladder on the Send button (idle → sending → sent). The stolen mechanic is acknowledgment itself — no Figma-style purple cursors copied for vibes.

Why it passes. Every user turn gets a system turn; the steal is a behavior, not a prestige name-drop (Conventions: steal mechanic).

Ch 2 — P3: Systems over pages — Example

Concept. UI is grammar: roles, type, elevation, space, named patterns; pages are utterances (§2.2.3).

Scenario. A Ledgerline squad builds a new “Payouts” page.

Example. The squad writes zero new CSS colors. The page is composed from grammar: PageHeader (type.title), DataTable (space.8 cell padding, tabular figures), StatusPill, EmptyState(variant="never-used"), semantic tokens only. Review comment that enforces it: "Line 82: raw #6B7280 — import color.text.secondary instead (L1). Pages are utterances; don't invent page-local paint."

Why it passes. Importing semantics rather than inventing paint is exactly how Material 3 / Spectrum / Polaris succeed per the philosophy.

Ch 2 — P4: Outcomes over aesthetics — Example

Concept. Craft is a moat on critical paths, not a coat of polish on every tile (§2.2.4).

Scenario. Ledgerline has one sprint of design capacity.

Example. Option A: restyle 12 dashboard tiles with new elevation and hover motion. Option B: checkout field honesty — inline validation on blur, error text naming the fix ("Card number is 15 digits — Amex starts with 34 or 37"), latency budget on card tokenization (ack ≤100ms, resolve indicator if >1s). Sprint goes to B. Post-ship: checkout error recovery rate 71% → 89%.

Why it passes. Stripe-Checkout-style field honesty is the moat; tile polish without a job is theater.

Measure. Error recovery rate and payment success — the metric decides, not the mood board.

Ch 2 — P5: Opinionated defaults — Example

Concept. Defaults teach the happy path; changing a default is a migration, not a tweak (§2.2.5).

Scenario. Nestly changes its default notification cadence from daily push to weekly digest.

Example. Treated as a migration: (1) announcement in-product "We're switching most updates to a weekly digest on July 22 — you'll get fewer pings. Keep daily instead"; (2) existing users who ever adjusted cadence are excluded from the auto-switch; (3) rollout 10% → 50% → 100% with opt-out rate watched; (4) settings deep link in the announcement. No silent flag flip.

Why it passes. The default teaches the happy path (digest, §4.7g) and the change is handled with migration discipline, not a tweak.

Rejected. Shipping the flag flip silently and letting support absorb the confusion.

Ch 2 — P6: Accessibility is quality — Example

Concept. Situational disability is normal; “nothing about us without us”; AA floor + humane ceiling + plain language beats compliance theater (§2.2.6).

Scenario. Ledgerline password-reset flow.

Example. Floor: labels visible (not placeholder-only), contrast 4.5:1 (1.4.3 AA), target 44×44 on the submit button (craft; AA floor is 24×24 per 2.5.8). Humane ceiling: plain-language error summary at top of form on failure — "There's 1 problem: The reset code has expired. We've sent a new one to m•••@acme.example." — GOV.UK Error-Summary instinct. Lived experience: quarterly paid session includes this flow; a finding (“code field rejects paste, which blocks a user with tremor using a password manager”) blocks ship until fixed. Situational framing used in the PR: the paste fix also helps every user on a train.

Why it passes. Axe-green and task-green; disabled users hold real blocking power.

Ch 2 — P7: AI consumes your contract — Example

Concept. Ambiguous APIs and unnamed states become defects at generator scale; agent UX = intent, proposal, review, undo; side-effects need approval (§2.2.7).

Scenario. Trellix enables an internal LLM to scaffold new views from the design system.

Example. Before enabling: audit finds Banner accepts type, kind, and variant (synonyms) and has no named denied state. Generator dry-run produces 61 near-duplicate banner usages, 12 with color-only status. Fixes shipped first: one tone prop, named state set matching the L6 taxonomy, catalog entries with a11yKeyboard fields (§4.3h) fed into the generator context. Post-fix dry-run: 0 synonym usages; status always text+icon.

Why it passes. The contract was made unambiguous before being multiplied at machine speed — ambiguity scales into industrial defects.

Ch 2 — T1: Density vs air — Example

Concept. Prefer density: daily driver, tables, power users. Prefer air: first-run, marketing, empty states. Failure if wrong: middling padding that serves neither (§2.3).

Scenario. Trellix triage table vs its never-used empty state.

Example. Triage table (Prefer A): row height 32px, cell padding space.8, 13px type.body-dense, 50 rows visible on a 1080p display. First-run empty state (Prefer B): 64px illustration, space.48 padding, one CTA "Create your first issue". Both in one product, chosen per surface.

Why it passes. Each surface picks a cell and names the accepted failure (dense empty state would fail first-run clarity; airy table fails the tool test).

Rejected. The averaged compromise: 40px rows everywhere — “middling padding is the characteristic failure of teams that average the debate” (§2.3 reading notes).

Measure. Rows visible per viewport + triage task time on the dense surface vs first-run activation (time-to-first-issue) on the airy one — the metric pair exposes an averaged compromise that serves neither.

Ch 2 — T2: Consistency vs flexibility — Example

Concept. Prefer consistency: auth, forms, focus, destructive patterns. Prefer flexibility: brand moments, campaigns. Failure: flat brand or unmanageable debt (§2.3).

Scenario. Meridian Bank Halloween campaign page + login form.

Example. Campaign page (Prefer B): custom illustrated header, one-off type treatment, campaign palette — allowed on the Open/marketing surface. Login form (Prefer A): must use the Locked AuthForm pattern — same field order, same focus ring token focus.ring (2px, contrast-aware), same error pattern — even inside the campaign funnel. Review rule: “the campaign may restyle everything except the moment trust is exchanged.”

Why it passes. Brand gets expression where it acquires; consistency holds where errors and focus cost trust.

Measure. Error-recovery rate and focus-visible audit pass on the campaign-funnel login vs the standard login — the Locked AuthForm must show zero delta; campaign conversion is measured separately and never traded against it.

Ch 2 — T3: Optimistic vs pessimistic UI — Example

Concept. Prefer optimistic: cheap rollback, local edits. Prefer pessimistic: money, legal, mass notify, shared destroy. Failure: silent wrong state / confirm tax everywhere. Classified by blast radius and rollback cost (§2.3).

Scenario. Ledgerline rename vs charge.

Example. Rename an invoice (Prefer A, optimistic): title updates instantly in the list, syncs in background; on failure, reverts with toast "Rename failed — restored 'Q3 Retainer'. Retry". Charge a card (Prefer B, pessimistic): button "Pay $1,240.00" → "Processing…" (disabled, spinner) → success screen only after the processor’s 200. No optimistic "Paid!".

Why it passes. Optimistic insert with undo is talkative and reversible; optimistic “Paid!” before the bank responds is the named trust defect.

Rejected (both directions). "Paid!" before settlement; and a confirm modal on every rename (confirm tax without safety).

Ch 2 — T4: Polish vs speed — Example

Concept. Prefer polish: high trust×frequency, competitive post-PMF. Prefer speed: discovery, internal tools, rare admin. Failure: theater before learning / shoddy fintech (§2.3).

Scenario. Ledgerline (post-PMF fintech) vs its internal support-ops dashboard.

Example. Checkout (Prefer A): full polish budget — motion on transform/opacity only, both-theme contrast pass, AT smoke, microcopy review. Internal refund-ops tool (Prefer B): default table components, no custom motion, ships in a week — but still passes the floors (24×24 minimum targets, keyboard operability), because speed never licenses exclusion (L14 note, §3.6.5).

Why it passes. Each surface names its cell; “shoddy checkout errors in a trust market” is explicitly not the same choice as pre-PMF speed (§1.4).

Measure. Trust×frequency score decides the budget: checkout error recovery rate and payment success for the polish cell; days-to-usable ship time for the speed cell — with floor checks (keyboard operability, 24×24 targets) passing on both.

Ch 2 — T5: Disclosure vs discoverability — Example

Concept. Prefer disclosure: long-tail expert actions. Prefer discoverability: core path found without a tour. Failure: buried core action / chrome bloat (§2.3).

Scenario. Trellix issue actions.

Example. Discoverable (Prefer B): "New issue" is a persistent primary button, top-right, color.bg.accent, reachable by C shortcut — never inside a menu. Disclosed (Prefer A): "Export as CSV", "Clone with subtasks", "Move to another project" live in the ⋯ overflow and the ⌘K palette. Ladder per L8: primary → overflow → palette → settings.

Why it passes. Core action keeps scent; expert power doesn’t bloat the chrome.

Rejected. All 14 actions as toolbar buttons (chrome bloat), or “New issue” only inside ⌘K (buried core action).

Measure. First-click success on "New issue" without a tour (target >90%) plus findability of overflow actions via ⌘K usage logs — buried core action and chrome bloat each surface in one of the two numbers.

Ch 2 — T6: Growth vs trust (asymmetric) — Example

Concept. Prefer A when value is clear, trial reversible, cancel honest. There is no legitimate Prefer B for urgency theater on Locked trust paths. Failure: activation↑ trust↓ permanent (§2.3).

Scenario. Nestly pricing page proposals.

Example. Allowed (Guided surface, still obeying contrast and focus laws): labeled default "Most people choose Family — includes shared lists" where Family genuinely is the most-chosen plan (claim auditable from data); reversible trial "Try Pro free for 14 days — cancel in one tap from Settings"; cancel flow completable in ≤3 steps with no retention maze. Refused regardless of projected lift: countdown timer "Offer ends in 09:41" tied to nothing, decoy plan priced to make another look cheap, cancel link at 9px in color.text.tertiary.

Why it passes. The tension’s asymmetry is respected: honest defaults get a column; fake urgency does not.

Measure. Refuse to worsen: cancel clarity, "how do I cancel?" tickets, chargebacks (§1.5b guardrails).

Ch 2 — T7: Platform parity vs native — Example

Concept. Prefer parity: semantics, IA, tokens. Prefer native: gestures, nav chrome, materials. Failure: shrunk-web or three unrelated apps (§2.3).

Scenario. Trellix web + iOS + Android.

Example. Parity table kept in the repo:

Layer Parity? Detail
Semantic tokens, type roles Yes color.text.danger identical meaning on all three
IA / object model Yes Project → Board → Issue everywhere
Navigation chrome No iOS tab bar + swipe-back; Android predictive back; web sidebar
Destructive pattern Yes (class) Quarantine trash on all; presentation uses native sheets on mobile
Gestures No iOS swipe-to-archive; web hover actions + keyboard

Why it passes. Semantics yes, chrome no — avoids both the shrunk-desktop app and three unrelated products.

Measure. Cross-platform task-success parity on shared jobs (same IA, same undo classes must yield the same completion rates); platform-store complaints tagged “doesn’t feel native” as the counter-signal.

Ch 2 — T8: Checklist floor vs lived-experience gate — Example

Concept. Automated floor always runs; lived-experience sessions can block Locked releases even when the checklist is green. Failure: axe-green, unusable (§2.3).

Scenario. Ledgerline sign-up flow, release week.

Example. CI floor (always): axe serious=0, contrast job both themes, require-focus-visible lint. Gate: quarterly paid sessions with 5 disabled participants on auth/checkout/create. Session finding: TalkBack reads the OTP input as "edit box" with no name; participant abandons at 100% rate. Release ticket labeled blocker/lived-experience — the Eng lead cannot override it; only the Research owner (RACI, §4.2g) can close it after a re-test passes.

Why it passes. Two opposite failures prevented: shipping without floors, and shipping with floors only.

Rejected. “Axe is green, ship it” — the exact compliance theater the tension names.

Ch 2 — T9: Brand expression vs forced-colors — Example

Concept. Prefer brand: marketing illustration. Prefer system: High Contrast / forced-colors modes. Failure: broken HC or lifeless product UI (§2.3).

Scenario. Ledgerline status pills under Windows High Contrast.

Example.

/* Base theme: brand-subtle background + a transparent 1px border.
   Forced-colors mode repaints that border with a system color automatically,
   so the pill keeps a visible boundary when its background is stripped. */
.status-pill { background: var(--color-bg-success-subtle); border: 1px solid transparent; }
@media (forced-colors: active) {
  /* No forced-color-adjust opt-out: let the system strip the brand background.
     Icon + text carry the meaning, not the background. */
  .status-pill .icon { fill: CanvasText; }
}

Status always pairs icon + text ("✓ Paid"), so when forced-colors strips brand backgrounds, meaning survives (also L11) — the code deliberately does not set forced-color-adjust: none, which would preserve the brand-subtle background against system colors and risk failing contrast with CanvasText. If an opt-out is ever needed (e.g. a color-swatch chip whose color is the content), it is scoped to that single element with a stated reason. Marketing hero illustration keeps full brand color — it’s decorative, and forced-colors may flatten it without harm.

Why it passes. Brand expresses where decoration is safe; system palettes win where meaning must survive — and the code matches the prose: the background is stripped, the border and icon+text survive.

Measure. Forced-colors / Windows High Contrast smoke on status surfaces each release: 0 statuses conveyed by background alone; pill text/icon legible against Canvas/CanvasText.

Ch 2 — T10: Systemize vs leave local — Example

Concept. Prefer systemize: ≥3 real uses on a Locked surface. Prefer local: one-off experiment. Failure: shadow libraries or premature API. Implements L12 early (§2.3).

Scenario. A Trellix squad builds an inline “quick-assign” popover.

Example. First use: lives in the squad’s folder as a local recipe with a comment // local recipe — do not import cross-squad (L12). Third real use (board, issue detail, and the mobile sheet all need it, two on Locked surfaces): promotion request filed with the three usage links, a11y keyboard map, and do/don’t. Systems team promotes it to pattern, then to AssignPopover@1.0.0.

Why it passes. Three real uses + Locked surface = promote; one clever wrapper “for consistency” is named premature abstraction.

Rejected (both). Copy-pasting it into five squads’ folders (shadow library) or shipping @org/ui-popover-kit after use #1 (premature API).

Measure. Real-use count against the promotion threshold (3, ≥1 Locked); near-duplicate implementations of the same behavior found in the quarterly override review (the shadow-library indicator).

Ch 2 — T11: Brand-hero vs quiet tool — Example

Concept. Prefer brand-hero: marketing/acquisition. Prefer quiet tool: product work surfaces. Failure: pretty tool / forgettable brand (§2.3).

Scenario. Nestly homepage vs its weekly-planner screen.

Example. Homepage: full-bleed brand illustration, display type 56px, color.brand.saffron everywhere the eye lands — passes the brand test with the nav cropped. Planner: chrome desaturated to color.bg.surface and color.text.secondary; the loudest pixels are the user’s meals and grocery list; brand shows only in the 24px logo and the accent on the single primary action.

Why it passes. Both tests pass on their own surfaces instead of one look failing both (§1.3c).

Measure. Nav-cropped brand recognition rate on the homepage (brand test); chrome-saturation / squint-test audit pass on the planner (tool test) — each surface is scored by its own test’s metric.

Ch 2 — 2.4: Philosophies applied to gap-audit surfaces — Examples (a–g)

Concept. §2.4’s seven applications — philosophies are hardest to keep on settings and safety.

Scenario. Ledgerline applies each philosophy where it’s least glamorous.

Example.

  • (a) Clarity in settings: taxonomy of 7 areas (§4.7a) + in-settings search ("Search settings…" matching synonyms: “dark mode” finds Appearance › Theme) — not a flat list of fifty toggles.
  • (b) Conversation in privacy: export completes with a receipt — email subject "Your Ledgerline data export is ready", body listing "2,118 invoices, 214 contacts, 3 workspaces · link expires July 22" — never a silent HTTP 204.
  • (c) Systems in admin: one Locked DangerConfirm and one Locked ImpersonationBanner pattern used by all operator tools — no per-squad scary modals with different typed-confirm rules.
  • (d) Outcomes in help: the help panel’s success metric is return-to-job (user resumes the failed flow within 5 min), not article pageviews.
  • (e) Defaults in notifications: quiet hours default ON where timezone is known (22:00–08:00 local); weekly digest is the default class; critical interrupts reserved for safety/security per the textbook rule — plus payment failure as Ledgerline’s documented product-level decision, since a failed payment is a safety-of-funds event in a fintech — each with an in-notification "Why did I get this?" link.
  • (f) Accessibility in consent banners: the cookie banner is a proper dialog — focus moves in, Esc works, buttons "Accept all" / "Reject non-essential" are equal size and both ≥4.5:1 contrast; it never covers the page behind an untrappable overlay.
  • (g) AI contract in disclosure: generated invoice summaries carry AIProvenanceBadge ("Drafted with AI — edited by you"), and the off switch lives in Settings › AI assistance, one level deep — labeled, not buried, where policy requires it.

Why it passes. Each philosophy survives contact with its least-glamorous surface, which is the §2.4 test.

Chapter 3 — Fourteen Laws

Each law example includes the observable break so a PR can be failed against it (§3.1).

Ch 3 — L1: Roles, not hexes — Example

Concept. Product UI consumes semantic tokens only. Breaks when raw palette values appear in components or app CSS.

Scenario. Ledgerline PR adds a “past due” style to the invoice row.

Example.

/* REJECTED in review — breaks L1 */
.invoice-row--overdue { color: #B91C1C; background: #FEF2F2; }

/* MERGED */
.invoice-row--overdue {
  color: var(--color-text-danger);
  background: var(--color-bg-danger-subtle);
}

CI lint no-raw-color (§4.3g) fails the first version automatically.

Why it passes. Semantic roles survive theme switch, forced-colors mapping, and generator consumption (§1.6a).

Measure. Raw-hex count in app CSS = 0 (lint-enforced).

Ch 3 — L2: Hierarchy before paint — Example

Concept. Weight, space, and position beat color; one focus per region. Breaks when: equal card shadows everywhere; status by color alone.

Scenario. Ledgerline dashboard has six equally-shadowed cards and a red dot for “payment failed.”

Example (fix). Structure first: the “Payment failed” card moves to position 1, gets type.title (20px/600) heading and space.24 isolation; the other five drop to a flat 1px-border grid — zero shadows (also L4). Status becomes multi-channel: "⚠ Payment failed — card ending 4242" (icon + text + color.text.danger), not a lone red dot (also L11). Only one region on the page now claims focus.

Why it passes. The fix changed weight/space/position before touching color; color is now reinforcement, not the message.

Rejected. “Make the red redder” — fixing structure with accent color.

Ch 3 — L3: Type & rhythm are contracts — Example

Concept. Named roles, locked role scale, 4/8 space. Breaks when: ad-hoc px type; seven unused sizes; spacing from taste.

Scenario. Trellix type and space tokens.

Example.

{
  "type.display": { "size": "32px", "line": "40px", "weight": 700 },
  "type.title":   { "size": "20px", "line": "28px", "weight": 600 },
  "type.body":    { "size": "14px", "line": "20px", "weight": 400 },
  "type.meta":    { "size": "12px", "line": "16px", "weight": 400 },
  "type.code":    { "size": "13px", "line": "20px", "family": "mono" },
  "space": [4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48]
}

PR comment enforcing it: "font-size: 15px is outside the locked role scale — use type.body or make a scale-change proposal to Systems (L3)." Note the textbook’s own correction: this is a locked role scale, not a modular-ratio claim (Edition notes #3).

Why it passes. Roles are named (Display, Title, Body, Meta, Code per §3.3), the scale is closed, spacing snaps to 4/8.

Measure. Lint count of font-size declarations outside the locked role scale in app CSS (target 0); spacing values off the 4/8 grid (target 0); unused type roles pruned at quarterly review.

Ch 3 — L4: Elevation means modality — Example

Concept. Raise = temporary; flat = durable. Breaks when: random shadows on static panels; durable pages that look like overlays.

Scenario. Ledgerline settings page uses box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.12) on every static card “for hierarchy.”

Example (fix). Elevation map enforced: elevation.0 (flat, 1px color.border.subtle) for pages, tables, settings cards; elevation.1 (0 2px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.10)) for dropdown menus; elevation.2 (0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.16)) for modals/popovers — temporary things only. Settings cards go flat; hierarchy is rebuilt with type roles and space.24 grouping (L2/L3 do the job shadows were faking).

Why it passes. Elevation now encodes exactly one thing — modality — so a raised surface reliably means “temporary, dismissible.”

Rejected. Decorative shadow on a static settings card — the textbook’s named break.

Measure. Elevation audit: shadowed static (non-dismissible) surfaces = 0; every elevation.1+ usage maps to a temporary, dismissible surface in the component inventory.

Ch 3 — L5: Acknowledge ≤100ms — Example

Concept. Tiered latency budgets for press, work, resolve. Breaks when: silent controls; blank full-page waits with no local pending state.

Scenario. Trellix “Run automation” button triggering a 3–8s server job.

Example. Budget tiers: ack ≤100ms — button pressed state + label "Queued…" instantly, from local state, no network wait. Work — if >1s, inline progress ("Running · step 2 of 4"); the page never blanks. Resolve — result row inserted with highlight, or inline error "Automation failed at 'Notify' — Retry". Skeleton screens only for initial loads >500ms; optimistic row insert used where rollback is cheap (T3).

Why it passes. Ack, work, and resolve each have a budget and a visible state; no silent 3s gap.

Measure. p95 time-to-first-acknowledgment ≤100ms in RUM; count of interactions with no state change within 100ms = 0.

Ch 3 — L6: State is designed — Example

Concept. Empty, loading, partial, error, offline, denied, syncing are distinct designed states. Breaks when: “No data” for every gap; toast-only failure; spinner with no meaning.

Scenario. Ledgerline invoice list ships a full state matrix (see Ch 3 — 3.5 for all row-level CTAs).

Example. State matrix committed next to the component:

type ListState =
  | "never-used-empty"    // "Create your first invoice" + template CTA
  | "filtered-to-zero"    // "No invoices match · Clear filters"
  | "loading"             // skeleton rows, not a bare spinner
  | "partial"             // rows + banner "Showing 50 of 2,118 — Load more"
  | "error"               // inline "Couldn't load invoices — Retry · Contact support"
  | "offline"             // "You're offline — showing cached data from 14:02"
  | "denied"              // "You need the Billing role · Request access"
  | "syncing";            // "Syncing 3 changes…" indicator, list stays usable

PR review requires a screenshot per state before merge (design-quality OS ritual 1, §4.6).

Why it passes. Filtered-to-zero ≠ true empty; denied ≠ error; syncing ≠ loading — the distinctions §3.3 names are separately designed.

Rejected. One "No data" illustration for all of them (breaks L6, and L8 by hiding the right recovery).

Ch 3 — L7: Undo > confirm — Example

Concept. Confirm only for external irreversibility. Breaks when: confirm-on-archive; no soft delete; toast undo for team-visible destroy.

Scenario. Trellix classifies four actions (mirrors Review Q8).

Example.

Action Class UI
Archive personal draft Soft Toast "Draft archived. Undo" — 7s
Delete shared production database Hard Typed confirm: "Type 'acme-prod' to delete. 3 services depend on this database."
Send campaign to 40k recipients Hard Modal names blast radius: "This emails 40,212 people immediately and cannot be recalled."
Toggle notification digest None needed Instant apply; the toggle itself is the reversal

Why it passes. Confirm is spent only where irreversibility is external (mass mail, prod destroy); everything local gets recovery instead of a confirm tax.

Rejected. "Are you sure you want to archive?" modal (confirm-on-archive), and a 7s toast-undo as the only guard on the shared prod database (toast undo for team-visible destroy — the named break).

Ch 3 — L8: Progressive disclosure — Example

Concept. Primary → overflow → palette → settings. Breaks when: expert control dump on first run or core action buried.

Scenario. Trellix board header action design.

Example. The disclosure ladder, explicitly assigned: Primary (always visible): "New issue", view switcher. Overflow (⋯): "Export board", "Duplicate board", "Board settings". Palette (⌘K): all of the above plus 40 long-tail commands ("Toggle swimlanes", "Bulk re-estimate"), fuzzy-searchable. Settings: durable preferences (default assignee, automation rules). First-run shows exactly two controls.

Why it passes. The core action keeps maximal scent; expert power exists but doesn’t tax the first run.

Rejected (both breaks). All 40 commands as first-run toolbar icons; or "New issue" reachable only via ⌘K.

Measure. First-run task success without a tour (core action found); always-visible toolbar control count stays within budget (2 here); ⌘K adoption among daily users as the disclosure ladder’s health signal.

Ch 3 — L9: Focus is a cursor — Example

Concept. Keyboard and AT are peer paths; restore focus to trigger. Breaks when: outline: none without replacement; focus dumped on body after modal close.

Scenario. Ledgerline “Delete client” flow via keyboard.

Example.

:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring);   /* ≥2px, contrast-aware ring (§3.3) */
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

<Dialog
  onOpen={() => firstFocusableRef.current.focus()}   // trap inside while open
  onClose={() => triggerRef.current.focus()}          // restore to the ⋯ button
/>

Keyboard walkthrough in the PR: Tab reaches the row’s ⋯ (visible ring) → Enter opens menu → Delete client → dialog traps focus → Esc closes → focus returns to the ⋯ trigger, not body. Skip link "Skip to invoice list" is the first tab stop on the page.

Why it passes. DOM order, visible ring, trap-with-restore, skip link — focus behaves as a first-class cursor.

Rejected. outline: none “because the ring is ugly” with no replacement — the named break.

Measure. Keyboard task completion rate on the delete flow; count of focus-lost-to-body events after dialog close in the automated focus audit (target 0).

Ch 3 — L10: Native first, APG second — Example

Concept. Native elements beat ARIA reimplementation; APG patterns only when native is insufficient. Breaks when: fake roles without keyboard maps; div theater with ARIA lipstick.

Scenario. Trellix needs a select and a multi-token combobox.

Example. Single choice among 6 options → native <select> (or platform picker on mobile): free keyboard support, AT support, forced-colors support. Multi-token assignee combobox → native is insufficient, so the APG combobox pattern is implemented completely: role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-activedescendant, and the full keyboard map (↓ opens, ↑/↓ move, Enter selects, Esc closes and restores) — plus it ships via the adopted headless primitive rather than hand-rolled (§4.3i).

Why it passes. Native by default; APG only where native genuinely can’t do the job, and then the whole pattern, not the role attribute alone.

Rejected. <div class="select" role="listbox"> with click handlers and no keyboard map — div theater with ARIA lipstick.

Measure. AT smoke pass on the combobox’s full keyboard map (NVDA + VoiceOver); count of custom-role widgets shipped without a complete APG keyboard map (target 0, checked via the catalog’s a11yKeyboard field).

Ch 3 — L11: Multi-channel + reflow — Example

Concept. Never color alone; usable at 320px CSS width / 400% zoom. Breaks when: red-only errors; essential horizontal scroll at zoom; charts without labels/patterns.

Scenario. Ledgerline revenue chart + form errors, zoom audit.

Example. Form error: color.text.danger plus icon ⚠ plus text "Card expired — update your card" plus aria-describedby linkage — four channels. Chart: each series gets a label and a distinct line pattern (solid/dashed/dotted), with a data-table toggle "View as table". Reflow: at 320px CSS width (≈400% zoom on a 1280px viewport, WCAG 2.2 1.4.10 AA), the invoice table reflows to stacked key-value cards; only the optional chart may scroll horizontally inside its own container — no essential content does.

Why it passes. Meaning survives color-blindness, forced-colors (T9), and magnification.

Measure. CI viewport test at 320px: no horizontal scrollbar on document body on critical paths.

Ch 3 — L12: Abstract after three — Example

Concept. Recipe → pattern → component. Breaks when: one-off “shared” wrappers; prop soup; shadow libraries.

Scenario. The AssignPopover from T10, followed through the promotion path.

Example. Use 1 (recipe): local file, comment header naming it a recipe. Use 3 (pattern): written up in the pattern doc — anatomy, a11yKeyboard: "↓ open · type to filter · Enter assign · Esc close/restore", do ("use for ≤1 assignee change"), don’t ("don't use for bulk assign — use the bulk bar"). Component: AssignPopover@1.0.0 — semver, tests, Storybook, catalog entry (§4.3h). Prop review kills soup: the proposed 9 booleans (compact, dense, mini…) collapse to size: "sm" | "md".

Why it passes. Abstraction is paid for by three real uses; each promotion step adds contract (docs, a11y, versioning), not just indirection.

Rejected. SharedPopoverWrapper created at use #1 “for consistency” — the named one-off wrapper break.

Measure. Near-duplicate implementations found per quarter (shadow-library indicator); props per component (soup indicator — the 9-boolean proposal collapsed to one enum); promotion requests granted vs refused, with reasons logged.

Ch 3 — L13: Version the contract — Example

Concept. Semver tokens/APIs; deprecate with CI bans. Breaks when: silent breaking renames; eternal dual APIs; Figma drift without code SoT.

Scenario. Ledgerline renames color.text.subtle → color.text.secondary.

Example. This changes the name of a semantic role → MAJOR per the token bump rules (§4.3e): tokens@4.0.0. Ship kit: changelog entry, codemod (npx ledgerline-codemod token-rename-4), 90-day deprecation window during which the old name resolves with a build-time warning, then CI rule no-banned-import fails builds still using color.text.subtle after the sunset date (Oct 13). Figma Variables renamed the same week; the weekly drift check (§4.3d) confirms parity.

Why it passes. No silent rename, no eternal dual API (the window closes), no Figma drift (code is SoT, Figma mirrors).

Rejected. Keeping both names forever “to be safe” — eternal dual APIs are a named break.

Ch 3 — L14: Craft ∝ trust × frequency — Example

Concept. Polish money, identity, and daily paths. Breaks when: dashboard theater; shoddy checkout errors; rare admin polished before pay.

Scenario. Ledgerline sprint review discovers the mismatch.

Example. Audit finds: the admin “audit log” page (trust 3 × freq 1) received custom motion and illustrations last quarter, while checkout (5 × 4) still shows the generic error "Something went wrong" on card decline. Correction per L14: checkout errors rewritten field-honestly ("Your bank declined this card. Try another card or contact your bank — no charge was made."), latency budgets applied (L5), AT smoke added; the audit-log illustrations are left as-is but the pattern of pre-pay admin polish is flagged in the quarterly review (§4.6). Note the boundary from §3.6.5: L14 allocates craft — it does not excuse exclusion on rare paths; the audit log still meets keyboard and contrast floors.

Why it passes. Craft budget re-flows to where trust × frequency is highest; floors remain universal.

Measure. Checkout error recovery rate; support tickets tagged payment-confusion.

Ch 3 — SC1–SC7: Supporting constraints (§3.4) — Examples

Concept. Default ship gates unless a documented exception exists.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s release checklist implements each constraint.

Example.

  • SC1 Touch targets. Primary actions ≥44×44 (Apple HIG / Material craft bar). Dense table rows may not shrink hit areas below the WCAG 2.2 2.5.8 AA floor of 24×24; a 32px-tall row’s 16px icon button gets invisible hit-slop padding to 32×32 — comfortably above the 24×24 AA floor — and 44×44 where it’s a primary action: .icon-btn { position: relative; } .icon-btn::after { content:""; position:absolute; inset:-8px; } (the -8px inset adds 8px on every side of the 16px control: 16 + 8 + 8 = 32×32 hit area)
  • SC2 Reduced motion. @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .toast { transition: opacity 120ms linear; transform: none; } } — opacity/instant alternatives; shared components animate only transform/opacity in the first place (budget §4.3f).
  • SC3 Logical CSS / RTL. margin-inline-start: var(--space-16) not margin-left; the “next” chevron flips via [dir="rtl"] .chevron { transform: scaleX(-1); }; meaning is never carried by physical left/right alone.
  • SC4 Tabular figures. .money, td.numeric { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; } so $1,240.00 and $918.75 align in columns and totals don’t jitter while live-updating.
  • SC5 Media & flashing. Product-tour video ships captions + transcript; the “payment succeeded” celebration is checked against the >3 flashes/sec seizure limit (it pulses once, 400ms).
  • SC6 Auth & CAPTCHA. Visible <label> (not placeholder-only), autocomplete="email" / autocomplete="current-password" / autocomplete="one-time-code" so password managers work; passkeys and email OTP preferred over puzzle CAPTCHA; where a challenge is unavoidable, an accessible alternative (audio + server-side risk fallback) is always present.
  • SC7 Consistent Help (WCAG 3.2.6 — Level A). Help lives in a consistent slot (bottom-right ? on every Locked trust path). Published WCAG 2.2 lists 3.2.6 Consistent Help at Level A (the textbook’s §3.4 “Help Mechanisms is AAA” label predates the published numbering — flagged upstream), so consistent placement is already required inside an AA conformance claim; the craft bar — help linked from every denial and error state — goes beyond the SC. The VPAT labels levels accurately (A vs AA vs AAA).

Why it passes. Each constraint is a checkable gate with a number or a selector, not a footnote.

Ch 3 — Undo/Soft: Soft class — Example

Concept. 5–10s toast with Undo; prefer for local, reversible, frequent actions (§3.4b).

Scenario. Ledgerline “Undo send” on internal invoice notes and archive.

Example. Archive: toast "Invoice archived. Undo" — 7s window, role="status" (polite), Undo reachable by keyboard (Tab or shortcut ⌘Z while toast lives), toast queue so rapid archives stack rather than replace (§4.4d). Note dismissal, email-style "Sending in 5s… Undo" delay-send.

Why it passes. Local + reversible + frequent = Soft per the taxonomy; no confirm modal tax on a many-times-daily action.

Rejected. "Are you sure you want to archive?" modal every time — the taxonomy’s named rejected column.

Ch 3 — Undo/Quarantine: Quarantine class — Example

Concept. Trash/recycle ~30 days; prefer for recoverable destroy where regret is common (§3.4b).

Scenario. Trellix page/file delete in a shared workspace.

Example. "Delete page" → page moves to Trash immediately (no modal); banner in Trash: "Pages are permanently deleted after 30 days." Each item shows "Deleted by Maya · Jul 3 · Restore". Restore returns it to its original location with a toast "'Q3 Roadmap' restored to Product wiki." Team-visible: the trash event appears in the space’s activity feed.

Why it passes. Destroy is recoverable for the whole regret window; team-visible destruction gets more than a 7s toast — using Soft here is the taxonomy’s named rejection (“Soft toast for team-visible destroy”).

Measure. Restore rate from Trash (a high rate signals mis-scented delete affordances).

Ch 3 — Undo/Hard: Hard confirm class — Example

Concept. Modal names blast radius; typed confirm for extreme; for money, legal, mass notify, prod destroy, account erase (§3.4b).

Scenario. Meridian Bank admin deletes an organization.

Example. Modal copy names the blast radius in numbers: "Delete the 'Acme Corp' organization? This permanently erases 34 users, 12,408 records, and 3 active API keys. Integrations will stop within 60 seconds. This cannot be undone." Typed confirm: "Type acme-corp to confirm"; the destructive button ("Permanently delete organization", color.bg.danger) stays disabled until the string matches; a 5s cooldown before the button enables prevents click-through. The action is audit-logged (§4.7b).

Why it passes. External/shared irreversibility that cannot be reconstructed cheaply earns the one legitimate confirm; the blast radius is named, not implied.

Rejected. One-click delete “for speed” — the taxonomy’s named rejection.

Ch 3 — 3.5: L6 state distinctions — all six rows — Example

Concept. The gap-audit table sharpening L6: each situation gets distinct meaning and CTA (§3.5).

Scenario. Ledgerline invoice list, one string per state, side by side.

Example.

Situation Microcopy CTA
Never-used empty "No invoices yet. Most teams start from a template." "Use a template" · "Create blank invoice"
Filtered to zero "No invoices match 'status: overdue, client: Acme'." "Clear filters" (primary) · "Edit query"
True empty collection "All invoices archived. Nice and tidy." "Create invoice" · "Import CSV"
Error "Couldn't load invoices (request timed out)." "Retry" · "Contact support"
Denied "You need the Billing role to view invoices." "Request access from Maya (admin)" · link "About roles"
Offline / syncing "You're offline — showing data saved at 14:02." / "Syncing 3 changes…" queued-changes indicator · "Resolve conflict" when needed

Why it passes. Filtered-to-zero recovers via the filter, never-used recovers via creation, denied recovers via access — one "No data" string would misdirect all three recoveries (breaking L6 and L8).

Chapter 4 — Company Strategy & Design-Quality OS

Ch 4 — 4.2a: Pre-PMF / unknown problem — Example

Concept. Optimize clarity + learning speed; do not build visual theater or a mega design system (§4.2).

Scenario. A 4-person startup, “Plotline,” testing a podcast-notes product.

Example. Investments: stock headless primitives skinned with ~20 semantic tokens (one afternoon), plain type roles, instrumented critical path (sign-up → first note → share), weekly user interviews. Refused: a custom icon set, a 60-component library, motion design. Kept anyway (floors are not theater): visible labels, focus rings, 24×24 minimum targets.

Why it passes. Speed of learning is the legitimate pre-PMF optimization (§1.4); the mega design system is the named “do not.”

Ch 4 — 4.2b: Trust market — Example

Concept. Optimize polish + pessimistic patterns + a11y on money/identity paths early; no growth dark patterns on checkout (§4.2).

Scenario. Ledgerline (fintech) at seed stage.

Example. Even pre-scale, checkout ships with: pessimistic payment (T3), field-honest errors (P4), AT smoke on pay/auth, hard-confirm on refunds. The growth team’s countdown-timer proposal for checkout is refused outright per T6’s asymmetry.

Why it passes. In a trust market the “early” qualifier moves a11y and pessimism ahead of scale — shoddy checkout errors here are a spine failure, not lean speed (§1.4).

Ch 4 — 4.2c: Daily pro tool — Example

Concept. Optimize density, keyboard, latency, Cmd-K; no marketing bento inside the app (§4.2).

Scenario. Trellix core loop.

Example. 32px rows, full keyboard map (J/K move, X select, C create, ⌘K palette), latency budget p95 ack ≤100ms / route change ≤400ms, density honesty scored on the craft scorecard (§4.6b). A marketing-style bento grid proposed for the in-app home screen is rejected; the home screen stays a work queue.

Why it passes. The daily driver optimizes for the thousandth session, not the screenshot.

Ch 4 — 4.2d: Consumer viral — Example

Concept. Optimize fast experiment + honest cancel; fake urgency is not default growth (§4.2).

Scenario. Nestly growth program.

Example. Experiment velocity: weekly A/B slots on Guided surfaces (home feed layout, template ordering). Non-negotiables shipping with every test: cancel in ≤3 steps from Settings › Account, "You'll keep Pro until Aug 3" honesty, no dark-pattern retention maze. The urgency-banner experiment is allowed only when the deadline is real ("Family plan price changes July 31" — an actual price change).

Why it passes. Speed lives on Guided surfaces; trust guardrails (§1.5b) ride along with every experiment.

Ch 4 — 4.2e: Multi-brand enterprise — Example

Concept. Shared grammar + forked tokens; never forked component trees per brand (§4.2).

Scenario. Meridian Bank runs three brands: Meridian, Northbridge, Kestrel.

Example. One component tree (@meridian/ui), three semantic-token themes:

// themes/northbridge.json — only the semantic layer forks
{ "color.bg.accent": "{palette.teal.600}", "color.text.brand": "{palette.teal.800}",
  "radius.control": "2px", "type.display.family": "Northbridge Serif" }

Button behavior, focus management, undo classes, and state taxonomy are identical across brands; only the theme file differs.

Why it passes. Grammar shared, expression forked — three brands without three codebases.

Rejected. northbridge-button.tsx as a separate component tree — the named “do not,” which triples every a11y fix.

Ch 4 — 4.2f: Multi-platform — Example

Concept. Shared semantics; native chrome/gestures; no pixel-identical cross-platform fantasy (§4.2).

Scenario. Trellix web/iOS/Android — the parity table from T7 operationalized.

Example. Governance rule in the repo: any PR touching packages/semantics/* (tokens, IA, state names, undo classes) requires all three platform leads’ review; PRs in platform/ios/chrome/* need only the iOS lead. The rule encodes “semantics yes, chrome no” as code ownership.

Why it passes. The org structure enforces the tension cell instead of relying on memory.

Ch 4 — 4.2g: RACI + override rate — Example

Concept. The §4.2 RACI sketch, adjusted names, kept seams; override rate as a strategy metric with Systems-accountable remediation.

Scenario. Ledgerline adopts the RACI; then override rate spikes on CheckoutField (mirrors Review Q13).

Example. RACI as adopted: Locked primitives + tokens — A: Design Systems (Priya), R: DS + Eng; Guided surfaces — A: Product Design; A11y CI + lint — A: Eng, C: A11y specialist; Critical-path metrics — A: PM; Lived-experience sessions — A: Research; Override-rate remediation — A: Design Systems, R: Product + Systems.

Spike response (first two weeks, Systems-accountable): week 1 — query the lint telemetry: 23 of 31 overrides add a helperText slot the component lacks; interview two overriding squads. Week 2 — decide promote or fix: ship CheckoutField@2.1.0 with helperText (MINOR — adds capability), file codemod removing the 23 local patches, and post the finding in the weekly review. Overrides fall from 11% to 3%.

Why it passes. “High overrides mean the system failed the product, or the product is forking without promotion” — the accountable seam ensures shadow libraries don’t win by neglect.

Measure. Override rate per component; target <5%; trend reviewed quarterly (§4.6a ritual 4).

Ch 4 — 4.3a: Token layers — Example

Concept. Primitive → Semantic → rare Component; product imports semantic only (L1) (§4.3).

Scenario. Ledgerline token pipeline.

Example.

primitives.json    palette.blue.600: #2563EB          ← never imported by product code
semantic.json      color.bg.accent: {palette.blue.600} ← the only layer product imports
component.json     button.primary.bg: {color.bg.accent} ← rare; only where a component
                                                          must fork from the semantic default

ESLint boundary: importing from tokens/primitives in apps/* is an error.

Why it passes. The layer boundary is enforced by tooling, making L1 structural rather than aspirational.

Measure. Primitive-layer imports in apps/* (ESLint-enforced, target 0); share of product color/space values resolving through the semantic layer = 100%.

Ch 4 — 4.3b: Locked / Guided / Open partition — Example

Concept. Label Open explicitly so “exception” doesn’t become the unmarked default (§4.3).

Scenario. Trellix surface registry.

Example. A checked-in surfaces.yaml:

- surface: auth/*            tier: locked   # AuthForm pattern mandatory; lived-exp gate
- surface: checkout/*        tier: locked
- surface: settings/*        tier: guided   # system components; layout freedom
- surface: boards/*          tier: guided
- surface: labs/experiments/* tier: open    # explicitly labeled; may use local recipes,
                                            # still passes automated a11y floor

CI reads the registry: a raw-color lint failure is blocking on locked/guided, warning-only on open.

Why it passes. Open is a named tier with a boundary, not the silent default every exception drifts into.

Measure. Routes registered in surfaces.yaml = 100%; unregistered (“drifted”) surfaces discovered per quarter = 0; lint-block rate by tier reviewed for tier misassignment.

Ch 4 — 4.3c: Promotion path — Example
