Concept. Local recipe → documented pattern (a11y + do/don’t) → versioned component (§4.3).

Scenario. AssignPopover (continuing T10/L12) — the artifact at each stage.

Example. Stage gates checklist used by Systems:

  1. Recipe → Pattern requires: 3 real uses linked; ≥1 on a Locked surface; written anatomy; a11yKeyboard map; one do and one don’t with screenshots.
  2. Pattern → Component requires: semver package; unit + interaction tests (incl. focus restore); Storybook stories for every L6-relevant state; catalog entry (§4.3h); named owner.

Refusal example (mirrors Review Q22): a squad requests promotion after 2 uses, both on Open surfaces — refused with "Re-apply at 3 uses incl. one Locked (L12)."

Why it passes. Each arrow adds contract; refusal criteria are as explicit as acceptance criteria.

Measure. Promotion-gate pass/refusal log with reasons; post-promotion override rate on the new component (<5% target, §4.2g) — a high rate means the pattern was promoted with the wrong contract.

Ch 4 — 4.3d: Source of truth + drift check — Example

Concept. Code is SoT for product; Figma Variables mirror token names; weekly drift check on renames (§4.3).

Scenario. Ledgerline design-eng sync.

Example. Monday CI job diffs semantic.json against the Figma Variables export via API; output posted to #design-systems: "DRIFT: figma has color.text.subtle (renamed in code to color.text.secondary in tokens@4.0.0). 2 files reference the stale name." Figma is updated the same week; the drift report must be empty before the next token release.

Why it passes. Drift is detected mechanically weekly, so Figma remains a mirror rather than a competing source of truth (also L13’s “Figma drift without code SoT” break).

Measure. Weekly drift-report row count (must be 0 before each token release); stale token names still referenced in Figma files at release time.

Ch 4 — 4.3e: Semver SLA + token bump rules — Example

Concept. MAJOR = rename/remove/change meaning of a semantic role; MINOR = add role/alias; PATCH = primitive ramp tweak behind same semantic (visual diff required); ~90-day deprecation; codemods; CI bans after sunset (§4.3).

Scenario. Three real changes classified.

Example.

Change Bump Kit
Rename color.text.subtle → color.text.secondary MAJOR (4.0.0) codemod + 90-day window + no-banned-import after Oct 13
Add color.bg.warning-subtle MINOR (4.1.0) changelog only
Darken palette.blue.600 #2563EB → #1D4ED8 behind unchanged color.bg.accent PATCH (4.1.1) visual diff required — Chromatic run attached; contrast re-checked (5.2:1 → 6.7:1 on white)

Why it passes. Every consumer can predict breakage from the version number alone; the PATCH rule’s visual-diff requirement catches “harmless” ramp tweaks that break contrast.

Ch 4 — 4.3f: Budgets — Example

Concept. Example budgets: core kit JS ≤150KB gzip incremental; no raw hex/px in app CSS; motion in shared components via transform/opacity only (§4.3).

Scenario. Ledgerline CI budget job.

Example. budgets.config.js enforced on every PR: { coreKitGzipKB: 150 } — a PR adding a 40KB date-picker dependency to the core kit fails with "core kit 178KB > 150KB budget: lazy-load or slim the dep"; stylelint rules reject #-hex and rogue px type sizes in apps/**/*.css; a lint scans shared-component keyframes for animated properties outside transform/opacity (e.g. animating box-shadow fails — repaint cost and reduced-motion hazard).

Why it passes. Budgets are numbers wired to CI, so the argument happens at PR time, not in a retro.

Measure. Core-kit gzip size vs the 150KB budget on every PR; budget-failing PRs merged = 0; keyframe-property violations caught pre-merge rather than in a perf retro.

Ch 4 — 4.3g: Lint catalog — Example

Concept. no-raw-color, no-synonym-variant, no-unlabeled-icon-button, no-banned-import, require-focus-visible (§4.3).

Scenario. One PR trips three rules.

Example. CI annotations on a Trellix PR:

✖ no-raw-color            Line 41: '#EF4444' — use var(--color-text-danger) (L1)
✖ no-unlabeled-icon-button Line 88: <IconButton icon="trash"> lacks aria-label (L9/L10)
✖ no-synonym-variant      Line 102: variant="main" — canonical is variant="primary" (§1.6)
✔ no-banned-import         clean
✔ require-focus-visible    clean

Why it passes. Each rule mechanizes a law: the catalog is the laws compiled to CI.

Measure. Violations per rule per week (trend must fall after adoption); % of UI PRs passing the lint catalog on first push.

Ch 4 — 4.3h: Catalog schema — Example

Concept. Minimum { id, name, props[], tokens[], a11yKeyboard, do, dont, status } for humans and codegen (§4.3).

Scenario. The AssignPopover catalog entry consumed by docs and the codegen agent.

Example.

{
  "id": "assign-popover",
  "name": "AssignPopover",
  "props": [{ "name": "size", "type": "\"sm\" | \"md\"", "default": "md" },
            { "name": "onAssign", "type": "(userId: string) => void" }],
  "tokens": ["color.bg.surface-raised", "elevation.2", "space.8", "focus.ring"],
  "a11yKeyboard": "ArrowDown opens; type to filter; Enter assigns; Esc closes and restores focus to trigger",
  "do": "Use for changing a single assignee inline.",
  "dont": "Don't use for bulk assignment — use the selection bulk bar.",
  "status": "stable"
}

Why it passes. One machine-readable record serves human docs, review checklists, and the generator’s context (P7) — the same contract for both audiences.

Measure. Catalog coverage: % of shipped components with a complete entry including a11yKeyboard (target 100%); generator dry-run misuse count against the schema (the P7 audit’s 61 → 0).

Ch 4 — 4.3i: Adopt vs build — Example

Concept. Prefer battle-tested behavior primitives (e.g. Radix, React Aria); skin with tokens. Build when the contract is missing; don’t wrap once “for consistency” (§4.3).

Scenario. Trellix needs a dialog and a Gantt-style dependency editor.

Example. Dialog → adopt: Radix Dialog (focus trap, restore, Esc, aria-modal proven), skinned with elevation.2, color.bg.surface-raised, radius.control. Dependency-drag Gantt editor → build: no battle-tested primitive carries that contract; it’s built in-house with an APG-informed keyboard map and enters the promotion path as a recipe. Refused: OurDialog that wraps Radix Dialog 1:1 adding only a renamed prop — a wrap-once-for-consistency with negative value.

Why it passes. Behavior risk is delegated where the ecosystem has solved it; invention is spent only where the contract is genuinely missing (also L12).

Measure. Behavior-bug count in adopted vs built primitives (focus, keyboard, AT regressions); wrapper components that add no contract (target 0, flagged in review).

Ch 4 — 4.4a: Feedback loop — Example

Concept. Trigger → acknowledge → work → resolve → undo (§4.4).

Scenario. Trellix bulk “Move 18 issues to Sprint 12.”

Example. Trigger: bulk bar button "Move to…". Acknowledge: ≤100ms — bar swaps to "Moving 18 issues…" (L5). Work: inline progress "12 of 18 moved"; list rows gray-and-relocate optimistically (cheap rollback, T3). Resolve: "18 issues moved to Sprint 12." Undo: the same toast carries "Undo" (Soft, 8s) — the loop’s last stop is built in, not bolted on.

Why it passes. All five stages present and visibly distinct — the company-level loop is checkable per interaction.

Measure. p95 acknowledgment ≤100ms in RUM; % of bulk actions resolving with a visible undo affordance = 100%; undo-after-bulk usage rate (a mis-scent indicator when high).

Ch 4 — 4.4b: Dual device models — Example

Concept. Not shrunk desktop; native nav and gestures where the platform demands (parity: semantics yes, chrome no) (§4.4).

Scenario. Ledgerline mobile invoice review.

Example. Mobile is re-modeled, not shrunk: the 9-column desktop table becomes a card list (client, amount in tabular figures, status pill); row actions become an iOS swipe (swipe left → "Archive", Soft undo) and a bottom sheet, matching platform muscle memory; navigation is a native tab bar, not the desktop sidebar squeezed to 320px. Semantics identical: same status names, same undo classes, same color.text.danger meaning.

Why it passes. The parity table splits exactly as §4.4 demands — the product is one language (P3) in two native dialects.

Measure. Mobile vs desktop task-success parity on invoice review; app-store complaints tagged “feels like a website” as the shrunk-desktop signal.

Ch 4 — 4.4c: Offline + conflict prefer-when — Example

Concept. Sync indicator required. Conflicts: keep both (equal peer edits) / choose (one clearly stale) / merge (structured fields) (§4.4).

Scenario. Trellix offline edits collide on reconnect.

Example. Persistent indicator: "Offline — 3 changes queued" → "Syncing…" → "All changes saved." Conflict routing:

  • Two teammates edited the same issue description offline (equal peer edits) → keep both: "Maya's version" / "Your version" saved side-by-side with a compare view — nothing silently lost.
  • Your cached edit is 3 days old; the field changed twice since (clearly stale) → choose: "This field changed since you went offline. Keep server version · Keep mine (from Jul 12)."
  • Both edited different structured fields (you: due date; Maya: assignee) → merge silently; the activity log records both.

Why it passes. The prefer-when picks the resolution class by data shape and staleness instead of one lossy global rule.

Measure. Silent-overwrite incidents = 0; conflict-resolution completion rate; support tickets tagged lost-my-edit (must trend to zero after shipping the routing).

Ch 4 — 4.4d: Interruptions — Example

Concept. One modal at a time; toasts queue; never steal focus from typing unless assertive error (§4.4).

Scenario. Ledgerline: a session-expiry warning fires while the user types a client note and two toasts are pending.

Example. Toast queue: "Invoice sent" shows, "Export ready" waits its turn — no stacking chaos, no replacement loss. The session warning is not an assertive emergency yet: it renders as a non-focus-stealing banner "Session expires in 5:00 — Stay signed in"; the user’s caret never leaves the note field. Only at hard expiry does an assertive modal appear — and it’s the only modal (a pending “new feature” modal is suppressed by the one-modal rule). The note draft is preserved through re-auth.

Why it passes. Focus theft is reserved for the one genuinely assertive case; everything else waits in line.

Rejected. The feature-announcement modal opening on top of the expiry modal — two modals is the named break.

Measure. Focus-steal events while typing (target 0 outside assertive errors); toasts dropped instead of queued = 0; draft loss through re-auth = 0.

Ch 4 — 4.4e: Permissions just-in-time — Example

Concept. Ask at intent; denial explains, links to settings, offers a degraded path — not a dead end (§4.4).

Scenario. Nestly asks for camera access to scan a grocery receipt.

Example. No launch-time permission blitz. When the user taps "Scan receipt", a pre-prompt explains value first: "Nestly uses your camera only while scanning receipts — nothing is stored." → OS prompt. On denial, the screen shows: "Camera access is off. You can type items instead, or enable the camera in Settings." with "Type items manually" (degraded path, primary) and "Open Settings" (deep link).

Why it passes. Intent-timed ask, explained denial, settings link, and a working degraded path — all four §4.4 requirements; also L6’s denied state done properly.

Measure. Camera grant rate at intent (vs launch-blitz baseline); % of denials that continue via "Type items manually" rather than abandoning the task.

Ch 4 — 4.4f: AI interaction strategy — Example

Concept. Stream + cancel; citations; tool side-effects need approval; diff → apply → undo; track reject/override as trust metrics (§4.4).

Scenario. Trellix agent triages 40 stale issues.

Example. Proposal streams as it computes ("Analyzed 24 of 40…", "Stop" button live); each recommendation cites its evidence ("No activity for 94 days; assignee left the org (directory)"); the plan renders as a diff — 31 close, 6 reassign, 3 skip — with per-row checkboxes. The step "email the 6 new assignees" is fenced behind an explicit approval card. Apply → Soft toast "37 issues updated. Undo" (10s) + activity-log batch entry. Dashboards track accept and reject and post-apply override rates; a rising override rate pages the AI team as a trust regression, not a tuning curiosity.

Why it passes. Every §4.4 AI clause is a visible mechanism; the metric set prevents accept-rate-only optimization (§1.6b).

Ch 4 — 4.5a: A11y in primitives + release gates — Example

Concept. Contrast-gated tokens, focus rings, labeled APIs, APG maps in primitives; release-blocking gates on critical paths (§4.5).

Scenario. Ledgerline primitive-level inclusion + the checkout release gate.

Example. Primitives: token build fails if any color.text.*-on-color.bg.* documented pair drops below 4.5:1 (1.4.3 AA) in either theme; Button requires a label (children or aria-label — type error otherwise); focus.ring ships in every interactive primitive; APG maps live in the catalog (§4.3h). Release gate on checkout: keyboard-only task pass, axe serious=0, both-theme contrast job, focus-visible audit, NVDA smoke on pay — any red blocks the train.

Why it passes. Inclusion is a property of primitives plus a blocking gate — not a late audit (§1.4 negation 5).

Measure. Gate pass rate per release; regressions caught pre-merge vs post-release.

Ch 4 — 4.5b: AT matrix + legal floor — Example

Concept. VoiceOver+Safari; NVDA+Chrome/Firefox; TalkBack+Chrome; JAWS for enterprise; Voice Control once on mobile core. Legal floor: WCAG 2.2 AA; EAA/ADA/508 by market; VPAT/ACR when enterprise sells (§4.5).

Scenario. Meridian Bank’s compliance-and-testing grid.

Example. Test rota per release: NVDA+Chrome and NVDA+Firefox (primary pairings per the §4.5 matrix, every release), VoiceOver+Safari (every release, macOS+iOS), TalkBack+Chrome (mobile releases), JAWS (quarterly — enterprise deals require it), Voice Control (once on the mobile core flows, re-run on nav changes). Legal mapping: EU customers → EAA; US → ADA; government contracts → Section 508 with a current VPAT/ACR produced from the audit, claims labeled honestly at AA (3.2.6 Consistent Help is Level A and therefore part of the AA claim itself; genuinely AAA criteria such as 3.3.9 are noted only where actually met, per SC7).

Why it passes. Coverage is a scheduled matrix, and the conformance claim matches what was tested — no AAA inflation.

Ch 4 — 4.5c: Lived-experience program — Example

Concept. Paid sessions on critical paths each quarter; findings can block ship on Locked surfaces (§4.5, T8).

Scenario. Ledgerline Q3 program.

Example. Q3 plan: 6 paid participants (2 screen-reader, 1 switch access, 1 low-vision/zoom, 1 motor/tremor, 1 cognitive) × 3 Locked paths (auth, checkout, create-invoice); compensation at professional consulting rates; findings triaged in the weekly failure-path review with a blocker/lived-experience label whose closure authority sits with Research (RACI). Q3 outcome: 2 blockers (OTP field name; zoom reflow break at 320px on the plan-picker), both fixed before release.

Why it passes. “Nothing about us without us” is budgeted, scheduled, and wired to blocking power — not a goodwill gesture.

Ch 4 — 4.6a: Design-quality OS rituals — Example

Concept. (1) PR critique checklist; (2) weekly failure-path review with ~5 replays; (3) release gates; (4) quarterly usability + override review with promote/fix/delete verdicts (§4.6).

Scenario. Trellix runs all four rituals; one artifact each.

Example.

  1. PR critique checklist (pasted in every UI PR): hierarchy ✅ · state matrix (7 states) ✅ · undo class named: Soft ✅ · focus/AT: restore verified ✅ · contrast/reflow: both themes, 320px ✅ · tokens only (no raw hex) ✅ · growth/trust: n/a (not a Locked path) ✅.
  2. Weekly failure-path review (Thursdays, 45 min): screenshots of empty/error/denied/offline on one flow + 5 session replays of failures. This week’s find: 38% of "filtered to zero" sessions end in abandonment because "Clear filters" sits below the fold — moved into the empty-state body.
  3. Release gates: the §4.5a automated floors + manual/AT smoke on critical paths; a red gate stops the train without debate.
  4. Quarterly review: override dashboard + usability findings → each UI bet gets a verdict: promote (AssignPopover → component), fix (CheckoutField + helperText), or delete (the “insights” dashboard tiles — scored 2/5 vs rivals on opinionated defaults and used by 4% weekly — killed).

Why it passes. The rituals make L14 and inclusion recurrent and boring — no heroics required.

Ch 4 — 4.6b: Competitive craft scorecard — Example

Concept. Score 1–5 vs top rivals: trust-path quality · density honesty · opinionated defaults · undo honesty · checkout a11y · scent of core action (§4.6).

Scenario. Trellix vs rivals “Kanbanly” and “Sprintbase” (mirrors Review Q14).

Example.

Dimension Trellix Kanbanly Sprintbase Verdict
Trust-path quality 3 4 3 fix: billing-change flow silent on failure
Density honesty 5 2 3 ship: our triage density is the moat — market it
Opinionated defaults 4 3 2 hold
Undo honesty 4 2 4 hold
Checkout a11y 3 3 5 fix: Sprintbase beats us; gate next release
Scent of core action 4 5 3 fix: “New issue” hidden on mobile

One ship (density as differentiator), one kill decided in the same review (dashboard tiles, per 4.6a).

Why it passes. Craft debates become a scored comparison with named ship/kill outcomes — evidence, not logo worship.

Ch 4 — 4.7a: Settings IA — Example

Concept. Taxonomy beats a scroll of toggles; the seven-area starter map; in-settings search; deep links from denial states (§4.7).

Scenario. Ledgerline settings, full IA.

Example.

Settings
├─ Account          — name, email, password/passkeys, active sessions ("MacBook · Berlin ·
│                     now — Sign out"), 2FA. Security indicators here AND in-session.
├─ Workspace        — members, roles, billing entry point (admin depth lives in the
│                     admin console, not here — separation per §4.7b)
├─ Notifications    — per-class controls (see 4.7g), quiet hours, digest cadence
├─ Privacy & data   — consent, "Export my data", "Delete account" (hard delete,
│                     clearly ≠ trash), connected apps with per-scope revoke
├─ Appearance       — theme (Light/Dark/System), density (Comfortable/Compact —
│                     implemented as token maps: row 44px → 32px, space.16 → space.8),
│                     language
├─ AI assistance    — disclosure preferences, assist defaults on/off,
│                     "Use my data to improve models" (off by default where applicable)
└─ Advanced         — long-tail expert controls (L8 disclosure)

In-settings search with synonyms ("dark mode" → Appearance › Theme; "stop emails" → Notifications). Deep link honored from denial states: the notification-denied banner’s "Open notification settings" lands directly on the right pane.

Why it passes. Clear taxonomy (P-applied 2.4a), density as token maps not one-off CSS, hard-delete separated from soft-delete, AI assistance a first-class area — every §4.7 note implemented.

Rejected. AI disclosure and data export buried under “Advanced” — they carry legal and trust weight and must be findable (Review Q15’s trap).

Measure. Settings task success (e.g. “turn off marketing email” found in <30s); in-settings zero-result search rate; support tickets asking where a setting lives.

Ch 4 — 4.7b: Admin / operator consoles — Example

Concept. Scoped mass actions with blast-radius copy + hard confirm (L7); readable/exportable audit logs; impersonation obvious, time-boxed, logged; separation from end-user surfaces (§4.7).

Scenario. Ledgerline support-ops console; impersonation design (mirrors Review Q16).

Example. Mass action: "Suspend 214 accounts matching 'chargeback > 2'? They lose access immediately and receive the suspension email. Type SUSPEND to continue." — scoped by an explicit filter chip row the operator can inspect, Hard confirm. Audit log: human-readable rows ("14:22 · j.chen suspended acct #88231 · reason: chargeback policy · via bulk action"), filterable, "Export CSV". Impersonation: full-width persistent banner in color.bg.warning: "Viewing as maya@acme.example — expires in 28:41 · End session" — visible in every view while active, auto-expires at 30 min, every action double-logged (operator + impersonated context). Separation: the console is a separate app shell; its density and mass-action affordances never leak into consumer IA. Per L14: less visual polish than checkout is acceptable here — but not less inclusion (operators with disabilities complete these tasks), and never silent irreversibility.

Why it passes. All four §4.7 admin requirements plus the L14 boundary condition are concrete and checkable.

Ch 4 — 4.7c: Privacy, consent, data rights — Example

Concept. Minimize consent theater; preference centers as findable as upgrade paths; export/deletion as hard workflows with receipts and legally-required delays; revocable connected apps (§4.7).

Scenario. Ledgerline data-rights suite (distinguishes trash vs account deletion vs OAuth revoke — Review Q17).

Example. Consent: asked at the moment of need in plain language ("Allow Ledgerline to read your bank feed? Used only to match transactions to invoices.") — no “accept all” maze; reject is one equal-weight click. Preference center: reachable in 2 clicks from the account menu — the same depth as "Upgrade" (growth-vs-trust parity made literal). Export: request → "We're preparing your export — usually under 10 minutes" → receipt email with contents summary and 7-day link (2.4b). Account deletion: not the trash pattern — identity re-auth, consequence list ("Erases 2,118 invoices and cancels your subscription"), typed confirm (Hard class per §3.4b: account erase), then honest delay copy where law requires: "Deletion begins now and completes within 30 days as required; you'll get a confirmation email." Connected apps: each OAuth grant lists scopes in plain words ("Zapier — can read invoices, cannot send them") with one-click "Revoke" (no support archaeology); revoke is instant and confirmed with a receipt toast — its own class: immediate, no quarantine, because continued access is the harm.

Why it passes. Three deliberately different irreversibility designs: Quarantine for content trash, Hard for account erase, instant-revoke for grants — matched to blast radius, with receipts throughout.

Measure. Export/deletion completion without a support contact; receipt delivery = 100%; time-to-revoke a connected app (one click, no ticket); preference-center findability at parity with the upgrade path (click depth ≤ upgrade’s).

Ch 4 — 4.7d: Trust and safety — Example

Concept. Report, block, mute, appeal as product flows: clear categories/consequences, receipt confirmation, honored timelines, non-void appeals, temporary-vs-permanent enforcement messaging (§4.7).

Scenario. Nestly community recipe comments.

Example. Report: categorized picker ("Spam · Harassment · Dangerous food advice · Other") with consequence preview ("Our team reviews reports; repeated violations can lead to removal"); receipt: "Thanks — report #4821 received. We review most reports within 48 hours." and a status page for the reporter. Block/mute: block is immediate and bidirectional ("You won't see Dana's content, and they can't contact you"); mute is the lighter tool ("You'll stop seeing Dana's comments — they won't know"). Enforcement messaging to the reported user distinguishes classes: "Your commenting is paused for 7 days" (temporary, with the specific rule cited and the end date) vs "Your account is permanently closed for repeated harassment — you can appeal within 30 days." Appeal: a real form with a tracked case number and a committed reply window — not a void mailbox.

Why it passes. Safety is treated as a critical path for people being harmed — every §4.7 requirement is a flow with states, receipts, and honest copy, not a legal footer.

Measure. Report-to-receipt time; % of appeals answered within the committed window = 100%; post-block contact from the blocked party = 0 (block is bidirectional); reporter status-page usage as a receipt-clarity signal.

Ch 4 — 4.7e: Help mechanisms — Example

Concept. Contextual links from errors/denials; plain language with GOV.UK Error-Summary instinct; search that admits zero results; in-product curricula over carousels (§4.7).

Scenario. Ledgerline bank-connection failure.

Example. The error state links help contextually: "Couldn't connect to your bank (error BC-14). Fix connection issues" — the link opens a panel over the flow (job preserved), not a new tab into a KB home page. The article is GOV.UK-plain: 4 short steps, sentence length ≤20 words, starting "1. Check your bank hasn't asked you to re-approve Ledgerline." Form failures use an Error Summary at top: "There are 2 problems: · Account number must be 8 digits · Sort code is missing" — each item an anchor to its field. Help search admits defeat honestly: "No articles match 'BC-14 timeout'. Contact support (replies ~2h) · Check system status." Onboarding remains the identity→artifact→share→return-cue curriculum (1.5c), not a carousel.

Why it passes. Success is defined as return-to-job (2.4d), the AAA-labeled Help Mechanisms mindset (SC7) ships as craft on Locked paths, and dead ends are designed out.

Measure. Return-to-job within 5 minutes of a help view; zero-result search rate.

Ch 4 — 4.7f: AI disclosure & provenance — three layers — Example

Concept. (1) Mutation control: propose → review → undo; (2) Disclosure: user knows when model-assisted; (3) Provenance/watermarking where required. Reject/override are trust metrics; agents never email/charge/change permissions without approval (§4.7).

Scenario. Ledgerline’s AI-drafted payment-reminder emails.

Example. Layer 1 — mutation control: the AI drafts, the user reviews a diff against their last manual reminder, applies, and gets Soft undo (the 1.6b loop). Layer 2 — disclosure: the composer shows "Drafted with AI" chip; after the user edits, it updates honestly to "Drafted with AI — edited by you". The recipient-facing footer, where workspace policy requires it: "Parts of this message were generated with AI assistance." Layer 3 — provenance: outbound content embeds C2PA-style machine-readable provenance metadata where the market requires signals — without theater (no giant watermark defacing an invoice). Hard line: the agent may stage the reminder but the send — an email to a customer — always requires explicit approval: "Ready to send to 12 clients — Review & send." Dashboards track reject/override rates alongside accept rate.

Why it passes. The three layers are kept distinct (provenance ≠ mutation control, per the settings note in §4.7a), disclosure is honest without burying the off switch, and the side-effect rule is absolute.

Measure. Reject and override rates tracked alongside accept rate (a rising override rate is a trust regression, §4.4f); unapproved side-effect executions = 0; disclosure-label accuracy audited (edited drafts must show the edited variant).

Ch 4 — 4.7g: Notification classes — all four — Example

Concept. Critical interrupt / batched digest / muteable / quiet hours; lifecycle mail must not hijack marketing patterns; security alerts distinct; preference centers are operable UI (§4.7). (Mirrors Review Q18.)

Scenario. Ledgerline classifies four real notifications.

Example.

Notification Class Behavior & prefs
New sign-in from unrecognized device Critical interrupt Breaks through quiet hours; push + email; "Why did I get this? Security alerts can't be fully disabled, but you can change channels." — hard to disable (safety), still explainable
Weekly product tips Muteable One-click "Turn off tips" in the email footer that actually works — honest unsubscribe
"Your export is ready" Batched digest (class default) — delivered immediately as a documented product-level exception within the class, because the user is actively waiting on it Exception recorded in the notification spec; cadence prefs don’t apply to it; never marketing-dressed
Marketing newsletter Muteable Separate consent; unsubscribe ≤2 clicks
Activity roundup (mentions, payments received) Batched digest Default class for non-critical; cadence selectable "Daily · Weekly · Off"
Quiet hours applied to all non-critical Default ON 22:00–08:00 where timezone known; critical interrupts exempt

Lifecycle honesty: the "Trial ends in 3 days" email uses the transactional template (plain, no promo hero image) — it must not hijack marketing patterns; the security alert keeps a visually distinct scent (shield glyph, color.text.danger accent, no CTA buttons besides "Review activity"). The email preference center is real UI: labeled checkboxes, visible focus, changes confirmed with "Saved — takes effect immediately."

Why it passes. Every notification maps to one of the textbook’s four classes (Critical interrupt / Batched digest / Muteable / Quiet hours) with its prescribed behavior and prefs — immediate delivery of the export notice is an exception inside the digest class, not a fifth class; the two named integrity rules (lifecycle ≠ marketing; security stays distinct) are visible in the artifacts.

Measure. Opt-out rate per class; spam-complaint rate; quiet-hours breakthrough count (non-critical breakthroughs target 0).

Ch 4 — 4.8: Visual strategy posture — Example

Concept. Quiet chrome/loud content; type specimens in the system; icon grid + metaphor glossary; label primary nav until learnability proven; viz = position/length first, color with labels, patterns for a11y; marketing full-bleed stays out of product (§4.8).

Scenario. Ledgerline’s one-page visual posture doc, each line enforced somewhere.

Example.

  • Quiet chrome / loud content: chrome saturation capped (chrome uses only color.bg.surface/color.text.secondary); enforced by the squint heuristic in PR review (1.3b).
  • Type specimens live in the system: the locked role scale (L3) renders as a Storybook specimen page — the source of truth designers link to, not a slide.
  • Icon grid + metaphor glossary: 24px grid, 2px stroke; glossary entries prevent drift — "trash = Quarantine delete only; never use trash for Soft archive — archive uses the box icon."
  • Label primary nav: sidebar icons ship with text labels ("Invoices · Clients · Reports"); icon-only mode is unlocked only after learnability data (>90% first-click success) proves it — until then, labels stay.
  • Data viz: revenue comparison uses a bar chart (position/length — the strongest channels) before any pie; series are colored and labeled inline; print/colorblind fallback uses fill patterns (L11).
  • Brand-hero stays out: the marketing team’s full-bleed gradient hero is welcome on ledgerline.example; the lint-guarded product shell cannot import marketing/* assets behind dense data (T11).

Why it passes. Posture is stated as enforceable rules with owners and gates — visual strategy as operations, not taste.

End of Part I Foundations examples companion.

Modern UI — Part II Companion Examples: Visual Systems (Chapters 5–9)

Purpose. This document is the official examples companion for Part II — Visual Systems of Modern UI (Chapters 5–9). Every major concept, law, tension, table row-group, taxonomy, and pattern in Chapters 5–9 gets at least one concrete, auditable example: a realistic product scenario, real microcopy in quotes, real code (CSS/HTML/JSON/TS pseudo-API), real numbers (px, ms, ratios), and named tokens in the textbook’s own naming style. Headings mirror the textbook’s numbering so coverage can be checked line-by-line against the source. Laws are cited as L1–L14, WCAG floors carry their exact SC numbers and AA/AAA labels, touch targets follow the textbook’s 44×44 craft bar / 24×24 WCAG 2.5.8 AA floor convention, and cross-domain examples (law + token + WCAG SC in one decision) are marked [Cross-domain].

Coverage index

Chapter 5 — Type, Space, Hierarchy

Ch 5 §5.1-A: Hierarchy before paint — weight/space/position beats color (L2)

Concept. Hierarchy is encoded first by weight, size, position, and space—then color (5.1 prefer-when rows 1–2; L2 Hierarchy before paint).

Scenario. “Ledgerline,” a B2B invoicing tool, has an Invoices table where overdue rows were shipped as red text on red-tinted rows. Support tickets: colorblind users can’t find overdue invoices; every row with any status tint reads as equally urgent.

Example. Redesign of the status column:

  • Overdue row: status pill "Overdue 12 days" set in Meta (14px / 500), icon alert-triangle at 16px, pill background danger-subtle, text fg-on-danger-subtle. The row itself stays surface — no row-wide tint.
  • Paid row: pill "Paid" with check icon, success-subtle.
  • The primary visual differentiator is position (fixed status column, third from left) and weight (invoice number column in Body 16/600; everything else 400/500). Color is the last channel, and it is never alone — text + icon always accompany it (L11 multi-channel).

Why it passes. One focal point per region: the eye lands on the bold invoice number column, then scans the fixed status column. Status survives grayscale because the words "Overdue 12 days" carry the meaning; color merely reinforces. This is the 5.1 table row “Weight / space / position → Product UI, dense tools, status in tables.”

Rejected. The named failure mode from the prefer-when table: color-only status (red text with no label/icon) and equal card shadows (wrapping every table section in an identical elevated card so nothing steps down).

Measure. Print the table grayscale; overdue rows must still be findable in <5s in a usability pass.

Ch 5 §5.1-B: Air + Display for first-run vs Density + Body/Meta for the daily driver

Concept. 5.1 prefer-when rows 3–4: Air + Display type for first-run/empty/marketing hero; Density + Body/Meta for daily-driver lists. Managed tension: density vs air.

Scenario. “Relay,” a support-ticket tool. The first-run empty inbox and the working inbox of an agent handling 300 tickets/day.

Example.
- First-run empty state: centered block, max-width 480px, space-7 (48px) above and below. Headline in Title (22/600): "No conversations yet". One sentence in Body: "Connect your support address and new tickets will land here." One primary button: "Connect email". Small spot illustration above, alt="".
- Working inbox: dense list rows at 36px height (compact mode), Body 16 for subject, Meta 14 muted for "Sarah K. · 2h ago · #4812". Zero decorative padding beyond space-3 row padding.

Why it passes. Each surface gets the treatment its job demands; the failure named in the table — “middling padding everywhere” — is avoided by committing fully to air on first-run and density on the daily path. Note the empty state uses Title, not Display: Display (32) is reserved for marketing/brand hero per the 5.2 scale.

Rejected. “Marketing bento inside the app”: shipping the working inbox as a grid of airy cards with 32px padding each, which caps the agent at ~6 visible tickets instead of ~20.

Ch 5 §5.2-A: Locked role scale — the five roles as tokens

Concept. 5.2 locked type scale: Display/Title/Body/Meta/Code with exact size, weight, line-height, letter-spacing. Contract rule 1: named roles only, never raw font-size in app CSS (L3 Type & rhythm are contracts).

Scenario. Ledgerline’s design system publishes the type roles as tokens consumed by components.

Example.

{
  "type": {
    "display": { "size": "32px", "weight": 700, "lineHeight": 1.15, "tracking": "-0.02em" },
    "title":   { "size": "22px", "weight": 600, "lineHeight": 1.25, "tracking": "-0.01em" },
    "body":    { "size": "16px", "weight": 400, "lineHeight": 1.5,  "tracking": "0" },
    "meta":    { "size": "14px", "weight": 500, "lineHeight": 1.35, "tracking": "0.01em" },
    "code":    { "size": "14px", "weight": 400, "lineHeight": 1.4,  "tracking": "0", "family": "mono", "numeric": "tabular-nums" }
  }
}

// Component API — role, not px:
<Text role="title">Invoices</Text>
<Text role="meta" tone="muted">Last synced 4 min ago</Text>
// Lint rule `no-raw-type` fails: style={{ fontSize: 18 }}

Why it passes. Components say text.style = title; no app CSS carries font-size: 18px. The scale is a locked role scale — a practical contract, not a false claim that every step equals ratio 1.125 (edition note 3).

Rejected. The review-question anti-pattern: a squad adds font-size: 18px because “Title feels too loud, Body feels weak.” The correct fix is hierarchy by weight and space — keep the widget title at Body 16 but weight 600 with space-2 below it — not a sixth size.

Measure. Ch 5 measure line: “no ad-hoc px in product” — grep/lint count of raw font-size declarations in app code must be 0.

Ch 5 §5.2-B: Contract rules 2–3 — no speculative sizes; brand pairing over default stacks

Concept. 5.2 contract rules: don’t ship seven unused intermediate sizes “for flexibility”; pair one distinctive display face with one readable UI sans; avoid default Inter/Roboto/Arial stacks as the brand voice.

Scenario. “Fieldnote,” a research-notes product, is rebranding. The old system shipped text-xs through text-7xl (11 sizes); telemetry shows 6 were never used.

Example. New pairing decision record:

  • Brand/Display face: “Tiempos Headline” (serif) — used only for Display role on marketing and the account-upgrade moment.
  • Product face: “Söhne” (UI sans) — Title/Body/Meta/Code.
  • Deleted sizes: the 6 unused intermediates are removed in a MAJOR type-token release; migration codemod maps text-lg (18px) → title or body case-by-case.
  • Specimen page in the design system shows all five roles in light, dark, and on accent surfaces (contract rule 4), e.g. Meta on accent fill checked at 4.5:1.

Why it passes. Flexibility without roles is drift (contract rule 2); the pairing gives brand voice without sacrificing product readability (rule 3); specimens make the contract reviewable (rule 4).

Rejected. Keeping all 11 sizes “in case marketing needs them” and setting the whole brand in default Inter.

Ch 5 §5.2-C: Tabular figures for code and money

Concept. 5.2: “Code and money always use tabular figures”; 5.3 optical row “Numerals in tables → tabular-nums; right-align money.”

Scenario. Ledgerline’s invoice table shows amounts $1,240.00, $86.10, $11,905.50. With proportional figures the decimal points wobble column-to-column and scanning totals is error-prone.

Example.

.table-cell--money {
  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;
  text-align: right;
  font-feature-settings: "tnum"; /* legacy fallback */
}

Rendered column (right-aligned, digits in fixed-width cells):

   $1,240.00
      $86.10
  $11,905.50

Why it passes. Tabular figures make every digit the same advance width, so magnitude comparison happens by position/length — the same channel priority Ch 8.4 demands for data viz. Money right-aligns so decimal points stack.

Rejected. Proportional oldstyle figures centered in the cell — pretty in prose, unreadable as a ledger.

Ch 5 §5.3-A: Icon beside label — center to cap height

Concept. 5.3 optical craft rows 1 and 3: icon vertically centered to cap height, not the full line-box; icon+text buttons use icon optical middle with an 8px gap.

Scenario. Relay’s “Assign to me” button (user-check icon + label) looks like the icon is floating high because it was flex-centered against a line-box inflated by the font’s ascender/descender.

Example.

.button__icon {
  /* 16px Body cap height ≈ 11.5px; nudge icon down ~0.5px from geometric center */
  margin-block: auto;
  transform: translateY(0.5px); /* optical correction — value verified against the type specimen at 100% and 200% zoom */
  margin-inline-end: 8px;        /* space-2 gap, per 5.3 row 3 */
}

Design-review note in the PR: "Icon centered to cap height of Body/16, not line-box; verified at 100% and 200% zoom."

Why it passes. Optical alignment beats mathematical centering (5.3 headline rule). The 8px gap is the specified icon–text gap.

Rejected. “Don’t center to emoji ascent” — aligning to the full em-box because an emoji in the label stretched the line-box.

Ch 5 §5.3-B: Text field padding — more top than bottom

Concept. 5.3 row 2: text fields often need more padding-top than bottom so the glyph sits optically centered.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s 40px-tall inputs looked bottom-heavy: equal 10px/10px padding made lowercase text (which hangs from the cap line, not the descender) appear to sag.

Example.

.input {
  height: 40px;
  padding: 11px 12px 9px; /* +2px top bias; glyph box optically centered */
  font: 400 16px/1 var(--font-ui); /* Body role, single-line */
}

Why it passes. The asymmetric 11/9 padding compensates for the visual center of the glyph box sitting above the mathematical center — exactly the 5.3 optical rule.

Rejected. padding: 10px 12px and closing the ticket as “mathematically centered.”

Ch 5 §5.3-C: All-caps labels get tracking; never all-caps for long reading

Concept. 5.3 rows 5 and closing paragraph: caps/small-caps labels take +0.02–0.05em tracking; tracking is a role property, not a one-off; no ad-hoc kerning of individual words.

Scenario. Relay’s sidebar section labels — "INBOX", "ASSIGNED TO ME", "SNOOZED" — are set in uppercase Meta.

Example.

.nav-section-label {
  font: 500 12px/1.35 var(--font-ui);
  text-transform: uppercase;
  letter-spacing: 0.04em; /* within the +0.02–0.05em band, defined ON the role */
  color: var(--fg-muted);
}

Token definition: type.label-caps.tracking = 0.04em — every uppercase chrome label inherits it.

Why it passes. Uppercase forms need air between letters to stay legible; putting the tracking on the role (not sprinkled per-instance) keeps it a contract. Long reading text is never uppercased.

Rejected. “Ad-hoc tracking is the typographic equivalent of raw hex” — a marketer hand-tracking one hero word letter-spacing: 0.31em in page CSS with no tracked specimen in brand guidelines.

Ch 5 §5.3-D: Baseline alignment in mixed-weight toolbars

Concept. 5.3 row 4: align baselines across Title/Body/Meta in a toolbar.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s page header row contains "Invoices" (Title 22/600), a count "1,204" (Body 16), and "Updated 4 min ago" (Meta 14, muted). Flex align-items: center made the three sit on three different baselines.

Example.

.page-header__row { display: flex; align-items: baseline; gap: 12px; }

Result: the bottoms of “Invoices”, “1,204”, and “Updated…” share one baseline; the size step-down reads as deliberate hierarchy instead of misalignment.

Why it passes. Baseline alignment is the optical rule for mixed-weight/size rows; the hierarchy (Title → Body → Meta) does the ranking work per L2.

Ch 5 §5.4-A: Variable font earns its keep — wght replaces four files

Concept. 5.4 table row wght: prefer when one family covers 400–700 without separate files; avoid when you only need two weights forever.

Scenario. Fieldnote currently ships Soehne-Book.woff2, -Medium, -Semibold, -Bold (4 files, ~4×28KB). The type roles use weights 400, 500, 600, 700.

Example. Swap to one variable file:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Sohne VF";
  src: url("/fonts/soehne-vf.woff2") format("woff2-variations");
  font-weight: 400 700; /* one file serves the whole role scale */
  font-display: swap;
}
.text-title { font-weight: 600; }  /* exact axis value, no faux-bold */

Payload: 1 file at ~44KB vs 4 files at ~112KB; and density modes can later use intermediate weights (e.g. 550 for dense Meta) without new files.

Why it passes. The variable font replaces multiple static files and exposes an axis the system actually uses — the 5.4 earn-their-keep test.

Rejected. Adopting a 6-axis variable font for a product that only ever uses Regular and Bold (“you only need two weights forever” → static cuts are cheaper).

Ch 5 §5.4-B: opsz — caption-optimized small text, display-optimized hero [Cross-domain]

Concept. 5.4 opsz guidance: at ≤14px Meta/Code prefer caption optical size (higher x-height, looser forms); at Display 32+ prefer display optical size; never fake opsz with tracking alone.

Scenario. Ledgerline uses “Fraunces” (opsz 9–144) for marketing Display and a UI sans with opsz 8–24 for product chrome. Meta timestamps at 14px looked pinched using the text master.

Example.

:root { font-optical-sizing: auto; } /* browser maps px → opsz */

/* Explicit pin where auto misfires: */
.text-meta   { font-size: 14px; font-variation-settings: "opsz" 10; } /* caption master */
.text-display{ font-size: 32px; font-variation-settings: "opsz" 32; } /* display master */

The 14px caption master raises x-height and opens counters, which also helps the fg-muted Meta text hold its 4.5:1 (WCAG 1.4.3 AA) legibility budget — small dark-mode text with tight apertures is where contrast passes numerically but fails visually.

Why it passes. Optical size axes are used for their actual job (small-size legibility vs display refinement), integrating type craft (5.4) with the contrast floor (6.2).

Rejected. The family lacks opsz, so the team “fakes it” by adding +0.06em tracking to Display — explicitly banned: “do not fake it with tracking alone—pick a pairing or accept the static cut.”

Ch 5 §5.4-C: font-display: swap with metric-adjusted fallback

Concept. 5.4 closing rule: ship font-display: swap with size-adjusted fallback metrics (ascent-override / size-adjust) so hierarchy doesn’t jump on load; subset aggressively for product UI.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s webfont loads ~800ms after first paint on 3G; the Arial fallback is ~6% wider, so the Title wraps to two lines then snaps back to one — a visible layout jump.

Example.

@font-face {
  font-family: "Sohne-fallback";
  src: local("Arial");
  size-adjust: 94.3%;
  ascent-override: 96%;
  descent-override: 24%;
  line-gap-override: 0%;
}
body { font-family: "Sohne VF", "Sohne-fallback", sans-serif; }

Product subset: unicode-range: U+0000-00FF, U+2013-2014, U+2019, U+20AC (~180 glyphs); marketing loads the fuller set with ligatures.

Why it passes. The adjusted fallback occupies the same metrics, so the swap is invisible; hierarchy (line counts, heading positions) never jumps.

Measure. CLS contribution from font swap ≈ 0 in Lighthouse (ties to Ch 7 measure line: layout shift within budget).

Ch 5 §5.4-D: wdth for density modes; italic as a true axis

Concept. The two remaining 5.4 axis rows: wdth — prefer for compact table headers and density modes, avoid for stretching body text “for personality”; italic-as-axis — prefer when true italic masters are available, avoid a slanted roman sold as italic.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s dense-mode invoice table has 14 column headers competing for width; Fieldnote needs italic emphasis inside note text.

Example.

/* Dense mode: narrow the header glyphs via the variable font's wdth axis */
.table--dense th {
  font-variation-settings: "wdth" 87;  /* true condensed master — counters and stroke contrast stay intact */
}
/* NOT: transform: scaleX(0.9) — geometric squeeze thins verticals unevenly and blurs hinting */

The header "Outstanding balance" now fits its column at wdth 87 without truncation; body cells stay at the default width — like weight in 5.4-A, width is remapped only where density earns it (same discipline as 5.5-C: density remaps values, never deforms roles).

Italic note. Fieldnote’s inline emphasis uses the family’s true italic axis (font-variation-settings: "ital" 1 — drawn italic masters with cursive letterforms), scoped to emphasis spans in notes. Rejected: letting the browser synthesize an oblique from the roman via bare font-style: italic with no italic face loaded — a slanted roman sold as italic, the 5.4 avoid cell verbatim. If the family ships no italic masters, pick a pairing or use weight for emphasis; do not fake the slant.

Rejected. transform: scaleX(0.9) on body paragraphs “for personality” — the named avoid cell: body text is never width-distorted.

Ch 5 §5.5-A: The 4-based space ladder in a real card

Concept. 5.5 space tokens space-1 (4) … space-7 (48): components consume tokens, not magic pixels.

Scenario. Relay’s “Customer context” card in the ticket sidebar.

Example.

.context-card {
  padding: var(--space-5);        /* 24 — card internal */
}
.context-card__title { margin-bottom: var(--space-2); } /* 8 */
.context-card__row   { padding-block: var(--space-3); } /* 12 — compact list row */
.context-card__icon  { margin-inline-end: var(--space-1); } /* 4 — icon-text micro gap */
.context-card + .context-card { margin-top: var(--space-4); } /* 16 */
.sidebar__section + .sidebar__section { margin-top: var(--space-6); } /* 32 — section break */

Why it passes. Every gap resolves to a named token from the 4-based ladder used at its documented “typical use”; a reviewer can audit the card without a ruler.

Rejected. padding: 18px 22px 14px — magic pixels; “space is a contract, not a vibe.”

Ch 5 §5.5-B: Form rhythm — the locked recipe on a billing form

Concept. 5.5 form rhythm table: label→control 4–8; control→next field 16–24; group→group 32+; helper/error 4–8 below, error replaces helper in place.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s “Payment details” form: Cardholder name, Card number, Expiry+CVC, then a separate “Billing address” group.

Example.

.field label          { margin-bottom: var(--space-2); }  /* 8: label → control */
.field + .field       { margin-top: var(--space-4); }     /* 16: control → next field */
.field-group + .field-group { margin-top: var(--space-6); } /* 32+: group → group */
.field__helper, .field__error { margin-top: var(--space-1); } /* 4: under control */

Helper under Card number: "We never store your full card number."
On validation failure that same slot swaps to the error — no layout growth:
"Check the card number — it should be 16 digits."

Why it passes. Exact locked-recipe distances; error replacing helper in place means no reflow jump at the worst moment. Proximity encodes grouping (label hugs its control at 8; groups separate at 32) — hierarchy by space per L2.

Rejected. Uniform 20px between everything: label-to-control equals group-to-group, so the eye can’t tell which label owns which input.

Ch 5 §5.5-C: Density modes remap tokens, never invent sizes [Cross-domain]

Concept. 5.5 closing rule: comfortable / compact / dense remap the same semantic roles to different token steps; they do not invent new type sizes. Integrates with 8.5 dense-row heights and the 44/24 touch rule.

Scenario. Relay ships a density switcher for its ticket list.

Example.

{
  "list-row": {
    "comfortable": { "paddingY": "space-4", "height": 48, "leadingIcon": 24 },
    "compact":     { "paddingY": "space-3", "height": 38, "leadingIcon": 20 },
    "dense":       { "paddingY": "space-2", "height": 34, "leadingIcon": 16 }
  }
}

In all three modes: primary text stays Body (16), meta stays Meta (14) — never shrunk below 14. On touch devices, dense 34px rows extend hit slop so the effective row target is ≥44px tall:

.row--dense .row__action { position: relative; }
.row--dense .row__action::before {
  content: ""; position: absolute; inset: -5px -10px; /* 34 visual → 44 hit */
}

Why it passes. Density is a token remap (space-4 → space-3 → space-2), not a new scale; type roles are untouched (L3). Touch stays at the 44×44 craft bar via hit slop even though the visual row is 34 — well above the WCAG 2.5.8 AA floor of 24×24.

Rejected. A “dense” theme that sets body text to 12px — inventing a size and breaking the type contract.

Measure. Ch 5 measure line: “Compact/dense remaps tokens — does not invent sizes”; audit the density theme diff for any font-size change (must be none).

Ch 5 §5.6-A: Measure by surface — marketing prose vs settings form

Concept. 5.6 rows: marketing body prose ~60–70ch (content ~640–720px); marketing hero headline full-bleed OK with text block ≤12–14 words; settings/forms 1-col control column 480–560px; docs 65–75ch.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s marketing “Why Fieldnote” page and its in-app Settings → Profile form.

Example.

.marketing-prose { max-width: 68ch; }            /* ≈ 680px at Body 16 */
.settings-form   { max-width: 520px; }           /* focused control column */
.docs-article    { max-width: 72ch; }             /* long-form reading */

Settings form fields (Display name, Email, Timezone) each span the full 520px column; the “Save changes” button sits left-aligned at the column start where the eye already is.

Hero headline audit (5.6 row 2). Ledgerline’s marketing hero headline — "Invoices that close themselves." (Ch 7 §7.4-A) — is 4 words, well inside the ≤12–14-word cap, so its text block may run full-bleed with no max-width: for a hero, the word cap (one claim), not a reading measure, is what keeps it scannable. Rejected: the 23-word draft "Ledgerline is the modern invoicing platform that helps small businesses everywhere chase payments, reconcile accounts, and file their paperwork without lifting a finger" — it wraps to three full-bleed Display lines and reads as a paragraph, not a claim.

Why it passes. Each surface’s measure matches its intent from the 5.6 table: readability for prose, one full-bleed claim for the hero, focused tasks for forms. The 5.6 rule holds: removing the 68ch cap makes a 1440px-wide paragraph unreadable → restore it.

Rejected. Full-width form inputs on a 27” display — a 2200px-wide email field where the label sits half a meter from the value.

Ch 5 §5.6-B: Tables full-bleed; dialogs sized sm/md/lg

Concept. 5.6 rows: data tables take full shell width, horizontal scroll only for non-essential columns; dialogs sm 400 / md 560 / lg 720; toasts never full-bleed paragraphs.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s invoices table and its “Void invoice” dialog.

Example.
- Table: width: 100% of the content shell; columns Invoice #, Customer, Amount, Status, Due are always visible; optional columns (PO number, Memo) live beyond a horizontal scroll boundary.
- Void dialog: md (560px) — title "Void invoice #4812?", one Body paragraph, two buttons.
- Toast: "Invoice #4812 voided — Undo" at content width (~340px), single line, never a full-width banner paragraph.

Why it passes. The 5.6 rule verbatim: “If adding a max-width clips a table’s primary columns, remove it and redesign columns instead.” The dialog uses the named md token; the toast stays glanceable.

Rejected. Wrapping the table in the marketing 720px prose container and forcing horizontal scroll on the Amount column (an essential column).

Ch 5 §5.6-C: Two-column settings — labels ≤ ⅓

Concept. 5.6 row: settings 2-col label|control at 720–960px with labels ≤⅓.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s Admin → Organization settings on desktop (bp-lg).

Example.

.settings-2col {
  max-width: 880px;
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) minmax(0, 2fr); /* label ⅓ | control ⅔ */
  column-gap: var(--space-5); /* 24 */
  row-gap: var(--space-5);
}

Row: label cell "Company legal name" (Meta, fg-muted, top-aligned to control’s first line) | control cell with the input + helper "Appears on invoices and receipts." At bp-md and below the grid collapses to one column (label above control at space-2).

Why it passes. Labels cap at ⅓ so controls keep a usable width; the 720–960 band keeps label→control eye travel short.

Ch 5 §5.7-A: Intent-named breakpoints for the app shell

Concept. 5.7: name breakpoints by layout intent, not device names; viewport breakpoints govern shell navigation.

Scenario. Relay’s app shell.

Example.

/* bp-sm 320–639: single column; bottom primary nav */
/* bp-md 640–959: two columns possible; side panels become sheets */
/* bp-lg 960–1279: persistent nav + content; tables usable */
/* bp-xl 1280+: optional third rail */

@media (min-width: 960px) { /* bp-lg: nav rail becomes persistent */
  .shell { grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr; }
}
@media (min-width: 1280px) { /* bp-xl: context rail appears */
  .shell { grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr 320px; }
}

Design-doc naming: "At bp-md the ticket-details panel presents as a bottom sheet; at bp-lg it docks as the third rail." No design ticket ever says “on iPad.”

Why it passes. Intent names (“side panels become sheets”) describe behavior that survives new device sizes; device names rot.

Rejected. $ipad-breakpoint: 768px — the moment a 744px-wide tablet ships, the name is a lie.

Ch 5 §5.7-B: Container query recipes — toolbar and entity card

Concept. 5.7 container query recipes, rows 1–2: toolbar icon-only → icon+label at ~280–320cqi; entity card drops side meta first below ~360cqi. (Rows 3–4 — filter bar and page header — are worked in §5.7-D.)

Scenario. Fieldnote’s note-editor toolbar renders inside both a full-width editor and a narrow split-pane.

Example.

.toolbar { container-type: inline-size; container-name: toolbar; }

.toolbar__button span.label { display: none; }        /* icon-only default */
@container toolbar (min-width: 300px) {
  .toolbar__button span.label { display: inline; }    /* icon + label */
}

.entity-card { container-type: inline-size; }
@container (max-width: 360px) {
  .entity-card__side-meta { display: none; }          /* drop side meta first */
  /* title + primary action always survive */
}

Why it passes. The component adapts to its container, so the same toolbar works docked in a 280px pane and a 900px editor — local chrome uses container queries, shell nav uses viewport breakpoints, exactly the 5.7 split.

Rejected. Driving the toolbar off @media (min-width: 640px): in the split-pane the container is 300px even though the viewport is 1400px, so labels overflow and clip.

Ch 5 §5.7-C: Reflow law — 320px and 400% zoom [Cross-domain]

Concept. 5.7 reflow law: WCAG 1.4.10 (AA) — usable at 320 CSS px and 400% zoom; stack; DOM order = reading order; no essential two-dimensional scrolling.

Scenario. A low-vision Ledgerline accountant runs the app at 400% browser zoom on a 1280px display — an effective viewport of 320 CSS px.

Example. At 320px, the invoice-detail page:
- Two-column summary (Amounts | Customer) stacks to one column; DOM source order (amounts first) equals visual order.
- The sticky action bar collapses to a single full-width primary button "Record payment" (48px tall ≥ 44 craft target).
- The line-items table linearizes: each row renders as a keyed card — "Item: Design retainer / Qty: 1 / Amount: $1,240.00" — instead of forcing horizontal scroll of essential data.

Why it passes. No essential 2-D scrolling; content stacks per bp-sm intent; the reflow is a designed layout (bp-sm single-column intent), not an accidental squish. Cross-domain: intent breakpoint (5.7) + WCAG 1.4.10 AA + 44px craft target in one decision.

Measure. Manual pass at 320px/400% on the invoice trust path is a ship gate.

Ch 5 §5.7-D: Container query recipes — filter bar and page header

Concept. The two remaining 5.7 recipe rows: filter bar — horizontal chips → a “Filters” sheet trigger in a narrow container; page header — inline actions → overflow menu when title + actions collide.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s invoices view renders both in the full shell (~1100px container) and inside a 300px “attach invoice” side panel.

Example.

/* Filter bar: chip row ↔ single sheet trigger */
.filter-bar { container-type: inline-size; container-name: filterbar; }
.filter-bar__trigger { display: none; }
@container filterbar (max-width: 320px) {
  .filter-bar__chips   { display: none; }          /* hide the horizontal chip row */
  .filter-bar__trigger { display: inline-flex; }   /* one button opens the filter sheet */
}

/* Page header: inline actions ↔ kebab overflow */
.page-header { container-type: inline-size; container-name: pageheader; }
.page-header__overflow { display: none; }
@container pageheader (max-width: 520px) {  /* measured width where "Invoices" + 3 actions collide */
  .page-header__actions--secondary { display: none; }        /* "Export", "Duplicate" leave the row */
  .page-header__overflow           { display: inline-flex; } /* kebab menu now holds them */
  /* the primary action ("New invoice") always survives inline */
}

Microcopy: the collapsed trigger reads "Filters (3)" — label plus active-filter count — so narrowing the container never hides that filtering is in effect (a filtered-to-zero list stays explainable). Tapping it opens a bottom sheet containing the same chips as toggles.

Why it passes. All four 5.7 recipe rows now have concrete container-driven rules (toolbar and entity card in §5.7-B; filter bar and page header here); the two things that never collapse away are the primary action and the active-filter count.

Rejected. Truncating overflowing chips with overflow: hidden (active filters silently invisible), and letting header actions wrap to a second line that pushes the table below the fold.

Ch 5 §5.8-A: Grid choices — marketing 12-col vs product shell vs form grid

Concept. 5.8 table: marketing modular 12-col (gutter 16–24); product shell = fluid content + fixed nav 240 / rail 320; form grid 1-col mobile with optional 2-col desktop for short fields only; dense list = single column at full content width, row padding from space tokens, vertical scan path; dashboard widgets auto-fit minmax(280px, 1fr).

Scenario. One product, three surfaces: Fieldnote’s marketing homepage, its app shell, and its signup form.

Example.

/* Marketing: 12-col modular, edges align across bands */
.mkt-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(12, 1fr); gap: 24px; }
.hero__copy { grid-column: 2 / 7; } .hero__media { grid-column: 7 / 12; }

/* Product shell: fluid + fixed */
.shell { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 240px minmax(0, 1fr) 320px; gap: 16px; }

/* Form: 1-col; 2-col only for short paired fields */
.form-row--short { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 16px; }
/* First name | Last name = OK. Address, error-prone fields = full width, 1-col. */

/* Dense list: single column, full content width; rows pad with space tokens */
.dense-list { display: block; max-width: none; } /* scan path vertical — row anatomy worked fully in Ch 8 §8.5-A */

/* Dashboard widgets — peer objects only */
.widgets { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr)); gap: 16px; }

Why it passes. Each grid matches its 5.8 row: marketing aligns edges across sections; the tool keeps content fluid and un-carded; 2-col form usage is limited to short fields (never long text or fields whose errors need full-width messages); the dense list stays one full-width column whose rows pad with space tokens (row heights, separators, and scan path are worked in Ch 8 §8.5-A); the widget grid is used only because dashboard widgets are genuine peer objects.

Ch 5 §5.8-B: The card-grid anti-pattern

Concept. 5.8 anti-pattern: “Card-grid everything. Cards are for interactive containers; flat sections with type hierarchy are the default for durable content (L2, L4).”

Scenario. A Ledgerline redesign proposal wraps the Settings page in 9 identical elevated cards: “Profile” card, “Notifications” card, “Danger zone” card, each with box-shadow and 16px radius.

Example (the fix). Settings becomes one flat surface page:

<section aria-labelledby="h-profile">
  <h2 id="h-profile" class="text-title">Profile</h2>
  <!-- fields ... -->
</section>
<hr class="rule--subtle"> <!-- border-subtle hairline, space-6 above/below -->
<section aria-labelledby="h-notifications">…</section>

Cards survive only where the container is genuinely interactive as a unit — e.g. the draggable dashboard widgets.

Why it passes. Elevation means modality (L4): static settings content is durable → flat. Hierarchy comes from Title roles and space-6 section breaks, not nine equal shadows that give the eye nowhere to land (L2).

Measure. Ch 6 measure line applies: “No decorative shadow on durable flat panels” — count of box-shadow on non-overlay surfaces trends to 0.

Chapter 6 — Color, Theme, Materials, Elevation

Ch 6 §6.1-A: Semantic roles consumed by components (L1) [Cross-domain]

Concept. 6.1 semantic role table (canvas, surface, surface-raised, fg-default, fg-muted, fg-on-accent, border-subtle, accent, danger/warning/success/info, focus-ring); primitives only in the theme layer; lint no-raw-color.

Scenario. Relay builds a “Merge conversations” confirmation banner.

Example.

.banner {
  background: var(--surface);
  border: 1px solid var(--border-subtle);   /* ≥3:1 vs surface when structural — WCAG 1.4.11 AA */
  color: var(--fg-default);                  /* ≥4.5:1 — WCAG 1.4.3 AA */
}
.banner__action-primary {
  background: var(--accent);
  color: var(--fg-on-accent);                /* contrast-gated pair */
}
.banner__action-primary:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring);      /* ≥2px, ≥3:1 vs adjacent */
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Theme layer (the only place hex lives):

{ "primitive": { "blue": { "600": "#2456d6" } },
  "semantic":  { "accent": "{primitive.blue.600}",
                 "fg-on-accent": "#ffffff" } }

Lint config: "no-raw-color": "error" — a component containing #2456d6 fails CI.

Why it passes. Product imports semantic only (L1 Roles not hexes); every role in the snippet carries its contract from the 6.1 table, and three WCAG SCs (1.4.3, 1.4.11, focus visibility) are satisfied by role definition rather than per-component heroics. Cross-domain: L1 + tokens + WCAG in one banner.

Rejected. background: #2456d6 inline in the component — the defect no-raw-color exists to ban.

Ch 6 §6.1-B: Token semver — MAJOR / MINOR / PATCH

Concept. 6.1: MAJOR = rename/remove/change meaning of a role; MINOR = add role; PATCH = ramp tweak behind same role (visual diff required).

Scenario. The Ledgerline design-tokens package @ledgerline/tokens ships three changes over a quarter.

Example.

Change Version Why
Add fg-on-danger role for text on danger fills 3.4.0 → 3.5.0 (MINOR) New role; nothing existing changes meaning
Nudge primitive.blue.600 from #2456d6 to #2050cc for dark-mode contrast; accent unchanged in meaning 3.5.0 → 3.5.1 (PATCH) Ramp tweak behind the same role — release notes attach the visual diff screenshots (light + dark)
Rename surface-raised → surface-overlay and repoint warning from amber to orange family 3.5.1 → 4.0.0 (MAJOR) Rename + change of meaning; ships with codemod npx tokens-migrate v4

Why it passes. Consumers can trust that a PATCH never changes what a role means, only how it renders — and even that is proven with a required visual diff.

Rejected. Shipping the surface-raised rename as a patch “because it’s just a name” — every consumer’s build breaks on a Tuesday.

Ch 6 §6.1-C: Rare component alias — the third layer used sparingly

Concept. 6.1 token layers: Primitive ramp → Semantic role → rare Component alias.

Scenario. Relay’s Badge component needs a background that is semantically “info surface” everywhere, but design wants room to tune badges independently later.

Example.

{ "component": { "badge": { "bg": "{semantic.info-subtle}", "fg": "{semantic.fg-on-info-subtle}" } } }

The alias points at semantics — never at primitives — and exists only because badges are a proven, system-wide tuning point. There are 4 component aliases in the whole system, not 400.

Why it passes. The alias is rare and resolves through the semantic layer, preserving the L1 chain. A theme (dark, HC) that remaps info-subtle automatically restyles badges.

Rejected. component.badge.bg: {primitive.blue.100} — a component alias that tunnels past semantics, silently breaking dark mode.

Ch 6 §6.2-A: Contrast floors on a form — 4.5:1 / 3:1 exact numbers

Concept. 6.2 contrast table: normal text 4.5:1 (WCAG 1.4.3 AA); large text (≥18.66px bold / 24px) 3:1; non-text UI (icons, boundaries, focus) 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11 AA); disabled controls exempt but must not look primary.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s checkout form audit.

Example. Audit table shipped with the PR:

Element Pair Ratio Floor Verdict
Body label fg-default on surface #1a1d21 / #ffffff 16.9:1 4.5:1 AA (1.4.3) Pass
Helper fg-muted on surface #5c636b / #ffffff 5.5:1 4.5:1 AA (used as text) Pass
Placeholder (old) #a3a8ae / #ffffff 2.6:1 4.5:1 AA Fail → darkened to #6e747c (4.9:1)
Input border border-subtle #c9ced4 / #ffffff 1.6:1 → structural? yes 3:1 AA (1.4.11) Fail → #949aa2 (3.1:1)
Title 22/600 on surface #1a1d21 / #ffffff 16.9:1 4.5:1 AA (1.4.3 — held as normal text) Pass
“Total due” figure 24px/400 on surface #5c636b / #ffffff 5.5:1 3:1 AA (1.4.3 large text: ≥24px non-bold) Pass
Disabled “Pay” button exempt as inactive — must not look primary Pass: surface fill + fg-muted, no accent

Classification note (Title row). Title 22/600 is deliberately held to the 4.5:1 normal-text floor, not the 3:1 large-text floor: 22px is below the 24px non-bold threshold, and weight 600 (semibold) does not reliably count as WCAG bold — hold semibold sub-24px text to 4.5:1 (1.4.3 AA). The 3:1 large-text floor (≥18.66px bold / ≥24px) is demonstrated instead by the 24px/400 “Total due” figure, which qualifies unambiguously.

Why it passes. Exact AA numbers applied to the exact pairings the SCs govern; the two named “usual failures” from 6.2 — placeholder text and muted chrome — are precisely what the audit caught and gated; and the borderline Title case is classified conservatively rather than under-held at 3:1.

Measure. Dual-theme contrast CI (see 6.2-B) green on the checkout trust path.

Ch 6 §6.2-B: Dual-theme contrast audit in CI

Concept. 6.2: every semantic pair ships light and dark; CI or visual regression fails contrast on both.

Scenario. @ledgerline/tokens repo CI.

Example.

// tokens.contrast.test.ts (pseudo-API)
const PAIRS: ContrastPair[] = [
  { fg: "fg-default", bg: "canvas",  floor: 4.5, sc: "1.4.3 AA" },
  { fg: "fg-default", bg: "surface", floor: 4.5, sc: "1.4.3 AA" },
  { fg: "fg-muted",   bg: "surface", floor: 4.5, sc: "1.4.3 AA (text usage)" },
  { fg: "fg-on-accent", bg: "accent", floor: 4.5, sc: "1.4.3 AA" },
  { fg: "border-subtle", bg: "surface", floor: 3.0, sc: "1.4.11 AA (structural)" },
  { fg: "focus-ring", bg: "surface", floor: 3.0, sc: "1.4.11 AA" },
];
for (const theme of ["light", "dark"]) {
  for (const p of PAIRS) expect(ratio(resolve(p.fg, theme), resolve(p.bg, theme)))
    .toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(p.floor);
}

A dark-theme PR that dims fg-muted to 4.2:1 fails the build with: "fg-muted on surface (dark) = 4.21:1 < 4.5:1 [1.4.3 AA]".

Why it passes. Contrast is enforced as a property of the token contract in both themes, catching the dark-mode regressions humans miss.

Ch 6 §6.2-C: Multi-channel status — never color alone (L11)

Concept. 6.2: status must be multi-channel — color + text and/or icon and/or pattern; red-only errors fail.

Scenario. Relay’s SLA indicator on ticket rows.

Example. Each state is a triple (color, icon, text):

  • Breached: danger pill + alert-octagon icon + "SLA breached"
  • At risk: warning pill + clock icon + "Due in 32 min"
  • On track: success pill + check icon + "On track"

Screen-reader output for the row includes the text: "Ticket 4812, SLA breached, assigned to you."

Why it passes. Meaning survives grayscale, color-blindness, and forced-colors because the words and icons carry it; color reinforces (L11 multi-channel).

Rejected. A bare 8px red dot as the only breach indicator — “red-only errors fail.”

Ch 6 §6.3-A: Dark mode is separate tonal ramps, not inversion

Concept. 6.3 table: dark surfaces elevate by lightening slightly, hairlines are 10–20% white, accents dim chroma, shadows give way to border/surface steps, danger/success desaturate and rely on label.

Scenario. Ledgerline dark theme for its data-heavy invoices view.

Example.

{
  "dark": {
    "canvas":         "#101214",
    "surface":        "#16191d",              /* +1 lightness step, not a shadow */
    "surface-raised": "#1d2126",              /* elevation by lightening */
    "border-subtle":  "rgba(255,255,255,0.14)", /* 14% white hairline — in the 10–20% band */
    "accent":         "#6b96f2",              /* dimmed chroma vs light-mode #2456d6 */
    "fg-on-accent":   "#0d1526",              /* re-checked: 8.1:1 */
    "danger":         "#e5736b",              /* desaturated; the label "Overdue" carries meaning */
    "shadow-overlay": "0 8px 24px rgba(0,0,0,0.5)" /* reserved for true overlays only */
  }
}

Menus in dark mode differentiate by surface-raised (lighter step) + hairline, not by heavy shadow (“shadows wash out”).

Why it passes. Every row of the 6.3 light/dark table has a concrete value; nothing is a hex flip of the light theme.

Rejected. filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg) on :root — “not inverted light”; it destroys photos, charts, and the accent contract at once.

Ch 6 §6.3-B: Dark preference — system + persistent toggle

Concept. 6.3 prefer-when: honor prefers-color-scheme plus an explicit persisting product toggle; don’t force brand-dark marketing look onto dense data tables without a product dark ramp.

Scenario. Fieldnote appearance settings.

Example. Settings → Appearance offers "System" (default), "Light", "Dark"; choice persists per account:

type ThemeMode = "system" | "light" | "dark";
// resolution:
const resolved = mode === "system"
  ? matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches ? "dark" : "light"
  : mode;
document.documentElement.dataset.theme = resolved;

Meanwhile marketing ships a near-black brand-dark hero — but the app’s tables use the product dark ramp from 6.3-A, not the marketing hero palette.

Why it passes. User preference respected by default, user override respected forever; marketing dark and product dark are different jobs.

Rejected. Reusing the marketing hero’s #0a0014 purple-black as the table canvas — brand-dark without a product ramp.

Ch 6 §6.4-A: Forced-colors — preserve system semantics [Cross-domain]

Concept. 6.4 do/don’t table: use system color keywords; keep control borders; keep focus visible via system Highlight; never paint over Canvas/ButtonText/Highlight/LinkText with brand fills; never outline: none without replacement.

Scenario. A Relay agent uses Windows High Contrast (forced-colors). The old build painted brand purple over everything and the primary button vanished (its only boundary was a shadow).

Example.

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .button--primary {
    forced-color-adjust: none;      /* only where we then use SYSTEM colors */
    background: ButtonFace;
    color: ButtonText;
    border: 1px solid ButtonText;   /* border restores the boundary shadow used to fake */
  }
  .card { border: 1px solid CanvasText; }  /* keep borders that define controls */
  .blur-overlay { backdrop-filter: none; background: Canvas; } /* decorative blur disabled */
  a { color: LinkText; }
  :focus-visible { outline: 2px solid Highlight; outline-offset: 2px; }
}

Why it passes. Semantic meaning is preserved with system keywords; borders replace shadow-only affordances; focus rides system Highlight. Cross-domain: forced-colors (6.4) + material rule “disable decorative blur” (6.5 Contrast layer / 6.7) + focus-ring contract (6.1) in one media query.

Rejected. Both named failures of the 6.4 tension: brand purple fills that wipe Canvas (broken HC) — and equally, gutting all brand expression from marketing where illustration may legitimately carry it. Product must choose HC correctness.

Ch 6 §6.4-B: The brand-vs-forced-colors tension resolved by surface

Concept. 6.4 tension: brand expression vs forced-colors — prefer illustration on marketing; preserve system semantics on product UI.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s marketing homepage uses a rich duotone illustration; the app’s editor chrome is token-driven.

Example. Under forced-colors: active:
- Marketing hero illustration remains as an <img> (images are not remapped) with real alt text: alt="A researcher's desk with tagged notecards" — brand survives as content.
- Every piece of product chrome (toolbar, buttons, links, focus) remaps to system colors per 6.4-A.
- Test plan explicitly splits the two: "HC pass: marketing (illustration legible, CTAs system-colored) / product (all controls bordered, focus visible)."

Why it passes. Brand lives where it’s content (illustration on marketing); semantics rule where it’s chrome (product) — the textbook’s stated preference, avoiding both “broken HC” and “lifeless product chrome” by assigning each failure mode to the surface that can afford the fix.

Ch 6 §6.5-A: Theme layer stack — brand → mode → contrast → campaign

Concept. 6.5: themes stack Brand → Mode → Contrast → Campaign; later layers override without forking component trees; campaign layers are time-boxed aliases and never touch Locked checkout tokens.

Scenario. Ledgerline runs a “Year-end close” October campaign accent while supporting light/dark and high contrast, and sells a white-label variant to a bank.

Example.

{
  "layers": [
    { "name": "brand/ledgerline", "owns": ["primitive ramps", "type pairing", "radius"] },
    { "name": "brand/norbank",    "owns": ["primitive ramps", "type pairing", "radius"], "note": "white-label = token fork, not component fork" },
    { "name": "mode/dark",        "remaps": ["canvas", "surface", "border-subtle", "accent", "..."] },
    { "name": "contrast/high",    "remaps": ["border-*: solid 1px minimum", "blur-overlay: solid-overlay"] },
    { "name": "campaign/year-end-close",
      "remaps": { "accent-marketing": "{primitive.amber.500}" },
      "sunset": "2026-11-01",
      "guard":  "MUST NOT remap: accent on /checkout, danger, focus-ring" }
  ]
}

Why it passes. Multi-brand is a token fork (Brand layer), never a component-tree fork; the campaign is time-boxed (sunset) and guarded off the Locked checkout tokens; Contrast is a real layer (HC borders, blur disabled), not “a pastel gray theme.”

Rejected. The 6.5 avoid-column items: forking a norbank-components repo; shipping HC as gray-on-gray pastels; letting the campaign alias restyle the checkout’s primary button.

Measure. 6.5 smell metric: override-rate on Locked surfaces after the campaign layer ships — if checkout components carry campaign overrides in November, remediate.

Ch 6 §6.5-B: Campaign layer with a sunset date

Concept. 6.5 Campaign row: temporary accent alias / landing skins, prefer for marketing launches with sunset date.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s “Back to research” September landing page.

Example. Campaign token file header:

# campaign/back-to-research.tokens.yaml
# OWNER: growth-design  SUNSET: 2026-10-01 (CI warns after; blocks after +14d)
accent-campaign: "{primitive.green.600}"
hero-skin: "gradient(160deg, {primitive.green.100}, {primitive.cream.50})"

CI job token-sunset-check posts on 2026-10-01: "campaign/back-to-research is past sunset — remove or renew."

Why it passes. The campaign is machine-expirable; seasonal skin can’t silently become permanent debt.

Ch 6 §6.6-A: Elevation ladder in one screen (L4)

Concept. 6.6 elevation table: 0 Flat (z 0) pages/tables · 1 Raise (z 100) menus/popovers/sticky bars · 2 Overlay + scrim (z 200) modals/sheets · 3 Telemetry (z 300) toasts · Critical blocker (z 400).

Scenario. Ledgerline’s invoices screen with a row-actions menu open, then a “Void invoice” modal, during which an unrelated "Export ready" toast arrives; later the session expires.

Example.

:root {
  --z-flat: 0; --z-raise: 100; --z-overlay: 200; --z-toast: 300; --z-blocker: 400;
}
.table            { background: var(--surface); }          /* level 0: no shadow */
.menu             { background: var(--surface-raised);
                    box-shadow: var(--shadow-raise); z-index: var(--z-raise); }
.modal            { z-index: var(--z-overlay); }
.modal-scrim      { background: rgba(0,0,0,0.5); z-index: var(--z-overlay); } /* 40–60% band */
.toast            { z-index: var(--z-toast); }              /* above scrim, below blockers */
.session-blocker  { z-index: var(--z-blocker); }            /* rare: legal/session hard stop */
