Sequence: menu raises at 100 → modal + 50% scrim at 200 (menu closes) → toast "Export ready — Download" appears at 300 above the scrim → session expiry blocker at 400 stops everything.

Why it passes. Raise means temporary; the durable table stays flat; each layer’s z-index token matches its modality level, and toasts remain visible over modals per the level-3 definition — exactly the stack the Part II review question 2 asks for.

Rejected. Random z-index: 9999 on the toast and box-shadow on the static table container (“random shadows on static panels destroy hierarchy”).

Ch 6 §6.6-B: Sticky header — elevation-1 look without modal implication

Concept. 6.6 closing note: sticky headers sit at elevation 1 visually but must not imply modality; prefer hairline borders over shadow for durable content. Integrates 8.5: shadow only while stuck.

Scenario. Relay’s ticket-list sticky column header.

Example.

.table-header { position: sticky; top: 0; background: var(--surface);
                border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-subtle); z-index: var(--z-raise); }
.table-header.is-stuck { box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,0.08); } /* scroll-driven class */

<!-- The sentinel sits directly ABOVE the table, never inside it: a div is
     not valid next to thead, and browsers foster-parent it out of the table,
     leaving the observer watching the wrong geometry -->
<div class="sticky-sentinel" style="height:1px" aria-hidden="true"></div>
<table>
  <thead class="table-header">…</thead>
  <tbody>…</tbody>
</table>

// Sentinel scrolls out of view ⇒ header is stuck; scrolls back in ⇒ unstuck.
const header   = document.querySelector(".table-header")!;
const sentinel = document.querySelector(".sticky-sentinel")!;
new IntersectionObserver(
  ([e]) => header.classList.toggle("is-stuck", !e.isIntersecting),
  { threshold: 0 }
).observe(sentinel);

Why it passes. At rest the header is hairline-only (durable, flat-feeling); the whisper of shadow appears only while stuck, avoiding “permanent fake elevation.”

Ch 6 §6.6-C: Radius tokens — full sparingly

Concept. 6.6 radius tokens: sm 4 · md 8 · lg 12 · full sparingly (avatars, icon buttons) — not on every card.

Scenario. Fieldnote component sweep.

Example. radius-sm 4 → inputs, checkboxes; radius-md 8 → buttons, menus, cards; radius-lg 12 → modals, sheets; radius-full → avatars and circular icon buttons only. A PR adding border-radius: 999px to note cards is rejected in review with: "full is reserved for avatars/icon buttons — cards take radius-md."

Why it passes. Radius is tokenized like space and type; full stays a signal (this thing is a person or a round control), not a style fad.

Ch 6 §6.7-A: Scrim spec on a destructive modal [Cross-domain]

Concept. 6.7 scrim material: neutral black 40–60% opacity; prefer for modal/sheet focus dimming durable UI beneath; avoid as soft decorative tint behind forms.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s "Void invoice #4812?" modal.

Example.

.scrim { background: rgba(10, 12, 14, 0.5); }  /* 50% — inside the 40–60 band */

Modal content sits on surface-raised (fully opaque). Body: "This voids the invoice and notifies the customer. You can restore it for 30 days." Buttons: "Cancel" / "Void invoice" (danger). The void is a Quarantine undo class — recoverable for 30 days — so the modal explains recovery instead of shouting.

Why it passes. The scrim encodes modality (level-2 overlay per 6.6), not decoration; text sits on a solid plate so contrast is guaranteed regardless of what’s beneath. Cross-domain: material token (6.7) + elevation law L4 + undo class (Quarantine, Ch 3/10 taxonomy) in one dialog.

Rejected. A 12% lavender wash behind an inline form “for depth” — decorative tint, no modality.

Ch 6 §6.7-B: Blur overlay only over rich canvases; solid for data

Concept. 6.7 blur-overlay (backdrop-filter: blur(8–16px) + translucent fill): prefer for floating panels over rich canvases (design tools); avoid on data tables, checkout, long reading. Rule 1: glass/blur = overlays only; solid for data. Rule 3: text on glass must meet contrast against the worst-case backdrop or sit on a solid scrim plate.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s moodboard canvas has a floating layers palette; Ledgerline’s checkout does not.

Example.

/* Design-canvas palette — allowed */
.palette {
  backdrop-filter: blur(12px);
  background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--surface) 72%, transparent);
  border: 1px solid var(--border-subtle);   /* hairline per glass spec */
}
.palette__label {
  background: var(--surface);               /* solid plate under text — worst-case-proof */
  color: var(--fg-default);
}

/* Checkout — solid only */
.checkout-summary { background: var(--surface); }  /* no blur, ever */

Why it passes. Blur appears only on a floating overlay above a rich canvas; text gets a solid plate so 4.5:1 (1.4.3 AA) holds even when a photo slides beneath; checkout/data stays solid per rule 1.

Rejected. The research anti-pattern by name: “glass everywhere” — frosted table rows and a translucent checkout card whose total becomes unreadable over a busy background. Also banned by rule 4: glow + multi-layer shadow stacks as hierarchy substitutes (L2).

Ch 6 §6.7-C: prefers-reduced-transparency and the solid fallback

Concept. 6.7 rule 2: respect prefers-reduced-transparency — swap blur → solid; solid-overlay row: opaque surface-raised for accessibility, HC, reduced transparency. vibrancy row: platform-native only.

Scenario. A Fieldnote user with vestibular/visual sensitivity enables Reduce Transparency at the OS level.

Example.

@media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) {
  .palette { backdrop-filter: none; background: var(--surface-raised); } /* solid-overlay */
}
@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .palette { backdrop-filter: none; background: Canvas; border-color: CanvasText; }
}

iOS native shell: the tab bar uses UIKit’s system material (true vibrancy); the web app does not fake vibrancy with CSS on its dense note grid.

Why it passes. The material degrades to solid-overlay on user preference and in HC; vibrancy is used only where the platform HIG expects it — every avoid-cell of the 6.7 table respected.

Chapter 7 — Motion & Loading

Ch 7 §7.1-A: Motion as meaning — the “decorates or changes known state?” test

Concept. 7.1: motion acknowledges state change (press, open, resolve); motion that doesn’t change understood state is theater — cut it. Shared components animate transform and opacity only.

Scenario. Relay design review of two proposed animations: (a) checkbox check-draw + row slide-out when a ticket is archived; (b) a perpetual 3° float on the empty-state illustration.

Example. Review verdicts using the cheat-sheet question:

  • (a) Keep. The 160ms slide-out (transform: translateX) + fade communicates “this item left the list because of your action” — state change made legible.
  • (b) Cut. The float loops forever and encodes nothing — theater.
.row--archiving {
  transition: transform 160ms var(--ease-accel), opacity 160ms var(--ease-accel);
  transform: translateX(24px); opacity: 0;   /* transform + opacity ONLY */
}

Why it passes. Every surviving animation maps to a state transition; the implementation stays on compositor-friendly properties (no height, top, or box-shadow animation), honoring the systems budget.

Rejected. Animating margin-top for the slide (layout thrash) and the decorative infinite float.

Ch 7 §7.2-A: Motion tokens applied — menu, sheet, toggle

Concept. 7.2 token table: motion-fast 100–150ms ease-out · motion-default 150–250ms ease-in-out · motion-slow 300–400ms · motion-enter decelerate · motion-exit ≤ enter, accelerate · motion-reduced 0–1ms/opacity-only.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s interaction inventory.

Example.

:root {
  --motion-fast: 120ms;  --motion-default: 200ms;  --motion-slow: 320ms;
  --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1);       /* decelerate — enter */
  --ease-in:  cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1);       /* accelerate — exit  */
  --ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1);
}
.toggle__knob   { transition: transform var(--motion-fast) var(--ease-out); }      /* 120ms press */
.menu[data-open]{ animation: pop-in var(--motion-default) var(--ease-out); }        /* 200ms enter */
.menu[data-closing]{ animation: pop-out 150ms var(--ease-in); }                     /* exit ≤ enter, snappier */
.sheet[data-open]{ animation: rise var(--motion-slow) var(--ease-out); }            /* 320ms large overlay */

Why it passes. Every duration is a named token inside its documented band; enters decelerate, exits accelerate and never exceed the enter duration (“snappier exit”).

Rejected. A 600ms bouncy spring on the dropdown — outside every band, and the bounce implies physicality that encodes nothing.

Ch 7 §7.2-B: Latency tier — acknowledge ≤100ms, then progress UI (L5) [Cross-domain]

Concept. 7.2 latency tier note: acknowledge control press ≤100ms (often CSS :active / optimistic); longer work needs progress UI, not a longer animation.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s "Record payment" button triggers a 1.4s server call.

Example.

  • 0ms: CSS :active press state (transform: scale(0.98), --motion-fast) — acknowledgment inside the 100ms budget.
  • ~120ms: button enters pending — label swaps to spinner + "Recording…", aria-busy="true", button disabled against double-submit.
  • 1.4s: resolve — success row updates; toast "Payment recorded — Undo" (Soft undo class).

Why it passes. L5 acknowledgment is instant and local; the 1.4s of real work is shown as progress UI (pending button per the 7.5 100–300ms+ tier), not a stretched 1.4s animation pretending latency is choreography. Cross-domain: L5 + motion tokens + loading tier + Soft undo in one control.

Rejected. A 1.4s “satisfying” checkmark animation timed to mask the request — when the request takes 3s the animation lies.

Ch 7 §7.3-A: Reduced-motion peer path — sheet, list insert, skeleton

Concept. 7.3 table: sheet slide 300ms → instant + optional 100ms fade; list fly-in → opacity/instant; parallax → static; skeleton shimmer → static pulse ≤2Hz or solid; confetti → checkmark + text. Reduced motion is a peer path, shipped and tested.

Scenario. Relay under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce.

Example.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .sheet[data-open]   { animation: fade-in 100ms linear; }   /* was: rise 320ms */
  .row--new           { animation: none; opacity: 1; }        /* was: fly-in */
  .skeleton__shimmer  { animation: pulse 1s steps(2) infinite; } /* ≤2Hz static pulse */
  .hero-parallax      { transform: none !important; }         /* static layout */
}

Success moment: instead of confetti, reduced-motion users get "✓ Inbox zero — nice work." as text with a static check icon.

Why it passes. Each full-motion behavior has a designed peer, not an absence; nothing essential is communicated only through movement.

Rejected. * { animation: none !important } dumped globally — it kills the loading spinner that tells users work is happening, breaking L6 state design.

Measure. Ch 7 measure line: “No essential meaning lost under prefers-reduced-motion” — QA runs the create/archive/load flows with the OS setting on.

Ch 7 §7.3-B: Test both paths as a release check

Concept. 7.3: “Ship both; test both.”

Scenario. Fieldnote’s release checklist for any PR touching motion.

Example. PR template checkbox block:

- [ ] Ran flow with `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` (macOS: Reduce Motion)
- [ ] No state change communicated by movement alone
- [ ] Shimmer replaced by static pulse ≤2Hz
- [ ] Screen recording of BOTH paths attached

Why it passes. The peer path is verified per change, not assumed once.

Ch 7 §7.4-A: Marketing hero budget and ≤3 scroll scenes

Concept. 7.4 table: first viewport = brand, one headline, one sentence, one CTA group, one dominant image — no stats strips/schedules/secondary promos; ≤3 scroll scene changes, one job each; parallax subtle or none; sticky storytelling keyboard-operable with content in DOM order; autoplay video captioned + pausable, no >3 flashes/sec.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s marketing homepage rebuild.

Example. First viewport contents (audited against the budget):

  1. Logo + nav (brand)
  2. Headline (Display 32/700): "Invoices that close themselves."
  3. One sentence (Body): "Ledgerline chases payments, reconciles them, and files the paperwork."
  4. CTA group: "Start free" (accent) + "See pricing" (quiet link)
  5. One product screenshot (dominant image)

Cut in review: a logos strip, a G2 badge row, and a webinar banner — all deferred below the fold. Scroll scenes: (1) “Chase” (2) “Reconcile” (3) “File” — three scenes, one claim each, revealed with a subtle 24px translate + fade; every scene’s text is in DOM order and reachable by keyboard; the demo video has captions and a visible "Pause" control. The demo video also passed a PEAT flash analysis confirming no region flashes more than 3 times per second (WCAG 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold, Level A) — the result is recorded as a line item in the launch checklist alongside the caption and pause checks.

Why it passes. Exactly one job per viewport unit; scene count at the ≤3 cap; parallax subtle; a11y constraints (keyboard, DOM order, captions, flash limit) honored.

Rejected. The 7.4 anti-patterns verbatim: scroll-jacking that pins the wheel until a Lottie finishes; and any of this inside the product app.

Ch 7 §7.4-B: Product must not scroll-jack

Concept. 7.4 last row: product app — no scroll-jacking, no bento theater inside tools. Anti-patterns: dashboard confetti on every save; scroll-jacked settings.

Scenario. A growth PM proposes reusing the marketing scroll-scene engine for Relay’s onboarding settings, plus confetti on every ticket close.

Example (the rejection memo). "Settings scroll normally — a wheel tick moves the page, period. Onboarding is a checklist, not a cinematic. Confetti is reserved for ≤1 rare milestone (first inbox-zero week), not every close: celebration on a 300×/day action is noise by L14 (craft ∝ trust × frequency — high-frequency actions get quiet, fast feedback)." Ticket close feedback becomes: row slide-out (160ms) + count decrement.

Why it passes. The frequency lens sizes the feedback: daily-driver actions get sub-200ms quiet acknowledgment; theater is confined to marketing where sequencing claims is the actual job.

Ch 7 §7.5-A: Loading tiers assigned to one screen (L6)

Concept. 7.5 latency table: <100ms no loader · 100–300ms control pending · 300ms–2s local skeleton/inline progress · >2s determinate progress or skeleton + status text · full-page only for true route-level first paint without shell.

Scenario. Relay’s ticket view: opening a ticket (~150ms cached), loading its history (~800ms), generating an AI summary (~6s), and cold-booting the app.

Example.

Action Latency Treatment
Open cached ticket ~80ms No loader — content just appears (<100ms tier)
“Assign to me” ~180ms Button pending: spinner-in-button + disabled (100–300ms tier)
Load history pane ~800ms Local skeleton in the pane only; shell + ticket header stay live (300ms–2s tier)
AI summary ~6s Determinate-ish progress: "Summarizing 42 messages… (step 2 of 3)" (>2s tier)
Cold boot first paint Full-page skeleton of the shell — the only full-page treatment allowed

Why it passes. Each latency band gets its prescribed treatment; loading is a designed state (L6), scoped as locally as possible.

Rejected. A full-page spinner between every internal navigation (the review-question 3 failure) — route changes inside a mounted shell must never blank the shell.

Ch 7 §7.5-B: Skeleton recipe, all seven steps, for a dense issue list

Concept. 7.5 skeleton recipe: (1) shape match, (2) token surfaces, (3) shimmer with reduced-motion fallback, (4) no fake text, (5) preserve chrome, (6) crossfade exit ≤150ms with reserved min-heights, (7) timeout → error with retry.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s “All notes” dense list route (36px rows, avatar + title + meta).

Example.

<div class="skeleton-list" role="status" aria-label="Loading notes">
  <!-- 12 rows, each mirroring final geometry: -->
  <div class="skel-row" style="height:36px">
    <span class="skel skel--circle" style="width:20px;height:20px"></span> <!-- avatar -->
    <span class="skel skel--bar" style="width:46%;height:14px"></span>      <!-- title -->
    <span class="skel skel--bar" style="width:18%;height:12px"></span>      <!-- meta -->
  </div>
</div>

.skel { background: var(--surface); border-radius: 4px; }        /* (2) token surface vs canvas — no pure gray flash in dark */
.skel--bar { position: relative; overflow: hidden; }
.skel--bar::after { /* (3) slow shimmer */
  content:""; position:absolute; inset:0;
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, transparent, rgba(255,255,255,0.06), transparent);
  animation: shimmer 1.6s linear infinite;
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .skel--bar::after { animation: pulse 1s steps(2) infinite; }   /* static pulse ≤2Hz */
}
.list-container { min-height: 432px; }  /* (6) 12 × 36px reserved — no jump */
.content-enter { animation: fade 140ms ease-out; }               /* (6) crossfade ≤150ms */

// (7) failure handoff — skeleton never spins forever
const t = setTimeout(() => showRegionError({
  message: "Notes are taking too long to load.",
  action: { label: "Retry", onClick: refetch },
}), 8000);

(1) Rows mirror final geometry (36px, circle avatar, two bars). (4) No lorem-ipsum text — shapes only. (5) The nav rail and user menu stay mounted; only the content pane skeletons.

Why it passes. All seven recipe steps are implemented with numbers; the skeleton is a designed loading state that terminates in either real content or a real error (L6).

Rejected. A generic gray card grid that looks nothing like the list (“shape match” violation), pure #e0e0e0 blocks flashing in dark mode, and a skeleton that shimmers forever on network failure.

Measure. Ch 7 measure line: skeleton→content CLS within budget (target <0.02 for this route); loader appears only when latency exceeds its tier threshold.

Ch 7 §7.5-C: Partial loading — stream sections, optimistic insert

Concept. 7.5 partial loading: prefer streaming rows / section-ready over blocking the whole view; Linear-style optimistic list insert beats full-page reload when rollback is cheap.

Scenario. Relay creates a ticket from the composer while the list is loading.

Example.

  • The list streams: header + first 20 rows paint at 300ms; remaining rows hydrate as they arrive — no full-view block.
  • Creating a ticket inserts the row optimistically at 0ms with a subtle pending dot; on server ack (~400ms) the dot resolves to the real ID #4813. On failure, the row is removed and a toast appears: "Couldn't create ticket — Retry" (rollback is cheap: nothing else depended on it yet).

Why it passes. Section-ready beats view-blocked; the optimistic insert is the named Linear-style steal, used precisely because rollback is cheap.

Chapter 8 — Icons, Illustration, Photography, Data Viz + Dense-List Craft

Ch 8 §8.1-A: Icon production grid — 24px master with a 20px live area

Concept. 8.1 production grid: 24×24 master (16/20/32 derived); 20×20 live area (2px padding); 1.5–2px optical stroke at 24; don’t scale stroke naively to 16 — cut a 16 master or use variable stroke; round vs square caps chosen once; circles/diagonals get +0.5–1px optical weight; currentColor/semantic fg-* only.

Scenario. Fieldnote commissions a 120-glyph icon set.

Example. Icon spec sheet (excerpt):

Master: 24×24 grid, live area 20×20 (2px safe padding all sides)
Stroke: 1.75px at 24; 16px size uses dedicated 16-master at 1.5px (NOT scaled 1.16px)
Caps/joins: ROUND (friendly set) — locked product-wide
Optical: circle glyphs (record, user) drawn at 20.5px effective diameter (+0.5 weight);
         diagonal strokes (share-arrow) +0.5px weight
Corners: 1.5px radius (slightly tighter than radius-md 8 scaled)
Color: fill="none" stroke="currentColor" — NO baked hex in product SVGs

<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.75"
     stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true">…</svg>

Why it passes. Every grid-table row has a numeric decision; currentColor lets the icon inherit fg-default/fg-muted and survive dark mode and forced-colors automatically (L1).

Rejected. Exporting the 24px master at 16px with a resulting 1.16px stroke that antialiases to mush; brand-blue hex baked into SVG fills.

Ch 8 §8.1-B: Icon touch targets — 44 craft / 24 AA floor with hit slop [Cross-domain]

Concept. 8.1 touch row: primary actions get ≥44×44 craft hit target (HIG/Material); WCAG 2.5.8 AA floor is 24×24; dense rows at 32–36 tall are legal if hit slop yields ≥44×44 or expand-on-focus is offered; visible glyph may be 20–24.

Scenario. Relay’s dense ticket rows (34px tall) show a 20px star “prioritize” icon button.

Example.

.icon-button {
  width: 44px; height: 44px;                /* craft target */
  display: grid; place-items: center;
}
.icon-button svg { width: 20px; height: 20px; }  /* visible glyph 20 */

/* Dense row variant: visual button 28×28, hit slop expands to 44×44 */
.row--dense .icon-button { width: 28px; height: 28px; position: relative; }
.row--dense .icon-button::before { content: ""; position: absolute; inset: -8px; } /* 28+16 = 44 */

Audit note: "28×28 visual exceeds the 24×24 WCAG 2.5.8 AA floor on its own; slop brings it to the 44 craft bar. Adjacent slop regions must not overlap — row actions spaced ≥44 center-to-center."

Why it passes. Both numbers from the textbook convention are used correctly: 24×24 is the legal minimum (2.5.8 AA), 44×44 is the product craft bar, and the dense-row hit-slop recipe reconciles density with touch. Cross-domain: icon craft (8.1) + density (8.5) + WCAG 2.5.8 AA.

Measure. Ch 8 measure line: “Dense rows still provide ≥44×44 hit (padding/slop) or expand-on-focus” — automated bounding-box check in component tests.

Ch 8 §8.1-C: Metaphor glossary — one meaning per symbol

Concept. 8.1 metaphor glossary: Settings = gear or sliders (pick one); Delete = trash, never X in primary toolbars (X = dismiss); Search = magnifier; Share ≠ Send airplane if Send exists; More = kebab or meatball (pick one), never hamburger for overflow.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s audit finds three “settings” metaphors (gear, wrench, sliders) and X used for both “close panel” and “delete line item.”

Example. Published glossary (design-system page, enforced in icon-set PRs):

Concept Approved Banned in this product
Settings gear wrench, sliders
Delete trash x (X = dismiss only)
Dismiss/close x —
Search magnifier spyglass-tilted
Share node-branch paper-plane (that’s Send — we have a Send)
More/overflow kebab (vertical) meatball, hamburger (hamburger = nav menu only)

Line-item delete becomes trash; panel close stays x. A lint on the icon import map flags any component importing a banned synonym.

Why it passes. One concept ↔ one metaphor product-wide; the X/trash split removes a destructive-action ambiguity.

Measure. Ch 8 measure line: “No metaphor collisions in primary nav” — glossary diff review each release.

Ch 8 §8.1-D: Labeling — icon + text nav; no-unlabeled-icon-button; decorative aria-hidden

Concept. 8.1 labeling: primary navigation stays icon + text until learnability is proven; lint no-unlabeled-icon-button for destructive and primary actions; decorative icons next to text get aria-hidden="true"; solo icons need accessible names.

Scenario. Relay’s left nav and its row actions.

Example.

<!-- Primary nav: icon + text (labels are not collapsed until telemetry proves learnability) -->
<a href="/inbox"><svg aria-hidden="true">…</svg> Inbox</a>

<!-- Solo icon button: accessible name required -->
<button aria-label="Delete ticket" class="icon-button">
  <svg aria-hidden="true"><use href="#trash"/></svg>
</button>

Lint output on a bare destructive button: error no-unlabeled-icon-button: <button> with icon "trash" has no aria-label/visible text (destructive action).

Why it passes. Text carries meaning for new users and screen readers; the decorative duplicate icon is hidden from AT; destructive actions can never ship nameless.

Rejected. An icon-only sidebar on day one “because it looks clean” — learnability unproven.

Ch 8 §8.2-A: Empty-state illustration vs marketing hero art

Concept. 8.2 table + “empty vs marketing art”: marketing art = brand atmosphere with a real visual anchor (not generic purple blobs), full-bleed OK; empty state = quieter, smaller, subordinate to one CTA, decorative alt=""; never reuse the hero as a permanent empty state.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s marketing hero vs its empty “Tags” screen.

Example.

  • Marketing hero: full-bleed illustration of a researcher’s desk with tagged notecards (a real anchor — the product’s actual object), duotone brand palette.
  • Empty tags screen: a 96×96 spot illustration (small, muted palette mapped to semantic tokens), alt="", above: Title "No tags yet", Body "Tags help you find related notes fast.", one CTA "Create your first tag", optional "Start from a template" link.
  • Explicit rule in the design doc: "Hero art may not be reused in empty states — it becomes wallpaper and kills the scent of the action."

Why it passes. Each illustration serves its 8.2 row: brand atmosphere on marketing (with a real anchor, not blobs); one encouraged next action in-product. Spot palette maps to tokens so dark mode gets a dark variant instead of a white-boxed PNG.

Rejected. Generic purple-blob abstract art on marketing; the full hero painting parked permanently behind the empty tags list.

Ch 8 §8.2-B: Error illustration — calm clarity, path forward

Concept. 8.2 rows: error/denied = calm clarity, no blame humor obscuring recovery, always a path forward; in-product celebration rare, prefer quiet success text; onboarding = curriculum (identity → artifact → share → return cue), not carousel.

Scenario. Relay’s 403 “no access to this workspace” screen.

Example. Small neutral illustration (locked folder, muted tones), then:

  • Title: "You don't have access to this workspace"
  • Body: "Ask an admin to invite you, or switch to a workspace you belong to."
  • Actions: "Request access" (primary) · "Switch workspace" (secondary)

Onboarding, by contrast, is a 4-step curriculum: create your profile (identity) → import your first inbox (artifact) → invite a teammate (share) → "We'll email you when your first ticket lands" (return cue) — not a 5-slide swipe-through carousel of feature art.

Why it passes. The error screen is calm, unblaming, and always offers a forward path; celebration stays quiet ("✓ Access requested"), reserved per trust×frequency (L14).

Rejected. "Whoopsie! Our hamster fell off the wheel 🐹" with no recovery action — blame-adjacent humor obscuring the path forward.

Ch 8 §8.3-A: Photography — crop, grade, text-safe zones

Concept. 8.3: subject-aware crop with defined focal point for object-position; one shared grade per brand; reserve text-safe zones; never Display text on busy midtones without a scrim plate; full-bleed hero on marketing, not inset rounded cards (unless system requires).

Scenario. Ledgerline’s customer-story page: a photo of a bakery owner behind a Display headline.

Example.

.story-hero__img {
  width: 100%; height: 56vh; object-fit: cover;
  object-position: 68% 30%;  /* focal point: subject's face, defined in the asset's metadata */
}
.story-hero__plate {          /* scrim plate under Display text */
  background: linear-gradient(180deg, transparent, rgba(10,12,14,0.55));
}
.story-hero__title { color: #fff; }  /* measured 7.2:1 vs the darkest plate band */

Asset pipeline note: "All story photos share grade preset 'LL-Warm-01'; no mixing cinematic teal-orange with flat product shots on one page. Left third reserved text-safe in all hero crops."

Why it passes. Focal point drives object-position at every breakpoint; the scrim plate guarantees Display contrast over unpredictable midtones; one grade keeps the page coherent — and the hero is edge-to-edge full-bleed per the treatment row.

Rejected. White Display text laid straight onto a busy midtone counter-top region; three stock photos in three different grades.

Ch 8 §8.3-B: Alt text and performance discipline

Concept. 8.3 rows: informative photos get real alt; decorative get empty alt; never “image123”; responsive srcset; priority only on the LCP hero. Plus the brand test: remove the nav — if the first viewport could be another company, photography + type failed.

Scenario. The same customer-story page, performance and a11y pass.

Example.

<!-- fetchpriority="high" on the LCP hero ONLY; all below-fold imgs are loading="lazy" -->
<img src="/img/bakery-1200.avif"
     srcset="/img/bakery-640.avif 640w, /img/bakery-1200.avif 1200w, /img/bakery-2000.avif 2000w"
     sizes="100vw"
     fetchpriority="high"
     alt="Maya Chen arranging pastries in her Portland bakery, where Ledgerline handles her invoicing">

Decorative divider texture: alt="". Brand test applied in review: nav removed from the mock — the bakery-owner-with-invoices composition and the Tiempos/Söhne pairing still read as Ledgerline, so photography + type pass.

Why it passes. Alt text is informative and specific (never "image123"); only the LCP hero gets fetch priority; the brand test is run as a literal review step.

Ch 8 §8.4-A: Encoding priority — position/length first, color last

Concept. 8.4 channel priority: 1 position/length · 2 direct labels · 3 shape/pattern · 4 color · 5 motion (transition on filter only).

Scenario. Ledgerline’s “Revenue by plan” chart (4 plans).

Example. Chosen form: horizontal bar chart (length encodes magnitude), bars sorted descending, each bar directly labeled ("Growth — $412k") instead of a color legend; plans additionally distinguished by subtle pattern (one hatched) so print/grayscale survives; color applies the categorical ramp last; when the user filters by quarter, bars transition once over 200ms (motion-default) — no continuous animation.

Why it passes. The encoding walks the priority list in order: position/length carries the data, labels remove legend round-trips, pattern covers a11y/print, color is reinforcement, motion is transition-only.

Rejected. A donut chart where 4 similar hues are the only differentiator and values live in a hover-only tooltip — color-first, position-last, inaccessible.

Ch 8 §8.4-B: Ramp selection — sequential vs diverging vs categorical vs status

Concept. 8.4 ramp rules: sequential = magnitude, one hue family, dark-mode checked; diverging = deviation with a clear neutral midpoint; categorical ≤6–8 then aggregate/facet; status pairs with icon/text.

Scenario. Relay’s analytics dashboard: (a) heatmap of ticket volume by hour, (b) SLA delta vs target, (c) tickets by channel (11 channels), (d) queue-health tiles.

Example.

Chart Ramp Decision
(a) Volume heatmap Sequential One hue family chart-seq-1..7 (light→dark blue); dark-mode variant re-anchored so step 1 isn’t invisible on canvas
(b) SLA delta Diverging Blue ← neutral gray midpoint (0) → orange; midpoint explicitly chart-neutral, never a saturated color
(c) 11 channels Categorical Aggregate: top 6 channels + "Other (5 channels)" — over the ≤6–8 cap, so aggregate rather than an 11-hue ramp
(d) Queue health Status success/warning/danger tokens each paired with icon + label "Healthy" / "Slowing" / "Backed up"

Why it passes. Each ramp type is used only for its 8.4 job; the 11-category case triggers the aggregate rule instead of inventing indistinguishable hues; status never rides color alone (L11).

Ch 8 §8.4-C: Chart tokens, gridline contrast, and table fallback [Cross-domain]

Concept. 8.4 dual-theme: export chart-1…chart-n, chart-axis, chart-grid as semantics; gridlines subtle but ≥3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11 AA) if they define relied-on structure. Fallbacks: data table or summary; keyboard-focusable points or a table toggle — tooltips are not the only access path.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s revenue chart in light and dark, used by a keyboard-only accountant.

Example.

{ "chart": {
    "1": "{semantic.accent}", "2": "{primitive.teal.500}", "3": "{primitive.amber.500}",
    "axis": "{semantic.fg-muted}",
    "grid": "{semantic.border-subtle}"   /* resolves ≥3:1 in both themes when structural */
} }

<figure aria-labelledby="rev-title">
  <figcaption id="rev-title">Revenue by plan, Q2 2026</figcaption>
  <!-- Interactive chart: the container must NOT be role="img" — an atomic
       image hides its subtree from AT, so the focusable bars inside would
       be swallowed. role="img" + a summary label is for STATIC charts only. -->
  <svg role="group" aria-label="Bar chart, 4 bars. Use Tab to read each value.">
    <!-- each bar: <rect tabindex="0" role="img" aria-label="Growth: $412,000"> -->
  </svg>
  <button aria-expanded="false">View as table</button>
  <table hidden><!-- same data, real <th scope> headers --></table>
</figure>

Why it passes. Chart colors are semantic tokens (L1), so dark mode retints without touching chart code; gridlines meet the 3:1 non-text floor where users read against them; the data has three access paths — labeled bars, keyboard-focusable points, and a real table. The container is a non-atomic role="group" so each bar remains its own tab stop and announcement; a role="img" wrapper would flatten the chart into one atomic graphic and hide the bars from AT. Cross-domain: token layer + 1.4.11 AA + keyboard access in one chart.

Measure. Ch 8 measure line: “Chart meaning survives grayscale + labels” — print the dashboard grayscale; series must remain identifiable via labels/patterns.

Ch 8 §8.4-D: AI diffs — never red/green alone

Concept. 8.4 final rule (Case D tie-in): AI diffs / code hunks must not rely on red/green alone; include +/− markers and readable wording.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s AI “suggest edit” review pane shows changed lines.

Example.

− The study included 12 participants.        [line marker "−", danger-subtle wash]
+ The study included 14 participants (two    [line marker "+", success-subtle wash]
  added in the March cohort).

Header microcopy: "AI suggests 1 change: participant count updated from 12 to 14." The −/+ glyphs sit in a dedicated gutter column; the wash is reinforcement.

Why it passes. A colorblind or grayscale reader gets identical information from the gutter markers and the sentence summary; color is channel #4, not #1.

Ch 8 §8.5-A: Density tiers on a real list — comfortable/compact/dense

Concept. 8.5 table: row heights 44–48 / 36–40 / 32–36 (dense still ≥44 touch via slop); separators full hairline vs zebra-or-hairline (never both heavy); primary text Body, never below 14; meta drops optional columns first; leading icon 24 / 20–24 / 16–20; trailing actions visible+overflow / overflow-first / reveal-on-select.

Scenario. Relay’s ticket list shipping all three densities.

Example.

{
  "ticket-row": {
    "comfortable": { "height": 46, "separator": "hairline", "leadingAvatar": 24,
                     "trailing": ["assign", "overflow"] },
    "compact":     { "height": 38, "separator": "hairline", "leadingAvatar": 20,
                     "trailing": ["overflow"] },
    "dense":       { "height": 34, "separator": "zebra",    "leadingAvatar": 16,
                     "trailing": "reveal-on-select-or-focus",
                     "drops": ["channel-column", "last-reply-column"] }
  }
}

In dense mode: subject stays Body 16 (never shrunk), meta stays Meta 14, the two optional columns drop before any type shrinks, zebra striping replaces hairlines (not both), and mobile hit slop keeps row actions at ≥44×44.

Why it passes. Every 8.5 column maps to a concrete value per tier; density is achieved by dropping optional content and remapping space — never by inventing sub-14 text (ties to 5.5-C).

Rejected. “Both heavy”: zebra stripes plus strong borders, doubling visual noise; 12px primary text to “fit more.”

Ch 8 §8.5-B: Scan path — identity column, fixed status, selected-row encoding [Cross-domain]

Concept. 8.5 scan path: (1) users scan down the primary column — align it; (2) status pills in a fixed column, multi-channel; (3) sticky header hairline + surface, elevation-1 without modality; (4) selected row = surface-raised or low-alpha accent wash plus checkbox/aria-selected — not color alone; (5) visible focus ring per row/action; don’t steal horizontal scroll.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s invoices table, keyboard + pointer.

Example.

  • Column order: [✓] Invoice # (identity, Body 600, left-aligned) · Customer · Amount (right, tabular) · Status (fixed col) · Due.
  • Selected row:
.row[aria-selected="true"] {
  background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent) 8%, var(--surface)); /* low-alpha wash */
}
.row[aria-selected="true"] .row__checkbox { /* checkbox reflects state — never color alone */ }
.row:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring); outline-offset: -2px; }
  • Status pills (from 6.2-C) live in one fixed column so vertical scanning works.
  • Arrow keys move row focus; horizontal scroll of the optional-columns region is only via the region’s own scrollbar/shift-wheel — row focus never hijacks it.

Why it passes. The scan path (identity → primary → meta) is architected, selection is triple-encoded (wash + checkbox + aria-selected), and focus is visible per row. Cross-domain: dense-list craft (8.5) + selection semantics + focus-ring token (6.1) + L11 multi-channel.

Measure. Ch 8 measure line: “Scan path (identity · primary · meta) holds in usability” — 5-user pass: find invoice #4812 and its status in <5s.

Ch 8 §8.5-C: Sticky identity column + Linear-style steal with a progressive path

Concept. 8.5: pin identity columns first; freeze header on vertical scroll; shadow only while stuck. Linear-style steal: issue-row density, instant insert, keyboard scent — without assuming keyboard-native users (progressive path).

Scenario. Ledgerline’s wide invoices table (14 columns) on a 13” laptop; power users want speed, new bookkeepers don’t know shortcuts.

Example.

.col--invoice-id { position: sticky; left: 0; background: var(--surface); z-index: 1; }
.table-header    { position: sticky; top: 0; }  /* + .is-stuck shadow from Ch 6 §6.6-B */

Keyboard scent, progressively disclosed: hovering the “Assign” action shows "A" as a keycap hint; the command palette (⌘K) lists every action with its shortcut beside it; nothing is keyboard-only — every shortcut has a clickable button peer. Creating an invoice inserts the row instantly (optimistic, per 7.5-C).

Why it passes. Identity stays visible during horizontal scroll; the steal is the behavior (density + instant insert + shortcut scent), and the progressive path (visible buttons + discoverable shortcuts) covers non-keyboard-native users, exactly as 8.5 qualifies the steal.

Chapter 9 — Email, Print & Safe Areas

Ch 9 §9.1-A: Transactional receipt email — the constrained runtime kit

Concept. 9.1 element table: 600px content table, fluid ≤100%; system-stack type 14–16px body / titles ≤22–24; hierarchy by weight + space with one primary CTA; solid CTA button ≥44px tall with link fallback text; inline hex with semantic intent + dark-client testing; width attributes + alt on images, CTA never image-only; cell padding not margins; plain-language unsubscribe footer. Transactional mail = trust-path craft: quiet chrome, tabular-ish amounts, no growth dark patterns.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s “Payment received” receipt email.

Example.

<table role="presentation" width="600" style="max-width:100%; margin:0 auto;">
  <tr><td style="padding:24px; font-family:-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Arial,sans-serif;">
    <h1 style="font-size:22px; font-weight:600; margin:0 0 8px; color:#1a1d21;">
      Payment received — $1,240.00</h1>
    <p style="font-size:16px; line-height:1.5; color:#1a1d21; margin:0 0 16px;">
      Invoice #4812 from Chen's Bakery was paid on July 14, 2026.</p>
    <!-- amounts: right-aligned numeric column, monospace-ish fallback for lining -->
    <table role="presentation" width="100%">
      <tr><td style="padding:8px 0; font-size:14px; color:#5c636b;">Subtotal</td>
          <td align="right" style="font-size:14px;">$1,200.00</td></tr>
      <tr><td style="padding:8px 0; font-size:14px; color:#5c636b;">Tax</td>
          <td align="right" style="font-size:14px;">$40.00</td></tr>
    </table>
    <!-- ONE primary CTA, solid fill, ≥44px tall -->
    <a href="https://app.ledgerline.com/invoices/4812"
       style="display:inline-block; background:#2456d6; color:#ffffff;
              padding:14px 24px; border-radius:8px; font-size:16px;
              text-decoration:none;">View receipt</a>
    <p style="font-size:14px; color:#5c636b;">
      Button not working? https://app.ledgerline.com/invoices/4812</p>
  </td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:16px 24px; font-size:14px; color:#5c636b;">
    <a href="…" style="color:#5c636b;">Manage email preferences</a> ·
    <a href="…" style="color:#5c636b;">Unsubscribe from payment notifications</a>
  </td></tr>
</table>

A plain-text twin ships alongside (Content-Type: multipart/alternative). Test matrix: Apple Mail light/dark, Gmail light/dark, Outlook desktop.

Why it passes. Every 9.1 spec row is instantiated: 600px table, system stack, 16px body / 22px title, weight+space hierarchy, exactly one 44px+ solid CTA with a link fallback line, cell padding, alt-covered images (none critical), and a footer whose unsubscribe is as legible as any upsell would be. Quiet chrome + clear amounts = trust-path craft (L14: receipts are high-trust).

Rejected. The 9.1 don’t column: the receipt total baked into a hero image (invisible with images blocked); layout built on CSS grid (collapses in Outlook); a newsletter-style dashboard of upsells around the amount.

Ch 9 §9.1-B: One job per email; live text for claims

Concept. 9.1 do/don’t: one job per email; live text for claims; prefers-plain-text twin for transactional; never a newsletter-as-dense-dashboard.

Scenario. Relay’s weekly digest tries to include: metrics, three feature announcements, a webinar, and a survey.

Example (the fix). The digest is split: the weekly email keeps one job — "Your week: 214 tickets resolved, median first reply 42 min" as live text with a single CTA "See full report". Feature announcements move to a monthly product-notes email. The claim "42 min median first reply" is HTML text, not a rendered PNG chart headline, so it survives image blocking and is searchable.

Why it passes. One job per email; the load-bearing claim is live text; images (a small sparkline) are enhancement with alt "First-reply time trend, improving".

Ch 9 §9.2-A: @media print for a receipt — strip chrome, survive B&W

Concept. 9.2 table: hide nav/chrome/toasts; expand accordions; show link URLs where needed; break-inside: avoid on rows; assume B&W with patterns/labels for status; 10–12pt body, margins ≥0.5in; headers/footers with title/date/page; print user-entered values, not empty widgets.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s in-app receipt view gets a "Print receipt" action.

Example.

@media print {
  .nav, .sidebar, .toast-region, .sticky-actions { display: none; }
  .accordion__panel { display: block !important; }        /* expand all */
  a[href^="http"]::after { content: " (" attr(href) ")"; font-size: 9pt; }
  .line-item { break-inside: avoid; }
  body { font-size: 11pt; color: #000; }
  @page {
    margin: 0.5in;
    @bottom-right { content: counter(page) " of " counter(pages); font-size: 9pt; } /* page number: "1 of 2" */
  }
  .status-pill { background: none !important; border: 1pt solid #000; }
  .status-pill--paid::before { content: "✓ "; }            /* label + mark, not fill color */
  .page-footer { position: fixed; bottom: 0; font-size: 9pt; }
  /* footer renders: "Ledgerline receipt — Invoice #4812 — printed 2026-07-15 — Page 1 of 2" */
}

Where @page margin boxes are unsupported (most browser print engines), the fixed .page-footer carries the rendered "Page 1 of 2" string from the PDF pipeline — the 9.2 header/footer row (title, date, page number) is complete either way. The payment-method field prints its value ("Visa •••• 4242"), not an empty select widget. When the document requires a confidentiality marking, the footer adds it: the enterprise SLA report variant (§9.2-B) stamps "Confidential — Norbank internal" in the footer of every page — the fourth, conditional element of the 9.2 header/footer row.

Why it passes. Chrome gone, accordions expanded, rows unbreakable, status survives B&W via border + ✓ + the word "Paid" (multi-channel under grayscale, L11), 11pt body within the 10–12pt band, 0.5in margins, and a footer carrying all required elements: document title, date, page number — plus confidentiality when required.

Measure. Ch 9 measure line: “Critical content within margins; B&W still legible” — print-to-PDF in grayscale as a release check on the receipt trust path.

Ch 9 §9.2-B: PDF export — print-faithful preview, tagged PDF

Concept. 9.2: export buttons preview a print-faithful layout when legal/money is involved; tagged PDF when enterprise sells; selectable text and real headings — never a flattened screenshot; no “Download PDF” that screenshots a glass dashboard.

Scenario. Relay sells to enterprises that require quarterly SLA compliance reports as PDF.

Example. The "Export PDF" flow opens a preview rendered from the print stylesheet (not the dashboard DOM): white background, solid fills, H1 "SLA Compliance Report — Q2 2026", real <h1>/<h2> tag structure carried into a tagged PDF with selectable text, table headers marked as header cells, and the charts re-rendered with pattern fills + direct labels for grayscale. Every page’s footer carries "SLA Compliance Report — Q2 2026 · generated 2026-07-15 · Page N of M", and because Norbank’s contract classifies the report, the footer additionally stamps "Confidential — Norbank internal" (the conditional confidentiality element of the 9.2 header/footer row). File properties carry title and language.

Why it passes. The export is a first-class print surface: faithful preview before commit (money/legal), tagged and selectable for enterprise accessibility procurement.

Rejected. html2canvas(dashboard) → a 3MB flattened screenshot of a dark glassmorphic dashboard, unreadable in B&W and opaque to screen readers.

Ch 9 §9.3-A: Safe-area insets on a sticky pay bar [Cross-domain]

Concept. 9.3: env(safe-area-inset-*) on shell edges and fixed CTAs; bottom primary CTA uses padding-bottom: max(space-4, env(safe-area-inset-bottom)); primary targets ≥44×44.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s mobile invoice view has a sticky "Pay now" bar; on an iPhone with a home indicator, the old build’s button was half-covered by the indicator zone (review question 5’s scenario).

Example.

.pay-bar {
  position: fixed; inset-inline: 0; bottom: 0;
  background: var(--surface);
  border-top: 1px solid var(--border-subtle);
  padding: var(--space-3) var(--space-4);
  padding-bottom: max(var(--space-4), env(safe-area-inset-bottom)); /* 16px or the inset, whichever is larger */
}
.pay-bar__button { min-height: 48px; width: 100%; } /* ≥44 craft target */

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, viewport-fit=cover">

Why it passes. The exact textbook recipe (max(space-4, env(safe-area-inset-bottom))) keeps the CTA clear of the home indicator on notched devices while falling back to space-4 elsewhere; the 48px button clears the 44 craft bar (and trivially the 24×24 WCAG 2.5.8 AA floor). Cross-domain: safe-area layout (9.3) + space token (5.5) + touch-target convention in one bar.

Measure. Ch 9 measure line: “Primary CTA clear of home indicator / notch” — device-lab screenshot on a notched iPhone in the release checklist.

Ch 9 §9.3-B: Gestures, notch landscape, and hover-only failure

Concept. 9.3: keep destructive swipes away from system back-gesture edge zones; no primary controls in the landscape camera-cutout band; hover-only affordances fail on mobile — sheets + buttons instead; don’t lock orientation unless the task is inherently media-canvas with an alternative.

Scenario. Relay mobile: swipe actions on ticket rows, plus a video-review screen.

Example.

  • Row swipe: "Archive" swipe starts only after a 24px dead zone from the screen’s left/right edges, so iOS/Android back gestures don’t trigger archiving; archive is Soft-undo anyway ("Archived — Undo" toast) as defense in depth.
  • Landscape ticket view: the toolbar insets padding-left: env(safe-area-inset-left) so no button sits in the camera-cutout band.
  • Row actions that were hover-revealed on desktop become an explicit per-row overflow button on touch, opening a bottom sheet with "Assign" / "Snooze" / "Archive" buttons — no hover required.
  • The video-review screen suggests landscape but never locks it; portrait shows the same controls stacked.

Why it passes. Destructive gestures respect system gesture zones (with an undo net), cutout bands hold no primary controls, every hover affordance has a touch peer, and orientation reflows rather than locks.

Rejected. Hover-only row actions shipped to mobile (the named anti-pattern) and a hard landscape lock on a form screen.

Ch 9 §9.3-C: Foldables and desktop window chrome

Concept. 9.3: foldables — two logical panes over one form stretched across the crease; no interactive targets on the hinge; desktop PWA/Electron — honor traffic-light/drag regions; no controls under window chrome.

Scenario. Relay on a Galaxy Fold and as an Electron desktop app.

Example.

  • Fold posture: with the hinge vertical, Relay presents list pane (left) | ticket pane (right) using the viewport segments API; the composer’s "Send" button is explicitly kept ≥24px away from the hinge band; a single form is never stretched across the crease.
  • Electron: the custom title bar declares -webkit-app-region: drag, with buttons carved out via no-drag; the top-left 80×36px traffic-light region contains no app controls; the tab strip starts after it.

Why it passes. Panes map to physical segments instead of fighting them; nothing interactive lives on the hinge or under OS window chrome.

Ch 9 §9.4-A: Cross-surface checklist run on one artifact — the paid invoice

Concept. 9.4 checklist: (1) same semantic roles across web/email/native; (2) brand-hero on marketing/email headers, quiet tool in product + transactional mail; (3) safe-area padding on every fixed edge control; (4) print path verified for trust documents; (5) forced-colors/dark clients sampled. (This is also review question 5, worked.)

Scenario. Ledgerline invoice #4812 exists as: in-app receipt view, email receipt, and PDF download.

Example (checklist run, recorded in the ship review).

# Check Evidence
1 Same roles In-app uses surface/fg-default/accent; email maps the same intents to inline hex (#ffffff/#1a1d21/#2456d6) from the token export tokens-to-email.json; native iOS uses the same semantic names
2 Brand vs quiet Marketing header carries the hero illustration; the receipt email and in-app view are quiet chrome — logo, amounts, one CTA
3 Safe areas Sticky "Pay now" bar uses max(space-4, env(safe-area-inset-bottom)) (9.3-A)
4 Print path @media print receipt verified grayscale (9.2-A); PDF export tagged (9.2-B)
5 FC/dark sampling Web receipt checked under forced-colors: active; email screenshot set: Gmail dark (partial-invert client) + Apple Mail dark — amount text confirmed legible in both

Why it passes. One trust artifact traced through every surface with the five checklist items evidenced — type/measure (email 600px vs in-app 520px form column), grayscale contrast, single-CTA hierarchy, and safe-area behavior all resolved consistently. Craft ∝ trust × frequency (L14): a receipt is maximal-trust, so it gets the full cross-surface pass.

End of Part II companion examples.

Interaction & Information Work (Chapters 10–14)

Section headings mirror the textbook’s numbering so coverage is auditable. Laws are cited L1–L14; undo classes as Soft / Quarantine / Hard; WCAG success criteria with their conformance level (A / AA / AAA); touch targets as 44×44 craft bar vs 24×24 WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 AA floor.
