Chapter 10 — Feedback, Latency, Undo & State

Ch 10.1 — The feedback loop (trigger → ack → work → resolve → undo) — Example

Concept. All five loop phases and their failure modes (§10.1); silence is a bug; L5 + L7.

Scenario. “Archive conversation” in a team inbox product (“Helm Inbox”), the highest-frequency mutation in the app (~40×/day per user → L14 says spend craft here).

Example. One action, five phases:

Phase What ships Numbers / tokens
Trigger Archive button visible on row focus/hover and in row overflow menu; keyboard E. Hit target 44×44px (craft bar; ≥24×24 SC 2.5.8 AA floor). size.target.touch = 44px
Acknowledge Button gets pressed state (opacity 0.7 via motion.fast 120ms) within one frame; row begins collapse. ack ≤100ms (L5)
Work Optimistic: row leaves the list immediately; no spinner needed because rollback is cheap. 0 network wait shown
Resolve Polite status region: "Conversation archived." Toast at elevation tier 3. aria-live="polite" (SC 4.1.3 Status Messages, AA)
Undo Toast: "Archived. Undo" — Undo focusable via keyboard, window 7s. Soft undo, 5–10s class

Why it passes. Every phase answers its question: no ambiguous target (trigger), no dead button (≤100ms ack), no blank wait (optimistic work), no toast-only failure (resolve pairs status text + row state), and undo replaces a confirm (L7). Acknowledgment is treated as infrastructure — the Slack-send-state / Linear-optimistic-insert steal mechanic.

Rejected. The silent version: click → nothing for 800ms → row vanishes with no toast → user unsure whether they archived or deleted. Silence is a bug (§10.1).

Measure. Time-to-ack (p95 ≤100ms), undo usage rate, support tickets containing “where did my conversation go.”

Ch 10.2-A — Latency budget tiers (L5) — Example

Concept. The five tiers Instant / Fast / Perceptible / Interrupt / Long with matched UI patterns (§10.2).

Scenario. Five real actions in a project-management app (“Trellum”), one per tier.

Example.

Tier Action Budget UI shipped Microcopy
Instant Toggle “Star project” 0–100ms Icon fills instantly; ripple 120ms (motion.fast); button disabled 300ms against double-fire —
Fast Rename inline title, commit on blur 100–300ms Inline pending: title stays put, 16px spinner replaces the checkmark in place — layout stable —
Perceptible Load board with 200 cards 300ms–1s Layout-matched skeleton: 3 columns × 5 card skeletons at exact card height 88px —
Interrupt Export board to PDF 1–5s Determinate bar "Exporting… 60%" + "Cancel" (safe to cancel) “Exporting… 60%”
Long Import 10,000 rows from CSV >5s Job persists; modal releases immediately: "Import started — we'll notify you when it's done." Notification on completion deep-links to result. “Import started — we’ll notify you when it’s done.”

Why it passes. Acknowledge ≤100ms in all five; never a blank full-page wait for a button press; the Long tier never holds the modal hostage (§10.2 table, last row).

Rejected. A full-page spinner for the rename (Fast-tier action treated as Interrupt), and a modal that blocks for the whole CSV import (Long-tier work hostage-holding).

Measure. p50/p95 per action against its tier budget; % of Long jobs whose completion notification is clicked.

Ch 10.2-B — Optimistic vs pessimistic prefer-when — Example

Concept. Optimistic when rollback is cheap; pessimistic when money/legal/mass-notify/shared blast radius (§10.2 prefer-when).

Scenario. Same product, two mutations side by side.

Example.
- Optimistic — “Create draft doc”: doc appears in the list instantly with a subtle Saving… chip; on server ack the chip flips to nothing; on failure the doc row shows "Couldn't save — Retry" inline and the draft body is kept locally.
- Pessimistic — “Invite all 214 workspace members”: button shows in-place pending "Sending invites…"; nothing is claimed until the server confirms; request carries idempotency key invite_batch:ws_88a1:attempt_9f2c — a client-generated attempt ID minted once per user action and reused verbatim on every retry, so a flaky connection can never send the batch twice. (A wall-clock timestamp in the key would mint a new key per retry and defeat the dedupe — see Ch 10.2-C.)

Why it passes. Draft-create rollback is cheap (delete a local row); invite-all is mass-notify — external irreversibility, so pessimistic + idempotent (§10.2).

Rejected. The failure-if-wrong pair named by the textbook: optimistic invite-all that says “Invited!” before the server (silent wrong state), and a confirm dialog on every draft create (confirm tax).

Ch 10.2-C — Double-submit protection — Example

Concept. Disable + in-place pending + idempotent request keys on once-only actions (§10.2, 10.F).

Scenario. “Pay $149.00” in checkout.

Example.

// TS pseudo-API — the key belongs to the ATTEMPT, not the button:
// minted when an attempt starts, reused verbatim for transport retries
// of that attempt, and replaced before any new attempt (decline, edited
// card, changed total) so the processor can't replay the old response.
let attemptKey: string | undefined;

async function onPayClick() {
  attemptKey ??= `order_7741:${crypto.randomUUID()}`; // new attempt → new key
  payBtn.disabled = true;                     // no second click possible
  payBtn.label = "Processing…";               // in-place pending, layout stable
  try {
    await api.charge({
      amountCents: 14900,
      idempotencyKey: attemptKey,             // server dedupes transport retries
    });
  } catch (err) {
    // Transport failure: keep the key — the retry is the SAME attempt.
    // Anything else (decline, validation): clear it — the next submit
    // is a NEW attempt and must carry a fresh key.
    if (!isTransportError(err)) attemptKey = undefined;
    throw err;
  }
}

Retry after network failure reuses the same idempotencyKey, so a flaky connection can never double-charge — while a resubmit after a decline or a changed total gets a fresh key, so the corrected attempt is never mistaken for a replay (same contract as Ch 10.2-B’s “minted once per user action”).

Why it passes. §10.2 double-submit rule verbatim: disable + in-place pending + idempotent keys on pay. L14: checkout is maximum trust × meaningful frequency.

Ch 10.3 — Motion as feedback, not noise — Example

Concept. Motion duration tokens fast/default/slow/reduced; animate transform/opacity only; never motion as sole success signal (§10.3, L11).

Scenario. A filter sheet opening on mobile, and a “copied” confirmation.

Example.

:root {
  --motion-fast: 120ms;      /* press/hover ack: 100–150ms */
  --motion-default: 200ms;   /* state transitions: 150–250ms */
  --motion-slow: 320ms;      /* sheets/large reveals: 300–400ms */
}
.sheet { transition: transform var(--motion-slow) ease-out; } /* transform only */
.chip  { transition: opacity var(--motion-fast); }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .sheet, .chip { transition-duration: 1ms; } /* `reduced` token: instant */
}

Copy-link success is not just a bounce animation: the button also swaps label to "Copied" for 2s and fires a polite status message — icon + text, multi-channel (L11).

Why it passes. Every animation marks a known state change (sheet opened, copy succeeded); durations sit inside the token ranges; prefers-reduced-motion honored; success never signaled by motion alone.

Rejected. A checkmark that only pulses green with no text (motion + color as sole channel — violates L11 and fails users with reduced motion).

Ch 10.4-A — Soft undo — Example

Concept. Soft undo class: 5–10s toast with Undo; prefer for archive, mute, send, local delete (§10.4).

Scenario. “Send email” in Helm Inbox — the Gmail Undo Send steal mechanic.

Example. On Send, message enters a 10s hold queue. Toast: "Sending… Undo" with a visible countdown ring. Undo pulls the draft back into the composer with cursor position restored. After 10s: "Sent."

Why it passes. Send-to-one-person becomes locally reversible by delaying the external event — undo > confirm (L7) without adding a confirm dialog to every send.

Rejected. Soft toast for a team-visible permanent destroy (§10.4 reject column) — a 7s toast is not consent for deleting the shared workspace wiki.

Measure. Undo-send usage rate; “recall this email” support requests (should approach 0).

Ch 10.4-B — Quarantine — Example

Concept. Quarantine class: Trash/recycle ~30d for recoverable user-owned content (§10.4).

Scenario. Deleting a personal document in a Drive-like product.

Example. Delete moves the doc to Trash immediately (no modal). Toast: "Moved to Trash. Items in Trash are deleted after 30 days. Undo". Trash view shows per-item "Deleted Jul 15 · auto-removes Aug 14" and a "Restore" action. Restore returns the doc to its original folder and announces "Report Q3.pdf restored to /Finance."

Why it passes. Drive-Trash steal mechanic verbatim; recoverable object, user-owned content → Quarantine, not Hard confirm.

Rejected. Pretending Trash is soft undo for shared ACL deletes without notice (§10.4 reject): if deleting revokes 12 collaborators’ access now, quietly trashing it hides a shared blast radius.

Ch 10.4-C — Hard confirm — Example

Concept. Hard confirm class: modal with blast radius named; only for external irreversibility (§10.4).

Scenario. Deleting a production database in a cloud console.

Example. Modal copy:

Delete production database orders-primary?
This permanently destroys 214 GB of data and disconnects 3 running services (checkout-api, reports, webhooks). This cannot be undone.
Type orders-primary to confirm.
[Cancel] [Delete database]

Confirm button disabled until the typed name matches (GitHub dangerous-zone steal mechanic — type-to-confirm because blast is extreme). Focus is trapped in the modal; on cancel, focus returns to the trigger (L9).

Why it passes. Confirm is reserved for prod destroy; the blast radius is named with numbers, not “Are you sure?”; type-to-confirm scales friction to consequence.

Rejected. Confirm-on-every-archive and custom scary modals per page (§10.4 reject) — the confirm tax that trains users to click through.

Ch 10.4-D — Bulk operation partial failure — Example

Concept. Bulk ops: show N selected; on partial failure keep successes, report failures with retry (§10.4, §12.5 #4).

Scenario. “Archive 40 issues” (textbook review prompt #37).

Example. Toolbar showed "40 selected". Server archives 37, fails 3. Result region (not toast-only):

"37 of 40 issues archived. 3 failed:"
- #812 Payment retry loop — permission denied
- #799 Dark mode QA — network error [Retry]
- #754 Import crash — network error [Retry]
[Retry all 3] [Dismiss]

The 37 stay archived; the 3 remain selected in the list.

Why it passes. Successes kept, failures listed per-item with retry — never a silent whole-batch rollback (§10.4 bulk rule).

Rejected. "Something went wrong" toast that rolls back all 40 silently — user redoes 37 successful archives.

Ch 10.5 — Interruptions & live regions — Example

Concept. One modal at a time; toast queue at elevation tier 3; never steal focus from typing; polite vs assertive (§10.5; SC 4.1.3 Status Messages AA; L9).

Scenario. User is typing a comment while a PDF-export progress dialog is open and three background events fire: export finished, teammate joined, session about to expire.

Example.
- “Export ready” and “Ana joined” enter the toast queue (max 1 visible, 5s each, z token elevation.3 — above scrim, below critical blockers). Both announce via role="status" / aria-live="polite". Focus never leaves the comment box; toast actions ("Open export") are reachable by keyboard (F6/documented shortcut) but focus is not moved into them.
- “Session expires in 60s — your comment will be preserved” is a blocking risk: rendered as role="alert" (assertive) with an "Extend session" button. This is the sparing assertive case: an error about to destroy work.
- One modal at a time: when the 60s countdown hits 0 and the session-expiry alert must escalate to a blocking re-auth modal, the still-open PDF-export progress dialog is closed first — the export continues as a background job (Long-tier pattern, §10.2) and its “Export ready” toast simply waits in the queue. The re-auth modal opens alone; two stacked modals never exist, and the queued toasts drain only after the modal is dismissed.

Why it passes. Polite for status, assertive only for the blocking case (WCAG 4.1.3: status vs alert); one modal at a time — demonstrated at the export-dialog / re-auth collision, where the earlier modal yields rather than stacking; typing focus stolen only when destructive risk requires it.

Rejected. Three stacked toasts each grabbing focus, throwing away half-typed characters.

Ch 10.6 — The designed state matrix (L6) — Example

Concept. All seven baseline states with real chrome/content (§10.6).

Scenario. The “Projects” list screen in Trellum.

Example.

State Shipped UI Microcopy
Empty Air + one primary CTA + 3 template cards “Create your first project” / “Start from template”
Loading Skeleton: 6 rows at exactly 56px row height, matching avatar+title+meta layout —
Partial First 25 rows real; below them, 3 skeleton rows + inline "Loading 25 more…" “Loading 25 more…”
Error Region error card in the list area, list chrome intact “Couldn’t load projects. [Retry] [Contact support]”
Offline Persistent banner; list shows cache “You’re offline — showing projects from 12 min ago.”
Denied Explanation + path “You don’t have access to this team’s projects. [Request access]”
Syncing Explicit affordance next to page title “Syncing… 2 changes pending” (not an unlabeled spinner)

Skeletons are layout-matched so content never jumps (§10.6 forms note): the skeleton row grid uses the same grid-template-columns: 40px 1fr 120px 80px as the loaded row.

Why it passes. “No data” is not a state — each of the seven answers a different user question with distinct chrome and a next step (L6).

Rejected. One centered spinner covering all seven situations, or an “Error” that dumps the empty-state illustration.

Measure. Count of states with designed UI in the component spec (must be 7/7 before ship gate).

Ch 10.7 — Empty vs zero vs error taxonomy — Example

Concept. The 8-row critical taxonomy with distinct CTAs (§10.7).

Scenario. Same “Projects” list; textbook drill #6 answered with headline + CTA per situation.

Example.

Situation Headline Primary CTA Anti-pattern avoided
Never-used “Create your first project” [New project] + 3 templates 12-step carousel
True empty “All projects archived or deleted” [New project] · “Restore from Trash” Reusing “Welcome!” copy
Filtered-to-zero “0 results — 3 filters active” + chips Status: Done × Owner: me × Q3 × [Clear filters] “No projects yet” while filters are on
Search zero “No matches for ‘roadmpa’ — did you mean roadmap?” [Clear search] · “Search all teams” Fake results / silent fallback to popular
Error “Couldn’t load projects” [Retry] · Contact support Toast-only failure + empty art
Denied “You don’t have access to Design team projects” [Request access] Dead end
Offline empty “You’re offline. Showing 14 cached projects.” [Retry when online] Spinner forever
Partial / stale “Updated 26 min ago” staleness chip [Refresh] Presenting stale as live

Ch 10.7-B — Taxonomy decision rule — Example

Concept. The if/else classifier (§10.7 decision rule).

Scenario. Frontend state resolver for the list above.

Example.

function classifyListState(s: ListSnapshot): ListState {
  if (s.httpStatus === 401 || s.httpStatus === 403) return "denied";
  if (s.requestFailed)                              return "error";
  if (s.items.length > 0)                           return "populated";
  if (s.query.length > 0)                           return "search-zero";
  if (s.activeFilters.length > 0)                   return "filtered-to-zero";
  if (s.userEverCreated)                            return "true-empty";
  return "never-used";
}

Why it passes. Implements the rule verbatim: clearing filters/search would reveal items → zero states, never first-empty; 403/401 → denied; failure → error; teaching UI only when legitimately vacant with no active refine.

Ch 10.7-C — Case B: Empty → first artifact → habit — Example

Concept. Case B (§10.7): air + one CTA + template → return to density.

Scenario. New Trellum workspace, day 0.

Example. Never-used screen: generous whitespace, one primary button "Create a project", three template cards (“Sprint board”, “Bug triage”, “Launch plan”) that pre-populate 8 realistic cards each so the future is simulated. The moment the first project exists, the shell returns to the dense default list — the empty art never becomes permanent furniture.

Why it passes. Case B exactly; templates teach by artifact, not tour.

Rejected. Permanent empty illustration and a hard-commit template with no revert (Case B rejects both — template application is Soft-undoable: "Template applied. Undo").

Measure. Time-to-first-artifact (target <2 min) and D7 return rate.

Ch 10.8 — Optimistic vs pessimistic decision matrix — Example

Concept. The six-row context matrix (§10.8).

Scenario. One product (“Trellum”) mapping each matrix row to a real control.

Example.

Control Bias shipped Concrete behavior
Star project Optimistic + Soft undo Instant fill; toast “Starred. Undo” 6s
Archive my draft Optimistic + Quarantine Instant move; “In Archive — restore anytime”
Delete shared board Hard confirm Blast-radius modal (see Ch 10.4-C style): “…removes access for 9 members”
Upgrade plan ($ charge) Pessimistic + idempotent “Processing…” until bank confirms; key sub_upgrade:ws_88a1:<attempt-uuid> — fresh per attempt, reused only on transport retry (Ch 10.2-C)
Email all watchers (312) Undo Send window 10s hold + “Sending to 312 watchers… Undo”
AI “clean up all card titles” Diff → apply → undo See Ch 14.5

Ch 10.8-A — Case A: Checkout — Example

Concept. Case A (§10.8): pessimistic; field errors; receipt.

Scenario. Card declined during a $149.00 checkout.

Example. Submit → in-place pending on Pay button → bank declines → form re-renders with input preserved, field-local error on the card group: "Your card was declined. No charge was made. Try another card or contact your bank." Error Summary at top links to the field. Success path ends on a receipt page with order number #7741, amount, and emailed copy.

Why it passes. Pessimistic where money moves (L14 trust × frequency); field errors preserve input (§10.6); receipt closes the Resolve phase honestly.

Rejected. Optimistic "Paid!" before the bank answers (Case A reject).

Measure. Payment success rate, error-recovery rate (declines that convert on retry), keyboard-only completion rate, chargeback rate.

Ch 10.8-B — Case C: Shared destructive delete — Example

Concept. Case C (§10.8): confirm with blast radius or Trash 30d; focus trap + announced result + focus restore.

Scenario. Deleting a shared folder “Q3 Launch” with 9 collaborators.

Example. Because the object is recoverable, the team ships Quarantine with notice instead of Hard confirm: "Move 'Q3 Launch' to Trash? 9 people will lose access until it's restored. [Cancel] [Move to Trash]". Dialog traps focus; on completion a polite status announces "'Q3 Launch' moved to Trash"; focus returns to the row that follows the deleted one (trigger is gone), per L9.

Why it passes. Blast radius named even in the Quarantine path; soft toast alone was not enough for a team-visible destroy (Case C reject); full L9 focus contract.

Ch 10.F — Forms & auth playbook — Example

Concept. All eight playbook rows (§ Forms & auth playbook, expanded).

Scenario. Sign-up + billing-address form for Helm Inbox.

Example.

Rule Shipped
Labels <label for="email">Email</label> always visible above the field; placeholder used only for format hint "name@company.com" — never as the label
Validation Email format checked on blur; required-set checked on submit; nothing flags while the user is mid-keystroke
Errors Field-local: "Enter an email address, like name@company.com" under the field, aria-describedby linked; GOV.UK Error Summary at top: "There are 2 problems:" with anchor links #email, #postcode — focus moves to the summary on failed submit
Layout Trust path = 1 column, 480px max-width; only the paired short fields City / Postcode go 2-col, and only when the container query reports ≥560px
Double-submit “Create account” disables + "Creating…" in place; idempotent key on the create call
Auth autocomplete="email", autocomplete="new-password"; passkey offered first, password fallback; paste allowed in password field (password-manager friendly). Passkey/OTP-first also satisfies SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA — no memorization puzzle required
CAPTCHA Risk-based challenge with an accessible alternative (audio + email fallback) — no puzzle-only gate (Case F)
Session "Your session expires in 2 minutes. [Stay signed in]" warning; on timeout, the half-finished billing form is restored from local draft after re-auth — which also honors SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, Level A (don’t make users re-enter what they already gave)

Why it passes (cross-domain). One decision — the session-timeout draft restore — spans law (L6 state + L7 reversibility of interruption), token (space.stack.form = 24px consistent 1-col rhythm), and WCAG (3.3.7 Redundant Entry, Level A; 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA). That is the visual × interaction × a11y integration the rubric scores.

Rejected. Placeholder-as-label; validate-on-every-keystroke; clipboard-blocked password field (“false security theater”, §13.7).

Ch 10.F-B — Typeahead / combobox — Example

Concept. Prefer native <datalist> or full APG combobox; don’t fake autocomplete with divs (§ playbook).

Scenario. Two pickers in Trellum: a static “Country” field on the billing form, and the dynamic “Assignee” picker.

Example — native <datalist> branch (prefer for simple static suggestion lists).

<label for="country">Country</label>
<input list="countries" id="country" name="country" autocomplete="country-name" />
<datalist id="countries">
  <option value="Germany"></option>
  <option value="Ghana"></option>
  <option value="Greece"></option>
</datalist>

Two lines of markup buy browser-native keyboard, screen-reader, and autofill behavior with zero JS. Prefer-when: native <datalist> for simple, static suggestion lists where the browser’s default rendering is fine; step up to the full APG combobox only when you need async filtering, custom option rendering (avatars, metadata), or aria-activedescendant control — as the assignee picker below does.

Example — full APG combobox branch (async, custom-rendered).

<label for="assignee">Assignee</label>
<input id="assignee" role="combobox" aria-expanded="true"
       aria-controls="assignee-list" aria-activedescendant="opt-3"
       aria-autocomplete="list" />
<ul id="assignee-list" role="listbox">
  <li id="opt-3" role="option" aria-selected="true">Priya Raman</li>
</ul>

Arrow keys move aria-activedescendant; Enter selects; Esc closes and restores the typed text; typing filters after a 200ms debounce.

Why it passes. Both playbook branches shown with the boundary between them: cheap native <datalist> where it suffices, and the full APG combobox contract (arrow keys, typeahead, aria-activedescendant) where async filtering demands it — never a div stack that only mouse users can operate.

Ch 10.F-C — Offline form matrix — Example

Concept. Read-only / queue / conflict offline modes (§ playbook offline matrix).

Scenario. Editing a customer record on a train.

Example.
- Read-only offline: the “Change billing plan” button is disabled with inline reason "Unavailable offline — plan changes need a connection."
- Queue offline: name/notes edits save locally; banner "Offline — 3 changes queued"; on reconnect the banner flips to Syncing then clears.
- Conflict: a colleague edited the same record; see Ch 13.10 / Ch 14.4 for the keep-both/choose/merge UI.

Why it passes. Each mode is explicit L6 state with honest copy — mutating controls are never silently broken.

Chapter 11 — Search, Filter, Sort & Pagination

Ch 11.1 — Findability system map — Example

Concept. Five surfaces (global search/Cmd-K, in-place search, facets, sort, pagination) acting as one system (§11.1).

Scenario. Inventory admin for an e-commerce back office (“Stocklane”), 48,000 SKUs.

Example. All five surfaces write to one state object and one result region:

/inventory?q=usb-c&filters=status:low,warehouse:eu-1&sort=stock:asc&cursor=czE4NDI

Typing in the in-place search, toggling the Status: Low stock chip, or clicking the “Stock ▲” header all update: (1) the same table region, (2) the same URL, (3) the same result count line "37 of 48,102 SKUs", and (4) route to the same zero-state playbook (Ch 11.7). Cmd-K exists too — but it jumps to objects and actions (“Open SKU 8841”, “Create purchase order”), it does not replace this page.

Why it passes. Changing search/filter/sort updates the same region, URL, and recovery taxonomy (§11.1 rule); Cmd-K is a palette, not the search product (§11.2 opening).

Rejected. Filters that re-render a different component with its own hand-rolled empty state, so “0 results” looks different depending on how you got there.

Ch 11.2 — Search product requirements 1–8 — Example

Concept. The eight requirements of a complete search experience (§11.2).

Scenario. Global search in Stocklane.

Example.

  1. Query — visible in a persistent field, one-click clearable (× button, 44×44 target).
  2. Scope — segmented control above results: [This warehouse] [All warehouses] [Orders] [People]; default This warehouse labeled, not implied.
  3. Results — ranked list with type labels (SKU, Order, Supplier); ↑/↓ moves, Enter opens, type label announced.
  4. Empty query state — "Recent: USB-C hub 65W · Order #5521" + "Suggested actions: Create purchase order" — never a blank void.
  5. Zero results — "No matches for 'usbc hub 90w' in This warehouse." CTAs: [Clear search] · [Search all warehouses] · “Try ‘usb-c’”.
  6. Ranking honesty — see Ch 11.2-B.
  7. Error / denied — "Search is temporarily unavailable. [Retry]" vs "You don't have access to Orders search. [Request access]" — distinct from zero (Ch 10.7 taxonomy).
  8. Performance — keystroke echoed instantly in the field (≤100ms, L5); network debounced 200ms; pending shown as a thin progress bar above the result list so the list never thrashes.

Why it passes. All eight present; scope is obvious; zero is honest; error ≠ zero ≠ denied.

Rejected. Cmd-K-only strategy with no visible Search in chrome — the textbook’s steal note demands a progressive path for users who never learn the shortcut (Linear steal mechanic caveat).

Ch 11.2-B — Ranking honesty — Example

Concept. Never silently rewrite the query; announce fallbacks (§11.2 #6).

Scenario. User searches "chagrer" (typo).

Example. Result header: "Showing results for 'charger' (corrected). Search instead for 'chagrer'" — the fallback is declared and reversible in one click. When fuzzy stemming broadens "cables" → "cable", a quiet note "Including matches for 'cable'" appears.

Why it passes. Fall back with a declaration, never silently (§11.2 #6).

Rejected. Silently returning popular items disguised as matches (§11.2 #5 anti-pattern — fake results destroy ranking trust).

Ch 11.3 — Filter & faceted refine patterns — Example

Concept. Four filter patterns with prefer-when, plus the five rules (§11.3).

Scenario. Stocklane inventory on desktop and mobile.

Example.

Pattern Where shipped Concrete spec
Chip filters Desktop, ≤4 active dims Removable chips above table: Status: Low × EU-1 × + "Clear all"; chips 32px tall, hit slop to 44px
Filter sheet (mobile) Phone viewport <600px Bottom sheet, motion.slow 320ms; footer [Cancel] [Apply — show 37 results] count preview before commit
Sidebar facets Desktop power view Sticky left rail 240px; every change syncs URL
Inline column filters Table columns Filter icon with text tooltip + accessible name "Filter by status" — not a mystery icon only

Rules in force: active filters always visible as chips (never invisible constraints); result count announced on change ("12 of 480" via polite live region); filtered-to-zero uses [Clear filters] (Ch 10.7); URL persistence (Ch 11.6).

Why it passes. Pattern chosen by facet count and viewport, not fashion; count preview on the mobile sheet prevents blind Apply.

Rejected. Invisible constraints — a saved filter silently applied on page load with no chip showing, making “0 results” a lie the user can’t see.

Ch 11.3-B — Facet-count honesty — Example

Concept. Facet counts should not lie; disable or show 0 for dead ends (§11.3 last rule).

Scenario. Sidebar facet “Warehouse” while Status: Low stock is active.

Example.

Warehouse
◉ EU-1 (37)
○ US-2 (12)
○ APAC-1 (0)        ← rendered, shown as 0, non-clickable, aria-disabled="true"

Why it passes. APAC-1 given the current selection would be a dead end; showing (0) and disabling gives signal instead of a trap.

Rejected. Offering APAC-1 as a live option that lands the user on an unexplained zero.

Ch 11.4 — Sort — Example

Concept. Default sort expectations; header sort a11y; multi-sort; sort under search (§11.4).

Scenario. Stocklane table sorted while a search is active.

Example.

<th aria-sort="ascending" scope="col">
  <button>Stock <span aria-hidden="true">▲</span></button>
</th>
  • Default sort = Last updated ↓ (recent activity — the user expectation for an ops table); under an active search, default flips to relevance, and the sort control shows "Sort: Relevance" explicitly so switching to Stock ▲ is a visible, reversible choice — relevance is never silently dropped.
  • Click/Enter toggles asc → desc; change announced politely: "Sorted by stock, ascending."
  • Multi-sort is behind the column menu ("Then sort by…") and, when active, rendered as ordered badges 1· Stock ▲ 2· Name ▲ — the order is explicit.

Why it passes. Direction indicated (aria-sort + arrow + label — multi-channel, L11), keyboard supported, polite announcement, relevance/field choice surfaced (§11.4 all four bullets).

Rejected. Silently dropping relevance ranking the moment any column is clicked, with no way back.

Ch 11.5 — Pagination vs infinite scroll vs load-more — Example

Concept. Prefer-when / avoid-when for the three traversal patterns + hard rules (§11.5).

Scenario. Three surfaces in one company’s products.

Example.

Surface Pattern Why (textbook prefer-when)
Stocklane SKU table Paged (50/page) + sticky header Need item N; row actions; stable address; “select all” math stays sane
Mobile activity feed in Trellum Load more button after 30 items User-controlled growth; mobile-friendly
Consumer discovery feed Infinite scroll + "Load more" keyboard peer + footer relocated to a sidebar Discovery, low per-item commitment; AT path preserved

Hard rules honored: the infinite feed provides a load-more peer reachable by keyboard and landmarks so screen-reader users are not trapped; back-navigation restores scroll position and selection; count line reads "~2,400 items" — approx honesty, no fake precision; the table explicitly does not use infinite append (breaks sticky-header math and select-all).

Why it passes. Pattern chosen by task; every choice keeps an AT-reachable path (§11.5 hard rules).

Rejected. Infinite scroll on the admin table — footer unreachable, “Select all” meaningless, position N unaddressable.

Ch 11.6 — URL persistence & deep links — Example

Concept. Encode q/filters/sort/page|cursor; prefer cursors for large mutable sets; Back restores refine state (§11.6).

Scenario. A teammate shares a filtered view in Slack.

Example.

https://stocklane.app/inventory
  ?q=usb-c
  &filters=status:low,wh:eu-1      ← stable keys ("wh"), not display labels ("Warehouse EU One")
  &sort=stock:asc
  &after=czE4NDI                   ← opaque cursor token, not page=3

Cursor chosen because SKUs insert constantly — page numbers would drift. Opening the link reproduces the exact view. From row → detail page → browser Back: query, chips, sort, and scroll offset restore from history state; the list does not reset to defaults. For a privacy-sensitive view (filter by employee salary band in an HR tool), filters live in session storage instead, with an explicit "Save view" action.

Why it passes. All four params encoded with stable keys; cursor over page for mutable sets; Back restores refine state; the privacy exception implemented exactly as the textbook allows.

Rejected. Back returning the user to an unfiltered page-1 default — destroying five minutes of refine work.

Ch 11.7 — Search + filter zero-state playbook — Example

Concept. The six-row zero-state matrix with copy + CTA (§11.7).

Scenario. Stocklane results region (answers textbook drill #12/#36).

Example.

State Copy shipped CTA
Empty query, no filters “Recent: USB-C hub 65W · Suggested: Low-stock report” Focus in search field; [Browse all SKUs]
Query, 0 hits “No matches for ‘usbc hub 90w’“ [Clear search] · [Search all warehouses]
Filters, 0 hits “No SKUs match these filters:” + chips Low stock × EU-1 × [Clear filters]
Query + filters, 0 hits “No matches for ‘hub’ with filters Low stock × EU-1 ×” — the chips rendered inline, so both constraints are named, not counted [Clear search] or [Clear filters] — both offered
Error “Couldn’t load results” [Retry]
Denied “You don’t have access to search Orders” [Request access]

Offline variant (drill #36): "You're offline — showing cached results from 14:02" + [Retry when online].

Why it passes. Both constraints named when both are active; each state’s CTA removes exactly the blocking constraint (§11.7 matrix).

Ch 11.8 — Search accessibility & performance — Example

Concept. Visible label, role="search", throttled polite announcements, 150–300ms debounce, in-flight cancel, keyboard map (§11.8; L9).

Scenario. The in-place search field above the SKU table.

Example.

<form role="search">
  <label for="sku-search">Search SKUs</label>  <!-- visible, not placeholder-only -->
  <input id="sku-search" type="search" />
</form>
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" class="visually-hidden" id="result-count"></div>

const search$ = fromInput(input).pipe(
  debounceTime(200),               // inside the 150–300ms band
  switchMap(q => api.search(q))    // switchMap cancels in-flight on new keystroke
);
announceThrottled("37 results", 1000); // polite, ≤1 announcement/second

Keyboard: ↓ enters results, ↑/↓ traverse, Enter opens, Esc clears query (first press) then closes the overlay (second press), focus restored to the trigger on close (L9).

Why it passes (cross-domain). One field decision combines L5 (keystroke echo instant, network debounced), L9 (focus restore), SC 4.1.3 AA (throttled status), and the labeled-landmark structure rule — the rubric’s cross-domain integration in miniature.

Chapter 12 — Selection, Tables & Drag-and-Drop

Ch 12.1 — Selection models — Example

Concept. Five models (single, multi-toggle, shift-range, scoped select-all, marquee) + the five rules (§12.1).

Scenario. Trellum issues list, 1,842 issues match the current filter, 25 per page.

Example.
- Single: clicking a row opens the detail inspector; click another replaces the selection.
- Multi-toggle: row checkbox toggles; Cmd/Ctrl-click on the row adds without opening.
- Shift-range: click row 4 (anchor), Shift-click row 12 → rows 4–12 selected. Keyboard: Space toggles, Shift+↓ extends from anchor, Ctrl/Cmd+A selects the scoped all.
- Scoped select-all: see Ch 12.1-B.
- Marquee: in the roadmap canvas view, drag-rectangle selects cards — with the keyboard alternative (Shift+Arrow range in list view) always available.

Rules: "9 selected" shown in the anchored toolbar; changing filters with an active selection announces "Selection cleared — filters changed" rather than silently dropping it; at 0 selected the bulk bar hides entirely (no enabled Delete button pointing at nothing).

Why it passes. All five models mapped to real surfaces; every rule from §12.1 has a shipped behavior.

Rejected. Cmd-click-only multi-select with no checkboxes (fails touch and discoverability — see Ch 14 review drill #32).

Ch 12.1-B — Scoped select-all microcopy — Example

Concept. “Select all” scope must be explicit; progressive-disclose the large scope (§12.1; textbook drill #14).

Scenario. Header checkbox clicked on the filtered list (25 on page, 1,842 matching).

Example. Checking the header checkbox selects the page and shows an inline banner:

"All 25 issues on this page are selected." [Select all 1,842 issues matching your filters]

Clicking the escalation link updates to:

"All 1,842 matching issues are selected." [Clear selection]

Destructive bulk on the large scope triggers a blast preview: "Archive 1,842 issues across 12 projects?"

Why it passes. The universe-scope is opt-in via a second explicit step, never the default (§12.1 rule 2) — the Gmail-style steal made honest.

Rejected. Header checkbox silently meaning “all 1,842” so a bulk delete nukes 1,817 rows the user never saw.

Ch 12.2 — Selection-anchored toolbar — Example

Concept. Contextual bulk bar when N>0; placement; partial failure; Esc (§12.2).

Scenario. 9 issues selected in Trellum.

Example. A bar slides in (motion.default 200ms, transform-only) pinned above the table header — a predictable sticky position that never covers row 1’s checkbox:

[9 selected]  [Archive] [Assign…] [Add label…]  [⋯ More]  [× Clear]

Primary bulk actions visible, long tail in ⋯ overflow (L8). Esc with focus in the list clears selection (shortcut listed in the ? shortcut sheet). Partial failure follows Ch 10.4-D.

Why it passes. Figma-style contextual chrome; selection count is the bar’s first element; overflow keeps the bar scannable.

Rejected. A floating bar that materializes on top of the first selected row, hiding the very checkbox the user just clicked.

Ch 12.3-A — Table structure & semantics — Example

Concept. Real <table>, <th scope>, sticky header, status not color-alone (§12.3 structure; L11).

Scenario. Stocklane SKU table.

Example.

<table>
  <thead class="sticky">   <!-- position: sticky; top: 0; background: var(--color-bg-surface) -->
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">SKU</th>
      <th scope="col" aria-sort="none"><button>Stock</button></th>
      <th scope="col">Status</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">USB-C Hub 65W</th>
      <td>12</td>
      <td><span class="badge badge--warn">▲ Low stock</span></td> <!-- icon + text, not color-only -->
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

Sticky header keeps an opaque --color-bg-surface background so text never overlaps rows, and focus rings on header buttons are not clipped by the sticky edge — SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA.

Why it passes (cross-domain). Semantics (real table + scope), interaction (sticky sort header), token (color.bg.surface), law (L11 status = icon+text+color), and WCAG 2.4.11 AA in one component.

Rejected. Div soup: <div class="row"> grids that give screen readers no column context, with red/green dots as the only status channel.

Ch 12.3-B — Column behaviors — Example

Concept. Six column behaviors: resize, reorder, show/hide, pin, inline edit, row actions (§12.3 column table).

Scenario. Power users configuring the SKU table.

Example.

Behavior Shipped spec
Resize 8px drag handle on column edge (hit-slop to 24px — SC 2.5.8 AA floor for this non-primary target); keyboard: header focus → Alt+←/→ resizes in 16px steps; widths persisted per user (prefs.table.inventory.widths)
Reorder Drag column or header menu “Move left / Move right”; on drop announce "Status column moved to position 2 of 6"
Show/hide Column picker popover with checkboxes; the identity column “SKU” is listed but disabled — required identity can’t be removed
Pin / freeze “SKU” pinned left on horizontal scroll; pinned cell keeps elevated shadow.raised edge so the boundary is visible
Inline edit Enter opens edit in the Stock cell; Esc cancels and restores prior value; blur commits with Soft undo toast "Stock updated 12 → 8. Undo"
Row actions Primary action “Reorder stock” visible per row; rest in ⋯ menu; on touch the menu is tap-reachable — never hover-only

Why it passes. Every behavior has a keyboard peer and a persistence/undo story; the inline-edit commit is explicitly assigned an undo class (§12.3: “commits with undo class”).

Ch 12.3-C — APG grid keyboard map — Example

Concept. Arrow cell navigation, Home/End, Enter/F2 edit, visible focus (§12.3 keyboard; answers drill #38).

Scenario. Spreadsheet-like bulk-edit mode of the SKU table.

Example.

Key Action
↑ ↓ ← → Move cell focus
Home / End First / last cell in row; Ctrl+Home/End = first/last cell of grid
Page Up / Down Jump one virtualized window (50 rows)
Enter or F2 Enter edit mode on editable cell
Esc (editing) Cancel edit, restore value, focus back on cell
Enter (on header button) Toggle sort; aria-sort updated; change announced
Space (on row checkbox) Toggle selection

Focus ring: 2px solid --color-border-focus with ≥3:1 contrast against adjacent colors; never outline: none.

Why it passes. Full APG grid map; focus visible ≥2px contrast ring exactly as §12.3 requires; sortable headers are real buttons inside <th>.

Ch 12.3-D — Table loading, filtered-to-zero, density — Example

Concept. Skeleton rows matching columns; in-table zero; error preserving setup; density token maps (§12.3 loading/empty + density).

Scenario. Same table, three moments.

Example.
- Loading: 8 skeleton rows using the table’s own grid-template-columns — column ghosts, not one grey slab.
- Filtered-to-zero: the <tbody> region shows "No SKUs match these filters" + [Clear filters], inside the table frame with the filter chips still visible above — not a full-page marketing illustration.
- Error: error region replaces rows only; header, column widths, and sort state preserved; [Retry].
- Density: toggle Comfortable / Compact / Dense as token maps, not one-off padding:

{
  "density": {
    "comfortable": { "row.height": "56px", "cell.padding.y": "16px", "font.size": "14px" },
    "compact":     { "row.height": "40px", "cell.padding.y": "8px",  "font.size": "13px" },
    "dense":       { "row.height": "32px", "cell.padding.y": "4px",  "font.size": "12px" }
  }
}

Newcomers land on Comfortable with template views; Dense is one toggle away — the Superhuman/Gmail-class mechanic without density elitism.

Why it passes. Zero state lives inside the region it describes; error never destroys column setup; density is systemic (token maps) per §12.3.

Ch 12.4 — Drag-and-drop requirements — Example

Concept. All nine DnD requirement rows (§12.4 table); SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements AA.

Scenario. Reordering sections in a Trellum project sidebar (desktop + touch + keyboard + screen reader).

Example.

Concern Shipped
Visible equivalent Row ⋯ menu: “Move up”, “Move down”, “Move to…” — the buttons/menu peer required by SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, AA
Gesture limit The mobile list has exactly one swipe action (swipe-left = Archive); reorder is via handle long-press or Move to… — never a second competing swipe
Desktop reorder Explicit 24×24 grip handle (⠿) at row start; the row body remains a plain click-to-open target — no ambiguous whole-row drag
Drop targets 2px insertion line --color-border-accent plus the moving row’s ghost label "Drop below 'Backlog'" — valid targets get the line, invalid get a ⃠ cursor + "Can't move into a locked section"; multi-channel, not color alone (L11)
Keyboard Space on handle = pick up ("Grabbed 'Sprint 12', position 3 of 8"), ↑/↓ = move ("Position 2 of 8"), Space = drop, Esc = cancel — APG pattern; “Move to…” dialog as the second peer
Screen readers All grab/move/drop strings above fired per step through a dedicated aria-live="polite" region (the APG default — each announcement is short, and the user’s own keypress just caused it, so polite queues cleanly); the region is emptied on drop/cancel so stale positions are never re-read. Assertive stays reserved for blocking errors per §10.5 — e.g. the drop failing server-side after an optimistic move would qualify; routine position updates do not
Touch Long-press 300ms on the handle initiates drag; page scroll still owns plain vertical pans; handle hit area ≥44×44
Undo Drop is Soft-undoable: "Moved 'Sprint 12' to position 2. Undo" (7s)
Reduced motion With prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, rows swap instantly — no fling/spring theater

Why it passes (cross-domain). One feature satisfies L7 (soft undo), L11 (multi-channel drop validity), the 44 craft / 24 AA target split, SC 2.5.7 AA (single-pointer alternative), and the reduced motion token.

Rejected (all named by textbook). Hover-only mobile DnD; drag-only merge for sync conflicts (Case H); color-only drop validity.

Ch 12.4-B — DnD prefer-when: handles vs move-to vs confirm — Example

Concept. Handles for desktop reorder; move-to dialog for deep hierarchies; confirm on permission-crossing drops (§12.4 prefer-when).

Scenario. Dragging a document between folders in a workspace tree.

Example. Shallow same-folder reorder = handle drag. Moving into a 6-level-deep tree = "Move to…" dialog with a searchable folder picker (dragging across 6 collapse levels is error-prone). Dropping into the folder “Externally shared / Clients” crosses a permission boundary → confirm: "Move 'Pricing.xlsx' to 'Clients'? 4 external guests will gain view access. [Cancel] [Move]".

Why it passes. Each prefer-when row mapped to the situation that triggers it; the ACL-crossing drop gets exactly one Hard-style confirm because access widens externally.

Ch 12.5 — Bulk operations checklist — Example

Concept. All six checklist items in one flow (§12.5; drill #37).

Scenario. “Archive 40 issues” end to end.

Example.
1. Scope: header checkbox = 25 on page; banner escalation to all 40 matching (Ch 12.1-B pattern).
2. N + blast preview: bar reads "40 selected"; Archive is non-destructive so no modal — a Delete of the same 40 would preview "Deletes 40 issues from 3 projects."
3. Idempotent: POST /issues:bulkArchive with operationId: "bulk_a91f" — retry-safe.
4. Partial success: 37/3 pattern from Ch 10.4-D.
5. Undo class matches blast: archive = Soft ("37 issues archived. Undo"); the delete variant = Quarantine (Trash 30d).
6. Announce + focus: polite status "37 issues archived, 3 failed"; focus stays on the bulk bar’s Retry control — sensible, not reset to <body>.

Why it passes. Six for six, and the undo-class assignment demonstrates the Soft-vs-Quarantine distinction on the same selection with different verbs.

Chapter 13 — Navigation, History, Disclosure, Teaching, Share, Autosave, Clipboard, Notifications & Collab

Ch 13.1 — Navigation shells, scent, landmarks — Example

Concept. Platform chrome bias; shared IA, native chrome; labeled core scent; skip link + landmarks (§13.1; L10).

Scenario. Trellum ships web, iOS, and Android.

Example.
- Web: left side nav + Cmd-K. iOS: bottom tab bar (Home / Inbox / Boards / Search). Android: Material nav bar. The IA — the four destinations and their names — is identical everywhere; the chrome is native everywhere (no pixel parity, L10).
- Scent: primary nav items are icon + label (“Boards”, not a lone kanban glyph) — icon-only primary nav stays banned until learnability is proven with data.
- Landmarks:

<a class="skip-link" href="#main">Skip to main content</a>
<header role="banner">…</header>
<nav aria-label="Primary">…</nav>
<!-- tabindex="-1": main is not focusable by default, and a skip link that
     only scrolls leaves focus behind — the next Tab re-enters the nav -->
<main id="main" tabindex="-1"><h1>Boards</h1> … </main>
<footer role="contentinfo">…</footer>

Heading outline h1 Boards → h2 Sprint 12 → h3 In progress mirrors the visual IA. Chrome is quiet (neutral --color-bg-chrome), content is loud — the tool test.

Why it passes. “Semantics & IA — yes; chrome — no” implemented literally; core action scent labeled; a11y structure landmarks complete.

Rejected. Shrunk-desktop web view wrapped in a native shell, and icon-only left rail where the third icon is anyone’s guess.

Ch 13.2 — History, deep links & Back — Example

Concept. Addressable objects; Back restores refine + focus; in-app back = real history; dirty guard only when needed; modal focus restore (§13.2; L9).

Scenario. Board → card detail → back.

Example. Every card has a URL (/b/sprint-12/c/TRL-812) — pasteable into Slack, openable cold. In-app “‹ Back” calls history.back() — it never maintains a parallel stack that fights the browser. Returning to the board restores filter chips, sort, scroll offset, and puts focus on card TRL-812’s tile. Because the card editor autosaves (13.6), Back never warns; the one dirty guard in the app is the unsent invite composer (autosave off): "Discard invite draft? [Keep editing] [Discard]". Closing the card modal returns focus to the tile that opened it (L9).

Why it passes. Deep links + honest history + refine restore + guard-only-when-data-would-be-lost, all four §13.2 rules.

Rejected. SPA “back” arrow that pops an internal stack while browser Back exits the app entirely.

Ch 13.3 — Progressive disclosure layers (L8) — Example

Concept. Primary / Overflow / Palette / Settings layers; disclosure vs discoverability tension; hover-card keyboard peers (§13.3; answers drill #19).

Scenario. Actions on a Trellum card.

Example.

Layer Actions placed there Why
Primary (on card) “Assign”, “Set status”, “Comment” Core path — must be found without a tour
Overflow (⋯ menu) “Duplicate”, “Move to board…”, “Copy link” Frequent enough for one click
Palette (Cmd-K / /) “Convert to epic”, “Export card JSON”, “Set custom field: Risk” Long-tail expert actions
Settings “Default card template”, “Auto-archive done after 30d” Rare preferences — not a feature dumping ground

Hovering an assignee avatar shows a hover card; the same card opens on keyboard focus, and dismiss is delayed + cancellable so the pointer can travel into it. The hover card is never the only path — “View profile” also lives in the ⋯ menu.

Why it passes. Long tail disclosed, critical path discoverable — the tension resolved per rule; hover has a focus peer.

Rejected (both textbook failure modes). All 14 actions as toolbar buttons on every card (expert dump), or “Assign” hidden in the palette only (buried core action).

Ch 13.4 — Teaching & first-artifact curriculum — Example

Concept. Identity → Artifact → Share → Return cue; reject carousels (§13.4; drill #20).

Scenario. New Trellum user, first session.

Example.
1. Identity: "What should teammates call you?" + role chip (one field, not a 9-step profile wizard).
2. Artifact: dropped straight into a real board pre-seeded from the chosen template; first card creation is celebrated once and is undoable (Soft).
3. Share: inline nudge after 3 cards: "Boards are better with people — invite one teammate" (skippable).
4. Return cue: if they leave mid-setup, next-day email "Your 'Launch plan' board is waiting — 3 cards to triage" deep-links to the exact board.

Help is in-context: a "?" next to “Epics” opens a 2-sentence explainer with a link to searchable docs. One primary action per screen; chrome predictable.

Why it passes. Teaching happens by making a real thing, not watching slides; templates simulate the future; every step maps to the four-step curriculum.

Rejected. Permanent onboarding carousel / modal wall on first launch — dismissed blind, teaches nothing, delays the artifact.

Measure. Time-to-first-value (first real card, target <3 min) and find-rate of core action without docs (target >90% in usability sessions).

Ch 13.5 — Share sheets & ACL — Example

Concept. Obvious entry; plain-language ACL; invite vs anyone-with-link; revoke parity; hard confirm on private→public (§13.5).

Scenario. Sharing the doc “2027 Compensation Plan”.

Example. "Share" is a labeled button in the doc header (not buried in ⋯). Sheet:

Share “2027 Compensation Plan”
People with access: You (owner) · Priya — can edit · Finance team — can view
[Invite people…] role select: Can view / Can comment / Can edit
——
Link sharing: Off → toggling to “Anyone with the link can view” triggers:
"Make this document visible to anyone with the link? Anyone — including people outside JAH Inc — could read it. [Cancel] [Turn on link sharing]"

Revoke is one click on the same row that granted ("Remove"), logged to the enterprise audit trail. “Copy link” is optimistic (instant "Link copied" toast) with the ACL badge "Anyone with link · view" shown beside the copied confirmation; the invite send is pessimistic (external notification).

Why it passes. Widening private→public gets the one Hard confirm; ACL words are “view/comment/edit”, not “role: 3”; revoke as easy as grant; optimistic-copy/pessimistic-send split exactly per §13.5.

Rejected. A link toggle that flips to public silently, with permissions labeled by internal enum names.

Ch 13.6 — Autosave & drafts — Example

Concept. Autosave+versions vs explicit Save vs Draft/Publish; visible save states; never lose input; guard only on loss (§13.6; drill #21).

Scenario. Three surfaces in one suite.

Example.

Surface Pattern Why
Doc editor Autosave + version history (“Version from 14:02 — restore”) Long-form document
SOC-2 attestation form Explicit [Sign & submit] Legal attestation — the commit must be a deliberate act
Blog CMS Draft + [Publish] Publish notifies 2,400 subscribers

Save-state chip in the doc header cycles the L6 map: "Saved" → "Saving…" → "Offline — changes queued" → "Couldn't save — retrying (draft kept on this device)". A transient 500 never discards keystrokes: the local draft persists and retry is automatic.

Why it passes. Pattern chosen by consequence (notify-on-publish, legal commit); all four save states visible; input survives transient error (§13.6 UI requirements verbatim).

Rejected. Autosave on the legal attestation (accidental half-signed state) or a dirty-navigation modal on a fully-autosaved doc (guard without possible loss).

Ch 13.7 — Clipboard & paste — Example

Concept. Copy toast; sanitize rich paste; JIT paste permission; grid paste as one undo unit; never block password paste (§13.7).

Scenario. Five clipboard moments across the suite.

Example.
- Copy link: "Link copied" Soft toast, 3s, polite announcement.
- Rich paste into doc: pasted HTML is sanitized (scripts/styles stripped); pasting a 40-row table pops a preview: "Paste as: [Table] [Plain text]".
- Web paste permission: clicking [Paste from clipboard] (a user gesture) triggers the browser prompt; on deny: "Clipboard access is blocked. Paste with Ctrl+V instead, or enable access in site settings." — degraded path, not a dead end (Ch 14.3 pattern).
- Grid paste: pasting a 6×4 spreadsheet range into the SKU table highlights the exact 6×4 target cells before commit; one Ctrl+Z reverts the entire paste as a unit.
- Password field: paste allowed — onpaste never suppressed. Password-manager-friendly and consistent with SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication AA intent.

Why it passes. Every §13.7 bullet has a shipped behavior; paste undo granularity matches the user’s mental “one action”.

Rejected. Blocking paste in the password confirm field — “false security theater” that punishes password-manager users.

Ch 13.8 — Notifications IA — Example

Concept. Critical interrupt / batched digest / muteable tiers; center rules; badge honesty (§13.8; drill #22 assignment included).

Scenario. Helm Inbox’s notification system.

Example.

Event Tier Behavior
Payment failed Critical interrupt Modal on next focus + email; cannot be muted
Password reset requested Critical interrupt Assertive alert + email (security)
New comment on your doc Batched digest Notification center + optional daily email digest
Weekly tips Muteable Off-by-default marketing tier; per-type mute; obeys quiet hours 22:00–08:00 local

Notification center: unread items carry a 8px dot + bold title (dot and weight — L11); "Mark all as read"; each item deep-links to the object; three distinct empty states (drill #39) — never-used: "Notifications about comments, mentions, and billing will appear here" vs zero-unread: "You're all caught up" vs muted-all: "All notification types are muted, so nothing new will arrive here. [Review notification settings]" — the muted-all copy names the cause and its CTA repairs it, where “caught up” would be a lie (Ch 10.7 discipline applied). Badge count equals real unread count — no manufactured "1" to farm opens.

Preference center is a plain matrix (rows = types, columns = In-app / Email / Push), not a maze; “unsubscribe all non-critical” is one switch.

Why it passes. Tier assignment matches consequence; quiet hours spare non-critical; badge honesty resolves the growth-vs-trust tension on the trust side.

Rejected. Fake urgency badges and an unsubscribe flow spread across four screens (dark-pattern maze).

Ch 13.9 — Wizards & multi-step flows — Example

Concept. One job per step; honest progress; Back-safe; review-step Error Summary (§13.9).

Scenario. 4-step workspace import wizard (“Choose source → Map fields → Options → Review”).

Example. Header: "Step 2 of 4 — Map fields" (honest N of M — no surprise step 5). Back returns to step 1 with every choice intact; draft persists between steps (leaving and returning resumes at step 2). Review step re-validates everything and renders an Error Summary: "1 problem: Field 'Priority' isn't mapped — Fix in step 2" with a link that jumps back with context. A competing 3-field “quick import” skips the wizard entirely — progressive disclosure beats a five-page wizard when fields are few.

Why it passes. All four §13.9 bullets; the user is never stranded on step 4 by a silent step-2 error.

Rejected. "Step 3 of 3" that spawns steps 4 and 5, and Back that wipes the field mapping.

Ch 13.10 — Live collaboration & conflict prefer-when (Case H) — Example

Concept. Presence, cursors optional, anchored comments, awareness/locks, keep both / choose / merge; reject silent overwrite (§13.10; drills #23, #40).

Scenario. Two teammates edit the same customer profile; one was offline.

Example.
- Presence: avatar stack "Priya, Marcus viewing" in the header; cursor-following is opt-in ("Follow Priya"), never required to edit.
- Comments: anchored to the field they discuss; "Resolve" state visible.
- Awareness: while Priya edits the “Bio” field it shows her avatar chip and a field-level soft lock: "Priya is editing" — the rest of the form stays editable.
- Conflict (Case H), structured fields → merge, field-level choose:

Sync conflict — Customer profile edited in two places
| Field | Your offline change | Marcus (14:02) | |
|—|—|—|—|
| Name | — | — | (identical — auto-merged) |
| Title | “VP Ops” | “VP Operations” | ( • Keep yours / • Keep Marcus’s ) |
| Bio | 3 paragraphs rewritten | 1 sentence added | [Keep both — review side by side] |
[Apply choices]

Strategy per prefer-when: Name merges (no overlap), Title is a choose (one field, clear either/or), the overlapping prose Bio is keep-both. Whole radio group and Apply are keyboard-operable. Remote non-conflicting changes announce politely ("Marcus updated Title"); focus is never stolen mid-keystroke — assertive handling reserved for an actually destructive collision.

Why it passes. All five collab signals + the exact keep-both/choose/merge prefer-when mapped to field types; silent overwrite is structurally impossible.

Rejected. Last-write-wins that vaporizes the offline rewrite (silent overwrite — Case H’s named reject) and drag-only merge UI (§12.4 reject).

Chapter 14 — Mobile, Gestures, Permissions, Offline & AI UI

Ch 14.1 — Dual device models — Example

Concept. Shared: semantic roles, IA, undo classes. Native: gestures, chrome, materials. Density comfortable-biased on small screens; ≥44×44 touch; safe areas (§14.1; answers drill #25).

Scenario. Trellum board on desktop web vs iPhone.

Example.
- Shared (must match): color.role.danger means destructive everywhere; archive is Soft-undo with the same 7s window on both; IA = same four destinations.
- Native (must differ): iOS gets bottom tab bar + swipe-back + sheet materials; desktop gets side nav + hover cards. Mobile hover cards are demoted to tap-to-open sheets; row actions become visible buttons/sheets, not hover reveals.
- Density: desktop defaults Compact (40px rows); phone defaults Comfortable (56px rows), primary touch targets 44×44.
- Safe areas: the sticky [Add card] bar uses padding-bottom: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-bottom)) so the home indicator never traps the CTA; foldable hinge treated as an inset, content flows around it.

Why it passes. Exactly three shared / three distinct, matching §14.1’s table; comfortable bias on small screens.

Rejected. Pixel-identical React-Native fantasy, and shrunk-web with hover-only row actions (the two named rejects).

Ch 14.2 — Gestures — Example

Concept. All seven gesture rules (§14.2; drill #26).

Scenario. Helm Inbox mobile message list.

Example.
- ≤1 swipe per row: swipe-left = Archive. That’s the only swipe. (Snooze, delete, etc. live in the row’s long-press sheet.)
- Visible equivalent: every gesture action also exists as a button in the row sheet — Archive, Snooze, Delete all tappable.
- Vertical scroll wins: the swipe recognizer requires a horizontal lock angle (>30° off vertical, >12px travel) before it claims the touch; ambiguous pans scroll.
- Desktop reorder: handles per Ch 12.4.
- System gestures: iOS edge swipe-back navigates back — the app never claims the left edge; Android back closes the top sheet first, then navigates.
- Discoverability: the first-ever visit shows a one-time inline hint "Tip: swipe a message to archive" on the first row — once, then never again; archive is always reachable without the gesture.
- Motor a11y: no hold-only exclusive path (long-press sheet duplicates into the ⋯ button); pointer-cancel supported — drag the finger off the row before release and the swipe aborts; row spacing 8px minimum between adjacent targets.

Why it passes. Rules 1 and 3 interact exactly as drill #26 asks: because only one horizontal gesture exists and it must win an angle-lock, the main vertical axis is never hijacked.

Rejected. Left-swipe and right-swipe and edge-swipe on one row, fighting each other and the scroll axis.

Ch 14.3 — JIT permissions — Example

Concept. Request at moment of intent; pre-prompt; denied = L6 state with settings path + degraded feature; never loop the OS prompt (§14.3; drill #27, camera).

Scenario. Scanning a receipt with the camera in an expenses app.

Example.
1. Intent: user taps [Scan receipt].
2. Pre-prompt (product UI): "To scan receipts, Expenses needs camera access. Your photos stay on this device until you submit." [Allow camera] [Not now]
3. OS prompt: system sheet appears only after [Allow camera].
4a. Granted: viewfinder opens immediately — the task continues.
4b. Denied: the scan screen becomes a designed Denied state: "Camera access is off. [Open Settings] — or [Upload a photo] / [Enter amounts manually] instead." The OS prompt is never re-fired in a loop; the settings deep-link + two degraded paths keep the job completable.

Notifications variant: the pre-prompt is deferred until the user does something notification-worthy ("Want to know when Priya approves this report?") — never a launch-day permission bundle.

Why it passes. All four steps; Denied is an L6 state with a CTA and a feature-degraded path (§14.3 rule verbatim).

Rejected. Launch-time bundle of camera+location+notifications dialogs, and an app that re-triggers the OS prompt every open after denial.

Ch 14.4 — Offline & sync — Example

Concept. Offline / Syncing / Synced / Conflict states; queue with idempotent replay; per-item failure (§14.4; Case H; drill #28).

Scenario. Field-sales rep edits 5 customer records on a plane.

Example.

State UI
Offline Banner: "Offline — changes queued" + per-record queued chip "Queued · will sync"
Syncing On reconnect: "Syncing 5 changes…" with a real count, not a mystery spinner
Synced Banner clears; quiet meta "Last synced 09:41" in the footer
Conflict Record 4 collides → the Ch 13.10 keep-both/choose/merge sheet, keyboard-accessible 
queue.replay(change => api.mutate(change, { idempotencyKey: change.id }));
// per-item resolution: 4 sync, 1 conflicts — never "sync failed" for the batch

Why it passes. Case H’s requirements: banner copy is the textbook’s own ("Offline—changes queued"); syncing is explicit; conflicts show both versions; per-item surfacing.

Rejected. Silent overwrite of the server copy, and one opaque “Sync error” that hides which of the 5 records failed.

Ch 14.5 — AI UI: intent → proposal → review → apply → undo (Case D) — Example

Concept. The five-step agent loop; stream+cancel; citations; side-effect approval; colorless diff; reject/override metric; AI disclosure (§14.5; drills #29–30).

Scenario. “Clean up all 214 card titles to sentence case and fix typos” — AI bulk edit in Trellum (Case D).

Example.
1. Intent: user types the request in the AI panel.
2. Proposal: results stream into a review list with a persistent [Stop generating] button — the UI is never blocked without escape.
3. Review — diff primary:

~ TRL-812   − "Fix Payment Retry LOOP"      + "Fix payment retry loop"
~ TRL-799   − "darkmode QA pass"            + "Dark mode QA pass"
= TRL-754   (no change)

Hunks are labeled −/+ and ~ changed / = unchanged textually — readable without red/green (L11). Keyboard: J/K next/prev hunk, A accept, R reject per hunk. Where the AI cites style rules, a provenance chip links the source (“Workspace style guide §2”).
4. Apply: explicit [Apply 212 changes] — nothing mutates before this. A step that would send (e.g. “email the summary to watchers”) is a tool side-effect and gets its own approval: "The assistant wants to email 312 watchers. [Review email] [Don't send]".
5. Undo: post-apply toast "212 titles updated. Undo all" (Soft, single unit) + version history entry. Applied changes carry an "AI-edited" marker in card history — disclosure where it matters for trust.

Why it passes. All five loop steps with stream+cancel, citations, colorless diff, side-effect approval, and mandatory undo; Copilot/Cursor apply-review steal, not ghostwriter theater.

Rejected (Case D + §14.5 failure modes). Autocomplete that silently mutates titles as you watch; optimizing accept-rate alone; red/green-only hunks; the agent emailing 312 people unattended.

Measure. Track reject/override rate per suggestion type — not accept rate alone. A 98% accept rate with a rising post-apply undo rate means users are rubber-stamping, then repairing: trust is falling while the vanity metric climbs.

Ch 14.6 — Mobile + AI + offline intersections — Example

Concept. Reconnect honesty; sheet-based mobile review; JIT mic for multimodal; offline AI queueing rules (§14.6).

Scenario. The Ch 14.5 bulk edit, attempted on a phone on hotel Wi-Fi.

Example.
- Stream drops mid-proposal → "Connection lost — 118 of 214 suggestions received. [Resume]" — never a list silently presented as complete.
- Review opens in a full-height sheet; Accept/Reject are 48×48px paired buttons under each hunk (≥44 craft bar) — no hover required anywhere.
- Voice input: mic permission is JIT with pre-prompt, and denial degrades to the text box (Ch 14.3 pattern).
- Fully offline: the AI entry point is disabled with "AI suggestions need a connection" — the product cannot fulfill queued AI requests later, so it does not pretend to queue them.

Why it passes. Each of the four §14.6 bullets shipped; the queue rule’s honest branch (“otherwise disable with explanation”) chosen deliberately.

Ch 14.7 — Platform parity snapshot — Example

Concept. What must match vs stay native across web/iOS/Android (§14.7 table).

Scenario. Cross-platform audit checklist row for Trellum’s release gate.

Example.

Check Web iOS Android Verdict
color.role.danger = destructive semantics ✓ ✓ ✓ Must match — pass
Archive soft-undo window 7s 7s 7s Must match (5–10s band) — pass
Nav chrome Side nav Tab bar Nav bar Must differ — pass
Swipe-back none system system Native — pass
Focus visible intent 2px ring focus engine focus engine Intent matches — pass

Why it passes. The audit tests intent parity for semantics/undo/focus and deliberate divergence for chrome/gestures — exactly the §14.7 split.

Rejected. A parity ticket demanding the iOS tab bar be rebuilt on web “for consistency” — chrome parity is explicitly a non-goal.

Part III Quick Reference — Integration drill

QR-1 — One flow audited against the quick-reference card — Example

Concept. The Part III quick-reference numbers + critique-checklist excerpt applied end-to-end (answers review drill #31’s flow, fixed).

Scenario. The broken flow from drill #31 — swipe-deletes a shared document; no undo toast; “Are you sure?” confirm; failure shows a toast and an ambiguous empty row — rebuilt.

Example (fixed flow, with the card’s numbers).

Checklist item Broken Fixed
Feedback ≤100ms + right tier Swipe → 900ms silence Swipe acknowledged in-frame; delete is Fast-tier inline pending
Undo class matches blast Hard “Are you sure?” for a recoverable object; no undo Shared + recoverable → Quarantine: "Moved to Trash — 9 people lose access until restored. Undo" (blast named; 30d Trash)
State matrix complete Failure = toast + ambiguous empty row Failure = row restored + inline "Couldn't delete — Retry"; error ≠ empty (Ch 10.7)
Gesture rules Swipe is the only path Delete also in row ⋯ menu (visible peer); one swipe max
Focus restore Focus lost to <body> Focus lands on adjacent row; result announced politely
Scent / filtered-to-zero / AI checks n/a n/a — flagged not-applicable, not skipped

Quick-reference numbers exercised: ack ≤100ms · Soft toast 5–10s (used elsewhere) · Quarantine ~30d · touch ≥44×44 · undo classes soft/quarantine/hard · taxonomy error≠empty.

Why it passes. Every violated law in the drill (L5 silence, L7 confirm-instead-of-undo, L6 ambiguous state, L9 focus, L11 toast-only failure) is repaired using the exact quick-reference biases — demonstrating the card as a working audit tool, which is its job.

End of Part III examples companion. Source: research/modern-ui-textbook.md, Part III (Chapters 10–14, review questions, and quick reference).

Modern UI — Companion Examples, Part IV: Design Systems (Chapters 15–17)

Purpose. This document is the official worked-examples companion to Part IV of Modern UI. Every major concept, law application, tension, table row-group, taxonomy, and pattern in Chapters 15 (Tokens, APIs, Promotion, Governance), 16 (Component & Layout Inventory), and 17 (Internationalization) gets at least one concrete example: a realistic product scenario, real microcopy in quotes, real code (CSS/HTML/JSON/TS), real numbers (px, ms, ratios, %, KB), and named tokens in the textbook’s own style. Section headings mirror the textbook’s numbering so coverage is auditable. Laws are cited L1–L14; undo classes as Soft/Quarantine/Hard; WCAG success criteria with their conformance-level labels (A/AA/AAA — Level A criteria such as 4.1.2 and 1.4.1 sit inside the WCAG 2.2 AA conformance floor); touch targets as 44×44 craft bar / 24×24 WCAG 2.2 2.5.8 AA floor. The recurring product used across examples is “Ledgerline” — a B2B invoicing tool with web, iOS, and Android clients, a marketing CMS, and 14 shipped locales.

Chapter 15 — Tokens, APIs, Promotion, Governance

Ch 15.1 — What a design system is for (semantic contracts; L12; L13) — Example

Concept. §15.1: a design system is opinionated infrastructure for outcomes — encode semantic contracts, make the right path the easy path (for humans and codegen), scale decisions, and version them so change is a migration. L12 (abstract after three real uses) and L13 (version the contract) govern.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s AI-assist feature generates invoice-settings screens from prompts. Two squads also hand-build settings pages. Before the system existed, the codegen model produced style={{ color: '#2563eb' }} buttons and invented a variant="brand" prop that didn’t exist.

Example. The system publishes one contract that all three consumers (squad A, squad B, codegen) import:

// @ledgerline/ui — the contract
export type ButtonTone = 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'destructive' | 'ghost';
export type Size = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg';
// v3.2.0 — changes to this union are MAJOR (L13)

The codegen prompt preamble is literally the catalog JSON (Ch 15.5-C), so the model can only emit props that exist. When squad B asked for a fourth settings-card layout, the systems team counted uses: only two real ones existed, so the request was parked as a recipe (L12: abstract after three real uses, not before).

Why it passes. The right path is the easy path: the AI cannot invent brand because the union is exhaustive; humans cannot ship raw hex because lint blocks it; and when secondary is renamed someday, that is a MAJOR migration with a codemod, not a Friday find-replace.

Rejected. The “Figma sticker sheet” system: a beautifully organized library with no published TypeScript contract. Codegen and squads each re-derive the button from screenshots; three synonym buttons ship in a quarter.

Measure. Count of distinct button implementations in the app bundle (target: 1); % of codegen output that compiles against the published unions without manual fixup.

Ch 15.2-A — Token layers: primitive / semantic / component — Example

Concept. §15.2 table: three layers; product code imports semantic only; component tokens are rare aliases.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s token repo, trimmed to the invoice-form slice.

Example.

/* LAYER 1 — PRIMITIVE (token pipeline only; never imported by product code) */
:root {
  --blue-500: #2f6fed;
  --blue-600: #1f56c4;
  --gray-900: #16181d;
  --gray-050: #f6f7f9;
  --red-600:  #c92a2a;
  --space-4:  4px;
  --space-8:  8px;
  --space-16: 16px;
  --space-24: 24px;
  --font-size-14: 14px;
  --font-size-16: 16px;
}

/* LAYER 2 — SEMANTIC (the only layer product UI may reference) */
:root {
  --color-text-primary:   var(--gray-900);
  --color-bg-canvas:      var(--gray-050);
  --color-action-primary: var(--blue-500);
  --color-action-primary-hover: var(--blue-600);
  --color-text-danger:    var(--red-600);
  --space-field-gap:      var(--space-16);
  --space-group-gap:      calc(var(--space-24) + var(--space-8)); /* 32 */
  --font-size-body:       var(--font-size-16);
}

/* LAYER 3 — COMPONENT (rare; component internals only) */
.ll-button {
  --button-bg: var(--color-action-primary);
  --button-bg-hover: var(--color-action-primary-hover);
}
.ll-toast {
  --toast-duration-soft: 7000ms; /* Soft-undo window, 5–10s band */
}

Product code:

/* invoice-form.css — legal */
.invoice-form { gap: var(--space-field-gap); color: var(--color-text-primary); }

Why it passes. The pipeline can retune --blue-500 (PATCH, §15.6) without touching a single product file; product code never knows a hex exists. --toast-duration-soft is a legitimate component token because it is meaningless outside the Toast.

Rejected. .invoice-form { color: #16181d; gap: 16px; } — raw palette and raw px in app CSS. Also rejected: a fourth “page layer” of tokens per screen (--invoice-page-blue), which is just hexes with extra steps.

Ch 15.2-B — Roles, not hexes (L1) + code as source of truth + Figma drift check — Example

Concept. §15.2 rules: no raw palette in app CSS or style props (L1); code is source of truth for what ships; Figma Variables mirror token names with a weekly drift check on renames.

Scenario. A designer renames the Figma variable color/text/primary to color/text/default on Tuesday without telling engineering.

Example. The Friday drift-check CI job diffs Figma Variable names (via API export) against the code token manifest:

DRIFT REPORT — 2026-07-10
  ✗ figma: color/text/default  |  code: --color-text-primary   (name mismatch)
  ✓ 212 / 213 variables match
Action: revert Figma rename OR open a token MAJOR proposal (see 15.6). Code is SoT.

Slack message auto-posted: “Figma variable color/text/default has no code counterpart. Code is source of truth — renames land in code first, mirrored to Figma the same week (see §15.6).”

Why it passes. What ships is what’s true; design tooling mirrors it. The weekly cadence bounds drift to ≤7 days, so specs never silently reference roles that don’t exist.

Rejected. “Figma is source of truth” — the app then ships tokens nobody renamed, and specs reference roles the build has never heard of.

Measure. Drift-report mismatch count per week (target 0); time-to-reconcile a rename (target ≤5 business days).

Ch 15.2-C — Token pipeline (Style Dictionary → platforms) — Example

Concept. §15.2 rules: pipeline emits CSS custom properties + iOS/Android artifacts from one source.

Scenario. One source JSON drives web, iOS, and Android so --color-action-primary means the same thing on all three (parity matrix §16.8: semantic color roles must match).

Example.

// tokens/semantic/color.json (source of truth)
{
  "color": {
    "action": {
      "primary": { "value": "{blue.500}", "type": "color" }
    }
  }
}

Build outputs:

/* dist/web/tokens.css */
:root { --color-action-primary: #2f6fed; }

// dist/ios/LLTokens.swift
public enum LLColor { public static let actionPrimary = UIColor(hex: 0x2F6FED) }

<!-- dist/android/values/colors.xml -->
<color name="ll_color_action_primary">#2F6FED</color>

Why it passes. One edit → three artifacts; no platform can drift on a semantic role. Semver applies to the source names, not the generated files.

Rejected. Hand-maintained colors.xml that an Android engineer “fixes” to #2F70EE locally — a fork the drift check can’t see because it never went through the pipeline.

Ch 15.2-D — Theme layers compose, don’t fork — Example

Concept. §15.2: theme layers are brand → mode (light/dark) → high-contrast/forced-colors → rare campaign overlays. Marketing may fork expression; Locked surfaces stay on semantic roles.

Scenario. Ledgerline runs a two-week “Tax Season” marketing campaign with a green accent, while a user on Windows High Contrast pays an invoice in dark mode.

Example. Cascade of layers on one root, never parallel token trees:

/* Layer 1: brand */
:root { --color-action-primary: var(--blue-500); }

/* Layer 2: mode */
:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  --color-text-primary: #e8eaef;
  --color-bg-canvas: #101216;
  --color-action-primary: var(--blue-400); /* 4.6:1 on dark canvas */
}

/* Layer 3: forced colors — defer to system semantics */
@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .ll-button { border: 1px solid ButtonText; } /* don't force broken hex */
}

/* Layer 4: campaign overlay — MARKETING SURFACES ONLY */
.mkt-taxseason { --color-action-primary: var(--green-500); }

The checkout page (Locked) is outside .mkt-taxseason; its “Pay $1,240.00” button stays on the brand-layer role.

Why it passes. Four composable layers, one tree. The campaign can’t touch the Pay button (Locked, §15.3), and forced-colors preserves system semantics instead of forcing hexes (ship gate, Part V).

Rejected. tokens-dark.css as a copied-and-diverged fork of tokens-light.css — six months later, dark mode is missing 14 roles added only to light.

Measure. Dual-theme contrast audit: semantic text ≥4.5:1 (WCAG 1.4.3 AA), non-text UI ≥3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11 AA) in both modes, in CI.

Ch 15.2-E — Density as token maps (cross-domain: token × touch target × WCAG 2.5.8) — Example

Concept. §15.2 density table: comfortable / compact / dense are named maps of control height, field gap, and row padding — exposed as data-density, never ad-hoc px, never inventing type sizes outside the locked scale.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s invoice list is a power-user data grid (dense), its settings forms are daily-tool compact, and its first-run onboarding is comfortable. On mobile, the primary “New invoice” CTA must stay a real touch target even in dense mode.

Example.
