:root, [data-density="compact"] {       /* default product */
  --density-control-height: 36px;       /* 36–40 band */
  --density-field-gap: var(--space-16); /* 12–16 band */
}
[data-density="comfortable"] {          /* first-run, empty states */
  --density-control-height: 48px;       /* 44–48 band */
  --density-field-gap: var(--space-24); /* 16–24 band */
}
[data-density="dense"] {                /* invoice grid */
  --density-control-height: 28px;       /* 28–32 band */
  --density-field-gap: var(--space-8);  /* 8–12 band */
}
/* Cross-domain guard: dense rows still get hit-slop so interactive
   targets never fall below the 24×24 WCAG 2.2 2.5.8 AA floor;
   primary mobile CTAs stay at the 44×44 craft bar regardless of density. */
[data-density="dense"] .ll-row-action {
  min-height: 28px;
  position: relative;
}
[data-density="dense"] .ll-row-action::after {
  /* 28 + 2 + 2 = 32px tall (≥ the 24px floor), 8px extra per inline side.
     Vertical slop is capped at 2px so adjacent dense-row targets never
     overlap — a -8px inset would make 44px-tall hit areas on ~36px row
     pitch and cause mis-taps. 44×44 is the craft bar for primary mobile
     CTAs, not a requirement for every dense row action. */
  content: ""; position: absolute; inset: -2px -8px;
}

<section data-density="dense"> <!-- invoice grid -->
<section data-density="comfortable"> <!-- onboarding -->

Type does not change per density map: dense maps body text to the existing --font-size-14 role; it never mints a 13.5px size outside the locked scale.

Why it passes. Density is a semantic theme attribute (one attribute flips three coordinated values), the dense grid keeps 2.5.8 AA compliance via hit-slop while visually staying 28px, and mobile primary CTAs hold the 44 craft bar. Law + token + WCAG SC in one decision.

Rejected. “Tighter padding somewhere”: a squad hardcodes padding: 3px 7px on their table rows. It looks dense but breaks the touch floor and can’t be flipped back to comfortable for onboarding reuse.

Measure. Automated target-size scan on dense surfaces: 0 interactive targets with effective hit area <24×24.

Ch 15.3-A — Locked / Guided / Open partition — Example

Concept. §15.3 table: Locked (auth, checkout, destructive, focus/a11y primitives, money/identity — no product restyle), Guided (documented escape hatches), Open (label explicitly; promote or delete).

Scenario. Three requests hit the Ledgerline systems team in one week.

Example.

  1. Locked. Growth squad wants to restyle the checkout error state — replace the red inline error with a subtler gray tooltip to “reduce anxiety.” Denied. Checkout validation is Locked: no product restyle of validation, focus, or semantics. The error stays --color-text-danger text tied via aria-describedby, not a tooltip (§16.3-G: never tooltips for errors).
  2. Guided. Reports squad forks the standard FilterBar pattern to add a saved-views dropdown. Allowed with paperwork: they file docs/forks/filterbar-reports.md — “Fork reason: saved views need per-user persistence the pattern lacks; revisit when 3 consumers exist (L12).”
  3. Open. Marketing builds a parallax annual-report page with custom purple gradients. Allowed, labeled: the package is @ledgerline/open-annualreport-2026 with header comment /* OPEN surface — delete after 2026-09-30 or propose promotion */.

Why it passes. Each surface got the policy its blast radius deserves: money/identity paths are non-negotiable; common patterns bend with documentation; brand moments run free but carry a label and an expiry so they get promoted or deleted, never silently absorbed.

Rejected. Treating everything as Guided — the checkout tooltip ships, error discoverability drops, and the “escape hatch” becomes the trunk.

Ch 15.3-B — Prefer systemize vs leave local; the two failure modes — Example

Concept. §15.3: systemize when ≥3 real uses on Locked/Guided surfaces; leave local when a one-off with unclear reuse. Failure modes: shadow libraries or premature API.

Scenario. The StatusPill question. Month 1: billing squad builds a pill showing “Paid / Overdue / Draft”. Month 2: approvals squad copies it for “Approved / Pending”. Month 3: payroll squad is about to copy it again.

Example — the decision memo (verbatim):

Proposal: promote StatusPill recipe → pattern.
Real uses: 3 (billing, approvals, payroll — all Guided surfaces). L12 threshold met.
Shared contract: tone: 'positive' | 'warning' | 'neutral' | 'danger', text label required (no color-only status, WCAG 1.4.1 A use-of-color — within the AA conformance floor).
NOT promoted: billing’s blinking-overdue animation (1 use — stays local, labeled Open).

Counter-example in the same memo: the ComparisonSlider used once on the marketing site is explicitly left local — “unclear reuse; revisit if a second real use appears.”

Why it passes. Promotion is triggered by counted evidence (≥3), not enthusiasm; the one-use flourish stays local, avoiding premature API (prop soup for hypothetical consumers); the third copy-paste is intercepted before it becomes a shadow library (three drifting pills with different color mappings).

Measure. Quarterly shadow-library scan: grep -r "border-radius: 999px" outside @ledgerline/ui as a smoke test for un-promoted pill clones; count should trend to 0.

Ch 15.4-A — Promotion pipeline: recipe → pattern → component — Example

Concept. §15.4 table: Recipe (local impl + note; a11y baseline) → Pattern (docs + a11y notes + do/don’t; ≥3 consumers; states designed; keyboard path) → Component (semver package + tests + Storybook; stable API; tokens only; CI gates; catalog entry).

Scenario. The StatusPill from 15.3-B travels the full pipeline over two quarters.

Example.

  • Stage 1 — Recipe (week 1). apps/billing/components/StatusPill.tsx + note in the squad wiki: “Pill for invoice status. Uses --color-* roles only. Text label always rendered (a11y baseline: not color-only).”
  • Stage 2 — Pattern (week 9, at 3 consumers). Docs page ships with: do/don’t (“Do pair tone with a text label. Don’t use danger tone for merely-unusual states.”), a designed state matrix (default, with-icon, truncated-at-160px-container), and the keyboard note: “Pill is static text; if made interactive it must become a Chip (§16.4-D) with keyboard remove.”
  • Stage 3 — Component (week 20). @ledgerline/ui v3.4.0 (MINOR: additive) exports <StatusPill tone size>; tests assert the label renders; Storybook meets DoD (§15.8); the lint rule no-banned-import now flags the three legacy squad copies; catalog entry added (see 15.5-C).

Why it passes. Each stage has entry requirements, so the org never pays component-grade maintenance costs (semver, VR, Storybook, catalog) for an idea that hasn’t proven three real uses.

Rejected. “Straight to component” — a squad publishes @billing/pill v0.0.1 to the internal registry after one use. Now there are two packages, and the promotion pipeline has been bypassed into a shadow library.

Ch 15.4-B — Don’t wrap a third-party once “for consistency”; adopt behavior + skin with tokens — Example

Concept. §15.4: prefer Radix / React Aria (or platform equivalents) for behavior; build only when the contract is missing.

Scenario. Ledgerline needs a combobox for “Assign invoice to client” (2,000+ clients, typeahead required).

Example.

// GOOD: adopt behavior, skin with tokens
import { Combobox } from '@ariakit/react';
// @ariakit/react is Ledgerline's ONE chosen behavior lib — it fills the
// "Radix / React Aria (or platform equivalents)" slot from §15.4. Any
// APG-mapped lib in that class works; picking exactly one is the rule.

export function ClientCombobox(props: ClientComboboxProps) {
  return (
    <Combobox
      className="ll-combobox"      /* skin: tokens only */
      autoSelect
      {...props}
    />
  );
}

.ll-combobox {
  block-size: var(--density-control-height);
  border-color: var(--color-border-input);
  font-size: var(--font-size-body);
}

What the team did not do: write <LedgerlineDropdownV2> from a <div> — the focus management, aria-activedescendant wiring, typeahead, and screen-reader announcements are exactly the solved behavior the library provides. What they did build from scratch: CheckoutField (domain-specific Locked flow — card entry with Ledgerline’s fraud-check states) because no library carries that contract.

Why it passes. Behavior (hard, standardized, APG-mapped) is adopted; expression (tokens) is owned; building is reserved for missing contracts.

Rejected. A 40-line passthrough wrapper around the library “so imports look consistent” — it adds a version-lag layer and an API to maintain while changing nothing. Also rejected: three squads adopting three different combobox libs — that’s the synonym fork the “ban synonym forks” rule exists for.

Ch 15.5-A — Semantic props, composition, exhaustive unions — Example

Concept. §15.5: props are tone / size / density, not blue / big / tightish; asChild/slot for polymorphism; exhaustive TS unions with no synonym variants (primary ≠ brand ≠ cta); “AI consumes your contract.”

Scenario. The Button API, v3.

Example.

export type ButtonTone = 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'destructive' | 'ghost';
export type ButtonSize = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg';

interface ButtonProps {
  tone?: ButtonTone;        // semantic role, not color
  size?: ButtonSize;
  asChild?: boolean;        // composition: render as consumer's element
  'aria-label'?: string;    // required by lint when children are icon-only
}

Polymorphism via composition, not a href prop that secretly renders an <a>:

<Button asChild tone="secondary">
  <a href="/invoices/export">Export CSV</a>
</Button>

When the AI codegen assistant emitted <Button tone="cta"> in a generated PR, the build failed at typecheck:

error TS2322: Type '"cta"' is not assignable to type
  '"primary" | "secondary" | "destructive" | "ghost"'.

Why it passes. The union is the whole vocabulary; a synonym cannot compile, so it cannot scale. tone="destructive" carries meaning the system enforces (confirm/undo pairing, --color-text-danger), which red never could.

Rejected. <Button blue big> boolean-prop soup, and the synonym trio primary/brand/cta mapping to the same pixels — one human shortcut that an AI generator will replicate ten thousand times (industrial defect).

Ch 15.5-B — Lint catalog (all five rules) — Example

Concept. §15.5: no-raw-color, no-synonym-variant, no-unlabeled-icon-button, no-banned-import, require-focus-visible. §15.7: lint is how Locked contracts survive growth.

Scenario. One squad PR trips all five rules; here is the actual CI output.

Example.

eslint --plugin @ledgerline/design-lint

src/invoices/Row.tsx
  14:22  error  Raw color "#c92a2a" — use a semantic token
                (--color-text-danger)                     ll/no-raw-color
  22:10  error  Variant "cta" is a synonym of "primary" —
                one name per meaning                      ll/no-synonym-variant
  31:6   error  Icon-only <Button> without accessible name —
                add aria-label (WCAG 4.1.2 A name/role/value)
                                                          ll/no-unlabeled-icon-button
  3:1    error  Import from "apps/billing/components/StatusPill"
                is banned — use @ledgerline/ui StatusPill
                (deprecated 2026-05-01, sunset passed)    ll/no-banned-import

src/invoices/row.css
  9:3    error  "outline: none" without :focus-visible
                replacement (WCAG 2.4.7 AA)               ll/require-focus-visible

✖ 5 problems (5 errors) — PR blocked

Why it passes. Each rule mechanizes a chapter law: L1 (roles not hexes), the synonym ban, name/role/value (WCAG 4.1.2 A), the deprecation sunset (§15.6), and focus visibility (WCAG 2.4.7 AA / ship gate). None of these survive growth as “taste” — only as blocking lint.

Rejected. The same five rules as a “best practices” wiki page. Wiki pages don’t fail PRs.

Ch 15.5-C — Catalog JSON min schema — Example

Concept. §15.5: { id, name, props[], tokens[], a11yKeyboard, do, dont, status } for humans + codegen.

Scenario. The catalog entry for Toast — the same JSON is rendered as the docs page and injected into the codegen system prompt.

Example.

{
  "id": "toast",
  "name": "Toast",
  "status": "stable",
  "props": [
    { "name": "tone", "type": "'neutral' | 'success' | 'danger'", "default": "'neutral'" },
    { "name": "action", "type": "{ label: string; onAction(): void }", "default": null },
    { "name": "durationMs", "type": "number", "default": 7000, "note": "Soft-undo band 5000–10000" }
  ],
  "tokens": ["--toast-duration-soft", "--color-bg-elevated", "--space-16"],
  "a11yKeyboard": "Announced via polite live region; F6/shortcut moves focus to toast region; Tab reaches action button; Escape dismisses focused toast. Focus is never stolen on show.",
  "do": "Use for transient acknowledgment and Soft undo: \"Invoice deleted — Undo\".",
  "dont": "Don't report hard failures via toast only; don't move focus for every toast."
}

Why it passes. Machine-readable (codegen can enumerate legal props and required a11y wiring) and human-readable (do/don’t is real microcopy, not lorem). status gates what codegen may emit: it never suggests experimental or deprecated components.

Measure. % of catalog entries with non-empty a11yKeyboard (target 100%); codegen prop-hallucination rate before/after catalog injection.

Ch 15.6-A — Semver SLA: MAJOR / MINOR / PATCH for tokens and components — Example

Concept. §15.6 table. L13: version the contract.

Scenario. Three real changes in one release train, classified from the changelog.

Example — @ledgerline/tokens and @ledgerline/ui CHANGELOG:

## tokens 4.0.0 (MAJOR)
- RENAMED semantic role `--color-text-subtle` → `--color-text-secondary`.
  Meaning unchanged, name changed ⇒ MAJOR. Alias bridge active until 2026-10-13.
- CHANGED MEANING: `--color-bg-warning` now reserved for blocking warnings
  (previously also used for promos) ⇒ MAJOR even though the hex is identical.

## tokens 3.9.0 (MINOR)
- ADDED role `--color-bg-selected-subtle` (new; nothing breaks).

## tokens 3.8.2 (PATCH)
- Primitive `--blue-500` #2f6fed → #2e6ce6 behind unchanged semantic roles.
  Visual diff attached (VR run #4471, 14 stories, all deltas approved).

## ui 5.2.0 (MINOR)
- Button: added `tone="ghost"` (additive variant).

## ui 6.0.0 (MAJOR)
- Dialog: `onClose` renamed `onOpenChange(open: boolean)` — breaking prop change.
  Codemod: `npx @ledgerline/codemods dialog-onopenchange`.

Why it passes. The tricky rows are handled exactly per the SLA: a meaning change is MAJOR even with identical pixels; a primitive ramp tweak is PATCH only because the visual diff requirement was met (otherwise “PATCH is a lie,” §15.9).

Rejected. Shipping the --color-text-subtle rename as a PATCH “because it’s just a name.” Every consumer stylesheet referencing the old name silently resolves to nothing — an unversioned rename, the industrial defect L13 exists to prevent.

Ch 15.6-B — Deprecation ops: 90-day window, alias bridge, codemod, CI sunset, Figma same-week, override rate — Example

Concept. §15.6 deprecation row, end to end.

Scenario. The --color-text-subtle → --color-text-secondary rename from 15.6-A, operated across 90 days (2026-07-15 → 2026-10-13).

Example.

Day 0 — alias bridge ships in the same MAJOR:

/* deprecated-bridge.css — auto-generated, removed at sunset */
:root {
  --color-text-subtle: var(--color-text-secondary); /* @deprecated 2026-07-15, sunset 2026-10-13 */
}

Day 0 — codemod published: npx @ledgerline/codemods token-rename --map color-text-subtle=color-text-secondary (rewrites CSS, TS style objects, and Tailwind config).

Day 0–5 — Figma Variables renamed the same week as the code SoT (per §15.2/§15.6), so no spec references the dead name for more than 5 days.

Day 30/60 — bot comments on the 12 remaining repos: “--color-text-subtle sunsets 2026-10-13 (43 days). Run the codemod; CI will fail after sunset.”

Day 91 — bridge file deleted; the token-scoped lint rule flips from warn to error:

ll/no-deprecated-token: "--color-text-subtle" was removed 2026-10-13.
Use --color-text-secondary. (stylelint, runs on all app CSS + TS style objects)

(ll/no-banned-import stays scoped to banned module paths — e.g. the legacy apps/billing/components/StatusPill import in 15.5-B; a CSS custom-property usage is not an import, so token sunsets get their own rule.)

Post-migration watch: the systems dashboard tracks override rate on Text and Field components (per Case E): if squads start writing local color: overrides after the migration, the rename confused the role’s meaning and needs docs or a follow-up.

Why it passes. Consumers get a working bridge (nothing breaks on day 0), a mechanical migration path (codemod), a hard deadline enforced by CI (not memory), design-tool parity within the week, and a trailing signal (override rate) that verifies the migration didn’t damage the contract’s usability.

Rejected. “Deprecated in the docs” with no bridge, no date, no CI — three years later both names live forever and no one knows which is real.

Measure. Repos still importing the deprecated name at day 30/60/89 (target 0 by sunset); override rate on affected components ±30 days around sunset.

Ch 15.7 — Budgets & lint as governance — Example

Concept. §15.7: core kit ≤150KB gz incremental on critical paths; no raw hex/px in app CSS; shared motion only via transform/opacity; dual-theme contrast audited.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s CI “governance” stage, as configured.

Example.

# .github/workflows/governance.yml (excerpt)
- name: Bundle budget (critical paths)
  run: size-limit
  # .size-limit.json:
  # [{ "path": "dist/checkout.js", "limit": "150 KB",
  #    "gzip": true, "note": "core kit incremental on Locked path" }]

- name: No raw hex/px in app CSS
  run: stylelint "apps/**/*.css" --config .stylelint-tokens.json
  # rules: color-no-hex: true; declaration-property-value-allowed-list
  #        forbids literal px on margin/padding/gap/font-size (tokens only)

- name: Motion property allowlist (shared components)
  run: node scripts/check-motion.js
  # fails on transitions/animations of top/left/width/height/margin
  # in @ledgerline/ui — transform/opacity only (compositor-friendly)

- name: Dual-theme contrast audit
  run: node scripts/contrast-audit.js --themes light,dark
  # asserts: semantic text roles ≥4.5:1 (WCAG 1.4.3 AA, large text ≥3:1),
  #          non-text UI roles ≥3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11 AA) in BOTH themes

Real failure it caught: a promo experiment added a 62KB confetti library to the checkout chunk (162KB total > 150KB) — CI blocked it; confetti moved to a lazy-loaded Open surface.

Why it passes. Every budget is a blocking check with a number, not a value statement. Lint is not optional taste; it is how the Locked checkout contract survived a growth squad’s quarter.

Measure. The budgets are themselves the measures: 150KB gz; 0 raw hex/px violations; 0 non-compositor animated properties in shared code; 0 contrast failures across 2 themes.

Ch 15.8 — Storybook definition of done (all seven gates) — Example

Concept. §15.8 DoD table: CSF, States, A11y addon, Interaction, Docs, RTL/pseudo-loc, Themes.

Scenario. The Dialog component (Locked, since destructive confirms live in it) cannot be marked stable in the catalog until this file passes review.

Example.

// Dialog.stories.tsx (excerpt)
export default { title: 'Locked/Dialog', component: Dialog };

// CSF: default + each variant/density/tone
export const Default = {};
export const Destructive = { args: { tone: 'destructive' } };
export const DenseDensity = { parameters: { density: 'dense' } };

// States (L6 taxonomy as applicable)
export const Loading = { args: { busy: true } };
export const ErrorState = { args: { error: 'Couldn’t save. Retry?' } };
export const DisabledConfirm = { args: { confirmDisabled: true } }; // typed-confirm gate not yet satisfied
// DoD checklist declares: empty / partial / offline = N/A for Dialog
// (a modal task has no collection to be empty of; offline surfaces via
// the ErrorState arm). N/A must be DECLARED per state, never skipped.

// Interaction: keyboard open/close + focus restore
export const KeyboardPath = {
  play: async ({ canvas, userEvent }) => {
    await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete invoice' }));
    await expect(canvas.getByRole('dialog')).toHaveFocus(); // trap engaged
    await userEvent.keyboard('{Escape}');
    await expect(canvas.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete invoice' }))
      .toHaveFocus(); // restore trigger
  },
};

// RTL / pseudo-loc where layout can break
export const PseudoLoc = { parameters: { locale: 'en-XA' },
  args: { title: '[!!! Ðéļéţé îñvöîçé !!!]' } };
export const RTL = { parameters: { direction: 'rtl' } };

// Themes: light + dark via global decorator matrix
export const DarkTheme = { parameters: { theme: 'dark' } };

A11y addon config: parameters: { a11y: { config: { rules: [...] } } } with CI failing on serious axe violations for anything under Locked/.

Docs tab renders: purpose, props table (from types), do/don’t (“Don’t stack modals”), tokens used (--color-bg-elevated, --space-24), and the a11y keyboard map (“Tab cycles inside; Escape closes; focus returns to trigger”).

Why it passes. “Renders in one happy path” is explicitly insufficient: all seven gates have artifacts a reviewer can point at, and the interaction play function makes focus restore a test, not a hope.

Rejected. A single Default story plus a screenshot in the wiki — the pseudo-loc clip and the broken Escape path ship undetected.

Ch 15.9 — Visual regression as a fail-the-PR gate — Example

Concept. §15.9: scope = Locked + high-traffic Guided; agreed pixel budget; triggers = token PATCH, layout CSS, density map edits; flake control = no non-deterministic motion, fixed dates in Intl stories.

Scenario. The --blue-500 PATCH from 15.6-A (#2f6fed → #2e6ce6) lands.

Example — the VR run record:

Chromatic build #4471 — tokens 3.8.2 (trigger: token PATCH, primitive ramp)
Scope: 96 stories (Locked: Button, Dialog, Field, Toast; Guided: Table, FilterBar)
Diffs: 14 stories changed, max delta 0.9% pixels (budget: flag >0.2%, block >5%
       without review)
Review: approved by @design-systems (intentional — ramp retune)
Flake controls verified:
  - Skeleton shimmer disabled via prefers-reduced-motion force in VR env
  - Intl stories pinned to fixed date 2026-01-15T12:00:00Z ("Jan 15, 2026",
    not "3 minutes ago")
Result: PASS with approval — PATCH classification upheld

Counter-run two weeks later: a “harmless” density map edit (--density-field-gap 16→12 in compact) triggered VR, 41 stories shifted, and the review revealed it silently compressed the Locked checkout form — change reverted, reclassified as needing design review.

Why it passes. VR is the mechanism that makes §15.6’s “PATCH requires visual diff” true; without it, PATCH is a lie. Deterministic stories (no shimmer, fixed dates) keep the signal-to-noise usable.

Rejected. Screenshots pasted into a wiki after merge (“VR without gates”), and VR on raw-hex CSS (“VR without semantic tokens is noise” — every brand tweak diffs everything, so reviewers rubber-stamp).

Ch 15.10 — Analytics hooks on Locked CTAs (cross-domain: instrumentation × Locked partition × find-rate) — Example

Concept. §15.10: Locked primary CTAs emit cue → action → reward with stable component_id + surface; system wrappers accept analyticsId; measure find-rate without docs; pair with override rate.

Scenario. The “Pay” button on Ledgerline checkout.

Example.

<Button tone="primary" analyticsId="checkout.pay">
  Pay $1,240.00
</Button>

The system wrapper — not product code — emits:

{ "event": "cue",    "component_id": "button", "surface": "checkout.pay", "ts": 1784112000021 }
{ "event": "action", "component_id": "button", "surface": "checkout.pay", "ts": 1784112004310 }
{ "event": "reward", "component_id": "button", "surface": "checkout.pay",
  "outcome": "payment_confirmed", "latency_ms": 1180 }

cue fires when the CTA becomes visible and enabled; action on activation (click, Enter, or Space — keyboard activations are the same event, so keyboard users aren’t invisible in funnels); reward when the success state renders.

Dashboard pairing: checkout.pay find-rate without docs = 96.4% of sessions reach action within 30s of cue; override rate on checkout chrome = 0% (Locked). When the reports squad’s forked FilterBar (Guided, 15.3-A) shows an 11% override rate, that’s the remediation trigger in the RACI (15.14).

Why it passes. Instrumentation lives in the system once, with stable IDs — no squad copy-pastes track() with drifting event names, and the Locked partition guarantees the funnel’s denominator is trustworthy.

Rejected. Ad-hoc onClick={() => { track('PayBtnClick_v2_final'); pay(); }} — five squads, five event names, and keyboard activations missed because someone bound analytics to mousedown.

Measure. Find-rate of core actions without docs; override rate on Locked/Guided chrome; cue→action latency distribution.

Ch 15.11 — Feature-flag UI states (all four flag effects) — Example

Concept. §15.11 table: hidden feature, partial rollout, kill switch mid-session, experiment variant.

Scenario. Ledgerline rolls out “Recurring invoices” behind flag recurring_v1.

Example.

  1. Hidden feature. Flag off ⇒ the “Recurring” nav item is absent from the IA, not rendered-disabled: no <NavItem disabled> ghost teasing a feature support can’t explain.
  2. Partial rollout (10%). Enabled cohort sees the same Locked Field/Dialog patterns as everything else. The PM’s request for a purple “BETA” ribbon over the form header was rejected because the proposed ribbon text was 2.7:1 on purple — beta chrome may not break contrast (WCAG 1.4.3 AA requires 4.5:1). Approved alternative: a standard Badge “Beta” using --color-bg-info-subtle at 5.1:1.
  3. Kill switch mid-session. A billing bug forces recurring_v1 off while 214 users are mid-form. They do not get a blank page; they get the error-boundary template (§15.12): “Recurring invoices is temporarily unavailable. Your draft is saved — we’ll restore this page when it’s back. [Back to invoices]” Draft state persisted; session preserved.
  4. Experiment variant. The A/B on the creation flow tests copy (“Set schedule” vs “Repeat this invoice”) — both arms are AA and neither arm may test a dark pattern on the Locked payment step (e.g., no variant that pre-checks auto-renew).
  5. Flag × component documented in Storybook. Because recurring_v1 changes the invoice CreateBar’s behavior (an extra “Repeat” schedule control appears), the DoD requires a story pair: Invoices/CreateBar (recurring_v1: off) and Invoices/CreateBar (recurring_v1: on) — export const FlagOn = { args: { flags: { recurring_v1: true } } }. Reviewers and the VR run (§15.9) see both arms; the off-arm story is what proves “hidden feature” leaves no dead control behind.

Why it passes. Flags are treated as designed product states: no dead nav, no contrast-breaking beta chrome, explain-and-recover on kill (L6: no blank states), experiment ethics bounded on trust paths, and every flag × component divergence has a reviewable Storybook artifact rather than living only in runtime config.

Rejected. The kill switch that swaps the route to null — users mid-form get a white screen and a lost draft; support tickets spike within the hour.

Ch 15.12 — Failure chrome templates (404, error boundary, crash, permission denied) — Example

Concept. §15.12 table: systemized failure chrome — plain language, recovery paths, focus management, correlation IDs; Guided→Locked candidates.

Scenario. The four templates as shipped in @ledgerline/ui/failure, with real microcopy.

Example.

  • Route 404. Heading: “We can’t find that page.” Body: “The link may be old, or the invoice may have moved.” Actions: “Go to Dashboard” (primary), “Open Invoices” (workspace), plus an inline search field. No cute skeleton-cowboy illustration with zero links.
  • Error boundary. Heading (focus moves here on mount, tabindex="-1"): “Something went wrong loading this panel.” Body: “Your other work is unaffected.” Actions: “Retry” · “Report issue”. The rest of the page keeps working — the boundary wraps the panel, not the app; focus is placed, not trapped. Steal mechanic: the move-focus-to-a-plain-language-heading behavior is stolen from GOV.UK’s Error Summary pattern — on form error, GOV.UK focuses an “There is a problem” heading with links to each failing field; Ledgerline copies the focus-the-explanation behavior, not the branding.
  • Crash / hard fail. “500 — Our server hit an error.” (status-code honesty, not “Oops! Something magical happened”). “Support reference: req_8fd2c91a. If this keeps happening, contact support with that code.” The correlation ID is selectable text.
  • Permission denied. “You don’t have access to Payroll exports.” Body: “Your role: Bookkeeper. Payroll exports need the Admin role.” Actions: “Request access from Dana K. (Admin)” · degraded path: “View summary totals instead”. Never a blank screen (L6).

Why it passes. Squads don’t invent panic UI: tone, focus behavior (heading focus, no trap), recovery links, and analytics (surface: "error.boundary") are shared. These start Guided and are promoted toward Locked as usage proves the contract.

Rejected. A dead-end 404 with only a joke and a logo; a permission wall that just says “Access denied.” with no who/why/how-to-request.

Measure. Recovery rate: % of 404/denied sessions that reach a valid destination within 60s.

Ch 15.13 — CMS / RTE as a consumer of the contract — Example

Concept. §15.13: map CMS blocks to system components; enforce contrast + heading order in RTE allowlists; alt policy (decorative vs informative); no CMS-invented button variants or raw hex.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s help center runs on a headless CMS; marketing editors write articles.

Example — the block map config:

{
  "blocks": {
    "heading":  { "component": "Heading", "levels": [2, 3, 4],
                  "rule": "must descend without skipping (h2→h3, never h2→h4)" },
    "callout":  { "component": "Banner", "tones": ["info", "warning"] },
    "button":   { "component": "Button", "tones": ["primary", "secondary"],
                  "rule": "no custom colors; tone only" },
    "image":    { "component": "Figure",
                  "altPolicy": "required; editor must choose 'informative' (alt text mandatory, 5–125 chars) or 'decorative' (alt=\"\" emitted)" }
  },
  "forbidden": ["rawHtml", "inlineStyle", "customColor"]
}

Editor-facing validation messages: “Heading level skipped: this section jumps from H2 to H4. Choose H3.” and “This image is marked informative but has no alt text. Describe it (e.g., ‘Invoice settings page with the Recurring tab open’) or mark it decorative.”

When marketing pasted a hex #7b2ff7 “Get started” button from their agency, the RTE stripped it and rendered <Button tone="primary">Get started</Button>.

Why it passes. Content that escapes the React tree still lands on system components, so contrast (WCAG 1.4.3 AA), heading order, and the alt policy (Chapter 19) hold in territory engineers never review.

Rejected. A freeform HTML field “for flexibility” — within a month it contains <font color="#9aa">, an <h5> after an <h2>, and a third button variant.

Ch 15.14 — RACI sketch (systems ops) — Example

Concept. §15.14 table: who is Accountable/Responsible/Consulted for Locked primitives+tokens, Guided patterns, a11y CI+lint, override-rate remediation, lived-experience on Locked.

Scenario. The FilterBar override-rate spike from 15.10 (11%), traced through the RACI in one week.

Example — the incident thread, annotated:

Mon. Dashboard alert: FilterBar override rate 11% (threshold 5%). Per RACI, Systems is Accountable for override-rate remediation, Product is Responsible — the Systems lead opens the ticket but assigns investigation to the reports squad’s PM.
Tue. Root cause: the pattern’s escape hatch doc never covered saved views, so three more squads forked it. Because Guided patterns have Product design Accountable, Squad eng Responsible, Systems Consulted, the pattern update is designed by product design, built by squad eng, reviewed by Systems.
Wed. The fix adds a savedViews slot — a MINOR (ui 5.3.0). The a11y lint update (saved-view menu needs APG menu keys) lands via Eng (A and R for a11y CI + lint), with Systems/a11y Consulted.
Fri. Because FilterBar sits on a reporting path (Guided, not Locked), no lived-experience session is triggered; had this been checkout, Research (A/R for lived-experience on Locked) would schedule paid sessions before ship.

Why it passes. Every hand-off in the thread names a row in the RACI — nobody debated ownership during the incident, which is the entire point of writing the matrix before you need it.

Rejected. “The design system team owns everything” — Systems becomes a ticket sink, squads stop feeling responsible for their own Guided forks, and override remediation dies in a backlog.

Ch 15.15 — Prefer-when: adopt vs build — Example

Concept. §15.15 matrix: adopt behavior lib + token skin for focus traps, menus, tabs, dialogs (APG-mapped), combobox/listbox, toast queues, portals; build for domain-specific Locked flows, unique data-viz encodings, and where platform chrome already broke parity. Don’t wrap once; do ban synonym forks.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s annual build-vs-adopt review, actual outcomes.

Example.

Need Decision Reasoning (from the memo)
Dialog focus trap Adopt (Ariakit Dialog + --color-bg-elevated skin — same @ariakit/react chosen in 15.4-B) “APG map exists; our focus-restore bugs cost 3 sprints last year.”
Combobox (client picker) Adopt (see 15.4-B) Solved behavior; skin with tokens.
Toast queue + portal Adopt Queue semantics + live-region wiring are commodity.
CheckoutField (card entry with fraud states) Build Domain-specific Locked flow; no library carries our contract.
Cash-flow “river” chart Build Unique data-viz encoding the brand owns.
iOS date picker Build on platform (use native UIDatePicker) Parity already broken by platform chrome (§16.8: nav/gesture chrome need not match web).

Governance rider in the same memo: “Squads may not adopt a second menu library. @ariakit/react is the one behavior lib for overlay primitives — a second one is a synonym fork and will be flagged by ll/no-banned-import.”

Why it passes. The line is drawn at contract, not code volume: adopt where the behavior contract is standardized (APG), build where the contract is yours alone.

Rejected. Building “LedgerlineTabs” from divs for brand feel (re-solving arrow-key APG behavior badly), and the one-line wrapper package created “for consistency.”

Chapter 16 — Component & Layout Inventory

(States follow L6 — never-used empty / filtered-to-zero / loading / partial / error / offline / denied / syncing / conflict — unless noted.)

Ch 16.1-A — Button — Example

Concept. §16.1: Button triggers an action; tone (primary/secondary/destructive/ghost), size, visible label or aria-label; pending disables + in-place status. Don’t: icon-only without name; synonym cta/brand; confirm-everything.

Scenario. Ledgerline’s “Send invoice” flow.

Example.

<Button tone="primary" size="md" onClick={send} pending={isSending}>
  {isSending ? 'Sending…' : 'Send invoice'}
</Button>

While pending: the button disables, keeps its width (no layout jump), and swaps its label in place to “Sending…” with aria-live="polite" status — no separate spinner overlay. The icon-only trash button next to it: <Button tone="ghost" aria-label="Delete draft"><TrashIcon aria-hidden /></Button> — passing ll/no-unlabeled-icon-button and WCAG 4.1.2 A (name/role/value — Level A, within the WCAG 2.2 AA conformance floor).

Why it passes. Action semantics, exhaustive tones, accessible name always present, and pending communicated in place (talkative obligation) without confirm dialogs for a safe, reversible send-draft action.

Rejected. <Button tone="cta"> (synonym, won’t compile — 15.5-A); a confirm dialog on every button including “Save draft” (confirm-everything trains click-through, devaluing the confirms that guard Hard deletes).

Ch 16.1-B — Link vs Button — Example

Concept. §16.1: Link navigates via real <a href>; visually distinct from Button; external indicated when needed. Don’t: div onClick navigation.

Scenario. Invoice row: open the invoice (navigation) vs duplicate it (action).

Example.

<a href="/invoices/INV-2041" class="ll-link">INV-2041 — Acme Corp</a>
<button type="button" class="ll-button" data-tone="ghost">Duplicate</button>
<a href="https://stripe.com/receipts/re_9x2" class="ll-link">
  View Stripe receipt <span class="ll-external" aria-hidden="true">↗</span>
  <span class="visually-hidden">(opens Stripe, external)</span>
</a>

Because it’s a real anchor: middle-click opens a new tab, Cmd-click works, right-click → “Copy link address” works, and the URL is crawlable/sharable.

Why it passes. Role matches behavior: navigation announces as “link” and inherits browser link affordances; action announces as “button.” External destination is indicated in both visible and accessible channels.

Rejected. <div onClick={() => router.push('/invoices/INV-2041')}> — no keyboard focus, no role, no middle-click, invisible to AT (fails WCAG 4.1.2 A name/role/value and 2.1.1 A keyboard).

Ch 16.1-C — Breadcrumb — Example

Concept. §16.1: hierarchy scent; landmark/nav label; current page not a link. Don’t: truncate middle without accessible full path.

Scenario. Deep client hierarchy: Clients → Acme Corp → 2026 → Q2 invoices.

Example.

<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
  <ol class="ll-breadcrumb">
    <li><a href="/clients">Clients</a></li>
    <li>
      <button aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Show 2 hidden levels: Acme Corp, 2026">…</button>
    </li>
    <li><a href="/clients/acme/2026/q2">Q2 invoices</a></li>
    <li aria-current="page">INV-2041</li>
  </ol>
</nav>

The middle collapse is a disclosure button that expands the two hidden levels in place — the full path exists for keyboard/AT, not just visually elided.

Why it passes. Labeled nav landmark, aria-current="page" on the non-link current node, and collapse-with-recovery per §17.6 (“Breadcrumbs: collapse middle with accessible full path”).

Rejected. Clients / … / INV-2041 where “…” is inert text — touch and AT users can never reach “Acme Corp.”

Ch 16.1-D — Nav shells + prefer-when — Example

Concept. §16.1: sidebar/top/tab-bar chosen platform-appropriately; labels on primary items until learnability is proven; no marketing bento inside tool chrome. Prefer-when: sidebar for multi-section pro tools; top for simpler IA; native tab bars on iOS/Android (parity: chrome need not match web).

Scenario. Ledgerline has 7 primary sections on web (Dashboard, Invoices, Clients, Payments, Reports, Payroll, Settings), 4 on mobile.

Example. Web ships a sidebar (multi-section pro tool) with icon + label on every item: “Invoices,” “Clients,” “Payments” — not icon-only, because internal find-rate testing hasn’t proven icon learnability. iOS ships a native tab bar with 4 items + “More”; Android ships its own nav bar. The marketing site’s bento-grid feature cards never appear inside the app shell — the tool test: chrome must not compete with the user’s work.

Collapse behavior (see 16.7): the sidebar collapses to icons only below a 240px container width, and each icon keeps its accessible name (aria-label="Invoices") plus tooltip.

Why it passes. Platform-appropriate chrome (parity matrix §16.8 says nav chrome must not match across platforms), labels retained until data says otherwise, and semantics (which section, which state) identical everywhere.

Rejected. Icon-only primary nav on day one (“it looks cleaner”) — unlearnable per §17.2’s nav-label row; and a React Native web-clone tab bar on iOS that ignores the platform’s own navigation grammar.

Ch 16.2-A — Field (label + control + help + error) — cross-domain Example

Concept. §16.2: visible label; aria-describedby for help/error; preserve input on error. Don’t: placeholder-as-label. Cross-domain: Locked validation (§15.3) + tokens + WCAG 3.3.1/3.3.2 A + 3.3.7 A redundant entry (all Level A, within the AA conformance floor).

Scenario. Checkout billing email field errors after submit.

Example.

<div class="ll-field" data-invalid="true">
  <label for="billing-email">Billing email</label>
  <input id="billing-email" type="email" autocomplete="email"
         value="dana@acme" aria-invalid="true"
         aria-describedby="billing-email-help billing-email-error" />
  <p id="billing-email-help">Receipts go here.</p>
  <p id="billing-email-error" class="ll-field-error">
    Enter a complete email address, like dana@acme.com.
  </p>
</div>

.ll-field-error { color: var(--color-text-danger); } /* 5.9:1 on canvas */
.ll-field [aria-invalid="true"] { border-color: var(--color-border-danger); border-inline-start-width: 3px; }

The typed value dana@acme is preserved — the user fixes 4 characters, not 9. Because Field is Locked chrome, the growth squad cannot restyle this error presentation (15.3-A).

Why it passes. Visible label (WCAG 3.3.2 A labels-or-instructions), programmatic help/error association via aria-describedby, error identified in text not color alone (WCAG 3.3.1 A + 1.4.1 A), input preserved (in the spirit of 3.3.7 A redundant entry — never make users re-supply what they gave you), and the whole thing runs on semantic tokens under a Locked contract. Law + token + WCAG in one component.

Rejected. <input placeholder="Billing email"> with no label — the “label” vanishes on first keystroke, and errors that wipe the field.

Ch 16.2-B — Input — Example

Concept. §16.2: correct type/autocomplete; password-manager-friendly auth fields. Don’t: disable paste on passwords.

Scenario. Ledgerline sign-in (Locked: auth).

Example.

<input id="email" type="email" autocomplete="username" inputmode="email" />
<input id="pw" type="password" autocomplete="current-password" />
<!-- sign-up variant: autocomplete="new-password" -->

Paste is enabled on the password field; a “Show password” toggle button (labeled, 44×44 craft target) sits inline. Password managers autofill both fields because the autocomplete tokens are correct.

Why it passes. Correct types drive the right mobile keyboards; correct autocomplete supports password managers, which is what WCAG 3.3.8 AA (accessible authentication — minimum) is protecting: no cognitive function test like memorizing/transcribing, because paste + autofill are honored.

Rejected. onpaste="return false" on the password field — it punishes password-manager users into weaker passwords and violates the intent of 3.3.8 AA.

Ch 16.2-C — Textarea — Example

Concept. §16.2: resize policy; character limits announced when enforced. Don’t: auto-grow without max that breaks layout at 400% zoom.

Scenario. “Note to client” on an invoice (500-char limit).

Example.

<textarea id="note" maxlength="500" rows="3"
          aria-describedby="note-count" style="max-block-size: 12lh;"></textarea>
<p id="note-count" aria-live="polite">440 characters left</p>

Auto-grows from 3 lines up to a max of 12 line-heights, then scrolls internally. The live counter switches to assertive phrasing at 0: “Character limit reached — 500 of 500 used.”

Why it passes. The limit is announced (not a silent stop), and the growth cap means at 400% zoom (WCAG 1.4.10 AA reflow context) the textarea can’t push the “Send” button off-viewport.

Rejected. Unbounded auto-grow: at 400% zoom a 20-line note makes the primary action unreachable without scrolling past a wall of text; and a maxlength that silently eats keystrokes with no counter.

Ch 16.2-D — Select — Example

Concept. §16.2: native when sufficient; APG listbox when custom. Don’t: fake select without keyboard map.

Scenario. Two dropdowns: “Currency” (24 options, plain) and “Assign client” (2,000 options, needs search + avatars).

Example. Currency ships as native:

<select id="currency" autocomplete="transaction-currency">
  <option value="USD">USD — US Dollar</option>
  <option value="EUR">EUR — Euro</option>
</select>

Native gets platform pickers on mobile for free. “Assign client” genuinely exceeds native (typeahead over 2,000 entries, avatar rendering) — so it uses the adopted APG combobox (15.4-B) with the full keyboard map: Down opens, arrows move aria-activedescendant, typing filters, Enter selects, Escape closes.

Why it passes. The escalation to custom is justified by a capability gap, not styling taste, and the custom control carries a complete APG keyboard contract.

Rejected. A styled <div class="select"> for Currency because the native chevron “looks off-brand” — no keyboard map, no mobile picker, an a11y bug bought for a chevron.

Ch 16.2-E — Checkbox — Example

Concept. §16.2: group legend; indeterminate only for “partial children.” Don’t: clickable row without name.

Scenario. Invoice-export options + the select-all header in the invoice table.

Example.

<fieldset>
  <legend>Include in export</legend>
  <label><input type="checkbox" checked /> Line items</label>
  <label><input type="checkbox" /> Payment history</label>
  <label><input type="checkbox" /> Client notes</label>
</fieldset>

Table header select-all: with 3 of 8 rows selected, the header checkbox is set indeterminate = true via JS and announces “mixed” — genuinely “partial children,” the only sanctioned use.

Why it passes. The legend gives every option its group context (“Include in export — Line items, checkbox, checked”), and indeterminate maps to a real partial-selection state, not a styling whim.

Rejected. A whole table row that toggles selection on click but contains no named checkbox — pointer users can select, keyboard/AT users can’t (fails WCAG 4.1.2 A name/role/value).

Ch 16.2-F — Radio — Example

Concept. §16.2: fieldset/legend; equal visual weight. Don’t: card-radio without radio semantics.

Scenario. Payment terms picker, rendered as selectable cards.

Example.

<fieldset class="ll-radio-cards">
  <legend>Payment terms</legend>
  <label class="ll-radio-card">
    <input type="radio" name="terms" value="net15" />
    <span class="ll-radio-card-title">Net 15</span>
    <span class="ll-radio-card-meta">Due within 15 days</span>
  </label>
  <label class="ll-radio-card">
    <input type="radio" name="terms" value="net30" checked />
    <span class="ll-radio-card-title">Net 30</span>
    <span class="ll-radio-card-meta">Due within 30 days</span>
  </label>
</fieldset>

The real radios are visually hidden but focusable; :focus-visible draws the 2px ring on the card via :has(). Both cards use identical --color-border-input weight — the recommended option gets a “Popular” Badge, not a heavier border that biases the choice.

Why it passes. Card visuals, radio semantics: arrow keys move within the group, the legend names the question, and equal visual weight keeps the choice honest.

Rejected. <div class="card" onClick={select}> cards — they look identical but have no group, no arrow-key behavior, no checked state for AT. The pattern’s named anti-pattern: “card-radio without radio semantics.”

Ch 16.2-G — Switch — Example

Concept. §16.2: immediate binary setting; label states on/off. Don’t: switch for “submit form”; switch for navigation.

Scenario. Settings → Notifications.

Example.

<button role="switch" aria-checked="true" id="reminder-switch">
  <span class="ll-switch-track" aria-hidden="true"></span>
</button>
<label for="reminder-switch">Payment reminders</label>
<p class="ll-switch-state">On — clients get a reminder 3 days before due date.</p>

Toggling applies immediately (no Save button on this row) and confirms in place: state text flips to “Off — no automatic reminders.”

Why it passes. A switch’s contract is instantaneous effect; the visible state text says which side is active in words, not just thumb position (color/position-only state fails low-vision users).

Rejected. A “switch” at the end of a form that does nothing until “Save changes” is pressed — that’s a Checkbox wearing a costume; and a switch that navigates to another page when flipped.

Ch 16.2-H — Form layout matrix + gap tokens — Example

Concept. §16.2 matrix: 1-column for critical tasks/checkout/mobile/cognitive load; 2-column for related short fields on large screens. Gaps: label→control 4–8, field→field 16–24, group→group 32+ (space tokens).

Scenario. Checkout (Locked) vs the admin client-record editor.

Example. Checkout is strictly 1-column top to bottom: Email → Card → Billing address → Pay. The one sanctioned 2-column moment appears inside the address group on ≥720px containers: City | Postal code — related short fields. The admin client editor (28 short fields, large viewports, daily-use admins) runs 2-column throughout but stacks to 1-column under container reflow (16.7).

.ll-form { display: grid; row-gap: var(--space-field-gap); } /* 16 */
.ll-field { display: grid; row-gap: var(--space-4); }        /* label→control 4 */
.ll-form-group { margin-block-start: var(--space-group-gap); } /* 32 */
.ll-form-row-2col { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; column-gap: var(--space-16); }
@container form (max-width: 560px) {
  .ll-form-row-2col { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
}

Why it passes. The critical/trust path gets single-column linearity (eye never zigzags near money); the dense admin tool earns 2-column on evidence (many short fields + large viewports), and it still stacks under reflow. All three gap bands are tokens, so density maps (15.2-E) can retune them coherently.

Rejected. A 2-column checkout with “Password” beside a promo-code field — label/control misalignment plus an unrelated pairing exactly as the matrix’s avoid-column warns.

Ch 16.3-A — Tabs — Example

Concept. §16.3: peer panels; one tablist; APG arrow keys; only selected panel in tab order. Don’t: nested tabs; tabs for sequential wizards.

Scenario. Client detail page: Overview / Invoices / Activity / Files.

Example.

<div role="tablist" aria-label="Client sections">
  <button role="tab" aria-selected="true" id="tab-overview" aria-controls="panel-overview">Overview</button>
  <button role="tab" aria-selected="false" id="tab-invoices" tabindex="-1" aria-controls="panel-invoices">Invoices</button>
  <!-- … -->
</div>
<div role="tabpanel" id="panel-overview" aria-labelledby="tab-overview">…</div>

Keyboard: Left/Right arrows move between tabs (roving tabindex — only the selected tab is in the Tab order), Tab jumps into the active panel. When product asked to add sub-tabs inside the Invoices panel, the answer was a segmented filter Chip row instead — no nested tablists.

Why it passes. APG contract complete; peer content (any order works). The 4 sections are genuinely parallel views of one client.

Rejected. A 3-step invoice-creation wizard rendered as tabs “Details | Line items | Review” — steps are sequential and validated; tabs imply free order. Wizards get a stepper.

Ch 16.3-B — Accordion — Example

Concept. §16.3: progressive disclosure; button headers; expand policy documented. Don’t: accordion as fake navigation.

Scenario. Invoice settings advanced options.

Example.

<h3><button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="sect-late-fees">Late fees</button></h3>
<div id="sect-late-fees" hidden>…</div>
<h3><button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="sect-tax">Tax handling</button></h3>
<div id="sect-tax" hidden>…</div>

Documented policy in the catalog entry: “Settings accordions are multi-expand (users compare sections). FAQ accordions are single-expand. Pick per surface and document it.”

Why it passes. Headers are real buttons inside real headings (SR users get both the heading outline and the expand/collapse state), content stays on the page (disclosure, not navigation).

Rejected. An accordion where expanding “Tax handling” actually routes to /settings/tax — that’s navigation cosplaying as disclosure; the back button and expand state fight each other.

Ch 16.3-C — Dialog — Example

Concept. §16.3: modal task; focus trap; Escape; restore trigger; labelled title. Don’t: stack modals; steal focus from typing for non-assertive noise. Cross-domain with Hard-delete confirm.

Scenario. Deleting a client with 34 invoices — a Hard destructive action (cascades; not recoverable by Soft undo), so it earns a real confirm.

Example.

<div role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="del-title">
  <!-- tabindex="-1" makes the heading programmatically focusable — a bare h2
       cannot receive focus, so "focus the heading on open" would silently fail -->
  <h2 id="del-title" tabindex="-1">Delete Acme Corp?</h2>
  <p>This permanently deletes the client and 34 invoices. This can't be undone.</p>
  <label for="confirm-name">Type <b>Acme Corp</b> to confirm</label>
  <input id="confirm-name" autocomplete="off" />
  <button class="ll-button" data-tone="destructive" disabled>Delete client</button>
  <button class="ll-button" data-tone="secondary">Cancel</button>
</div>

Focus moves into the dialog on open — deliberately to the heading (tabindex="-1" + .focus()), not to a button, so the blast-radius copy is read before any control is armed. Tab cycles inside (trap), Escape cancels, and on close focus restores to the “Delete client” trigger in the page. A request to open a second “Are you really sure?” modal on top was rejected: one modal at a time. Steal mechanic: the typed-name confirm is GitHub’s repository-delete behavior — “Please type the repository name to confirm” keeps the destructive button disabled until the exact name is typed, converting a reflex click into a deliberate act; Ledgerline steals the type-to-arm behavior for Hard deletes only.

Why it passes. Full modal contract (trap/Escape/restore/labelled) and the confirm is earned: Hard blast radius justifies typed confirmation, whereas the same squad’s “Archive invoice” (Soft) ships with a 7s undo Toast and no dialog at all.

Rejected. Stacked modals; and a “session expiring” dialog that yanks focus while the user is mid-keystroke in the note field for what is merely polite-level information.

Ch 16.3-D — Sheet — Example

Concept. §16.3: mobile/contextual panel; same focus rules as Dialog; drag handle is not the only dismiss. Don’t: sheet without visible close.

Scenario. Mobile invoice quick-actions sheet.

Example. Tapping an invoice row opens a bottom sheet: title “INV-2041 — Acme Corp”, actions “Mark paid”, “Send reminder”, “Duplicate”, “Delete…”. Chrome: a drag handle at top and a visible “Close” button (44×44) in the corner and Escape/scrim-tap dismissal. Focus is trapped while open and restored to the row on close.

Why it passes. Drag-to-dismiss is a bonus gesture, not the contract — switch-access and keyboard users get the labeled Close button. Same Dialog focus rules apply because a sheet is a modal in a different coat. (Gesture-only dismissal would also collide with WCAG 2.5.7 AA dragging-movements: single-pointer non-drag alternative required.)

Rejected. A sheet whose only exit is the swipe-down gesture — no close button, no Escape.

Ch 16.3-E — Menu — Example

Concept. §16.3: actions on an object; APG menu; typeahead when long. Don’t: hover-only open on mobile.

Scenario. Row overflow menu (“⋯”) on the invoice table.

Example. <button aria-haspopup="menu" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Actions for INV-2041">⋯</button> opens on click/Enter/Space/Down-arrow (not hover). Menu items: “Duplicate”, “Send reminder”, “Export PDF”, separator, “Delete…” (rendered with --color-text-danger). Arrows move, Home/End jump, typing “e” jumps to “Export PDF” (typeahead — this menu has 9 items), Escape closes and returns focus to the ⋯ button.

Why it passes. Full APG menu contract, activation works identically for touch (no hover dependency), and the trigger names its object so SR users hear which row they’re acting on.

Rejected. A CSS :hover-revealed menu — unopenable on touch, and it vanishes when a tremor briefly exits the hover zone.

Ch 16.3-F — Popover — Example

Concept. §16.3: non-modal anchored content; focus return; dismissible. Don’t: modal dialog dressed as popover.

Scenario. “Payment status” info popover on the dashboard.

Example. Clicking the “On hold ⓘ” trigger opens an anchored popover: “Payments are on hold while your bank verification completes (1–2 business days). [Check verification status]”. It’s non-modal: the page behind stays interactive; Escape or outside-click dismisses; on dismiss, focus returns to the trigger. Content stays hoverable and dismissible without moving the pointer (WCAG 1.4.13 AA content-on-hover-or-focus).

Why it passes. Non-modal contract matches non-blocking content — the user can read it and keep working.

Rejected. A “popover” containing a required form with Save/Cancel that closes on any outside click, eating input — that’s a modal task; use Dialog.

Ch 16.3-G — Tooltip — Example

Concept. §16.3: supplementary name/hint; keyboard accessible; never sole instruction. Don’t: tooltips for errors or essential copy.

Scenario. Toolbar icon buttons in the invoice editor.

Example. The “Bold” icon button shows a tooltip “Bold (Ctrl+B)” on hover and on keyboard focus, after 300ms, dismissible with Escape without moving focus (WCAG 1.4.13 AA). The button independently carries aria-label="Bold" — the tooltip is redundancy, not the name.

Why it passes. Supplementary by construction: remove every tooltip and the UI still works, because names and errors live elsewhere.

Rejected. Field validation delivered as a tooltip on the input (touch users may never see it; it vanishes on scroll) — the exact “tooltips for errors” ban; see 16.2-A for the correct error pattern.

Ch 16.3-H — Interruption rules — Example

Concept. §16.3: one modal at a time; toasts queue; never steal focus from typing unless assertive error.

Scenario. A user is typing a client note when three things happen within 2 seconds: a background export finishes, a collaborator comments, and the auth session hits its hard expiry.

Example. Export completion → Toast, queued, polite live region: “Export ready — Download” (no focus change; the user’s caret never leaves the note). Comment → queued second; the toast stack shows them one at a time, 7s each. Session hard-expiry (data loss imminent, action required) → this is the one sanctioned interruption: assertive Dialog “Your session ends in 60 seconds. [Stay signed in]”, focus moved to it, and the note draft is preserved either way.

Why it passes. Two polite events queue without touching focus; only the assertive, action-required error may interrupt typing — and even it protects the user’s work.

Rejected. The export toast that autofocuses its Download button mid-word — the user’s next keystroke, Space, activates a download they didn’t ask for.

Ch 16.4-A — Toast (Soft undo) — cross-domain Example

Concept. §16.4: transient acknowledgment / Soft undo; queue; polite live region; 5–10s soft undo; actions keyboardable. Don’t: move focus for every toast; toast-only hard failures. Cross-domain: undo class + component token + live region (WCAG 4.1.3 AA status messages).

Scenario. User archives invoice INV-2041.

Example.

toast({
  tone: 'neutral',
  message: 'Invoice INV-2041 archived',
  action: { label: 'Undo', onAction: unarchive },
  durationMs: 7000, // --toast-duration-soft; within the 5–10s Soft band
});

<div role="status" aria-live="polite">Invoice INV-2041 archived. Undo available.</div>

The timer pauses on hover and on focus-within; a documented shortcut moves focus to the toast region so keyboard users can reach “Undo” before expiry; the countdown never shortens below 5s. Archive is Soft (instant, in-place reversal). Steal mechanic: the behavior copied here is Gmail’s “Message sent — Undo” — Gmail holds the send for a user-configurable window (5–30s) so “Undo” is a true cancellation, not a compensating action; Ledgerline’s archive toast steals the held-window-with-inline-Undo behavior at 7s. Contrast: a failed payment is never toast-only — it gets an inline Banner on the payment panel (persistent) because a hard failure must not evaporate in 7 seconds.

Why it passes. Undo-instead-of-confirm for a reversible action, class-correct duration via a component token, announced via polite status (WCAG 4.1.3 AA) without stealing focus, and the action is genuinely keyboard-reachable. Law + undo class + token + WCAG SC in one component.

Rejected. “Payment failed” as a 5s toast (toast-only hard failure), and a toast system that focuses itself on every show (16.3-H).

Measure. Undo click-through rate on archive (healthy: >0 — proves reachability) and time-to-undo distribution vs the 7000ms window.

Ch 16.4-B — Banner — Example

Concept. §16.4: persistent inline status; role="status" or alert as appropriate; dismiss + undo class match blast radius. Don’t: color-only severity.

Scenario. Bank verification pending vs payment failure.

Example. Info banner (polite, dismissible): icon + “Verification in progress” + “Payouts resume when your bank confirms — usually 1–2 business days.” — role="status", --color-bg-info-subtle, and a dismiss “×” because pending-info is safe to hide. Failure banner (assertive, not dismissible while unresolved): role="alert", icon + bold “Payment failed” + “Acme Corp’s card was declined. [Retry payment] [Update card]”. Severity is carried by icon + title text, not background color alone.

Why it passes. Persistence matches consequence (a failure can’t be swiped away and forgotten); the role choice maps politeness to urgency; severity survives grayscale (WCAG 1.4.1 A use-of-color).

Rejected. A red-vs-yellow background as the only difference between “failed” and “pending” — indistinguishable to ~8% of male users with color-vision deficiency and to anyone in grayscale mode.

Ch 16.4-C — Badge — Example

Concept. §16.4: count/meta marker; text alternative for counts; don’t animate seizure-risk. Don’t: badge as only error signal.

Scenario. Sidebar “Invoices” item shows unpaid count.

Example. Visual: Invoices (12) pill. Accessible name of the nav item: aria-label="Invoices, 12 overdue" — the count has a text alternative with units and meaning, not a bare floating “12.” The badge appears without animation (no infinite pulse; anything flashing must stay under 3 flashes/second — WCAG 2.3.1 A threshold — but the system simply bans badge animation).

Why it passes. Count is perceivable and meaningful in the accessibility tree; no seizure-risk motion.

Rejected. A red dot on the Settings gear as the only signal that billing failed — a badge cannot carry an error; the failure also needs the Banner (16.4-B) and, if blocking, its own screen state.

Ch 16.4-D — Chip — Example

Concept. §16.4: filter token / selected attribute; removable chips named; keyboard remove. Don’t: chip clusters as primary IA.

Scenario. Invoice list filtered by two chips.

Example.

<ul aria-label="Active filters">
  <li><button class="ll-chip">Status: Overdue <span aria-hidden="true">×</span>
      <span class="visually-hidden">— remove filter</span></button></li>
  <li><button class="ll-chip">Client: Acme Corp <span aria-hidden="true">×</span>
      <span class="visually-hidden">— remove filter</span></button></li>
</ul>

Each chip is one focusable button whose accessible name is “Status: Overdue — remove filter”; Enter/Space or Delete removes it, focus moves to the next chip (or the filter bar when none remain), and the results-count status region announces “18 invoices match.”

Why it passes. Removal is named and keyboardable; focus never drops to <body> on removal.

Rejected. Chips as the app’s primary navigation (“Dashboard” “Invoices” “Settings” as a chip cloud) — chips mark attributes of a set, they are not IA; and an inert “×” glyph that only responds to mouse.

Ch 16.4-E — Avatar — Example

Concept. §16.4: person/entity; initials fallback; alt empty if adjacent name present. Don’t: avatar-only identity in lists.

Scenario. Activity feed: “Dana Kim marked INV-2041 as paid.”

Example.

<li>
  <img src="/u/dana.jpg" alt="" class="ll-avatar" /> <!-- alt="" : name is adjacent -->
  <p><b>Dana Kim</b> marked <a href="/invoices/INV-2041">INV-2041</a> as paid · 2:41 PM</p>
</li>

When Dana’s photo fails to load, the fallback renders initials “DK” on --color-bg-accent-subtle — deterministic per user, so DK is always the same hue. In the compact collaborator stack, avatars alone are never the identity: hover/focus reveals the name and the accessible name is on the element (aria-label="Dana Kim"), because a photo-only list is unnameable.

Why it passes. alt="" avoids the double-speak “Dana Kim, Dana Kim”; the fallback preserves identity without a network; lists never rely on face recognition.

Rejected. alt="avatar" (noise) or alt="Dana Kim" next to the visible text “Dana Kim” (duplication), and an assignee column that is nothing but 24px faces.

Ch 16.4-F — Skeleton — Example

Concept. §16.4: layout-matched placeholder; respect reduced motion. Don’t: shimmer as entertainment; mismatch causing layout jump.

Scenario. Invoice table initial load (~700ms p50).

Example. The skeleton renders 8 rows at exactly 44px row height with the same 5 column widths (checkbox 32px / number 120px / client 1fr / amount 96px / status 88px) as the real table, so content pops in with 0px cumulative layout shift. Shimmer is a subtle opacity pulse (0.6→1.0, 1200ms) — transform/opacity only per §15.7 — and under @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) it becomes a static block.

Why it passes. The skeleton’s only job is to promise the layout; matching geometry makes the promise true, and reduced-motion users get stillness.

Rejected. Three generic gray bars replaced by a 5-column table (layout jump; users mis-click as rows shift), and a rainbow shimmer that’s more entertaining than the data.

Ch 16.5-A — Table — Example

Concept. §16.5: real <table> or APG grid; headers/scope; sticky headers careful with focus; keyboard cell nav when grid; no div soup; no color-only status columns.

Scenario. The invoice table (read-mostly → real <table>, not grid).

Example.

<table class="ll-table">
  <caption class="visually-hidden">Invoices — 48 rows, filtered to Overdue</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col"><input type="checkbox" aria-label="Select all invoices" /></th>
      <th scope="col" aria-sort="descending"><button>Due date</button></th>
      <th scope="col">Client</th>
      <th scope="col" class="ll-num">Amount</th>
      <th scope="col">Status</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><input type="checkbox" aria-label="Select INV-2041" /></td>
      <td>Jun 30, 2026</td>
      <th scope="row"><a href="/invoices/INV-2041">Acme Corp</a></th>
      <td class="ll-num">$1,240.00</td>
      <td><span class="ll-statuspill" data-tone="danger">● Overdue</span></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

Status = dot + word (“Overdue”), never dot alone. The sticky header is position: sticky visual-only — DOM order is untouched, so tabbing never teleports, and a focused row scrolled under the sticky header is scroll-margined back into view (WCAG 2.4.11 AA focus-not-obscured-minimum). Because this table is read-and-navigate (links, checkboxes) rather than cell-editable, it stays a semantic <table>; the budgeting spreadsheet elsewhere in the app is a true APG grid with arrow-key cell navigation.

Why it passes. Real semantics give SR users row/column context for free; scope wiring, visible sort state (aria-sort), text-bearing status, and sticky-header focus care are each named rules from the row.

Rejected. <div class="table"><div class="row">… — no header association, no row/col announcement; and a status column of colored dots only.

Ch 16.5-B — Pagination — Example

Concept. §16.5: “Page X of Y” clarity; preserve filters in URL; components must support URL state and focus-to-results status; infinite scroll only with footer/keyboard escape hatches.

Scenario. Invoice list, 48 results, 25 per page, filtered to Overdue.

Example. URL: /invoices?status=overdue&sort=due_desc&page=2 — reload, share, and back-button all reproduce the exact view (filters preserved in URL).

<nav aria-label="Pagination">
  <a href="?status=overdue&sort=due_desc&page=1" aria-label="Previous page">‹ Prev</a>
  <span aria-current="page">Page 2 of 2</span>
</nav>
<!-- tabindex="-1": role="status" does not make a div focusable — without
     it the documented focus-to-results move silently fails -->
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" tabindex="-1">Showing 26–48 of 48 overdue invoices</div>

On page change, focus moves to the results-status element so keyboard/SR users hear the new range instead of being stranded on a link that may have disappeared. The team considered infinite scroll and kept pagination: the page has footer tasks (bulk export, totals row) that infinite scroll makes unreachable.

Why it passes. URL is the state container; position is explicit (“Page 2 of 2”); the announced range is the results status the section demands.

Rejected. Infinite scroll with a footer nobody can reach and no keyboard equivalent to “load more,” and pagination links that drop status=overdue so page 2 shows a different dataset than page 1.

Ch 16.6 — Layout primitives; content-shaped layouts; cards are not default — Example

Concept. §16.6: Stack / Inline / Cluster / Grid / Cover replace flex soup; quiet chrome, loud content; cards only when they bound an interaction.

Scenario. Rebuilding the invoice-detail page without one-off flexbox.

Example.

<Stack gap="group">            {/* --space-group-gap: 32 */}
  <Inline gap="16" align="center">
    <h1>INV-2041</h1>
    <StatusPill tone="danger">Overdue</StatusPill>
  </Inline>
  <Grid columns="2fr 1fr" gap="24" collapseAt="640px">
    <Stack gap="field">…line items…</Stack>
    <Stack gap="field">…totals…</Stack>
  </Grid>
  <Cluster gap="8">              {/* action buttons wrap gracefully */}
    <Button tone="primary">Record payment</Button>
    <Button tone="secondary">Send reminder</Button>
    <Button tone="ghost">Download PDF</Button>
  </Cluster>
</Stack>

Every gap value resolves to a space token; no component writes margin. Card audit result on this page: the line-items region is not a card (it’s the page’s content — quiet chrome, loud content); the single card is the “Record payment” panel, because it bounds a discrete interaction with its own state. The client logo thumbnail uses Frame at 1:1 with object-fit: cover — cropping decoration, never cropping UI controls.

Why it passes. Five primitives express the whole page; rhythm is token-governed so density maps retune it globally; card usage matches the “bounds an interaction” rule instead of card-as-wallpaper.

Rejected. Twelve nested display:flex divs with bespoke margins, and everything-in-a-card: cards inside cards until elevation means nothing.

Ch 16.7 — Container-query recipes (all five) + reflow laws — Example

Concept. §16.7: viewport breakpoints lie inside nested shells; CQ for component-local adaptation. Five recipes; plus reflow: usable at 320 CSS px + 400% zoom, DOM order = reading order, no essential 2D scroll (WCAG 1.4.10 AA).

Scenario. Ledgerline’s split view — invoice list (left pane, resizable 280–600px) + detail (right). The viewport is 1440px, so viewport breakpoints think everything is “desktop”; the left pane is effectively a phone.

Example.

.ll-pane { container: pane / inline-size; }

/* 1. Toolbar responsive: icon-only → icon+label above a concrete
   length threshold (a cqi condition here would be self-referential —
   48cqi of the pane's own inline size is effectively always true) */
@container pane (min-width: 420px) {
  .ll-toolbar .ll-button-label { display: inline; }
}

/* 2. Card meta demotion: drop side meta, keep title + primary action */
@container pane (max-width: 360px) {
  .ll-invoice-card .ll-meta-side { display: none; }
}

/* 3. Form split: 2-col → 1-col by CONTAINER width (see 16.2-H) */
@container form (max-width: 560px) { .ll-form-row-2col { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } }

/* 4. Data table: column priority + overflow menu */
@container pane (max-width: 480px) {
  .ll-table [data-priority="secondary"] { display: none; } /* moved into row ⋯ menu */
}

/* 5. Nav collapse: labels persist until proven; icons keep accessible names */
@container shell (max-width: 240px) {
  .ll-nav-label { position: absolute; clip-path: inset(50%); } /* visually hidden, name preserved */
}

Reflow verification on the same surfaces: at 320 CSS px viewport and at 400% zoom (both resolve to the same CSS-pixel reality), the detail pane stacks under the list, DOM order still matches reading order (the meta demotion uses display:none, never order: reshuffling), and only the data table scrolls horizontally — inside its own container, as a last resort, with column priority applied first (WCAG 1.4.10 AA).

Why it passes. Each recipe adapts to the component’s actual available width; the sidebar-in-a-wide-viewport case that breaks viewport breakpoints is handled by construction. Hidden secondary columns remain reachable (overflow menu), and collapsed nav icons keep their names.

Rejected. @media (min-width: 1024px) deciding the left pane is “desktop” and rendering the 5-column table into a 300px pane; and CQ demotion via CSS order that makes visual order diverge from DOM order (breaks WCAG 1.3.2 A meaningful sequence).

Measure. Automated reflow pass at 320px/400% on the five recipe surfaces in CI (0 horizontal page scroll, 0 clipped primary actions).

Ch 16.8 — Platform parity matrix — Example

Concept. §16.8: semantics match; chrome may differ. Must-match: semantic color roles, type-role intent, density maps, 5–10s toast soft-undo, Locked destructive confirms. Must-NOT-match: nav chrome, swipe-back. Company bet: shared semantics, native gestures; reject pixel-identical RN fantasy.

Scenario. “Delete draft invoice” reviewed across web, iOS, Android.

Example — the parity review sheet:

Concern Web iOS Android Verdict
Archive undo window Toast, 7s Snackbar-style, 7s Snackbar, 7s ✅ must match (5–10s band) — all 7000ms from the shared token source
Destructive confirm (Hard delete) Dialog w/ typed confirm Native alert w/ destructive-role red action Material dialog, same copy ✅ Locked pattern semantics match; native chrome renders it
--color-action-primary #2f6fed LLColor.actionPrimary #2F6FED ll_color_action_primary #2F6FED ✅ pipeline-generated (15.2-C)
Type roles --font-size-body 16px body 17pt (SF norm) body 16sp ✅ intent match, not px twins
Focus ring geometry :focus-visible 2px ring, --color-focus-ring System focus engine (UIFocusSystem) System focus engine (talkback/keyboard) ✅ intent yes — a visible, contrast-aware indicator everywhere; web draws its own 2px token ring, native platforms use their focus engines
Density maps data-density="compact" → 36px rows compact map → 44pt rows (HIG floor) compact map → 40dp rows ✅ yes — same named maps, values may differ per platform norms
Nav chrome Sidebar Native tab bar Native nav bar ✅ correctly different — must NOT match
Swipe-back Rare System edge-swipe System back ✅ native, untouched
Frosted panel --color-bg-elevated w/ subtle blur token System material (thin) Surface tone ✅ intent; iOS uses real material rather than a faked web blur
RTE/CMS help blocks Full block map (15.13) Limited renderer (heading/callout/image only) Limited renderer ✅ shared content rules — heading order, alt policy, and no-custom-color hold on all three even where the mobile renderers support fewer blocks

The one flagged item that quarter: an RN contractor shipped a pixel-cloned web sidebar on iOS — rejected in review with the matrix row cited (“Nav chrome: No — native”).

Why it passes. Trust-bearing semantics (roles, undo timing, destructive patterns) are identical everywhere; platform grammar (nav, gestures, materials) stays native. That is the company bet, executed.

Rejected. The pixel-identical RN fantasy as default strategy: web chrome cloned to iOS, breaking edge-swipe and platform muscle memory to win a screenshot-parity argument.

Ch 16.9 — Core kit status & contribution; promote or delete — Example

Concept. §16.9: every named component exists once in the catalog with status: experimental | stable | deprecated; contribution = the promotion pipeline; shadow libraries get promoted or deleted.

Scenario. Quarterly catalog audit, Q3 2026.

Example — audit excerpt:

[
  { "id": "button",    "status": "stable" },
  { "id": "statuspill","status": "stable",       "note": "promoted Q2 (see 15.4-A)" },
  { "id": "sheet",     "status": "experimental", "note": "2 consumers; component-grade early because mobile Locked flows need it — revisit Q4" },
  { "id": "modal-v1",  "status": "deprecated",   "note": "sunset 2026-09-01; use dialog; ll/no-banned-import active" }
]

Shadow-library findings: the audit script found two Accordions (@ledgerline/ui + a copy in apps/help) and three Toast implementations. Resolution ruling: help-center Accordion deleted (migrated to the kit in one PR); one squad Toast had a genuinely missing capability (progress toasts) — that feature was promoted into the kit Toast as ui 5.4.0 (MINOR) and the fork deleted; the third Toast was a stale copy — deleted.

Why it passes. One catalog row per concept; parallel implementations are treated as governance failures with exactly two exits — promote the novel part, delete the rest — never a third tolerated fork.

Measure. Duplicate-component count per audit (trend to 0); mean age of experimental status (flag anything experimental >2 quarters).

Chapter 17 — Internationalization

Ch 17.1 — ICU message architecture — Example

Concept. §17.1: ICU MessageFormat for all user-facing strings — plurals (never concatenate), select only with real data, named variables (never English word order), rich text as structured tags. API rule: no embedded English in Locked primitives.

Scenario. The invoice-list summary line and a “sent by” notification, shipped in en, pl (Polish has one/few/many/other), and ar.

Example.

// messages/en.json
"invoice.summary": "{count, plural, one {# invoice} other {# invoices}} due {dueDate}",
"invoice.sentBy": "{name} sent {count, plural, one {an invoice} other {# invoices}} to <clientLink>{client}</clientLink>",

// messages/pl.json — four plural categories, impossible with count + " items"
"invoice.summary": "{count, plural, one {# faktura} few {# faktury} many {# faktur} other {# faktury}} — termin {dueDate}"

// Rich text: translators write <clientLink>, never HTML
t('invoice.sentBy', {
  name: 'Dana Kim', count: 3, client: 'Acme Corp',
  clientLink: (chunks) => <Link href="/clients/acme">{chunks}</Link>,
});

Named variables mean Polish can reorder freely: “termin {dueDate}” puts the date last where English needed it last too — but Arabic reorders the whole sentence and nothing breaks, because there is no "due " + dueDate concatenation anywhere. select for formality exists only in the German locale ({formality, select, formal {Bitte prüfen Sie…} other {Bitte prüf…}}) because Ledgerline actually collects a workspace formality setting — not guessed from names.

API rule enforced in the kit: <Button> renders children — the Locked primitive contains zero English. The empty-state component takes title/body message IDs; the one hardcoded “Save” found in a Locked Field was flagged by the pseudo-loc gate (17.4).

Why it passes. Plural categories come from CLDR via ICU (Polish’s few/many are unrepresentable in count + " items"); word order is the translator’s to own; rich text is componentized so translators can’t inject HTML; and primitives stay language-free.

Rejected. `${count} invoice${count === 1 ? '' : 's'}` — wrong in Polish, Russian, Arabic, Welsh; and translators handed raw <a href=...> inside strings.

Ch 17.2 — Expansion budgets (all five rows) — cross-domain Example
