Concept. §17.2 table: buttons/tabs allow ~30–40% growth (wrap or taller control over ellipsis on critical actions); nav prefers wrap/scroll over icon-only fallback; toasts multi-line with tokenized max width; table column min-widths from content; dialogs grow with content.

Scenario. German (de) and Finnish (fi) launch. English “Save changes” (12 chars) becomes German “Änderungen speichern” (20 chars, +67% — beyond the 40% planning band, which is why budgets are enforced, not assumed).

Example — the five rows, as shipped:

  1. Button. .ll-button { max-inline-size: 100%; white-space: normal; min-block-size: 44px; } — the primary checkout button grows wider up to its container, and when the label no longer fits it wraps to two lines and the control grows taller (44→~64px). It never renders “Änderungen sp…”. (Not min-inline-size: max-content — that pins the minimum width to the unwrapped label, so the button overflows the container instead of wrapping.) Cross-domain note: the taller control still meets the 44×44 craft target and trivially clears the 24×24 WCAG 2.5.8 AA floor.
  2. Nav labels. Finnish “Laskutusasetukset” (billing settings) wraps to two lines in the sidebar item rather than triggering an icon-only collapse — icon-only fallback is the last resort, not the expansion strategy.
  3. Toast. .ll-toast { max-inline-size: var(--toast-max-width); /* 400px */ } — the German archive-undo toast runs two lines; the “Rückgängig” (Undo) action stays fully visible. A clipped Soft-undo action would silently delete the undo affordance.
  4. Table. The Status column’s min-width derives from the longest shipped status string per locale (de “Überfällig” > en “Overdue”), computed at build time; horizontal scroll remains the documented last resort.
  5. Dialog. The delete-confirm dialog (16.3-C) has max-block-size: 85dvh with internal scroll — German legal copy grows the dialog; the “Kunde löschen” / “Abbrechen” actions are pinned visible, never clipped below the fold of an English-sized fixed height.

Why it passes. Every element has a named growth strategy (wrap, grow, min-content, pinned actions) instead of a prayer; the budgets are enforced by the pseudo-loc CI gate (17.4), not by screenshots.

Rejected. text-overflow: ellipsis on the checkout primary action (“Truncated ‘Save’ equivalents”), and a dialog locked to the English screenshot’s 360px height clipping German buttons.

Measure. Pseudo-loc CI run: 0 clipped primary actions on Locked surfaces at +40% padded strings.

Ch 17.3 — Locale formats with Intl (all six rows) — Example

Concept. §17.3: never hand-roll dates, numbers, currency, lists, relative time, or collation; currency-code clarity when multi-currency; absolute-on-demand for trust paths; server/client timezone agreement for money/legal timestamps.

Scenario. One invoice rendered for a de-DE accountant and an en-US founder.

Example.

const d = new Date('2026-07-15T14:30:00Z');

new Intl.DateTimeFormat('de-DE', { dateStyle: 'medium' }).format(d);   // "15. Juli 2026"
new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-US', { dateStyle: 'medium' }).format(d);   // "Jul 15, 2026"

new Intl.NumberFormat('de-DE').format(12480.5);                        // "12.480,5"

// Multi-currency workspace ⇒ code clarity, not bare symbol:
new Intl.NumberFormat('de-DE', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD',
  currencyDisplay: 'code' }).format(1240);                             // "1.240,00 USD"
// ("$" alone is ambiguous across USD/CAD/AUD in one client list)

new Intl.ListFormat('de', { type: 'conjunction' })
  .format(['Acme', 'Birke', 'Corax']);                                 // "Acme, Birke und Corax"

new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('en', { numeric: 'auto' })
  .format(-3, 'day');                                                  // "3 days ago"

['Åberg', 'Zimmer', 'Öhman'].sort(new Intl.Collator('sv').compare);
// sv: ["Zimmer", "Åberg", "Öhman"] — Å/Ö sort AFTER Z in Swedish;
// naive .sort() would wrongly file Åberg first.

Trust-path rule applied: the activity feed shows “Paid 3 days ago”, but hover/focus and the detail view show the absolute “Paid Jul 12, 2026, 09:14 (UTC+02:00, Europe/Berlin)” — relative time never stands alone on a money timestamp, and the server sends the IANA zone + UTC instant so client rendering can’t disagree with the ledger. Product tables render amounts with font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums so “12.480,50” columns align (visual-system tie-in).

Why it passes. Six concerns, six Intl APIs, zero hand-rolled formatters; currency codes disambiguate a multi-currency list; absolute-on-demand keeps trust paths auditable.

Rejected. date.toLocaleDateString() with no locale on the server (renders in the server’s locale), "$" + amount.toFixed(2), and names.sort() shipping Swedish names in English order.

Ch 17.4 — Pseudo-localization gates (all four techniques) — Example

Concept. §17.4: pseudo-loc is a ship gate — accents+brackets catch hardcoded strings and clipping; padding catches expansion overflow; bidi marks/fake RTL catch mirroring bugs; long compounds catch nav/table breaks. Fail PRs when Locked surfaces clip primary actions.

Scenario. The en-XA pseudo-locale build runs on every PR’s Storybook (per §15.8 DoD).

Example — one CI run, four catches:

pseudo-loc gate — build #5512 (locale en-XA)

[accents+brackets]  Checkout/PayButton: renders "Pay now" — expected
                    "[!!! Þåý ñöŵ !!!]". Hardcoded string in Locked
                    primitive.                                   ⛔ FAIL (blocks PR)

[padding +40%]      Toast/ArchiveUndo: "xxxÐéļéţéðxxx — xxxÛñðöxxx"
                    action clipped at 400px max width. Soft-undo action
                    unreachable.                                 ⛔ FAIL

[fake RTL marks]    Breadcrumb: separator chevrons did not mirror under
                    dir="rtl"; path reads backwards.             ⚠ FAIL (Guided)

[long compounds]    Sidebar: "Rechnungsstellungseinstellungenxxx" (28+
                    chars, unbroken) overflowed the 240px nav — needs
                    overflow-wrap: anywhere on nav labels.       ⚠ WARN

The first two are on Locked surfaces and hard-block the merge; the developer fixes the hardcoded “Pay now” by routing it through the message layer (17.1) and adds the wrap rule from 17.2.

Why it passes. All four techniques run mechanically on every PR — layout truth comes from pseudo-loc, not from English screenshots — and the blocking policy matches the partition: clipped primary actions on Locked surfaces fail the build.

Rejected. Pseudo-loc as a one-time demo before launch: the four bug classes reappear with the next quarter’s features and nobody re-checks.

Ch 17.5 — Logical CSS, RTL, mixed bidi — Example

Concept. §17.5: logical properties over physical; dir="rtl" on document or islands; don’t mis-mirror meaning-bearing icons; bidi-isolate usernames/URLs/code/phones in RTL prose; truncation with a non-hover accessible path (title alone is insufficient).

Scenario. Arabic (ar) launch of the invoice detail page.

Example.

/* Logical: one rule serves LTR and RTL */
.ll-field-error { border-inline-start: 3px solid var(--color-border-danger);
                  padding-inline-start: var(--space-8); }
.ll-nav-item    { margin-inline-end: var(--space-16); }
/* NOT: border-left / margin-right — those point the wrong way in ar */

Icon policy applied: the back chevron mirrors in RTL (direction-bearing — “back” points right in Arabic UI, per platform convention); the media play triangle does not mirror (playback direction is not reading direction); the search magnifier doesn’t mirror (no direction).

Mixed bidi in an Arabic activity line:

<p dir="rtl">أرسلت <bdi>Dana Kim</bdi> فاتورة إلى
   <bdi>support@acme.com</bdi> — <bdi dir="ltr">+1 415-555-0134</bdi></p>

Without <bdi>/dir="auto", the phone number’s punctuation jumps and “+1” detaches to the wrong end of the line.

Truncation with a real accessible path (client name in a narrow list):

<a href="/clients/acme-industrial" class="ll-truncate"
   aria-label="Acme Industrial Fabrication GmbH">Acme Industrial Fa…</a>

text-overflow: ellipsis truncates on the logical end (start-side in RTL automatically); the full name lives in the accessible name and in a focus-triggered popover — title="" alone was rejected because touch and AT users never receive it.

Why it passes. One logical stylesheet serves 14 locales; mirroring is per-icon-meaning, not blanket transform: scaleX(-1); bidi isolation keeps Latin fragments intact inside Arabic prose; and truncated text remains fully available without hover.

Rejected. A rtl.css fork overriding hundreds of margin-lefts (drifts within a sprint); mirroring every icon including play; title as the only full-text path.

Ch 17.6 — Truncation strategy (all five rows) — Example

Concept. §17.6 table: critical action labels wrap (don’t truncate); secondary meta truncates with AT-available full text; list titles truncate end but stay unique in SR lists; numbers/currency never truncate mid-value; breadcrumbs collapse middle with accessible full path.

Scenario. The 320px-wide invoice list pane (16.7) under German strings.

Example — one surface, five rulings:

  1. Critical action. “Zahlung erfassen” (Record payment) wraps to two lines on its button; the ellipsized variant “Zahlung erf…” was rejected in review with this row cited.
  2. Secondary meta. “Zuletzt bearbeitet von Dana Kim vor 3 Tagen” truncates to “Zuletzt bearbeitet von Da…” visually, with the full string in a visually hidden span: <span class="visually-hidden">Zuletzt bearbeitet von Dana Kim vor 3 Tagen</span>.
  3. Primary list titles. Two clients truncate to “Acme Industrial Fa…” — audit found their SR names collide, so the row’s accessible name is extended with the distinguishing suffix: aria-label="Acme Industrial Fabrication GmbH" vs "Acme Industrial Facilities AG"; the SR list stays unique.
  4. Numbers/currency. $1,240,580.00 never renders as $1,240,5…; the narrow column either wraps the amount or uses the explicit compact format "$1.24M" (a formatted abbreviation via Intl.NumberFormat notation: 'compact', labeled in the column header “Amount (approx.)”) — never a mid-digit chop.
  5. Breadcrumbs. As built in 16.1-C — middle collapse behind an expandable “…” button whose aria-label enumerates the hidden levels.

Why it passes. Each content class gets the strategy its stakes demand: actions keep their whole verb, meta stays recoverable, identity stays unique, money is never visually falsified, and paths stay traversable.

Rejected. One global .truncate { text-overflow: ellipsis } utility slapped on everything — which is precisely how “$1,240,5…” and “Zahlung erf…” ship.

Ch 17.7 — i18n × a11y × systems checklist — Example

Concept. §17.7: correct lang on page and islands; pseudo-loc (not screenshots) as layout truth; quarterly SR smoke in a non-English shipped locale; CMS translators inherit expansion rules.

Scenario. The pre-launch checklist run for the Arabic release, with evidence links.

Example — the filled checklist:

  • ✅ Lang attributes. <html lang="ar" dir="rtl">; the embedded English legal-terms block is an island: <section lang="en" dir="ltr">. Verified by audit script — without the island attribute, VoiceOver read the English ToS with Arabic pronunciation rules (garbled).
  • ✅ Layout truth. Docs screenshots regenerated from the pseudo-loc + ar builds; the Figma English frames carry a banner: “Layout truth = pseudo-loc CI, not this frame.”
  • ✅ SR smoke, non-English. Quarterly VoiceOver (iOS, ar) run on checkout: land → skip to main → complete “ادفع الآن” (Pay now) → hear the card error → dismiss dialog → focus restored. Logged as passing in the release ticket.
  • ✅ CMS. Translator guidelines updated: Arabic help articles use the same block map (15.13); a lint on CMS content flags manual <br> line-break sculpting that assumed English line lengths.

Why it passes. Each line is verified with an artifact (script output, CI run, session log), and the checklist spans systems (CMS block map), a11y (SR smoke, lang islands), and i18n (pseudo-loc) in one gate — the intersection the section exists to police.

Rejected. Shipping ar because “RTL CSS is done” — flipped layout with lang="en" still on the root, unpronounceable to TalkBack, and help articles line-broken for English.

Ch 17.8 — Prefer-when: ICU day one vs labeled hardcode — Example

Concept. §17.8: full ICU + Intl from day one for any product that will leave one locale; English-only hardcode acceptable only for a throwaway internal spike labeled Open with a delete date; pixel-perfect English layouts never for Locked surfaces.

Scenario. Two new codebases start the same month.

Example. (1) The customer-facing “Estimates” module: even though it launches en-only, every string goes through the message layer from commit 1 — retrofitting ICU onto 2,400 concatenated strings later was quoted at 6 engineer-weeks; wiring it now cost ~2 days. (2) An internal ops dashboard spike: hardcoded English is explicitly permitted, with the required label in the repo root:

<!-- README.md -->
> **OPEN surface — English-only hardcode sanctioned.**
> Throwaway internal spike. Delete date: **2026-10-01.**
> If this survives past the delete date, it enters the promotion
> pipeline and gets ICU like everything else.

(3) A designer’s request to lock the checkout layout to the polished English mock (“can we freeze it exactly like this?”) is denied with the row cited: pixel-perfect English layouts — never for Locked surfaces; the mock is re-annotated with the 17.2 growth strategies.

Why it passes. The expensive discipline is applied exactly where the future demands it (customer product), waived exactly where it’s waste (labeled, expiring spike), and the “never” row is enforced where money flows.

Rejected. The unlabeled “temporary” internal tool that quietly becomes customer-facing in Q4 with 2,400 unlocalizable strings — the precise failure the Open label + delete date exists to prevent.

End of Part IV examples. Cross-references: undo classes and state taxonomy per Chapters 3/10; WCAG ship gates per Part V; promotion Case E (override rate) per Chapter 21.

Modern UI — Companion Examples, Part V: Accessibility & Inclusion (Chapters 18–20)

Purpose. This document is the official examples companion to Part V of Modern UI. Every major concept, law, tension, table row-group, taxonomy, and pattern in Chapters 18–20 gets at least one concrete example: a realistic product scenario, real microcopy in quotes, real code, real numbers, and named tokens. Headings mirror the textbook’s chapter/section numbering so coverage is auditable. Conventions follow the textbook exactly: laws cited as L1–L14 (Ch 3), undo classes Soft / Quarantine / Hard (Ch 3 & 10), Locked / Guided / Open partition (Ch 15), WCAG 2.2 AA as legal floor with AAA labeled where claimed, touch targets 44×44 craft bar vs 24×24 AA floor (2.5.8), and semantic token naming in the --color-text-primary / --space-field-gap style. The running scenario products are LedgerLine (B2B invoicing SaaS — a trust path product), Fieldnote (a daily-driver research notes tool), and Wayfare (a consumer travel-booking app), so trust × frequency (L14) allocation is visible across examples.

Chapter 18 — Inclusive Design Philosophy & Verification

Ch 18 — 18.1.1: Situational disability is normal — Example

Concept. Designing for situational disability under-scopes reality if you only build “permanent disability personas” (18.1 item 1).

Scenario. Wayfare’s boarding-pass screen. Users open it: in bright sun at a gate (low effective contrast), one-handed while dragging a suitcase (motor), in a loud terminal (audio useless), sometimes with a sprained wrist (temporary injury).

Example. The boarding-pass surface is specified against situational personas, not only disability personas:

  • Text uses --color-text-primary on --color-surface-raised at 7:1 measured in both themes (exceeds the 4.5:1 AA floor of 1.4.3, because sun glare eats margin).
  • The single primary action “Show QR code” is a 56×56 px target anchored bottom-center — above the 44×44 craft bar, reachable with either thumb.
  • Gate-change alerts fire as a role="alert" live region and a visible banner and an optional haptic — never sound-only.
  • QR brightness boost is automatic; no gesture required.

Why it passes. One design decision serves the blind user, the sunburned user, and the one-handed user simultaneously — the textbook’s point that situational disability makes inclusive choices majority choices. Craft budget is justified by L14: boarding is maximal trust × frequency for a travel app.

Measure. Task success (“present pass to scanner”) in field testing under 50k lux simulated glare; one-handed completion rate.

Ch 18 — 18.1.2: Nothing about us without us — Example

Concept. Paid participants with relevant disabilities on critical paths; findings can block ship on Locked surfaces (18.1 item 2).

Scenario. LedgerLine is redesigning the Pay Invoice flow (a Locked surface). The a11y CI is green.

Example. Research runs the quarterly lived-experience panel before the release train:

  • 8 paid participants: 2 NVDA users, 2 VoiceOver users, 1 TalkBack user, 1 switch-access user, 1 low-vision 400%-zoom user, 1 participant with aphasia. Compensation: $125/hour, paid regardless of findings.
  • Task: “Pay the March invoice using the saved card.” No coaching.
  • Finding P0-2026-041: the card-CVC field’s error (“Security code is incomplete”) is injected into a container with aria-hidden="true", so NVDA users retried silently and abandoned. Two of two NVDA participants failed the task.
  • Per policy, a P0 lived-experience finding on a Locked path blocks ship. The release train holds 4 days; fix is verified by re-testing with one of the original participants.

Why it passes. The finding could not have been produced by axe (the ARIA was technically valid); only lived experience answers “can a person complete the job with their tools?” (18.5). Blocking ship operationalizes “nothing about us without us” instead of quoting it.

Measure. Lived-experience task success on Pay ≥ overall task success − 5 points; count of P0 findings that actually held a release (if the number is always zero, the gate is theater).

Ch 18 — 18.1.3: AA floor / humane ceiling — Example

Concept. Meet WCAG 2.2 AA everywhere; exceed it where trust × frequency demands (18.1 item 3, GOV.UK posture).

Scenario. LedgerLine’s account-deletion flow (rare but maximal trust) vs its internal icon-glossary admin page (rare, low trust).

Example. Both pages pass AA. The deletion flow additionally gets ceiling treatment:

  • Plain language at ~grade-7 reading level: “Deleting your account removes all invoices after 30 days. Until then you can restore everything.” — not “Account deletion is irreversible upon elapse of the retention window.”
  • GOV.UK-style Error Summary on validation failure (see 19.7 example).
  • One-column layout, one primary action per view (20.5).
  • Target: 7:1 text contrast (the 1.4.6 AAA number) even though only 4.5:1 AA is claimed in the VPAT.

The icon-glossary admin page gets the AA floor and nothing more.

Why it passes. Floors are uniform; ceilings are allocated by L14 (craft ∝ trust × frequency). Labeling matters: the VPAT claims AA — AAA-level touches are unclaimed craft, so no compliance overstatement occurs (18.2, 20.13 discipline of labeling AA vs AAA).

Rejected. Spending the AAA-contrast and plain-language budget on the admin glossary while checkout errors remain jargon — the L14 failure mode “rare admin polished before pay.”

Measure. Reading-grade level of critical-path copy (deletion flow target ≤ grade 7); ceiling spend audited against the L14 trust×frequency ranking — AAA touches appearing on low-rank pages before high-rank ones is the failure signal.

Ch 18 — 18.1.4: Bake into primitives — Example

Concept. Contrast-gated tokens, focus rings, labeled APIs, APG keyboard maps live in Locked primitives so squads don’t reinvent accessible Dialog quarterly (18.1 item 4). Cross-domain: L1 + L9 + tokens + WCAG in one decision.

Scenario. LedgerLine’s design system team ships @ledgerline/primitives v4.

Example. Three baked-in guarantees:

/* 1. Contrast-gated token pipeline: CI computes ratios at build time.
   A PR that maps --color-text-secondary to a primitive failing 4.5:1
   on --color-surface-default in EITHER theme fails the build. */
:root {
  --color-text-secondary: var(--gray-700);   /* 5.9:1 on surface-default (light) — pass */
  --focus-ring-color: var(--blue-600);        /* 3.4:1 vs adjacent surfaces — pass 1.4.11 */
  --focus-ring-width: 2px;
  --focus-ring-offset: 2px;
}

/* 2. Focus ring is a primitive, not per-squad CSS */
.ll-focusable:focus-visible {
  outline: var(--focus-ring-width) solid var(--focus-ring-color);
  outline-offset: var(--focus-ring-offset);
}

// 3. Labeled API: the icon-only button REQUIRES a name at the type level.
type IconButtonProps =
  | { icon: IconName; 'aria-label': string; onPress(): void }
  | { icon: IconName; labelledBy: string; onPress(): void };
// <IconButton icon="trash" /> is a compile error, not a lint warning.

The Locked Dialog ships the full APG dialog keyboard map (trap, Escape, focus restore to trigger) so product squads never write it.

Why it passes. L1 (roles, not hexes) makes contrast enforceable at the token layer; L9 (focus is a cursor) is satisfied once, centrally; the labeled API turns a WCAG 4.1.2-class name failure into a compile error. This is “accessibility as a property of primitives, not a late audit” (Ch 1 §1.4).

Measure. Count of outline: none and raw-hex violations caught in CI per quarter; number of squad-local Dialog implementations (target: 0, per L12 shadow-library rule).

Ch 18 — 18.1.5: Checklist floor vs lived-experience gate — Example

Concept. Automated/axe floor always; lived experience required when the path is essential — auth, pay, create, delete, appeal (18.1 item 5). Failure mode: axe-green, unusable.

Scenario. Two LedgerLine PRs land the same week.

Example.
- PR #4812 restyles the marketing pricing page. Gate applied: automated floor only — axe clean of serious issues, contrast tokens, keyboard pass. Ships same day.
- PR #4820 changes the invoice create flow (essential path: “create”). Gate applied: automated floor plus the flow is queued for the quarterly lived-experience panel; because it ships mid-quarter, an interim 90-minute session with two AT users is run against the staging build before merge to Locked.

Rejected (the named failure mode: “axe-green, unusable”). The earlier v2 invoice editor passed axe with zero violations. Every field had a programmatic label, every contrast pair passed. But line items were added via a hover-revealed “+” button with no keyboard path, and totals recalculated with no live region — a VoiceOver user could reach every control and still not finish an invoice. Axe measures attributes; it cannot measure task completion. Inclusion beats compliance theater.

Measure. For essential paths: AT-user task completion rate, tracked next to axe violation count. If the first is unknown, the second is a vanity metric.

Ch 18 — 18.2: Legal & market floors — Example

Concept. WCAG 2.2 AA baseline; EAA / ADA / Section 508 as market-triggered obligations; VPAT/ACR as enterprise sales evidence; internal ship gates stronger than marketing claims (18.2).

Scenario. LedgerLine sells to (a) EU mid-market, (b) US enterprises, (c) a US federal agency pilot.

Example. The compliance map the legal + a11y leads maintain:

Market trigger Instrument Concrete obligation
All markets WCAG 2.2 AA Baseline SC set; the internal ship gates (18.4) enforce it per release
EU sales (post-June-2025 services) EAA Accessibility statement published; feedback channel; conformance evidence kept current
US private-sector ADA Litigation exposure framed to execs as “WCAG AA is the de facto bar courts reference”
US federal pilot Section 508 Buyer requires an ACR on the VPAT 2.5 template before contract; sales cannot self-declare — the a11y team authors it, listing “Supports / Partially Supports” per SC with remarks
Internal Ship gates Stronger than the marketing claim: marketing says “WCAG 2.2 AA”; internal gates also run SR smoke and forced-colors checks that no statute names

Microcopy on the public accessibility statement: “LedgerLine targets WCAG 2.2 Level AA. Found a barrier? Email access@ledgerline.example — we respond within 2 business days.”

Why it passes. Legal compliance ≠ product quality, but the map shows nobody is treating “ignore the floor” as a strategy. The VPAT/ACR row exists because enterprise procurement asks for evidence, not vibes.

Rejected. A marketing page claiming “fully ADA compliant and beyond AAA” with no ACR, no statement, no gates — a claim stronger than the verification behind it, inverted from the textbook’s rule that internal gates should be stronger than marketing claims.

Measure. ACR freshness (age of the current VPAT 2.5 ACR ≤ two release trains); accessibility-statement feedback response time ≤ the promised 2 business days; zero public claims stronger than the gate evidence behind them.

Ch 18 — 18.3a: AT matrix (P0/P1/P2) — Example

Concept. Prioritized verification environments (18.3 table).

Scenario. LedgerLine’s release train runs every 2 weeks. QA capacity is finite; the matrix decides what runs when.

Example. The team’s test-run configuration file:

# at-matrix.yaml — verification environments per release train
p0_every_release:
  - { at: VoiceOver, browser: Safari,        os: macOS + iOS, why: "Apple ecosystem" }
  - { at: NVDA,      browser: Chrome+Firefox, os: Windows 11,  why: "Windows baseline" }
  - { at: TalkBack,  browser: Chrome,          os: Android 15,  why: "Android" }
p1_every_release_train_or_enterprise_deal:
  - { at: JAWS,          browser: Chrome+FF,  os: Windows 11, why: "Enterprise sales" }
  - { at: VoiceControl,  scope: mobile-core-path, cadence: once-per-release-train }
p2_scheduled:
  - { at: switch-access, scope: Locked flows }
  - { at: keyboard-only-marathon, scope: "full critical-path map, no pointer, 60 min" }
paths_under_test: [auth, checkout, create-invoice]

Why it passes. Matches the textbook priority order exactly: P0 combinations run on every release for auth/checkout/create; JAWS is funded because enterprise deals ask for it; Voice Control at least once per release train on the mobile core path; switch access and the keyboard-only marathon cover motor access on Locked flows.

Measure. Matrix coverage per release (target: 100% of P0 rows on the three named paths); escaped-defect count by AT, to re-weight priorities annually.

Ch 18 — 18.3b: SR smoke script — Example

Concept. The four-step screen-reader smoke run on auth / checkout / create each release (18.3).

Scenario. Release 2026.14, NVDA + Chrome, LedgerLine checkout.

Example. The tester’s checklist, with expected utterances:

  1. Land on page → skip to main. Press Tab once. Expect visible skip link and NVDA reading: “Skip to main content, link.” Press Enter; focus lands on #main.
  2. Complete primary CTA. Tab to card fields, complete them, reach “Pay $1,240.00, button”, press Enter.
  3. Hear errors. Submit with an expired card. Expect the Error Summary to receive focus and NVDA to read: “There is a problem, heading level 2. Your card has expired — check the expiry date or use a different card, link.”
  4. Dismiss modal → focus restored. Open “Apply promo code” dialog, press Escape. Expect focus back on the “Apply promo code” button (the trigger), announced by name — not on document.body.

Any step failing on auth, checkout, or create is a release blocker (ship gate row “SR smoke”, 18.4).

Why it passes. The script is short enough to run every release (a floor, not a research study) and covers the four survivability moments: entry, primary job, failure, and modal recovery — the exact places L5/L6/L9 failures strand SR users.

Measure. Pass/fail per path per release; time-to-run (should stay under 30 minutes so it is never “skipped for schedule”).

Ch 18 — 18.4: Ship gates — Example

Concept. Six release-blocking checks on critical paths (18.4 table): keyboard task pass, axe clean of serious issues, dual-theme contrast, focus visible, SR smoke, forced-colors/HC.

Scenario. LedgerLine’s CI pipeline plus manual gate checklist for the checkout PR train.

Example. The gate report a PR must render green:

{
  "path": "checkout",
  "gates": {
    "keyboard_task_pass":  { "status": "pass", "evidence": "Completed Pay with keyboard only, 47 tab stops, no traps" },
    "axe_serious":         { "status": "pass", "serious": 0, "moderate": 2, "note": "moderate tracked, not blocking" },
    "dual_theme_contrast": { "status": "pass", "rules": "text 4.5:1, large text 3:1, non-text UI 3:1", "themes": ["light","dark"], "worst_pair": "5.1:1 --color-text-secondary/--color-surface-raised (dark)" },
    "focus_visible":       { "status": "pass", "ring": "2px solid var(--focus-ring-color), offset 2px", "outline_none_without_replacement": 0 },
    "sr_smoke":            { "status": "pass", "script": "18.3b", "at": "NVDA+Chrome" },
    "forced_colors":       { "status": "pass", "note": "No forced hex; ButtonText/Canvas semantics preserved; checked in Windows HC Aquatic" }
  },
  "verdict": "SHIP"
}

The forced-colors CSS that makes the last gate pass:

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .ll-button-primary {
    /* don't fight the user's palette; keep system semantics */
    background: ButtonFace;
    color: ButtonText;
    border: 1px solid ButtonText; /* border survives when bg is stripped */
    forced-color-adjust: auto;
  }
}

Why it passes. Every row of the 18.4 table is present with its exact bar: 4.5:1 / 3:1 / 3:1 contrast, ≥2px contrast-aware ring, zero outline: none without replacement, axe clean of serious issues (moderate logged, not release-blocking), SR smoke per 18.3b, and forced-colors preserving system semantics rather than forcing broken hex.

Measure. Gate pass rate at first CI run (a chronically failing gate means the primitive layer, not the squads, needs fixing — see 18.1.4).

Ch 18 — 18.5: Dual verification model — Example

Concept. Automated + checklist answers contrast/name-role-value/ARIA mistakes; lived experience answers real task success, cognitive load, AT-quirk survivability. Neither substitutes for the other (18.5). Cadence: paid sessions on critical paths each quarter; P0 findings block Locked ship.

Scenario. Q3 planning at LedgerLine: an exec asks, “We pay for axe DevTools and CI — why also pay research participants?”

Example. The a11y lead’s one-slide answer, drawn from last quarter’s actual defects:

Defect Caught by automated? Caught by lived experience?
--color-text-meta at 3.9:1 in dark theme Yes (contrast gate) Unlikely to be reported precisely
Icon button missing accessible name Yes (axe serious) Yes, but expensive way to find it
Totals recalculating with no status announcement No — no attribute is wrong Yes — NVDA user: “I can’t tell if the discount applied”
Wizard step 3 cognitive overload (14 fields, 3 primary-looking buttons) No Yes — 2 of 3 participants abandoned
VoiceOver + Safari swallowing aria-live inside display: contents No Yes — AT-quirk survivability

Q3 plan: automated floor on every PR (cost ≈ CI minutes); one paid lived-experience round on auth, pay, create (8 participants × 90 min × $125/h ≈ $1,500 plus recruiting). P0 findings block Locked ship, per policy.

Why it passes. The table is the textbook’s 18.5 matrix instantiated: rows 1–2 are the automated layer’s jurisdiction; rows 3–5 are things “automated cannot answer alone.” The quarterly cadence and P0-blocks-Locked rule are stated as budget commitments, not aspirations.

Measure. Defect-escape analysis per quarter: every production a11y bug tagged with which layer should have caught it.

Ch 18 — 18.6: Ownership — Example

Concept. Eng owns a11y CI + lint (R); Design Systems owns accessible primitives (A); Research owns lived-experience sessions (R); PM owns that metrics don’t incentivize exclusion (A) (18.6).

Scenario. A Wayfare growth PM proposes an A/B test: replace the labeled “Email me a sign-in code” button with an unlabeled sparkle icon to “reduce visual noise” and lift conversion.

Example. How the RACI resolves it:

  • Eng (R, a11y CI + lint): lint rule icon-button-requires-name fails the PR; eng does not hand-waive it.
  • Design Systems (A, primitives): the IconButton primitive’s typed API (18.1.4) will not compile without a name; DS declines an exemption.
  • Research (R, lived experience): flags that Voice Control users say the visible label to activate controls (20.4) — an unlabeled sparkle is unspeakable.
  • PM (A, metrics don’t incentivize exclusion): the experiment’s success metric is rewritten from “overall conversion” to “overall conversion AND AT-user completion not worse” — the 20.10 rule against conversion-only A/Bs that hide exclusion.

Outcome: icon ships with a visible text label “Email code”; conversion hypothesis tested without excluding anyone.

Why it passes. Each owner exercises exactly their letter: R’s do the work (CI, sessions), A’s are accountable for the contract (primitives, metrics). No single hero; the system catches it four times.

Measure. Number of experiments shipped with an AT-completion guardrail metric (target: 100% on Locked paths).

Chapter 19 — Structure, Focus, Name/Role/Value

Ch 19 — 19.1: Landmarks & skip links — Example

Concept. Landmark roster with rules — banner once, labeled multiple navs, exactly one main, labeled asides, contentinfo, search role, named forms — plus skip-link completeness (19.1).

Scenario. Fieldnote’s app shell: top bar, primary sidebar nav, in-page table-of-contents nav, notes canvas, quick-capture form, related-notes panel, footer, global search.

Example.

<a class="skip-link" href="#main">Skip to main content</a>
<a class="skip-link" href="#global-search">Skip to search</a>

<header>                                   <!-- banner: once per page -->
  <nav aria-label="Primary">…</nav>        <!-- label because there are 2 navs -->
  <div role="search" id="global-search" tabindex="-1">
    <!-- skip target: tabindex="-1" because a div is not focusable by default —
         without it the skip link only scrolls, focus stays on the link, and
         the next Tab lands in the nav instead of the search field -->
    <form aria-label="Search notes">       <!-- named: page has 2 forms -->
      <label for="q">Search notes</label>
      <input id="q" type="search" />
    </form>
  </div>
</header>

<nav aria-label="On this page">…</nav>     <!-- second nav, distinct label -->

<main id="main" tabindex="-1">             <!-- exactly one; skip target -->
  <h1>Interview synthesis — Q3 riders study</h1>
  <form aria-label="Quick capture">        <!-- named: page has 2 forms -->
    <label for="cap">Capture a thought</label>
    <input id="cap" type="text" />
    <button>Add note</button>
  </form>
  …
</main>

<aside aria-label="Related notes">…</aside>
<footer>…</footer>                          <!-- contentinfo -->

.skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  left: -9999px;
}
.skip-link:focus {
  left: var(--space-2);          /* 8px */
  top: var(--space-2);
  z-index: 100;
  padding: var(--space-2) var(--space-3);
  background: var(--color-surface-raised);
  outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring-color);
}

Why it passes. Every row of the 19.1 table is instantiated: one banner, two labeled navs so a screen-reader’s landmark list reads “Primary navigation / On this page navigation” instead of “navigation / navigation”, exactly one main that is the skip target, labeled aside, contentinfo, role="search" because a search region exists, and — the table’s “Form” row — because the page has two forms (search and quick capture), each carries a distinguishing name (aria-label="Search notes" / aria-label="Quick capture") so the landmark list never reads “form / form”. Skip completeness: Fieldnote is a dense tool, so “Skip to search” is added beside the required “Skip to main content”, and both are keyboard-visible on focus (never display: none).

Rejected. left: -9999px without the :focus reveal — the skip link technically exists, is announced, and can never be seen by a sighted keyboard user. Also rejected: three <nav>s with no labels, and two anonymous <form>s.

Measure. Landmark lint in CI (exactly one main, zero unlabeled duplicate landmarks — navs or forms) per release; skip-link usage rate in keyboard session replays.

Ch 19 — 19.2: Heading hierarchy; style ≠ level — Example

Concept. One h1; no level skips for convenience; visual style comes from type roles while heading level follows the outline; prefer sectioning with headings over aria-label alone for long content (19.2). CMS/RTE enforce heading allowlists (Ch 15 tie-in).

Scenario. A LedgerLine settings page. The designer wants the “Danger zone” section title to look small and red, but it is structurally a peer of “Billing” and “Team”.

Example.

<h1 class="type-title">Workspace settings</h1>       <!-- one h1: page purpose -->

<section>
  <h2 class="type-section">Billing</h2>
  <section>
    <h3 class="type-subsection">Payment method</h3>
  </section>
</section>

<section>
  <h2 class="type-section">Team</h2>
</section>

<section>
  <!-- Visually small + danger-colored, structurally still an h2 -->
  <h2 class="type-meta" style="color: var(--color-text-danger)">Danger zone</h2>
  <button>Delete workspace…</button>
</section>

type-title / type-section / type-meta are the locked type roles (L3); the level (h2) follows the outline, the style follows the role. The CMS heading allowlist for Guided content editors permits only h2–h4 inside an article body, so no editor can mint a second h1 or jump h2 → h4 “because h3 looked too big”.

Why it passes. The screen-reader heading list reads as a truthful outline: 1 “Workspace settings” → 2 “Billing” → 3 “Payment method” → 2 “Team” → 2 “Danger zone”. Style ≠ level is honored by decoupling type roles from heading elements.

Rejected. <h4>Danger zone</h4> chosen purely because h4’s default size matched the mock — a level skip for convenience that makes the outline fiction, the exact 19.2 anti-rule. Also rejected: <section aria-label="Billing"> with no heading inside — the region appears in the landmark list but vanishes from the heading outline, so heading-navigation users (the majority screen-reader navigation mode) never find it; the 19.2 “Sections” row says prefer sectioning with headings over aria-label alone for long content — use a real h2 inside the section.

Measure. Heading-outline lint per release: pages with more than one h1 or any level skip (target 0); count of long-content sections carrying aria-label with no heading inside (target 0).

Ch 19 — 19.3a: Modal focus trap & restore — Example

Concept. Modals trap focus, close on Escape, restore the trigger (APG dialog); L9 focus is a cursor (19.3).

Scenario. LedgerLine’s “Void invoice” dialog opened from row 14 of the invoices table.

Example.

<!-- index.html: the dialog layer is a SIBLING of the app root, so inerting
     #app-root can never inert the dialog itself -->
<body>
  <div id="app-root"><!-- app renders here --></div>
  <div id="dialog-root"><!-- dialogs portal here --></div>
</body>

import { createPortal } from 'react-dom';

function VoidInvoiceDialog({ triggerRef, onClose }) {
  const dialogRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const previouslyFocused = document.activeElement as HTMLElement;

    // Make the trap REAL, not asserted: everything outside the dialog is
    // inert while it is open, so Tab/Shift+Tab can only cycle inside and
    // screen-reader virtual cursors can't wander into the background.
    // This only works because the dialog is portaled OUTSIDE #app-root —
    // `inert` on an ancestor of the dialog would inert the dialog too.
    const appRoot = document.getElementById('app-root');
    appRoot?.setAttribute('inert', '');

    dialogRef.current?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[data-autofocus]')?.focus();

    return () => {
      appRoot?.removeAttribute('inert');
      // L9: restore the cursor to where the user was — the trigger.
      (triggerRef.current ?? previouslyFocused)?.focus();
    };
  }, []);

  return createPortal(
    <div role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="void-title" ref={dialogRef}
         onKeyDown={(e) => e.key === 'Escape' && onClose()}>
      <h2 id="void-title">Void invoice #1042?</h2>
      <p>The invoice stays in your records marked “Void”. You can restore it for 30 days.</p>
      <button data-autofocus onClick={onClose}>Cancel</button>
      <button onClick={voidInvoice}>Void invoice</button>
    </div>,
    document.getElementById('dialog-root')!
  );
}

Tab and Shift+Tab cycle inside the dialog because the background is inert — the trap is a mechanism in the code, not a comment. The portal to #dialog-root (a sibling of #app-root) is load-bearing: it keeps the dialog outside the inert subtree. If your stack can’t portal, don’t inert the root — inert each non-dialog sibling of the dialog instead. In production, trap + Escape + inert background live inside the Locked Dialog primitive (18.1.4); squads compose it and never hand-roll this file.

Why it passes. Full APG dialog contract: trap (via inert on everything outside), Escape, aria-modal, labelled by its own h2, and — the part squads forget — focus restored to the “Void…” button in row 14, so a keyboard user’s place in a 200-row table is not destroyed. This is L9’s “restore focus to trigger” clause, shipped once in the Locked Dialog primitive (18.1.4).

Rejected. Closing the dialog and letting focus fall to document.body — L9’s named failure mode. Also rejected: a dialog whose “trap” exists only in the PR description — aria-modal="true" alone does not stop Tab from leaving in every browser/AT pairing; without inert (or an equivalent sentinel trap), a novice copying the snippet ships an untrapped dialog. Also rejected: rendering the dialog inside #app-root and then inerting #app-root — the trap eats itself: the dialog becomes inert too, autofocus is suppressed, and keyboard/AT users can interact with nothing at all.

Measure. Focus-restore assertions in the Dialog primitive’s test suite (open from trigger → close → document.activeElement === trigger); SR-smoke step 4 (“Dismiss modal → focus restored”, 18.3b) pass rate per release.

Ch 19 — 19.3b: SPA route announcements — Example

Concept. On route change, move focus to h1 or main; update document.title; optional polite status “Navigated to {title}” (19.3).

Scenario. Fieldnote is a React SPA. Clicking “Projects” swaps the view with no full page load, so screen readers hear nothing by default.

Example.

// route-announcer.tsx — mounted once in the app shell
function onRouteChange(newTitle: string) {
  document.title = `${newTitle} — Fieldnote`;

  const h1 = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>('main h1');
  (h1 ?? document.getElementById('main'))?.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1');
  (h1 ?? document.getElementById('main'))?.focus({ preventScroll: false });

  // Optional polite status for SR users who missed the focus move
  announcer.textContent = `Navigated to ${newTitle}`;
}

<div id="route-announcer" role="status" aria-live="polite" class="visually-hidden"></div>

NVDA after clicking “Projects”: “Projects, heading level 1” then (politely) “Navigated to Projects”.

Why it passes. All three textbook clauses: focus moves to the h1 (the new page’s purpose, per 19.2), document.title updates so the browser tab and SR title report match, and the polite status is role="status" — not assertive — per the 20.2 discipline. No focus theft mid-typing occurs because navigation is user-initiated.

Rejected. Announcing routes with aria-live="assertive" on every navigation (interrupts everything for a routine event) or doing nothing (silent SPA — “silence after a click is a bug”).

Measure. E2E assertion that the SR announcement fires on 100% of route changes; document.title mismatch count (routes whose title does not match the rendered h1’s page purpose).

Ch 19 — 19.3c: Delete/destroy — announce result, restore sensibly — Example

Concept. After delete: announce the result and restore focus sensibly, not to document.body (19.3). Cross-domain with L7 (undo > confirm) and the Soft + Quarantine undo classes (Ch 3.4b).

Scenario. Fieldnote note list: user presses Delete on note 7 of 20.

Example. Deleting a personal note gets a Soft undo (a 5–10s toast with Undo, per Ch 3.4b — local delete) layered over a Quarantine trash window (~30 days), the Drive-Trash steal mechanic. No confirm dialog: confirm is reserved for external irreversibility (Hard class). On delete:

  1. The row is removed; focus moves to the next row (note 8), or the previous row if the last was deleted, or the list’s empty-state heading if none remain.
  2. The status live region announces: “‘Interview with R. Alvarez’ moved to trash. Undo, button available.”
  3. A toast renders: “Note moved to trash — Undo”, visible for 8s (inside the Soft class’s 5–10s window; the toast does not steal focus, per 20.2). When the toast expires, the note is still recoverable from the Quarantine trash for ~30 days.
<div role="status" aria-live="polite">
  “Interview with R. Alvarez” moved to trash. Undo, button available.
</div>

Why it passes. L7: a local, recoverable delete gets undo, not confirm — Soft (5–10s toast) for the immediate reversal, Quarantine (~30d trash) as the safety net beneath it; the confirm dialog is reserved for Hard-class external irreversibility. L9: focus lands somewhere sensible and adjacent to the user’s task, never document.body. The 4.1.3-class status message announces the result — including that an Undo control exists — without moving focus, and the snippet’s text is exactly what NVDA speaks.

Rejected. “Are you sure you want to delete this note?” confirm on this action (L7 failure “confirm-on-archive”); a Soft toast alone with no Quarantine beneath it (the toast expires in seconds — for anything a user might regret at minute two, the trash window is the real recoverability); and post-delete focus dumped on body so the next Tab starts from the top of 20 rows.

Measure. Post-delete focus-target assertions in the list’s test suite (never document.body); Undo-click rate inside the 5–10s Soft window vs trash-restore rate afterward (both nonzero means both layers earn their keep).

Ch 19 — 19.3d: Focus visible + interruptions — Example

Concept. Contrast-aware ring ≥2px; don’t steal focus from typing unless an assertive error requires it (19.3; ship gate 18.4).

Scenario. Wayfare checkout. A designer asks to remove “that blue box” from the brand-styled Pay button; separately, a promo toast appears while the user types a passport number.

Example.

/* Replacement, not removal: brand-styled but still ≥2px and 1.4.11-contrast-aware */
.wf-button:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring-color);   /* 3.2:1 against both adjacent surfaces */
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
/* Forbidden by lint: outline: none / outline: 0 without a replacement rule */

The promo toast (“Prices dropped on 2 saved trips”) renders as role="status" polite and does not move focus — the user’s caret stays in the passport field. The only thing allowed to interrupt typing is an assertive error such as “Your session expires in 2 minutes — Extend session” (20.6), which is a role="alert".

Why it passes. The 18.4 gate is met (ring ≥2px, contrast-aware, no outline: none without replacement) while the brand keeps a styled ring — the gate bans removal, not restyling. The interruption rule preserves L9: focus is the user’s cursor; marketing does not get to grab it.

Rejected. *:focus { outline: none; } in a reset stylesheet “because the ring clashed with the brand” — the ship-gate’s named violation.

Measure. outline: none/outline: 0-without-replacement lint violations per release (target 0, per the 18.4 gate); focus-steal-while-typing incidents found in session replays (target 0 outside role="alert" errors).

Ch 19 — 19.3e: Native first, APG second (L10) — Example

Concept. Use native elements; if you fake roles, you own the full keyboard map (19.3, L10).

Scenario. A Fieldnote squad needs (a) a settings toggle and (b) a combobox with async search.

Example.
- (a) Native wins. The toggle ships as <input type="checkbox" role="switch"> wrapped by the Locked Switch — native focus, Space activation, form semantics, forced-colors rendering all free.
- (b) APG with the full bill paid. No native combobox matches async filtering, so the team uses the design system’s Combobox (built on a battle-tested behavior primitive per Ch 15 adopt-vs-build), which implements the complete APG combobox contract:

Key Behavior owned
↓ / ↑ Move active option (aria-activedescendant)
Enter Select active option, close list
Escape Close list; second press clears
Home / End First / last option
Printable chars Filter
Tab Commit and move on — never trapped

Plus role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-controls, and options as role="option" with aria-selected.

Why it passes. L10’s order of operations: native first because the platform has already paid the AT-compatibility bill; APG second, and only with the entire keyboard map — half an APG pattern is div theater (19.5).

Rejected. <div class="toggle" onClick=…> with role="switch" and no tabindex, no Space handling, no aria-checked updates — “fake roles without keyboard maps; div theater with ARIA lipstick” (L10 failure text).

Measure. APG keyboard-map conformance tests on Combobox green per release (every key row above is an assertion); count of squad-local role fakes caught in review or by the role-without-keyboard-handler lint (target 0).

Ch 19 — 19.4: CSS order and flex/grid traps — Example

Concept. order, positive tabindex, and absolute positioning create keyboard/AT order ≠ visual order bugs (WCAG 1.3.2 / 2.4.3 class); reorder in DOM instead; lint any order: in product CSS (19.4).

Scenario. Wayfare’s flight-results card shows price visually first on mobile but the source order is airline → times → price. A developer reaches for order: -1.

Example — Rejected version first (the trap).

/* BUG: visual order says price first; tab/reading order still says airline first */
.fare-card { display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.fare-card .price { order: -1; }

A screen-reader user hears “Delta… 9:05–11:40…” and only then “$214” — while a sighted phone user is told price is the headline. Worse, the “Select” button visually beside the price is reached three tab stops later. Classic 1.3.2/2.4.3-class failure.

Example — Preferred fix. Reorder in the DOM; render price first in source for the mobile layout:

// Same data, DOM order = reading order = visual order
<article class="fare-card">
  <p class="price">$214</p>
  <p class="carrier">Delta</p>
  <p class="times">9:05–11:40</p>
  <button>Select</button>
</article>

Lint rule shipped with the design system: any order: in product CSS fails review without a written justification; tabindex values other than 0 / -1 are flagged; focusable elements inside aria-hidden="true" are an error.

Why it passes. DOM order = reading order = tab order, the 19.4 “prefer” column verbatim. The lint item makes the rule enforceable rather than folklore.

Measure. order: / positive-tabindex lint hits requiring written justification per quarter; E2E assertion that tab order matches visual reading order on the fare-card path (pass rate 100%).

Ch 19 — 19.5: Name, role, value — Example

Concept. Every interactive control needs an accessible name, correct role, and updated value/state; per-control sources per the 19.5 table.

Scenario. Fieldnote’s editor toolbar and note-properties panel.

Example. One of each table row:

<!-- Icon button: name from aria-label; state via aria-pressed -->
<button aria-label="Bold" aria-pressed="true">
  <svg aria-hidden="true">…</svg>
</button>

<!-- Input: name from <label for>; error state via aria-invalid + describedby -->
<label for="note-title">Title</label>
<input id="note-title" aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="note-title-err" />
<p id="note-title-err">Enter a title — it can’t be blank.</p>

<!-- Custom checkbox (APG pattern, only because a styled tri-state was needed) -->
<div role="checkbox" tabindex="0" aria-checked="mixed"
     aria-labelledby="sel-all-label"></div>
<span id="sel-all-label">Select all notes</span>
<!-- + Space toggles, updates aria-checked between true/false/mixed -->

<!-- Tabs: name is the tab's text; state via aria-selected -->
<div role="tablist" aria-label="Note views">
  <button role="tab" aria-selected="true"  id="tab-edit">Edit</button>
  <button role="tab" aria-selected="false" id="tab-history">History</button>
</div>

VoiceOver reads the first as “Bold, toggle button, selected” — name (Bold), role (toggle button), value (pressed).

Why it passes. Name source matches the 19.5 matrix per control type; states (aria-pressed, aria-invalid, aria-checked, aria-selected) are updated on change, which is the “value” half teams skip.

Rejected — ARIA div theater (the named anti-pattern).

<!-- Looks accessible in a DOM inspector; unusable -->
<div role="button" class="btn-bold"><svg>…</svg></div>

Role without name, no tabindex, no Enter/Space handling, no pressed state. Divs with roles but incomplete keyboard support — L10’s failure mode wearing a role attribute.

Measure. Axe serious name/role/value violations per release on critical paths (target 0, per the 18.4 gate); state-update assertions (aria-pressed/aria-checked/aria-selected change on interaction) in the toolbar’s component tests.

Ch 19 — 19.6: Product alt / accessible-name matrix — Example

Concept. The nine-row alt policy: decorative art, informative image, complex diagram, icon-next-to-text, icon-only control, avatar-beside-name, avatar-alone, chart, CAPTCHA image (19.6).

Scenario. One LedgerLine dashboard page happens to contain every row of the matrix.

Example.

<!-- 1. Decorative empty-state art -->
<img src="empty-invoices.svg" alt="" />

<!-- 2. Informative image: purpose, not “image of” -->
<img src="qr-payment.png" alt="QR code to pay invoice #1042" />
<!-- NOT: alt="image of a QR code" -->

<!-- 3. Complex diagram: short alt + long description -->
<img src="cashflow-sankey.png" alt="Cash flow by category, Q3" aria-describedby="sankey-desc" />
<a href="#sankey-desc">Full description and data table</a>

<!-- 4. Icon next to visible text: icon hidden -->
<button><svg aria-hidden="true">…</svg> Download</button>

<!-- 5. Icon-only control: non-empty name -->
<button aria-label="Filter invoices"><svg aria-hidden="true">…</svg></button>

<!-- 6. Avatar beside the person's name: empty alt -->
<img src="mira.jpg" alt="" /> <span>Mira Chen</span>

<!-- 7. Avatar alone (assignee cell with no text): name the person -->
<img src="mira.jpg" alt="Mira Chen" />

<!-- 8. Chart: summary + table fallback (see 20.3) -->
<figure aria-labelledby="rev-summary">…</figure>

<!-- 9. CAPTCHA image: DON'T. Provide a non-visual alternative (see 20.10). -->

Why it passes. Each row applies the matrix policy exactly: decorative content is silent (alt="", not focusable), duplication is avoided (rows 4 and 6 — the adjacent text already carries the name), information is preserved (rows 2, 3, 7, 8), and row 9 is a design rejection, not an alt-text writing exercise — no alt string makes a visual puzzle accessible.

Rejected. alt="logo" on decorative art (noise), alt="chart" on the revenue chart (information destroyed), and describing the CAPTCHA image (“distorted letters reading X4T9”) — which would defeat the CAPTCHA and still not help.

Measure. Alt-policy lint: images with a missing alt attribute (target 0 — note alt="" passes, absent alt fails); quarterly manual audit of alt quality on a sample of informative images (purpose stated, no “image of” prefixes).

Ch 19 — 19.7: Forms structure — Example

Concept. Visible labels (not placeholder-only); fieldset/legend grouping; GOV.UK Error Summary linked to fields with focus management; preserve input on failure with field-local errors (19.7).

Scenario. LedgerLine “Add bank account” form fails validation on 2 of 5 fields.

Example.

<!-- On failed submit, this summary is injected at top and receives focus -->
<div class="error-summary" role="group" aria-labelledby="err-h" tabindex="-1">
  <h2 id="err-h">There is a problem</h2>
  <ul>
    <li><a href="#routing">Routing number must be 9 digits</a></li>
    <li><a href="#acct-type">Select an account type</a></li>
  </ul>
</div>

<form>
  <label for="holder">Account holder name</label>
  <input id="holder" value="Dana Okafor" autocomplete="name" />
  <!-- preserved on failure — user does not retype -->

  <label for="routing">Routing number</label>
  <span id="routing-hint">9 digits, printed at the bottom-left of a check</span>
  <input id="routing" inputmode="numeric" value="12345"
         aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="routing-err routing-hint" />
  <p id="routing-err" class="field-error">Routing number must be 9 digits</p>

  <fieldset aria-describedby="acct-type-err">
    <legend>Account type</legend>
    <!-- group error lives INSIDE the fieldset and is tied to it via
         aria-describedby, so SR users entering the group hear it — a bare
         <p> after the fieldset is invisible to them -->
    <p id="acct-type-err" class="field-error">Select an account type</p>
    <label><input type="radio" name="acct-type" id="acct-type" /> Checking</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="acct-type" /> Savings</label>
  </fieldset>

  <button>Save bank account</button>
</form>

Behavior: focus moves to the Error Summary; each summary link jumps to and focuses its field; every entered value is preserved; errors also render field-locally.

Why it passes. All four 19.7 bullets: visible persistent labels (placeholder never carries the name — it vanishes on input), radio group named by legend so SRs read “Account type, Checking, radio button, 1 of 2” (with the group error announced on entry via aria-describedby on the fieldset), the GOV.UK Error Summary pattern with linked errors and managed focus, and preserved input honoring the reversibility obligation. Plain-language error strings do double duty for 20.5.

Rejected. Placeholder-only labels (“Routing number” disappearing the moment you type), a generic toast “Please fix the errors below” with no links and no focus move, and a form that clears itself on failure.

Measure. Form error-recovery completion rate (failed submit → successful resubmit); % of failed submits followed by abandonment — the metric that catches “technically labeled, practically hostile” validation.

Chapter 20 — Perception, Motor, Cognitive, Media

Ch 20 — 20.1a: Contrast floors — Example

Concept. Text 4.5:1 normal / 3:1 large (1.4.3); non-text UI 3:1 (1.4.11) (20.1). Cross-domain with L1 tokens.

Scenario. LedgerLine token review for the invoice table in light theme.

Example. The contrast-gate report (the 18.1.4 pipeline’s output):

Token pair Measured Floor Verdict
--color-text-primary on --color-surface-default 13.2:1 4.5:1 pass
--color-text-secondary on --color-surface-default 5.9:1 4.5:1 pass
--color-text-meta (12px) on --color-surface-raised 4.6:1 4.5:1 (normal text — 12px is NOT large) pass, flagged low-margin
Page title 24px semibold on --color-surface-default 3.4:1 3:1 (large text) pass
--color-border-input vs --color-surface-default 3.1:1 3:1 (non-text UI, 1.4.11) pass
--focus-ring-color vs adjacent surfaces 3.4:1 3:1 (1.4.11) pass
Disabled button text 2.4:1 exempt (disabled) logged, not gated

Why it passes. The exact 20.1 numbers, applied per token role (L1) so a passing pair passes everywhere the role is used. Meta text at 12px is correctly held to 4.5:1 — “large” is a size/weight definition, not a vibe.

Rejected. Declaring 16px light-gray #9aa0a6 on white (2.6:1) acceptable “because it’s secondary” — secondary is a hierarchy role, not a contrast exemption.

Measure. Contrast-gate pass rate at first CI run per theme; count of low-margin pairs (within 0.5 of the floor, like --color-text-meta at 4.6:1) tracked so a future ramp tweak can’t silently tip them under.

Ch 20 — 20.1b: Dark theme ramps, forced-colors, solid-for-data — Example

Concept. Dark theme uses separate tonal ramps, not inverted light; forced-colors preserves ButtonText/Canvas semantics; glass/blur for overlays only — solid surfaces for data (20.1).

Scenario. Fieldnote ships dark mode plus a frosted-glass command palette.

Example.

/* Separate ramps — dark is authored, not math-inverted */
:root[data-theme="light"] {
  --color-surface-default: var(--gray-0);
  --color-text-primary:    var(--gray-900);   /* 13.2:1 */
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  --color-surface-default: var(--gray-925);   /* not pure black; authored ramp */
  --color-text-primary:    var(--gray-75);    /* 12.1:1 — re-measured, not assumed */
}

/* Glass ONLY on the transient palette overlay */
.fn-command-palette { backdrop-filter: blur(12px); background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-surface-raised) 78%, transparent); }

/* The notes TABLE (data) is solid — no blur, no translucency */
.fn-table { background: var(--color-surface-default); }

Dual-theme audit runs the 20.1a gate against both ramps; forced-colors handling as in 18.4’s example (ButtonFace/ButtonText, no forced hex).

Why it passes. Authored dark ramps keep semantic meaning per theme (L1: --color-text-primary means “primary text” in every theme, at verified contrast). Glass is confined to a temporary overlay (elevation = modality, L4) while data sits on solid surfaces where translucency would randomize contrast against whatever scrolls beneath.

Rejected. filter: invert(1) dark mode (broken images, accidental 2:1 pairs) and a frosted-glass data table where row text measures 4.9:1 over one background region and 2.2:1 over another.

Measure. Dual-theme contrast audit green on both authored ramps per release; forced-colors manual check on the release checklist; count of glass/translucent surfaces containing data (target 0 — lint on backdrop-filter outside overlay components).

Ch 20 — 20.1c: Reflow — 320 CSS px / 400% zoom — Example

Concept. Content reflows at 320 CSS px width / 400% zoom; stack; no essential two-dimensional scrolling (1.4.10) (20.1, L11).

Scenario. LedgerLine’s two-column “New invoice” form on a 1280px desktop, zoomed to 400% (effective viewport 320 CSS px).

Example.

.invoice-form {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr;
  gap: var(--space-4);                 /* 16px */
}
@container form-region (min-width: 640px) {
  .invoice-form { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }
}
/* Line-items table: the ONE allowed horizontal scroller, self-contained */
.line-items-wrap { overflow-x: auto; }

At 400% zoom the form stacks to one column; labels stay above fields; the sticky summary bar collapses to a single-line “Total $1,240 — Review” disclosure. The only horizontal scrolling is inside the data-table wrapper (tables are the recognized exception), and every action on a row is also reachable from a row-overflow menu that fits in 320px.

Why it passes. 1.4.10 verbatim: stack at 320 CSS px, no essential 2D scroll — the page never requires scrolling right to find the Save button. Container queries mean the reflow is a layout contract, not a coincidence. This is L11’s reflow clause.

Measure. Manual gate: complete “create invoice” at 400% zoom in Chrome, keyboard only. Automated: CI viewport screenshot at 320px flags horizontal scrollWidth > clientWidth outside whitelisted wrappers.

Ch 20 — 20.1d: Color not alone (L11) — Example

Concept. Never communicate by color alone; pair text, icon, and/or pattern with color (20.1, L11).

Scenario. LedgerLine invoice status: Paid / Overdue / Draft.

Example. The StatusBadge primitive encodes three channels:

<Badge tone="success" icon="check">Paid</Badge>     // green + ✓ + the word
<Badge tone="danger"  icon="alert">Overdue</Badge>  // red + ⚠ + the word
<Badge tone="neutral" icon="pencil">Draft</Badge>   // gray + ✎ + the word

In the revenue chart, the “Overdue” series additionally uses a dashed stroke pattern so deuteranopic users can separate it from “Paid” without relying on red vs green (see 20.3).

Why it passes. A user who cannot distinguish the hues still reads the word and the icon; 1.4.1-class intent plus L11 explicitly. Because it’s baked into the Locked Badge, no squad can ship a color-only status by accident (18.1.4).

Rejected. A table of colored dots — green dot, red dot — with a legend only in a tooltip. L2’s failure text: “status communicated by color alone.”

Measure. Color-only-status lint (a Badge rendered without icon or text label fails the build); grayscale screenshot audit per release — every status and chart series must remain distinguishable with hue removed.

Ch 20 — 20.2: Live regions matrix — Example

Concept. Status/polite for toasts and soft undo; alert/assertive for blocking errors and session expiry; log for sequential feeds; progressbar for determinate long tasks. Polite by default, assertive sparingly; toasts don’t move focus (20.2, WCAG 4.1.3).

Scenario. Four moments in one LedgerLine session.

Example.

<!-- 1. STATUS: autosave + Soft undo toast — polite, no focus move -->
<div role="status" aria-live="polite">Draft saved</div>
<div role="status" aria-live="polite">Invoice moved to trash. Undo available.</div>

<!-- 2. ALERT: blocking failure / session expiry — assertive, earned -->
<div role="alert">Payment failed: your card was declined. No charge was made.</div>
<div role="alert">Your session expires in 2 minutes. Select “Stay signed in” to continue.</div>

<!-- 3. LOG: the support chat feed — additions announced in sequence -->
<div role="log" aria-live="polite">
  <p>Agent: “I’ve reissued invoice #1042.”</p>
</div>

<!-- 4. PROGRESSBAR: determinate export, named -->
<progress id="export" max="100" value="62" aria-labelledby="export-label"></progress>
<span id="export-label">Exporting 2026 invoices — 62%</span>

Discipline rules enforced in the Toast primitive: role="status" only; focus never moves on toast render; a search-as-you-type results counter announces at most once per settled query (“14 results”), never per keystroke.

Why it passes. Each row of the 20.2 matrix uses its designated politeness: routine confirmations never interrupt (polite), the two genuinely blocking events use alert, chat uses log so messages queue in order instead of clobbering, and the long task has a named determinate progressbar (a spinner “with no meaning” would break L5/L6).

Rejected. The matrix’s own “avoid” column: flooding every keystroke (“1 result… 3 results… 14 results” ×14), role="alert" on “Draft saved”, and role="log" for a one-shot error (it would be read as feed history, not a failure).

Measure. Live-region utterances per session (a flooding detector — a spike means someone is announcing keystrokes); count of assertive/alert usages per release outside blocking errors and session expiry (target 0).

Ch 20 — 20.3: Charts & data-viz a11y — Example

Concept. Position/length encoding first; color + labels + patterns; text summary; data-table fallback; keyboard access to interactive points; dual-theme series contrast (20.3).

Scenario. LedgerLine’s “Revenue vs Overdue, last 6 months” bar chart.

Example.

<figure role="group" aria-labelledby="rev-title" aria-describedby="rev-summary">
  <h3 id="rev-title">Revenue vs overdue — Jan–Jun 2026</h3>
  <p id="rev-summary">
    Revenue grew from $84k in January to $132k in June. Overdue invoices fell
    from 12% to 4% of billed value; March was the peak at 15%.
  </p>
  <svg><!-- bars: series use chart-1 / chart-2 tokens; overdue bars carry a
       diagonal-hatch pattern fill in addition to color; direct value labels
       on bars; interactive bars are focusable with Enter opening detail --></svg>
  <details>
    <summary>View as data table</summary>
    <table>
      <caption>Revenue and overdue percentage by month</caption>
      <tr><th>Month</th><th>Revenue</th><th>Overdue %</th></tr>
      <tr><td>Jan</td><td>$84,000</td><td>12%</td></tr>
      <!-- … -->
    </table>
  </details>
</figure>

Series colors are semantic chart tokens (chart-1…chart-n, chart-axis, chart-grid) audited in both themes; structural gridlines meet 3:1.

Why it passes. All five 20.3 layers: bar length carries the quantity (position/length first), color is supplemented by hatch pattern and direct labels (L11), the takeaway exists as text (the summary answers “what should I conclude?” without seeing anything), a real table fallback exists, and interactive points are keyboard-focusable rather than hover-only. Dual-theme via chart tokens.

Rejected. “Color-only charts are an anti-pattern”: a red/green line pair distinguishable only by hue, values only on hover, no summary, exported as a PNG (see 20.9 — image export is not a data-accessibility strategy).

Measure. Data-table fallback open rate (proves the fallback is real and discoverable, not decorative); E2E assertion that every interactive data point is keyboard-reachable (pass rate 100%).

Ch 20 — 20.4a: Touch targets & spacing — Example

Concept. ≥44×44 primary controls (craft); 24×24 is the 2.5.8 AA floor; avoid adjacent tiny targets; density maps still respect primary targets on touch (20.4, 20.13).

Scenario. LedgerLine mobile invoice list in compact density.

Example.

/* Primary row action: full craft bar */
.ll-row-primary-action { min-width: 44px; min-height: 44px; }

/* Dense-row secondary icon: visual 28px, hit-slop to 44 effective */
.ll-row-icon {
  width: 28px; height: 28px;
  position: relative;
}
.ll-row-icon::after {          /* extends the hit area without moving pixels */
  content: ""; position: absolute; inset: -8px;   /* 28 + 8 + 8 = 44 */
}

/* Adjacent-target spacing: undo/redo pair separated */
.ll-toolbar > * + * { margin-inline-start: var(--space-2); }  /* 8px */

Density note: compact remaps row padding from space-4 (16px) to space-3 (12px) per the density token maps — but on touch devices the primary “Open invoice” target keeps its 44px effective size regardless of density mode.

Why it passes. Craft bar (44×44) on primary controls; even the visually-28px icon exceeds the 24×24 AA floor before hit-slop and reaches 44 effective with it — the textbook’s dense-row hit-slop recipe. 8px separation prevents the “adjacent tiny targets” fat-finger failure. Density changes tokens, not target law.

Measure. Mis-tap rate on row actions (taps followed by immediate back/undo within 2s); target-size lint in the mobile snapshot suite.

Rejected. A 20×20 close button flush against a 20×20 overflow button — below even the 24px AA floor, with zero spacing.

Ch 20 — 20.4b: Pointer cancellation, hold-only, gestures — Example

Concept. No irreversible action on pointerdown alone (2.5.2); alternatives to long-press-only; ≤1 swipe action per row with a visible button equivalent; vertical scroll wins (20.4).

Scenario. Wayfare’s saved-trips list on mobile.

Example.

  • Pointer cancellation: “Delete trip” fires on pointerup inside the target; sliding a finger off the button before lifting cancels. Even then, deletion is Soft class — a “Trip deleted — Undo” status toast follows (L7 backs up 2.5.2).
  • Hold-only alternative: long-press on a trip opens the context menu, and every card has a visible “⋯ More options” button (44×44) that opens the same menu.
  • Gestures: exactly one swipe action per row (swipe-left reveals “Archive”); the same “Archive” appears in the ⋯ menu; the swipe recognizer requires a horizontal intent angle so vertical scrolling always wins over accidental swipes.

Why it passes. 2.5.2 is met twice over — up-event activation plus undo. Long-press and swipe are accelerators, never the only path, so switch users and tremor users lose nothing. One swipe per row honors the gesture budget.

Rejected. Swipe-left = archive, swipe-right = delete, long-swipe = share, with no visible equivalents — three invisible, undiscoverable, motor-hostile paths; and a delete that commits on pointerdown (no cancel, no undo).

Measure. Accidental-swipe rate (archives undone within 5s of a swipe); CI assertion that every destructive handler binds to pointerup/click, never pointerdown alone.

Ch 20 — 20.4c: Voice Control & switch access — Example

Concept. Visible names match spoken labels; avoid unlabeled icons; operable via keyboard path; no timing-only traps (20.4).

Scenario. A Voice Control user and a switch user both operate Wayfare checkout.

Example.
- The pay button’s visible text is “Pay $412.00” and its accessible name starts with the same string: aria-label="Pay $412.00 for Lisbon trip". Saying “Tap Pay” works, because the spoken label matches the visible label (2.5.3-class intent).
- The seat-map’s icon-only “aisle seat” toggles get visible text on focus/hover and numbered-grid fallback works because they are real <button>s.
- Switch access: the entire checkout is completable on the keyboard path (Tab/Enter/Space only — verified by the 18.3 keyboard-only marathon); the 3-D-Secure step’s 5-minute window shows a visible countdown and offers “Need more time?” — no timing-only trap.

Why it passes. Voice users can speak what they see; the accessible name doesn’t contradict the visible name (which would make “Tap Pay” fail silently). Switch operability rides the keyboard path, which is why the keyboard task gate (18.4) is P2 switch coverage’s foundation.

Rejected. <button aria-label="Confirm transaction">Pay $412.00</button> — the visible text and the name diverge, so “Tap Pay four twelve” matches nothing.

Measure. Voice Control task pass on the mobile core path once per release train (the 18.3 P1 row); lint for accessible names that do not start with the control’s visible text (2.5.3-class mismatch, target 0).

Ch 20 — 20.4d: Accessible drag-and-drop — Example

Concept. Keyboard alternative (move up/down or “Move to…”), multi-channel drop feedback + live region, named discoverable handles, Escape cancels, SR announcements for grab/target/drop (20.4). Ties to 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA, 20.13) and desktop-reorder handles.

Scenario. Fieldnote lets users reorder sections in a research report.

Example.

<li>
  <button class="drag-handle" aria-label="Reorder: Methods section"
          aria-describedby="dnd-hint">⠿</button>
  <span>Methods</span>
  <button aria-label="Move Methods up">↑</button>
  <button aria-label="Move Methods down">↓</button>
</li>
<p id="dnd-hint" class="visually-hidden">
  Press Space to lift, arrow keys to move, Space to drop, Escape to cancel.
</p>
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" id="dnd-status"></div>

Announced sequence for a keyboard reorder: “Methods, lifted. Current position 2 of 5.” → (ArrowDown) “Moved to position 3 of 5, after Findings.” → (Space) “Dropped. Methods is now section 3 of 5.” Escape at any point: “Move cancelled. Methods returned to position 2.” Drop feedback is also visual (insertion line + row highlight for 800ms), so it’s multi-channel. The visible ↑/↓ buttons are the single-pointer non-drag alternative; a “Move to…” menu exists for long lists.

Why it passes. Every row of the DnD table: keyboard alternative (↑/↓ + Move to…), multi-channel feedback with a live region, a named grip (⠿ alone is unspeakable — the aria-label names it), Escape restores, and grab/target/drop each announced. 2.5.7 AA is satisfied because dragging is never the only path; desktop discovery uses handles, not secret drag zones.

Rejected. Drag-only reorder discovered by hovering rows until the cursor changes — no handle, no keyboard path, no announcements, drop feedback color-only (also an L11 failure).

Measure. Keyboard-reorder completion rate vs drag completion rate (a keyboard path that exists but fails users is 2.5.7 theater); Escape-cancel assertion in the reorder tests.

Ch 20 — 20.5a: Cognitive patterns — Example

Concept. One primary action per critical view; predictable chrome (3.2.3/3.2.4 class); chunked wizards; plain language; quiet mode; opinionated defaults over infinite settings (20.5).

Scenario. LedgerLine’s “Set up payouts” — a compliance-heavy task users dread.

Example.
- Chunking: one 14-field form becomes a 4-step wizard — “1. Business details → 2. Bank account → 3. Verify identity → 4. Review” — with a visible progress indicator (“Step 2 of 4”) and per-step save.
- One primary action: each step renders exactly one primary button (“Continue”); secondary “Back” and tertiary “Save and finish later” are visually subordinate.
- Predictable chrome: nav stays put; the Help control stays top-right on every step (see 20.11).
- Plain language: legal requirement copy reads “We’re required by law to check who owns this business. You’ll need a photo ID.” — not “Pursuant to KYC obligations, beneficial-ownership attestation is mandated.”
- Quiet mode: users can enable “Reduce distractions” in Appearance settings: non-essential badges hide, promotional banners suppress, motion drops to reduced (20.7).
- Opinionated defaults: payout schedule defaults to “Weekly, Fridays” with a one-line “Change schedule” disclosure — not a 9-field cron builder up front.
- Error Summary: validation failures on any wizard step render the GOV.UK linked Error Summary (see 19.7) — a cognitive pattern as much as a structural one: it externalizes the to-do list (“There is a problem” + linked items) instead of making users hunt through 14 fields and hold the failures in working memory.

Why it passes. Each 20.5 row is embodied — including Error Summary, which the 20.5 table lists alongside plain language; chunking + one-primary-action cut working-memory load on a path where abandonment is expensive (L14 justifies the craft spend). Progressive disclosure (L8) carries the defaults philosophy: primary → disclosure → settings.

Rejected. The “expert dump”: all 14 fields, three equally-loud buttons (“Submit”, “Verify now”, “Add another account”), and jargon errors — plus the infinite-settings anti-pattern of shipping the cron builder as the default UI.

Measure. Per-step wizard abandonment (a spike at one step localizes the cognitive overload); error-comprehension in usability tests (“what would you do next?” answered correctly after a validation failure).

Ch 20 — 20.5b: Redundant entry & session restore — Example

Concept. Don’t make users re-supply what they already gave; don’t punish timeouts with total data loss (20.5 “Session restore”, 20.6 “Preserve”).

Scenario. A Wayfare user is 12 minutes into booking; step 3 asks for the lead traveler; the user already entered their name and email at sign-up. Mid-form, they’re pulled away for 40 minutes and the session expires.

Example.
- Redundant entry avoided: step 3 pre-fills “Lead traveler: Dana Okafor (dana@…) — Use my details” as the default, with “Someone else” as the alternative. The billing step offers “Same as traveler address” as a checkbox, checked by default.
- Session restore: on re-auth after expiry, the booking resumes at step 3 with every field intact: “Welcome back — we saved your booking details. Pick up where you left off.”

Why it passes. Re-asking known information is a cognitive tax that falls hardest on users with memory, attention, or motor constraints; pre-fill + “same as” checkboxes remove it. Restoring drafts after re-auth is the 20.6 “Preserve” row and the Reversible obligation applied to time, not just actions.

Rejected. Re-typing passport number, name, and address twice in one flow; and the silent-logout wipe: “Your session expired” over an empty form.
