Measure. Redundant-entry events per booking (the same value typed twice in one flow, target 0); resumed-session completion rate after re-auth vs completion rate of uninterrupted sessions.

SC note: published WCAG 2.2 has a dedicated success criterion for this redundant-entry pattern; this companion defers to the textbook’s SC table for numbering — see the editorial note at 20.13.

Ch 20 — 20.6: Timeouts & sessions — Example

Concept. Warn before expiry with time remaining (alert); primary “extend” action; preserve drafts after re-auth; never silent logout mid-form; timing extendable unless essential security — and then with alternatives (20.6; WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable intent).

Scenario. LedgerLine enforces a 30-minute idle timeout for financial data.

Example.

<!-- Fires at T-2:00; assertive is earned here (20.2 alert row) -->
<div role="alertdialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="to-title" aria-describedby="to-desc">
  <h2 id="to-title">You’ll be signed out in 2 minutes</h2>
  <p id="to-desc">For your security, sessions end after 30 minutes of inactivity.
     Your invoice draft is saved either way.</p>
  <button data-autofocus>Stay signed in</button>   <!-- primary; one keypress extends -->
  <button>Sign out now</button>
</div>

The countdown is announced at T-2:00 and T-0:30 only (not every second — that would flood, per 20.2 discipline). If expiry happens anyway, re-auth returns the user to the same invoice with the draft intact (autosave, Soft recovery). The security team’s exception — a 10-minute hard cap on the payout-details step — is documented as essential security, and even there the draft persists across re-auth.

Why it passes. Warn / Extend / Preserve / Avoid, all four rows: clear alert with time remaining, primary continue action, drafts restored, no silent mid-form logout. The essential-security carve-out is used narrowly and still pairs with preservation — the “alternatives” clause.

Measure. Percentage of expired-session users who successfully resume with data intact; support tickets containing “lost my work”.

Ch 20 — 20.7: Motion & seizure safety — Example

Concept. Motion tokens fast 100–150 / default 150–250 / slow 300–400 ms; honor prefers-reduced-motion with opacity/instant alternatives; no flashing >3 times/sec; scroll storytelling must not trap keyboards or gate meaning behind motion (20.7).

Scenario. Wayfare’s marketing homepage has a parallax hero; the app has panel transitions and a “deal alert” pulse.

Example.

:root {
  --motion-fast: 120ms;      /* micro feedback: hover, press */
  --motion-default: 200ms;   /* panels, menus */
  --motion-slow: 320ms;      /* full-view transitions */
}

.wf-panel { transition: transform var(--motion-default) ease-out; }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .wf-panel { transition: opacity var(--motion-fast) linear; transform: none; }
  .wf-hero-parallax { transform: none !important; animation: none; }
  .wf-deal-pulse { animation: none; }   /* the badge stays visible, just static */
}

The “deal alert” pulse animates at 1 pulse per 1.2s (≈0.8 flashes/sec — far under the 3/sec ceiling), and the reduced-motion variant is a static badge. The marketing scroll story is plain scrollable sections: every panel’s content is real text in the DOM, reachable by Tab and readable with motion off; scroll-jacking is banned.

Why it passes. Tokens sit inside the textbook’s exact ranges (fast 100–150, default 150–250, slow 300–400); reduced-motion swaps movement for opacity/instant per the rule; nothing approaches 3 flashes/sec; the story degrades to plain content, so keyboard users are never trapped and meaning never requires motion.

Rejected. A 5Hz flashing “SALE” badge (seizure risk, >3/sec), and a scroll-hijacked story where content exists only as animation frames.

Measure. Lint: 100% of animated components have a prefers-reduced-motion branch; animation-frequency audit — nothing in the codebase animates above 3 cycles/sec; keyboard completion of the marketing story with motion disabled.

Ch 20 — 20.8: Media players — Example

Concept. Captions with speaker ID; transcript; keyboard-operable controls; no autoplay with sound; audio description when visuals carry unique info (20.8).

Scenario. LedgerLine embeds a 4-minute “Set up payouts” tutorial video in onboarding.

Example.
- Captions: human-reviewed, with speaker IDs since two people speak: [PRIYA] Head to Settings, then Payouts. [SAM] I'll show the bank side. Accuracy bar: speech verbatim, not auto-caption soup.
- Transcript: full text transcript expandable below the player (“Read transcript”), including descriptions of on-screen actions: “(Priya opens Settings → Payouts and selects Add bank account.)”
- Keyboard: play/pause (Space/Enter/K), seek (←/→), mute (M), volume (↑/↓), captions toggle (C) — all focusable real buttons with names (“Play”, “Mute”, “Captions”).
- No autoplay with sound: the video renders paused with a poster; nothing plays until the user acts.
- Description: because Priya’s clicks convey unique info not in the narration, the described version adds “Selecting Add bank account opens a two-field form” — offered as an “Audio description” track toggle.

Why it passes. Every “must have” row: multi-speaker captions with IDs, transcript (which also serves deaf-blind braille users and people who skim), full keyboard operation, autoplay respect, and description where visuals are load-bearing.

Rejected. Auto-playing with sound on page load (hostile to SR users, whose speech it talks over), captionless “just watch the cursor” tutorials, and a <div> play button with no name.

Measure. Caption-accuracy sample audit per published video (verbatim speech + speaker IDs, human-reviewed); transcript open rate (proves the transcript is discoverable, and quantifies how many users prefer reading).

Ch 20 — 20.9: PDF & export a11y — Example

Concept. Tagged PDF when promised (reading order, headings, alt text — never scan-only sold as accessible); prefer CSV/XLSX for data with documented encoding; image export is not an accessibility strategy (20.9).

Scenario. LedgerLine’s “Download report” menu on the revenue dashboard.

Example. The export menu offers, in order:

  1. “CSV (best for data)” — UTF-8 with BOM, documented in the help entry: “Exports are UTF-8 CSV; dates are ISO 8601 (2026-07-15); currency is a plain number plus a currency column.”
  2. “XLSX” — one table per sheet, header row marked.
  3. “Accessible PDF” — generated as tagged PDF: H1 “Revenue report — Q2 2026”, logical reading order (summary → chart alt text + data table → notes), figure alt “Bar chart: revenue by month; data table follows”, document language set, title metadata set. Before the label “accessible” shipped, the file was verified with NVDA + Acrobat reading order — not screenshots (the textbook’s verification rule).

Why it passes. Data prefers CSV/XLSX (structured beats paginated); the PDF claim is backed by tags, order, headings, and alt; the claim was AT-verified. Encoding is documented so downstream screen-reader users in Excel aren’t handed mojibake.

Rejected. “Export as PNG” as the only option for the data (image export is not an accessibility strategy), and a scanner-style flattened PDF labeled “accessible report” — a promise the file cannot keep.

Measure. AT verification pass (NVDA + Acrobat reading order) recorded before any export labeled “accessible” ships or changes template; support tickets mentioning unreadable/garbled exports.

Ch 20 — 20.10: Auth & CAPTCHA (Case F) — Example

Concept. Prefer passkeys / email OTP; visible labels + password-manager autocomplete; always an accessible alternative if a challenge is required; measure AT-user completion and overall conversion; never puzzle-CAPTCHA-only, never disable paste (20.10; 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) AA, 20.13).

Scenario. Wayfare’s sign-in gets bot-attacked; the fraud team proposes a puzzle CAPTCHA.

Example. The shipped design:

<h1>Sign in to Wayfare</h1>

<button>Sign in with a passkey</button>   <!-- primary: no memory, no puzzle -->

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" autocomplete="username" />
<button>Email me a sign-in code</button>  <!-- OTP path -->

<details><summary>Use a password instead</summary>
  <label for="pw">Password</label>
  <input id="pw" type="password" autocomplete="current-password" />
  <!-- paste allowed; PM autofill works; visible label, not placeholder-only -->
</details>

Bot defense: invisible risk scoring first; a challenge only on high-risk traffic — and when challenged, the user gets a choice: audio challenge, email-link verification, or “Contact us to verify” — an accessible alternative always exists. Success metrics: overall conversion and AT-user completion tracked separately in the experiment dashboard.

Why it passes. 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (AA): no cognitive function test as the only path — passkey and OTP paths require neither memorized secrets nor puzzle-solving, and the challenge has non-visual alternatives. autocomplete attributes keep password managers working (the SC’s PM-friendly clause). The dual metric closes the 20.10 loophole of conversion-only A/Bs that hide exclusion.

Rejected. Every “Avoid” cell: puzzle CAPTCHA as the sole gate (“select all traffic lights” — unsolvable non-visually), onpaste="return false" on the password field, placeholder-only labels, and the phrase from the table: treating blind users as “edge cases.”

Measure. Overall conversion and AT-user completion tracked as separate series (the Case F dual metric); fraud catch rate; time-to-OTP success; auth support tickets.

Ch 20 — 20.11: Help mechanisms — Example

Concept. Help consistent in placement and identification across pages (3.2.6 Consistent Help, Level A — already required within an AA claim; the textbook’s craft bar goes beyond the SC’s letter); human contact, self-help, disclosed-AI chatbot with human escalation, inline field help via aria-describedby not hover-only; denial/error states link to help (20.11).

Scenario. LedgerLine standardizes help across its 40-odd product pages.

Example.
- Consistent placement: a “Help” button sits at the top-right of the app bar on every page — same position, same label “Help”, same icon. It opens a panel with, always in the same order: “Search help articles”, “Chat with us”, “Email support (reply within 1 business day)”.
- Chatbot disclosure & escalation: the chat opens with “You’re chatting with LedgerLine’s AI assistant. Type ‘agent’ anytime to reach a person.” The widget is keyboard-operable and announced as a role="log" feed (20.2).
- Inline field help: the routing-number hint is tied via aria-describedby="routing-hint" (19.7) — not an ⓘ tooltip that appears only on hover.
- No dead ends: the “Payouts unavailable in your region” denial screen links “See supported regions” and “Contact support” — the permissions-JIT pattern applied to denial states.

Why it passes. 3.2.6 Consistent Help (Level A) asks for consistency of help placement/identification, so it is already inside LedgerLine’s AA conformance claim — not an optional extra. The craft bar from 20.11 and 18.1.3’s humane ceiling (help linked from every denial and error state, disclosed-AI escalation) goes beyond the SC’s letter. AI disclosure honors the Ch 1 obligation; hover-only help would exclude touch and keyboard users.

Rejected. Help living top-right on Billing, in the footer on Invoices, and absent on Payouts; a chatbot pretending to be “Sam from support”; and error pages that end with “Access denied.” and nothing else.

Measure. Help-control position/label consistency check across all pages (automated screenshot-diff of the app-bar region, target 100% consistent); count of dead-end denial/error screens with no help or settings link (target 0).

Ch 20 — 20.12: Part V synthesis — bake, verify, include — Example

Concept. The five-line synthesis: bake into tokens and Locked components; verify with gates + AT matrix; include lived experience as a ship gate where it matters; structure before ornament; perception/motor/cognitive/media as peer concerns (20.12).

Scenario. A single LedgerLine feature — “Bulk-send invoice reminders” — traced through the whole Part V pipeline as an integration example (L1 + L7 + L9 + L11 + WCAG in one decision).

Example.
1. Bake: the feature composes only Locked primitives — Table (keyboard selection model), Dialog (APG map), Badge (multi-channel status), Toast (role="status"), all on contrast-gated tokens (--color-text-primary, --focus-ring-color). Zero new ARIA is written by the squad.
2. Verify: the 18.4 gates run on the path (keyboard bulk-select 50 rows → send; axe serious = 0; dual-theme; ring ≥2px; SR smoke; forced-colors). AT matrix P0 rows execute because “send mass notification” is a critical path.
3. Include: because bulk reminder = mass notification to customers, it is external irreversibility → L7 says this one earns a confirm (“Send reminders to 50 customers? They’ll each receive an email.”) — and it goes to the quarterly lived-experience panel; a P0 finding would block the Locked ship.
4. Structure before ornament: the review rejects a decorative glass panel until the selection-count live region (“50 invoices selected”) and heading outline are correct.
5. Peer concerns: the review checklist covers perception (badge contrast + pattern), motor (44px row targets, no drag-only selection), cognitive (plain confirm copy, one primary action), and media (the tutorial video per 20.8) as equal rows — none is “post-launch backlog.”

Why it passes. The synthesis is visible as sequence: primitives make the floor cheap, gates make it verified, lived experience makes it true, and the four concern families get peer review status.

Measure. The 18.4 gate report green on the path before merge; zero unresolved P0 lived-experience findings at Locked ship; zero squad-authored ARIA in the feature diff (primitives did the work).

Ch 20 — 20.13: WCAG 2.2 additions — Examples (one per SC)

Concept. The explicitly-taught WCAG 2.2 additions with their published numbers and levels (20.13 table, corrected to the published W3C numbering — see the editorial note below).

Scenario. One concrete artifact per row, spread across the running products.

Example.

  1. 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) — AA. Fieldnote’s 56px sticky header plus a 96px cookie banner: a CSS scroll-margin rule makes the browser’s automatic scroll-on-focus keep the control clear of the sticky chrome — no JS needed:
    css :focus-visible { scroll-margin-top: 72px; scroll-margin-bottom: 112px; }
    (72px clears the 56px header with margin; 112px clears the 96px banner.) Separate note for programmatic focus moves — e.g. the 19.3b route announcer calling .focus() — the same scroll-margin values also apply when code calls scrollIntoView(), so one rule covers both paths. Test: Tab through the page with the banner open; every focused element must be at least partially visible. (Cross-ref 19.3.)

  2. 2.5.7 Dragging Movements — AA. Fieldnote section reorder (20.4d): the ↑/↓ buttons and “Move to…” menu are the single-pointer, non-drag alternative to dragging. No path exists where dragging is the only way.

  3. 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) — AA. LedgerLine dense rows (20.4a): every target ≥24×24 effective (the AA floor), primary controls at ≥44×44 (the product craft bar). Both numbers appear in the lint config, labeled floor: 24 / craft: 44.

  4. 3.3.7 Redundant Entry — A. Wayfare’s session-timeout re-auth restores the half-finished booking form from a local draft, and checkout’s “Billing address same as shipping” checkbox auto-fills previously entered data — the user never re-supplies information they already gave in the same process. (Same mechanic as the 20.5b redundant-entry example.)

  5. 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) — AA. Wayfare sign-in (20.10): no cognitive function test (puzzle) as the only auth path; passkeys, email OTP, and password-manager-friendly fields (autocomplete="current-password", paste allowed).

  6. 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) — AAA. LedgerLine’s enterprise SSO tier advertises the enhanced criterion to a government buyer. Because it is AAA and claimed, the ACR labels it explicitly: “3.3.9 (AAA): Supports — no cognitive function test of any kind is required at any step; object-recognition challenges are not used.” The textbook rule: stricter, and label AAA if claimed — never fold it silently into an “AA” claim.

  7. 3.2.6 Consistent Help — A. LedgerLine’s consistent top-right “Help” (20.11). Because this criterion is Level A, consistent help placement is already required inside the public AA claim; the craft bar (help linked from every denial/error state) goes beyond the SC and the VPAT notes that as an exceed.

Why it passes. Each SC gets its published number, its published level label (A vs AA vs AAA), and the textbook’s own practice column made concrete. The level-labeling discipline is itself demonstrated in items 6–7.

Measure. Each of the seven SCs mapped to at least one shipping artifact plus one gate or lint (the mapping above); AAA criteria appear in the ACR only when explicitly labeled AAA — never folded into an AA claim.

Editorial note — SC numbering (companion diverges from textbook 20.13; flagged upstream). The textbook’s 20.13 SC table (and edition note 6) mislabels several WCAG 2.2 additions. Because readers use this companion as compliance guidance (ACR/VPAT mapping), it follows the published W3C numbering: 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (Level A), 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (Level AA), 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (Level AAA), and 3.2.6 Consistent Help (Level A) — not the textbook’s labels (which present 3.3.7 as authentication and 3.2.6 as AAA “Help Mechanisms”). This is the companion’s only deliberate divergence from the textbook; it is flagged upstream for the textbook’s next edition, which should correct 20.13, edition note 6, and §3.4’s “Help Mechanisms (3.2.6) is AAA” line in the same pass.

End of Part V examples companion.

Modern UI — Part VI Practice: Official Companion Examples

Companion to: Part VI — Practice (Chapters 21–25) of Modern UI: Philosophies, Principles, Strategies & Tactics, Edition 1.1.
Purpose: This document supplies at least one concrete, shippable example for every worked case (Ch 21 A–K), every anti-pattern row (Ch 22), every north-star mechanic (Ch 23), every decision-cheat-sheet row group and PR-checklist section (Ch 24), and every capstone exercise plus the scoring sheet (Ch 25). Every example uses realistic product scenarios, quoted microcopy, real numbers (px, ms, ratios, day counts), named semantic tokens (--color-*, --space-* style per Ch 15), the textbook’s undo classes (Soft / Quarantine / Hard), and its exact WCAG 2.2 SC numbers with AA/AAA labels. Where the textbook names a rejected alternative, the anti-pattern version appears under Rejected so critique discipline stays falsifiable, not taste.

Ch 21 — Worked Decisions (Cases A–K): Examples

Ch 21-A — Case A: Checkout (trust × frequency) — Example

Concept: Payment path craft under L14 (craft ∝ trust × frequency), L5 (acknowledge ≤100ms), L7 (confirm only for external irreversibility → pessimistic submit), Locked partition. Ch 21 Case A.

Scenario: “Ledgerly,” a B2B invoicing SaaS, ships a card-payment step for annual plan upgrade ($1,188.00 charged once). Trust market: customers are accountants.

Example (the concrete artifact):

  • Visual: fields sit on --color-bg-surface (solid — no glass on data), one accent used exactly once on the Pay button via --color-action-primary. Money set in the mono-tabular type role: font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; so “$1,188.00” and “$988.00” align. Field label→control gap --space-field-gap: 8px; group gap --space-24.
  • Interaction: pessimistic submit. On press, button acknowledges within 100ms (L5): label swaps to “Processing payment…” with inline spinner, disabled + aria-disabled="true", form fields locked. Success renders a receipt state, not a toast: “Payment received — $1,188.00 on Jul 15, 2026. Receipt #INV-20481 emailed to bowie@example.com.”
  • Idempotency (double-submit ban, checklist row 13):
// Locked PayButton contract — one idempotency key per PAYMENT ATTEMPT.
// Transport retries of the same attempt (timeout, dropped connection,
// double-click) reuse the key, so the bank sees one charge. A NEW attempt —
// resubmit after a decline, an edited card, a recalculated total — mints a
// fresh key; reusing the old one makes the processor replay the prior
// response or reject the changed params as a mismatch.
let payKey = crypto.randomUUID(); // minted when the attempt starts, NOT per click

await api.pay({ amountCents: 118800, currency: "USD" }, {
  headers: { "Idempotency-Key": payKey } // retry-safe within this attempt
});

// on decline or any change to amount/card: payKey = crypto.randomUUID()
// before the next submit — new attempt, new key
  • Errors: field-local message + GOV.UK-style Error Summary at top, focus moved to the summary. Summary heading: “There’s a problem with your payment” — each item links to its field: “Card number — check the 16-digit number on the front of your card.” Field wiring:
<label for="card">Card number</label>
<input id="card" name="cardnumber" autocomplete="cc-number" inputmode="numeric"
       aria-describedby="card-err" aria-invalid="true">
<p id="card-err">Check the 16-digit number on the front of your card.</p>
  • A11y (cross-domain): visible labels (never placeholder-only), text contrast ≥4.5:1 in both themes (1.4.3 AA), error not color-only (L11) — icon + text. Keyboard-complete pay path; SR smoke script run before ship. Pay button 48px tall (≥44 craft bar; 24×24 is only the 2.5.8 AA legal floor).

Why it passes: L14 says polish concentrates where trust × frequency peaks — money is maximum trust stakes. Pessimistic submit is correct because cheap rollback does not exist once money moves (prefer-when, Ch 21-A.1). Error Summary + aria-describedby satisfies the a11y lens; idempotent key kills “I was charged twice” tickets, the exact measure the case names.

Rejected: Optimistic “Paid! 🎉” fired before bank settlement; failure reported only in a 5s toast the user misses; Pay button restyled by the growth squad with a marketing gradient behind the card fields; a countdown “Offer ends in 4:59” pinned above the card form (banned growth trick on Pay).

Steal mechanic: Stripe Checkout — field honesty, visible label + inline error pairing, docs-as-product clarity (Ch 23.2) — steal the form’s behavior, not the marketing site’s gradients inside it.

Measure: payment success rate · error recovery rate (% of users with a validation error who complete within the session) · keyboard completion of pay path · chargebacks and support tickets containing “charged twice.”

Ch 21-A.1 — Prefer-when reminder: optimistic is wrong here — Example

Concept: The optimistic-vs-pessimistic tension flips on money. Ch 21 Case A prefer-when note.

Scenario: Same Ledgerly team also ships “add a draft invoice line” — there, optimistic insert with Soft undo (7s toast, “Line added — Undo”) is correct because rollback is one array splice. On Pay, the identical pattern is a defect.

Example: Decision rule as code comment shipped in the Locked kit:

// PayButton: pessimistic ONLY. Optimistic UI requires cheap rollback (L7).
// A settled charge has no cheap rollback → acknowledge ≤100ms locally,
// but never claim success before the processor's 2xx.

Why it passes: Encodes the prefer-when in the contract so AI codegen and new hires can’t “feel fast” their way into a chargeback.

Ch 21-B — Case B: Empty → first artifact → habit — Example

Concept: First-run curriculum identity → artifact → share → return; air before density; L6 (state is designed), L8 (progressive disclosure). Ch 21 Case B.

Scenario: “Fieldnote,” a research-repository tool. New workspace, zero studies.

Example:

  • Never-used empty state: generous air (--space-64 above the block), one primary CTA “Create your first study”, and three templates rendered as simulated futures — a template card titled “Usability test — 5 participants” showing a realistic filled-in study preview, not lorem ipsum. Decorative empty illustration carries alt="" so it’s silent to screen readers; the CTA’s accessible name is the full “Create your first study” (not an icon “+”).
  • The first create is one click, lands directly in an editable artifact, and is undoable (Soft class, “Study created — Undo” toast, 7s) — no hard commit, no 12-step wizard.
  • Return visit lands on the artifact (“Continue ‘Usability test — 5 participants’”), not a dashboard of zeros.
  • Skip link “Skip to main content” still reaches #main; on load, focus order reaches the primary create button without tabbing through marketing chrome.
  • Systems: the empty state is built from the documented empty-state recipe (never-used vs filtered-zero vs error vs denied variants), not a squad snowflake.

Why it passes: Optimizes time-to-first-artifact and D7 return — the case’s real measures — instead of tour completion (named vanity). One undoable create honors L7; air-then-density honors the density-vs-air tension for new users.

Rejected: A 12-step onboarding carousel ending on an empty dashboard; a card-grid of twelve starter options (choice paralysis, no artifact); a permanent empty illustration with no action; hard-commit first create with no revert.

Steal mechanic: Notion / Figma templates — start the user inside a real artifact shape (“Usability test — 5 participants” pre-filled), not a slideshow about artifacts.

Measure: time-to-first-artifact (target: median <90s) · D7 return · find-rate of the create action without docs · tour completion tracked but never optimized alone.

Ch 21-B.1 — State distinction: empty ≠ zero-with-filters ≠ error ≠ denied — Example

Concept: Each zero-looking state needs a different CTA. Ch 21 Case B state note + L6 taxonomy (never-used empty · filtered-to-zero · loading · partial · error · offline · denied · syncing · conflict).

Scenario: Fieldnote’s study list, four different “nothing here” moments.

Example (copy matrix):

State Copy Primary CTA
Never-used empty “No studies yet. Start from a template or create your own.” “Create your first study”
Filtered-to-zero “No studies match your current filters.” “Clear filters” (query preserved)
Error “We couldn’t load your studies. Your data is safe.” “Retry”
Denied “You don’t have access to this team’s studies.” “Request access”

Why it passes: Same visual slot, four distinct recoveries — the wrong CTA (“Create a study” on a permissions failure) strands the user. This is the exact defect Ch 22.21 catalogs.

Ch 21-C — Case C: Shared destructive delete — Example

Concept: Team-visible destroy: confirm with blast radius or Quarantine — never Soft toast alone. L7 (undo > confirm; confirm only for external irreversibility), L9 (focus restore). Ch 21 Case C.

Scenario: “Relay,” a team wiki. A space owner deletes the space “Q3 Launch Plan” that 12 teammates use.

Example:

  • Because Relay has a Trash, the chosen class is Quarantine 30d: delete moves the space to Trash immediately, with plain blast-radius copy in the confirm dialog: “Delete ‘Q3 Launch Plan’? This space and its 47 pages will move to Trash for all 12 members. You can restore it from Trash for 30 days.”
  • Dialog is the Locked DestructiveConfirm (APG dialog pattern): focus trapped inside, role="dialog" with aria-labelledby pointing at the title, buttons “Delete space” (danger) and “Cancel”. On confirm, result announced in a polite live region — “‘Q3 Launch Plan’ moved to Trash. Restore from Trash within 30 days.” — and focus restores to the element that opened the dialog (the space’s overflow menu button), never to body.
  • Danger-zone patterning: destructive action isolated in a “Danger zone” section with --color-action-danger on the button only; no playful trash-can animation.
  • Audit: deletion writes an audit-log entry (actor, spaceId, memberCountAtDelete: 12, restorableUntil).

Why it passes: L7 — quarantine gives reversibility without a confirm tax on every archive; the blast radius (“12 members”, “47 pages”) makes consequence legible; L9 focus trap + restore keeps keyboard/AT users oriented.

Rejected: One-click delete with a 5-second Soft toast for a team-visible destroy (“speed”); a per-page custom scary modal instead of the Locked DestructiveConfirm; focus dumped on document.body after close; a cute animation that minimizes consequence.

Steal mechanic: GitHub danger-zone typed confirm when irreversible; Google Drive Trash quarantine when recoverable — pick the class that matches recoverability, never mix (mapped in Ch 21-C.1).

Measure: accidental-delete tickets · quarantine restore rate · keyboard completion of the confirm · time-to-recover a deleted space.

Ch 21-C.1 — Undo class map — Example

Concept: Soft (5–10s) / Quarantine (30d) / Hard confirm mapped to blast radius. Ch 21 Case C class map + L7.

Scenario: Relay’s three destroy-shaped actions, one map.

Example:

Action Blast radius Class Artifact
Remove a tag from my own page Local, reversible Soft — toast “Tag removed — Undo”, --toast-duration-soft: 7000ms Undo restores instantly
Delete shared space (12 members) Shared, recoverable Quarantine 30d — Trash + restore Confirm states the window
Purge Trash / delete workspace account External irreversibility Hard — typed confirm: “Type Q3 Launch Plan to permanently delete” No undo claimed anywhere

Why it passes: Picks the class by recoverability, never mixes them (“do not mix” — the case’s steal-mechanic note: GitHub typed confirm when irreversible, Drive Trash when recoverable).

Ch 21-D — Case D: AI bulk edit proposal — Example

Concept: AI loop intent → proposal → review → undo; silent mutation ban; diff readable without color (L11). Ch 21 Case D.

Scenario: “Copydeck,” a CMS. The user asks the assistant: “Update our product name from ‘Sendly’ to ‘Sendly Mail’ across all published pages.” The model proposes edits to 214 records.

Example:

  • Proposal streams in with a visible Cancel button (stream + cancel). Nothing mutates until the explicit Apply press.
  • Diff is the primary surface, readable without color: removed lines carry a “−” glyph and strikethrough pattern, added lines a “+” glyph and underline pattern, plus aria-label="removed line" / "added line" — never red/green alone (L11).
  • The proposal is a typed contract object:
{
  "proposalId": "prop_8f2c",
  "intent": "Rename 'Sendly' → 'Sendly Mail' in published pages",
  "diff": [{ "recordId": "page_112", "field": "body", "hunks": ["…"] }],
  "scope": { "records": 214, "collections": ["pages"] },
  "sideEffects": [
    { "kind": "notify_watchers", "count": 38, "requiresApproval": true }
  ]
}
  • The side effect (“Notify 38 page watchers of the change”) is listed with its own unchecked approval checkbox: “Also notify 38 watchers — requires your approval.” Apply without checking it performs the edit but sends nothing.
  • After Apply: Soft undo — “Applied to 214 pages — Undo” (10s toast) plus a persistent “Revert this change” entry in version history.
  • Keyboard: j/k between hunks, a apply-hunk, x reject-hunk, all reachable by Tab as buttons too; each hunk announced (“Hunk 3 of 12, page ‘Pricing’, 2 lines changed”).
  • Systems: this review surface is a Guided pattern; after 3 product teams adopt it, it’s promoted toward Locked (L12).

Why it passes: Human stays the authority on side effects; explicit Apply + undo-after-apply preserves the conversation contract; instrumenting reject/override rate (not accept rate) makes trust measurable, not theatrical.

Rejected: Autocomplete that silently rewrites published pages; an agent that emails/notifies customers unattended; a red/green-only diff; a team leaderboard for “AI acceptance %.”

Steal mechanic: Copilot / Cursor apply-review — the human remains the authority on side effects — not autocomplete that writes production truth silently.

Measure: override/reject rate · undo-after-apply rate · side-effect incidents (target: 0) · time-to-review a 214-record diff · trust NPS on AI features.

Ch 21-E — Case E: Token rename (systems ops) — Example

Concept: Semver + alias bridge + 90-day deprecation; code is SoT; Figma renamed same week; L1 (roles not hexes), L12 (abstract after three), L13 (version the contract). Ch 21 Case E.

Scenario: The design-systems team at “Ledgerly” renames the semantic role --color-accent → --color-action-primary because “accent” had drifted into three meanings. AI codegen consumes the token docs, so a sloppy rename multiplies.

Example:

  • Classification: rename of a semantic role → MAJOR (tokens v4.0.0).
  • Alias bridge ships first, so product UI keeps working during the window:
/* tokens v4.0.0 — alias bridge, sunset 2026-10-13 (90 days) */
:root {
  --color-action-primary: var(--blue-600);
  --color-accent: var(--color-action-primary); /* @deprecated → --color-action-primary */
}
  • Codemod distributed with the release:
npx ledgerly-tokens-codemod rename \
  --from color-accent --to color-action-primary --paths "src/**/*.{css,tsx}"
  • CI ban after sunset: stylelint rule ledgerly/no-deprecated-token flips from warn to error on day 91; the deprecated alias is deleted in v5.0.0.
  • Figma Variables renamed the same week as code; the weekly drift check diffs Figma variable names against the token JSON and files a ticket on mismatch.
  • A11y gate rides along: both-theme contrast checks (4.5:1 text / 3:1 UI — 1.4.3 & 1.4.11 AA) re-run in visual regression, because a rename PR is exactly when an unreviewed dark-ramp swap sneaks in.

Why it passes: L13 — the change is a migration with a dated window, not a Friday find-replace; L1 stays intact because product code never touched --blue-600 directly; override-rate on affected components is watched as the fork early-warning.

Rejected: Big-bang find-replace on a Friday; “just tweak the hex” that silently changes the role’s meaning without a MAJOR; eternal dual APIs (alias never sunset); design library drifting 3 months behind code.

Steal mechanic: Style Dictionary token pipeline + semver discipline from mature kits (Polaris / Spectrum / Carbon contribution models, Ch 23.6) — promotion and deprecation as scheduled ops, not hero refactors.

Measure: deprecated-import CI failures trending to zero before sunset · override rate on affected components · Figma-vs-code drift check results · time-to-sunset (target ≤90 days) · visual-regression failures caught pre-merge.

Ch 21-E.1 — Token bump rules — Example

Concept: MAJOR = rename/remove/meaning change · MINOR = add role or alias · PATCH = primitive ramp tweak behind same semantic (diff required). Ch 21 Case E bump table.

Scenario: Three changes land in one quarter at Ledgerly.

Example:

Change Bump Why
--color-accent → --color-action-primary MAJOR (v4.0.0) Semantic rename
Add --color-bg-warning-subtle MINOR (v4.1.0) New role, nothing breaks
--blue-600: #2456d6 → #2050cc (same role mapping, contrast re-verified 6.8:1 on white — comfortably ≥4.5:1, 1.4.3 AA) PATCH (v4.1.1) Primitive tweak behind same semantic; visual-regression diff attached

Why it passes: Consumers (human and AI) can trust that a PATCH never changes meaning — the exact promise L13 requires.

Ch 21-F — Case F: CAPTCHA vs conversion — Example

Concept: Fraud pressure vs completion; accessible alternative always; L10 (native first), L11 (multi-channel), WCAG 2.2 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA. Ch 21 Case F.

Scenario: “Parcelo,” a shipping marketplace, sees bot signups spike 4× and the growth team proposes a drag-the-puzzle-piece CAPTCHA on login.

Example:

  • Ladder shipped instead: (1) passkey login first, (2) email OTP fallback (“We sent a 6-digit code to t•••@example.com — it expires in 10 minutes”), (3) risk-engine silent scoring, (4) only for residual high-risk sessions a challenge — and the challenge always carries a non-visual alternative (“Can’t complete this? Get a code by email instead”), plus a human-review path (“Contact us and we’ll verify you within 1 business day”).
  • Auth chrome quiet: visible labels (“Email address”), autocomplete="email" / autocomplete="one-time-code" so password managers and OTP autofill work (this is also what 3.3.8 AA wants — no cognitive-function test without alternative; no re-transcription burden, tie to 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, A).
  • Vendor isolation: the CAPTCHA vendor sits behind an adapter whose TypeScript contract makes the alt path unskippable:
interface ChallengeAdapter {
  render(el: HTMLElement): void;
  altPath: { kind: "email-otp" | "human-review"; label: string }; // required, not optional
}
  • Measurement is segmented: overall conversion and AT-user completion tracked separately, so an aggregate A/B can’t hide an assistive-tech failure.

Why it passes: “Blind users are edge” is a defect statement — the case’s own words. Passkey/OTP-first converts better and includes; the adapter makes inclusion a compile-time property of the system rather than a review catch.

Rejected: Puzzle-only CAPTCHA; hold-the-button or visual-only challenges with no alternative; an Open-partition paste of the vendor iframe with no alt contract; shipping puzzle-only “because aggregate bounce looked fine.”

Steal mechanic: Passkeys / email OTP with a documented fallback path, plus GOV.UK-style plain language (Ch 23.8) wherever a challenge must be explained — not “prove you’re human” theater.

Measure: overall conversion · AT-user completion · fraud catch rate · auth support tickets · time-to-OTP success (target: median <30s from request to accepted code).

Ch 21-G — Case G: Honest paywall — Example

Concept: Growth vs trust: clear value + reversible trials beat urgency theater; checkout stays Locked; L14. Ch 21 Case G.

Scenario: “Fieldnote” adds a Pro plan ($16/user/mo). Marketing owns the pricing page (Guided surface); the subscribe flow reuses Locked checkout.

Example:

  • Three comparable plan columns with identical row order (Seats, Storage, AI credits, Support). Default plan labeled honestly: “Pro — our default for teams of 3+” — a factual label, not a decoy-styled “MOST POPULAR” trap that dims the cheaper column.
  • Trial copy states the reversal path in the same breath as the offer: “14-day free trial. Cancel anytime before Jul 29 and you won’t be charged. Cancel in Settings → Billing in two clicks.”
  • The cancel path is at least as clear as upgrade: “Cancel plan” is a visible button on Settings → Billing, not a support-chat scavenger hunt.
  • A11y: full plan comparison operable by keyboard; price difference conveyed in text (“$16/user/mo — $8 more than Starter”), never color-only (L11); all pricing text ≥4.5:1 (1.4.3 AA); focus order matches the visual reading order of the columns; plan detail rows expand on click/Enter, not hover-only.
  • Systems boundary: the campaign theme may restyle the pricing hero, but PayButton and CheckoutField token contracts are untouched — no Locked overrides.
  • Experiment governance: the trial→paid A/B ships with guardrail metrics — it auto-fails if cancel-completion drops or “how do I cancel?” tickets rise >10% week-over-week.

Why it passes: Growth is allowed to experiment on the Guided marketing surface only while billing-trust guardrails hold; L14 says the trust path (checkout, cancel) gets the polish, not the confetti.

Rejected: Purple glass paywall over the plan table; hidden cancel; auto-charge obfuscation (“your trial converted” with no prior notice); a fake countdown timer; campaign theme breaking the PayButton contract.

Steal mechanic: Notion / Linear pricing clarity — labeled default (“Pro — our default for teams of 3+”), comparable plan outcomes row-for-row, cancel discoverable in two clicks — not dark-pattern playbooks.

Measure: trial→paid · cancel completion rate · support “how do I cancel?” volume · chargebacks · trust NPS on billing.

Ch 21-G.1 — Competitive craft scorecard — Example

Concept: Ship/kill UI bets from measured gaps, not taste debates. Ch 21 Case G scorecard.

Scenario: Fieldnote’s quarterly bet review against two rivals.

Example (filled 1–5):

Dimension Us Rival A Rival B Action
Trust-path quality 4 5 3 Fund checkout error-recovery work (close −1 gap)
Density honesty 5 3 4 Hold; publicize density toggle
Opinionated defaults 4 4 2 Hold
Undo honesty 5 3 4 Hold
Checkout a11y 4 5 2 SR smoke debt sprint (close −1 gap)
Core-action scent 5 4 3 Hold

Why it passes: Two funded bets fall directly out of the two −1 gaps; nothing is funded by “I feel our paywall is ugly.”

Ch 21-H — Case H: Sync conflict (offline) — Example

Concept: L6 state matrix must include syncing and offline; conflict resolution prefer-when: keep both / choose / merge. Ch 21 Case H.

Scenario: “Relay” wiki on a train: user edits the page “Retro notes” offline for 22 minutes; a teammate edited the same page online.

Example:

  • Going offline: persistent banner (not a toast) — “Offline — your changes are being saved locally and will sync when you’re back.” The banner is role="status" (polite live region, 4.1.3 Status Messages AA), plus a text label “Offline” next to the sync icon — never a color-only dot.
  • Reconnect with conflict: dialog (APG dialog pattern) shows both versions with clear labels: “Your version — edited offline, 2:14 PM” and “Maya’s version — edited online, 2:20 PM,” each with a preview.
  • Resolution prefer-when applied:
  • Keep both offered first because these are equal peer edits to overlapping prose (unknown merge): “Keep both — Maya’s version stays on the page; yours is saved as ‘Retro notes (your offline copy)’.”
  • Choose would be primary instead if one side were clearly stale (e.g., yours only touched a typo fixed identically upstream).
  • Merge is primary only for structured fields with no overlapping prose (e.g., you changed the status property, Maya edited the body → auto-merge both, announce it).
  • All three choices are named buttons, keyboard-reachable; no drag-to-merge-only interaction (also respects 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, AA).

Why it passes: Data integrity > faux realtime — the user never discovers silently vanished edits; the state matrix covered offline and syncing explicitly (L6); the conflict pattern is Guided now, promoted to Locked once ≥3 products use it.

Rejected: Silent last-write-wins overwrite (“magic”); a meaningless spinner; a color-only “out of sync” badge; drag-only merge UI; hiding conflicts to protect delight metrics.

Steal mechanic: Figma-style explicit presence + conflict as a conversation of state (Ch 23.3) — both versions labeled and offered — not last-write-wins pretending to be magic.

Measure: conflict rate · resolve success without data loss · time-to-acknowledge offline (banner within 2s of connectivity loss) · support tickets “my edits vanished.”

Ch 21-I — Case I: Search zero-with-filters — Example

Concept: Findability: no-query ≠ zero-for-query ≠ zero-with-filters ≠ error; primary CTA on filtered-zero = Clear filters (preserve query); URL persistence; Cmd-K ≠ retrieval product. Ch 21 Case I + decision tree.

Scenario: “Copydeck” CMS asset search. User searches q=hero banner then stacks filters type:video, updated:last 7 days → 0 results, though 34 image assets match the query.

Example:

  • Active filters render as dismissible chips: [type: video ×] [updated: last 7 days ×] — each chip a real button with accessible name “Remove filter: type video,” dismissible by keyboard (Enter/Space), active state conveyed by border + label, not color alone.
  • Zero-with-filters state copy: “No matches with current filters. 34 results for ‘hero banner’ are hidden by your filters.” Primary CTA: “Clear filters” (keeps q=hero banner); secondary “Clear all.” The never-used empty illustration does not appear here.
  • Decision tree shipped as code:
// unfilteredCount = results for the same query with filters cleared —
// the "34" the zero-state copy displays, so the UI already needs it.
function zeroState(q: string, filters: Filter[], results: Asset[],
                   unfilteredCount: number, error?: Error) {
  if (error) return { kind: "error", cta: "Retry" };                    // never masquerade as zero
  if (results.length > 0) return { kind: "results" };
  // Promise "Clear filters" only when clearing them actually reveals results.
  // A bad query with filters stacked on top is still zero-query — offering
  // "Clear filters" there strands the user on a second zero screen.
  if (filters.length > 0 && unfilteredCount > 0)
    return { kind: "zero-filtered", cta: "Clear filters", keepQuery: true,
             hiddenCount: unfilteredCount };
  if (q) return { kind: "zero-query", cta: "Check spelling or broaden scope" };
  return { kind: "no-query-coaching", examples: ["hero banner", "logo dark"] };
}
  • URL persists everything: /assets?q=hero+banner&type=video&updated=7d — refresh, share, and back-button all reproduce the state.
  • A11y: result count announced in a polite live region on every refine — “0 results with 2 filters active”; the search input is a native <input type="search"> inside a labeled combobox per APG; focus is not lost when the result list re-renders.
  • Ranking honesty: no fake fullness — the list never pads with “related” upsell cards to hide a weak retrieval.

Why it passes: The filtered-zero recovery path (chips + Clear filters, query preserved) is the completeness gap the case exists to close; error never masquerades as zero; URL persistence makes search a real retrieval product, not a palette.

Rejected: One generic “No results” for all four states; silently auto-clearing filters; infinite skeleton on timeout; hover-only facet panel; count not announced; a card-grid of unrelated upsells in the zero state; Linear-style Cmd-K presented as the only search.

Steal mechanic: Faceted-search recovery from mature commerce/docs search — filter chips + “Clear filters” as first-class citizens — not Linear’s Cmd-K alone (a command palette is not a retrieval product, Ch 22.22).

Measure: find success rate · zero-with-filters recovery rate · clear-filter CTR from the zero state · time-to-first-successful-open · queries-with-refine that end in an open.

Ch 21-J — Case J: Account delete / data-rights — Example

Concept: Legal erase/export ≠ document soft-delete; Hard confirm class; copy must match legal reality; Locked DataRights patterns. Ch 21 Case J.

Scenario: “Parcelo” must support GDPR/CCPA rights. IA: Settings → Privacy & data.

Example:

  • Preference center offers four actions: “Download my data (export)” · “Delete my account” · “Manage consent” · “Limit data use.”
  • Delete flow, Hard class: plain-language consequences screen — “Deleting your account permanently erases your profile, shipment history, and saved addresses within 30 days. We keep invoices for 7 years where tax law requires it.” Erased-vs-retained is an explicit two-column list, then a typed confirm: “Type delete my account to continue.”
  • Receipt + timeline: confirmation email “We received your deletion request on Jul 15, 2026 (ref DR-5521)” and an in-product status timeline: Requested → Processing → Done, with “Done expected by Aug 14, 2026.”
  • Export: if the export build takes minutes and the session nears timeout, warn + extend (“Your session expires in 2 minutes — Stay signed in”) rather than expiring mid-export.
  • If a fraud gate protects the flow, it carries the Case F accessible alternative — never a puzzle-only gate in front of a legal right.
  • SR announces submission in a live region: “Deletion request submitted. Reference DR-5521.” Any challenge failure renders a GOV.UK-style Error Summary.
  • Systems: DataRights patterns are Locked with rights-specific strings — the file-delete DestructiveConfirm copy (“Move to Trash…”) is not reused; legal strings accept no Open-partition copy overrides.

Why it passes: External irreversibility + compliance = Hard class (L7); the disclosed grace window (“within 30 days”) matches policy reality, so user-facing copy never over- or under-promises; Legal + PM co-own cancel/export/delete clarity.

Rejected: Soft toast “Account deleted — Undo”; the delete link buried in a footer paragraph; same flow/strings as archiving a project; silent partial delete with no retained-data disclosure; retention dark patterns (“contact support to leave”); a timer expiring mid-export.

Steal mechanic: Honest preference centers — GOV.UK plain language (Ch 23.8) + Stripe-level receipt honesty (Ch 23.2): retention exceptions stated plainly, export offered before delete — not “contact support to leave.”

Measure: time-to-complete export/delete · support “how do I delete/export” tickets · incomplete-request rate · regulatory complaints · trust NPS on privacy settings.

Ch 21-J.1 — Contrast with Case C — Example

Concept: File/team delete maps Soft/Quarantine/Hard by blast radius; account erase is legal Hard plus any disclosed grace window. Ch 21 Case J contrast note.

Scenario: Parcelo has both a “delete saved address” action and “delete account.”

Example: “Delete saved address” = Soft undo toast (7s) — local, reversible. “Delete account” = typed Hard confirm + email receipt + 30-day disclosed processing window. The same engineer builds both in one sprint; the undo-class map (Ch 21-C.1) is the review artifact that keeps them from sharing a pattern.

Why it passes: “Never ship account delete as a 5-second undo toast” — the case’s closing law, honored by classifying on irreversibility, not on how similar the buttons look.

Ch 21-K — Case K: Table selection + bulk partial failure — Example

Concept: Scoped select-all, N-selected toolbar, bulk soft-undo, partial failure keeps successes; structure a11y (<th scope>); DnD needs a Move up/down peer. Ch 21 Case K.

Scenario: “Ledgerly” ops console: 1,240 invoices, filter status:overdue active (312 match, 50 per page). An admin bulk-archives.

Example:

  • Selection grammar: click selects a row; Shift-click range-selects; the header checkbox is scoped: its accessible name is “Select all 50 on this page,” and only after that does a secondary, explicit link appear: “Select all 312 overdue invoices” — whole-corpus selection is never one silent click.
  • Selection-anchored toolbar appears with the count as text: “312 selected · Archive · Export · Clear selection.”
  • Bulk archive = Soft undo class (“Archived 312 invoices — Undo”, 10s) because archive is reversible.
  • Partial failure keeps successes:
{
  "requested": 312, "succeeded": 297, "failed": 15,
  "failures": [
    { "id": "inv_1021", "reason": "locked_by_dispute" },
    { "id": "inv_1088", "reason": "locked_by_dispute" }
  ]
}

UI: “297 of 312 archived. 15 couldn’t be archived because they’re locked by open disputes.” CTA: “Review 15 failed” filters the table to the failures with per-row error text — the 297 successes are not rolled back.
- Structure a11y: real <table> with <th scope="col"> headers; sticky header via position: sticky; top: 0 that doesn’t break reading order; documented keyboard model (Tab into table, Arrow keys row-to-row, Space toggles selection); status column is icon + text (“Overdue”), tabular figures for amounts.
- Row reorder (saved views) offers “Move up / Move down” menu items as the drag peer (2.5.7 Dragging Movements, AA).
- Systems: shared DataTable + BulkBar, currently Guided, promotion to Locked queued at the third product adoption (L12).

Why it passes: Selection grammar and scoped select-all are safety rails — the accidental whole-corpus archive is structurally impossible; partial-failure UX turns a support fire into a 30-second recovery.

Rejected: Silent whole-corpus select-all behind the header checkbox; all-or-nothing bulk that rolls back 297 successes over 15 locked rows (or worse, fails silently); card-per-row layout for a 1,240-row ops surface; color-only status dots; div-soup grid without headers; drag-only reorder.

Steal mechanic: Linear / Gmail scoped selection + selection-anchored bulk bar (Ch 23.1 / 23.9), plus partial-failure reporting that keeps successes and names each failure.

Measure: bulk completion rate · partial-fail recovery rate (% of failed subsets resolved within session) · accidental whole-corpus selects (target 0) · keyboard task success on select→archive→undo.

Ch 22 — Anti-Patterns Catalog: Examples (why / repair)

Format per row: the Rejected artifact is the anti-pattern as shipped; the Example is the repair, naming a law, token, or pattern — not a vibe.

Ch 22.1 — AI-SaaS purple / cream-terracotta cliché

Concept: Brand test failure — remove the nav and marketing could be any company. Ch 22 row 1.
Scenario: A startup’s site: purple-to-violet gradient hero, cream body, terracotta CTAs — identical to four competitors.
Rejected: background: linear-gradient(135deg, #7c3aed, #a78bfa) hero reused inside the app shell, forcing weak product chrome.
Example (repair): Pick a distinctive scarce accent (e.g., signal orange used only on primary actions, --color-action-primary), split marketing and product into separate systems (Stripe dual-system mechanic, Ch 23.2), and run a dual-theme audit so the accent holds 3:1 against both surfaces (1.4.11 AA).
Why it passes: Passes the brand test by scarcity + distinctiveness; product chrome stays quiet per the tool test.

Ch 22.2 — Card-grid everything

Concept: Equal elevation destroys hierarchy (L2/L4); cards imply interactivity. Ch 22 row 2.
Scenario: A settings page where every read-only info block is a shadowed card.
Rejected: 14 sibling cards, all box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.12) — no focal point, users click inert cards.
Example (repair): Flat sections separated by --space-32 and section headings; cards reserved for the two genuinely interactive containers (plan card, payment-method card). One focal point per region.
Why it passes: L2 hierarchy from weight/space/position; L4 elevation only where raise means something.

Ch 22.3 — Glass / glow everywhere

Concept: Backdrop blur hurts data readability; elevation-as-modality lies. Ch 22 row 3.
Scenario: A dashboard whose KPI table sits on backdrop-filter: blur(12px) over a gradient.
Rejected: Glass table where “$12,481.20” ghosts against moving background; contrast measured 2.7:1 — fails 1.4.3 AA (needs 4.5:1).
Example (repair): Data on solid --color-bg-surface; blur/scrim only on true overlays (modal scrim rgba(0,0,0,.5) + blurred sheet), where raise = temporary (L4).
Why it passes: Solid surfaces restore ≥4.5:1; modality signal becomes truthful.

Ch 22.4 — Default Inter / Roboto / system stacks

Concept: No specimen contract → product type drifts. Ch 22 row 4.
Scenario: Three squads each “just used Inter” at 13px, 14px, and 15px body.
Rejected: font-family: Inter; font-size: 14.5px ad hoc in a feature stylesheet.
Example (repair): Purposeful pairing (e.g., a grotesque for UI + tabular mono for numbers) with a locked role scale (Ch 5): --font-body: 14px/20px, --font-title: 20px/28px, --font-mono-tabular for money — published as specimens in the system docs.
Why it passes: L3 — type roles are contracts; drift becomes a lint failure, not a taste debate.

Ch 22.5 — Onboarding carousel

Concept: Delays first artifact; confuses the curriculum. Ch 22 row 5.
Scenario: 6-slide product tour before the user may touch anything.
Rejected: “Next (3/6)” carousel; tour completion 71%, time-to-first-artifact 9 minutes.
Example (repair): Case B curriculum — identity → artifact → share → return cue: land in a template-seeded artifact in <90s (see Ch 21-B).
Why it passes: Optimizes the outcome metric (time-to-first-artifact, D7) instead of tour vanity.

Ch 22.6 — Icon-only primary nav

Concept: Learnability debt; fails until find-rate proven. Ch 22 row 6.
Scenario: A sidebar of seven unlabeled glyphs; new users hover-hunt.
Rejected: <button><svg…/></button> ×7, tooltips as the only names.
Example (repair): Label primary nav (“Inbox”, “Reports”, “Settings”); collapse to icon+tooltip only via a container-query switch after find-rate is proven, and every icon button keeps an accessible name (aria-label="Reports"), enforced by the no-unlabeled-icon-button lint.
Why it passes: Learnability first; the CQ switch makes icon-only an earned density, not a default.

Ch 22.7 — Confirm-all / no undo classes

Concept: Confirm tax or irreversible accidents — both from missing L7 classes. Ch 22 row 7.
Scenario: “Are you sure?” on archive, on tag-remove, on delete — users click through blindly, then lose real data.
Rejected: One generic confirm modal for everything.
Example (repair): Classify: archive = Soft toast 7s undo; shared delete = Quarantine 30d Trash; workspace purge = Hard typed confirm (Ch 21-C.1 map).
Why it passes: L7 — undo > confirm; confirm reserved for external irreversibility keeps it meaningful.

Ch 22.8 — outline: none without replacement

Concept: Kills the keyboard cursor (L9). Ch 22 row 8.
Scenario: A reset stylesheet nukes outlines “for aesthetics.”
Rejected: *:focus { outline: none; }
Example (repair):

:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--color-focus-ring); /* ≥2px, ≥3:1 vs adjacent (1.4.11 AA) */
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Why it passes: L9 — focus is a cursor; :focus-visible keeps mouse aesthetics without blinding keyboard users; also supports 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA.

Ch 22.9 — Placeholder-as-label

Concept: Disappears on input; AT/label failure. Ch 22 row 9.
Scenario: Checkout form with placeholder="Card number" and no label.
Rejected: <input placeholder="Card number"> — label vanishes the moment typing starts; SR users hear nothing.
Example (repair): Visible <label for="card">Card number</label> + aria-describedby="card-hint" for “16 digits, no spaces” (see Ch 21-A HTML).
Why it passes: Persistent label; help/errors programmatically associated.

Ch 22.10 — ARIA div theater

Concept: Fake roles without keyboard maps (L10). Ch 22 row 10.
Scenario: <div role="listbox"> dropdown that only mouse users can open.
Rejected: role attributes sprinkled on divs, zero key handlers — “ARIA lipstick.”
Example (repair): Native <select> first; if design demands custom, implement the full APG listbox map (ArrowUp/Down, Home/End, typeahead, aria-activedescendant) — the whole map or the native element.
Why it passes: L10 — native first, APG second; a role is a promise of behavior.

Ch 22.11 — Infinite settings

Concept: Neutrality abdication; discoverability rot. Ch 22 row 11.
Scenario: 84 toggles including “show borders on hover cards.”
Rejected: A settings page as the dumping ground for every design dispute.
Example (repair): Opinionated defaults; keep the 6 settings with measured demand; move expert toggles behind progressive disclosure (primary → overflow → palette → settings, L8).
Why it passes: L8 — the product has an opinion; settings stop being an apology.

Ch 22.12 — Dashboard / confetti theater

Concept: Polish off the critical path (L14). Ch 22 row 12.
Scenario: Confetti burst on login streaks while checkout error copy still says “Error 422.”
Rejected: Animated celebration budget > error-recovery budget.
Example (repair): Starve non-path chrome; reassign the sprint to the pay path; instrument cue→action→reward on the habit loop instead of decorating it.
Why it passes: L14 — craft budget flows to trust × frequency.

Ch 22.13 — Premature abstraction

Concept: Prop soup; shadow libraries (violates L12). Ch 22 row 13.
Scenario: A SuperCard wrapper created for one usage, now with 23 props.
Rejected: <SuperCard variant="v2" legacyPadding compactish …/>
Example (repair): Abstract after three real uses: recipe (docs snippet) → pattern (copyable composition) → component (Locked API). Delete SuperCard, inline its one usage.
Why it passes: L12 — three uses prove the seam; promotion is earned.

Ch 22.14 — Hover-only on mobile

Concept: Primary path missing on touch. Ch 22 row 14.
Scenario: Row actions appear on :hover; iPhone users can’t archive.
Rejected: .row:hover .actions { opacity: 1 } as the only path.
Example (repair): Visible overflow button per row (≥44×44 target — craft bar; 24×24 is only the 2.5.8 AA floor) opening an action sheet; hover reveal kept as desktop enhancement only.
Why it passes: Touch parity; every gesture/hover affordance has a visible equivalent.

Ch 22.15 — Puzzle CAPTCHA only

Concept: Excludes AT users; growth vs inclusion failure. Ch 22 row 15.
Rejected: Drag-the-puzzle-piece CAPTCHA as the only gate on login.
Example (repair inline): Passkey first, email OTP fallback (“We sent a 6-digit code to t•••@example.com — it expires in 10 minutes”), and a vendor adapter whose contract makes altPath a required field — no challenge ships without a non-visual alternative (3.3.8 AA). Full ladder: Ch 21-F.
Why it passes: Inclusion can block ship; the alt path is contractual, not a review catch.

Ch 22.16 — Color-only charts / status

Concept: Fails L11; fragile in high-contrast/forced-colors. Ch 22 row 16.
Scenario: A revenue chart where “Won” vs “Lost” differ only by green/red; status dots in tables.
Rejected: Two same-shape lines distinguished by hue alone; forced-colors mode flattens both to CanvasText.
Example (repair): Direct line labels (“Won”, “Lost”), differing dash patterns (stroke-dasharray: 4 2 on one series), point markers of different shapes; table status = icon + text “● Overdue” with the word always present.
Why it passes: L11 multi-channel; survives forced-colors and 400% zoom.

Ch 22.17 — Silent AI mutation

Concept: Breaks conversation + trust. Ch 22 row 17.
Rejected: Autocomplete that silently rewrites 214 published pages the moment the model finishes.
Example (repair inline): Nothing mutates before explicit Apply; the proposal is a typed contract with sideEffects: [{ kind: "notify_watchers", count: 38, requiresApproval: true }] needing its own checked approval; after Apply, “Applied to 214 pages — Undo” (10s Soft toast) plus a version-history revert. Full loop: Ch 21-D.
Why it passes: The human remains the authority on side effects; diff → apply → undo preserves the conversation.

Ch 22.18 — Trap cancel / fake urgency

Concept: Permanent trust loss; legal risk. Ch 22 row 18.
Scenario: Cancel requires a phone call; countdown timer resets on refresh.
Rejected: “Offer expires in 4:59” (it doesn’t); “To cancel, contact retention.”
Example (repair): Cancel ≥ upgrade clarity — “Cancel plan” button in Settings → Billing, 2 clicks, immediate email confirmation (Ch 21-G).
Why it passes: Honest growth UI; the guardrail metric (cancel completion) is first-class.

Ch 22.19 — Shadow component libraries

Concept: Drift; override-rate explosion. Ch 22 row 19.
Scenario: A squad maintains @growth/ui-buttons forked from the kit 8 months ago.
Rejected: Two Buttons diverging in focus ring, disabled contrast, and API.
Example (repair): Promote or delete: fold the fork’s one real improvement (loading state) into the kit as a MINOR; add CI banned-imports ("@growth/ui-buttons": "error"); weekly drift check.
Why it passes: L12/L13 — one contract, versioned; override-rate returns as the health signal.

Ch 22.20 — Inverted-light “dark mode”

Concept: Contrast lies; muddy surfaces. Ch 22 row 20.
Scenario: Dark theme generated by filter: invert(1)-style ramp flips; saturated brand blue vibrates on near-black.
Rejected: --color-bg-surface: #0a0a0a with light-theme’s --blue-600 (#2456d6) text at 3.2:1 — fails 4.5:1 (1.4.3 AA).
Example (repair): Separate tonal ramps: dark surfaces desaturated (#111318, #1a1d24), text ramps re-picked to ≥4.5:1, accent lightened one step (--blue-400) in the dark map; dual-theme audit in CI.
Why it passes: Both themes independently pass; the theme layer composes (brand → mode → high-contrast), never forks the tree.

Ch 22.21 — One empty state for all zeros

Concept: Wrong CTA; users can’t recover filters. Ch 22 row 21.
Rejected: One illustration titled “Nothing here!” reused for never-used, filtered-to-zero, error, and denied.
Example (repair inline): Four states, four CTAs — filtered-to-zero: “No studies match your current filters.” + primary “Clear filters” (query preserved); denied: “You don’t have access to this team’s studies.” + “Request access”; error gets “Retry”, never-used gets “Create your first study”. Full matrix: Ch 21-B.1; search variant: Ch 21-I.
Why it passes: L6 — state is designed; recovery CTA matches cause.

Ch 22.22 — Cmd-K as only search

Concept: Palette ≠ retrieval; long-tail, zero/filter UX missing. Ch 22 row 22.
Scenario: A docs product where the only finder is a command palette with prefix match.
Rejected: Cmd-K returning 10 title matches, no facets, no URL, no zero-state recovery.
Example (repair): Full search product — query + scope selector + facet chips + ?q=&type= URL schema + Case I zero states — and keep Cmd-K strictly for commands/navigation.
Why it passes: Retrieval and command invocation are different jobs; conflating them starves the long tail.

Ch 22.23 — Select-all across universe

Concept: Mass-destroy risk; partial-failure chaos. Ch 22 row 23.
Rejected: Header checkbox silently selecting all 1,240 records across every page.
Example (repair inline): Header checkbox accessibly named “Select all 50 on this page”; the whole corpus only via a second, explicit link — “Select all 312 overdue invoices” — with the count as text in a selection-anchored toolbar (“312 selected · Archive · Clear selection”). Full grammar + partial-failure handling: Ch 21-K.
Why it passes: Selection scope is a safety rail; blast radius stays legible.

Ch 22.24 — Table as div soup

Concept: Keyboard cell nav and headers fail. Ch 22 row 24.
Scenario: <div class="table"> grid; SR reads it as undifferentiated text.
Rejected: Divs with display: grid, no role, no headers.
Example (repair): Real <table> with <th scope="col">/<th scope="row">, or full APG grid with documented Arrow-key model; sticky-header plan that preserves reading order; table a11y in the Definition of Done.
Why it passes: Structure gives AT users column context per cell; keyboard model is explicit.

Ch 22.25 — Account delete as soft toast

Concept: Legal irreversibility ≠ document undo. Ch 22 row 25.
Rejected: “Account deleted — Undo” as a 5-second toast.
Example (repair inline): Replace the toast with a Hard flow — typed confirm “Type delete my account to continue”, erased-vs-retained disclosure (“invoices retained 7 years — tax law”), email receipt “ref DR-5521”, and a Requested → Processing → Done status timeline. Full flow: Ch 21-J.
Why it passes: L7 Hard class; copy matches legal reality.

Ch 22.26 — axe-green ship without task pass

Concept: Compliance theater. Ch 22 row 26.
Scenario: Checkout passes axe with zero violations, but a keyboard user cannot reach “Apply promo code” (focus trap in a custom dropdown).
Rejected: “axe is green, ship it.”
Example (repair): Ship gates require keyboard task pass (complete checkout end-to-end by keyboard) + SR smoke + lived-experience gate on Locked paths — paid disabled-user sessions can block ship even with green axe.
Why it passes: Tools catch attribute bugs; only task passes catch broken journeys.

Ch 22.27 — Synonym public API (primary/brand/cta)

Concept: AI + humans scale defects (L13). Ch 22 row 27.
Scenario: Button accepts variant="primary" | "brand" | "cta" — three names, one meaning; codegen picks all three across the repo.
Rejected: type ButtonVariant = "primary" | "brand" | "cta" | string;
Example (repair):

type Tone = "neutral" | "primary" | "danger";      // exhaustive union, no synonyms
type Size = "sm" | "md" | "lg";
interface ButtonProps { tone: Tone; size?: Size }  // rename before codegen amplifies

Why it passes: L13 — one name per meaning; exhaustive unions make invalid states unrepresentable for humans and AI alike.

Ch 22.28 — Raw hex / px in app CSS

Concept: Breaks the semantic contract (L1/L3). Ch 22 row 28.
Scenario: A feature PR adds color: #6b7280; margin-top: 13px;.
Rejected: Raw palette + off-grid spacing in product code.
Example (repair): color: var(--color-text-secondary); margin-top: var(--space-12); enforced by stylelint no-raw-color and a space-token rule (4/8 rhythm) — CI fails the PR otherwise.
Why it passes: L1 roles-not-hexes; L3 rhythm as contract; theming and contrast audits stay possible.

Ch 22.29 — Focus to body after modal

Concept: Disorients AT/keyboard users (L9). Ch 22 row 29.
Scenario: Closing a delete dialog drops focus at document top; SR user is lost.
Rejected: dialog.close() with no restore.
Example (repair):

const trigger = document.activeElement as HTMLElement; // capture on open
dialog.showModal();
dialog.addEventListener("close", () => trigger.focus()); // APG: restore to trigger

Why it passes: L9 + APG dialog pattern — the cursor returns to where the journey paused.

Ch 22.30 — Marketing gradients inside tool tables

Concept: Tool test failure; trust-path noise. Ch 22 row 30.
Scenario: The rebrand team applies the launch gradient to the invoice table header.
Rejected: Brand hero treatment competing with the user’s numbers.
Example (repair): Stripe dual-system split (Ch 23.2): marketing forks expression freely; product chrome stays quiet (--color-bg-surface, 1px --color-border-subtle), content loud.
Why it passes: “If chrome competes with the user’s work, the product failed” — the tool test, honored structurally.

Catalog completeness note (unnumbered): all 30 catalog rows above (Ch 22.1–22.30) are exemplified. Rows that share a worked case carry a one-line inline repair and cross-reference the full case. No catalog row is left without a concrete repair naming a law, token, or pattern.

Ch 22.31 — Override-rate signal — Example

Concept: Frequent forks of Locked primitives usually mean premature rigidity or a wrong default — fix the system (Systems is Accountable), don’t blame squads. Ch 22 closing note.

Scenario: Ledgerly’s Locked Modal shows a 34% override rate this quarter; 11 of 14 overrides add a wider size.

Example: Systems team response: ship size: "sm" | "md" | "lg" | "xl" as a MINOR (new capability, no break), migrate the 11 forks via codemod, and re-measure. Override rate drops to 6% in the next quarter’s drift report.

Why it passes: The signal was read as a systems defect (missing default), not squad indiscipline; the fix went through the L13 versioned contract.

Ch 23 — North Stars: Steal the Mechanic — Examples

Ch 23.1 — Linear — Example

Concept: Steal issue row density, Cmd-K for long-tail, optimistic create when rollback is cheap. Ch 23 Linear entry.
Scenario: “Trackly,” a QA-issue tool for daily-driver test engineers.
Example: 36px issue rows (dense map: control height 28px, row padding --space-8, meta type role 12px/16px); Cmd-K palette for commands and jump-to-issue; pressing c then Enter optimistically inserts the new issue at the top of the list instantly, with Soft undo — rollback is one client-side removal.
Why it passes: Pro tool + high frequency + keyboard-willing users + reversible create — every “apply when” condition holds.
Rejected (cargo-cult): Assuming all users are keyboard-native (no templates or empty guidance for new users); reusing optimistic create on Trackly’s paid-plan checkout — money paths stay pessimistic (Case A).

Ch 23.2 — Stripe — Example

Concept: Steal dual systems (marketing vs product), label + error pairing, docs-as-product. Ch 23 Stripe entry.
Scenario: Ledgerly (trust market) separates ledgerly.com (marketing, expressive gradients allowed) from app.ledgerly.com (quiet Locked chrome).
Example: Two token themes composed from one primitive set; checkout fields use visible label + inline error pairs (Ch 21-A HTML); public API docs get the product team’s polish budget because docs deflect support.
Why it passes: Trust market + Locked checkout + support-reducing docs — the exact “apply when.”
Rejected (cargo-cult): Copying stripe.com’s animated gradients into the dashboard tables (Ch 22.30); treating docs as an afterthought while imitating the homepage.

Ch 23.3 — Figma — Example

Concept: Steal selection/presence as conversation and the contextual toolbar on selection. Ch 23 Figma entry.
Scenario: “Boardroom,” a multiplayer retro-board app.
Example: Selecting three sticky notes summons a floating toolbar anchored to the selection (“3 selected · Group · Color · Delete”); collaborators’ cursors carry name labels; when Maya selects a note you’re viewing, its border shows her presence with her name — state talks (Talkative obligation).
Why it passes: Multiplayer canvas + selection-scoped actions — presence prevents edit collisions before they need conflict UI.
Rejected (cargo-cult): Forcing the desktop canvas IA onto the mobile app; presence avatars flooding a solitary billing form where they’re noise.

Ch 23.4 — Apple HIG — Example

Concept: Steal material = temporary vs durable (elevation-as-modality), VoiceOver craft, prefers-reduced-motion. Ch 23 Apple entry.
Scenario: Parcelo’s iOS app: shipment detail page vs quick-actions sheet.
Example: The detail page is flat and durable (no shadow); the quick-actions sheet rises with a blurred material + scrim because it is temporary (L4). All motion honors the media query:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .sheet { transition: none; } /* fade only, no slide */
}

Why it passes: Modality is legible from elevation alone; reduced-motion users get the same information without the animation.
Rejected (cargo-cult): Copying iOS translucent materials onto the dense web ops table (Ch 22.3); decorative blur on data.

Ch 23.5 — Material 3 — Example

Concept: Steal role-based color, tonal surfaces, systematic state layers. Ch 23 Material entry.
Scenario: Ledgerly builds its semantic ramp with M3’s role logic, not its default hue.
Example: Roles like --color-bg-surface-container, --color-text-on-primary generated from Ledgerly’s own brand seed; state layers systematized (hover = 8% overlay of the on-color, pressed = 12%) so every component’s states derive from one rule.
Why it passes: Semantic roles + Android parity of roles — token ramps become generative, not hand-picked per component.
Rejected (cargo-cult): Shipping default M3 purple as “your brand” (Ch 22.1); inventing role soup (40 roles, no promotion rule).

Ch 23.6 — Polaris / Spectrum / Carbon — Example

Concept: Steal the contribution model — docs, do/don’t, escape hatches, token discipline. Ch 23 entry.
Scenario: Ledgerly’s design system serves 6 squads; squads keep asking for one-off variants.
Example: A published contribution path: proposal issue template → do/don’t doc requirement → 2-week RFC window → MINOR release with migration notes and a semver SLA (“deprecations live ≥90 days”); a documented escape hatch (unsafe_className) that is lint-flagged and counted in the override-rate report.
Why it passes: Multi-squad enterprise + Locked kit governance — contribution becomes ops, not hero refactors.
Rejected (cargo-cult): A monolith with no Locked/Guided/Open partition; “contribution theater” (a template nobody triages, no semver SLA).

Ch 23.7 — Radix / React Aria / shadcn-style kits — Example

Concept: Steal behavior primitives (focus management, APG keyboard maps); own the skin with tokens. Ch 23 entry.
Scenario: Trackly needs a combobox; building APG-correct focus/typeahead from scratch is a quarter of work.
Example: Adopt the headless primitive for behavior, skin it entirely with semantic tokens:

<Combobox.Input className="field" />  /* .field uses --color-bg-surface,
  --color-border-subtle, --space-field-gap — zero vendor styles */

Why it passes: Adopt-vs-build resolved correctly: proven behavior (focus, ARIA, keys) is the expensive part; skin is yours via tokens.
Rejected (cargo-cult): Copy-pasting a styled kit without understanding its focus/ARIA (then breaking it); wrapping the library once “for consistency” with no second use (violates L12).

Ch 23.8 — GOV.UK — Example

Concept: Steal the Error Summary (linked list of errors), plain language, one-column critical tasks. Ch 23 entry.
Scenario: Parcelo’s customs-declaration form — high-anxiety, legal consequences.
Example: On failed submit, focus jumps to a summary box: heading “There is a problem”, list items are links — “Enter the recipient’s postcode” → clicking focuses the postcode field; the whole form is one column; copy at plain-language reading level (“We’ll use this to calculate duty” not “Duty calculation requires locale data”).
Why it passes: Forms/auth/legal/data-rights are exactly the “apply when”; linked summary + field-local errors is the Case A / Case J error pattern.
Rejected (cargo-cult): Using plain-language austerity as an excuse for a lifeless acquisition homepage — marketing surfaces may still carry brand.

Ch 23.9 — Gmail / Superhuman — Example

Concept: Steal the Undo Send window (Soft undo class), density toggle, keyboard power with a progressive path. Ch 23 entry.
Scenario: “Heraldo,” a customer-messaging tool sending outbound emails.
Example: Send holds the message for a user-configurable 10s window with a persistent “Sending… Undo” affordance (Soft class applied to an otherwise-external action by delaying the side effect); density toggle switches the thread list between comfortable (52px rows) and compact (36px); keyboard shortcuts discoverable via a ? overlay so power is progressive, not gatekeeping.
Why it passes: High-frequency communication + reversible-by-delay sends; the undo window converts an irreversible act into a Soft one honestly.
Rejected (cargo-cult): Keyboard elitism with no templates/empty guidance; an “undo window” on a hard legal erase (Case J) — delay theater cannot soften genuine irreversibility.

Ch 23.10 — Cross-mechanic synthesis (steal stacks) — Example

Concept: Needs map to stacks of mechanics, not single heroes. Ch 23 synthesis table.
Scenario: Parcelo plans two quarters: Q3 “trust path” (checkout + customs), Q4 “daily density” (ops console).
Example:

Need Stack as shipped
Q3 Trust path Stripe field honesty (Ch 23.2) + GOV.UK Error Summary (Ch 23.8) + Locked CheckoutField/PayButton primitives
Q4 Daily density Linear 36px rows (Ch 23.1) + Superhuman density toggle (Ch 23.9) + Cmd-K for long-tail commands
Multiplayer (backlog) Figma presence + selection toolbar (Ch 23.3)
System scale (ongoing) Polaris-style contribution (Ch 23.6) + Radix behavior primitives (Ch 23.7) + M3 roles (Ch 23.5)
Inclusion (gate) GOV.UK language + HIG reduced-motion + AT-matrix ship gates

Why it passes: Behavior and structure are stolen per need; no logo worship — each line names the mechanic, where it applies, and (via the linked entries) the cargo-cult to avoid.

Ch 24 — Decision Cheat-Sheet & PR Critique Checklist: Examples

Ch 24.1 — Decision cheat-sheet, worked end-to-end — Example

Concept: The 18 ordered questions applied to one real feature, biasing to the right-column default unless prefer-when flips it. Ch 24.1.

Scenario: Trackly ships “Bulk close stale issues” — an ops action on a filtered table, with an optional AI suggestion of which issues are stale.

Example (every question answered):

# Question Answer for this feature
1 Marketing or product? Product → quiet tool chrome, no brand hero
2 Pre-PMF or trust market? Post-PMF daily tool → polish the flow now
3 New or daily? Daily → density + keyboard (36px rows, shortcuts)
4 Reversible? Close is reversible → Soft undo, “Closed 57 issues — Undo” (10s)
5 Money / identity / shared blast / legal erase? Shared blast only if “delete”; close = no → optimistic allowed
6 ≥3 real uses + Locked concern? BulkBar at 3rd use → promote to component (L12)
7 Decorates or changes known state? Confetti on close proposed → cut (decoration)
8 Color sole signal? Stale badge = icon + “Stale 90d+” text (L11)
9 Synonym API? tone="danger" only — no variant="destructive" twin (L13)
10 Growth on trust path? N/A — not a trust path (one-line why recorded)
