11 AI side effect? AI only suggests the stale set → diff-style review list + explicit Apply + undo
12 High override rate? BulkBar overrides at 4% — healthy, no action
13 axe-green but task fail? Keyboard task run: select→close→undo passes
14 Empty vs filtered-zero vs error? Filtered-zero shows “Clear filters” preserving query (Case I)
15 Search or command? The stale filter is retrieval (URL-persisted facet), not a Cmd-K trick
16 Table/grid needed? Yes → <th scope>, sticky header plan, Arrow-key model, scoped select-all
17 Account/data rights? N/A
18 Offline possible? Web-only ops console, online-required; queue not built — recorded as out of scope

Why it passes: Every row got a decision or an explicit justified N/A — the checklist’s own rule (“Check N/A only with a one-line why”). Four laws (L7, L11, L12, L13) were invoked by number, so the review is auditable.

Ch 24.2-A — Section A: Hierarchy & visual grammar (rows 1–7) — Example

Concept: Rows 1–7: hierarchy, type roles, elevation, space rhythm, semantic color + contrast, forced-colors, motion. Ch 24.2-A.

Scenario: PR #482 adds a “Payment insights” panel to Ledgerly’s dashboard.

Example (row-by-row review artifact):

  1. Hierarchy: one focal point — the headline number $48,210 in role stat-lg; supporting rows demoted by weight and --space-16, not by a second accent (L2). ✔
  2. Type: roles stat-lg (28px/36px) and meta (12px/16px) from the locked role scale — the PR’s original font-size: 27px flagged and replaced (L3). ✔ after fix
  3. Elevation: panel is durable → flat, 1px solid var(--color-border-subtle), no shadow (L4). ✔
  4. Space: 4/8 rhythm (--space-8/16/24); reflows single-column at 320px CSS width and at 400% zoom with no horizontal scroll (1.4.10 Reflow, AA). ✔
  5. Color: semantic tokens only (L1); secondary text --color-text-secondary measured 4.6:1 light / 4.8:1 dark (≥4.5:1, 1.4.3 AA); large-text case: the muted prior-period figure “$41,890” in stat-lg (28px bold — over both large-text thresholds: 24px regular / 18.66px bold) measured 3.4:1 against the surface — passes 1.4.3 AA as large text (3:1 floor) even though it would fail the 4.5:1 body floor; chart gridlines ≥3:1 (1.4.11 AA). ✔
  6. Forced-colors: no forced hex on buttons; @media (forced-colors: active) verified — controls inherit ButtonText/Canvas. ✔
  7. Motion: count-up animation is decorative → removed; remaining 150ms fade uses opacity only, disabled under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce. ✔

Why it passes: Each row cites the law or SC deciding it — the reviewer never says “looks off.”

Ch 24.2-B — Section B: Interaction & state (rows 8–14) — Example

Concept: Rows 8–14: feedback ≤100ms, L6 state matrix, empty≠zero≠error, undo class, disclosure, double-submit, bulk. Ch 24.2-B.

Scenario: Same PR #482 adds “Refresh data” and a bulk export.

Example:

  1. Feedback: Refresh acknowledges in ~50ms (button → pending spinner in place); work tier shows skeleton ≤1s; resolve announces “Data updated” (L5). ✔
  2. State matrix: designed states shipped for empty / loading / partial (“Showing cached data from 2:14 PM”) / error / offline / denied / syncing (L6). ✔
  3. Empty ≠ zero ≠ error: insights-with-filters zero shows “Clear filters”; API failure shows “Retry” — never shared copy. ✔
  4. Undo class: export is additive — no undo needed; recorded as N/A with why. ✔
  5. Disclosure: primary “Export CSV” visible; “Export as XLSX with pivot” in overflow (L8). ✔
  6. Double-submit: Export button disables + pending on press; the export POST carries an idempotency key. ✔
  7. Bulk: export of selected rows uses scoped selection + “12 selected” count; partial failure lists the 2 rows that failed without discarding the 10 that succeeded. ✔

Why it passes: State coverage is enumerated against the L6 taxonomy, not vibes; the one N/A carries its one-line why.

Ch 24.2-C — Section C: Search, filter & findability (rows 15–18) — Example

Concept: Rows 15–18: scope clarity/ranking honesty, zero-with-filters, live-region counts, Cmd-K vs search. Ch 24.2-C.

Scenario: Copydeck search PR (the Ch 21-I build) under review.

Example: 15. Scope selector visible (“Assets ▾”), no fake fullness padding ✔ · 16. Filtered-zero explains filters, “Clear filters” primary, ?q=&type=&updated= persists ✔ · 17. “34 results” announced via role="status" polite region on each refine (4.1.3 AA) ✔ · 18. Cmd-K exists but is command-only; the reviewer confirms it doesn’t pretend to be retrieval ✔.

Why it passes: Each row maps to a Case I artifact already specified — the checklist verifies, the case designed.

Ch 24.2-D — Section D: Tables, grids & selection (rows 19–23) — Example

Concept: Rows 19–23: semantics, keyboard model, sticky headers, selection, inline edit. Ch 24.2-D.

Scenario: Ledgerly invoice table PR (the Ch 21-K build).

Example: 19. Real <table>, <th scope="col"> ✔ · 20. Documented model: Tab enters table, Arrows move rows, Space selects; no trap ✔ · 21. Sticky header position: sticky preserves DOM/reading order; focused row never hidden under it (2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, AA) ✔ · 22. Shift-range works as claimed; toolbar anchors to selection; bulk delete (unlike archive) raises DestructiveConfirm with blast radius ✔ · 23. Inline amount edit: Esc cancels, Enter saves with “Saved” ack, error renders in-row (“Amount must be positive”) not in a distant toast ✔.

Why it passes: Row 22’s destructive-bulk branch shows the checklist catching a class upgrade (Soft archive vs Hard-gated delete) inside one surface.

Ch 24.2-E — Section E: Accessibility structure (rows 24–31) — Example

Concept: Rows 24–31: landmarks, headings, focus, names, live regions, SR smoke, touch, auth. Ch 24.2-E.

Scenario: Parcelo auth + shell PR.

Example:

  1. Landmarks: <header role="banner">, <nav>, <main id="main" tabindex="-1"> (focusable skip target); “Skip to main content” first-focusable ✔
  2. Headings: one h1 (“Sign in”), no h2→h4 skip for styling ✔
  3. Focus: DOM order = reading order; 2px --color-focus-ring on :focus-visible; modal close restores to trigger (L9) ✔
  4. Names: the eye “show password” icon button carries aria-label="Show password"; no-unlabeled-icon-button lint clean ✔
  5. Live regions: “Code sent” = polite role="status"; “Session expired” = assertive role="alert" (blocking); streamed AI progress lines (“Verifying device… Checking risk score…”) append into a role="log" region so each new line is announced without re-reading the whole container — status vs alert vs log disciplined per 4.1.3 AA ✔
  6. SR smoke script run: land → skip → primary CTA → trigger error → hear it → open/dismiss modal → focus restored ✔
  7. Touch: primary buttons 48×48px (≥44 craft; the 24×24 2.5.8 AA floor is noted as the legal minimum only) ✔
  8. Auth: visible labels, autocomplete="email"/"one-time-code" for password-manager/OTP autofill; challenge has an accessible alternative (3.3.8 AA; Case F) ✔

Why it passes: Cross-domain in one section: L9 + named tokens (--color-focus-ring) + three SC numbers (2.5.8, 3.3.8, 4.1.3) decide rows — no reviewer taste involved.

Ch 24.2-F — Section F: Systems & AI (rows 32–36) — Example

Concept: Rows 32–36: partition, tokens, API shape, promotion, AI loop. Ch 24.2-F.

Scenario: Trackly’s AI bulk-close PR (Ch 24.1 feature).

Example: 32. Surface labeled Guided in the PR description; one override (custom stale-badge) justified in a line ✔ · 33. Zero raw hex/px — stylelint gate green (L1/L3) ✔ · 34. Props are tone/size/density; reviewer rejects a proposed variant="destructive" synonym for the existing tone="danger" (L13) ✔ after fix · 35. BulkBar is at its 3rd use → promotion issue filed instead of a 4th copy (L12) ✔ · 36. AI: suggestion list → explicit Apply → Soft undo; no side effects, so sideEffects: [] shipped explicitly; override rate instrumented ✔.

Why it passes: Row 34 shows the checklist as a codegen firewall — the synonym dies in review, before AI replicates it.

Ch 24.2-G — Section G: Strategy, growth & privacy (rows 37–40) — Example

Concept: Rows 37–40: outcome metric, growth/trust, data-rights honesty, i18n. Ch 24.2-G.

Scenario: Fieldnote paywall PR (Ch 21-G build).

Example: 37. Outcome declared: trial→paid, guarded by cancel completion — L14 check: this is a trust-adjacent path, so polish justified ✔ · 38. No dark patterns on Locked checkout; cancel path reviewed side-by-side with upgrade path for parity ✔ · 39. Data-rights copy audited: “Cancel anytime” verified against actual billing behavior — copy is not softer than policy reality ✔ · 40. i18n: plan-column headers given a +35% German expansion budget; prices via Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency" }); layout uses logical properties (margin-inline-start) for RTL readiness ✔.

Why it passes: The strategy section forces the PR to name its metric and its guardrail — theater dies at row 37.

Ch 24.2-Gates — Ship gates (release-blocking) — Example

Concept: Six release-blocking checks on critical paths. Ch 24.2 ship gates.

Scenario: Ledgerly checkout release candidate, Jul 15 cut.

Example (gate log):

  • [x] Keyboard task pass — full pay flow completed keyboard-only, 3 testers
  • [x] axe clean of serious — 0 serious/critical (2 moderate ticketed, non-blocking)
  • [x] Both-theme contrast — token audit: all text ≥4.5:1, UI ≥3:1, light & dark
  • [x] Focus visible — :focus-visible ring verified on every control incl. custom card input
  • [x] SR smoke on checkout — NVDA + VoiceOver script passed (land → error → pay → receipt)
  • [ ] Lived-experience findings addressed — BLOCKED: paid session found the promo-code disclosure unreachable with switch access → release holds until fixed

Why it passes (by failing): The sixth gate blocks ship even though axe is green — the lived-experience gate outranks compliance theater, exactly as the convention table promises.

Ch 24.2-Template — PR summary template, filled — Example

Concept: The paste-into-review template. Ch 24.2 template.

Scenario: The Ch 21-K bulk-archive PR.

Example:

Path job: Ops bulk-archive of filtered invoices (daily-driver table)
Undo class: Soft (archive reversible; delete branch = Quarantine via Trash)
Partition: Guided (DataTable/BulkBar — promotion to Locked filed at 3rd use)
States covered: empty, filtered-to-zero, loading, partial (bulk 297/312), error, denied
Search/table/a11y-structure notes: <th scope="col">; scoped select-all named
  "Select all 50 on this page"; result/selection counts in polite live region;
  sticky header keeps focus visible (2.4.11 AA)
Metrics touched: bulk completion, partial-fail recovery, accidental corpus selects
Rejected alternatives: silent whole-corpus select-all; all-or-nothing bulk rollback;
  card-per-row layout

Why it passes: Every field filled including Rejected alternatives — skipping rejects collapses pedagogy into taste (Part VI opening rule).

Ch 25 — Capstone Exercises: Examples

Each example is a worked excerpt of the deliverable a passing submission would contain — enough to calibrate scoring, not a full answer key.

Ch 25.1 — Capstone 1: Trust-path checkout slice — Example

Concept: Single-page subscription-upgrade checkout; trust market; no growth theater. Ch 25 Capstone 1.

Scenario: Student specs Ledgerly’s annual-upgrade page (card + tax + Pay).

Example (passing excerpt):

  • Prefer-when table row: “Submit strategy → Pessimistic, because settled charges have no cheap rollback (L7/L14); optimistic reserved for cart edits.”
  • Locked contracts named: CheckoutField (visible label, aria-describedby error, autocomplete="cc-number"), PayButton (idempotency key minted per payment attempt — transport retries reuse it, a resubmit after a decline or changed total mints a fresh one, per Ch 21-A; disabled+pending ≤100ms after press per L5).
  • Error Summary spec: focus target, heading “There’s a problem with your payment”, items linked to fields (GOV.UK mechanic).
  • Tabular money: font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums on all amounts; both-theme contrast table attached (all text ≥4.5:1, 1.4.3 AA).
  • Receipt state mock: “Payment received — $1,188.00 · Receipt #INV-20481 emailed.”
  • Keyboard + SR smoke script included (7 steps, two screen readers).
  • ≥3 rejected alternatives listed: optimistic “Paid!”, placeholder-only labels, marketing gradient behind fields.
  • Ch 24 checklist attached with all six ship gates checked.

Measure (plan): payment success · error recovery rate · chargebacks/”charged twice” tickets.

Rejected (auto-fail per brief): Optimistic “Paid!” claim; placeholder-as-label fields; gradient hero behind the card form.

Why it passes: Hits every “must include” with numbers, named tokens/components, SC citations, and a measure plan — scoring rubric’s Accuracy + Tactical specificity columns are directly evidenced.

Ch 25.2 — Capstone 2: Findability — search + filters + zero recovery — Example

Concept: Product search with facets, URL persistence, zero-with-filters recovery; Cmd-K commands-only. Ch 25 Capstone 2.

Scenario: Student specs Fieldnote’s study search.

Example (passing excerpt):

  • Four-state copy table (no-query coaching / zero-query “No matches for ‘diary study’” / zero-filtered “No matches with current filters” + Clear filters preserving query / error “Retry” — never masquerading as zero).
  • URL schema: /studies?q=diary+study&method=usability&updated=30d — refresh/share/back reproduce state.
  • Chips: dismissible, keyboard-operable, accessible names (“Remove filter: method usability”), active state = border + label, not color alone (L11).
  • Live region: “12 results, 2 filters active” polite announcement per refine (4.1.3 AA).
  • Combobox: native-first note, APG fallback map documented (L10).
  • Mobile: filter sheet (temporary → elevated per L4) with Apply/Clear.
  • A11y structure notes for the results page: <main id="main" tabindex="-1"> landmark as a focusable skip-link target; one h1 “Search studies”; the results count rendered as an h2-level heading doubling as the role="status" announcement target; filter panel as <aside aria-label="Filters"> (complementary landmark).
  • Case I decision tree reproduced as the routing function.

Measure (plan): find success · zero-with-filters recovery rate · clear-filter CTR.

Rejected (auto-fail per brief): One generic empty; silent filter auto-clear; color-only active facets.

Why it passes: The decision tree + IA + a11y structure notes are all present — Completeness (25-weight criterion) is demonstrably covered.

Ch 25.3 — Capstone 3: Data table with selection & bulk destroy — Example

Concept: Admin table: sortable columns, sticky header, scoped select-all, bulk delete with correct undo class for shared records. Ch 25 Capstone 3.

Scenario: Student specs Relay’s admin page-management table.

Example (passing excerpt):

  • Selection model spec: click / Shift-range / header checkbox scoped (“Select all 50 on this page”) / explicit corpus escalation link; “N selected” toolbar.
  • Undo-class justification paragraph: “Pages are shared and recoverable → Quarantine 30d Trash with blast-radius confirm (‘Deletes 8 pages for 12 members — restorable 30 days’); Hard typed confirm reserved for Trash purge; Soft rejected because team-visible destroy exceeds toast blast radius (L7).”
  • Partial failure behavior: successes kept, failures listed per-row with reasons and a “Review failed” filter.
  • Ch 24 sections D+E filled row-by-row (as in Ch 24.2-D/E above); focus restore to triggering row’s menu button.
  • Rejected “div soup grid” written up: why headers/scope and the keyboard model die in divs.

Measure (plan): bulk completion · partial-fail recovery · accidental whole-corpus selects (target 0) · keyboard task success.

Rejected (auto-fail per brief): Unscoped corpus select-all; Soft toast for team-visible destroy; no keyboard path.

Why it passes: The undo-class justification names blast radius and cites L7 — the exact reasoning Capstone 3 exists to test.

Ch 25.4 — Capstone 4: AI proposal review on a Guided surface — Example

Concept: “Apply suggestions across N items”: stream, cancel, diff, apply, undo; one side effect requiring approval. Ch 25 Capstone 4.

Scenario: Student specs Copydeck’s assistant applying tone edits across 60 articles, with side effect “notify watchers.”

Example (passing excerpt):

  • Case D-style five-lens matrix with a rejected column per lens.
  • Stream + cancel: the proposal streams progressively — per-article rows appear as they’re generated (“Article 14 of 60: 3 lines changed”) — with a persistent Cancel button throughout; nothing mutates before explicit Apply (mirrors Ch 21-D).
  • Contract excerpt: sideEffects: [{ kind: "notify_watchers", count: 22, requiresApproval: true }] — Apply ships edits; notification requires its own checked approval.
  • Diff readable without color: +/− glyphs, underline/strikethrough patterns, per-hunk announcements; keyboard apply/reject map (a/x, Tab-reachable buttons).
  • Instrumentation plan: override/reject rate and undo-after-apply as the trust dashboard; explicit note that accept rate alone is a banned success metric.
  • Promotion plan: Guided now; Lock when 3 products adopt and override rate <10% for a quarter (L12).

Measure (plan): override rate · undo-after-apply · side-effect incidents (target 0).

Rejected (auto-fail per brief): Accept-rate-only metric; unattended watcher notification; red/green-only diffs.

Why it passes: Side-effect approval is contractual, not copy — the human-authority principle survives implementation.

Ch 25.5 — Capstone 5: Privacy preference center + account delete — Example

Concept: Settings → Privacy: consent minimize, export, delete; legal erase ≠ document delete; grace-window copy only if policy supports it. Ch 25 Capstone 5.

Scenario: Student specs Parcelo’s privacy center (the Ch 21-J product).

Example (passing excerpt):

  • Case J matrix; IA tree: Settings → Privacy & data → {Download my data, Delete my account, Manage consent}.
  • Hard confirm spec: consequences screen with erased-vs-retained two-column list (“invoices retained 7 years — tax law”); typed confirm; email receipt “ref DR-5521”; status timeline Requested → Processing → Done (“by Aug 14, 2026”).
  • Grace window: policy supports 30 days → copy discloses it explicitly; the submission notes that if policy had no grace window, the copy must not invent one.
  • Session timeout on export: warn + extend at T−2:00.
  • Fraud gate carries the Case F accessible alternative (3.3.8 AA).
  • Contrast-with-Case-C paragraph: “Document delete maps Soft/Quarantine/Hard by blast radius; account erase is legally Hard regardless of how small it feels — a 5-second undo toast here is a compliance defect, not a UX choice.”
  • Ch 24 section G rows filled; plain-language Error Summary for failed identity challenges.

Measure (plan): time-to-complete export/delete · “how do I delete/export” tickets · incomplete-request rate.

Rejected (auto-fail per brief): Soft-toast account delete; buried delete link; puzzle-only gate; reused file-delete strings.

Why it passes: Copy is pinned to legal reality in both directions (no over-promise, no dark-pattern under-promise) — the case’s core discipline.

Ch 25.6 — Capstone scoring sheet + revision loop — Example

Concept: Per-exercise scoring against the textbook rubric; pass >90 weighted; revision loop on failure. Ch 25 scoring sheet.

Scenario: A student’s first Capstone 3 submission is scored by two peers + one lead (averaged).

Example (filled sheet, round 1):

Criterion Weight Score (1–100) Note
Accuracy 20 94 Undo classes correct; 2.5.8 AA floor cited correctly (24×24 vs 44 craft)
Completeness 25 82 Missing: partial-failure recovery spec; denied state absent
Pedagogical clarity 15 92 Rejected column present per lens
Tactical specificity 20 90 Row heights, toast durations, token names given
Cross-domain integration 10 88 L7 + --color-action-danger + focus restore tied in one decision

Weighted total 89.0 — FAIL (≤90) 94×.20 + 82×.25 + 92×.15 + 90×.20 + 88×.10 + 91×.10 = 18.8 + 20.5 + 13.8 + 18.0 + 8.8 + 9.1

Revision loop applied: failing criterion = Completeness → repair with numbers/rejects/measures: add the 297/312 partial-failure spec (kept successes, per-row reasons, “Review 15 failed” filter) and the denied-state copy (“You don’t have access to manage these pages” + “Request access”). Re-score round 2: Completeness 82 → 93 adds 11 × 0.25 = +2.75 → weighted 91.75 — PASS.

Why it passes: The loop targets the named failing criterion with concrete artifacts, not prose polish — mirroring the textbook’s own R1 (~88, fail) → R2 (93.2, pass) history.

Chapter 1 — Foundations of Human-Centered Design

Worked examples: See the companion Chapter 1 examples for bad-vs-good scenarios tied to every teachable concept.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Explain why meaning and conceptual models matter more than feature lists in product design.
  2. Distinguish affordances, signifiers, and feedback, and apply each deliberately.
  3. Map gulfs of execution and evaluation in a real interface and propose ways to shrink them.
  4. Design for error using knowledge in the world, forgiveness, and recovery—not blame.
  5. Prioritize design decisions using a safety-first human-centered hierarchy.

Human-centered design begins with a deceptively simple claim: people do not use products; they pursue meaning. A calendar is not a grid of cells. It is a promise that you will show up on time, that a team will align, that a life will feel less chaotic. When designers start from features—“add a share button,” “support dark mode,” “ship AI summaries”—they optimize for inventory. When they start from meaning, they optimize for understanding, trust, and successful action. This chapter establishes the foundations that make that shift practical: conceptual models, the gulfs between intention and outcome, the language of affordances and feedback, and a priority order that keeps safety and recovery ahead of delight.

1.1 Meaning Over Features

A feature is a capability. Meaning is the reason that capability matters in someone’s life. Users rarely invent feature requests from a blank slate; they invent stories of friction. “I can’t tell if this payment went through” is not a request for a toast notification—it is a request for certainty. “I accidentally deleted the wrong client” is not a request for a confirmation dialog—it is a request for forgiveness and reversible history.

Human-centered practice therefore treats features as hypotheses about meaning. Before specifying UI, ask: What is the person trying to accomplish? What must they understand to succeed? What fear or cost makes failure expensive? Those questions expose the job beneath the control. In AI-assisted products, this distinction is especially sharp. Generating text is a feature; producing a draft the user can trust, edit, and attribute is meaning. Autocomplete that invents plausible but wrong facts fails the meaning test even when the feature “works.”

Design implication: Write product stories in the language of outcomes and understanding, then derive features. If a feature cannot be tied to a clearer model, safer action, or better recovery, it is decoration.

1.2 Conceptual Models: What People Think the System Is

Don Norman’s core insight remains current: people act through a conceptual model—their internal story of how the system works. Designers hold a design model; the interface is the bridge. When that bridge lies or stays silent, users invent folklore: “refreshing three times helps,” “don’t touch Advanced or it breaks,” “the AI is smarter if I ask nicely.”

Callout — Norman’s fuller picture (and this book’s local policy)

Norman’s account is richer than “conceptual model” alone. It includes the design model (what designers intend), the system image (what the product actually communicates through behavior and UI), and the user’s conceptual model (what people infer). Misalignment among those three—not merely “bad labels”—is a primary source of folklore. Norman also frames interaction through the seven stages of action (goal → plan → specify → perform → perceive → interpret → compare), which maps closely to the gulfs of execution and evaluation. The priority hierarchy in §1.6 is this book’s local decision policy for colliding goals; it is practice scaffolding, not a claim that Norman ranked safety → delight that way.

A good conceptual model is coherent, limited, and teachable. Spreadsheets work because cells, formulas, and absolute references form a stable story. Direct manipulation of files in a folder works because location and naming map to physical metaphors—imperfectly, but usefully. Modal editors and invisible background sync often fail because the model (“what is selected?”, “what is saved?”) is incomplete.

On mobile and in AI surfaces, models must be even more explicit. Is the assistant editing my document or suggesting a draft? Is offline mode queued locally or lost? State labels and durable metaphors matter more than visual polish. The designer’s job is not to make users think like engineers; it is to make the system think like people—consistently enough that learning transfers.

1.3 Gulfs of Execution and Evaluation

Norman describes two distances that separate people from successful interaction.

The gulf of execution is the gap between what the user intends and what actions the system makes available or discoverable. If the intention is “stop this subscription,” but the only path is buried under billing → account → manage → cancel → survey, the gulf is wide. If a destructive action looks identical to a safe one, the gulf is not only wide—it is dangerous.

The gulf of evaluation is the gap between the system’s state and the user’s ability to perceive and interpret it. A spinner with no progress, a silent save, or an AI reply with no source or confidence cue leaves people guessing: Did it work? Is it done? Can I trust this?

Closing both gulfs is the everyday craft of interaction design. Shrink execution by matching controls to intentions, offering clear paths, and reducing hidden steps. Shrink evaluation by making state visible, feedback timely, and outcomes interpretable. In 2020s products—especially those with async jobs, push notifications, and generative outputs—evaluation failures are as common as execution failures. People click the right thing and still do not know what happened.

1.4 Affordances, Signifiers, Feedback, and Knowledge in the World

An affordance is a relationship between an object’s properties and an actor’s capabilities: a button affords pressing; a list affords scrolling; a text field affords typing. Affordances are not decorations—they are possibilities for action. A signifier communicates where that action is available: underlines, chevrons, cursor changes, haptic hints, “pull to refresh” teaching moments. Many modern interfaces fail not because they lack affordances, but because they lack signifiers—flat icons that look identical whether interactive or inert.

Feedback closes the loop: it tells the user that the system registered an action and how the state changed. Feedback can be visual, auditory, haptic, or linguistic. Absence of feedback is not minimalism; it is silence that forces people to probe nervously.

Norman also distinguishes knowledge in the head from knowledge in the world. Experts can carry complex shortcuts mentally; most people cannot and should not have to. Put structure in the world: labels, defaults, visible constraints, progress, breadcrumbs, undo. Password managers, passwordless auth, and inline validation are all ways of moving fragile knowledge out of memory and into the environment. Designing for error starts here: assume distraction, interruption, and imperfect recall—especially on phones, in multitasking, and when AI suggestions compete for attention.

1.5 Design for Error: Blame the System, Not the Person

Error is not a character flaw; it is a predictable outcome of complex tools used under pressure. Human-centered design treats slips (wrong action, right intention) and mistakes (wrong intention, coherent action) as design inputs.

Effective error design includes: constraints that prevent illegal states; clear undo; non-destructive defaults; reversible deletes; explicit confirmation only when recovery is hard or costly; and messages that explain what happened, why it matters, and what to do next—never “Error 500” as a lifestyle. Confirmation theater—dialogs that train users to click OK without reading—creates the illusion of safety while destroying attention. Prefer forgiveness (undo, trash, version history) when the cost of recovery is low; reserve hard gates for irreversible, high-stakes actions (wiring money, deleting a production database, sharing health data).

1.6 A Priority Hierarchy for Human-Centered Decisions

When goals collide, use an explicit order of precedence:

  1. Safety — Prevent irreversible harm, data loss, privacy breaches, and accessibility barriers that exclude people from critical tasks.
  2. Model and recovery — Make the conceptual model clear; make mistakes reversible and states understandable.
  3. Inclusion — Design for diverse abilities, languages, devices, bandwidth, and contexts of use.
  4. Outcomes — Help people complete meaningful goals efficiently and with confidence.
  5. Systems — Align with platform conventions, performance budgets, and operational reality.
  6. Delight — Add pleasure only after the layers above are solid.

Critical-path accessibility failures that block task completion are Safety (#1) when they cause exclusion from an essential action; broader inclusive craft and co-creation sit in Inclusion (#3).

Delight without safety is marketing. Motion without feedback is noise. AI cleverness without a recoverable model is risk dressed as innovation.

Principles callout

  • Design for meaning first; features are hypotheses about meaning.
  • Teach one coherent conceptual model; silence invites folklore.
  • Shrink gulfs of execution and evaluation on every critical path.
  • Use affordances for possibility, signifiers for discoverability, feedback for certainty.
  • Put knowledge in the world; design for error and distraction.
  • Prefer forgiveness over confirmation theater.
  • Prioritize safety → model/recovery → inclusion → outcomes → systems → delight.

Practice Exercises

  1. Meaning audit. Pick a settings screen with five or more toggles. For each control, write one sentence of meaning (what life outcome it protects or enables). Flag any control that only describes a mechanism.
  2. Gulf mapping. Observe someone complete a cancel-or-refund flow (or walk it yourself). List every moment of execution gulf (unclear next action) and evaluation gulf (unclear result). Propose one change per gulf.
  3. Error redesign. Find a product error message that blames the user or reveals nothing actionable. Rewrite it using: what happened, why it matters, what to do next, and whether undo or retry is available.

Anti-Patterns

  • Feature stacking without a shared conceptual model, producing a toolkit no one can narrate.
  • Mystery meat navigation and unlabeled icons that rely on tribal knowledge.
  • Silent success (save, send, generate) with no perceivable state change.
  • Confirmation theater on low-stakes actions that trains people to dismiss dialogs.
  • Expert-only knowledge buried in docs instead of constraints, defaults, and inline guidance.
  • Delight-first animations or AI flourishes that obscure status, delay feedback, or hide failure.

Further Reading

  • Don Norman, The Design of Everyday Things (revised edition)—conceptual models, gulfs, affordances, and error.
  • Alan Cooper, Robert Reimann, David Cronin, & Christopher Noessel, About Face—goal-directed design and interaction principles.
  • Bill Verplank, interaction design sketches and “do/feel/know” framing (lectures and notes).
  • Dan Saffer, Microinteractions—triggers, rules, feedback, loops, and modes.
  • WCAG and platform HIG (Apple, Material, Fluent)—modern signifiers, feedback, and inclusion baselines.

Chapter 2 — Interaction Design: Behavior, Flows, and Feedback

Worked examples: See the companion Chapter 2 examples for bad-vs-good scenarios tied to every teachable concept.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Describe closed-loop interaction using Do / Feel / Know and apply it to screens and microinteractions.
  2. Choose between modes and modeless design, and apply direct manipulation where it clarifies action.
  3. Specify complete UI states (empty through locked and queued) for any asynchronous flow.
  4. Design navigation, forms, selection, notifications, and motion as feedback systems—not decoration.
  5. Decide when undo suffices and when version history is required for recovery and trust.

If Chapter 1 explained why people struggle with products, this chapter explains how interactions behave over time. Interaction design is the craft of sequences: what people do, what they feel in response, and what they come to know about the system. It spans microinteractions lasting a second and journeys lasting weeks. In contemporary products—mobile apps, collaborative editors, AI copilots, and offline-first tools—behavior is rarely a single click. It is a closed loop of triggers, rules, feedback, and modes, operating across incomplete and recovering states.

2.1 Closed-Loop Interaction and Do / Feel / Know

Bill Verplank’s compact framing remains one of the best teaching tools in the field: every interaction can be examined as Do, Feel, and Know.

  • Do — What actions are available? How does the person initiate change?
  • Feel — What sensory or emotional response does the system return (motion, sound, haptic, copy tone)?
  • Know — What understanding of state, consequence, and next step does the person leave with?

A loop that only supports Do without Feel is mute. A loop that Feel without Know is theatrical. Closed-loop design insists that action produces perceptible response, and response produces accurate knowledge. This is the operational form of shrinking Norman’s gulfs: execution lives in Do; evaluation lives in Feel and Know.

Dan Saffer’s microinteraction anatomy makes the loop concrete: a trigger (manual or system) initiates behavior; rules determine what happens; feedback communicates progress and result; loops and modes define repetition, timing, and whether the system is in a temporary condition (editing, recording, offline). Designing a “like,” a pull-to-refresh, or an AI “regenerate” is not inventing a widget—it is specifying this chain end to end. If rules are invisible (“sometimes it auto-saves”), users cannot form a stable model. If feedback is late or ambiguous, Know collapses.

2.2 Modes, Modeless Design, and Direct Manipulation

A mode is a temporary condition in which the same input means something different. Drawing tools, caps lock, “selection mode” for bulk delete, and voice-recording states are modes. Modes are powerful and dangerous: they multiply capability while multiplying opportunity for mode errors (“I typed a novel in the wrong field because focus was elsewhere”).

Prefer modeless design when possible: make actions visible, scoped, and reversible without requiring people to remember “which mode am I in?” When modes are necessary—as in cameras, editors, or multi-select—make them loud: persistent banners, distinct chrome, modal constraints that are hard to miss, and easy escape (Esc, Cancel, Done). Never rely on a tiny icon color change alone.

Direct manipulation, Cooper’s and Shneiderman’s shared inheritance, keeps objects visible and actions continuous: drag a file, resize a crop, reorder a list by touch. It shrinks the gulf of execution by letting people act on representations rather than through abstract commands. Direct manipulation still needs feedback (snap, highlight, ghost) and forgiveness (undo reorder). On touch and AI canvases, “direct” can mean pointing at a region and saying “make this shorter”—still an object-centered act if selection and result remain visible and editable.

2.3 State Completeness: Designing the Whole Truth

Most interface bugs are missing states. A professional interaction designer specifies not only the happy path but the full state set for every meaningful object and flow:

State Design question
Empty What does first-run or zero-data teach and invite?
Partial How is incomplete work shown and resumed?
Loading Is progress determinate? Can the user leave safely?
Success What changed, and what is the next useful action?
Failed What failed, why (in human terms), and how to recover?
Stale Is this data old? Can the user refresh or trust a timestamp?
Locked Who/what holds the lock, and how does wait or request access work?
Queued local Is the action saved offline and pending sync—distinct from “done”?

AI and mobile make stale, failed, and queued_local especially important. A generated answer may be outdated relative to live data. A send may succeed on device and fail on server. Treating “queued” as “success” trains false confidence; treating “loading” as infinite spinner trains abandonment. State completeness is how recovery and model clarity become visible in the UI—not merely in a requirements doc.

2.4 Navigation, Wayfinding, and Search

Information architecture (IA) is the structure of meaning; wayfinding is how people know where they are, what else exists, and how to get back. Labels, hierarchies, breadcrumbs, tabs, and persistent landmarks are not chrome—they are orientation. Search complements browsing: browsing teaches the model of the domain; search serves known-item and exploratory retrieval. Poor IA cannot be fixed by a search box alone, just as poor search cannot be fixed by deeper menus. Detailed IA methods (card sorting, tree testing, taxonomy design) are taught in Chapter 5B—this section covers interaction implications of wayfinding only.

For complex products, design landmarks (Home, Inbox, Library), scopes (project, account, workspace), and escapes (back, cancel, close) as first-class behaviors. On mobile, depth is expensive; prefer progressive disclosure and clear parent–child relationships over deep stacks that hide context.

2.5 Forms, Complex Input, Selection, and Bulk Actions

Forms are conversations with constraints. Good form design sequences fields by task, validates inline when helpful, explains errors next to causes, and never clears user input on failure. Complex input—dates, money, permissions, multi-step onboarding—should expose the model: what is required, what is optional, what is reversible. Defaults are ethics: they encode assumed norms.

Selection and bulk actions need explicit mode cues, clear counts (“3 selected”), and destructive differentiation. Bulk delete without undo is a trust-ending event. Prefer select → review → act → undo toast for moderate risk; require typed confirmation or staged deletion only for high-stakes irreversibility.

2.6 Notifications, Interruptions, Motion, Undo, and History

Notifications interrupt Do/Feel/Know loops in other tasks. Design them by urgency and recoverability: can this wait for inbox? Does it need action or only awareness? Bundling, quiet hours, and user-controlled channels are inclusion and safety practices, not niceties.

Motion and timing are feedback channels. Duration, easing, and choreography should answer: Where did this go? What changed? Is this waiting or done? Motion that exists only to impress widens the gulf of evaluation by delaying truth. Treat timing as latency-band heuristics (Ch. 8)—not absolute physiology laws: aim for immediate acknowledgment (~100–300 ms) for direct actions; polite-wait progress (~300–1000 ms) when work is real; async/out-of-band patterns when delays exceed a few seconds; skeleton states that preserve layout to reduce jarring shifts.

Undo restores a recent action; version history restores meaning across time and collaborators. Use undo for slips and local mistakes. Use history when work accumulates, when multiple people edit, or when AI transformations need audit (“what did we change?”). Confirmation theater is a poor substitute for either.

Principles callout

  • Every interaction is a closed loop: Do → Feel → Know.
  • Specify microinteractions as trigger → rules → feedback → loops/modes.
  • Prefer modeless design; when modes are required, make them unmistakable and escapable.
  • Design the full state set—including stale, locked, and queued_local.
  • Treat navigation, forms, and notifications as orientation and interruption systems.
  • Use motion as feedback; use undo for slips and history for durable recovery.
  • Keep the priority ladder: safety → model/recovery → inclusion → outcomes → systems → delight.

├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

│ understanding forming a continuous cycle.                   │
│ Do / Feel / Know — Verplank framing of action, response,    │
│ and resulting understanding.                                │

Practice Exercises

  1. Microinteraction spec. Choose one control (favorite, send, regenerate, offline sync). Write trigger, rules, feedback, loops/modes, and the Know statement a user should leave with. Identify missing states.
  2. Mode hunt. In an app you use daily, list every mode. For each, note how the mode is signified and how users exit. Redesign the worst mode error you can imagine preventing.
  3. State matrix. For a collaborative document with AI suggestions and offline editing, fill a table for empty / partial / loading / success / failed / stale / locked / queued_local. Sketch one UI treatment per cell that makes the model explicit.

Anti-Patterns

  • Open-loop UI — actions with no Feel/Know (tap void, hope).
  • Invisible modes — selection or recording states marked only by subtle tint.
  • Happy-path-only mocks — shipping without empty, failed, stale, or queued_local.
  • Search as IA substitute — dumping structure into a query box.
  • Interruptive spam — notifications that demand attention for low-urgency events.
  • Motion as mascara — animation that delays status or hides failure.
  • Undo theater — short toasts for irreversible bulk or AI overwrites without history.

Further Reading

  • Bill Verplank, “Interaction Design Sketchbook” and Do/Feel/Know lectures.
  • Dan Saffer, Microinteractions (trigger–rules–feedback–loops/modes).
  • Alan Cooper et al., About Face—direct manipulation, modes, and goal-directed flows.
  • Ben Shneiderman, direct manipulation principles; related HCI surveys on continuous representation.
  • Nielsen Norman Group articles on form design, empty states, and undo; platform guidelines on motion and notifications (Material Motion, Apple HIG).

Chapter 3 — Inclusive Design and Accessibility

Worked examples: See the companion Chapter 3 examples for bad-vs-good scenarios tied to every teachable concept.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Reframe disability as a mismatch between people and designed environments rather than a fixed personal deficit.
  2. Apply the Recognize → Learn → Solve cycle so that designing for one excluded person extends value to many.
  3. Use Persona Spectrum thinking (permanent, temporary, situational) to expand design constraints without inventing fictional “average users.”
  4. Map WCAG 2.2’s POUR principles and COGA patterns into concrete product decisions, including accessible authentication (SC 3.3.8).
  5. Practice Equity-Centered Community Design (ECCD) as co-decision, not consult-and-discard research.
  6. Design for offline use, shared devices, literacy variation, internationalization beyond RTL, motion sensitivity, media captions, color/contrast process, socioeconomic and metered-data constraints, and assistive-technology (AT) testing.
  7. Recognize legal baselines (ADA, EAA) and AI-related exclusion risks as product strategy concerns, not only compliance tickets.

3.1 Disability as Mismatch

Inclusive design begins with a definitional shift. Disability is not primarily a medical property of a body; it is a mismatch between what a person can do and what a product, place, or system demands. Stairs mismatch a wheelchair user; a CAPTCHA that requires sight mismatches a blind user; a checkout that assumes uninterrupted broadband mismatches someone on a prepaid mobile plan.

This framing matters because it relocates responsibility. If the problem is “the user’s limitation,” teams optimize for exceptions and charity. If the problem is mismatch, teams redesign the environment. Microsoft’s Inclusive Design toolkit and Kat Holmes’s Mismatch argue the same point from product practice: exclusion is designed in, and therefore can be designed out.

Mismatch also scales. A one-handed interaction pattern helps someone with a permanent limb difference, someone with a temporary cast, and someone holding a child while navigating an airport. The constraint is shared; the medical story is not. Inclusive design treats that shared constraint as a design brief.

3.2 Recognize → Learn → Solve: One Extends to Many

Holmes’s method is a deliberate cycle:

Recognize where people are excluded—by observation, complaints, analytics drop-offs, support tickets, and community partnership. Exclusion often hides in “edge cases” that are actually common contexts: glare outdoors, noisy kitchens, shared family phones, low literacy, intermittent connectivity.

Learn from the people at the extremes of the Persona Spectrum. Do not average them away. Extreme users reveal friction that middle-of-the-bell-curve testing softens into silence.

Solve for that person first, then ask who else benefits. A high-contrast mode built for low vision helps night drivers. Transcripts built for deaf users help search indexing and non-native speakers. Offline drafts built for unreliable networks help anyone on a subway.

Ethical and business arguments often align here—exclusion is rarely “niche,” and inclusive fixes can widen who succeeds—but they do not automatically converge. Inclusive work can cost time, conflict with growth tactics, or require saying no to stakeholders. Treat the multiplier as a frequent outcome of genuine “solve for one” empathy work, not as a guarantee that ethics and revenue always point the same way.

3.3 Persona Spectrum: Permanent, Temporary, Situational

Personas that describe “busy professionals who love productivity” rarely force hard choices. The Persona Spectrum does. For each capability (vision, hearing, mobility, cognition, speech, reach, attention), consider:

  • Permanent — e.g., blindness, deafness, dyslexia, limb difference.
  • Temporary — e.g., cataract surgery, broken arm, concussion, ear infection.
  • Situational — e.g., bright sunlight, loud café, one free hand, language unfamiliarity, driving.

A spectrum table is not a substitute for people; it is a constraint generator. If your product requires precise drag-and-drop with a mouse, you have mismatched permanent motor disabilities, temporary injuries, and situational mobile contexts at once. Redesigning for keyboard and large-touch targets is not “accessibility afterthought”—it is spectrum-aware product quality.

3.4 WCAG 2.2 POUR as Product Language

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 organize success criteria under POUR:

  • Perceivable — Information and UI components must be presentable in ways users can perceive (text alternatives, captions, adaptable layouts, distinguishable contrast and audio).
  • Operable — UI and navigation must be usable (keyboard access, enough time, seizure-safe motion, navigable structure, input modalities beyond pointer precision).
  • Understandable — Information and operation must be understandable (readable language, predictable behavior, input assistance).
  • Robust — Content must work with current and future user agents, including assistive technologies (valid markup, name/role/value).

Treat POUR as a product vocabulary in critiques, not only an auditor’s checklist. When a designer presents a motion-heavy onboarding, ask: Is it Perceivable without motion? Operable without a mouse? Understandable under cognitive load? Robust with a screen reader?

Accessible authentication (SC 3.3.8) is a concrete WCAG 2.2 addition with outsized product impact. It limits cognitive function tests (puzzles, memorizing/transcribing, object recognition) as authentication barriers unless an alternative exists. Password managers, passkeys, copy-paste of credentials, and non-puzzle second factors are not “nice-to-haves”—they are accessibility features that also reduce login abandonment.

3.5 COGA Patterns as Ship Craft

The W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force (COGA) publishes complementary guidance—Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities—and related design patterns. COGA is not a set of WCAG success criteria (SCs); it helps teams operationalize cognitive inclusion alongside POUR, without substituting for WCAG conformance claims.

Useful COGA-oriented craft includes:

  • Clear purpose on each page; avoid surprise navigation.
  • Consistent layout and controls; reduce working-memory load.
  • Plain language; define jargon; support multiple literacy levels.
  • Help in context; undo and error recovery that does not punish.
  • Chunked tasks; progress that can be saved and resumed.
  • Minimal distractions; control over timeouts and interruptions.

COGA is where “understandable” stops being abstract. A settings page with fifty unlabeled icons fails cognitive-usability guidance even if contrast ratios pass. Inclusive teams review flows for cognitive cost the way they review for visual polish.

3.6 ECCD: Co-Decision, Not Token Consultation

Equity-Centered Community Design (ECCD) insists that communities most affected by exclusion participate in decision-making, not only in interviews that validate a roadmap already frozen. Co-decision means:

  • Shared problem framing and success criteria.
  • Compensation and credit for community labor.
  • Power to change scope, not only provide quotes for a slide.
  • Feedback loops after launch—accessibility is maintained, not “shipped once.”

Without ECCD, inclusive design becomes extractive: teams learn from disabled people, then optimize for stakeholders who never feel the mismatch. With ECCD, accessibility acceptance criteria are co-owned.

3.7 Contexts Beyond the Desktop Ideal

Offline and unreliable networks. Progressive enhancement, local drafts, clear sync states, and non-blocking queues matter for rural users, travelers, and crisis contexts. An “always online” assumption is a socioeconomic and geographic exclusion.

Shared devices. Family tablets, library computers, and workplace kiosks require careful session design, privacy screens for sensitive content, easy sign-out, and avoidance of “remember me forever” defaults that expose personal data.

Kyōyōhin (共用品). Japanese inclusive practice emphasizes products good for everyone in ordinary use—not segregated “special” goods. A ramp that is also a stroller path is kyōyōhin thinking. In software: captions that also enable mute viewing; voice input that also speeds hands-busy use.

Literacy. Forms, errors, and legal copy must be readable. Icons alone are not universal. Support scanning, examples, and multilingual plain language.

Internationalization beyond RTL. Locale is more than flipping layout for Arabic or Hebrew. Handle locale-aware dates, currencies, address formats, name order and length, pluralization rules, sorting, and culturally meaningful imagery. A “first name / last name” Western form mismatches many naming systems worldwide.

Motion and vestibular safety vs. photosensitive seizure risk. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. Large parallax, autoplaying zooms, and infinite carousels can trigger vestibular symptoms (nausea, dizziness, disorientation)—distinct from photosensitive seizure triggers (flashing, strobing, high-contrast flicker). Design for both: reduce motion for vestibular safety; avoid flashing content and follow WCAG seizure guidance for photosensitive users. Provide pause and non-motion alternatives.

Media captions and transcripts. Captions are for deaf and hard-of-hearing users and for anyone who cannot play sound. Include speaker identification and non-speech information when meaningful. Audio descriptions matter for visual-only content.

Socioeconomic and metered data. Compress media, avoid autoplay video, offer low-data modes, and do not force app downloads when a light web flow would suffice. Data cost is an accessibility and equity issue.

3.8 Color, Contrast, and Process

Color accessibility is a process, not a palette:

  1. Design meaning with redundant cues (text, shape, pattern)—never color alone.
  2. Check contrast for text and meaningful non-text UI against WCAG thresholds early, not at handoff.
  3. Test in grayscale and with common color-vision simulations.
  4. Document tokens that meet contrast so engineers do not invent inaccessible variants.
  5. Recheck after brand refreshes; marketing gradients frequently break AA/AAA.

AA vs AAA (briefly). WCAG Level AA is the usual product and legal baseline referenced in procurement and settlements; Level AAA is a stricter set of criteria that is valuable where feasible but is not always practical as a whole-site bar. Aim for AA on the critical path; adopt AAA criteria selectively where they clearly reduce harm without breaking the experience.

Contrast is necessary but not sufficient: focus states, hit targets, and text resizing (up to 200% without loss of content) complete the picture.

3.9 Legal Baselines: ADA and EAA

Law sets floors, not ceilings. In the United States, treat ADA digital accessibility as a risk floor: related case law and settlements often push toward WCAG-referenced remediation, but doctrine for websites and apps remains unsettled in important respects—do not treat “ADA = WCAG AA everywhere” as settled statute. In the European Union, the European Accessibility Act (EAA) expands obligations for many products and services, with enforcement timelines that make accessibility a release-gate concern for companies selling into the EU.

Legal risk is real, but fear-based compliance produces brittle checklists. Strong teams use law as a minimum bar and inclusive design as the quality bar—because lawsuit avoidance does not automatically produce usable experiences for AT users.

3.10 Assistive Technology Testing Ladder

Build an escalating ladder:

  1. Automated scans — catch missing alt text, label issues, contrast failures; never treat green scores as done.
  2. Keyboard-only — tab order, focus visibility, no keyboard traps.
  3. Screen reader smoke tests — VoiceOver/TalkBack/NVDA on critical paths (auth, checkout, core task).
  4. Zoom and reflow — 200–400% zoom; mobile orientation.
  5. Speech and switch where relevant.
  6. Disabled user testing with compensated participants—preferred for high-stakes flows.

Automation without human AT testing is theater. Human testing without fixing systemic design system issues is endless whack-a-mole.

3.11 AI Exclusion Risks

Generative AI introduces new mismatches: models trained on biased data; interfaces that assume fluent typed English; voice agents that fail non-native accents; image generators that erase disability representation; automated moderation that flags assistive communication; “AI summaries” that omit critical accessibility content; captcha-like bot checks that block AT. Inclusive AI practice requires human override, accessible controls for AI features, transparent confidence, and evaluation with diverse users—not only accuracy benchmarks on majority datasets.

Key Terms

Mismatch; Persona Spectrum; POUR; WCAG 2.2; COGA; ECCD; kyōyōhin; SC 3.3.8 (accessible authentication); AT testing ladder; EAA; ADA.

Principles

  1. Disability is designed mismatch; redesign the system.
  2. Solve for one extreme; extend to many.
  3. Permanent / temporary / situational are equal design constraints.
  4. POUR (WCAG) is a conformance shipping bar; COGA is complementary cognitive-usability guidance—not WCAG SCs—but still craft you ship against.
  5. Co-decide with excluded communities.
  6. Context (offline, shared device, literacy, locale, data cost) is accessibility.
  7. Law is the floor; inclusion is the product bar.
  8. Test with AT and people, not only scanners.
  9. AI can scale exclusion unless governed inclusively.

Exercises

Exercise 1 — Spectrum brief. Pick one core task in a product you know. Build a Persona Spectrum table for vision, mobility, and cognition. List three mismatches and one redesign that helps permanent, temporary, and situational users simultaneously.

Exercise 2 — Auth audit. Evaluate a login/signup flow against WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8 and COGA patterns. Propose an alternative that supports password managers/passkeys and removes cognitive tests without weakening security goals.

Exercise 3 — AT ladder. Run steps 1–3 of the AT testing ladder on a public page. Document five issues by POUR category and prioritize fixes by user impact, not by ease.

Anti-Patterns

  • “We’ll add accessibility at the end.”
  • Accessibility as a segregated “special mode” that diverges forever from the main product.
  • Color-only status (red/green) without text or icons.
  • Motion as mandatory brand expression with no reduced-motion path.
  • CAPTCHA- or puzzle-gated auth as default.
  • Interviewing disabled users for inspiration quotes while excluding them from decisions.
  • Green automated a11y scores as a ship gate with no keyboard/AT verification.
  • Assuming high literacy, always-online, private personal devices.
  • Treating i18n as string translation only.
  • Shipping AI features that cannot be operated or understood via AT.

Further Reading

  • Kat Holmes, Mismatch: How Inclusion Shapes Design
  • Microsoft Inclusive Design manuals and Persona Spectrum materials
  • W3C, WCAG 2.2; WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices; COGA Design Patterns
  • Equity-Centered Community Design field guide (Creative Reaction Lab)
  • European Accessibility Act guidance; ADA digital accessibility case summaries
  • Apple Human Interface Guidelines — Accessibility; Android Accessibility help
  • World Wide Web Consortium guidance on making content usable for people with cognitive and learning disabilities

Chapter 4 — Product UX Strategy and Continuous Discovery

Worked examples: See the companion Chapter 4 examples for bad-vs-good scenarios tied to every teachable concept.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Frame product work with Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD) so strategy targets progress customers seek, not feature lists.
  2. Prefer outcomes over outputs and connect UX work to north-star metrics and input metrics across the product lifecycle.
  3. Practice continuous discovery, Opportunity Solution Trees (OST), dual-track agile, and the Research → Assumptions → Feedback (RAF) loop.
  4. Distinguish activation, retention, churn, and expansion—and design for monetization consent rather than dark-pattern revenue.
  5. Navigate B2B buyer-versus-user tension, PLG versus sales-led motions, experiment governance, research ops, and instrumentation.
  6. Use competitive teardown and support-as-product-surface as strategic inputs, not vanity monitoring.

4.1 Strategy Starts With Jobs, Not Roadmaps

Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD) is most closely associated with Clayton Christensen’s work (including Competing Against Luck) and with Anthony Ulwick’s outcome-driven innovation lineage. People “hire” products to make progress in a circumstance. A Job-to-be-Done is not a demographic and not a feature request. It is a stable intent under constraints—“When I commute on unreliable transit, I want to arrive prepared for my first meeting, so I don’t lose credibility.”

A related form—the job story (“When… I want to… so I can…”)—is a useful writing format for opportunities and stories; it is not identical to the full JTBD research method. Teresa Torres’s Continuous Discovery Habits is a discovery operating system (cadence, interviewing, OSTs), not the origin of JTBD. Marty Cagan’s product model shares the premise that teams own problems and progress, not feature inventories.

UX strategy fails when it catalogs screens. It succeeds when it clarifies: What progress are we hired for? What competing hires exist (including inertia and spreadsheets)? What anxieties and habits block switching? Feature roadmaps without JTBD become output factories: shipped volume rises while customer progress stalls.

4.2 Outcome Over Output

Outputs are artifacts: a redesigned checkout, three experiments, a design system release. Outcomes are meaningful changes in customer or business behavior: time-to-value drops; retention of a segment rises; support contacts for a task fall; expansion revenue grows because the product earned trust.

Teams that celebrate outputs reward busyness. Teams that manage to outcomes accept that the right response to a failed experiment is learning, not a quieter failure buried in a changelog. Cagan’s “empowered product teams” language is outcome language: the team owns a problem, not a backlog of predetermined solutions.

North-star thinking operationalizes this. A north star metric reflects delivered value (e.g., weekly active projects completed—not merely logins). Input metrics are leading indicators the team can influence (activation rate, time-to-first-success, invite acceptance). Vanity metrics (raw downloads, pageviews) inflate egos and starve strategy.

4.3 Continuous Discovery

Teresa Torres defines continuous discovery as weekly touchpoints with customers to inform decisions—by the team that builds the product, not a remote research guild that throws insights over a wall. Discovery is not a phase before delivery; it is a parallel cadence.

Cadence elements typically include:

  • Interviewing to understand opportunities (not to validate pet solutions).
  • Mapping opportunities and solutions visually.
  • Testing assumptions with the smallest honest experiment.
  • Feeding evidence into delivery priorities continuously.

Without continuous discovery, dual-track agile collapses into dual-track theater: “discovery” becomes stakeholder workshops, and delivery ships the HiPPO’s preference.

4.4 Opportunity Solution Trees (OST)

An Opportunity Solution Tree connects a desired outcome to:

  1. The outcome (clear, measurable).
  2. Opportunity spaces (customer needs, pains, desires uncovered in research).
  3. Solutions under each opportunity.
  4. Experiments under each solution to test assumption risk.

OSTs fight two failure modes: solution-first roadmaps (jumping to UI) and opportunity sprawl (endless insights with no compare-and-choose). Good OSTs make trade-offs visible: which opportunity, if solved, most moves the outcome? Which assumption, if wrong, kills the solution?

UX strategists use OSTs in critiques: “Show me the opportunity this prototype addresses, and the riskiest assumption it carries.”

4.5 Dual-Track and the RAF Loop

Dual-track agile runs discovery and delivery in parallel. Discovery reduces uncertainty about value and usability; delivery builds production-quality increments. The tracks inform each other: delivery reveals operational constraints; discovery prevents building the wrong thing faster.

A practical loop is RAF — Research → Assumptions → Feedback:

  • Research — interviews, observation, support mining, analytics patterns.
  • Assumptions — explicit bets (desirability, viability, feasibility, usability, ethics).
  • Feedback — gather signal against the outcome; update the OST; decide persevere, pivot, or kill.

Experiments (prototypes, concierge tests, A/B tests, carefully honest fake doors) are the primary mechanism inside Feedback/testing—not a fourth letter of the acronym. RAF is experiment governance in miniature: every test has a learning goal, a success/failure threshold, and an owner. Ungoverned experimentation creates metric thrash and user distrust.

4.6 Lifecycle Metrics: Activation, Retention, Churn, Expansion

Strategy must locate UX investment in the lifecycle:

  • Activation — users reach a first moment of value. UX owns clarity of onboarding, empty states that teach, and time-to-value. Premature paywalls and tour tooltips are not activation strategy.
  • Retention — users return and succeed repeatedly. Habit loops must be earned through reliable value, not notification spam.
  • Churn — users leave. Exit surveys and cohort analysis reveal whether churn is product failure, sales mismatch, or lifecycle completion. Designing win-back without fixing the job is cosmetic.
  • Expansion — users deepen usage or spend. In ethical products, expansion follows new jobs served well—not dark patterns that hide cancellation.

Map journeys to these stages. A beautiful marketing site with a confusing first-run experience is a strategy bug: acquisition without activation burns trust and CAC.

4.7 Monetization Consent

Revenue models are UX. Monetization consent means users understand what they pay, why, what they get, and how to leave. Contrast with dark patterns: hidden fees, obstructed cancel flows, guilt screens, forced continuity without clear reminders.

Consent-aligned monetization tends to improve retention quality even if it reduces short-term conversion tricks. In regulated contexts and brand-sensitive markets, consent is also risk management. Strategically, price packaging should map to jobs and segments—not to which button color converted 0.3% better in isolation from trust metrics.

4.8 B2B: Buyer Versus User

In B2B, the buyer (economic decision-maker, IT, security, procurement) and the user (daily operator) often diverge. Products that win RFPs but torment users accumulate “shelfware.” Products that delight users but fail security review never enter the account.

UX strategy must design for both surfaces: admin and compliance experiences as first-class products; end-user workflows that create internal champions; evidence (case studies, usage dashboards) that help buyers justify renewal. Ignoring either side is not “focus”—it is incomplete discovery.

4.9 PLG Versus Sales-Led

Product-led growth (PLG) uses the product as the primary acquisition and expansion engine: self-serve signup, freemium or trial, viral loops, in-product education. Sales-led motions rely on demos, RFPs, and human negotiation.

UX implications differ:

  • PLG demands exceptional activation, empty states, templates, and upgrade moments that feel like help.
  • Sales-led demands demo credibility, configurable enterprise flows, and admin tooling that survives procurement.

Many companies are hybrid. Strategy fails when PLG UX is bolted onto an enterprise backend—or when a sales-led team expects the product to “just be sticky” without investment in self-serve value.

4.10 Experiment Governance, Research Ops, Instrumentation

Experiment governance sets rules: what may be tested on whom; ethical limits (no deceptive fake charges); primary metrics paired with guardrails (accessibility, trust, support volume); duration and peeking policy; documentation of results so orphaned tests do not repeat.

Research ops makes continuous discovery sustainable: participant recruiting, incentives, GDPR/CCPA-aware consent, knowledge repositories, taxonomy of insights, and tooling so PMs/designers can research weekly without chaos.

Instrumentation connects UX to evidence: event taxonomy aligned to jobs and outcomes; funnels that match mental models; qualitative session replay used ethically; dashboards that show input metrics leading the north star. Without instrumentation, OSTs become opinion trees. Without research, dashboards become cargo cult.

4.11 Competitive Teardown and Support as Product Surface

Competitive teardown is structured learning: compare jobs served, activation paths, pricing consent, accessibility posture, and differentiation—not screenshot galleries of UI trends. Ask: Which opportunities do competitors own? Where are they mismatched with users you can serve?

Support is a product surface. Tickets, chat transcripts, and help centers reveal discovery gold and design debt. Deflecting support with unreadable FAQs is not efficiency; reducing contact drivers by fixing the product is strategy. Close the loop: top contact reasons become OST opportunities with owners.

Key Terms

JTBD; outcome vs output; continuous discovery; Opportunity Solution Tree (OST); dual-track agile; RAF; north star / input metrics; activation; retention; churn; expansion; monetization consent; PLG; sales-led; experiment governance; research ops.

Principles

  1. Strategy serves customer progress (jobs), not feature theater.
  2. Manage to outcomes; treat outputs as hypotheses.
  3. Discover continuously alongside delivery.
  4. Compare opportunities before falling in love with solutions.
  5. Instrument what you claim to improve.
  6. Earn activation and retention; do not coerce them.
  7. Monetize with consent; cancel is part of the product.
  8. In B2B, design for buyer and user.
  9. Match UX investment to growth motion (PLG vs sales-led).
  10. Mine support and competitors for opportunities, not vanity.

Exercises

Exercise 1 — JTBD to OST. Write one job story for a product you know. Define an outcome metric and sketch an OST with at least three opportunities, two solutions under one opportunity, and one experiment for the riskiest assumption.

Exercise 2 — Lifecycle diagnosis. Using public or imagined analytics, locate a failure in activation, retention, churn, or expansion. Propose one discovery interview guide and one experiment that tests a single assumption—not a full redesign.

Exercise 3 — Monetization consent review. Audit a paywall, trial, or upgrade flow for clarity of price, value, renewal, and cancellation. Rewrite the UX copy and flow to maximize informed consent while preserving a viable business model; list guardrail metrics.

Anti-Patterns

  • Roadmaps as prioritized solution lists with no outcomes.
  • Quarterly “discovery phases” with no weekly customer contact.
  • A/B testing UI chrome while ignoring job fit.
  • North stars that count logins instead of value.
  • Fake-door tests that punish users without follow-through.
  • Growth hacks that spike activation and destroy trust.
  • B2B UX that ignores admin, security, and procurement journeys.
  • PLG copy on a product that cannot self-serve.
  • Research insights trapped in slide decks nobody can search.
  • Treating support volume as a call-center problem rather than product truth.
  • Competitive “inspiration” that clones UI without comparing jobs.

Further Reading

  • Teresa Torres, Continuous Discovery Habits
  • Marty Cagan, Inspired and Empowered
  • Clayton Christensen et al., Jobs-to-be-Done theory and Competing Against Luck; Anthony Ulwick, outcome-driven innovation / JTBD practice
  • ResearchOps Community practices on scaling research infrastructure
  • Amplitude / Mixpanel / product analytics guides on north star and input metrics
  • Reforge and product-led growth literature on activation and expansion loops
  • Leah Tharin and PLG practitioners on monetization and self-serve UX
  • “Support is a product” operational essays from high-growth SaaS teams; ethical experimentation guides (e.g., avoid dark patterns in growth)

Chapter 5 — Design Systems and Craft at Scale

Worked examples: See the companion Chapter 5 examples for bad-vs-good scenarios tied to every teachable concept.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Describe a design system as layered architecture—from foundation tokens through kits—and explain what belongs at each layer.
  2. Distinguish consistency from flexibility, and decide when a system should constrain versus extend.
  3. Specify component APIs that encode state completeness, content slots, and accessibility by default.
  4. Treat documentation, contribution, and versioning as product work equal to components.
  5. Evaluate system health with measurable signals, and recognize when a system has become a zombie.

5.1 Why Design Systems Exist

A design system is not a component library with a logo. It is the shared language, constraints, and delivery mechanisms that let many teams build coherent product experiences without reinventing interaction grammar on every screen.

At scale, craft fails in predictable ways: buttons diverge by three pixels; “secondary” means something different in billing than in onboarding; dark mode is a late paint job; empty tables ship without empty states; motion is decorative noise. A healthy system prevents these failures by making the right choice the easy choice—and by documenting when deviation is legitimate.

Systems also encode content as interface. Labels, helper text, errors, and empty states are not afterthoughts pasted onto chrome; they are first-class parts of the interaction model. Frost-like atomic discipline, Polaris-style merchant clarity, and Spectrum-style accessibility rigor converge on the same idea: the system owns the contract between intent and presentation.

5.2 Atomic Composition and Semantic Tokens

Atomic composition builds UI from small, stable units: tokens → primitives → patterns → kits. Composition is not a style preference; it is how you keep change blast radius small. If spacing, color, and type are tokens, a density refresh does not require rewriting every card.

Semantic tokens name roles, not paint. Prefer color.bg.surface, color.text.critical, space.stack.md over blue-500 or 16px. Semantics survive rebrands, theming, and dark mode because consumers depend on meaning. Foundations may still hold raw ramps (blue.500), but product code should almost never reference them.

Token layers typically include:

Layer Examples Consumer
Core / palette hue ramps, type scales Foundation authors
Semantic text.primary, border.focus Primitive authors
Component button.bg.primary Rare; prefer semantic

Theming and dark mode are token remaps, not alternate component trees. If dark mode requires forked markup, the system has leaked presentation into structure. Test contrast, elevation, and focus rings under every theme before shipping a palette change.

5.3 Layers: Foundation → Primitives → Patterns → Kits

Healthy systems make layer boundaries explicit.

Foundation. Motion curves, duration tokens, type, color semantics, elevation, grid, iconography rules, content voice guidelines, accessibility baselines. Motion and content belong here—not as “nice-to-haves” bolted onto components later. A duration token without a “when to use” rule is decoration.

Primitives. Buttons, inputs, checkboxes, links, icons, tooltips. Primitives are intentionally boring. Their job is predictable behavior, complete states, and airtight APIs.

Patterns. Form layouts, filter bars, confirmation dialogs, data tables with selection, progressive disclosure. Patterns compose primitives and encode workflow wisdom.

Kits. Domain assemblies for recurring product surfaces: “settings page shell,” “checkout summary,” “admin user row.” Kits accelerate teams without pretending every product is identical.

Crossing layers carelessly creates zombie systems: kits that fork primitives, patterns that hard-code hex values, foundations that no one owns. Layer ownership and review gates matter as much as Figma libraries.

5.4 Consistency Versus Flexibility

Consistency reduces cognitive load; flexibility respects product diversity. The system fails when it becomes either a prison or a suggestion box.

Use strict consistency for: focus behavior, form validation timing, destructive action confirmation, navigation landmarks, error anatomy, table keyboard models.

Use guided flexibility for: page composition, illustration style within brand bounds, optional pattern variants, density modes, locale-specific content length.

A practical rule: if two teams solving the same user job produce incompatible interaction models, the system under-specified the pattern. If two teams solving different jobs are forced into the same layout kit, the system over-specified the kit.

5.5 State Completeness and Component APIs

Every interactive component has a state matrix. Incomplete matrices become production bugs.

Minimum states for most controls: default, hover, focus-visible, active/pressed, disabled, loading, error, empty (where applicable), read-only, selected. For data-bound UI, add: skeleton/loading, zero results, partial failure, offline, permission denied.

Component APIs should express intent, not CSS trivia. Prefer:

  • tone="critical" over className="red"
  • isLoading over hiding the label and hoping
  • content slots (label, helpText, errorMessage) over undocumented children conventions
  • controlled/uncontrolled clarity for form values

API design is UX design for engineers. Breaking changes to props break products; treat them like breaking changes to user-facing flows. Document defaults, accessibility hooks (aria-* wiring), and composition rules (what may wrap what).

Forms and tables deserve library-level investment. They concentrate density, validation, sorting, selection, bulk actions, and keyboard complexity. A system that only ships buttons while leaving tables to tribal knowledge will fragment fastest where users spend the most time.

5.6 Content, Motion, and Docs as Product

Content as interface means microcopy, structure, and hierarchy are specified alongside components. Empty states teach next steps; errors answer what / why / next; labels match user language, not schema names.

Motion as foundation means purposeful transitions: continuity (shared-element navigation), feedback (press, success), and orientation (panel open). Ban ornamental bounce that delays task completion. Prefer reduced-motion alternatives as first-class, not afterthoughts.

Docs-as-product means do docs ship with the same quality bar as components: live examples, do/don’t, accessibility notes, content guidelines, migration guides, and versioned changelogs. If the only truth lives in a Slack thread, you do not have a system—you have folklore.

Figma ↔ code parity is an operational goal, not a slogan. Shared naming, token export pipelines, and “source of truth” agreements (often: tokens and behavior in code; exploration in Figma) prevent design–engineering drift. When parity breaks, measure it: mismatched props, missing states, divergent spacing.

5.7 Contribution, RFCs, and Versioning

A system without a contribution model ossifies or forks.

Typical path: proposal → RFC (problem, options, migration cost, a11y impact) → prototype → review → release notes → adoption metrics. Versioning should be semantic and honest. Deprecations need timelines, codemods when possible, and dual-running guidance.

Gen-UI and AI-assisted layout must be constrained to the system: allowed components, tokenized styles, validated props, banned arbitrary CSS. Unconstrained generation recreates the pre-system chaos at machine speed.

5.8 Health Metrics and Zombie Systems

Track adoption (% of surfaces on current major), contribution latency, documentation freshness, a11y defect rate on system components, theme coverage, and “escape hatch” frequency (!important, one-off CSS, forked buttons).

A zombie system still has a website and a Figma library, but: versions lag years; teams fork silently; docs contradict code; no RFC path; dark mode is broken; nobody owns tokens. Kill or revive deliberately—neglect is the most expensive option.

Key Terms

Atomic composition — Building UI from layered, reusable units with clear ownership.
Semantic token — A design decision named by role/meaning rather than raw value.
