§1.1 Meaning Over Features

Example 1 — Meaning Over Features

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A feature is a capability; meaning is the reason that capability matters in someone’s life. Features are hypotheses about meaning — if a feature cannot be tied to a clearer model, safer action, or better recovery, it is decoration.

Scenario. Lumen, a mobile-first fintech app for freelancers, sees a spike in support tickets: “Did my invoice payment go through?” Average of 214 tickets/week; 41% of users who file one check the app more than five times in the following hour.

BAD (feature-first). The team hears “users want notifications” and ships a toast: “Payment sent! 🎉” that auto-dismisses after 3 seconds. Tickets drop only 9%. Users who were mid-distraction (on a train, between client calls) never see the toast; the underlying anxiety — is my money in flight, arrived, or lost? — is untouched. A second sprint doubles down by stacking more features onto the same unexamined hypothesis: a six-toggle notification-settings panel, an activity-feed widget, and a CSV export of payment events. Tickets drop only another 4%, and no one on the team can narrate the accreted toolkit as a single story of what a freelancer now understands — the chapter’s feature-stacking anti-pattern. The features “work”; the meaning fails.

GOOD (meaning-first). The team rewrites the product story in the language of outcomes: “A freelancer needs certainty that money reached the client’s bank, and proof they can show if it didn’t.” From that meaning they derive:

  • A persistent payment record with three named, durable states: Sent — leaves your account today, In transit — typically arrives in 1–2 business days, Deposited — confirmed by recipient's bank, Feb 12, 3:41 PM.
  • A “Share receipt” action producing a timestamped PDF — the proof.
  • If a payment stalls past 3 business days, the app says what to do next: “This is taking longer than usual. We’ve flagged it — no action needed yet. If it hasn’t arrived by Friday, tap here and we’ll trace it.”

Tickets fall 63% in six weeks; repeat status-checking sessions drop by half. Note what was not built: no confetti, no richer notification settings panel — those failed the “clearer model, safer action, or better recovery” test.

Why this works: The team treated “I can’t tell if this payment went through” as a request for certainty, not a request for a toast — exactly the chapter’s claim that people pursue meaning, and features are only hypotheses about it.

§1.2 Conceptual Models

Example 2 — Conceptual Model

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The user’s mental story of how a system works and what actions mean; a good one is coherent, limited, and teachable, and when the interface lies or stays silent, users invent folklore.

Scenario. Draftline, a 2025 AI writing assistant embedded in a docs tool, must answer the exact question the chapter poses: is the assistant editing my document or suggesting a draft?

BAD (silent model → folklore). V1 lets the AI rewrite paragraphs in place with a brief shimmer animation. Within a month, user interviews surface folklore: “I keep a copy in another tab because the AI sometimes eats my version,” “If you type while it’s thinking, it breaks,” and — verbatim from a session recording — “the AI is smarter if I ask nicely.” 28% of active users paste their text into a separate app before invoking the assistant. V1 also has the modal-state failure the chapter says makes modal editors fail: while a rewrite is pending, the editor is silently in a different mode — keystrokes replace the AI’s target selection instead of inserting at the cursor — and nothing on screen answers “what is selected? what will my next keystroke act on?” Users discover the mode only by losing a sentence to it. The system’s silence has taught a superstitious model.

GOOD (one coherent, teachable model). V2 commits to a single story the team can state in one sentence: “The AI never touches your words; it proposes, you dispose.” Everything in the UI reinforces it:

  • AI output appears in a right-hand panel labeled “Suggested draft — not applied”, never inline.
  • The only ways in are two explicit verbs: “Insert below” and “Replace selection” — and Replace immediately shows “Replaced 2 paragraphs · Undo” for 30 days via version history.
  • There is no hidden mode: the editor always behaves like an editor, even while a suggestion is pending. The target selection stays visibly highlighted with a labeled chip — “Replace will act on these 2 paragraphs” — so “what is selected?” always has an on-screen answer.
  • A first-run teaching moment, one screen, twelve words: “Draftline suggests. You decide. Your original text is always in History.”
  • Offline behavior states the model too: “You’re offline — your request is queued locally and will run when you reconnect.” (Queued locally, not lost — the distinction the chapter says mobile and AI surfaces must make explicit.)

The “backup copy in another tab” behavior drops to 4%; support questions about “lost text” fall from 130/month to 11.

Why this works: A coherent, limited, teachable story (“proposes, you dispose”) replaced silence, and once the model held, folklore had nothing left to explain — the designer made the system think like people, consistently enough that learning transfers.

Example 3 — Design Model, System Image, and the User’s Conceptual Model

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The design model is what designers intend; the system image is what the product actually communicates through behavior and UI; the user’s conceptual model is what people infer — and misalignment among the three, not merely “bad labels,” is a primary source of folklore.

Scenario. Nightreel, a streaming app, offers offline downloads for flights.

  • Design model (what the team intends): Downloads are licensed copies that expire 30 days after download or 48 hours after first play, whichever comes first, because of studio contracts.
  • System image (what the product communicates): A download icon, a checkmark when done, and… nothing else. No expiry shown anywhere.
  • User’s conceptual model (what people infer): “It’s on my phone now, like a file. I own it until I delete it.”

BAD (the system image stays silent). The collision detonates at the worst moment: mid-flight, airplane mode, a user taps a downloaded film and gets “Playback error (E-4012).” The license expired silently. App-store reviews fill with folklore: “downloads only work if you open them once at home first,” “re-download everything the night before you fly.” One-star reviews mentioning downloads: 340/month.

GOOD (repair the system image — the bridge). The team cannot change the contracts (design model) and should not expect users to intuit licensing law. So they change what the product communicates:

  • Each download shows a countdown chip: “Available offline for 23 more days.”
  • Starting playback surfaces the second rule once: “Heads up — once you press play, you have 48 hours to finish. Plenty for a flight.”
  • 72 hours before expiry, a queued local notification: “3 downloads expire this week. Renew them on Wi-Fi before you travel.” with a one-tap “Renew all.”
  • The old E-4012 dead end becomes: “This download’s license expired. Reconnect to renew it free — takes about a minute on Wi-Fi.”

Download-related one-star reviews fall from 340/month to roughly 60 — and then plateau there. Honest measurement matters here: the residual complaints target the 48-hour playback window itself, a contractual constraint that a truthful system image can soften but not remove. The team reports that residue upstream to the licensing negotiation instead of claiming design closed the gap. Renewal-before-flight does become the observed norm.

Why this works: The failure was never “bad labels” but a three-way misalignment; the interface is the bridge between design model and user model, and the fix made the system image finally tell the truth about the design model instead of leaving users to infer a false one.

Example 4 — Seven Stages of Action

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Norman frames interaction as goal → plan → specify → perform → perceive → interpret → compare — a cycle that maps closely to the gulfs of execution (first half) and evaluation (second half).

Scenario. Priya, 34, uses her state’s mobile portal, GovID, to renew her driver’s license before it expires Friday.

BAD (the 2023 portal). The home screen led with the agency-org-chart label “DMV e-Services Portal,” the vision step demanded “Attach form DL-62” with no plain-language gloss, and everything after payment was a blank page reading “Transaction complete.” Stages 5–7 of the cycle had no support at all: 31% of renewers phoned the call center within 48 hours to ask whether they were legal to drive.

GOOD (the redesign, walked through all seven stages). Walk Priya’s interaction through the cycle, noting where the design now supports each stage:

  1. Goal: “Have a valid license by Friday.” (Formed outside the app — designers must meet it, not assume users arrive knowing the system’s vocabulary.)
  2. Plan: She decides to renew online rather than visit an office. The home screen supports plan formation with a task-named tile — “Renew driver’s license” — not the agency-org-chart label “DMV e-Services Portal” it had in 2023.
  3. Specify: She must translate the plan into concrete actions. The flow shows a four-step map up front: “1. Confirm identity · 2. Vision certification · 3. Pay $42 · 4. Done” — she can specify her whole action sequence before performing any of it.
  4. Perform: She taps, types, and pays with Apple Pay. One stumble: the vision-certification step’s “Attach form DL-62” assumed she knew the form’s number; a redesign renamed it “Attach the eye-exam form your optometrist gave you (also called DL-62).”
  5. Perceive: After paying, the screen changes to a full-state confirmation — not a 3-second toast: “Renewal submitted — confirmation #R-88231.”
  6. Interpret: She must understand what that state means for her goal. The screen answers it directly: “Your current license stays valid while we process this. Your new card arrives by mail in 7–10 days.”
  7. Compare: Did the outcome match the goal (“valid by Friday”)? The interface closes the loop rather than leaving her to guess: “You’re covered for Friday — this receipt in your GovID wallet serves as proof of renewal if you’re asked.”

After the redesign, the confused-about-status calls fell from 31% of renewers to 6%.

Why this works: Each screen is doing named work for a specific stage of the action cycle — the first half shrinking the gulf of execution, the second half the gulf of evaluation — which is exactly why the chapter says the seven stages map onto the two gulfs.

§1.3 Gulfs of Execution and Evaluation

Example 5 — Gulf of Execution

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The gap between what the user intends and what actions the system makes available or discoverable — wide when the path is buried, dangerous when a destructive action looks identical to a safe one.

Scenario. CrateKitchen, a meal-kit e-commerce app. Intention: “skip next week’s box because I’m traveling.”

BAD (wide and dangerous). The path is buried five levels deep: Account → Billing → Manage plan → Delivery schedule → (long-press a week) → Skip. Nothing on the home screen hints that weeks are skippable. Worse, on the “Manage plan” screen, “Pause deliveries” and “Cancel subscription” are visually identical gray text buttons two rows apart — a destructive action indistinguishable from a safe one. Metrics tell the story: 22% of users who start looking for “skip” end up in the cancel flow; support logs 90 chats/week that begin “I didn’t mean to cancel.”

GOOD (match controls to intentions). The team lists the top user intentions from support transcripts — skip a week (58%), change delivery day (17%), swap meals (11%) — and puts controls where the intentions form:

  • The home screen’s next-delivery card gets a “Skip this week” button directly on it. One tap, then “Week of Mar 3 skipped. You won’t be charged. Unskip anytime.”
  • “Cancel subscription” moves to its own screen, styled distinctly, and is reworded to expose the safer near-neighbors first: “Need a break? You can skip up to 6 weeks or pause your plan — both keep your meal preferences.”
  • Hidden steps are removed: skipping no longer requires a reason survey (it was optional data dressed up as a required step).

Time-to-skip drops from a median 84 seconds to 6. Accidental cancellations fall 87%.

Why this works: The redesign shrinks the gulf of execution the way the chapter prescribes — matching controls to intentions, offering clear paths, reducing hidden steps — and removes the danger of a destructive action masquerading as a safe one.

Example 6 — Gulf of Evaluation

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The gap between the system’s state and the user’s ability to perceive and interpret it — in 2020s products with async jobs and generative outputs, people click the right thing and still don’t know what happened.

Scenario. ShipRail, a developer tool that deploys web services. Deploys are async jobs taking 2–9 minutes.

BAD (silent success + uninterpretable state). The developer runs a deploy from the dashboard. The button briefly shows a spinner with no progress, then returns to normal. Is the deploy running? Done? Failed? The only truth lives in a logs page three clicks away, rendered as a raw ANSI stream. Internal telemetry shows the classic evaluation-gulf signature: developers re-click “Deploy” an average of 1.8 times per deploy (spawning duplicate jobs), and 40% keep a terminal open running curl in a loop against production — probing nervously, exactly the behavior the chapter predicts when feedback is absent.

GOOD (make state visible, feedback timely, outcomes interpretable). The deploy becomes a persistent, named-state object:

  • A status card walks through explicit states: Queued (position 2) → Building — step 3/5, ~2 min left → Rolling out — 40% of traffic on v214 → Live — v214 serving all traffic since 14:32 UTC.
  • Failure states interpret themselves instead of demanding forensics: “Build failed at step 4 (tests). 2 tests failing — view the 11-line diff since the last green build.”
  • The AI-assisted layer earns trust the chapter’s way — interpretable, not just generated: “Suggested cause: missing env var STRIPE_KEY (added to code in this commit, absent in production config). Confidence: high — based on the error at line 212.” The suggestion cites its evidence rather than asserting.
  • The “Deploy” button disables during an active job and reads “Deploying v214…” — the control itself now reports state.

Duplicate deploys drop 92%; median time-to-diagnose a failed deploy falls from 19 minutes to 4.

Why this works: Every change attacks the evaluation side of the loop — visible state, timely feedback, interpretable outcomes (including a source-and-confidence cue on the AI reply) — closing the gap the chapter says now fails as often as execution does.

§1.4 Affordances, Signifiers, Feedback, and Knowledge in the World

Example 7 — Affordance

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A relationship between an object’s properties and an actor’s capabilities — a possibility for action, not a decoration.

Scenario. Thriftly, a secondhand-fashion marketplace, designs its mobile order-history rows.

Consider what the row-as-object actually affords, given a thumb on a 6.1-inch phone screen: a full-width list row affords tapping (large target, ~60 pt tall) and affords horizontal swiping (it’s a pannable surface under a touch-capable finger). A tiny 12-pt “…” glyph in the corner technically affords tapping too — but only barely, and only for users with fine motor precision; the relationship between object properties and this actor’s capabilities is what makes the affordance real. For a user with hand tremor, the 12-pt target affords almost nothing.

BAD (action possibilities that don’t exist where users expect them). V1 rows are inert images: tapping the product photo does nothing (only the tiny title text is linked), and swiping does nothing. Session recordings show users tapping photos 3–4 times, then rage-tapping. The photo looks like the object but affords nothing.

GOOD (design the possibility itself, then reveal it). V2 makes the entire row a single tap target opening the order; a left swipe on the row affords quick actions (“Track”, “Return”), with targets sized ≥44 pt so the possibility exists for the widest range of hands and abilities. A first-use teaching moment reveals the swipe once (that reveal is a signifier’s job — see Example 8; the affordance is the swipe-ability itself, which exists whether or not it’s communicated).

Tap-through on order rows rises from 31% to 79%; “how do I start a return” contacts drop by a third.

Why this works: The team designed relationships between object properties and actor capabilities — real, reachable possibilities for action — rather than treating interactivity as decoration, and kept the affordance/signifier distinction clean as the chapter requires.

Example 8 — Signifier

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A cue that communicates where and how action is available; many modern interfaces fail not because they lack affordances but because they lack signifiers.

Scenario. BenefitsNow, a state benefits portal used to manage food and childcare assistance — high stakes, many first-time and low-digital-literacy users, heavy mobile use.

BAD (mystery meat navigation). The 2024 dashboard is a row of five flat, unlabeled line icons: a leaf, a circle-with-arrows, a shield, a person, a bell. All are rendered in the same flat teal whether interactive or inert — the exact failure the chapter names. The circle-with-arrows (renew benefits — the single most important action, with a hard legal deadline) gets discovered by only 44% of users in usability testing; testers describe asking relatives which icon does what — tribal knowledge substituting for signifiers. 19% of households in the test cohort had missed a renewal deadline at least once.

GOOD (signify where and how to act). Same affordances, new cues:

  • Every icon gains a persistent text label: “Renew”, “My documents”, “Privacy”, “Profile”, “Alerts”.
  • Interactive elements are visibly distinct from inert ones: buttons get a filled shape and pressed states; static status text stays flat. Nothing that isn’t tappable looks tappable.
  • The renewal card adds a time-bound cue in words, not just color (color alone excludes colorblind users): “Renewal due in 12 days — takes about 10 minutes. Start now →” with a chevron signifying forward navigation.
  • On first visit, a one-time teaching moment shows that the document list is pull-to-refresh: “Pull down to check for new letters” — the pattern the chapter cites as a signifier teaching moment.

Renewal-action discovery in testing rises from 44% to 96%; on-time renewals improve 11 points quarter over quarter.

Why this works: The affordances were always there — the interface failed at communicating where action was available, and adding honest signifiers (labels, distinct interactive states, chevrons, teaching moments) fixed discoverability without adding a single capability.

Example 9 — Feedback

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Information that the system registered an action and how state changed — visual, auditory, haptic, or linguistic; absence of feedback is not minimalism, it is silence that forces people to probe nervously.

Scenario. DoseMate, a medication-tracking app for managing a parent’s blood-pressure regimen. The core action: logging “Mom took her 8 AM lisinopril.”

BAD (silent success). Tapping the pill row gives no visible change — the log is written to the database, the UI shows nothing. Caregivers double-log constantly (12% of entries are duplicates), and duplicates matter here: a double-logged dose can mask a missed dose in the adherence report the cardiologist reviews. Silence isn’t just annoying; in a health context it corrupts the record that clinical decisions lean on.

GOOD (multi-channel, state-changing feedback). One tap now produces layered confirmation matched to context:

  • Visual: the row transforms to a distinct logged state — checkmark, timestamp, changed background: “Lisinopril 10 mg — logged 8:04 AM”. Not a vanishing toast; a durable state change she can perceive even if she looks back a minute later.
  • Haptic: a single light tap confirms registration without requiring eyes on screen — useful when she’s simultaneously helping her mother.
  • Linguistic, for the queued-offline case: at the care facility with poor signal, the row shows “Logged — will sync when you’re back online” (queued locally, not lost), then flips to “Synced ✓ 9:12 AM”.
  • Feedback also carries recovery: the logged row offers “Undo” for 15 seconds, so confirmation and forgiveness travel together.

Duplicate log entries fall from 12% to 0.8%; the nervous pattern of opening the history screen right after logging drops by 70%.

Why this works: Every channel answers the two questions feedback exists to answer — was my action received, and how did state change? — replacing the silence that made a careful caregiver probe nervously and pollute a clinically meaningful record.

Example 10 — Knowledge in the World (vs. Knowledge in the Head)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Externalized structure — labels, defaults, visible constraints, progress, history — that reduces memory load, because most people cannot and should not have to carry complex shortcuts mentally.

Scenario. Relay, a team collaboration tool (channels, docs, tasks) used by a 40-person nonprofit whose staff includes seasonal volunteers.

BAD (expert-only knowledge in the head). Power actions live behind memorized shortcuts documented only in a help-center article: ⌘⇧M assigns a task, ⌘E archives a thread, and moving a doc requires remembering the exact channel name to type it, spelled precisely, from memory. Long-tenured staff fly; every seasonal volunteer cohort spends weeks asking “how do you…?” in a #help channel (median 26 such questions per new hire). The design assumes distraction-free experts; the reality is interrupted people on phones — precisely the conditions the chapter says to assume.

GOOD (put the structure in the world).

  • A command palette (⌘K — one thing to remember) exposes every action as searchable text: typing “assign” surfaces “Assign task to…” with the shortcut displayed alongside, so the world teaches the head over time instead of the reverse.
  • Moving a doc shows a browsable, recently-used-first channel picker — recognition over recall; no exact names to remember.
  • Inline validation moves rules out of docs and into the moment: naming a channel with a space triggers “Channel names use dashes, like grant-2026 — we’ve suggested one below” as-you-type, not as a post-submit error.
  • Sign-in switches to passkeys — “Sign in with your fingerprint — no password to remember” — moving the most fragile piece of knowledge-in-the-head out of memory entirely, the passwordless pattern the chapter cites.
  • Breadcrumbs (Programs / Grants / 2026 Renewal) and a visible version history (“Edited by Sam, 2:14 PM — view previous”) externalize “where am I?” and “what changed?”

New-volunteer #help questions drop from a median 26 to 7; task-assignment usage spreads from 9 power users to 31 of 40 staff.

Why this works: Each change relocates fragile knowledge from memory into visible structure — labels, defaults, constraints, history, recognition-based pickers — so the product works for distracted, interrupted, imperfect-recall humans rather than only for experts, which the chapter says is where designing for error starts.

§1.5 Design for Error

Example 11 — Slips, Mistakes, and Constraints (Blame the System, Not the Person)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Error is a predictable outcome of complex tools used under pressure, not a character flaw; slips (wrong action, right intention) and mistakes (wrong intention, coherent action) are design inputs, addressed with constraints that prevent illegal states, non-destructive defaults, and messages that explain what happened, why it matters, and what to do next.

Scenario. InfusaLink, a tablet app nurses use to program home-infusion pumps. Two distinct error types show up in incident reports:

  • A slip (wrong action, right intention): A nurse intends 10.0 mL/hr but, interrupted mid-entry by a patient call, types 100 — the classic decimal-entry slip under pressure.
  • A mistake (wrong intention, coherent action): A float nurse covering an unfamiliar patient coherently and carefully programs the morning protocol… for a patient who was switched to the evening protocol last week. Every action was correct for the wrong plan.

BAD (blame the person). V1 accepts any numeric input, then logs incidents as “user error — retraining scheduled.” Retraining does not change the conditions (interruption, unfamiliarity, time pressure) that produce the errors, so they recur: 14 dosing near-misses across the fleet in one quarter.

GOOD (treat both error types as design inputs).

  • Against the slip — constraints that prevent illegal states: the rate field enforces drug-specific hard limits from the formulary; entering 100 for this drug is simply not accepted: “100 mL/hr is above the maximum for this medication (12 mL/hr). Did you mean 10.0?” The illegal state cannot be reached, and the message says what happened, why it matters, and what to do next. A soft-range check (“11.5 mL/hr is within this medication’s limit but unusually high for this patient’s weight — confirm with the order”) catches values that are legal but improbable.
  • Against the mistake — fix the intention-forming context: the programming screen leads with the current order, pulled fresh: “Active protocol changed 6 days ago: EVENING schedule”, with the changed field highlighted. The mistake was coherent action on a stale model; the design puts the current model in front of the coherent actor.
  • Non-destructive defaults: starting a new program never overwrites the last one; the prior program remains one tap away under “Previous program (ended Mar 2)”.
  • Confirmation is reserved for the genuinely hard-to-recover step — starting the infusion — and it is informative rather than theatrical: it restates drug, dose, rate, and schedule in words a tired human can compare against the paper order.

Dosing near-misses drop from 14 to 2 per quarter; none in the following two quarters involve decimal-entry slips.

Why this works: The redesign treats the slip and the mistake as different design problems — constraints and limits for the slip, a corrected conceptual model at the point of intention for the mistake — and retires “user error” as an explanation, exactly the chapter’s blame-the-system stance.

Example 12 — Forgiveness (and the Confirmation-Theater Anti-Pattern)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Reversibility and recovery after error — undo, trash, version history — preferred over confirmation when recovery cost is low, with hard gates reserved for irreversible, high-stakes actions.

Scenario. ClientVault, a CRM for small agencies, handles two very different destructive actions: deleting a client record, and initiating a wire-transfer refund from escrow.

BAD (confirmation theater everywhere). V1 treats both actions — and archiving, and unsubscribing from a digest — identically: “Are you sure? OK / Cancel.” Users see the dialog ~30 times a week on trivial actions and, as the chapter predicts, learn to click OK without reading. Instrumentation shows median dialog-dwell time of 400 ms — nobody is reading. So when the dialog guards something real, it protects nothing: “I accidentally deleted the wrong client” tickets run 25/month, and each recovery requires a support-engineer database restore (median 2 business days). The illusion of safety has destroyed the attention safety needs.

GOOD (forgiveness where recovery is cheap; hard gates where it isn’t).

  • Delete client loses its dialog entirely. The action executes immediately with layered forgiveness: a snackbar — “Acme Design moved to Trash. Undo” — then a Trash that retains records for 30 days (“Restore” rebuilds the record, its notes, and its file links intact), backed by version history. Recovery cost is now near zero, so no gate is needed.
  • Wire a refund — irreversible, high-stakes, the chapter’s own “wiring money” case — gets a real gate, engineered to demand attention rather than a reflexive OK. It verifies both dimensions of the action: the recipient, by displaying the destination against the client record it must match (“Account name on file: Acme Design LLC · First Meridian Bank ···4417 — confirm this matches the refund request”), and the amount, by requiring it to be typed (“Type 4,250.00 to authorize”). Transfers over $1,000 add a 30-second hold with visible countdown, and the stakes are stated plainly: “Wire transfers cannot be recalled once sent.”
  • Low-stakes actions (archive, unsubscribe) get no dialog and no undo bar — just clear feedback — so the remaining gate stays rare and therefore meaningful.

“Deleted the wrong client” support tickets fall from 25/month to under 2 (all self-served via Trash); zero wire-recovery incidents are logged in the following year — the gate can verify amount and recipient-record match, though no confirmation can make a wrong underlying request impossible.

Why this works: Matching the mechanism to recovery cost — forgiveness for the cheap-to-recover, one attention-demanding hard gate for the irreversible — follows the chapter’s rule “prefer forgiveness over confirmation theater” and restores the scarce attention that real confirmations require.

§1.6 The Priority Hierarchy

Example 13 — The Priority Hierarchy as a Decision Policy

Definition (as this chapter uses it): When goals collide, decide in explicit order — safety → model/recovery → inclusion → outcomes → systems → delight — this book’s local decision policy (practice scaffolding, not a claim that Norman ranked it so), with critical-path accessibility failures that block essential tasks counting as Safety (#1).

Scenario. CareLoop, a telehealth app, is redesigning its “join your video appointment” flow for a spring release. Six proposals compete for the same two-sprint budget. The team resolves the collision by walking the hierarchy top-down and recording the calls in a decision log:

  1. Safety. Audit finds the “Join visit” button fails screen-reader labeling — it announces only “button” — so blind patients cannot join appointments at all. This is a critical-path accessibility failure blocking an essential action, so per the chapter it is Safety, not merely polish. Also at this layer: the “End visit for all” control sits one ambiguous tap from “Mute,” risking irreversible harm mid-consultation (a dropped clinical call). Both are fixed first, before anything below is even estimated. Fix: labeled controls (“Join your 2:30 PM visit with Dr. Osei”), and End-visit moved behind a distinct, described control.
  2. Model and recovery. Patients don’t understand pre-call state (“is it waiting for me or the doctor?”). The team ships named states — “Waiting room — Dr. Osei has been notified” vs. “Reconnecting — you’re still in your visit” — and makes call drops recoverable: rejoining within 10 minutes returns the patient to the same visit with the message “Welcome back — Dr. Osei is still here.”
  3. Inclusion. Real-time captions for deaf and hard-of-hearing patients; Spanish and Vietnamese localization (34% of the patient population); a low-bandwidth audio-only fallback that triggers automatically below ~250 kbps with the notice “Video paused to protect audio quality.” Devices tested down to a 2019 Android on 3G.
  4. Outcomes. With the layers above solid, the team streamlines the happy path: appointment reminders deep-link straight into the waiting room, cutting median time-from-notification-to-joined from 3 m 40 s to 55 s, and post-visit summaries arrive in the app within an hour.
  5. Systems. The flow adopts platform-native call UI conventions (CallKit/ConnectionService) so incoming visits behave like calls the OS understands, and the team holds a performance budget: waiting room interactive in under 2 s on the test floor device.
  6. Delight. Last and only now: a calming waiting-room animation and a gentle chime when the clinician joins. One proposed flourish — an AI-generated “your visit at a glance” splash card shown while connecting — is cut because it would delay feedback about connection state: the chapter’s line that delight must never obscure status.

The log’s ordering survives a real fight: marketing wanted the animated waiting room shipped first “for the app-store screenshots.” The hierarchy gave the team a shared, non-personal way to say no — delight without safety is marketing.

Why this works: Every trade-off was resolved by explicit precedence rather than taste or politics — safety and recovery before efficiency, inclusion before polish, delight strictly last — which is precisely the decision policy §1.6 exists to provide.

How to Use These Examples

For each concept, try the transfer test the chapter’s Practice Exercises encourage: take the BAD half of any example, find its analogue in a product you use this week, and write the GOOD half yourself — naming the states, drafting the actual UI copy, and checking your fix against the hierarchy (does it touch safety? model/recovery? inclusion?) before you polish anything.

Chapter 02 Worked Examples — Interaction Design: Behavior, Flows, and Feedback

This companion document gives one worked example for every teachable concept in Chapter 2: the core concept(s) of each numbered section plus every entry in the Key Terms list (merged where a key term and a section concept coincide). Each example follows the same structure — a one-line definition anchored to the chapter’s usage, a concrete scenario from a plausible 2024–2026 product with real UI copy, named states, flows, and numbers, a BAD vs GOOD contrast where instructive, and a one-sentence tie-back to the chapter principle. Every example honors the book’s priority ladder: safety → model/recovery → inclusion → outcomes → systems → delight.

§2.1 Closed-Loop Interaction and Do / Feel / Know

Example 1 — Closed-Loop Interaction

Definition (per this chapter): Action, perception, and updated understanding forming a continuous cycle — the action produces perceptible response, and the response produces accurate knowledge.

Scenario — “Pesa,” a mobile peer-to-peer payments app (fintech). A user sends KES 4,500 rent to a landlord on a spotty 3G connection.

  • Do: She taps “Send KES 4,500” on the confirm screen.
  • Feel: Within 150 ms the button depresses, a short haptic tick fires, and the button label changes to “Sending…” with a determinate arc. At 2.1 s (server ack), the arc completes and the sheet header reads “Sending to Daniel M. — undo within 30s” with a live countdown ring. The transfer is held server-side until the undo window lapses, and the copy refuses to say “sent” while undo is still possible — if it is undoable, it is not yet done (the same queued-vs-done honesty §2.3 demands). When the window closes at 30 s, the check animates in and the header flips to “Sent to Daniel M. · Today 14:02.”
  • Know: The screen states exactly what changed and what comes next, in both phases. During the hold: “KES 4,500 on its way. New balance: KES 11,320. Undo within 30s.” After the window closes: “KES 4,500 sent. Daniel will get an SMS receipt.” A “View receipt” control sits below.

BAD version (open-loop UI, the chapter’s “tap void, hope” anti-pattern): the tap dims the button for 400 ms, the screen returns to the home feed, and no balance change is visible for 20 seconds. In usability testing this version produced 31% duplicate sends — users re-tapped because the loop never closed. The GOOD version above cut duplicate sends to under 1% in the same 24-participant lab protocol; field telemetry later settled nearer 2% (double-taps on very old devices where the haptic never fires) — still a large win, honestly measured.

Why this works: The action produces perceptible response (Feel) and the response produces accurate knowledge of state, consequence, and next step (Know) — the closed loop is the operational form of shrinking Norman’s gulfs, and here it is also a safety fix (duplicate money movement) before it is a delight fix.

Example 2 — Do / Feel / Know

Definition (per this chapter): Verplank’s framing of every interaction as action available (Do), sensory/emotional response returned (Feel), and resulting understanding (Know).

Scenario — “Doserly,” a medication-adherence app (health). An 82-year-old user with reduced vision logs her evening warfarin dose.

  • Do: The home screen offers one dominant action per due dose: a 64-pt card reading “Warfarin 5 mg — due now. Tap when taken.” Nothing else competes for the tap; the action available is unmistakable.
  • Feel: On tap, the card flips green, plays a soft chime, gives a long haptic, and the copy tone stays calm: “Logged at 7:04 PM.” For a user with a screen reader, VoiceOver announces “Warfarin five milligrams, logged, seven oh four PM” — Feel is designed across senses, not just motion.
  • Know: The card settles into a summary: “Next dose: tomorrow 7 PM. Streak: 12 days.” She leaves knowing state (logged), consequence (nothing more tonight), and next step (tomorrow).

Diagnosing with the framing: an earlier build had strong Do and Feel (satisfying green flip) but weak Know — it never said which dose was logged, and 3 of 8 pilot users double-logged after the flip, a genuine overdose-risk defect. Per the chapter, a loop with Feel but no Know is theatrical; the fix was the explicit “Logged at 7:04 PM / Next dose tomorrow” copy, not more animation.

Why this works: Auditing the interaction column by column — Do, Feel, Know — located the failure in Know, exactly where the chapter says evaluation lives, and fixed a safety problem first rather than polishing delight.

Example 3 — Microinteraction (Trigger → Rules → Feedback → Loops/Modes)

Definition (per this chapter): A contained behavior specified end to end by its trigger (manual or system), rules, feedback, and loops/modes — designing a “like” or an AI “regenerate” means specifying this chain, not inventing a widget.

Scenario — the “Regenerate” control in “Draftmate,” an AI writing copilot. Full spec, the way the chapter’s Practice Exercise 1 asks for:

  • Trigger (manual): User taps “Regenerate” under an AI-drafted paragraph. Trigger (system): if generation stalls > 20 s, the system itself offers “Retry?” — a system trigger, distinct from the manual one.
  • Rules (made visible, not “sometimes it auto-saves”): Regeneration replaces only the selected paragraph, never the whole document; the previous version is always kept; each regeneration counts against a visible daily quota. The UI states the rule: “Regenerating this paragraph. Your current version is saved in History.”
  • Feedback: Button becomes “Regenerating…” with a determinate shimmer over the paragraph only (scope of change is visible); on completion, a diff-style highlight marks changed sentences for 3 s; a toast offers “Keep new · Restore previous.” Quota chip updates: “14 of 20 regenerations left today.”
  • Loops/modes: The control supports repetition — each tap loops the behavior with the same rules — and while generating, the paragraph enters a temporary condition (its text is read-only) marked by a labeled border: “Generating — tap to cancel.”
  • Know statement: “Only this paragraph changed; my old text is one tap away; I have 14 tries left.”

BAD version: an invisible-rules regenerate that silently rewrote the entire document and kept no previous version — the chapter’s warning that if rules are invisible, users cannot form a stable model. Support tickets tagged “AI deleted my work” fell from 47/week to a four-week average of 3–6/week after the spec above shipped; the residue traced to a separate mobile session-restore bug — a reminder that one fix rarely zeroes a metric.

Why this works: Specifying trigger, rules, feedback, and loops/modes end to end is exactly what the chapter says microinteraction design is, and putting model/recovery (saved previous version) ahead of speed follows the priority ladder.

§2.2 Modes, Modeless Design, and Direct Manipulation

Example 4 — Mode (and Mode Errors)

Definition (per this chapter): A mode is a temporary condition in which the same input means something different; modes multiply capability while multiplying opportunity for mode errors.

Scenario — voice-message recording in “Relay,” a team messaging app (collaboration tools). Holding the mic button enters recording mode: now the same gestures mean different things — swiping left (normally “reply”) means “cancel recording,” and releasing (normally nothing) means “send.”

BAD version (invisible mode, the chapter’s anti-pattern of a state “marked only by subtle tint”): the only cue was the mic icon turning from gray to slightly-red. A user in a loud open office believed recording had stopped, vented about a client, and the 40-second clip sent to the client channel. That is a mode error with real consequences — the same input (“release finger”) meant “send” in a mode she didn’t know she was in.

GOOD version (make the mode loud, as the chapter instructs):

  • Persistent full-width banner: “Recording voice message · 0:07” with a pulsing red waveform — distinct chrome, not a tiny icon color change.
  • Modal constraint: the message list dims and cannot be scrolled while recording.
  • Easy escape: a large “Cancel” target, Esc on desktop, and slide-to-cancel with the rail labeled “← Slide to cancel.”
  • Exit confirmation of the mode boundary: on release, a 3-second “Sending voice message… Undo” interstitial before delivery.

Accidental-send reports dropped 88% in the quarter after the redesign.

Why this works: The chapter’s rule is that necessary modes get persistent banners, distinct chrome, hard-to-miss constraints, and easy escape — never a subtle tint alone — because preventing the mode error (safety, recovery) outranks the minimalism of quiet chrome (delight).

Example 5 — Modeless Design

Definition (per this chapter): Prefer designs where actions are visible, scoped, and reversible without requiring people to remember “which mode am I in?”

Scenario — annotation in “Plotset,” a data-dashboard tool (developer/analytics tools). V1 used a classic modal toolbar: click the pencil to enter annotate mode, where clicking a chart adds a note; click the arrow to return to explore mode, where clicking a chart drills down. Instrumentation showed 23% of drill-down clicks happened while users were unknowingly still in annotate mode, littering dashboards with empty notes titled “Untitled annotation.”

GOOD, modeless redesign — the capability moved from a remembered global state into visible, scoped, reversible actions:

  • Clicking a chart always drills down (one input, one meaning — no mode to remember).
  • Annotation is invoked in place: hovering any data point reveals a ”+ Note” affordance; on touch, long-press opens a small sheet with “Add note · Drill down · Copy value.”
  • Every note is created with an inline “Undo” chip, so the action is reversible without ceremony.

Stray empty annotations fell to near zero, and annotation usage rose roughly 40% — though a redesigned onboarding tour shipped the same quarter, so the team credits the modeless change for only part of that lift. The error-class elimination, not the usage bump, is the defensible result.

Why this works: The chapter says to prefer modeless design when possible — making actions visible, scoped, and reversible removes the “which mode am I in?” memory burden entirely, eliminating the error class rather than signaling it better.

Example 6 — Direct Manipulation

Definition (per this chapter): Acting on visible objects with continuous, reversible representation — shrinking the gulf of execution by acting on representations rather than through abstract commands; on AI canvases, pointing at a region and saying “make this shorter” still counts if selection and result remain visible and editable.

Scenario — trimming a clip in “Cutlist,” a mobile video editor with AI assist (media).

  • The clip is a visible object: a filmstrip with draggable handles. Dragging the right handle trims continuously — the preview frame updates live at every pixel of drag (continuous representation), the handle snaps to detected scene boundaries with a haptic tick, a ghost outline shows the original length, and a highlight shows the retained region — the chapter’s snap/highlight/ghost feedback trio.
  • Forgiveness: releasing the handle shows “Trimmed 0:04 · Undo”; undo restores the exact prior in/out points (undo reorder/undo trim, as the chapter requires of direct manipulation).
  • AI-canvas extension: the user can also draw a selection over the timeline and say “tighten this section.” The selection stays visibly marked, the AI’s proposed cut renders as a dashed overlay labeled “Proposed: −0:12 · Apply · Discard,” and after Apply the change remains editable — an object-centered act, per the chapter, because selection and result remain visible and editable.

BAD contrast (abstract command): a dialog asking for numeric in/out timecodes — “Trim from 00:00:04:12 to 00:00:19:03” — forces users to translate intent into a command language, widening the gulf of execution the drag handles had closed.

Why this works: Keeping the object visible and the action continuous — with snap, highlight, ghost feedback and undo forgiveness — is exactly how the chapter says direct manipulation shrinks the gulf of execution, and the AI variant shows the principle surviving the shift from drag to language.

§2.3 State Completeness: Designing the Whole Truth

Example 7 — State Completeness (the Full Eight-State Matrix)

Definition (per this chapter): Explicit design for the full state set — empty, partial, loading, success, failed, stale, locked, queued_local — for every meaningful object and flow, because most interface bugs are missing states.

Scenario — a benefits application in “CivicFile,” a state government services portal (gov services). The design spec answers the chapter’s design question for each state of the application object:

State UI treatment (actual copy)
Empty First run teaches and invites: “You haven’t started an application. Most people finish in about 25 minutes. You can stop anytime — we save as you go.” Primary button: “Start application.”
Partial Incomplete work shown and resumable: dashboard card “Application 3 of 6 sections complete · Last edited May 2.” Button: “Continue where you left off.”
Loading Determinate and leavable: “Checking eligibility… step 2 of 3.” Copy beneath: “Safe to close — we’ll email you if anything is needed.”
Success What changed + next useful action: “Application submitted. Confirmation #TX-58291. Most decisions arrive within 10 business days. Next: upload proof of income to avoid delays.”
Failed What failed, why in human terms, how to recover: “We couldn’t verify your address against postal records. Your answers are saved. Fix the address, or upload a utility bill instead.” (Never a bare “Error 422.”)
Stale Old data flagged with a trusted timestamp and refresh: “Status as of 9:14 AM. Pull down to refresh.”
Locked Who holds the lock and how to wait/request: “A caseworker is reviewing your application. You can view but not edit. Request an edit window →”
Queued_local Saved offline, pending sync — distinct from done: “Saved on this phone · Will submit when you’re back online,” with a gray clock icon, never the green check.

BAD version (the chapter’s happy-path-only mocks anti-pattern): the original vendor mockups showed only empty → loading → success. In the field, “Failed” rendered as a blank white screen and “Locked” as silently discarded edits; 19% of applicants abandoned at exactly those unmocked moments.

Why this works: Specifying all eight states is how, per the chapter, recovery and model clarity become visible in the UI — not merely in a requirements doc — and in a benefits flow the failed/locked states are the safety-critical ones, so they are designed first, not last.

Example 8 — Queued_local vs. Success (Stale and Failed under Mobile/AI Conditions)

Definition (per this chapter): AI and mobile make stale, failed, and queued_local especially important — a send may succeed on device and fail on server, and treating “queued” as “success” trains false confidence, while an infinite spinner trains abandonment.

Scenario — “FieldNote,” an offline-capable inspection app for utility crews with AI defect-summaries. A lineworker files a damage report from a canyon with no signal.

GOOD design distinguishes the three truths:

  • On tap of “Submit report,” the item appears in the outbox as “Queued on device · Will upload when back in coverage” with a gray up-arrow badge — visually distinct from the green “Received by dispatch 11:32 AM” state. Queued is never dressed as done.
  • Back in coverage, sync runs; if the server rejects the report (photo over size limit), the state becomes honestly failed: “Upload failed — photo too large. Report is still saved on this phone. Compress and retry?” — device success and server failure are separate facts, exactly the split the chapter names.
  • The AI hazard summary on the dashboard is marked stale relative to live data: “AI summary generated 6:00 AM from 42 reports. 3 newer reports not included · Regenerate.” A generated answer may be outdated relative to live data, and the UI says so with a timestamp rather than implying freshness.
  • No infinite spinner anywhere: any wait over 3 s converts to an async pattern — “Uploading in background. You can keep working.”

BAD version: v1 showed a green check the instant the submit button was tapped offline. Crews drove home believing dispatch had their hazard reports; 12 reports from one storm arrived a day late, and one energized downed line went unbarricaded overnight. That is the “false confidence” the chapter warns about, at safety-incident scale.

Why this works: Making queued_local, failed, and stale first-class, visually distinct states keeps the user’s model true to the system’s actual truth — safety and model/recovery ahead of the reassuring-but-false green check (a misplaced delight).

§2.4 Navigation, Wayfinding, and Search

Example 9 — Wayfinding (Landmarks, Scopes, Escapes)

Definition (per this chapter): Cues that answer where am I, what’s here, where can I go — with landmarks, scopes, and escapes designed as first-class behaviors, because labels, hierarchies, breadcrumbs, tabs, and persistent landmarks are orientation, not chrome.

Scenario — “Ledgerly,” a small-business accounting app used across three client companies (fintech/professional services). A bookkeeper works in multiple companies and must never post an invoice to the wrong one.

  • Landmarks: A persistent bottom bar on mobile — Home, Invoices, Banking, Reports — never disappears; whatever depth she reaches, the landmarks remain one tap away.
  • Scopes: The current company is a loud, persistent header chip — “Acme Plumbing Ltd ▾” — colored per company and repeated on every money-moving confirm sheet: “Post invoice to Acme Plumbing Ltd?” Scope is stated at the moment of consequence, not just in a corner.
  • Escapes: Back always returns one level with context preserved; Cancel on any sheet discards nothing silently (“Discard draft invoice? Keep editing / Discard”); Esc closes overlays on desktop. Escapes behave identically everywhere — first-class, designed behaviors.
  • Mobile depth — progressive disclosure over deep stacks. This one earns its own contrast, because §2.4’s rule is specific: on mobile, depth is expensive.
  • BAD (deep stack): v1 buried a VAT line detail five screens deep — Reports → Tax → Quarter → Form → Line detail. Reaching it took a median of 9 taps; each screen replaced the last, so no parent context was visible; and Android’s hardware back popped the whole stack, dumping users to Home. 41% of mobile report sessions ended in a back-out before the detail was ever read.
  • GOOD (progressive disclosure): the Q2 VAT report is now one screen of collapsed, expandable sections — “Sales VAT ▸ · Purchases VAT ▸ · Adjustments ▸” — under a persistent breadcrumb “Reports / Q2 VAT.” Tapping a section discloses its lines in place, the parent stays visible above (clear parent–child relationship), and Back means one predictable step. Median taps-to-line-detail fell from 9 to 3, and back-out abandonment dropped by roughly half — disclosure showed depth without making users travel it.

BAD contrast: v1 showed the active company only as a small avatar tint. In one quarter, support logged 60+ “posted to wrong company” incidents — a wayfinding failure with financial consequences. After the scope chip and scoped confirm copy shipped, incidents fell to 4.

Why this works: Treating landmarks, scopes, and escapes as first-class behaviors answers where-am-I/what’s-here/how-do-I-get-back continuously, and stating scope at the point of action turns wayfinding into a safety mechanism, per the priority ladder.

Example 10 — Search Complements Browsing (Not an IA Substitute)

Definition (per this chapter): Browsing teaches the model of the domain; search serves known-item and exploratory retrieval — poor IA cannot be fixed by a search box alone, just as poor search cannot be fixed by deeper menus.

Scenario — “Stacksmith Docs,” documentation for a cloud developer platform (developer tools).

BAD version (the chapter’s search as IA substitute anti-pattern): the 2024 redesign collapsed the sidebar into a single AI-search box — “Ask anything about Stacksmith.” Known-item retrieval was fine (“rotate an API key” → answer in seconds), but new users had no way to learn what the platform even contained. Time-to-first-deploy for new accounts rose 35%, and the top AI-search query became, tellingly, “what can stacksmith do.” Structure had been dumped into a query box.

GOOD version — browse and search as complements:

  • Browsing rebuilt to teach the domain model: a persistent left rail with five stable top-level areas — Get Started, Build, Deploy, Observe, Reference — plus breadcrumbs (“Build / Queues / Retries”) so every search landing also orients.
  • Search kept for known-item and exploratory retrieval: the AI answer box remains, but every generated answer cites and links its source pages (“From: Deploy / Rollbacks”), so search results feed the browsing model instead of bypassing it.
  • Scoped search — “Search in: All docs ▾ / This section” — reuses the IA as the scoping structure.

Time-to-first-deploy recovered, and the “what can it do” query volume dropped 70% because browsing was answering it.

Why this works: The chapter’s point is that search and browsing serve different jobs — retrieval versus model-building — so the fix was restoring both and linking them, not making either one deeper or smarter alone.

§2.5 Forms, Complex Input, Selection, and Bulk Actions

Example 11 — Forms and Complex Input as Conversations with Constraints

Definition (per this chapter): Good form design sequences fields by task, validates inline when helpful, explains errors next to causes, never clears user input on failure, and exposes the model of complex input — what is required, optional, reversible.

Scenario — checkout at “Terraroot,” a mobile-first plant e-commerce shop (e-commerce).

BAD version: v1’s checkout was a database dump in form clothing — one long page ordered payment-first, the postcode field scolded “Invalid postcode” on the third keystroke, and a declined card threw a page-top “Payment error (code 05)” and reloaded the page, wiping the address, delivery window, and gift note. Checkout abandonment after a card decline ran 61%.

GOOD version — the form as a conversation with constraints:

  • Sequenced by task: delivery address → delivery window → payment — the order a shopper thinks in, not the order of the database schema. Progress is honest: “Step 2 of 3 — Delivery.”
  • Inline validation when helpful: the postcode field validates on blur, not per keystroke — “We deliver here Tue/Thu” appears in green under the field. The card number validates its checksum as typed but shows the error only after the field loses focus (no scolding mid-entry).
  • Errors next to causes: a declined card puts the message directly under the card field — “Your bank declined this card. No charge was made. Try another card or PayPal.” — human terms plus a recovery path, not a page-top “Payment error (code 05).”
  • Never clears input on failure: after the decline, address, window, and gift note remain exactly as entered. Preserving input cut post-decline abandonment from 61% to 24%.
  • Exposing the model of complex input: the delivery-window picker states what’s required, optional, and reversible — including what the option costs: “Required: pick a day. Optional: choose a 2-hour window (+ KES 150) — or keep free all-day delivery. You can change this until the order ships.”

Why this works: The chapter frames forms as conversations with constraints — sequencing, inline explanation beside causes, and preserved input keep the conversation coherent, and the “no charge was made” line services model/recovery before conversion optimizing (outcomes).

Example 12 — Defaults Are Ethics

Definition (per this chapter): Defaults encode assumed norms — the pre-selected choice is a value judgment the designer makes on the user’s behalf.

Scenario — onboarding for “Luna,” a period- and symptom-tracking app (health, privacy-conscious).

BAD version: v1’s onboarding pre-checked “Help improve Luna — share usage and health data with partners” and defaulted cloud backup on, with sync of symptom logs enabled. 91% of users never touched the toggles — meaning the default, not any choice, determined that intimate health data left the device. The assumed norm the default encoded was “sharing is normal”; users never actually agreed to it.

GOOD version, defaults rewritten as the norms the product is willing to defend:

  • Storage defaults to “On this device only.” The alternative is opt-in with plain consequences: “Encrypted cloud backup — Luna staff cannot read it. Off by default.”
  • Data sharing defaults off, with symmetric effort: turning it on is one tap, and so is turning it off later (Settings → Privacy → “Stop sharing and delete shared data”).
  • The AI insights feature states its default boundary up front: “Insights are computed on your phone. Nothing is uploaded.”

Post-change, opt-in sharing was chosen by 14% of users — a true measure of consent rather than of inertia. Regulators in two markets cited the pattern favorably; conversion to paid was unaffected.

Why this works: Because most users keep defaults, the default is the decision — the chapter’s “defaults are ethics” means the pre-set state must be the one that is safe and respectful if never revisited, putting safety and inclusion ahead of data-hungry outcomes.

Example 13 — Selection and Bulk Actions

Definition (per this chapter): Selection and bulk actions need explicit mode cues, clear counts, and destructive differentiation — select → review → act → undo toast for moderate risk; typed confirmation or staged deletion only for high-stakes irreversibility.

Scenario — bulk file cleanup in “Teamvault,” a shared-drive collaboration tool (collaboration). An admin clears out a project folder with 240 files, 12 of which are linked in live client documents.

  • Explicit mode cue: Long-press enters selection mode announced loudly (per §2.2): a top banner reads “Selection mode — 0 selected · Cancel,” checkboxes appear on every row, and the app chrome shifts to a distinct slate color.
  • Clear counts: the banner live-updates — “37 selected · 2 shared externally.” The count includes the risk-relevant sub-count, not just the raw number.
  • Destructive differentiation: “Move” and “Tag” are neutral buttons; “Delete” is red, placed apart, and disabled until at least one item is selected.
  • Moderate risk → select → review → act → undo toast: tapping Delete first shows a review sheet — “Delete 37 files? 2 are shared with external guests (shown below).” After confirming, files go to Trash (staged deletion, restorable 30 days) and a persistent toast offers “37 files moved to Trash · Undo” for 15 seconds.
  • High-stakes irreversibility → typed confirmation: emptying Trash permanently requires typing the folder name: “Type PROJECT-KESTREL to permanently delete 37 files. This cannot be undone.” Typed confirmation is reserved for this one truly irreversible step, so it stays meaningful.

BAD version: v1’s bulk delete was instant and permanent behind a generic “Are you sure? OK/Cancel.” One admin deleted a live client deliverables folder; the account churned. As the chapter says, bulk delete without undo is a trust-ending event — literally, in this case.

Why this works: The design matches ceremony to reversibility — undo toast plus staged deletion for the recoverable case, typed confirmation only for the irreversible one — exactly the chapter’s graduated prescription, with recovery machinery (Trash, Undo) doing the safety work that ritual dialogs cannot.

§2.6 Notifications, Interruptions, Motion, Undo, and History

Example 14 — Notifications and Interruptions

Definition (per this chapter): Notifications interrupt Do/Feel/Know loops in other tasks; design them by urgency and recoverability — can this wait for inbox? does it need action or only awareness? — with bundling, quiet hours, and user-controlled channels as inclusion and safety practices, not niceties.

Scenario — “Kite,” a news and podcasts app (media).

BAD version (the chapter’s interruptive spam anti-pattern): v1 pushed every recommendation — “You might like: 5 shows about sourdough 🍞” at 6:40 AM. Each push interrupted whatever Do/Feel/Know loop the person was in (a meeting, driving, sleep) for a zero-urgency event. 30-day notification opt-out ran at 58%, taking genuinely important alerts down with it.

GOOD version — triaged by urgency and recoverability:

  • Needs action now (rare): “Your download of ‘Longform Ep. 412’ failed — storage full. Fix” — actionable, time-relevant, allowed to interrupt.
  • Awareness only, can wait for inbox: new-episode and recommendation events land silently in an in-app Inbox tab with a badge; nothing buzzes.
  • Bundling: followed-show releases collapse into one daily digest — “3 new episodes from shows you follow” — at a user-chosen time (default 5 PM, not 6:40 AM).
  • Quiet hours and user-controlled channels: Settings offers per-channel toggles — Breaking news / New episodes / Recommendations / Account & security — each with Push, Inbox-only, or Off, plus “Quiet hours 10 PM–7 AM (follows system Focus).” Account & security cannot be silenced below Inbox — a safety floor.

Opt-out fell to 12–18% depending on cohort, and tap-through on the surviving pushes roughly tripled — though an OS-level notification-permission prompt changed in the same release, so attribution is directional rather than clean. Fewer, better interruptions either way.

Why this works: Routing each event by “action or awareness?” and “can it wait for inbox?” respects the loops the user is already in, and treating quiet hours and channel control as inclusion and safety practices — not engagement levers — follows the chapter’s framing exactly.

Example 15 — Motion and Timing as Feedback

Definition (per this chapter): Motion is a feedback channel whose duration, easing, and choreography must answer where did this go? what changed? is this waiting or done? — using latency-band heuristics, with skeleton states preserving layout; motion that exists only to impress widens the gulf of evaluation by delaying truth.

Scenario — “Cartwheel,” a grocery e-commerce app (e-commerce).

  • Immediate acknowledgment (~100–300 ms): tapping “Add to cart” shrinks a thumbnail that arcs into the cart icon in 240 ms while the cart badge ticks 3 → 4. The choreography answers where did this go — into the cart — and what changed — the count.
  • Polite-wait progress (~300–1000 ms): applying a promo code shows an inline determinate bar on the price row for the ~600 ms server round-trip, then the total animates from KES 3,180 → KES 2,862 with the changed line highlighted, answering what changed.
  • Async beyond a few seconds: slot availability checks (~4–8 s) never block; the checkout row shows “Checking delivery slots — we’ll update this row,” and the user keeps editing the cart — the out-of-band pattern the chapter prescribes for delays past a few seconds.
  • Skeleton states preserving layout: the order-history screen loads as gray bars in the exact final geometry, so content pops in without the jarring reflow shifts the chapter warns about.

BAD version (the chapter’s motion as mascara anti-pattern): a marketing-driven build added an 1,800 ms full-screen confetti sequence after “Place order” — and the sequence played before server confirmation. When orders failed, users saw celebration, then an error. Motion existed to impress, delayed truth, and briefly hid failure; the fix subordinated all celebratory motion to confirmed state (confetti only after the server 200, capped at 500 ms, honoring the OS reduce-motion setting — an inclusion requirement).

Why this works: Every animation above carries state information within the chapter’s latency bands — acknowledgment, progress, or async handoff — so motion narrows rather than widens the gulf of evaluation, and truth is never delayed for delight.

Example 16 — Undo vs. Version History

Definition (per this chapter): Undo restores a recent action (slips and local mistakes); version history restores meaning across time and collaborators — required when work accumulates, when multiple people edit, or when AI transformations need audit.

Scenario — “Quillboard,” a collaborative document editor with AI editing (collaboration tools + AI).

  • Undo for slips: a writer accidentally drags a paragraph into the wrong section; Cmd-Z (or the “Undo” chip on mobile) restores it instantly. Scope: her own recent, local actions on this device — the right tool for a slip.
  • History for accumulated, multi-person, AI-touched work: Tuesday, a teammate runs “AI: Tighten entire doc”, which rewrites 60 paragraphs; Thursday, the client asks, “where did the liability clause go?” Undo is useless — two days and three editors have passed. The History panel shows named snapshots — “Before AI tighten · Tue 2:14 PM · run by Marcus” — with per-author/per-AI color-coded diffs and “Restore this section only.” The clause is recovered in under a minute, and the AI change is auditable: the chapter’s “what did we change?” question has a first-class answer.
  • Rule of thumb shipped in the product: every AI transformation that touches more than one paragraph auto-creates a named snapshot before applying. Note the provenance: the one-paragraph threshold is Quillboard’s own applied heuristic, not a rule from this chapter — the chapter’s actual requirement is the reason behind it (version history wherever AI transformations need audit), and a team could defensibly draw the line elsewhere. Undo covers the last few minutes; history covers the document’s life.

BAD version (the chapter’s undo theater anti-pattern): v1 answered the AI rewrite with only a 5-second toast — “Document updated · Undo.” Anyone who blinked, or any collaborator who opened the doc later, had no path back: a short toast for an AI overwrite of accumulated work, without history.

Why this works: Matching the recovery tool to the loss — undo for local slips, version history for time-, collaborator-, and AI-spanning changes — is the chapter’s exact division of labor, and it is what makes aggressive AI transformation safe to offer (model/recovery before outcomes).

Example 17 — Confirmation Theater

Definition (per this chapter): Ritual confirmations that train dismissal without improving safety — a poor substitute for undo and history.

Scenario — “Shipyard,” a CI/CD and infrastructure console (developer tools).

BAD version: Shipyard v1 showed the same dialog — “Are you sure? OK / Cancel” — for everything: restarting a build, muting a flaky test, deleting a preview environment, and deleting the production database. Engineers confirmed ~40 of these a day; the ritual trained pure dismissal. Telemetry showed a median of 1.1 seconds between dialog open and OK. When an engineer one night got the identical dialog for “Drop database prod-eu-1,” muscle memory clicked OK. Nine hours of restore followed. The confirmations had never been safety; they were theater.

GOOD version — ceremony proportional to risk, with real recovery doing the work:

  • Reversible actions confirm nothing: restart build, mute test — they just happen, each with an “Undo” chip. Dozens of daily dialogs deleted outright.
  • Recoverable destructive actions get recovery, not ritual: deleting a preview environment shows “Environment deleted · Restore within 7 days” — staged deletion instead of a dialog.
  • The rare irreversible action gets friction that forces reading: dropping a production database requires typing the resource name — “Type prod-eu-1 to confirm” — beneath a plain-language blast-radius summary: “This will disconnect 3 services and delete 412 GB. No restore is possible.” The team deliberately stopped there: the chapter prescribes typed confirmation or staged deletion for high-stakes irreversibility, and stacking further ceremony on top (timed holds, cooldown countdowns, a second dialog) would restart the very dismissal-training the redesign had just removed. Because the typed confirm now appears perhaps once a quarter instead of 40 times a day, it still means something.

Over the following year Shipyard logged no accidental irreversible deletions, and accidental-but-recoverable destructive actions fell by roughly 70% (the 12 that occurred were all self-served via Restore) — a partial, honestly measured win achieved with fewer total confirmations, not more.

Why this works: The chapter’s verdict is that confirmation theater trains dismissal while real safety lives in undo, staged deletion, and history — so the redesign removed ritual where recovery exists and reserved heavyweight, comprehension-forcing confirmation for the one place nothing else can protect the user.

End of Chapter 02 worked examples. Cross-references: gulfs of execution/evaluation (Ch. 1), IA methods (Ch. 5B), latency-band heuristics (Ch. 8).

Chapter 03 Worked Examples — Inclusive Design and Accessibility

This companion document gives one concrete, worked example for every teachable concept in Chapter 3: the core concept of each numbered section (including each sub-concept of §3.7) and every entry in the chapter’s Key Terms list. Each example follows the same format — a one-line definition anchored to the chapter’s usage, a realistic 2024–2026 product scenario with actual UI copy and numbers, a BAD vs GOOD contrast where instructive, and a one-sentence tie-back to the chapter principle. Products and domains are deliberately varied (fintech, health, gov services, collaboration, e-commerce, media, developer tools) so no single scenario carries the chapter. Throughout, examples honor the book’s priority hierarchy: safety first, then model/recovery, then inclusion, then outcomes, then systems, then delight.
