Section 5B.1 — Visual Hierarchy: Structure Before Decoration

Example 1 — Visual Hierarchy (Type, Weight, Space)

Definition (per this chapter): Visual hierarchy is the ordered perceptual and cognitive priority created by type, weight, space, and color roles — the order in which a screen teaches the eye and the mind.

Scenario: Lumen, a consumer fintech app, redesigns its payment-confirmation screen after support tickets showed 11% of users didn’t realize a transfer had not yet sent (it was scheduled). The screen must teach, in order: (1) the amount and recipient, (2) the status “Scheduled — sends Mon, Jul 20”, (3) how to cancel, (4) metadata (reference number, fee breakdown).

BAD: Every line is 16px medium-weight. “Scheduled” sits in gray metadata next to “Ref: LMN-88412”. The amount “$1,250.00” and the disclaimer share the same size. Users’ eyes land on the big blue brand banner first, then wander. In moderated testing, 4 of 8 participants believed the money had already left their account — a model failure with real financial-safety consequences.

GOOD: The redesign uses four distinct type roles:

  • Title role, 28px semibold: “$1,250.00 to Priya Raman”
  • Status role, 17px medium with a clock glyph and the word: “Scheduled — sends Mon, Jul 20”
  • Action role, full-width secondary button: “Cancel this transfer”
  • Meta role, 13px text.muted: “Ref: LMN-88412 · No fee · From Everyday Checking”

Spacing does grouping work: 24px separates the status block from metadata; 8px binds the status line to its explanatory sub-line “You can cancel any time before it sends.” In the follow-up test, 8 of 8 participants correctly described the transfer state in under 5 seconds, and “did my money send?” tickets dropped 63% in the next release cycle.

Why this works: Size, weight, and proximity encode role (title, status, action, meta) rather than decoration, so the screen teaches what matters first — and here what matters first is the user’s mental model of whether money has moved, which sits above delight in the priority hierarchy.

Example 2 — Color as Structure and the Grayscale Craft Check

Definition (per this chapter): Color carries status, emphasis, and brand roles (semantic tokens like tone.critical, text.muted) — hierarchy must survive grayscale, or the design depended on decoration.

Scenario: DoseDay, a medication-reminder app used heavily by older adults and processed entirely on-device for privacy, shows today’s doses. The original design used color as the only differentiator: green pill rows = taken, red rows = missed, blue rows = upcoming.

BAD: A designer prints the screen in grayscale for the chapter’s craft check: “Cover the logo and brand color. Can a new user still answer: What is this page? What should I do first? What is secondary?” All three row types collapse into identical mid-gray cards. A user with deuteranopia — roughly 1 in 12 men — sees the same collapse in full color. Missing a warfarin dose because “missed” and “taken” look alike is a safety failure, not a style nit.

GOOD: The team rebuilds with semantic roles that survive grayscale:

  • Missed dose: tone.critical background plus a filled alert icon plus the label “Missed — take now if within 2 hours” in bold, sorted to the top of the list.
  • Upcoming: outlined clock icon, regular weight, “Warfarin 5 mg · 8:00 PM”.
  • Taken: checkmark icon, strikethrough-free but demoted to text.muted, collapsed under “Done today (3)”.

Position (missed doses first), icon shape, and weight now each independently carry the message; color reinforces rather than carries. The grayscale printout reads correctly.

Why this works: Treating color as structure — semantic roles redundant with type, space, and iconography — keeps the reading order intact when hue disappears, which the chapter demands (“if removing hue collapses the reading order, the design depended on decoration”) and which serves safety and inclusion before aesthetics.

Section 5B.2 — Layout Systems: Grid, Density, and Breakpoints

Example 3 — Grid as an Alignment Contract

Definition (per this chapter): A grid is a contract for alignment and rhythm — columns, gutters, margins — so related content lines up, scanning stays predictable, and deliberate breaks read as emphasis.

Scenario: Meridian News, a subscription news site, rebuilds its article-list homepage on a 12-column grid (72px columns, 24px gutters, 80px margins at the 1280px breakpoint).

BAD: The legacy page had five hand-placed modules: the lead story image was 634px wide, the opinion rail 310px, the podcast promo 298px, each with different internal padding (12px, 16px, 20px). Nothing shared an edge. Eye-tracking in a 12-person study showed erratic scan paths and a median 9.4 seconds to find the second-ranked story.

GOOD: On the grid: lead story spans columns 1–8, opinion rail spans 9–12, every card uses the same 16px internal padding and baseline rhythm. Headlines across modules sit on shared horizontal alignment lines. The one deliberate break: the weekly investigative feature spans all 12 columns with a full-bleed image — and then the page returns to the grid, so the break reads as editorial emphasis, not noise. Median time-to-second-story fell to 3.1 seconds.

Why this works: The grid is shared coordinates, not a cage — related content lines up so scanning stays predictable, and the single deliberate break earns its emphasis precisely because everything else keeps the contract.

Example 4 — Density and Density Modes

Definition (per this chapter): Density is how much information occupies a region without losing scannability; offer density modes when jobs differ, but keep hit targets, focus rings, and row heights accessible.

Scenario: Pipewright, a CI/CD developer tool, shows a build-run table. Two jobs collide: an on-call engineer triaging a red main branch wants 40+ runs on screen; a new teammate onboarding wants breathing room and visible column labels.

BAD: The team ships one “power” density: 24px rows, 11px text, icon-only status glyphs, hover-only action buttons. It crowds without completing: the failed-state cell shows only a red dot (no error summary), touch targets on the iPad app are 24px (below the 44px minimum), and keyboard focus rings clip inside the row. This is exactly the chapter’s warning that “density without state completeness produces crowded failures.”

GOOD: Pipewright ships two modes behind a persistent toggle labeled “Comfortable / Compact” (default Comfortable, remembered per user):

  • Comfortable: 48px rows, status word + glyph (“Failed · lint”), inline “Re-run” button.
  • Compact: 32px rows, ~42 runs visible on a 1440px display — but hit targets stay 44×44px via padded touch zones, focus rings render outside the row bounds, and every failed row still carries its one-line error summary (“exit 1 · test_auth.py::test_refresh”).

Support data after launch: on-call engineers chose Compact 78% of the time; time-to-locate a failing run in internal timing tests dropped from 14s to 6s with no rise in mis-taps.

Why this works: Density modes follow the jobs (triage vs. learn) while preserving accessibility and state completeness, matching the chapter’s rule that enterprise density must never trade away hit targets, focus rings, or complete states.

Example 5 — Adaptive Breakpoints as Interaction Change

Definition (per this chapter): An adaptive breakpoint is a viewport (or container) threshold at which the interaction model or content priority changes — not merely where boxes rearrange.

Scenario: TenderDesk, a B2B procurement tool, has a supplier-comparison view: on desktop (≥1024px), four supplier columns side-by-side with rows for price, lead time, compliance certificates, and carbon score; hover reveals per-cell source notes.

BAD: The first mobile pass “stacks on mobile”: the four columns shrink to 22% width each, text truncates to “Acme Fabr…”, hover notes become unreachable (no hover on touch), and users pinch-zoom to read numbers. It rescaled layout without redesigning interaction — the chapter’s definition of a fake responsive design.

GOOD: At the 768px breakpoint, the interaction model changes:

  • Side-by-side columns become a sequential accordion: one supplier expanded at a time, with a sticky compare bar pinned at the bottom — “Comparing 4 suppliers · Best price: Acme”.
  • Hover notes become an explicit tappable “ⓘ Source” chip (hover affordances replaced by explicit actions).
  • Content priority changes: on desktop the compliance-certificate row is fourth; on the phone — where field buyers verify certificates at a supplier site visit — it moves to the top of each accordion panel.
  • The left nav becomes a bottom bar with three landmarks: “Tenders,” “Suppliers,” “Approvals.”
  • The threshold is not viewport-only: the same compare table also renders inside a split-view side panel on desktop (a tender open on the left, suppliers on the right). A container query (@container (max-width: 640px)) switches the table to the accordion whenever its container — not the 1440px viewport — gets narrow, so the component adapts identically in the panel, the phone, and a future embed.

Mobile task success on “identify which supplier lacks ISO 14001” rose from 35% to 90% in an unmoderated test (n=20).

Why this works: Each breakpoint answered the chapter’s question “what interaction model changes?” — compare-columns → accordion, hover → explicit action, and content priority re-ranked for the mobile job, not just narrower boxes.

Section 5B.3 — Information Architecture Methods

Example 6 — Card Sorting

Definition (per this chapter): A method where participants group labeled items (open, closed, or hybrid) to reveal mental models and vocabulary — used early, while taxonomy is still plastic.

Scenario: The city of Ashfield is rebuilding its resident services portal. The IA lead runs an open card sort with 18 residents (recruited across ages 22–79, three via screen reader–compatible remote tooling) on 42 cards: “Report a missed bin collection,” “Pay a parking fine,” “Apply for a resident parking permit,” “Book a bulky-waste pickup,” “Register to vote,” etc.

Findings: Cluster analysis shows 83% of participants group bin collection, bulky waste, and recycling calendars together — and they name the group “Rubbish & Recycling,” not the department’s name “Environmental Operations.” Two outlier cards behave exactly as the chapter predicts: “Pay a parking fine” lands in a money-shaped group (“Payments & Fines”) for 11 participants but in “Parking & Streets” for 7. Rather than forcing one home, the team gives it a primary placement under “Parking & Streets” with a cross-link from “Payments,” and rewrites the ambiguous card “Environmental permits” (which scattered across five groups) into two clearer items.

Closed-sort validation: Six weeks later, with the eight candidate categories drafted (“Rubbish & Recycling,” “Parking & Streets,” “Payments & Fines,” “Housing,” “Elections & Voting,” …), the team runs a closed sort with a fresh cohort of 15 residents — participants must use the team’s categories rather than invent their own, which is exactly what makes it a validation method rather than a discovery one. 13 of 15 place 38 of the 42 cards where the team expected. The misses are informative: “Register to vote” splits between “Elections & Voting” (9) and a hoped-for “My Account” home (6), so the card gains a cross-link; and “Apply for a skip permit” strands with no confident home, so the team runs a small hybrid sort on the five stranded cards (use our categories, but you may create one) — three participants independently invent a “Building & Renovating” group, which becomes a new second-level node.

BAD contrast: The previous portal shipped the org chart as navigation — top-level items “Environmental Operations,” “Revenue Services,” “Highways & Civic Assets” — with no sort at all; 41% of sessions started with search because browse taught nothing.

Why this works: The open sort was used early, while the taxonomy was still plastic; the closed sort validated the proposed categories with the “use yours” constraint; the hybrid sort resolved the stragglers — all three chapter variants in their proper roles — and the outlier cards were treated as label problems and multiple-home candidates with clear primary placement, exactly the chapter’s analysis guidance.

Example 7 — Tree Testing

Definition (per this chapter): A findability test of a text-only hierarchy — no visual design — measuring success, directness, and time, catching IA failures that polished-screen usability tests would blame on “the button.”

Scenario: Benefly, an HR benefits platform, proposes a new three-level tree from its card-sort results. Before any visual design, the researcher runs an unmoderated tree test (n=60 employees) with eight tasks, e.g., Task 3: “You just had a baby. Find where to add your child to your health plan.”

Results table (excerpt):

Task Success Directness (no backtracking) Median time
Add child to health plan 52% 31% 38s
Download last year’s tax form 93% 88% 9s
Change 401(k) contribution 87% 74% 12s

Task 3 fails: first clicks split between “My Coverage” (where the answer lives, at My Coverage → Dependents → Add a dependent) and “Life Events” (where 44% of people go first). The path data shows heavy backtracking out of “Life Events” — a structure failure invisible to a hi-fi usability test, which would have recorded “user couldn’t find the button.”

Fix and retest: The team adds “Add a dependent” as a second entry point under Life Events → Birth or adoption (documented as a “see also” in the taxonomy) and retests with a fresh cohort: success 91%, directness 79%, median time 14s.

Why this works: Testing the text-only hierarchy measured findability of structure alone, and scoring success, directness, and time located the failure in the tree — not in pixels that didn’t exist yet — fulfilling the principle “IA is testable.”

Example 8 — Taxonomy

Definition (per this chapter): Controlled vocabularies and hierarchical categories for domain objects that must match user language more than org charts — shallow, well-labeled trees with documented synonyms and “see also” relationships.

Scenario: Toolbarn, a trade-supplies e-commerce app serving contractors on phones at job sites, inherits a supplier-driven taxonomy seven levels deep: Fasteners → Threaded → Machine Screws → Pan Head → Phillips → Zinc → M4.

BAD: Search-log analysis shows contractors type “m4 screws” (2,300 queries/month) and “drywall screws” (1,900/month), while zero users navigate past level four; 68% of category-page sessions bounce to search. The tree is deep and clever; nobody says its words.

GOOD: The taxonomy team flattens to three levels max (Fasteners → Screws → Drywall screws), renames nodes to trade language (“Twinfast” becomes “Drywall screws” with synonym: twinfast, sheetrock screws in the controlled vocabulary), and documents relationships in a governance sheet: Drywall screws — see also: Plasterboard fixings (UK locale), Drill drivers (accessories). Products can carry multiple category assignments, but each has one primary placement for breadcrumbs and canonical URLs. Synonym rings feed both search and the store’s AI shopping assistant, so “sheetrock screws” resolves correctly in chat, browse, and search alike. Category-page bounce-to-search drops from 68% to 29% in six weeks.

Why this works: A shallow, well-labeled tree in user language, with synonyms and “see also” documented as first-class taxonomy artifacts, makes the structure browsable instead of forcing search to rescue it forever.

Example 9 — Labeling

Definition (per this chapter): Labels are the UI’s spoken model — prefer the task and object language users use over internal schema, and test labels in context, because a word that survives a card sort can fail as a nav item under time pressure.

Scenario: Chorus, a team-collaboration suite, is naming the workspace-admin nav. Engineering’s internal names leak into the first draft: “IdP Config,” “Entitlements,” “RevOps_v3 Billing,” “Retention Jobs.”

BAD: In a five-second first-click study, admins asked “make sure ex-employees lose access automatically” click “Retention Jobs” 40% of the time — it’s actually the data-deletion scheduler; the correct home is “IdP Config” (SCIM deprovisioning). One mislabel here is a privacy and security exposure: an admin who thinks offboarding is automated when it isn’t leaves live accounts behind.

GOOD: The team rewrites labels in task/object language and tests them in-context (real nav rail, timed tasks), not just as loose cards:

  • “IdP Config” → “Sign-in & provisioning”
  • “Entitlements” → “Roles & permissions”
  • “RevOps_v3 Billing” → “Billing & invoices”
  • “Retention Jobs” → “Data retention & deletion”

Notably, “Provisioning” alone had passed an earlier card sort with IT participants, but failed in the nav under time pressure (first-click 55%) until paired with “Sign-in” — the chapter’s exact warning. Post-rename, first-click accuracy on the offboarding task hits 92%.

Why this works: Labels became the interface’s spoken model of tasks and objects (“Billing,” “Roles”) rather than internal schema, and in-context testing caught a failure the card sort could not — protecting a safety/privacy-critical task before polish.

Example 10 — Findability Tests

Definition (per this chapter): Methods beyond tree tests — first-click tests, search-query analysis, and “where would you expect…?” scenarios — that catch label and landmark failures after visual design arrives.

Scenario: Nightjar, a streaming media app, added “Downloads for offline” a year ago; only 8% of subscribers use it despite 60% of surveyed users commuting through dead zones. The team runs three combined findability methods on the shipped, fully designed app:

  1. First-click test (n=85): screenshot of the home screen, task “Save this series to watch on the subway with no signal.” Only 22% first-click the profile avatar (where “Downloads” hides); 47% click the series poster expecting a save action on the detail page; 18% click the search icon.
  2. Search-query analysis: in-app search logs show 5,600 monthly queries for “offline,” “download,” and “save” — queries that return content titles containing those words, not the feature. A top-10 recurring query with zero good results is a findability alarm.
  3. “Where would you expect…?” scenario interviews (n=12): 10 of 12 point at the series detail page — “right next to Play.”

Fix: A “Download” button with a downward-arrow glyph joins “Play” on every detail page; the Downloads library becomes a bottom-nav landmark; the search engine adds a feature-answer card (“Looking for offline viewing? → Downloads”). Weekly downloads-feature adoption rises from 8% to 31% in two months.

Why this works: The structure was fine and a tree test would have passed it — the failure was label-and-landmark placement in the visual design, which is precisely the failure class the chapter says findability tests exist to catch, in combination: sort proposes, tree validates, findability tests audit the shipped surface.

Section 5B.4 — Navigation Patterns and Wayfinding

Example 11 — Wayfinding

Definition (per this chapter): Cues that continuously answer Where am I? What else exists? How do I get back or go next? — unique titles, current-location cues, escape paths, and scope indicators.

Scenario: Ledgerline, a small-business banking app, serves owners who hold multiple entities (e.g., a café LLC and a personal account). Support logs show the most dangerous ticket category: payments sent from the wrong entity — 210 incidents last quarter.

BAD: Every screen is titled “Payments.” No indicator shows which business is active. After drilling into a transaction dispute flow, the only way out is the OS back gesture, which sometimes exits to the account list and loses the half-completed dispute form. Users answer none of the three wayfinding questions.

GOOD: The redesign makes orientation a product requirement:

  • Where am I? Unique page titles (“Dispute charge · Blue Fern Café LLC”) and a persistent scope chip at the top of every money-movement screen: “Acting as: Blue Fern Café LLC ▾” — tapping it switches entities with an explicit confirmation.
  • What else exists? Four bottom-nav landmarks — Home, Payments, Cards, More — visible on every screen, with the active tab shown by a filled icon and a label highlight (not color alone).
  • How back / next? Every modal flow has an explicit “Cancel” with a draft-saving confirmation (“Save dispute draft? · Discard”), and deep screens carry a labeled back affordance (“← Payments”) rather than relying on gesture alone.

Wrong-entity payment incidents fall to 34 the following quarter — a safety and recovery win, not a cosmetic one.

Why this works: Landmarks, unique titles, scope indicators, and escape paths answer the chapter’s three continuous questions, and the scope chip specifically targets the highest-severity wayfinding failure (acting in the wrong account) before any visual polish.

Example 12 — Navigation Pattern Selection

Definition (per this chapter): Choosing among top global + local tabs, sidebar, bottom nav, hub-and-spoke, breadcrumbs, and search + browse based on destination count, frequency, depth, and platform — each pattern fits specific conditions.

Scenario: Trailhead Gov, a state DMV mobile app, must expose ~30 services (renew registration, real-ID appointment, pay tolls, driving record, etc.) plus a small set of daily-use items.

BAD: Version 1 crams a five-item bottom nav with “Home, Services, Wallet, Offices, Settings” — where “Settings” is opened by 2% of users monthly (rare settings parked in high-frequency real estate, against the chapter’s rule) — and “Services” opens an endless push-navigation stack: Services → Vehicles → Registration → Renew → Fees → Payment, with no way home except tapping back six times. Session recordings show “stack fatigue”: users backing out three levels and abandoning.

GOOD: The team restructures by pattern-fit:

  • Bottom nav shrinks to three high-frequency peer landmarks: “Home,” “Wallet” (digital license + registration cards), “Appointments.” Settings moves behind a profile icon.
  • Hub-and-spoke controls depth: every service is a spoke off the “Home” hub; completing or exiting a spoke (“Renewal submitted — Done”) returns to the hub rather than growing the stack.
  • Search + browse coexist on the hub: a prominent search field (“Try ‘renew registration’”) serves known-item retrieval, while eight browsable, card-sorted groups (“Vehicles,” “Licenses & IDs,” “Records,” …) teach the domain model to first-time users.
  • Progressive disclosure replaces v1’s buried third-level menus: the “Vehicles” group page shows its five most-used services as full-width cards (“Renew registration,” “Replace a title,” …) with a single “Show all 14 vehicle services” expander beneath, instead of Services → Vehicles → Registration → Renew. On mobile, depth is expensive — the disclosed list costs one tap; the old menu chain cost three taps and taught nothing along the way.
  • Breadcrumbs appear only on the deep web help-center (“Help › Vehicles › Out-of-state transfer”), where the tree genuinely runs four levels — and page titles remain unique regardless, since breadcrumbs are not a substitute for them.

Task completion for “renew registration” rises from 61% to 88%; average depth per session drops from 5.7 screens to 3.2.

Why this works: Each pattern was matched to its chapter conditions — few high-frequency peers for bottom nav, hub-and-spoke for mobile depth control, progressive disclosure instead of buried third-level menus, browse to teach the model and search for retrieval — instead of one pattern being asked to do every job.

Example 13 — Top Global + Local Tabs and the Left Rail / Sidebar

Definition (per this chapter): Top global + local tabs fit broad products with clear primary areas (keep the global item count small); a left rail / sidebar fits dense tools and admin, paired with collapse rules and clear “you are here” indicators.

Scenario: Wardenly, a property-management SaaS used on desktop web, has two very different navigation problems in one product: the everyday workspace (broad areas, moderate depth) and a 34-page admin/settings area (dense, visited rarely but under pressure — payout schedules, tax forms, user permissions).

BAD: Version 1 uses one pattern for both. Eleven top-global items (“Dashboard, Properties, Units, Leases, Tenants, Payments, Maintenance, Vendors, Reports, Documents, Settings”) overflow into a “More ▾” menu on a 1280px laptop — and which four overflow changes with window width, so landmarks physically move between sessions. Inside Settings, a single ungrouped left rail lists all 34 pages; the collapsed mode shows unlabeled icons with no tooltips and no active indicator, and every page is titled just “Settings.” A support-log sample finds 19% of admin tickets contain some variant of “I can’t tell which page I’m on.”

GOOD: The team gives each area the pattern its conditions call for:

  • Top global + local tabs for the workspace: global tabs cut to five broad areas — “Home, Properties, Money, Maintenance, Reports” — small enough that nothing ever overflows. Local tabs scope within a record: opening a property shows “Overview · Units · Leases · Documents · Inspections”, so per-object destinations stop competing for global real estate.
  • Left rail / sidebar for Settings, with explicit collapse rules: the 34 pages group under seven labeled headings (“Payments,” “Team & permissions,” …); the rail auto-collapses to a 56px icon rail below 1200px and via a pin toggle whose state persists per user; collapsed icons keep tooltips and the active-item dot so collapse never costs orientation.
  • “You are here” indicators: the active item gets a filled background, a left accent bar, and aria-current="page"; its parent group auto-expands on load; page titles become unique (“Settings › Payments › Payout schedule”).

Time-to-find “payout schedule” in a first-click study drops from a median 41s (two dead-end clicks) to 12s, and “which page am I on” admin tickets fall from 19% of the category to 4% over the next quarter.

Why this works: The broad, shallow workspace got top global tabs with a deliberately small global count plus local tabs for scope, while the dense admin surface got the sidebar — with the chapter’s required pairings of collapse rules and visible current-location cues — rather than forcing one navigation pattern to serve conditions it doesn’t fit.

Section 5B.5 — The Prototyping Fidelity Ladder

Example 14 — Fidelity Ladder

Definition (per this chapter): The progression of prototype realism (paper → lo-fi → hi-fi → coded) matched to the risk of the question being answered — climb only when lower fidelity has answered its questions or a higher-risk claim demands stronger evidence.

Scenario: Scribeway, a clinical-notes product, is adding an AI feature: “Draft visit summary” generates a note from an ambient recording, which the physician must review and sign. The team has four open questions of escalating risk and answers each at the cheapest sufficient rung:

  1. Paper / whiteboard (question: does the concept flow make sense?). In a 45-minute session, sticky notes walk three physicians through record → draft → review → sign. One physician immediately objects: “I will never sign anything I haven’t diffed against what I actually said.” The team adds an evidence-linking step before drawing a single wireframe. Cost: one afternoon.
  2. Lo-fi wireframes (question: what’s the review-screen hierarchy and task sequence?). Grayscale Balsamiq-style frames test whether physicians review section-by-section or whole-note. 6 of 7 prefer section-by-section with an “Accept / Edit / Reject” control per section. No paint arguments occur because there is no paint — exactly why lo-fi was chosen.
  3. Hi-fi visual prototype (question: does the AI-content treatment read as “unverified draft”?). The open risk is now genuinely visual: will physicians perceive AI text as provisional? A Figma prototype tests a tone.caution left border, an “AI draft — not yet reviewed” badge, and dotted underlines linking each claim to its transcript evidence. Version A (badge only) fails — two participants say it “looks final.” Version B (badge + border + per-claim links) succeeds.
  4. Coded prototype (questions: real states, latency feel, screen-reader behavior). Only code can answer: what does a 9-second generation delay feel like; what happens when the model returns low confidence (“Couldn’t draft the Assessment section — write it manually or retry”); does VoiceOver announce “AI draft, unreviewed, 4 sections” on load; does the offline clinic queue the recording (“Saved — will upload when you’re back online”)? Two weeks of engineering answers all four; the low-confidence and offline/queued states — invisible in Figma — generate the most design changes.

BAD contrast: A rival team “hi-fi’d a question paper could answer”: six weeks of polished prototype impressing stakeholders (“brand buy-in theater”), which hid the missing evidence-diff step until pilot physicians refused to sign notes — the exact anti-pattern of hi-fi prototypes hiding missing states and unsettled structure.

Why this works: Each rung answered only the question whose risk it matched — paper for unsettled structure, lo-fi for task evidence without paint arguments, hi-fi for visual-hierarchy risk, coded for state truth — honoring “fidelity follows risk” and putting the safety-critical review model ahead of stakeholder impressiveness.

Section 5B.6 — Design–Engineering Handoff

Example 15 — Acceptance Criteria

Definition (per this chapter): Testable, behavioral handoff statements (Given / when / then) tied to states — never “looks like the Figma.”

Scenario: Loomery, a collaboration whiteboard tool, hands off “Comments on canvas objects” to engineering.

BAD: The handoff is a Figma link plus a Slack message: “Build this — comments work like FigJam basically.” Engineering invents behavior: comments on deleted objects throw an unhandled error, offline comments silently vanish, and screen-reader users get no announcement when a reply arrives. QA has nothing to test against; three “not a bug, it was never specified” disputes eat a sprint.

GOOD: The designer ships acceptance criteria an engineer can verify without opening Figma, each mapped to a state-matrix row:

  • AC-1 (empty): Given an object with zero comments, when the user opens the comment panel, then the panel shows “No comments yet — press C or click to start a thread” and the primary CTA focuses the composer.
  • AC-2 (offline/queued): Given the client is offline, when the user posts a comment, then it renders immediately with a “Queued — will send when online” chip, persists across app restart, and sends within 5 s of reconnect, firing comment_synced.
  • AC-3 (error with recovery): Given a post fails server-side, then the comment shows “Couldn’t post. Retry · Copy text” — the draft is never destroyed.
  • AC-4 (assistive tech): When a new reply arrives in an open thread, then an aria-live="polite" region announces “New reply from Dana Okafor.”
  • AC-5 (motion, only where it teaches): Given the ≤768px layout, when the user opens a thread, then the bottom sheet slides up from the tapped object’s comment pin in ≤200 ms — motion that teaches the continuity between canvas object and thread — and given prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, then the sheet appears instantly with no transition. No other motion is specified: transitions that teach nothing are omitted from the handoff by rule.

Content slots (“author name truncates at 24 chars with full name in tooltip”), the 768px breakpoint change (side panel becomes bottom sheet), and links to the design system’s CommentThread component API and spacing tokens complete the package — not a screenshot dump.

Why this works: Because each criterion is Given/when/then and testable, engineers ship complete behavior instead of inventing it — the chapter’s definition of handoff as acceptance criteria tied to states, with recovery and assistive-tech announcements specified rather than hoped for.

Example 16 — State Matrix

Definition (per this chapter): An explicit grid of interactive and data states — empty, loading, partial, success, failed, stale, locked, offline/queued, disabled, focus-visible, error-with-recovery — each specifying what the user sees, can do, what assistive tech announces, and what analytics event fires.

Scenario: Fieldmed, an app for community health workers who visit patients in low-connectivity rural areas, hands off the “Patient visit list” screen with a full state matrix. Excerpt:

State User sees User can do AT announcement Analytics
Empty “No visits scheduled today. Tomorrow: 4 visits.” + “Plan a visit” CTA Tap CTA; pull-to-refresh “No visits today, list empty, one action available” visits_empty_viewed
Loading 5 skeleton rows, ≤ 2 s before timeout messaging Cancel to cached list “Loading visits” (polite) visits_load_start
Partial 12 of 30 synced; banner “Showing 12 synced visits — 18 more syncing” Work with synced rows Banner text announced once visits_partial
Success All 30 visits listed, sorted by scheduled time; header “Synced 2 min ago” Open a visit; start check-in; pull-to-refresh “Visit list, 30 items, synced” visits_loaded
Offline/queued Cached list + header chip “Offline — changes saved on this phone”; edited rows show clock badge “Queued” Full read/edit; queue drains on reconnect “Offline mode, 3 changes queued” visits_offline_edit
Stale Data > 24 h old: “Last synced yesterday 4:12 PM — Refresh” Refresh; continue with caution Staleness stated before list visits_stale_viewed
Locked / permission denied “This patient’s record is restricted. Request access from your supervisor.” Request-access action; no data leak in the error copy Restriction announced, not the patient name visits_locked
Failed → recovery “Couldn’t sync. Your notes are safe on this device. Retry · View queued changes“ Retry; inspect queue Failure + safety of data announced visits_sync_failed
Focus-visible 2px high-contrast ring outside row bounds on every interactive row Full keyboard/switch operation n/a (visual affordance) n/a
Disabled “Start visit” grayed with reason inline: “Complete check-in first” Reason readable, not just gray Button “dimmed” with reason n/a

BAD contrast: The prior release specified only success — engineers improvised the rest, producing a blank white screen offline (health workers assumed patient data was lost and re-entered vitals, creating duplicate records) and a permission error that displayed the restricted patient’s full name, a privacy breach.

Why this works: Enumerating every cell — sight, action, announcement, event — before build means the riskiest states (offline/queued data safety, permission-denied privacy) are designed rather than improvised, which is the chapter’s minimum bar for professional handoff and the priority hierarchy’s demand that safety and recovery precede polish.

Section 5B.7 — Light Data-Visualization UX

Example 17 — Encoding Correctly

Definition (per this chapter): Prefer position and length over angle, area, and rainbow for quantitative comparison, and respect scale — never truncate axes to manufacture drama without labeling the break.

Scenario: Acorn, a personal-finance app, shows “Spending by category” and “Savings rate over time.”

BAD: Spending is a 9-slice pie chart in a rainbow palette; against a $2,270 monthly total, the “Dining $412” (18.2%) and “Transport $389” (17.1%) slices sit barely one percentage point of the whole apart — angles the eye cannot rank, so users misjudge their top category in testing (only 3 of 10 correctly identify the second-largest). Meanwhile the savings-rate line chart runs its y-axis from 6.1% to 6.9%, making a month-over-month change of 0.3 points look like a cliff; three App Store reviews call the chart “scary” and one user reports panic-moving money out of investments — an honesty failure with a safety edge.

GOOD:

  • Spending becomes a horizontal bar chart sorted descending, values labeled on the mark: “Dining ████████ $412 / Transport ███████▌ $389.” Position and length now carry the comparison; 10 of 10 rank categories correctly.
  • The savings line gets a 0–10% axis by default. Where zoom genuinely helps (detecting a slow trend), the app offers “Zoom to range,” and the truncation is labeled: the axis shows a break glyph (⌇) and a caption “Axis starts at 6% to show detail.”

Why this works: Position and length beat angle for quantitative comparison, and scale is respected or its break explicitly labeled — the chapter’s encoding discipline, applied so the chart informs decisions instead of manufacturing drama.

Example 18 — Decluttering and Chartjunk

Definition (per this chapter): Chartjunk is visual elements that do not support understanding of the data — unnecessary 3D, dual axes that lie, redundant legends, gridlines that compete with the marks.

Scenario: Quotawise, a sales-analytics tool, inherits a quarterly revenue chart built to “look impressive” for exec reviews.

BAD: A 3D extruded column chart with a perspective tilt (the Q3 column reads taller than Q2 despite being $40k lower, because 3D foreshortening distorts length), a dual y-axis pairing revenue ($0–2M, left) with deal count (0–90, right) whose independent scales make the two lines cross dramatically at an arbitrary, meaningless point, a drop-shadowed legend listing four series whose lines are already distinguishable, and dark gridlines every $50k that visually outweigh the data marks.

GOOD: The rebuilt chart: flat 2D columns (length honest again), the dual axis split into two stacked small charts sharing an x-axis — “Revenue ($M)” above, “Deals closed” below — so each scale is honest and the false crossover disappears; the legend deleted in favor of direct labels on the marks (“New business,” “Renewals” at line ends); gridlines reduced to three light-gray reference lines at $0.5M intervals behind the data. Ink that survives is ink that informs: the file’s element count drops from 61 drawn objects to 24 with zero data loss, and execs answer “which quarter grew fastest?” correctly in 4 seconds versus 15.

Why this works: Every removed element — 3D, the lying dual axis, the redundant legend, the heavy grid — was chartjunk by the chapter’s definition: it did not support understanding of the data, and several elements actively distorted it.

Example 19 — Accessible Charts

Definition (per this chapter): Never rely on color alone; add patterns, direct labels, or shapes; provide text alternatives or data tables; meet contrast; support keyboard focus for interactive points; offer reduced motion.

Scenario: A state public-health department publishes a respiratory-illness dashboard with a three-line trend chart (flu, RSV, COVID) that residents, journalists, and clinicians rely on weekly.

BAD: The three lines differ only by hue (green/red/teal — red and green indistinguishable for deuteranopic users), the legend is the sole label, hovering is the only way to read values (excluding keyboard users entirely), the chart is a <canvas> with no text alternative so screen readers announce only “graphic,” and the animated weekly-update transition ignores prefers-reduced-motion.

GOOD: The rebuilt chart:

  • Each line gets a distinct shape marker (● flu, ▲ RSV, ■ COVID) and a direct label at the line’s end — color becomes reinforcement, not the sole signal.
  • A “View as table” toggle renders the same data as an accessible HTML table with proper headers; the chart region carries a text summary: “Flu visits rose 12% this week to 340 per 100k; RSV flat; COVID declining 4th consecutive week.”
  • Interactive points are keyboard-focusable: Tab enters the chart, arrow keys walk data points, each announcing “Week of Jan 6, flu, 340 per 100k.”
  • All marks meet 3:1 contrast against the background; text labels meet 4.5:1.
  • With prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, the update transition is replaced by an instant redraw plus the caption “Updated Jan 13.”

An accessibility audit moves the page from 9 WCAG failures to 0, and screen-reader users can now answer the dashboard’s core question independently.

Why this works: Shapes, direct labels, a data-table alternative, contrast, keyboard focus, and reduced motion implement every clause of the chapter’s accessible-charts rule — and on a public-health surface, inclusion is not optional polish but a prerequisite for the outcome the dashboard exists to serve.

Example 20 — One-Job Dashboards

Definition (per this chapter): Each dashboard view answers one primary question; secondary metrics earn a second view or progressive disclosure; titles state the question, filters state the scope, and empty/error states explain missing data.

Scenario: Parcelo, a logistics company, rebuilds the warehouse-operations dashboard shown on a wall monitor and shift leads’ tablets.

BAD: The legacy “Ops Command Center” is widget wallpaper: 23 tiles — fuel prices, HR birthdays, a 12-month revenue sparkline, three carrier maps, and, buried in the third row, the only number the shift actually runs on. Shift leads keep a paper note taped to the monitor with the real target because the dashboard won’t say it.

GOOD: The new default view has one job, and its title states the question: “Are we on track for weekly fulfillment?” A scope line under the title states the filters: “Scope: Warehouse 4 · Week of Jul 7–13 · Updated 2 min ago.” Content: one large progress figure (“14,210 / 18,000 orders — 79%, target pace 81%”) with a pace line, a single exception list (“3 carrier pickups at risk today”), and nothing else. Secondary metrics earn progressive disclosure: a “Breakdowns” tab holds per-line throughput and staffing; revenue lives in a separate finance view with its own question. States are designed, not improvised: if the WMS feed drops, the panel shows “Order data unavailable since 9:42 AM — showing last known count (9:40 AM). Ops-data team has been paged.” rather than a silent frozen number a shift lead might act on; before the week starts it reads “Week begins Mon 6 AM — last week: 17,640 / 18,000 (98%).”

Shift leads answer the on-track question in a glance test in under 3 seconds (previously 22), and the taped paper note comes down.

Why this works: One view, one primary question — with title-as-question, scope-stating filters, progressive disclosure for secondary metrics, and explicit empty/error states — exactly the chapter’s “one job per view” principle, and the stale-data state protects users from confidently acting on wrong numbers (model/recovery before outcomes).

End of Chapter 05B worked examples. 20 examples covering all seven numbered sections, all six named navigation patterns, and all ten Key Terms.

Chapter 06 Worked Examples — Content, Trust, Privacy, and Service Continuity

This companion document gives one fully worked example for every teachable concept in Chapter 6: the core concept of each numbered section (6.1–6.9) plus every entry in the Key Terms list. Where a key term is the core of a section (what / why / next, severity ladder, just-in-time consent, support handoff, service blueprint lite), the section example and the key-term example are merged into one, per the chapter’s own framing. Examples span fintech, health, government services, e-commerce, media, collaboration, developer tools, telecom, and smart home so no single scenario carries the chapter. Every example honors the book’s priority hierarchy — safety, then model/recovery, then inclusion, then outcomes, then systems, then delight — and uses the chapter’s vocabulary exactly. One honesty note before you start: all before/after numbers in this document are illustrative teaching figures — invented to show what a team would measure and which direction a fix should move it — not empirical benchmarks to cite. Real results are rarely this tidy; where instructive, an example says so.

Chapter section / key term Concept Example
