Section: Mobile Interruption

Example 1 — Interruption-Native Design (Pause and Resume)

Definition (per this chapter): Flows built to pause, survive, and resume — durable drafts, visible recovery points, undo, and state that survives app death.

Scenario — “Meridian” mobile banking, scheduled bill-pay flow. Priya starts paying her utility bill on the bus: she has selected the payee, typed the amount ($142.60), and is choosing the funding account when a phone call arrives. Android kills the app in the background four minutes later to reclaim memory.

  • BAD (anti-pattern): A five-step wizard holds all state in memory. On relaunch, Priya lands on the account home screen. The payment is gone; she must re-search “City Power & Light,” re-type the amount, and re-answer “Is this a one-time or recurring payment?” She abandons; the bill goes late. Internal funnel data shows 31% of bill-pay sessions that background for >60 seconds never complete.
  • GOOD (fixed): Every field writes to a durable local draft on change. On relaunch, the home screen shows a recovery point card: “Resume payment to City Power & Light — $142.60 · Draft saved 4 min ago” with buttons “Resume” and “Discard draft.” Tapping Resume re-enters the flow at the funding-account step; nothing already answered is re-asked. Because a money transfer’s blast radius deserves more than zero friction, the flow ends on an explicit review step — “Pay City Power & Light $142.60 from Everyday Checking · Arrives tomorrow” with a full-width “Confirm payment” button — and only after sending does a 10-second “Undo” snackbar cover hurried-thumb mistakes, as a backup to the confirm, not a substitute for it. Completion rate for interrupted sessions rises from 69% to 93% over the next quarter (n ≈ 12,400 interrupted sessions), though the team notes a concurrent bill-reminder campaign likely contributed part of the lift.

Why this works: It designs for resume, not only first completion (Principle 1): the draft survives app death, the recovery point is visible, and re-entry avoids the cognitive restart tax the chapter warns multi-step wizards impose.

Example 2 — Time-to-Value Under Partial Attention

Definition (per this chapter): Primary actions must be reachable without reading a novel, and confirmations for irreversible actions must survive hurried thumbs — friction proportional to blast radius.

Scenario — “RouteRunner” gig-courier app, one-handed order handling. Marcus rides a bike and glances at his phone for ~2 seconds at red lights. Two actions matter: Accept order (low blast radius, reversible for 60 seconds) and Decline order (irreversible — it goes to another courier, and three declines pause his queue for the day).

  • BAD: Both actions are same-sized gray text links under a paragraph of pickup details. Decline fires instantly with no confirmation. Support logs show 18% of declines are followed within a minute by a “I declined by accident” chat ticket.
  • GOOD: “Accept — $11.75 · 2.1 mi” is a full-width thumb-zone button that acts in one tap, because acceptance is reversible: a banner offers “Undo accept” for 60 seconds. Decline — the irreversible action — gets friction proportional to its blast radius: a slide-to-confirm control labeled “Slide to decline · 2 of 3 declines used today.” Glanceable time-to-value: the payout and distance are the two largest elements on screen, readable in under a second. Accidental-decline tickets drop 84% in the first month (46/week → 7/week), then settle at roughly a 70% reduction once couriers acclimate to the slide control — and the team accepts a measured 1.9-second increase in median decline time as the cost of the protection.

Why this works: It puts the primary action within reach of a thirty-second glance while making the irreversible one survive hurried thumbs — exactly the chapter’s rule that friction scale with blast radius, model/recovery ahead of raw speed.

Section: Multi-Modal Continuity

Example 3 — Multi-Modal Continuity (Designing the Handoff)

Definition (per this chapter): Job state — identity, draft, cart, ticket, or conversation thread — progressable across channels and devices, with the handoff itself designed: what is summarized on return, what requires re-authentication, what is safe on a shared display.

Scenario — “Anchor Mutual” auto-insurance claim. After a fender-bender, Dana opens a claim by voice, captures evidence by phone camera, adds detail on a laptop, and closes the loop by SMS. The claim is a single addressable object, Claim #C-88412, not four channel-specific records.

  1. Voice (intent): Still parked at the scene, Dana tells her car’s assistant: “Ask Anchor Mutual to file a claim for my fender-bender.” Voice captures intent only — it creates Claim #C-88412 in state “Draft — opened by voice” and replies: “Started. I’ve sent a link to your phone to add photos.” No detail is negotiated by voice; the channel does the one thing it is good at.
  2. Phone (capture): Dana taps the link and photographs the damage in the app. The same claim advances to “Draft — photos received (4).”
  3. Laptop (detail): That evening, the web portal opens with a return summary: “Welcome back — Claim #C-88412 is 60% complete. Still needed: other driver’s info, repair-shop preference.” She is not asked to re-upload photos. Viewing the other driver’s personal details requires step-up re-authentication (passkey), because that PII is sensitive enough to demand fresh proof of identity. What is safe to show by default on a possibly shared display is the separate question the chapter also asks — the portal answers it by masking the other driver’s license number until re-auth succeeds.
  4. SMS (closure): Two days later: “Anchor Mutual: your estimate for claim C-88412 is ready. Reply YES to accept $1,840 or view details: anchor.mu/c/88412.” The lock-screen preview deliberately omits the dollar amount until the phone is unlocked.

BAD contrast: The phone app, portal, and IVR each invent their own object model — the call center asks “Do you have a claim number? Photos? We don’t see any” — forcing modality loyalty and repeated capture.

Why this works: Continuity is a product object, not a visual theme (Principle 2): voice captures intent, screen confirms detail, notification closes the loop — exactly the chapter’s division of modal labor — and the job progresses because the handoff (summary on return, re-auth threshold, lock-screen safety) was designed, not just each surface.

Section: AI as an Unreliable Teammate

Example 4 — AI as a Junior Teammate (Humans Own Outcomes)

Definition (per this chapter): Generative systems do not “know”; they sample. Treat AI as a junior teammate — fast at drafts, weak at accountability — never as an authoritative oracle.

Scenario — “Helm” customer-support platform, AI reply drafting. Helm’s model drafts responses to support tickets for a smart-thermostat company.

  • BAD (oracle framing): The feature is labeled “Auto-Resolve” and sends replies directly. On a ticket asking whether the thermostat is safe with a 2-wire heating system, the model confidently invents a wiring instruction. A customer follows it and trips a breaker. Confident harm, no accountable human.
  • GOOD (teammate framing): The panel is labeled “Suggested reply — review before sending.” The draft appears in the agent’s compose box with uncertain claims highlighted: “⚠ Unverified: wiring compatibility — check the hardware KB.” The Send button belongs to the human agent, whose name goes on the reply. Weekly metrics track edit distance before send (median 22%) as a signal the team is reviewing, not rubber-stamping; drafts on tickets tagged electrical-safety require a senior-agent send.

Why this works: Safety outranks outcomes in the book’s hierarchy: the design assigns accountability to a human, uses AI where it is genuinely fast (drafting), and refuses the oracle framing that the chapter says “produces confident harm.”

Example 5 — Propose → Confirm → Apply

Definition (per this chapter): For consequential AI-assisted actions: the system proposes with visible uncertainty; the human reviews a confirmation that shows what will happen; only then does the system apply — mutating durable state with undo and an audit trail.

Scenario — “Postmark AI” in a collaboration email client, “reply and reschedule” assist. The user asks: “Tell the vendor we accept the quote and move Thursday’s call to Friday.” This sends a message as the user and mutates a shared calendar — the chapter’s never-skip-confirm territory.

  1. Propose: A card shows the drafted email plus a plan list: “Will do 2 things: ① Send email to r.osei@vendorco.com (draft below) ② Move ‘Vendor sync’ from Thu 2:00pm to Fri 2:00pm — 3 attendees will be notified.” An uncertainty note reads: “Assumed Friday 2:00pm since no time was given — edit if wrong.”
  2. Confirm: Buttons: “Send & reschedule,” “Edit first,” “Cancel.” Not a vague “Looks good?” — the confirmation states exactly what will happen, including who gets notified.
  3. Apply: Only after confirm does state mutate. A toast offers “Undo (30s)”; the activity log records “Rescheduled by Postmark AI, confirmed by you at 10:42.”

BAD contrast — the “Accept all” anti-pattern: an earlier build collapsed everything behind a single “Accept all” button — one tap sent the email, moved the meeting, and deleted the superseded invite, with no per-action listing and no undo on the deletion. That is the chapter’s first anti-pattern verbatim: irreversible AI actions behind a single “Accept all.” A confirmation that hides what will happen is not a confirmation.

Contrast — where confirm is rightly skipped: the same product applies grammar tweaks inside the user’s private draft silently, because the blast radius is a private, unsaved draft.

Why this works: AI proposes; humans confirm; systems apply with undo (Principle 3) — and confirmation friction is spent only where effects leave the local draft.

Example 6 — AI Definition of Done (DoD)

Definition (per this chapter): An AI feature is not done when the model demos well; done means scoped job, listed failure modes, human confirm path for high risk, empty/error/refusal states, an evaluation set with known hard cases, provenance logging, escalation to a human, and latency targets under real load.

Scenario — “CarePath” patient app, medication-interaction checker. The demo answers “Can I take ibuprofen with lisinopril?” beautifully on office Wi‑Fi. The PM tries to ship. The design lead blocks launch until the DoD is met:

DoD item What CarePath shipped
Scoped job Interactions between the user’s saved med list and one queried drug — not general medical advice
Failure modes listed Hallucinated interaction, missed interaction, brand/generic confusion, dose ambiguity
Human confirm path Every answer ends: “Not a substitute for your pharmacist. Call to confirm: [Pharmacy · 555-0142]” — the app never presents advice as fact to act on alone
Empty/error/refusal states Unknown drug → “I can’t find ‘Xelora’ — check the spelling on the label”; out-of-scope (“should I stop my statin?”) → refusal + escalation card
Evaluation set 412 curated pairs including known hard cases (warfarin combinations, look-alike names); ship gate: 0 missed high-severity interactions
Provenance logging Every answer logs retrieved monograph IDs
Escalation “Talk to a pharmacist” button, staffed 8am–8pm
Latency under real load p95 = 3.8 s on real 4G, so the wait uses streaming + a determinate progress state, not a demo assumption

Why this works: “It answered in the happy path” is not done — the DoD converts a demo into a safety-governed feature, putting safety and recovery before outcome metrics.

Example 7 — Streaming

Definition (per this chapter): Stream tokens to reduce perceived wait and support early abort, edit, and steering of partial output — but never stream irreversible side effects; stream the proposal, apply only after confirm.

Scenario — “Forgeline” developer tool, AI database-migration generator. A developer types: “Add a nullable archived_at column to orders and backfill from status.”

  • BAD: The UI locks with a spinner for 14 seconds, then dumps a finished migration — and a beta build once began executing statements against staging as they generated. When the developer noticed the wrong table on line 3, ALTER TABLE had already run. Streamed side effects are irreversible by the time you can react.
  • GOOD: The SQL streams into an editable proposal pane token by token. The header reads “Drafting migration… (Esc to stop · click any line to edit).” At line 3 the developer sees ALTER TABLE order_items — wrong table — clicks the streamed line, corrects it to orders, and generation continues from the correction, drafting the backfill against the right table; total loss: ~4 seconds, because the job is “scan and steer” — interrupt, edit mid-stream, or reject — not “wait for the essay.” (Esc remains for full rejection and re-prompt.) Nothing executes until the separate “Run against staging” confirm step. Median time-to-first-token: 380 ms, so the wait feels conversational even though full generation takes 11 s.

Why this works: Streaming designs the wait as part of the interaction and preserves the propose→confirm→apply boundary — partial output is steerable, durable state is not touched mid-stream.

Example 8 — Provenance

Definition (per this chapter): A traceable basis for system claims — sources, retrieved documents, policy citations, or an honest “no source — model inference” — shown whenever stakes are non-trivial, so users can calibrate trust.

Scenario — “GovAnswers,” a state benefits portal assistant. A resident asks: “Do I still qualify for childcare assistance if I work 25 hours a week?”

  • BAD: “Yes, you qualify!” — no basis shown. Users either over-trust (file, get denied, lose weeks) or, after one bad answer, permanently discount the assistant. Pilot data: after a single uncited wrong answer, 62% of users never asked it another question.
  • GOOD: The answer separates claim from basis: “Likely yes — the work requirement is 20+ hours/week for households under 85% of state median income.” Below it, a Sources block: “📄 Admin Code 170-45-0230 (updated Jan 2026) — ‘minimum of 20 hours per week’ [view section]” and “⚠ Income estimate: no source — model inference from your earlier message. Verify with your caseworker.” A final line: “Eligibility is decided by the department, not this assistant.”
  • Each cited claim is tappable to the highlighted passage; claims without retrieval are explicitly flagged rather than dressed up.

Why this works: Provenance is not decoration — it is how users calibrate trust; separating cited policy from flagged inference lets a resident act on the strong claim and verify the weak one, honesty over optimistic confidence (Principle 5).

Example 9 — Agents (Allowlists, Budgets, Scopes, Kill Switch, Activity Log)

Definition (per this chapter): Agents chain tools (browse, write, purchase, message, configure) and must be bounded with allowlists, budgets of time/money/steps, explicit scopes, a surfaced plan before external effects, a kill switch, and a readable activity log.

Scenario — “Cartwright,” a shopping agent in a grocery e-commerce app. The user says: “Restock my usual pantry staples, keep it under $60.”

  • BAD (multi-agent haunted house): An earlier prototype split the job across a “deals agent” and a “checkout agent” that messaged each other, each with its own progress toast and no unified status feed. When an order arrived with the wrong milk, neither the user nor support could reconstruct which agent substituted it, when, or why — the un-debuggable haunted house the chapter predicts for multi-agent orchestration without a stable human-facing status model. The rebuilt Cartwright keeps one human-facing plan and one activity log regardless of how many agents run behind it:
  • Plan before tool use: Because effects leave the local draft (a real purchase), Cartwright first shows: “Plan: search your 12 usual staples → build cart (est. $54) → checkout with saved Visa •4821. Approve plan?”
  • Allowlist: The agent may call search_catalog, add_to_cart, and checkout — it cannot message anyone, change the delivery address, or leave the grocery domain.
  • Budgets: Hard caps shown in the header: “$60.00 limit · 25 steps max · 3 min max.” At $58.90 with two items unfound, it stops and asks rather than substituting a pricier brand.
  • Kill switch: A persistent “⏹ Stop agent” button; stopping mid-run leaves the cart as a reviewable draft, never a half-completed order.
  • Activity log: A human-readable feed — “10:31 Added oat milk ×2 ($7.98) · 10:31 Skipped tahini (out of stock) · 10:32 Paused: 2 items unresolved” — the single stable status model whose absence made the BAD prototype un-debuggable.

Why this works: Every boundary the chapter names — allowlist, budget, scope, surfaced plan, kill switch, readable log — is a visible UI object, keeping the human in control of consequential effects.

Section: Generative UI in a Stable Shell

Example 10 — Stable Shell Around Generative Regions

Definition (per this chapter): Persistent chrome — navigation, safety controls, account, critical wayfinding — stays consistent while generative content fills designated regions; dynamic regions are announced to assistive technology (AT), with no unlabeled custom controls.

Scenario — “Ledgerlight,” a small-business analytics tool with AI-generated dashboard widgets.

  • BAD (unbounded generation): The AI rebuilds the whole screen per session. On Monday “Invoices” is in the left nav; on Tuesday the model decides cash flow matters more and relocates navigation into a generated card stack. A screen-reader user’s landmarks vanish; a generated “slider-button” hybrid has no role or label. Learnability and accessibility are destroyed — task time for repeat visits increases week over week.
  • GOOD (stable shell): The shell never moves: top bar (account, search), left nav (Home · Invoices · Cash Flow · Reports), and the Export/Share safety chrome are fixed. Generation is confined to two designated regions: an “Insights for you” panel (AI-written summaries like “Receivables over 60 days grew 18% this month”) and a “Suggested views” row that can only compose from the design system’s existing chart and table components — never invent controls. The insights panel is an ARIA live region announced as “Insights updated, 3 new items,” and every generated card carries a “Generated · why this?” affordance.

Why this works: Generate inside a stable, accessible shell (Principle 4): users keep their learned wayfinding and AT users keep their landmarks — inclusion is not traded away for adaptive delight.

Section: Offline-First

Example 11 — Offline-First With Explicit Sync Semantics

Definition (per this chapter): Disconnection is normal: local-first reads and writes with real sync semantics — conflict resolution, queue visibility, honest indicators — never implying server success for a local write.

Scenario — “Sana,” a community-health-worker app used in rural clinics with hours-long dead zones.

  • BAD: The visit form shows “Saved ✓” after a local write. The worker’s phone dies before sync; three patient visits silently vanish. “Saved” was an optimistic lie.
  • GOOD:
  • Every record works locally first; the status is honest and specific: “Saved on device · Pending sync (3 records).” After sync: “Synced to clinic server · 14:22.”
  • A visible Outbox screen lists queued records with per-record retry, so queue visibility is a feature, not a mystery.
  • Conflict resolution: if a nurse edited the same patient’s weight at the clinic desktop, sync surfaces “Conflict: weight 61 kg (you, offline) vs 61.4 kg (Clinic desktop, 13:05) — keep which?” rather than silently last-write-wins on clinical data.
  • Low-connectivity degradation: critical paths (patient lookup, vaccine schedule) are pre-cached; media uploads defer to Wi‑Fi; and where the app cannot run at all, the program falls back to an SMS/USSD-style flow: text VISIT 4471 BCG to a shortcode.
  • Payload discipline: the sync bundle is 41 KB median, tested on throttled 2G profiles, not office Wi‑Fi.

Why this works: Honesty about offline beats optimistic lies (Principle 5), and explicit conflict/queue semantics protect the data-safety and recovery layers before any outcome metric.

Section: Shared Device

Example 12 — Shared-Device Session Hygiene

Definition (per this chapter): Devices belong to households, retail floors, clinics, and classrooms; design quick user switching, PIN/biometrics at sensitivity thresholds, hidden notification content, and clear “who is acting” indicators.

Scenario — “Readable,” a literacy app on a classroom cart of 12 shared tablets, which teachers also use for parent messaging.

  • BAD: The app stays signed in as whoever used it last. A student taps Back twice and lands in the teacher’s parent-message thread discussing another child’s IEP accommodations. A push notification — “Msg from Ms. Alvarez: about Deja’s reading eval…” — pops over a student’s quiz. Sensitive content is one Back gesture away.
  • GOOD:
  • Quick switch: Launch opens a class picker of avatar tiles: “Who’s reading today?” Switching users takes one tap, <2 seconds — hygiene that is fast enough to actually be used.
  • Sensitivity thresholds: Student activities need no credential; opening Teacher tools (grades, parent messages) always requires the teacher’s PIN, even mid-session.
  • Notification hygiene: On devices marked Shared — Classroom, notifications show only “Readable: 1 new message” with no names or content.
  • Who is acting: A persistent chip reads “Reading as: Deja M.”; progress and audio recordings attribute to the right student, and a wrong-profile fix exists: “Not you? Switch.”
  • Idle timeout returns to the class picker after 3 minutes.

Why this works: Session hygiene keeps another person’s sensitive content from being one Back gesture away — privacy safety and inclusion for a device the chapter reminds us belongs to a room, not a person.

Section: Performance Latency Bands

Example 13 — Latency Bands as Design Heuristics

Definition (per this chapter): Users experience delay in heuristic perceptual bands — instant (~0–100 ms), immediate (~100–300 ms), polite wait (~300–1000 ms), break in flow (~1–5 s), out of band (>5–10 s) — which guide the choice of progress, cancel, and async patterns, calibrated with your own measurements.

Scenario — “Lumen,” a mobile photo editor with AI features. The team maps each operation to a measured band and picks the pattern the band demands:

Operation Measured p95 Band Pattern shipped
Slider adjustments (exposure, warmth) 45 ms Instant Direct manipulation; no indicator at all
Apply preset filter 210 ms Immediate Crossfade only — still conversational
Auto-enhance (on-device model) 700 ms Polite wait Subtle shimmer on the image; no modal
AI object removal (cloud) 3.2 s Break in flow Determinate progress (“Removing… 60%”) + Cancel; low-res preview streams in as a useful partial
Generative sky replacement 22 s Out of band Async job: “We’ll notify you — keep editing.” Push on completion; result waits in Edits ▸ Ready (1)
  • BAD contrast: the first build showed the same indeterminate spinner for all five operations — a “spinner apology” that made 210 ms feel broken (users double-tapped, causing duplicate applies) and made 22 s feel like a hang (41% force-quit before completion).
  • The team also re-measured on real mid-tier Android over 4G rather than treating demo latency on office Wi‑Fi as production truth.

Why this works: Each band gets the progress/cancel/async pattern it needs, and the AI waits that land in later bands are designed as part of the interaction — streaming partials and async notification — not apologized for with a spinner.

Section: Platform Conventions

Example 14 — Platform Conventions as Interface Language

Definition (per this chapter): Respect platform navigation, typography scaling, permission idioms, back/gesture behavior, and notification norms; brand consistency does not excuse fighting conventions users already trust.

Scenario — “Vellum,” a news app shipping on iOS and Android.

  • BAD (brand over platform): To feel “immersive,” Vellum overrides Android’s predictive-back gesture with a custom right-edge swipe that opens a bookmarks drawer — so system Back exits the app mid-article. It renders headlines in a fixed 17 px custom font, ignoring iOS Dynamic Type, so large-text users get clipped two-line headlines. It builds a custom share panel missing AirDrop and the user’s usual targets, and on first launch fires the notification permission dialog before showing any value. Metrics: 1-star reviews citing “back button broken,” notification opt-in at 11%.
  • GOOD (fixed):
  • System Back and predictive-back animate correctly; the bookmarks drawer moves to a standard toolbar icon.
  • Text respects Dynamic Type / Android font scale up to 200%; layouts reflow instead of clipping — an inclusion requirement, not a preference.
  • Share uses the system share sheet, inheriting AirDrop, Nearby Share, and the user’s learned targets for free.
  • Notification permission follows the platform idiom: an in-context pre-prompt — “Get an alert when your saved topics break? “Not now” / “Enable”“ — shown after the user saves their first topic; the OS dialog fires only on “Enable.” Opt-in rises to 44%.

Why this works: Platform conventions are part of the interface language (Principle 6): custom chrome that breaks system Back or share sheets taxes every session forever, while respecting conventions buys learned behavior, accessibility, and trust at zero cost.

End of Chapter 08 worked examples — 14 concepts covering all eight sections and all seven Key Terms.

Chapter 09 Worked Examples — Operating Practice: Cadence, Gates, and Critique

This companion walks every concept in Chapter 9 through a concrete, modern (2024–2026) product scenario: real UI copy, named states, step-by-step flows, and plausible numbers. Products vary deliberately — fintech, gov services, health, e-commerce, collaboration, developer tools, media, field service — so you learn the practice, not one scenario. Every example honors the book’s priority hierarchy: safety / irreversible harm → mental model & recovery → inclusion on the critical path → job progress / outcomes → systems consistency → delight / differentiation.

Section: The Monday Loop

Example 1 — Monday Loop

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A weekly ritual, under thirty minutes, that reconnects intent, evidence, and capacity — aligning outcome, evidence delta, priority stack, risk scan, owners, and the midweek gate calendar.

Scenario — “Lumen,” a mobile budgeting app with AI spend categorization (squad of 6).

Monday, 9:30–9:55 a.m., 25 minutes on the clock. The facilitator (rotating; this week it’s the design lead, Priya) shares the one-pager on screen and runs the six steps:

  1. Outcome pulse (2 min). One sentence, read aloud: “This week we move first-week retention for new users who connect a bank account, currently 41%, target 48%.”
  2. Evidence delta (6 min). Since last Monday: (a) support saw 63 tickets tagged miscategorized-transaction, up from 38 — users say the AI labeled rent payments as “Entertainment”; (b) research ran 5 usability sessions on the “Fix category” sheet, 3 of 5 participants couldn’t find it; (c) analytics: 12% of users who hit a miscategorization churn within 48 hours; (d) one incident — the Friday model update briefly auto-recategorized historical transactions without a confirm step.
  3. Priority stack review (7 min). Two bets collide: “AI auto-budget suggestions” (growth’s favorite) vs. “Fix-category recovery flow.” Priya applies the priority hierarchy out loud: “Silent recategorization of history is a mental-model-and-recovery problem; auto-budget suggestions are job progress at best, delight at worst. Recovery outranks. Auto-budget demotes to P2; reason recorded in the decision log: ‘Demoted 2026-07-13 — recovery gap ranks higher per hierarchy.’”
  4. Risk scan (4 min). DoD gaps in flight: the Interrupt DoD is unmet for the fix-category sheet (a draft correction is lost if a call interrupts the app), and the Content DoD needs provenance (“Why did we label this Entertainment?”).
  5. Owner map (3 min). Fix-category flow → Priya. Model-update confirm gate → Tomás (eng). Provenance copy → Sam (content). No orphan work; the parked auto-budget bet gets a revisit date of Aug 4.
  6. Midweek gate calendar (3 min). “Wednesday noon: go/no-go on shipping the fix-category sheet — evidence required: 4 of 5 usability participants complete correction unaided; decider: Priya; default: no ship.”

BAD version (for contrast): the same meeting run as a 75-minute status theater — each person recites what they did last week, the strategy debate from March reopens (“should we even do AI categorization?”), no owner is named for the confirm-step gap, and the meeting ends with “let’s keep all three P0s hot.” Nothing is written down, so by Thursday two people disagree about what was decided.

Why this works: the loop reconnects intent, evidence, and capacity without re-litigating strategy from zero, uses the priority hierarchy to settle a bet collision with a recorded reason, and stays under thirty minutes — the chapter’s signal that the one-pager and stack are healthy.

Section: The One-Pager

Example 2 — One-Pager

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The team’s external memory — a living brief for intent, constraints, metrics, and risks, updated when reality changes, not only at kickoff.

Scenario — “RenewND,” a state benefits renewal portal (gov services).

BAD version — the kickoff deck that never updates. A 34-slide deck from January titled “Benefits Modernization Vision” with brand moodboards, a persona named “Busy Brenda,” and the goal “delight residents.” By July, the scope has changed twice, but the deck hasn’t. When the PM and the accessibility specialist disagree in a crit about whether screen-reader users are in scope for the pilot, both cite the deck — which is silent. The one-pager failed before the design did.

GOOD version — the living one-pager (fits on one screen, last edited Friday 2026-07-10):

Problem / job: Residents must renew SNAP benefits before their deadline; 31% currently miss it and lose coverage for a month.
Target segment & critical constraints: Renewers on mobile (78% of traffic); many on shared or borrowed devices; 14% use assistive technology; rural users on intermittent connectivity — every step must survive offline and resume.
Non-goals: New applications (renewals only); document upload redesign; English/Spanish only for pilot.
Success metrics & evidence bar: On-time renewal rate 69% → 80%; evidence bar: any claim of “residents understand X” requires ≥5 moderated sessions including ≥2 AT users.
Current priority stack (ranked): 1. Deadline reminder + resume flow. 2. Offline draft durability. 3. Plain-language eligibility summary. (Parked: chatbot — revisit Sept 15.)
Open assumptions (Ch. 7 map): “Residents recognize the state seal as legitimate in SMS” — untested, high risk.
Risks & DoD status: Auth ✅ · Privacy ✅ · Interrupt ⚠️ (resume point after ID verification unverified) · Content ✅ · Activation ⚠️ · Support ❌ (macros not yet matched to UI language — blocking; owner: Luís, support lead; unblock by the Wed Jul 15 gate or the pilot slice holds). A DoD owned by nobody is optional; this one has a name and a date.
Links: research repo · event dictionary · Figma prototype v14 · decision log.

When the scope changed on Friday, July 10 (legal required re-consent language), the one-pager changed the same day — with a decision-log link. Now when the PM and the AT specialist disagree, they open one document and the disagreement dissolves in ninety seconds.

Why this works: the one-pager holds intent, constraints (AT, connectivity, shared device), non-goals, the ranked stack, and DoD status in one living place — so “what we’re doing” is never a matter of memory or politics.

Section: Midweek Gates

Example 3 — Midweek Gate

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A scheduled go/no-go decision point with four parts — decision question, evidence required, decider, and default if undecided (usually “no ship”) — that prevents weekend heroics and Friday ambiguity.

Scenario — “Doselight,” a medication-reminder app adding an AI “Refill request” agent that can message pharmacies.

BAD version — no gate, no default. The feature is “basically done” Thursday afternoon. In Slack: “Any objections to turning on auto-send to pharmacies for the beta cohort?” Two people are heads-down and don’t reply. Silence becomes accidental yes; auto-send ships Friday at 5 p.m. Over the weekend the agent sends 212 refill requests, 9 of them for medications the user had discontinued, and there is no one online to abort. Safety — the top of the hierarchy — was decided by an unread Slack message.

GOOD version — the gate, written on the Monday-loop calendar:

Gate: Wednesday 12:00.
Decision question: May the AI refill agent send a pharmacy message without per-message human confirm for the beta cohort?
Evidence required: (1) eval set of 300 historical refill scenarios with ≥99% correct medication match and zero discontinued-med sends; (2) usability check that the confirm sheet — “Send refill request for Metformin 500mg to Walgreens on 5th Ave?” with buttons “Send request” / “Not now” — is understood by 5/5 participants; (3) abort path verified: “Cancel request” works within 60 seconds of send.
Decider: Clinical safety lead (Dr. Okafor).
Default if undecided: No ship — the agent stays in propose→confirm→apply mode.

Wednesday noon arrives; the eval set shows 98.3% match with two discontinued-med sends. Evidence bar not met → default holds → the feature ships with the confirm step, and a revisit gate is scheduled for July 29 after model retraining. No weekend heroics, no ambiguity, and the failure to hit the bar cost a calendar line, not a patient.

Why this works: defaults matter — without “default: no ship,” silence becomes accidental yes; the gate turned a safety-critical AI decision into a scheduled, evidence-based go/no-go instead of a Friday vibe check.

Section: Priority Stack

Example 4 — Priority Stack

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A forced-rank, ordered list of bets with displacement rules — one P0 human-attention consumer per squad, every item with an exit (ship, kill, or park with revisit date), and new work displacing old work explicitly.

Scenario — “Bazaari,” a mobile marketplace for handmade goods (e-commerce, squad of 5).

BAD version — stack fiction. The Notion board lists twelve items marked P0: “AI listing writer,” “Seller payouts v2,” “Dark mode,” “Checkout redesign,” “TikTok share,” “Offline seller mode,” and six more. When the VP asks “what’s the priority?” the answer is “all of it.” Engineers pick whatever is most fun; the checkout redesign — the one bet tied to the quarter’s outcome — has three half-finished branches. If everything is high, nothing is.

GOOD version — the forced-rank stack (from the one-pager, 2026-07-13):

Rank Bet Why here (hierarchy) Exit
P0 Checkout payment-failure recovery (“Your card was declined — your cart is saved” + retry) Mental model & recovery: 6.2% of checkouts fail with a dead end Ship by Jul 24 or kill
P1 Seller payout status visibility Job progress / outcomes Ship by Aug 7
P2 AI listing writer (propose→confirm→apply) Outcomes; gated on Content DoD Park if eval < bar; revisit Aug 18
Parked Dark mode Delight / differentiation Revisit Oct 1
Killed TikTok share Reason recorded: “No evidence delta supports it; stakeholder volume ≠ risk reduction” —

Then the displacement test arrives: sales requests “storefront video banners” for a demo in two weeks. The PM applies the rule — insertion requires displacement: “Video banners can enter at P1 only if payout visibility moves to P2 and its owner agrees the slip is recorded. Which do we want less?” Sales, forced to name the trade, withdraws the request. The stack stays true because it is sequenced by risk reduction and learning, not stakeholder volume.

Why this works: forced ranking plus explicit displacement keeps the stack from becoming fiction — every bet has an exit, only one P0 consumes the squad’s attention, and demotions carry recorded reasons.

Section: Conflict Playbooks

Example 5 — Conflict Playbook

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A structured, five-step resolution pattern for colliding goods — name the goods, restate user harm, consult evidence bars and DoDs, choose a time-boxed experiment or principled constraint, and record the decision with a revisit trigger — used before escalation.

Scenario — “PatchPilot,” a developer-tools product whose AI agent proposes dependency-upgrade fixes in CI. Growth wants one-click “Auto-merge safe fixes” to boost activation; platform engineering wants human review on every merge.

BAD version — improvisation and escalation-first. Growth PM DMs the VP: “Platform is blocking activation again.” Platform lead counter-escalates: “Growth wants to auto-merge into production.” The VP, with no framing, splits the difference arbitrarily (“auto-merge only on weekends?”). The team learns that politics beats method.

GOOD version — the playbook, run in a 40-minute working session:

  1. Name the colliding goods (not the people). “Activation speed for new repos” vs. “control and reviewability of production changes.” Not “growth vs. Dana.”
  2. Restate user harm if either side wins absolutely. If auto-merge wins outright: a bad transitive-dependency bump ships to production with no human in the loop — irreversible harm, top of the hierarchy. If manual review wins outright: median time-to-first-value stays at 3.4 days, and 44% of trials never merge a single fix — the product fails at its job.
  3. Consult evidence bars and DoDs. The Content DoD already requires editable AI proposals and provenance; the checklist requires propose→confirm→apply for AI paths. Much of the conflict dissolves: fully silent auto-merge was never available under the team’s own DoDs.
  4. Choose a time-boxed experiment within a principled constraint. Constraint (non-negotiable): propose→confirm→apply remains — nothing merges without an explicit human act. Experiment (3 weeks, 200 repos): a batched confirm — “PatchPilot proposes 4 low-risk patch bumps. Review diff summary → Approve all 4 / Review individually“ — with provenance links per patch and a one-click “Revert batch” for 72 hours. Revisit metric: time-to-first-merge < 24h AND revert rate < 2%.
  5. Record the decision and the revisit trigger. Decision log entry 2026-07-15: “Batched confirm experiment; revisit Aug 5; if revert rate ≥ 2%, fall back to per-patch confirm; escalate only if the experiment result is disputed.”

Why this works: the playbook converts a political collision into a method — the safety concern is honored by a principled constraint, the outcome concern by a time-boxed experiment, and escalation is reserved for after framing, so executive attention isn’t wasted.

Section: Anti-Pattern Critique Table

Example 6 — Anti-Pattern Critique Table

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A shared table used in design crits to critique the work, not the author — each anti-pattern paired with a symptom, a falsifiable critique question, and a remedy direction.

Scenario — “Currents,” a podcast/news media app, holds its Thursday 45-minute crit on the new “For You” home screen and AI episode-summary feature. The facilitator projects the anti-pattern table and the crit works row by row. Here is the full table applied to this one design:

Anti-pattern What the crit caught in “Currents” Critique question asked Remedy agreed
Preference theater Designer: “I feel the card grid is more premium.” “What behavior would falsify this?” Task-based test: 8 users, task “find and resume yesterday’s episode”; success bar 7/8
Happy-path only Mock shows a full feed; no state for new users, no offline “What happens on tunnel Wi-Fi / AT / denial?” State matrix added: empty-first-run, offline-cached, offline-empty, mic-permission-denied; each gets copy, e.g. offline: “You’re offline — 3 downloaded episodes ready”
AI oracle AI summary auto-posts to the user’s public profile after listening “Where is confirm + provenance?” Propose→confirm→apply: “Share this summary? Generated by AI from the transcript — edit before posting” with Edit primary
Dashboard hero First viewport: listening stats, streaks, trending panel, 3 carousels “What is the one job of this surface?” Single-composition redesign around “resume what I was listening to”
Metric theater Success metric proposed: “summary impressions” “Which decision does this metric change?” Replaced with “summaries edited-then-shared / shown,” tied to the evidence bar
Stack fiction Designer mentions this is one of “five P0 screens” “What did we demote?” Sent back to Monday loop for forced rank + displacement
Accessibility as phase Plan says “a11y audit after beta” “Who is screened into research now?” Screen-reader users added to this week’s screener; AT added to the flow’s DoD
Dark pattern creep Decline button on notifications sheet reads “No thanks, I hate staying informed” “Would we defend this in support?” Rewritten: “Turn on” / “Not now”; ethics + support DoD check added

Every open issue is ticketed before the crit ends (per the operating checklist: “Crit used anti-pattern table; open issues ticketed”). Nobody’s taste was debated; every objection came with a falsifiable question and a remedy direction, and the author leaves with work, not wounds.

Why this works: critiquing patterns instead of people, through falsifiable questions, turns crit from taste debate into a quality gate — and note the remedies track the hierarchy: the AI-oracle and dark-pattern fixes (safety, model/recovery, ethics) landed before the layout polish.

Section: Definitions of Done (DoDs)

Example 7 — DoD (the concept)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Ship criteria for a risk domain — DoDs convert values into ship gates; thresholds adapt to risk, but categories are never skipped, and “design approved” without DoD review is theater.

Scenario — how DoDs get wired into practice. At “Lumen” (Example 1), every Wednesday gate agenda ends with a six-line DoD roll call: Auth · Privacy · Interrupt · Content · Activation · Support — met, waived-with-owner, or blocking? A waiver is legal but loud: “Activation DoD waived for this slice by Marta (PM), Wednesday 2026-07-15 gate, revisit at GA” goes in the decision log. What is never legal is silence — an unchecked category defaults to blocking, mirroring “gates need defaults — usually do not ship.”

One roll call, verbatim (Lumen’s Wednesday 2026-07-15 gate, on the fix-category sheet):

Priya: “DoD roll call. Auth?” — Tomás: “Met — no change to the session model.”
Priya: “Privacy?” — Tomás: “Met — correction events retain no merchant history past 90 days.”
Priya: “Interrupt?” — Priya: “Met as of Tuesday — draft corrections survive a phone call; resume point verified.”
Priya: “Content?” — Sam: “Met — provenance line ships: ‘Labeled Entertainment because the merchant matched Ticketmaster.’“
Priya: “Activation?” — Marta: “Waived for this slice — first-run flow untouched. Waiver logged with my name and a GA revisit.”
Priya: “Support?” — (silence — the support lead is out sick and nobody prepared the category) — Priya: “Then Support is blocking by default. An unanswered category is not a passed category. Tomás owns matching macros to the new sheet copy by Friday 10 a.m., or the slice waits.”

The unchecked category did not slide through as accidental yes; it defaulted to blocking, with a named owner and a date. The six sub-examples below show each domain’s DoD catching a real gap.

Example 7a — Auth DoD

Definition: Clear session actor; recovery paths; shared-device logout; no secret leakage in URLs or notifications; step-up auth for sensitive actions.

Scenario — “KinBank,” a family banking app used on shared tablets. BAD: the teen and parent profiles share one session; the lock-screen notification reads “Transfer of $2,400 to Marcus approved — tap to view.” Anyone holding the tablet sees the amount, and password reset links carry a session token in the URL, which lands in the family’s shared browser history. GOOD after DoD review: profile switcher shows the session actor by name and avatar on every money screen (“Acting as: Dana”); lock-screen copy becomes “KinBank: You have a new account update”; reset links are single-use with no token in the visible URL; and transfers over $500 require step-up auth — Face ID plus “Confirm you’re Dana.” Shared-device logout: “Log out of all devices” verified to kill the tablet session within 10 seconds. Why this works: the Auth DoD treats shared devices and notification leakage as ship criteria, not QA niceties.

Example 7b — Privacy DoD

Definition: Data minimization; purpose limitation stated; consent where required; retention known; third-party sharing diagrammed; user-visible controls work.

Scenario — “Cyclia,” a period-tracking app (health, privacy-critical). BAD: onboarding requests location “to improve predictions,” retention is “indefinite,” and an analytics SDK receives symptom logs nobody diagrammed. GOOD after DoD review: data minimization drops location entirely (predictions never used it); purpose limitation is stated in-flow — “Your cycle data is used only to generate predictions on this device. It is never sold or shared.”; retention is user-set (“Keep history: 12 months / Forever / Delete on export”); the third-party sharing diagram shows exactly one processor (crash reporting, no health fields) and is reviewed at the gate; and the control “Delete all my data” is tested end-to-end — backend deletion confirmed within 24 hours, verified with a support-visible receipt ID. Why this works: every clause of the Privacy DoD becomes a checkable gate item, so consent and controls are working software, not policy prose.

Example 7c — Interrupt DoD

Definition: Draft durability; resume points; irreversible actions protected under hurried use; notifications safe on lock screen.

Scenario — “FieldFix,” an offline-capable inspection app for utility technicians. BAD: a technician is 40 minutes into a gas-leak inspection form when a phone call interrupts; returning to the app shows a fresh blank form — the draft is gone — and the hurried tech, redoing it in the rain, fat-fingers “Close ticket as resolved,” which is irreversible and unguarded. GOOD after DoD review: drafts autosave every field change to local storage (draft-saved state chip: “Saved offline · will sync”); reopening the app lands on a resume point — “Resume inspection #4417 (Section 3 of 5)?”; “Close as resolved” under hurried use requires a typed confirmation of the ticket number plus a 30-second Undo toast; and lock-screen notifications say “1 inspection pending sync” rather than exposing the site address. Why this works: the Interrupt DoD assumes real-world interruption and hurry — mental model and recovery outrank throughput.

Example 7d — Content DoD

Definition: Source/provenance for claims; localization plan; empty states; harmful/unsafe content handling; editable AI proposals.

Scenario — “Statuary,” a team status-update tool with AI-drafted weekly summaries. BAD: the AI summary states “Deployment failures dropped 40% this week” with no source; the empty state is a blank white screen; the Spanish localization is machine-translated with the button “Someter” (a mistranslation of “Submit”); and a summary once repeated a teammate’s private health mention from a DM-synced channel. GOOD after DoD review: every AI claim carries provenance — “Based on 12 updates and the #deploys channel · View sources”; the AI draft opens in an editor with “Edit draft” primary and “Post as-is” secondary (editable AI proposals); the empty state teaches — “No updates yet. Summaries appear after your team posts 3 updates.”; localization has a reviewed glossary (“Enviar,” not “Someter”); and a sensitive-content filter blocks health/HR terms from summaries with a named state, summary-redacted, explaining “Some content was excluded from this summary.” Why this works: the Content DoD makes provenance, editability, and safety of generated content ship criteria for any AI path.

Example 7e — Activation DoD

Definition: First-value path measurable; time-to-value target; dead ends instrumented; support escape hatch on first-run failure.

Scenario — “LedgerLite,” a receipt-scanning bookkeeping app for sole traders. BAD: first-value is undefined; 37% of new users hit the camera-permission-denied state, which shows only “Error: camera unavailable” — a dead end with no instrumentation and no way out. GOOD after DoD review: first value is defined and measured — “first receipt scanned and categorized,” with a time-to-value target of under 3 minutes from install (currently median 4:10); the event dictionary gains activation.dead_end.camera_denied so the funnel shows exactly where users stall; the denied state becomes recoverable — “Camera access is off. You can also add your first receipt by uploading a photo” with “Upload instead”; and a support escape hatch appears on any first-run failure: “Stuck? Chat with us” carrying the session’s diagnostic ID. Two weeks later, day-one activation moves from 52% to 64%. Why this works: the Activation DoD turns “onboarding is nice” into measurable ship criteria — instrumented dead ends and an escape hatch, so first-run failure is diagnosable and recoverable.

Example 7f — Support DoD

Definition: Failure modes diagnosable; logs/IDs users can cite; macros match UI language; known defects documented before launch.

Scenario — “Transitly,” a city transit ticketing app (gov-adjacent) launching offline ticket validation. BAD: when validation fails on the bus, the app shows “Something went wrong (code -1)”; the rider calls support, which has never heard of offline validation and whose macro says “please check your Wallet pass” — a feature Transitly doesn’t have. Nobody can diagnose anything; the rider pays a fine. GOOD after DoD review: every failure mode gets a named, user-citable state — “Ticket couldn’t validate offline. Show this code to the driver: TVAL-7F3K” — and the same failure name, validation.offline.clock_skew, appears in the event dictionary, the analytics dashboard, and the support console (per the checklist: “Support and analytics can see the same failure names”); macros are rewritten to match UI language word-for-word; and the two known defects (clock-skew failures on Android 13, double-scan on some readers) are documented in the support wiki before launch, with workarounds. First-week ticket resolution time: 9 minutes median instead of the projected 40. Why this works: the Support DoD means shipping includes the ability to diagnose and repair in the field — done isn’t done until support can see what users see.

Section: Worked Case Method

Example 8 — Worked Case

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A blameless, six-part post-incident learning artifact — case brief, timeline, evidence, principle failure, repair, teaching artifact — run monthly to turn incidents into durable practice.

Scenario — “Trailhand,” a field-sales CRM with offline/queued sync. The incident: 83 sales reps lost edited customer notes during a regional outage.

The team runs the worked case three weeks later, blameless framing stated up front by the facilitator: “We are studying the system that made this easy, not the people who touched it.”

  1. Case brief (user harm, not only downtime). During a 6-hour carrier outage, reps kept editing customer notes offline. On reconnect, the sync service resolved conflicts server-wins, silently discarding 1,204 offline edits across 83 reps. Harm: reps re-entered notes from memory; at least 11 customer commitments (“agreed to net-60 terms”) were lost, and two customers were promised conflicting prices. The harm was trust and money, not uptime.
  2. Timeline (decisions and skipped gates). May 6: conflict-resolution design marked “later” in crit. May 20: the Wednesday gate on offline conflict handling was skipped because the decider was traveling — no default was recorded, so the slice proceeded (silence became accidental yes). June 2: shipped. June 30: outage.
  3. Evidence (knew vs. assumed). Knew: 22% of sessions occur offline (analytics). Assumed: “conflicting edits are rare” — never tested; the assumption was on the Chapter 7 map but had no owner.
  4. Principle failure. The Interrupt DoD (draft durability, resume points) was checked for app interruption but never applied to sync conflict; and the gate lacked a default — violating “gates need defaults — usually do not ship.”
  5. Repair (product + process). Product: conflict state sync-conflict-detected with UI — “This note changed on another device while you were offline. Keep yours, keep theirs, or merge?” — plus a 30-day recoverable archive of discarded versions (“Restore previous version”). Process: every gate on the calendar now carries a written default; the screener for the next research round recruits reps who work offline weekly; the event dictionary adds sync.conflict.resolved.{mine,theirs,merged}.
  6. Teaching artifact. One paragraph and one new row added to the living anti-pattern table: “Sync roulette — Symptom: offline edits resolved silently — Critique question: who loses data, and do they know? — Remedy: conflict UI + recoverable archive.” The Monday loop’s risk scan now includes “queued sync paths?”

BAD version (for contrast): a postmortem titled “Sync Incident RCA” that identifies “human error by the sync engineer,” assigns a remediation ticket that ages out, and changes no gate, screener, or checklist. Blame was assigned; nothing was learned. Learning dies under humiliation.

Why this works: the six-part method converts one incident into three durable process changes and a taught anti-pattern — every serious failure becomes a taught case, and blameless framing keeps the knowledge flowing.

Section: Compact Operating Checklist

Example 9 — Compact Operating Checklist

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A pre-“ready” checklist that keeps teams honest under schedule pressure — run before you call something ready, with the launch default set to no if gate evidence is missing.

Scenario — “Mural Notes,” a collaboration whiteboard app, is five days from launching “AI Meeting Recap” (AI-generated action items from board activity), and the launch date is already announced. Under exactly the schedule pressure the checklist exists for, the EM runs it line by line in Thursday’s gate:

  • [x] One-pager current — updated Tuesday with the narrowed scope (recaps for boards ≤ 50 objects).
  • [x] Monday loop owners named; midweek gates dated — this gate is on the calendar; decider: design lead.
  • [x] Priority stack forced-rank — recap is the sole P0; “board templates v3” displacement recorded.
  • [ ] Evidence bar met for high-risk claims — FAIL. The claim “recaps correctly attribute action items to people” rests on 2 internal dogfood sessions; the bar requires 5 external. Not waived.
  • [x] Event dictionary updated — recap.generation_failed, recap.item_edited, recap.item_deleted added.
  • [ ] DoDs checked — Content ⚠️. Provenance link (“From sticky note in ‘Q3 Planning’ frame”) works, but AI proposals are not yet editable inline — “Edit item” ships in the build landing tomorrow; re-verify at Friday 10 a.m. mini-gate.
  • [x] AI paths: propose→confirm→apply — recap opens as a draft (“Review recap before sharing — AI-generated from board activity”), “Share to channel” requires explicit confirm; abort mid-generation works; eval set of 150 boards, 96% attribution accuracy.
  • [x] Mobile/offline/shared-device states designed, not promised — offline state recap-unavailable-offline copy: “Recaps need a connection. Your board is saved.”
  • [x] Latency bands accounted for — generation p90 is 14s; the UI shows progressive status (“Reading 32 notes…”) with a Cancel button rather than a spinner.
  • [x] Crit used anti-pattern table; open issues ticketed — Thursday crit caught a dashboard-hero recap screen; ticket MN-2141.
  • [x] Support and analytics see the same failure names — recap.generation_failed appears in both.
  • [x] Launch default is no if gate evidence missing — evidence is missing (two unchecked boxes), so the default applies: as of this gate, the plan of record is a one-week slip.

Outcome: the EM does not “gate it later.” With two boxes failed, the default is not a threat held in reserve — it is the plan: a one-week slip, with the announcement drafted for Friday noon. The announced date can be rescued, not assumed: if Friday’s 10 a.m. mini-gate shows both bars met — 5 external sessions passing on the attribution claim, and the inline “Edit item” build verified — the slip announcement is torn up and launch proceeds. If either misses, the drafted announcement goes out as written. The checklist made that conversation happen five days early instead of on launch morning.

BAD version (for contrast): under the same announced-date pressure, the EM skips the checklist — “we’ll gate it later; the date’s already public.” The attribution claim ships on two dogfood sessions, recaps mis-attribute action items in customer channels during launch week, and the team discovers the missing editable-proposals state from an angry support ticket instead of a gate. “We’ll gate it later” became launch day, exactly as the chapter’s anti-pattern list predicts.

Why this works: the checklist operationalizes the whole chapter under pressure — cadence, stack, DoDs, AI safeguards, offline states, and a “default is no” launch posture — so quality remains the path of least resistance precisely when schedule pressure tempts the team to skip it.

Nine sections, seven key terms, fifteen example entries — Ex. 1–9 plus 7a–7f, of which Ex. 7 is a concept overview and the other fourteen are worked scenarios. Cadence beats inspiration; write it down or it did not happen.

Chapter 10 Worked Examples — Case Studies and Capstone Practice

Chapter 10 is where the book’s methods stop being separate lenses and become one act of judgment: read a failure, name the harm, repair the critical path, prove it with honest metrics, and change the process so it cannot silently recur. The worked examples below give each teachable concept of the chapter — every numbered section’s core ideas plus every Key Term — its own concrete, modern scenario (2024–2026 era: mobile-first, AI-assisted, offline-capable, privacy-conscious). Products and domains vary deliberately so no single scenario carries the chapter. Every example honors the priority hierarchy (safety → model/recovery → inclusion → outcomes → systems → delight) and uses the chapter’s vocabulary exactly.

Key Terms already embodied by a section concept are merged into a single example, per the chapter’s own rule against duplication; the coverage map shows every mapping.
