Principle 3 — Redesign resume, confirm, and conflict states Resume points, hard confirms, and conflict UX — not only happy paths 7, 8, 12
Principle 4 — Metrics must detect silent failure and wrongful automation (Mapped above with Case C) 11
Principle 5 — Every case ends in a process fix Durable checklist / screener / anti-pattern-table changes 6, 17
Principle 6 — Capstones practice operating cadence Gates, priority stacks, and evidence over slide craft 15, 16

Section: How to Work a Case (Student Method)

Example 1 — Worked Case (Key Term: worked case)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A structured teaching artifact that moves from user harm to process repair, following the Chapter 9 sequence: brief → lens analysis → redesign → metrics → discussion.

Scenario. A student team writes a worked case about PayLoop, a mobile budgeting app whose “Autopay rules” feature double-paid a utility bill.

BAD (postmortem, not a worked case): PayLoop’s own internal postmortem opens with the stack trace, names the root cause as “user initiated a manual payment while an autopay rule was pending” — quietly blaming Darnell’s behavior — never restates the harm in human terms, and closes with “engineers reminded to check for race conditions.” No lens analysis, no metric, no discussion question, no process change: nothing prevents the next coupled-writers bug from shipping.

GOOD (their case document, in the five required parts):

  1. Brief. “Darnell, 62, on a fixed income, creates an autopay rule for his electric bill. A sync race between the rule engine and a manual payment he made the same morning sends two $214 payments. His checking account overdrafts; the bank charges $35. The app’s history shows one payment.” Harm restated in one sentence before any UI debate: “A user on a fixed income was overdrafted by software that then hid the evidence.”
  2. Lens analysis. HCD: the conceptual model “one bill, one payment” was violated with no visible reconciliation. IxD: no feedback that a rule and a manual payment collided. Inclusive: fixed-income users have zero slack for duplicate withdrawals — this is a safety-tier failure, not an inconvenience. Strategy: “autopay adoption” was the KPI; overdraft complaints landed in a different team’s queue.
  3. Redesign. Duplicate-payment guard on the critical path: before executing, the rule engine checks for same-payee payments within 72 hours and holds with the notice “We paused this autopay — you already paid Ridgeline Electric $214.00 on May 3. Send anyway / Skip this month.” History shows both attempts with states Executed and Held — possible duplicate.
  4. Metrics. Leading: duplicate-payment holds triggered per 1,000 rules; % of holds resolved in-app within 24h. Lagging: overdraft-adjacent support tickets per month (baseline 41 → target < 10).
  5. Discussion. “Should the guard default to Skip or Hold? Who owns harm that appears in bank fees, outside our product’s walls?”

Why this works: The case is a teaching artifact, not a postmortem — where the BAD version blames the user and files itself away, the worked case restates harm first and ends with judgment questions and a process repair, exactly the chapter’s arc from user harm to process fix.

Example 2 — Lens Analysis (Key Term: lens analysis)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Reading a single failure through four frames at once — HCD, IxD, Inclusive Design, and Strategy — so no lens’s blind spot decides the redesign alone.

Scenario. Verdant Health, a telehealth app, ships an AI-assisted “Request refill” flow. Rosa requests a blood-pressure refill; the AI intake asks three questions, then displays “Request sent to Dr. Okafor.” In reality it created a draft message the physician never sees unless she opens a “Pending intakes” tab. Rosa runs out of medication for four days.

BAD (single-lens read): The IxD-only review concludes “the confirmation copy is misleading — change ‘sent’ to ‘submitted.’” Copy tweak ships; drafts still rot in the hidden tab.

GOOD (four-lens read):

  • HCD: Rosa’s conceptual model is “my request is in the doctor’s hands.” The system’s model is “a draft exists in a queue nobody polls.” Repair the model, not the adjective.
  • IxD: Gulf of evaluation — no status object Rosa can check. Add states: Received → Under review → Approved → Sent to pharmacy, each visible on a “Your request” card.
  • Inclusive: Patients managing chronic conditions with limited English proficiency cannot chase a hidden queue; medication lapse is a safety-tier harm, top of the priority hierarchy.
  • Strategy: The clinic’s KPI was “intakes automated %” — the queue backlog was invisible in dashboards. Add “median time from request to clinician view” as a paired guardrail metric.

The four-lens redesign: an SLA timer that escalates any intake unviewed after 24 hours to the clinic’s triage nurse, with patient-visible status and a plain-language push: “Dr. Okafor hasn’t reviewed your refill yet. We’ve flagged it to the care team.”

Metrics. Median time from request to clinician view (the guardrail paired with “intakes automated %”); % of intakes escalated by the 24-hour SLA timer; medication-lapse reports per 1,000 refill requests.

Why this works: Only the combined lenses reveal that the failure spans model, feedback, equity, and incentives — the chapter’s warning that one failure usually spans multiple frames, and single-lens fixes become copy tweaks.

Example 3 — Naming Which DoDs Failed

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Step 2 of the student method — before redesigning, explicitly name which Definitions of Done (auth, privacy, interrupt, content, activation, support, AI) the broken experience violates.

Scenario. A state benefits portal, MyBenefits, launches a SNAP renewal flow. A caseworker audit finds a renewal that silently failed for Tran, whose benefits lapsed. The student team’s DoD audit, one row per domain:

DoD Pass/Fail Evidence
Auth Fail Session expires at 15 min with no warning; renewal form data is discarded on re-login.
Privacy Fail Case number and benefit amount appear in the browser tab title, visible on shared library computers.
Interrupt Fail No draft durability — closing the tab mid-renewal loses 40 minutes of document uploads.
Content Fail Rejection reason reads “Error E-4471”; support script cannot map it to a fix.
Activation Pass First-run explains required documents before starting.
Support Fail The failure screen offers no citeable ID; call-center agents cannot find Tran’s attempt.
AI N/A No AI features on this path.

The named failures set the redesign order: Interrupt and Auth first (recovery), then Support and Content (citable IDs — “Reference R-88213, we saved your documents”), then Privacy (generic tab title “MyBenefits”).

Why this works: Naming DoDs converts a vague “the renewal is broken” into an ordered, checkable repair list — the chapter’s point that one failure usually spans multiple DoDs, and you cannot fix what you have not named.

Example 4 — Critical Path (Key Term: critical path)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The minimum path to complete the user’s job under constraint — the thing you redesign first; polish comes later.

Scenario. TransitGo, a metro ticketing app, is redesigning after riders miss trains fumbling with the app at the fare gate. The user’s job under constraint: prove I have a valid fare, one-handed, in under 5 seconds, possibly with no signal underground.

BAD (polish-first): The team’s sprint plan opens with a rebranded home screen, animated route illustrations, and an AI trip-planning chat. The ticket QR code remains three taps deep behind a promo carousel, and it fails to render offline. Gate-line dwell time is unchanged; support logs still show “app stuck loading at gate.”

GOOD (critical path first): Forced ranking puts the fare-proof moment at #1. Redesign: the active ticket is the app’s launch state (“Your pass · Zone 1–2 · Valid · works offline”), QR pre-cached and rendered from local storage, screen brightness auto-boosts at the gate, one-handed reach verified on a 6.7” device. Offline state copy: “No signal — your pass still works.” Only after gate-line task success hits 98% in field testing does the team schedule the illustration polish.

Metrics. Time from app-open to scannable fare (median 1.4s, p95 3.9s); % of fare displays that succeed with airplane mode on (target 100%); missed-scan complaints per 10k rides.

Why this works: It applies the chapter’s rule directly — redesign the critical path first; delight (illustrations, AI chat) is the last layer of the priority hierarchy, never a substitute for the job.

Example 5 — Leading and Lagging Metrics That Measure Recovery, Inclusion, and Trust

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Step 4 of the student method — pick two leading and one lagging metric, chosen to detect recovery, inclusion, and trust rather than vanity engagement.

Scenario. Ledgerly, a mobile tax-filing product, adds an AI “Deduction finder.” The growth team proposes measuring “deductions suggested per user” and “minutes in app.”

BAD (vanity set): Both metrics rise when the AI suggests aggressive, low-confidence deductions users must untangle. Engagement up, audit risk up, trust down — the metrics reward the harm.

GOOD (recovery / inclusion / trust set):

  • Leading 1 (recovery): % of AI-suggested deductions the user edits or rejects before filing, segmented by confidence band. A healthy propose-and-review loop shows meaningful edit rates on low-confidence items; near-zero edits signal rubber-stamping.
  • Leading 2 (inclusion): Task success rate for “review and remove a suggested deduction” with screen reader and keyboard-only, within an agreed band of the mouse baseline (≤ 1.3× time-on-task).
  • Lagging (trust): Post-filing trust pulse — “I understand why each deduction was suggested” (5-point scale, target ≥ 4.2).

That is the complete worked set: two leading, one lagging, exactly as the method requires. The amended-return rate attributable to AI suggestions (target < 0.5%) is also tracked — but as a paired harm guardrail on the dashboard, not smuggled in as a second lagging metric. The dashboard sketch pairs each leading metric with the harm it predicts, so a rising number can never be read as unambiguously good.

Why this works: It fulfills Learning Objective 3 — outcome metrics that measure recovery, inclusion, and trust, not vanity engagement — and gives the midweek gate real evidence to rule on.

Example 6 — Process Fix / Teaching Artifact (Key Term: teaching artifact)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A durable change to a checklist, screener, or anti-pattern table — step 5 of the method — so the failure cannot silently recur; every case ends in one, or it will recur.

Scenario. Forgeline, a CI/CD developer tool, ships a “Rollback” button that, in one incident, rolled back the database migration along with the app version, destroying six hours of customer writes. The incident review produces a fix (rollback now excludes migrations by default) — but the team’s worked case is not done until it produces a teaching artifact.

BAD (no artifact): The fix ships; the postmortem doc is filed in a drive folder. Eight months later a new “Restore environment” feature repeats the same coupled-destruction pattern, built by an engineer who never saw the postmortem.

GOOD (three durable artifacts):

  1. Checklist row added to the release DoD: “Any destructive or bulk action: does the confirm screen enumerate everything that will change, and can each part be excluded? Sign-off required.”
  2. Anti-pattern table entry: “Coupled destruction — one control that silently mutates more than one system of record. Detection: confirm copy uses a vague plural (‘roll back changes’). Repair: itemized confirm with per-item opt-out.”
  3. Screener amendment: usability rounds for destructive flows must include one participant who is an on-call operator recruited mid-incident-fatigue conditions (recently paged), because tired operators are the real users of rollback.

Each artifact lives where work happens — the DoD checklist in the PR template, the anti-pattern table in the design-review doc — not in a postmortem archive.

Metrics. Recurrence of the coupled-destruction pattern in incident reviews (target 0); % of destructive-flow PRs with the itemized-confirm checklist row signed off; % of destructive-flow usability rounds that included a recently-paged operator.

Why this works: The chapter’s Principle 5 verbatim — every case ends in a process fix, or it will recur — and the fix is durable precisely because it changes checklists, screeners, and the anti-pattern table rather than one feature.

Section: Case A — Mobile Interrupted Delivery-Time Modification

Example 7 — Draft Durability and Resume Point Under Interruption (Interrupt DoD)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Persisting in-progress work as a local draft and reopening the exact step on return, so interruption — the default mobile condition — never destroys or falsifies user intent.

Scenario. ClaimSnap, a home-insurance app, lets policyholders file a storm-damage claim with photos. Priya starts a claim on her porch: 7 photos uploaded, damage description half-typed. Her toddler cries; the phone sits locked for 20 minutes; iOS evicts the app from memory.

BAD: On relaunch, ClaimSnap opens its home screen. The claim wizard restarts at step 1 of 5. Photos are gone (“uploads” were held in memory). Priya re-shoots in fading light; 31% of users in this state abandon and file by phone instead — median call time 24 minutes.

GOOD: Every wizard input writes to a local draft within 500 ms of change (state: Draft — on this phone). On relaunch, the app opens directly to step 3 with a banner: “Welcome back — we saved your claim draft. 7 photos · description in progress.” Photos were queued to upload in the background; two that failed show “Waiting to send · Tap to retry.” A sticky status chip reads “Not submitted yet” until the final confirm, so the draft can never masquerade as a filed claim. Drafts persist 30 days and sync to the account after submission consent — not before, keeping unsubmitted damage photos on-device (privacy-conscious default).

Metrics. % of claim flows resumed after ≥ 30 s backgrounding without data loss (target ≥ 99%); abandonment-to-phone-channel rate; time-to-file for interrupted vs. uninterrupted sessions.

Why this works: It treats the one-handed, interrupted, low-attention context as the default mobile condition — Case A’s Inclusive lens — and satisfies the Interrupt DoD with draft durability and a resume point instead of hoping users finish in one sitting.

Example 8 — Durable Confirmation and the Honest Queue: Instrumenting “Assumed Success”

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Confirming success through channels that survive app death, showing honest pending states when the network fails, and instrumenting failures that leave no angry click.

Scenario. Loop & Post, an e-commerce marketplace, lets sellers schedule a courier pickup for returns. Kenji, on a train with patchy 5G, taps “Schedule pickup — Thu 2–4pm.” The request POST times out as the train enters a tunnel.

BAD (assumed success): A spinner flashes, then the screen goes back to the returns list. Kenji assumes it worked — he tapped it. No courier comes Thursday. Because he never saw an error, he never retried and never contacted support until Friday: the classic “assumed success” failure that leaves no angry click and therefore no event in analytics.

GOOD (honest queue + durable confirmation):

  • The request enters a visible queue with honest copy: “Waiting to send · No connection · We’ll keep trying — or tap to retry.” The pickup card shows state Pending — not yet scheduled, never a checkmark.
  • On success, confirmation is durable across three surfaces: push notification (“Pickup confirmed: Thu 2–4pm, DHL”), an in-app receipt on the order timeline, and an email with reference PU-20417 — the same ID support macros cite.
  • Instrumentation for silent failure: the client emits a submit_attempted event on tap and the server emits submit_committed on write. A nightly job diffs the two; any attempted-without-committed older than 1 hour with no visible error shown fires an alert and an apologetic proactive push: “Your pickup didn’t go through — one tap to rebook.”
  • Forgiveness vs. hard confirm — the boundary drawn: everything up to dispatch lives in forgiveness territory — Kenji can edit the window, change the address, or cancel the queued request freely, and the honest queue absorbs mistakes at no cost. But dispatching a driver is an irreversible physical-world action, so it is soft-locked behind an explicit confirm screen (“Confirm pickup: Thu 2–4pm at 12 Elm St — a DHL driver will be dispatched”) whose answer is recorded server-side and survives app death: if the train tunnel kills the app mid-confirm, relaunch reopens the same confirm step with the same details — the system never assumes yes. After the driver is en route, the card flips to “Driver dispatched — changes now require a call,” making the boundary legible to the user, not just the codebase.

Metrics. Attempted-vs-committed gap rate (target < 0.1%); confirmation-receipt open rate; support tickets tagged “courier no-show after scheduling.”

Why this works: It answers both of Case A’s discussion questions directly — you instrument “assumed success” by measuring the gap between intent and commit, and you draw the forgiveness-vs-hard-confirm line where the chapter’s redesign does: forgiveness (drafts, undo, honest queue) for everything reversible, and an explicit confirm that survives app death for irreversible driver dispatch — putting model/recovery above the delight of a fast fake checkmark.

Section: Case B — B2B Admin Invite with Screen Reader

Example 9 — Critical-Path Assistive Technology Parity

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Treating screen-reader and keyboard operability of job-critical flows as ship-blocking — exclusion is product failure, not a niche bug deferred to “phase 2 accessibility.”

Scenario. Standup.io, a team collaboration tool, has a “Reassign task” flow used by project managers: open task → “Reassign” → pick teammate → optional handover note → “Confirm reassign.” Marcus, a blind PM using NVDA, must reassign 14 tasks before a sprint boundary.

BAD: “Reassign” opens a custom popover; focus stays on the trigger button, so NVDA reads nothing. The teammate picker is a div list with no roles — arrow keys do nothing. Confirmation is a visual toast (“Task reassigned to Amara ✓”) that is never announced; the task list updates silently. Marcus asks a sighted colleague to finish — in an employment context, that is an access failure with legal weight, and the company’s next enterprise deal requests a VPAT this path cannot survive.

GOOD:

  • The popover becomes a role="dialog" labelled by its title (“Reassign task: Q3 launch checklist”), initial focus in the search field.
  • Teammate picker is a listbox with accessible names (“Amara Diallo, Design, 3 open tasks”); arrow keys + type-ahead work; Escape closes and returns focus to the trigger.
  • Errors announce via an assertive live region; success via a polite live region using the same language as the visual toast: “Task reassigned to Amara Diallo.” A non-modal fallback page (/tasks/8841/reassign) offers the identical flow for AT users and low-end devices alike.
  • Process: the research screener now requires at least one AT user per round on any access-control or assignment flow, and “reassign with SR” is a midweek gate item — evidence attached, default no-ship.

Metrics. Task success with SR/keyboard-only on reassign (target = mouse baseline); time-on-task within the agreed 1.3× band; Sev1 WCAG issues on the critical path = 0; VPAT evidence current for the flow.

Why this works: It moves inclusion above outcomes in the priority hierarchy exactly as Case B demands: the job must be completable by AT users before any conversion or throughput number counts, and the fix is enforced by screener and gate, not goodwill.

Section: Case C — AI CRM Follow-Up Agent with Send Side Effects

Example 10 — Side-Effect Boundary: Propose → Confirm → Apply (Key Term: side-effect boundary)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The line where AI/agent proposals become external mutations — nothing crosses it without human confirmation, review surfaces, budget caps, and a kill switch (AI DoD).

Scenario. ShipMate, an AI release assistant for developer teams, can “prepare and publish releases”: bump versions, write changelogs, tag, publish to npm, and post release notes to customers.

BAD: An engineer types “release the payments SDK.” The agent tags v4.0.0 (it inferred a major bump from one renamed export), publishes to npm, and emails 2,300 customers release notes containing a hallucinated deprecation date. Publishing to a registry is irreversible; “undo” is a support ticket and a v4.0.1 apology release. Trust collapses inside the engineering org first — nobody lets the agent touch anything for months.

GOOD (the boundary made visible):

  • Everything up to the side-effect boundary is free: the agent drafts the changelog, computes the semver recommendation, and stages the tag — all reversible, all local.
  • At the boundary, a plan surface appears: “ShipMate proposes: ① Tag v3.9.0 (minor — 2 features, 0 breaking; disagree? see diff analysis) ② Publish to npm ③ Email release notes to 2,300 subscribers.” Each item shows data sources and confidence; the email step carries a policy flag: “⚠ 14 recipients are on active support escalations.”
  • Propose → confirm → apply: publishing requires an explicit typed confirm (“type the version to publish”); the customer email is a separate confirm with per-recipient review and is default = draft-only. Bulk send requires step-up confirmation and respects a budget cap (max 1 external blast/day).
  • An activity log records every applied action with one-click revoke where the provider allows (unpublish window, email recall); a global kill switch (“Pause all agent actions”) sits in the header. The evaluation set includes known hard cases: repos with renamed exports, dispute-tagged customers, and hallucinated-deprecation probes.
  • Midweek gate question, answered with evidence: “May the agent apply without human confirm?” Default = no.

Metrics. % of agent outputs human-edited before apply; wrongful-publish rate; time-to-revoke; engineer trust pulse.

Why this works: It draws Case C’s side-effect boundary as an explicit UI and policy line — the agent is framed as proposing accountable drafts, never “acting as me,” with safety and recovery ranked above the outcome metric of releases shipped.

Example 11 — Metric Theater and Wrongful-Automation Detection

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Refusing metrics that reward blast radius; choosing measures that detect silent failure and wrongful automation instead of celebrating activity.

Scenario. Currents, a news app, launches “AI Morning Brief” — an auto-generated audio summary of each user’s followed topics.

BAD (metric theater): The team’s north star is “briefs played per user per week.” The AI learns (via a bandit over headline styles) that alarmist framings boost plays. Plays climb 34% quarter over quarter; meanwhile, correction requests triple and a fabricated quote about a local election official circulates for six hours. The dashboard is green the entire time — the metric selected for harm, exactly the chapter’s “metric theater” failure. Two obvious gaming strategies the team never adversarially reviewed: auto-playing briefs on app open (plays without listening), and stretching briefs with filler (minutes without value).

GOOD (anti-gaming, harm-detecting set):

  • Wrongful-automation rate: corrections issued per 1,000 brief segments, with a hard threshold that pauses the feature per-topic (“Election coverage briefs paused pending review”) — a kill-switch metric, not a dashboard vanity.
  • Silent-failure detector: % of briefs containing claims that fail retrieval-grounding checks against cited sources, sampled daily by an automated eval set including known hard cases (breaking news, low-source-count topics).
  • Trust pair: “brief completed and source article opened” replaces raw plays — listening that leads to verification counts; autoplay impressions do not (plays with < 5 s listen are excluded).
  • Every activity metric on the dashboard is displayed with its paired harm metric; a green activity number with a red harm pair blocks the weekly ship review.

Metrics. Corrections issued per 1,000 brief segments (with the per-topic pause threshold); grounding-check failure rate on the daily sampled eval; completed-and-source-opened rate (replacing raw plays); time from harm-threshold breach to per-topic pause.

Why this works: It operationalizes Principle 4 — metrics must detect silent failure and wrongful automation — and answers Case C’s discussion prompt about stopping metric theater from selecting for harm by pairing every reward metric with the harm it can hide.

Section: Case D — Offline / Shared Handheld Field Inventory

Example 12 — Offline-First Explicit Sync States and Conflict Resolution UX

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Making local-vs-server truth visible with named sync states, and resolving conflicts with visibility — never auto-dropping data — so “Saved” never lies.

Scenario. VisitNote, an app for home-health nurses, records vitals and medication administration during visits — often in basements and rural areas with no signal.

BAD (optimistic lie): Nurse Aisha records “Warfarin 5 mg administered 10:12” in a dead zone. The app shows a checkmark instantly (optimistic UI). At sync, the record conflicts with an office-side edit to the same visit and is silently dropped as the “loser.” The chart now shows no dose given; the evening nurse administers Warfarin again. This is the safety tier of the priority hierarchy — the lie about “Saved” becomes a double-dose risk.

GOOD (explicit states, visible conflicts):

  • Every record carries a visible state chip: On device → Pending → Synced → Conflict. The medication entry shows “On device — will sync when connected”; a checkmark appears only at Synced.
  • The sync queue is inspectable: “3 records pending · last sync 10:47 · Sync now.”
  • On conflict, nothing is dropped. A conflict screen shows both versions side by side with timestamp, actor, and location: “You recorded Warfarin 5 mg, 10:12, at patient home · Office recorded visit rescheduled, 10:05, at clinic. Keep both and flag for supervisor review (default) / Keep mine / Keep office version.” Medication records can never lose to a scheduling edit; conflict class determines allowed resolutions.
  • Support DoD honored: every failed sync generates a citeable ID (“Sync issue S-3092”) that the help desk sees verbatim.

Metrics. Sync-success within a 15-minute SLA once connectivity returns; conflict resolution time; records lost to sync = 0 (audited); double-documentation incidents.

Why this works: It replaces Case D’s optimistic UI with an honest pending model — the conceptual model of local vs. server truth made visible — and treats conflict resolution as a designed state, ranking safety and model/recovery above throughput.

Example 13 — Shared-Device Identity and Lock-Screen Privacy (Auth and Privacy DoDs)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): On shared devices, the acting identity is always visible, switching users is fast, sensitive actions re-authenticate, and lock-screen surfaces leak nothing.

Scenario. A community food bank runs intake on shared tablets used by rotating volunteers via IntakeDesk, a nonprofit case-management app. Clients’ records include income and household data — sensitive, and in some cases (domestic-violence relocations) genuinely dangerous to expose.

BAD (silent identity continuity): Volunteer Sam logs in at 9 a.m.; the session never expires. At 1 p.m., volunteer Lee picks up the tablet and — still as Sam — edits records; the audit log is now fiction. The tablet’s lock screen shows notification previews: “New note on Maria G.: relocated after DV incident, new addr…” visible to anyone in the intake line.

GOOD:

  • A persistent header chip shows the session actor: “Acting as Sam R. · Switch user.” Switch-user is two taps + PIN (≤ 5 seconds, tested with gloves and glare in mind — the operating environment, not an edge case).
  • Auto-lock after 90 seconds idle; reopening any record marked sensitive requires PIN re-entry (“quick lock + PIN on sensitivity”).
  • Lock-screen notifications are minimized to counts only: “IntakeDesk · 2 updates” — no names, no content, ever, on a shared device profile.
  • Audit log entries carry actor, device, and timestamp; a mismatch between scheduled volunteer and session actor flags the coordinator.

Metrics. Time-to-lock after idle (p95 ≤ 90 s); accidental cross-user exposure incidents (target 0); % of record edits attributed to the correct actor in audit sampling; switch-user completion time.

Why this works: It applies Case D’s rule that shared-device patterns differ from personal-phone patterns — identity must be visible and cheap to switch, and Privacy/Auth DoDs must be working software, not paperwork, because exposure here is a safety-tier harm.

Section: Case E — Voice → Screen Multi-Modal Repair Booking

Example 14 — Handoff Object (Key Term: handoff object)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): One shared, addressable job state that every modality and device reads and writes — the cure for continuity theater.

Scenario. GridWatch, a utility’s outage service, takes reports by phone/IVR (“Press 2 to report an outage”), smart speaker, SMS, and app.

BAD (continuity theater): Dana calls at 9:02 p.m.: the IVR captures “power out, sparking line near the alley.” The call creates ticket IVR-2241. Dana then opens the app to add a photo of the sparking line — the app knows nothing about the call and starts a fresh wizard asking the same questions. Her second report becomes APP-9310. Dispatch sees two tickets, neither with both the “sparking line” detail and the photo; the crew is sent without the hazard flag. Channel metrics were siloed — IVR containment vs. app conversion — so the handoff was nobody’s P0.

GOOD (one addressable draft):

  • Every report, regardless of channel, is a single outage report object with a stable ID (OUT-55081) and slots: location, hazard flags, description, photos, callback number.
  • After the call, the IVR sends an SMS deep link: “We heard: power out at 414 Alder Ct, possible downed line — sparking. Add a photo or fix details: gridwatch.us/r/55081.” The link opens a summary of heard intent, proposed urgency (“Hazard: suspected — please confirm”), and missing slots — editable, not locked.
  • The screen confirms what voice cannot safely finalize: exact address unit and the hazard confirmation that triggers a priority dispatch. (Outage reports involve no payment step, but the chapter’s answer to “what must voice never finalize alone?” also names payment — in GridWatch’s sibling paid-service flow, booking an electrician after the outage, payment details are likewise confirmed on screen, never spoken and finalized in one breath.) Dynamic updates (“Crew assigned · ETA 45 min”) are announced to assistive technology and mirrored across SMS and app — deaf/hard-of-hearing users and voice-only users work from the same ticket model.
  • Priority stack decision on record: fund the handoff object before adding a new WhatsApp channel.

Metrics. Cross-modal resume rate (call → link opened → detail added); duplicate-ticket rate per incident (baseline 18% → target < 2%); re-ask rate on follow-up calls; time-to-dispatch from first utterance; accessibility task success on summary edit.

Why this works: It gives Case E’s “shared job object across modalities” a literal address, lets each modality do what it is safest at, and measures continuity without punishing modality switches.

Section: Capstone Project Brief (2 Weeks)

Example 15 — Capstone Gate (Key Term: capstone gate)

Definition (as this chapter uses it): A scheduled go/no-go review where evidence decides shipping and the default is no-ship.

Scenario. A capstone team of four is redesigning the “AI side effects” slice: an AI meeting assistant for Minute1, a collaboration tool, that drafts and sends action-item emails to attendees. Day 10, the scheduled gate. The gate is on the calendar from Day 4 — it cannot be quietly skipped when the demo looks shiny.

Gate agenda (45 minutes, evidence only):

  1. Question of record: “May the assistant send action-item emails without human confirm?” Default = no.
  2. Evidence presented: usability eval, n=6 (including one screen-reader participant): task success on “review and edit the AI draft before send” = 5/6; the SR participant could not reach the per-recipient remove button (Sev1). Mini eval set of 25 known hard cases: 2 hallucinated owners assigned to action items (8% wrongful-attribution rate).
  3. Decision: No-go on auto-send (evidence bar unmet: Sev1 AT blocker + wrongful attribution above the 2% threshold the team pre-registered on their one-pager). Go on draft-only mode behind propose → confirm → apply.
  4. Recorded output: DoD sign-off sheet shows AI DoD “human confirm before external send” = enforced; Inclusion DoD = blocked pending fix, re-gate scheduled Day 12.

BAD contrast: A rival team treats Day 10 as a demo rehearsal — “the gate is just a check-in” — ships auto-send because the happy path demos well, and discovers the hallucinated-owner rate from angry pilot users instead of their own eval set.

Metrics. Gates held on their scheduled date with no quiet skips (target 100%); % of gate decisions ruled against a pre-registered evidence bar; Sev1 issues caught at the gate vs. found in pilot; re-gate turnaround time for blocked items.

Why this works: The gate turns the priority hierarchy into an operating decision — safety and inclusion evidence can veto an outcome the team wants — and the default of no-ship means enthusiasm is never evidence.

Example 16 — Running the Two-Week Capstone: One-Pager, Priority Stack, Evidence-Backed Ship

Definition (as this chapter uses it): The capstone’s operating cadence — Week 1 discovery and framing (one-pager, assumption map, priority stack, gate calendar, DoD checklist), Week 2 prototype, evidence, gate, and teaching artifact — practicing process, not slide craft.

Scenario. Team “Spin Cycle” (4 students) picks the offline/interruption slice: CampusWash, their university’s laundry app, which fails in basement laundry rooms with no signal — students pay for machines that never start, and “payment processing…” spins forever.

Week 1 — Discovery & framing.
- Day 1–2, living one-pager: Problem (“students lose money and time when payments fail offline in basements”); segment (dorm residents, incl. one participant who uses VoiceOver); constraints (no hardware changes); non-goals (“no redesign of the rewards program”); success metrics (failed-payment refund tickets, resume-after-interrupt rate); open assumptions (“machines broadcast state over BLE even when Wi-Fi is dead — unverified”).
- Day 2–3: Assumption map + 5 task-based sessions in the actual basement, plus a synthesis of 90 support tickets. Key finding: 62% of failures are “assumed success” — students walk away mid-spinner.
- Day 4: Priority stack (forced rank): ① honest offline payment queue ② resume point after backgrounding ③ machine-status accuracy ④ dark mode (ranked last, explicitly delight). Midweek gate booked for Day 10. DoD checklist scoped to their risk domains: Interrupt, Support, Privacy.
- Day 5: Concept critique against the Chapter 9 anti-pattern table catches “optimistic checkmark before commit”; revised to Queued — will start machine when connected with copy “Hold on — payment not sent yet. Stay near the machine or we’ll refund automatically in 10 min.”

Week 2 — Design, evidence, ship decision.
- Day 6–8: Prototype the critical path including failure/empty/offline/interrupt states — the queued state, the auto-refund state, and the resume banner (“Your payment to Washer 12 is still queued”).
- Day 8–9: Usability eval: task success 9/10; one Sev2 (refund copy unclear); VoiceOver participant completes the queue-check task at 1.2× mouse baseline — inside band.
- Day 10: Gate passes on evidence; auto-refund logic gated in, dark mode explicitly cut.
- Day 11–12: Polish only because the gate passed; instrumentation plan (attempted-vs-committed payment diff) + support macros citing queue IDs (“Ref W12-Q-0387”).
- Day 13–14: Demo + teaching artifact: one worked-case paragraph and a checklist amendment their fictional team adopts (“Any payment flow must define its queued and auto-refund states before visual design begins”).
- Retrospective: the hardest trade-off sat at the model/recovery layer — honest queueing versus the growth instinct for an instant checkmark — and the priority hierarchy decided it.

Metrics. Attempted-vs-committed payment gap on the prototype’s instrumentation plan; resume-after-interrupt rate; failed-payment refund tickets per week in the pilot dorm (baseline 23 → target < 8); VoiceOver time-on-task within the agreed 1.3× band.

Why this works: Harm reduction and recoverability outranked visual novelty exactly as the grading emphasis demands, and the team practiced the operating cadence — gates, inclusion in research, honest metrics — that the capstone exists to teach.

Section: Turning Cases into Team Process Change (Learning Objective 4)

Example 17 — Facilitating the Case Discussion

Definition (as this chapter uses it): Learning Objective 4 — running a case discussion so it produces a durable team process change; facilitation is the bridge between a written case and an adopted fix.

Scenario. Ines, a design lead at Harborview Labs, facilitates a 50-minute discussion of the PayLoop double-payment case (Example 1) with her own payments team of eight.

BAD (case read, nothing changes): Ines presents the case as slides. The team nods (“wild that they shipped that”), someone says “we’d never do that,” and the meeting ends with “let’s be careful about race conditions.” No artifact changes. Three sprints later the team’s own scheduled-transfers feature ships without a duplicate guard — the exact failure class they discussed.

GOOD (facilitated toward process change):

  1. Pre-read + silent start. The case circulates 24 hours ahead; discussion opens with two minutes of silent writing — “Restate the harm in one sentence” — so everyone commits to a framing before the loudest voice supplies one.
  2. Lens rotation. Four people are each assigned one lens (HCD / IxD / Inclusive / Strategy) and speak in turn; Ines holds all solutioning until the fourth lens has spoken.
  3. The transfer question. After the case’s own discussion prompts, Ines asks the question that turns a case about them into a case about us: “Where in our product could two writers hit the same account state?” The team names their scheduled-transfers feature within four minutes.
  4. Commitment close. The final ten minutes are reserved for exactly one process change with an owner and a date: a new release-DoD row — “Any money-moving action: same-payee / same-amount collision check with a visible Held state” — owned by the platform lead, in the PR template by Friday.
  5. Logged where work happens. The outcome lands in the team’s DoD checklist, not in meeting notes, so the discussion leaves a teaching artifact rather than a memory.

Metrics. Process changes adopted per case discussion (target ≥ 1, each with owner and date); % of adopted changes still enforced 90 days later (audit sample); recurrence of the discussed failure class in the team’s own incident log.

Why this works: It fulfills Learning Objective 4 head-on — the discussion is engineered, not hoped, into a team process change — and it honors Principle 5: every case ends in a process fix, or it will recur, as the BAD version’s shipped duplicate-payment bug proves.

End of Chapter 10 worked examples. Seventeen examples cover all seven sections’ core concepts, all seven Key Terms, all six Principles, and Learning Objectives 3 and 4 (merged where the chapter’s own material already embodies a term).

Appendix A — Unified Glossary

Key terms from Chapters 1–10. Prefer these definitions in critiques and one-pagers.

Activation — First meaningful value for a new user; not signup alone.
Activation DoD — Ship bar for measurable first-value path and support escape hatches.
Affordance — Action possibility from object properties and actor capabilities.
Agent (AI) — Tool-chaining system; needs budgets, allowlists, and visible plans.
Anti-pattern — Recurring harmful design or process habit named for critique.
Assumption map — Beliefs under a bet, ranked by risk and ignorance.
Assistive technology (AT) — Mediating tools such as screen readers or switch input.
Audit trail — Durable who/what/when record for trust, support, and AI accountability.
Auth DoD — Ship bar for clear actor, recovery, shared-device hygiene, and step-up auth.
Blameless postmortem — Incident review aimed at systemic repair, not blame.
Capstone gate — Student/team go/no-go with a default of no-ship.
Cognitive load — Mental effort required to understand and act; design to reduce it.
Component — Reusable UI building block governed by a design system.
Conceptual model — User’s internal story of how the system works.
Conflict playbook — Steps for resolving colliding goods (e.g., growth vs. privacy).
Confirmation theater — Low-value confirms that train dismissal without safety.
Constraint — Real limit (AT, offline, shared device, latency) treated as design input.
Content DoD — Ship bar for provenance, localization, empty/unsafe states, editable AI.
Continuous discovery — Ongoing research paired with delivery, not a pre-build phase.
Critical path — Minimum path to complete the user’s job under constraint.
COGA — W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities guidance (Making Content Usable…); complementary to WCAG, not WCAG success criteria.
Dark pattern — UI that subverts user intent for business gain.
Decision log — Written record of significant product/UX decisions and reasons.
Definition of Done (DoD) — Explicit ship criteria for a risk domain.
Delight — Polish allowed only after safety, model, inclusion, and outcomes.
Design model — Designers’ intended explanation of system behavior.
Design system — Principles, tokens, components, and docs that scale craft.
Displacement — Rule that new priority-stack work must demote something explicitly.
Draft durability — Persistence of in-progress work across interrupt or handoff.
Dual-track — Running discovery and delivery in parallel so learning and shipping inform each other.
ECCD (Equity-Centered Community Design) — Co-decision with affected communities, not consult-and-discard research.
Empty state — Zero-data UI that teaches the next useful action.
Error (slip vs. mistake) — Slip: wrong action, right intent; mistake: wrong intent.
Evaluation set (AI) — Hard cases used to judge AI behavior before ship.
Evidence bar — Agreed evidence quality required to believe a claim.
Event dictionary — Shared names for failures/successes across product and support.
Feedback — Signal that an action registered and how state changed.
Focus order — Sequence in which interactive elements receive keyboard/AT focus.
Forgiveness — Reversibility after error (undo, history, soft-delete).
Generative UI — Model-produced UI fragments inside a stable shell.
Gulf of evaluation — Gap between system state and user perception/interpretation.
Gulf of execution — Gap between intention and available/discoverable actions.
Handoff object — Job state addressable across devices, channels, or modalities.
Happy path — Ideal flow without error, interrupt, or denial—insufficient alone.
Human-centered design (HCD) — Meaning, models, error, and outcomes over feature lists.
Inclusive design — Designing for diverse ability, language, device, and context.
Interaction design (IxD) — Behavior over time: flows, feedback, modes, microinteractions.
Interrupt DoD — Ship bar for drafts, resume, hurried irreversibles, safe notifications.
Job (JTBD) — Progress sought in a circumstance; frames outcomes beyond features (Christensen/Ulwick lineage).
Job story — Related writing form (“When… I want to… so I can…”); useful for stories/opportunities, not identical to full JTBD research.
Kill switch — Control that stops automation and leaves state inspectable.
Knowledge in the world — External structure (labels, constraints, history) vs. memory.
Latency band — Timing-tier heuristic (instant → out-of-band) guiding progress/cancel UX.
Live region — AT announcement mechanism for dynamic updates.
Mental model — Everyday term for conceptual model; keep teachable.
Metric theater — Vanity KPIs that do not change decisions or detect harm.
Microinteraction — Trigger–rules–feedback–modes loop (toggle, pull-to-refresh).
Midweek gate — Scheduled decision with evidence, decider, and default.
Modality — Interaction channel (touch, voice, keyboard, AT).
Monday loop — Weekly align of outcome, evidence, stack, risk, and owners (stack conflicts use the priority hierarchy).
Monetization consent — Clear pay/get/leave terms; revenue UX without dark-pattern coercion.
Multi-modal continuity — Progressing one job across channels without restart.
Non-goals — Explicitly deferred or rejected aims that protect focus.
Offline-first — Design assuming disconnection is normal, with honest sync states.
One-pager — Living brief: problem, segment, metrics, stack, assumptions, risks.
Opportunity solution tree — Links outcome → opportunities → solution experiments.
Persona of exclusion — Scenario highlighting who fails under current constraints.
Persona Spectrum — Permanent / temporary / situational capability framing (Microsoft Inclusive Design) used as a constraint generator.
Platform convention — OS/browser expected patterns that reduce learning cost.
POUR — Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust (WCAG critique vocabulary).
Priority hierarchy — Safety → model/recovery → inclusion → outcomes → systems → delight.
Priority stack — Forced-rank bets with displacement rules.
Privacy DoD — Ship bar for minimization, purpose, consent, retention, controls.
Progressive disclosure — Revealing complexity as needed without restart taxes.
Provenance — Visible basis for a claim—sources, retrieval, or “model inference.”
Propose → confirm → apply — Pattern for consequential AI/automation side effects.
RAF — Research → Assumptions → Feedback; experiments are the mechanism inside Feedback/testing.
Recovery — Paths restoring understanding and state after error or conflict.
Research screener — Recruiting criteria ensuring diverse abilities/contexts.
Resume point — Explicit place a user re-enters an interrupted flow.
Service blueprint — Frontstage/backstage map of a service over time.
Shared device — Multi-user hardware needing clear actor, lock, session hygiene.
Side-effect boundary — Where proposals become external or irreversible mutations.
Signifier — Cue showing where/how an action is available.
Stable shell — Consistent chrome containing generative or dynamic content.
State matrix — Empty/loading/error/offline/success permutations.
Streaming (AI) — Incremental output enabling early abort and steering.
Support DoD — Ship bar for diagnosable failures, citeable IDs, matching macros.
Sync conflict — Divergent local/server state needing visible resolution.
System image — What the product communicates about how it works (behavior + UI); bridges design model and user’s conceptual model.
Systems consistency — Alignment with platforms, tokens, and ops constraints.
Task success rate — Share completing a defined task without critical help.
Teaching artifact — Durable process change from a worked case.
Time-to-value — Time to first meaningful outcome under real attention.
Token (design system) — Named visual/decision value consumed by components.
Trust — Calibrated reliance via honesty, control, and recovery.
Usability severity — Rated impact of a finding used as a fix-before-ship bar.
Voice→screen handoff — Voice captures intent; screen confirms detail.
WCAG — Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (current reference: WCAG 2.2); accessibility baseline (AA usual product bar; AAA selective).
Wireframe — Low-fidelity structure for flow and hierarchy.
Wizard tax — Multi-step flow that punishes interruption with full restart.
Worked case — Harm → evidence → principle failure → repair → teaching artifact.
Wrongful send — External action without adequate confirm or policy check.

(Count: 103 terms.)
