Appendix C — Quick-Reference Checklists

C1 — Midweek Gate

  • [ ] Decision question is yes/no or A/B—not “discuss.”
  • [ ] Evidence required listed (tasks, eval set, AT, support).
  • [ ] Decider named; default if undecided = no-ship.
  • [ ] Blast radius stated; touched DoD domains checked or N/A with owner.
  • [ ] Outcome recorded; revisit date if parked.

C2 — AI Definition of Done

  • [ ] Job scoped; failure modes listed.
  • [ ] Propose → confirm → apply for consequential side effects.
  • [ ] Provenance or explicit “no source—model inference.”
  • [ ] Empty/error/refusal/abort + kill switch designed.
  • [ ] Eval set with hard cases; severity bar set.
  • [ ] Agent bounds: allowlists, budgets, activity log.
  • [ ] Latency/streaming/cancel specified; support logging ready.

C3 — Auth Definition of Done

  • [ ] Session actor always clear.
  • [ ] Login/logout/expiry recoverable; shared-device lock + switch user.
  • [ ] No secrets in URLs or lock-screen notifications.
  • [ ] Step-up auth for sensitive actions; recovery paths tested.

C4 — Privacy Definition of Done

  • [ ] Minimization + purpose limitation in plain language.
  • [ ] Honest consent; working retention/deletion/export.
  • [ ] Third-party sharing diagrammed; analytics reviewed for PII.
  • [ ] User-visible controls match real system behavior.

C5 — Priority Stack

  • [ ] Forced rank; one P0 attention consumer per squad.
  • [ ] Each item: ship, kill, or park + revisit.
  • [ ] New work displaces something (recorded).
  • [ ] Sequence by risk/learning, not stakeholder volume.
  • [ ] Critical-path AT/constraint risks are not “phase 2.”
  • [ ] Stack on the one-pager—twelve P0s = process bug.

Appendix D — Textbook Quality Scoring Rubric

Published for transparency. Target for v2.2 freeze: ≥ 90/100.

Student shorthand dimensions: Accuracy, Completeness, Practice, Modern, Coherence, Teachability, Ethics.

Dimension Wt Excellent (9–10) Adequate (6–8) Weak (0–5)
Accuracy 20 Matches canon/standards; no unsafe “best practice” Mostly sound; minor overclaims Material errors or harmful patterns endorsed
Completeness 15 Principles, terms, exercises, anti-patterns, reading Core ideas; thin practice Missing critical paths (error, AT, recovery)
Practice 20 Checklists/DoDs/cases runnable in a real week Conceptually helpful; awkward to run Theory or buzzwords only
Modern 15 Interrupt, inclusion, AI sides, offline/shared, multi-modal Light mentions Desktop happy-path only
Coherence 10 Shared vocab with hierarchy + Ch. 9 ops Minor term drift Contradicts hierarchy or DoDs
Teachability 10 Objectives, cases, capstone load-bearing Generic exercises No assessable outcomes
Ethics 10 Safety/privacy/inclusion before delight Ethics as appendix-only Engagement over harm

Method. Score each dimension 0–10; contribute (score × weight) / 10; sum to 100. Capstones may reuse this table, judging Practice by gate evidence and Teachability by the teaching artifact.

Edition rule. Any chapter < 8 on Accuracy or Ethics blocks release—regardless of total.

End of appendices. See Chapter 10 and Front Matter.

Appendix E — Shippable Accessibility Kit (WCAG 2.2 AA critical path)

Conformance levels, stated honestly

WCAG 2.2 defines three conformance levels. Level A is the floor: without it, many people cannot use the product at all (keyboard traps, missing names, unlabeled controls). Level AA is the practical shipping target for most public and enterprise products—contrast, reflow, focus visibility, target size, and consistent help. Level AAA is aspirational for most teams: valuable where feasible (e.g., enhanced authentication alternatives), but rarely a blanket release gate. Claiming “AA” means every applicable Success Criterion (SC) at A and AA is met for the scoped pages and user journeys—not that you ran an automated scan once.

This kit is a critical-path AA checklist, not a full WCAG inventory. Use it to gate release of primary flows; keep a fuller audit backlog for secondary surfaces.

Critical-path SC checklist (WCAG 2.2)

SC Level Ship question
1.1.1 Non-text Content A Meaningful images/icons have text alternatives; decorative content is hidden from AT
1.3.1 Info and Relationships A Structure (headings, lists, labels, tables) is programmatically determinable—not only visual
1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) AA Text meets 4.5:1 (normal) / 3:1 (large) against its background
1.4.4 Resize Text AA Text resizable to 200% without loss of content or function (no horizontal scroll for text alone)
1.4.10 Reflow AA Content usable at 320 CSS px width without two-dimensional scrolling (except maps, data tables, etc.)
1.4.11 Non-text Contrast AA UI components and graphical objects meet 3:1 against adjacent colors
2.1.1 Keyboard A All functionality available from keyboard
2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap A Focus can move away from every component using keyboard alone
2.4.3 Focus Order A Tab order preserves meaning and operability
2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) A Link purpose is clear from link text plus programmatically determined context
2.4.6 Headings and Labels AA Headings and labels describe topic or purpose
2.4.7 Focus Visible AA Keyboard focus indicator is visible
2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) AA Focused item is not entirely hidden by sticky headers, drawers, or cookie bars
2.5.7 Dragging Movements AA Drag-only actions have a single-pointer alternative
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) AA Pointer targets ≥ 24×24 CSS px (with allowed exceptions)
3.2.3 Consistent Navigation AA Navigational mechanisms that repeat appear in the same relative order
3.2.4 Consistent Identification AA Components with the same functionality are identified consistently
3.2.6 Consistent Help A Help mechanisms appear in the same relative order across pages
3.3.1 Error Identification A Errors are identified in text
3.3.2 Labels or Instructions A Inputs have labels/instructions
3.3.3 Error Suggestion AA Suggestions provided when known (unless security/purpose would be compromised)
3.3.7 Redundant Entry A Previously entered info is auto-filled or selectable (with allowed exceptions)
3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) AA Cognitive function tests are not required unless alternatives exist (object recognition, personal content, etc.)
3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) AAA No cognitive function test at all—note: AAA; track, don’t block AA ship unless product policy requires it
4.1.2 Name, Role, Value A Custom controls expose accessible name, role, states, and values
4.1.3 Status Messages AA Status updates are announced without moving focus

Treat failures on primary paths (auth, checkout, core create/edit, account) as release blockers. Secondary marketing pages can follow on a timed remediation track if legal/compliance allows.

Focus management recipes (point to APG)

Do not invent keyboard patterns. Implement from the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG):

  • Dialog (Modal): Open → move focus into dialog (first focusable or labeled container); Tab cycles within; Escape closes; restore focus to trigger on close. aria-modal="true"; inert or hide background.
  • Tabs: Arrow keys move between tabs; Tab moves into the active panel; selected tab has aria-selected="true"; panels linked via aria-controls / aria-labelledby.
  • Combobox: Text input + popup listbox; Arrow Down opens/moves options; Enter/Space selects per APG variant; Escape closes and returns focus to input; announce count/filter changes via live region when appropriate.

Verify with keyboard-only navigation before AT testing.

AT test script (expected outcomes)

Run on the critical path in one recent browser + OS pair each for:

  1. Screen reader (VoiceOver / NVDA / TalkBack): Every control has a spoken name and role; errors and status messages are announced; dialogs trap and restore focus correctly.
  2. Keyboard only: Complete the happy path and one error path with no mouse; focus never trapped; focus order matches reading order.
  3. Zoom / reflow: 200% zoom and ~320 px width—no loss of content or function on the critical path.
  4. Forced colors / high contrast (where available): Controls remain distinguishable; focus still visible.

Pass: Task completable with equivalent information and no WCAG critical-path SC fails above. Fail: Missing name/role, keyboard trap, invisible focus, contrast fails on primary UI, or status not announced.

COGA clarification

W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Guidance (COGA) is complementary guidance, not a set of WCAG Success Criteria. Pattern themes include: clear purpose and plain language; consistent navigation and help; enough time and reduce distractions; memory aids and avoid unnecessary recall; error prevention and recovery; and supportive authentication. Use COGA to improve inclusivity and backlog prioritization. Do not equate “we followed COGA themes” with “we ship WCAG AA.” Shipping criteria remain the numbered SCs (and applicable law).

EAA / ADA caveat

The EU Accessibility Act (EAA) and similar statutes set a legal floor for in-scope products and services; WCAG AA is often the referenced technical bar, but obligations, timelines, and scope are jurisdictional. In the U.S., ADA application to digital products remains doctrine unsettled across circuits—treat accessibility as risk management and inclusive quality, not as settled gospel that one checklist ends all liability. Seek counsel for regulated industries and public accommodations claims; this appendix is practice guidance, not legal advice.

Appendix F — Privacy & Compliance UX Ship Kit

Purpose

This kit aligns privacy UX with how the product actually processes data. Copy, flows, and settings must match backend behavior. It is UX-facing; seek counsel for legal determination of lawful bases, transfers, and DPIAs.

Lawful-basis map (UX-facing)

For each processing purpose visible in the product, record: purpose in plain language; data categories; claimed lawful basis (e.g., contract, consent, legitimate interests, legal obligation—labels vary by regime); where consent is collected in UI; and where users can withdraw or object. Designers own clarity and discoverability; counsel owns whether the basis is valid.

Rights UX

Expose or route to mechanisms for:

  • Access — see what you hold about me
  • Export — portable copy where required
  • Erase — delete or anonymize, with honest caveats (backups, legal holds)
  • Correct — fix inaccurate personal data
  • Object / restrict — object to certain processing or limit use where rights apply

Place these in account/settings or a privacy center; confirm requests; set expectations for timing. Do not promise instant erasure if the backend cannot deliver it.

Kids / teen note (when in scope)

If the product may be used by children or is directed to them, COPPA (U.S.) and age-appropriate design regimes (e.g., UK AADC-style expectations, regional equivalents) may apply. Default to privacy-preserving settings, minimize data, avoid dark-pattern nudges toward sharing, and involve counsel before launch. Out of scope products still need an honest age gate policy if falsely claiming “13+ only” while onboarding younger users.

Retention honesty

Product copy (“we delete after 30 days”) must match retention jobs, logs, and backups. If analytics linger longer, say so. Mismatch between UI promises and storage is a compliance and trust failure.

Cookies / ePrivacy as regional constraint

Cookie banners and preference centers are regional constraints (ePrivacy / national implementations, CCPA/CPRA “sale/share” controls, etc.), not a universal decoration. Load non-essential tags only after valid consent where required; honor reject as easily as accept; document tag inventory.

Privacy DoD gate checklist

  • [ ] Purpose → data → basis map reviewed for new processing
  • [ ] Rights flows tested end-to-end against real backend behavior
  • [ ] Retention statements match configured policies
  • [ ] Consent/reject UX meets regional rules for launch markets
  • [ ] Vendors/subprocessors reflected in notices where required
  • [ ] Counsel engaged for high-risk processing (sensitive data, profiling, children’s data, large-scale monitoring, cross-border transfers)
  • [ ] Incident/comms path known if breach notification UX is needed

Appendix G — AI Evaluation & Safety UX Kit

Risk tiers for AI features

Tier Examples UX / release bar
Low Rewrites, formatting, local suggestions with easy undo Lightweight eval; clear AI labeling
Medium Summaries, search ranking, recommendations affecting decisions Human review path; eval harness; provenance
High Medical/legal/finance advice, autonomous actions, agent tool use with side effects Strict confirm; audit logs; kill switch; counsel + safety review

Tier by blast radius (irreversibility, affected users, regulatory sensitivity), not by model novelty.

Propose → confirm → apply

Default pattern for consequential AI output: propose (show draft/diff), confirm (explicit user action), apply (mutate state). Never silently write high-impact changes. Keep the proposal inspectable; make reject as easy as accept.

Eval harness

Before ship and on model/prompt changes, maintain:

  • Golden sets — representative tasks with expected acceptable outputs
  • Adversarial / jailbreak cases — attempts to exfiltrate secrets, ignore policy, or escalate privileges via the UI
  • Disability / accent / low-connectivity cases — speech, captions, simplified language, offline/degraded modes; ensure AI features do not become the only path to success

Record pass/fail and regression owners. UX owns presentation of uncertainty and recovery; ML owns model metrics—both are required.

Provenance, logging / PII, kill / rollback

Show what generated the suggestion (model/feature version where useful) and allow users to dismiss. Log enough for debugging and abuse response without retaining unnecessary PII in prompts/completions. Ship a kill switch and rollback path for the feature flag or tool permissions—not only a model swap ticket.

Prompt injection as UX risk

When agents or tools browse, read email, or load user-supplied documents, treat untrusted content as hostile. UX must surface tool actions, constrain scopes, and avoid auto-trusting page text as instructions. Injection is not only a backend issue—it is a user-facing trust and control problem.

When auto-apply is allowed

Only for low blast radius actions: reversible, local, non-destructive, easily undone, and not security- or compliance-sensitive (e.g., optional grammar tint the user can clear). Anything that sends messages, moves money, deletes data, changes permissions, or notifies others requires confirm.

EU AI Act (emerging constraint)

The EU AI Act is an emerging product constraint: risk classification, transparency, and human oversight duties may apply depending on use case and role (provider vs deployer). Treat it as a roadmap input and counsel trigger, not as self-serve legal clearance from this appendix.

Appendix H — Accuracy Errata & Canon Notes (v1 → v2)

Short corrections to keep the book’s vocabulary honest:

  • Norman: Beyond “affordances,” remember the system image (how the design presents itself) and the seven stages of action (goal → plan → specify → perform → perceive → interpret → compare). Gaps between execution and evaluation explain many UX failures.
  • Priority hierarchy: The urgency/importance ordering used in this textbook is this book’s editorial policy, not a universal field canon. Teams may adopt different stacks; cite the policy explicitly when teaching.
  • JTBD schools: Distinguish Christensen (disruption / progress framing), Ulwick (Outcome-Driven Innovation / jobs-as-metrics), and job stories (When… I want… So I can…). Teresa Torres popularized continuous discovery; she is not the inventor of JTBD.
  • RAF redefined: For simplicity, RAF in v2 means Research → Assumptions → Feedback. Experiments are how assumptions are tested and feedback is obtained—not a fourth unexplained letter. (RAEF is avoided to reduce jargon churn.)
  • ResearchOps: Cite ResearchOps Community practice and practitioners in the vein of Kate Towsey—shared repositories, participant ops, knowledge systems—not invented authorities or fictional frameworks.
  • Latency bands: Perceived-performance thresholds (e.g., ~100 ms / ~1 s / ~10 s style guidance) are heuristics, not physical laws. Device, context, and expectation shift the bands.
  • Motion vs photosensitive seizure: Reduced-motion preferences and vestibular comfort are related to but distinct from photosensitive seizure risk (flashing, strobing). Do not conflate prefers-reduced-motion compliance with WCAG seizure safety (e.g., 2.3.x). Address both on purpose.

These notes supersede looser v1 phrasings where they conflict.

Appendix I — Evaluation Methods Mini-Unit

Expert inspection and light metrics catch many failures before costly research. They do not replace task-based user evidence, AT testing, or DoD gates. Use them to cheaply find issues and decide what to investigate next—not to declare a product “validated.”

1. Heuristic evaluation (Nielsen’s 10)

When useful. Early and mid design, when you need breadth over depth: wireframes, prototypes, redesigns of dense flows (forms, settings, admin). Best as a pre-filter before usability sessions or as a midweek gate when shipping a constrained change and you lack time for full research. Pair with inclusive review (keyboard, contrast, language) so “usability heuristics” do not silently exclude AT users.

Nielsen’s ten (use as critique vocabulary, not a scorecard religion): (1) visibility of system status; (2) match between system and the real world; (3) user control and freedom; (4) consistency and standards; (5) error prevention; (6) recognition rather than recall; (7) flexibility and efficiency of use; (8) aesthetic and minimalist design; (9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; (10) help and documentation.

How to run. Recruit 3–5 independent evaluators familiar with the domain or with UX method (more than five rarely pays off for inspection). Give a task set and scope (critical path only). Each evaluator inspects alone, notes issue → violated heuristic(s) → severity (cosmetic / minor / major / catastrophic), and cites location. A facilitator de-duplicates and consolidates; the team then prioritizes by user harm and frequency of independent discovery—not by who shouted loudest. Time-box: often half a day for a focused flow.

Limits. Heuristics find predicted problems, not proven ones. Experts miss novice folklore and over-flag style preferences as “minimalism violations.” Heuristic eval is weak on emotional trust, long-term adoption, and whether people want the job. It is not accessibility conformance. Never treat a clean heuristic pass as ship approval when Auth, Privacy, Interrupt, or AT DoDs are open.

2. Cognitive walkthrough

When useful. First-time or infrequent tasks where learnability matters: signup, invite, recovery, one-shot admin actions, “empty → first success.” Prefer walkthrough when the question is “Will a new user know what to do next?” rather than “Is this elegant for experts?”

Procedure. Define the user profile, the goal, and the correct action sequence. For each step, answer four questions honestly: (1) Will users try to achieve the right effect? (2) Will they notice the correct control is available? (3) Will they associate the control with the effect? (4) If they act, will feedback confirm progress? Record failure stories (what false belief or missing signifier causes a wrong turn). Fix the model, labels, and feedback—not only the layout.

Limits. Walkthroughs assume a rational, attentive newcomer following your intended path. They underplay interruption, multitasking, shared devices, and AT. They are poor for expert efficiency and for probabilistic AI outcomes. One designer walking alone becomes preference theater; use at least two people or rotate roles (actor vs. recorder).

3. SUS and SEQ — light metrics, not gospel

What they measure. The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a 10-item post-study questionnaire yielding a 0–100 score that roughly benchmarks perceived usability after defined tasks. It is not a diagnostic of which problems exist. The Single Ease Question (SEQ) asks, after each task, how easy that task felt (commonly 1–7). SEQ localizes pain to tasks; SUS summarizes the whole experience.

How to use lightly. Always pair with task success, errors, and time (or severity notes). Report SUS/SEQ with task context and sample description—never as a naked number in a slide. Use SEQ to compare tasks within a study; use SUS to track the same product slice over time under similar protocols. Treat shifts as signals to investigate, not as proof of quality.

Not gospel. Scores move with task difficulty, branding, facilitator effect, and who you recruit. A “good” SUS with failing AT paths or broken Interrupt DoD is still a fail. Do not gate releases on SUS alone; do not argue “industry average” as if it were a law. Prefer behavioral evidence and DoD checklists when harm is on the table.

4. Sample-size and evidence honesty

The “5 users” myth, caveated. Nielsen’s classic guidance—that a handful of users finds most usability issues in a narrow interface—is often true for homogenous users on a fixed task set in iterative design. It is not a universal sample size. Five convenience recruits will not represent AT users, languages, device constraints, or rare-but-catastrophic failure modes. Five sessions also do not power a quantitative claim (“conversion will rise 12%”).

When you need more. Add people when: segments diverge (novice vs. admin; permanent vs. situational disability); stakes are high (money, health, auth, irreversible AI side effects); you are comparing alternatives statistically; or prior rounds keep surfacing new issue classes. For inclusion, screen for constraints, not only headcount.

Saturation vs. power (high level). Qualitative saturation means new sessions stop adding meaningful themes for this research question—stop or refocus, don’t pad. Quantitative power means you have enough observations to detect a decision-relevant difference with acceptable uncertainty—usually far more than a lab week. Do not invent fake formulas in critiques. State your evidence bar (Chapter 7): what claim type requires which method and scale. Prefer honest “we don’t know yet” over theatrical confidence intervals on n = 6.

5. A/B test literacy

Primary metric + guardrails. Pick one primary metric tied to the job (e.g., task completion, successful refund, verified invite)—not vanity clicks. Pre-commit guardrails: error rate, support contacts, accessibility regressions, latency, opt-out, refund/chargeback, or trust complaints. A “win” that breaches a guardrail is a loss.

Peeking. Repeatedly checking results and stopping when “green” inflates false wins. Prefer a pre-registered duration or sample, or sequential methods designed for interim looks. If leadership peeks, treat early lifts as hypotheses, not ship orders.

Ethics. Do not A/B dark patterns, coercive consent, or hidden fees. Exclude or protect vulnerable flows (auth recovery, medical, financial irreversibles) unless risk review passes. Log who is in which arm for support. Respect privacy minimization. An experiment that improves a metric by harming users fails the book’s priority hierarchy regardless of p-values.

Mini-unit takeaway. Inspection finds cheap issues; walkthroughs stress learnability; SUS/SEQ summarize perception; sample size must match claim type; experiments need a primary metric, guardrails, disciplined stopping, and ethics. Wire all of them to midweek gates and DoDs—methods without ship criteria are theater.

Appendix J — Classical HCI Notes (short)

Fitts’s law (pointing difficulty). Pointing time grows with distance to a target and shrinks as the target gets larger (classically: harder to hit small, far controls). Use as layout intuition: enlarge primary actions, bring frequent targets closer, avoid tiny hit areas at screen edges on touch, and respect WCAG target-size thinking. Sticky headers that cover focus, icon-only toolbars with 16px targets, and “confirm” buried across a long scroll all fail the same intuition. Do not plug product screens into textbook formulas and declare a critique “scientific.” Device, input method, tremor, and occlusion change the story—measure when stakes are high.

Worked intuition (Fitts) — tiny touch targets. A field-ops inventory app puts “Mark received” as a 14×14 px glyph beside each line item, flush to the trailing edge of a phone screen. Under Fitts intuition the control is both small and far from a comfortable thumb arc, so miss-taps and accidental neighbor taps spike—especially with gloves, tremor, or one-handed use. The critique is not “compute ID = log₂(2D/W)”; it is: enlarge the hit area (or whole-row affordance), pull the primary action into the thumb zone, and verify against WCAG target-size guidance plus a hurried outdoor task. If support tickets say “I keep marking the wrong SKU,” you have behavioral confirmation of the same layout failure.

Hick’s law (choice time). Decision time tends to increase as the number of equally salient choices grows. Use it to justify progressive disclosure, smart defaults, and search over endless peer buttons—not to demand that every menu have ≤7 items as dogma. Experts with recognizable structure (muscle memory, categories, recent items) violate naive “more options = slower” readings. Clarity of labels, grouping, and defaults often matters more than raw count. When every action looks equally important, users stall; when hierarchy is honest, they don’t.

Caution (Hick) — too many nav items. A product nav that promotes twelve peer destinations (“Home, Inbox, Catalog, Orders, Inventory, Analytics, Team, Billing, Integrations, Help, Admin, What’s New”) treats every destination as equally urgent. Hick predicts slower first decisions for newcomers—and in practice you also get wrong-path starts, “I can’t find receiving,” and PMs adding a thirteenth item instead of grouping. The fix is hierarchy and progressive disclosure (e.g., primary job destinations vs. overflow settings), not a cargo-cult “max seven links” rule. Experts who live in Orders all day may still be fast; the law bites hardest when salience is flat and the job is infrequent. Pair nav cuts with task success evidence, not with a slide quoting Hick alone.

Direct manipulation (Shneiderman). Keep objects of interest visible; actions should feel continuous and reversible; feedback should be immediate and incremental. Dragging a file, resizing a crop, or reordering a list shrinks the gulf of execution versus opaque command languages. On modern canvases and AI UIs, “direct” still means: selection visible, result editable, side effects confirmable—not auto-mutate and hope. Direct manipulation does not replace accessible non-pointer paths; every drag needs a keyboard or single-pointer alternative (see Chapter 3 / ship kits).

Mapping (Norman). Controls should map naturally onto effects—spatial, cultural, and conceptual. A stove’s knobs matching burner layout; a slider that moves the same direction as the value; undo that restores the prior world. Bad mapping forces knowledge in the head; good mapping puts knowledge in the world. When critiquing, ask whether the system image teaches the conceptual model or invents folklore (“refresh three times”). Mis-mapped modes, invisible sync, and unlabeled toggles are mapping failures first, aesthetic failures second.

Use as intuition, not cargo-cult formulas in product critiques. Cite these ideas to sharpen why a control is hard, a menu overwhelms, or a gesture feels indirect. Do not wave Fitts or Hick numbers as proof without measurement, context, and user evidence. Classical HCI informs craft; modern DoDs, inclusion, and outcome metrics decide ship.

Appendix K — Course Week Map & Assessment

Twelve weeks align to the book’s full curriculum (Chapters 1–10 + 5B). Adjust pacing for shorter terms by merging Weeks 5–6 or running capstone as a studio intensive.

Week Focus Primary chapters Core artifacts
1 HCD foundations, gulfs, models 1 Gulf map; conceptual-model one-pager draft
2 Interaction, flows, feedback 2 Critical-path flow + failure states
3 Inclusive design & AT ladder 3 Persona Spectrum constraints; AT ladder steps 1–3
4 Strategy & continuous discovery 4 Assumption map; opportunity framing
5 Design systems & state completeness 5 Component state matrix (starter)
6 Visual craft, IA, prototyping 5B Prototype + IA outline; handoff notes
7 Content, trust, privacy, service 6 Content/Privacy DoD pass on one flow
8 Research methods & evidence bars 7 + App. I Study plan; heuristic or walkthrough write-up
9 Modern contexts (mobile, multi-modal, AI) 8 Constraint scenario + AI/interrupt risks
10 Operating practice 9 Monday loop live; midweek gate calendar
11–12 Cases & capstone 10 Capstone package; teaching artifact

Graded artifact rubrics (pass tied to book DoDs)

(1) Monday one-pager. Pass: Names problem/job, segment, critical constraints (AT/connectivity/shared device as relevant), non-goals, success metrics + evidence bar, ranked priority stack (≤ one true P0), open assumptions, Risks & DoD status for applicable domains (Auth, Privacy, Interrupt, Content, Activation, Support, AI if in scope), and links to research/prototype/decision log. Fail: branding brief only; twelve P0s; no DoD status; metrics without decisions.

(2) State matrix + midweek gate. Pass: Matrix covers default through focus-visible, disabled, loading, error, empty, and constraint states (offline/permission/partial failure where relevant); acceptance criteria are engineer-verifiable without Figma; gate states decision question, evidence required, decider, default = no-ship. Fail: happy-path-only matrix; gate with no default; “design approved” without DoD scan.

(3) AT test script run. Pass: Script covers critical path; evidence of ladder progress (at least automated + keyboard + screen-reader smoke, or documented equivalent); issues logged by POUR with severity by user impact; blockers tied to ship/no-ship. Fail: green axe score alone; no keyboard pass; AT deferred to “later.”

(4) Capstone. Pass: Living one-pager; prototype including failure/empty/offline/interrupt (and AI confirm/provenance if AI slice); evidence summary with honest sample limits; DoD sign-off for risk domains in play; metrics that detect silent failure; midweek-style go/no-go with default no; demo + teaching artifact (checklist or anti-pattern amendment). Harm reduction and recoverability outweigh visual novelty. Fail: restyle without gates; vanity metrics; no constraint-matched research; ship recommendation with open catastrophic DoD gaps.

Course pass criteria. Credit requires passing artifacts (1)–(4) at the bars above, plus participation in Monday loops and critiques using the Chapter 9 anti-pattern table. Methods from Appendix I may support evidence but never substitute for DoD-tied gates. Grade process honesty equal to craft: an elegant UI that fails Interrupt or AT DoDs does not pass.

Appendix L — Instructor Exemplars (v2.1)

Part of textbook v2.2. Filled examples for teaching and grading. Pair with Chapter 9 (operating practice), Chapter 4 (OST), Chapter 5 (state matrices), and Appendix K rubrics. Students may adapt structure; inventing empty theater does not pass.

These exemplars show what a pass looks like in prose—not templates to copy wholesale. Use them in studio critiques and grading calibration.

L1 — Exemplar Monday one-pager (delivery-time modify)

Squad: Field Inventory · Week of 2026-03-09
Outcome pulse: Cut wrong-SKU receives on intermittent warehouse Wi‑Fi without adding irreversible side effects under interrupt.

Field Content
Problem / job When a receiver is mid-count and connectivity drops, they need to modify delivery quantity/notes on a line and resume without restarting the receipt—so inventory stays honest and dock time does not explode.
Segment & constraints Warehouse associates; shared tablets; gloves; intermittent Wi‑Fi; occasional VoiceOver/TalkBack; hurried shifts. Persona Spectrum: temporary (one free hand), situational (bright aisle glare).
Non-goals Redesign put-away; new analytics dashboard; AI auto-correct of quantities this sprint.
Success metrics + evidence bar Primary: % of modify-quantity tasks completed offline→sync without restart or silent overwrite. Guardrails: duplicate-receive rate, support tickets tagged receive-conflict, AT critical-path blockers = 0. Evidence bar: ship only if (a) 5 task sessions under airplane-mode→reconnect include ≥1 AT user and show no catastrophic sync loss, and (b) Interrupt + Support DoD checklist signed. SUS alone does not clear the bar.
Priority stack P0: Offline modify + visible sync/conflict for delivery lines (displaces “bulk photo upload polish”). P1: Conflict copy + citeable receipt ID. P2 (parked): Suggested qty from ASN—revisit after sync honesty ships.
Open assumptions A1: Receivers understand “queued locally” vs “confirmed on server.” A2: Conflict resolution “keep mine / keep server” is learnable in <30s. Highest risk × ignorance: A1.
Risks & DoD status Interrupt: draft durability on qty/notes — in progress. Auth: shared-tablet lock — met. Privacy: no PII in lock-screen banners — met. Support: conflict events in dictionary — gap (owner: PM). Content: empty/offline copy — in progress. AI: N/A.
Links Research notes #recv-offline-12; prototype proto/recv-modify-v3; decision log ADR-041; event dictionary recv.modify.*.

Why this passes. It names a job under constraint, one true P0 with displacement, metrics that detect silent failure, an evidence bar tied to methods, and honest DoD gaps with owners. A branding paragraph (“delightful receiving experience”) with twelve P0s would fail Appendix K.

L2 — Exemplar state matrix (offline inventory)

Three objects × key states for offline receiving. Acceptance criteria must be engineer-verifiable without opening Figma.

Object Default Loading Empty Error Offline / queued Sync conflict Success / confirmed Disabled / focus-visible
Receipt header Shows site, PO#, actor Skeleton; “Loading receipt…” N/A once opened “Can’t load receipt” + retry + citeable ID Banner: “Working offline · changes queue on device” Banner: “Server differs · resolve before submit” “Synced · server confirmed 14:02” Submit disabled until lines valid; focus ring on Retry
Line item (SKU) Qty, unit, notes Row shimmer “No lines—scan or add” + primary CTA Inline “Save failed” on that row Badge Queued; qty editable locally Row highlight; Keep mine / Keep server Check + server qty Qty stepper disabled if receipt locked; focus order: SKU → qty → notes
Modify qty control Stepper + confirm Brief progress on confirm N/A “Couldn’t apply change” + undo restore Applies locally; announces via live region Blocked until conflict choice Live region: “Quantity 12, queued” then “confirmed” Min hit area ≥ WCAG; keyboard ±; AT name includes SKU

Sample acceptance criteria. (1) With network off, changing qty persists after app background ≥5 min and shows Queued. (2) On reconnect with server mismatch, neither value silently wins—user chooses Keep mine/Keep server; choice logged. (3) Screen reader announces queued→confirmed transition without focus trap.

Midweek gate (attach). Decision: “Ship offline modify for receipts?” Evidence: matrix AC green + 5 constrained sessions + Support dictionary entries. Decider: EM + Design lead. Default if undecided: no-ship.

L3 — Exemplar OST snippet with evidence bar

Desired outcome: Reduce dock rework from wrong or lost quantity edits during intermittent connectivity (proxy: conflict/rework tickets per 1k receives ↓ 40% in pilot site).

Outcome: Honest qty edits under flaky Wi‑Fi
├─ Opportunity: Receivers lose in-progress edits when the app reloads
│  ├─ Solution: Local draft durability + resume point on receipt
│  │  └─ Experiment: Prototype offline edit; task success offline→online
│  │     Evidence bar: ≥4/5 complete modify without restart; 0 silent overwrites
│  └─ Solution: Autosave every keystroke to server only
│     └─ Experiment: Kill—fails offline constraint (do not run)
└─ Opportunity: Receivers don’t trust whether the count “took”
   ├─ Solution: Explicit queued vs confirmed system status
   │  └─ Experiment: Comprehension probe after task (teach-back)
   │     Evidence bar: 4/5 correctly explain queued≠confirmed; else rewrite copy
   └─ Solution: Push notification “sync done”
      └─ Experiment: Parked—lock-screen privacy risk on shared tablets

Evidence bar (team contract). Opportunity ranking requires ≥2 independent signals (support themes + observed task failure) before a solution enters P0. Solution ship requires behavioral task evidence under the stated constraint—not preference votes or heuristic-only pass. Sample limits stated in the write-up (n=5, one AT user, one site)—no fake power claims.

L4 — Grading annotation: pass vs theater

Artifact signal Pass Theater (fail)
One-pager Job + constraints; one P0 with displacement; metrics change decisions; DoD gaps owned Vision poster; vanity KPIs; twelve P0s; “TBD accessibility”
State matrix Offline/conflict/AT focus included; AC testable without Figma Happy path only; “error TBD”; screenshots as “done”
OST / evidence Outcome→opportunity→experiment; pre-committed bar; honest n Solution-first tree; “users will love it”; SUS as ship gate
Gates Yes/no question, named decider, default no-ship “Align async”; silence = yes; design approved without DoD scan
Research Constraint-matched recruits; assumptions retired explicitly Five friends on campus Wi‑Fi; confirmation of the preferred mock

Instructor note. Grade process honesty equal to craft polish. An elegant UI that fails Interrupt or AT DoDs does not pass—even if the critique vocabulary is fluent. Reward students who demote work, record unknowns, and refuse to ship on theater.
